title: Engagements
text: It sounds like the Prime Minister does not have any red lines, because when he had the opportunity, he did not say so. Instead, he went on point scoring. I do not know why he is getting tetchy with me again, because if I do not hold him to account—[Interruption.] If I do not hold him to account, we know that he will end up giving the whole country away. I know he is not enjoying this—he prefers soft questions from people dancing around Downing Street. That is not what he is going to get from me. I asked the Prime Minister a very simple question. Instead, he wants me to congratulate him on a deal that is not yet done. This is important. This is about our students. Labour froze the student loan repayment threshold until 2030 at the last Budget. Because of that freeze, the Treasury says that British graduates will pay an extra £355 million a year. Those are not my numbers; they are Treasury numbers. Yet he is willing to spend at least £500 million a year subsidising tuition fees for EU students. Why is the Prime Minister making British graduates pay more, while agreeing to let EU students pay less?

title: Engagements
text: The right hon. Lady has mentioned my talking to influencers. It is true: I have spoken to influencers, and then I have to come to the House and speak to people who are the opposite of influencers. In relation to the deal, the right hon. Lady is referring to the European negotiating position, which is not the British negotiating position. That has not been put on the table, and it will not be put on the table, but she should address the substance of the deal—the overall package. What will the overall package do for growth in the British economy? She dismisses the fact that it adds up to 0.5% to the British economy, billions of pounds extra. Can we as a country really afford to turn our back on growth of that scale? It is the biggest growth measure that we could take in this Parliament. The party of low growth in the last decade is standing against an opportunity to boost British growth. The Conservatives keep on making the same old mistake over and over again. They want us to stick with a failed Tory Brexit deal—the failed status quo. We will not do that. We can improve it, and it is in the British national interest to do so.

title: Floods and Emergencies: Access to Remote Locations
text: I am more than happy to move on and talk about regional water councils, but it is incredibly disappointing if my hon. Friend’s council is not speaking to community groups impacted by flooding. Flooding is not political. It does not stay within a political boundary; it affects and impacts everyone regardless. I hope her council will think again. As I said, I am happy to intervene if I can be of support. The council absolutely must listen to communities impacted by flooding, work with them and try to mitigate it. We cannot stop all flooding, but we can be better prepared and try to mitigate the worst possible effects. My hon. Friend’s local highway authority has a statutory responsibility for maintaining local roads and should have the right understanding of what needs to be done. We are providing a record £7.3 billion for local highways maintenance across England starting from 2026-27, which gives authorities the certainty to plan ahead and invest. I want to say a bit about the regional water councils, because I know my hon. Friend is incredibly interested in them. Of course, there will be a role on them for Members of Parliament. I met with mayors just yesterday to talk about their role in regional water councils and how they will work. She is absolutely right; it is about thinking holistically across the whole river basin about the best way to deal with the challenges. We have new data from NaFRA2—the new national flood risk assessment—that tells us what our surface risk is not only now, but in the future. There is a role for MPs and I will make sure my hon. Friend is involved and informed about what is happening. We recognise that geographically isolated communities face particular recovery challenges. Flood resilience is a personal priority. I will continue working hard to make sure that the Government meet that responsibility. If my hon. Friend wants a meeting to follow up with officials, I can arrange that for her. Question put and agreed to.

title: Floods and Emergencies: Access to Remote Locations
text: I thank the hon. Gentleman for his invitation. We will pick up on that issue, and the issues raised in our conversation. I want to address the points made by my hon. Friend the Member for Tamworth. There are a number of significant projects reducing flood risk in her area. There is £15 million, which she knows a lot about, so I will not spend too long talking about that. The Environment Agency is also in the early stages of developing proposals to further enhance Tamworth’s flood risk management scheme. The project aims to better protect approximately 2,600 residential properties and 360 commercial properties. Development of those proposals remains on track. The first of three business cases, the strategic outline case, has been completed. The business case forecasts that the scheme will deliver approximately £900 million of economic benefit. I will write to my hon. Friend with all the details, because I am conscious of time. To give her some idea, if the project progresses into construction it would include improving or replacing ageing River Tame defences, potential new defences along the River Anker, making sure that flood defences are resilient to future changes in flood risk due to climate change—a very important point that my hon. Friend mentioned—opportunities to improve the amenity, environment and economic growth along the river corridors, and more. My hon. Friend made it clear how vulnerable communities in Tamworth are to flooding. She mentioned that Edingale village was cut off for the first time during Storm Henk. I recognise that there are further difficulties on the road network in her constituency, with the restrictions on Chetwynd bridge that have been in effect since 2019 causing lengthy detours, including for emergency services. I understand that Staffordshire county council has applied for funding to replace that bridge as part of the structures fund. The Department for Transport is currently assessing schemes submitted to the fund and expects to announce funding awards later this autumn. I have no doubt that my hon. Friend will tirelessly campaign to the Department for Transport on that issue. Responding to emergencies is always difficult, but it is particularly difficult in rural areas. For many parts of England and Wales, it is a significant risk and is recognised in many community risk registers. Local resilience forums—co-ordinating groups made up of all responders within a local area—are encouraged to develop multi-agency flood plans. Those plans allow for complicated issues, like the one my hon. Friend mentioned, such as how to get to villages when there is one access road. She is right that communities must be at the centre of emergency planning. If she does not feel like she is getting the support she needs in engaging with her local resilience forums, I am more than happy to intervene and support her where I can.

title: Floods and Emergencies: Access to Remote Locations
text: It is a pleasure to serve under your chairmanship, Sir Desmond. I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Tamworth (Sarah Edwards) for securing the debate and providing the opportunity to discuss the challenges faced by rural communities during floods and other emergencies. I also commend her on the hard work she is doing in her constituency to address these challenges. We spoke in January last year about the flooding that happened in Tamworth and the flood summit my hon. Friend held in 2024. I commend her on her local leadership and tireless campaigning on this issue. Members from across the House will be able to relate to many of the issues she has mentioned in her speech, such as being able to travel to work, disruption to local businesses and access to flooded homes, so it is important that we have the debate. On sandbags, the University of Hull did a really interesting study—I found it interesting, and I hope the hon. Member for Yeovil (Adam Dance) will too—on the most effective way to protect homes from flooding. It found that flood tape is way more protective than sandbags, and it costs only £14 a roll. Flood Mary, an incredible, amazing lady, has also looked at the best way to protect homes, and the best news is that people need flood tape, not sandbags. I advise everyone to be prepared and buy themselves a few rolls of flood tape, although obviously other tape is available. I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Stafford (Leigh Ingham), who is also a tireless campaigner—I have yet to enter the Tea Room without her raising the issue of flooding in Stafford with me—and all other Members who have contributed.

title: Floods and Emergencies: Access to Remote Locations
text: Absolutely—that is a problem in my constituency as well. People understand the need to build houses, but it is sometimes not considered in the wider context, and it can create known issues, particularly where sewers are concerned. We need a better system to make sure that what is proposed actually works for local people. We must listen to those who know their communities best, strengthen communication between agencies and communities, and give local people a meaningful role in shaping flood resilience measures. Regional water councils offer an opportunity to deliver that. They could provide a single point of accountability for regional water investment, covering sewage, water quality, flood resilience, drought and future water supplies. Bringing together agencies under one body could improve co-ordination and information sharing, but that must extend to local people too. Water councils must put local knowledge at their heart, delivering practical solutions to problems like access routes and securing investment, whether through redirecting water company fines or earmarking developer CIL funding for flood resilience. Can the Minister assure me that plans for regional water councils involve genuine consultation that accounts for the voices and views of local people? It cannot be devolution that gives water company bosses a seat at the table while communities are ignored, or consultation without the powers or funding to make a difference. How will the Minister ensure that the councils deliver tangible change and that community perspectives genuinely shape flood planning? Climate change is bringing wetter winters, more intense periods of rainfall and increasingly unpredictable weather patterns. In England, 38% of roads are at risk of flooding, and the figure is expected to rise to 46% by 2050. For rural communities where there may be only one or two roads connecting a village to the outside world, the consequences are particularly serious. The Government must reexamine how flood funding is allocated to ensure that smaller, rural communities are not disadvantaged by population-based cost-benefit assessments, and they must explore how regional water councils can deliver smaller, quicker and more practical interventions. In conclusion, I ask the Minister whether this Government will work with communities most exposed to flooding and emergencies to protect vulnerable citizens. Will the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs meet the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government to establish clear priorities for devolved powers over water and flooding infrastructure that can be measured, with the population impact clearly stated? Will villages such as Elford, Edingale, Whittington, Comberford, Harlaston and Fisherwick, and other similar places around the country, be prioritised in localised flooding strategies? Will the Minister take away my principle of a one route system and develop it into a basis for better flood preparedness and mitigation as we face a changing climate? Climate change will make flooding more frequent and severe, and the consequences of inaction will become increasingly costly, both financially and, sadly, in human life. We need to trust local people. They know how to fix this problem in their communities better than we do. They know what their area needs to can stay safe and connected, but they need our support. We must trust them, because they know their communities. We have an opportunity to act before the next emergency. We must not wait for tragedy to remind us why keeping rural communities connected matters. In a great many areas, it may not be as complicated or expensive as we think.

title: Floods and Emergencies: Access to Remote Locations
text: I thank the hon. Lady for raising that point. She is absolutely right; farmers play a crucial role in flood defences and often go above and beyond, including in helping people directly, whether by utilising their land or getting people through the floods. I hope that the agency will speed that process up; perhaps the Minister will be able to put some pressure on it to make sure that such things are resolved in a timely manner. We are spending £7 billion a year on HS2, which passes through my constituency. As rural communities ask for the small investments to ensure that they can still reach an ambulance, a hospital or their homes when the floodwaters rise, surely protecting people from being cut off from emergency services deserves to be a national priority. Councillors have told me directly that villages were low priority for flood defences simply because they have fewer houses, so the threat to life was deemed to be less. In the cost-benefit analysis, keeping people in villages and rural areas safe during flooding was not seen to be worth the money it would cost, but there are simple low-cost measures that could make a real difference. They just require clear engagement with local leaders who know their areas well, and funding for smaller community-based projects. I propose a simple approach to protecting our most remote areas with the one-route system. The flood strategy should identify a single route that could be protected so that access is maintained for villages, and simple and effective measures that could be deployed or installed to safeguard that route, which would be a minimum expectation. There are clear examples of how one route in and one route out could have high impact locally for little cost, for example between Edingale and Harlaston. There is a road that is often passable in a high enough vehicle, such as an off-road vehicle, but there are no depth gauges installed along the road to provide clarity on the depth of that water. Vehicles could drive through it, but of course most people will not take that risk. Similarly, the northern route out of Edingale is usually the one road that remains passable. Despite creating a 15-mile round trip for residents, it is usually open; but in the last few years it has flooded, cutting off the village entirely. For most ordinary cars, these flooded roads are completely impassable. With a small amount of capital investment, many roads could be transformed into flood-safe routes, for example by raising the road surface above the expected flooding levels so that they remain accessible during emergencies. We cannot prevent every flood, nor can we realistically protect every single road from this eventuality, but we can identify roads that are lifelines for rural communities and make them resilient enough to withstand increasingly severe weather. For an isolated village, building just one accessible route can be the difference between reaching an ambulance, receiving care at home or getting children to school, and being cut off from the outside world and unable to go to work. In villages such as Edingale, roads to the local hospital can be unusable for days at a time. Residents are cut off from GPs, hospitals, pharmacies and essential services, whether they need treatment for a flood-related injury or an unrelated medical emergency. Police officers can struggle with call-outs, and the violent incidents that can be attributed to people being stuck at home are impacting domestic abuse victims. Older and vulnerable residents may fall on dangerous, slippery roads and be unable to get help. Fire engines, which are expected to respond to flood rescue calls despite having no statutory funding or responsibility to do so, can struggle to get through to these communities. An accessible route means that ambulances can reach patients, carers can visit vulnerable residents, police can respond to emergencies and families can remain connected to the outside world. title: Floods and Emergencies: Access to Remote Locations
text: Although I have not shared my speech with my hon. Friend, it is almost as though she has predicted some of the things that I will be saying. I think we need to identify local interventions, and I will be arguing for a one-route system that sets a principle for those types of interventions. The summit made it clear that flooding cannot be tackled in silos. We need a co-ordinated and long-term approach that protects homes and businesses, maintains essential road access and ensures that no community is left isolated. The economic consequences of flooding are significant. Tamworth is a centre for logistics and manufacturing, and my flooding report found that more than two thirds of residents have struggled to get to work. Landlords at Lichfield Road industrial park, which is affected by flooding, have warned that businesses could leave the estate, and even leave Tamworth, because of the exposure to repeated flooding. The cost of doing nothing is measured not just in damaged homes, roads and bridges, but in jobs, disrupted businesses and the growing cost to the taxpayer of repeatedly repairing infrastructure.

title: Lobbying Transparency and Public Confidence
text: I thank the Minister for his comprehensive remarks and for recommitting to the Government’s broad ambition for reform in today’s enlivening debate. The hon. Member for Strangford (Jim Shannon) talked in considerable detail about his 41 years of service as an MLA, councillor and MP. He spoke up for his constituents in Northern Ireland, and he spoke of the need for registers of interest to be robust. He talked in detail about the Nolan principles and about being lobbied on pigs and poultry, which I found particularly insightful. My hon. Friend the Member for Alloa and Grangemouth (Brian Leishman) and I have differences of opinion on military spending, but I agree with his point in principle that money buys access. He was right to talk in detail about much-needed APPG governance reform. I was not expecting military spending multipliers to feature in today’s debate, but I thank him for his remarks. I thank the Lib Dem spokesperson, the hon. Member for Hazel Grove (Lisa Smart). She is right to say that lobbying can be helpful, to touch on special advisers being outside the current regime, and to focus on enforcement through the register. I also thank the shadow Minister, the hon. Member for Bridlington and The Wolds (Charlie Dewhirst), who displayed admirable transparency about his previous life as a lobbyist and his spouse not having a spousal pass because of a perceived conflict of interest. That is to be welcomed, and I am delighted that he quoted Spotlight on Corruption with approval. A distinction should be drawn between the lobbying of decision makers in the Executive and the lobbying of Back-Bench Members of this House. That is important because, as the Minister said, we are all lobbyists on behalf of our constituents, seeking to drive meaningful change in this place. When done in an ethical and transparent manner, lobbying leads to good policy outcomes. As the Minister, shadow Minister and Lib Dem spokesperson said, there is nothing wrong with lobbying in principle. The point under discussion today is transparency and building confidence in the system. I pay tribute to Doug Chalmers, chair of the EIC, for his team’s hard work in producing the report published over the summer that sets the groundwork for what I hope will be a fairly swift response from the Government. That is why I quoted one of the relevant trade bodies, the CIPR, with approval. I look forward to continuing to work with the Minister and his officials as we see the EIC’s recommendations implemented. Question put and agreed to. Resolved, That this House has considered lobbying transparency and public confidence.

title: Lobbying Transparency and Public Confidence
text: The hon. Member makes an important point. As he knows, I am the Intergovernmental Relations Minister, and I think it is important that there is as much consistency as possible in these issues. I of course respect the different arrangements in the devolved Administrations, but I think the public would expect us all to hold ourselves to similar standards of transparency. He is right to raise the importance of consistency in these measures. Under the current system, the Government’s publication of Ministers’ and senior officials’ meetings has carried the weight of our transparency obligations on lobbying over many years. That dataset is published to reflect those engagements that have received sufficiently serious consideration by the Government that the issue has warranted a meeting with the relevant Minister or senior official. The 2014 lobbying Act was designed to complement the dataset released by the Government. Where a Minister or senior official is meeting a consultant lobbying company, it would not be immediately clear whose interests were being advocated for within that meeting. The Act was designed to fill that gap, requiring all consultant lobbyists to publish a list of their clients. However, the Government recognise the view of many that the current system of transparency around lobbying does not have widespread support. It is not good enough. That is why the EIC was asked to look into the issue and make recommendations. As the Opposition spokesperson pointed out, its report was published in July. It recommended replacing the existing register of consultant lobbyists with a new register of all lobbying activity, which was a point reinforced by my hon. Friend the Member for Bolton West. We recognise that this would be a significant reform of the system, requiring primary legislation, and we are considering it carefully. As hon. Members have outlined, there are issues to balance here, and we must get it right. Registers of lobbying activity, rather than just of lobbyists, exist in other liberal democracies. Our friends in Canada and Ireland both have lobbying registers covering a much broader range of activity. We will consider the effectiveness of those registers as we consider reforming our own. I acknowledge the work of Baroness Hayter in the other place to bring this issue to prominence through her private Member’s Bill and her tireless campaigning and commitment to improving the transparency and integrity of our democracy. The Government expressed reservations about that Bill when it was debated prior to the publication of the EIC’s report. We also want to consider a broader range of issues in relation to the 2014 lobbying Act, rather than just the issue that the PMB addressed of bringing in-house lobbyists into scope of the Act. The EIC’s report made wide-ranging recommendations on how to reform the Act, recommending a comprehensive new system of transparency for anyone who seeks to influence Government policy. The question for Government is how to get any reforms to the system right, balancing the need for transparency against our obligation not to create undue burdens, as both the hon. Members for Hazel Grove (Lisa Smart) and for Bridlington and The Wolds identified, particularly on citizens wanting to engage with their Government. For example, we need to ensure that we do not create unnecessary or disproportionate obstacles to individual citizens’ routine engagement with the Government. There also needs to be consideration of the right balance between informing the public about meaningful lobbying engagements and not putting too much irrelevant or trivial information into a transparency scheme, potentially undermining its accessibility or usefulness. As well as thinking about increased transparency of lobbying activity, the Government keep the datasets we already publish under review. title: Lobbying Transparency and Public Confidence
text: It is an honour to serve under your chairmanship, Sir Desmond. I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Boston West (Phil Brickell)—sorry, for Bolton West; that is the second slip of the tongue I have made in a week—both for securing this debate and for his leadership and work in the APPG on these important issues. I thank Members from across the House for their contributions. As the Opposition spokesperson, the hon. Member for Bridlington and The Wolds (Charlie Dewhirst), said, trust in politics has never been more important. Public confidence and belief that the Government are putting citizens at the heart of their decision making is vital for building and maintaining trust in our institutions, and it is a central pillar of a well-functioning democracy. Policy that is made with the public’s interest at its heart must involve engaging with affected citizens and stakeholders and listening to outside advice, opinion and expertise. I agree very much with the comments from many hon. Members that “lobbying” is not in itself a bad word. I was amused to hear even Members of this House describe themselves as lobbyists, and I understand why. We all seek to represent our constituents and their interests in this place. Engagement with Government and Ministers is a core British right and value. Lobbying can indeed have a positive influence on policy. Representative bodies and pressure groups have successfully moved important issues higher up the agenda and made change happen. However, as Members have said this morning, transparency is also important. Without it, it can be unclear whether a single group or set of interests has undue or disproportionate influence. Uncertainty about who is influencing the Government, and how, can undermine trust in our political system, so while we must protect the right of citizens and stakeholders to engage with the Government, so must we also ensure transparency. That is why it is important to ensure that the system of transparency around lobbying is sufficient. As Members have noted, we asked the Ethics and Integrity Commission to look into this very question earlier this year. The answer was clear: the current system is not good enough. The EIC cites estimates that the existing register of consultant lobbyists covers just 4% to 6% of the lobbying that takes place. We are carefully considering the recommendations made by the EIC, including recommendations for legislative reform, and will present our response to Parliament once ready. As the Opposition spokesperson said, it is important that we take our time to get the balance right in these measures. In the meantime, we are listening and are determined to get that balance right.

title: Health Bill
text: My Lords, I know that anecdotal evidence can sometimes lead people to think that the speaker is simply referring to himself, rather than the issue at hand, but when I went to have my operation for prostate cancer, Mr Cross at Leeds hospital was very clear that nothing should be said to anybody and that they take patient confidentiality very seriously. They went out of their way to make sure that nothing leaked out—to such an extent that, at the registration, my name was there but there was no question of “Archbishop”. But it amused me that, in the section on religion, they had put down “Unknown”. That was one way of ensuring that I was going to be protected and that nobody would do to me what happened to Desmond Tutu, whose diagnosis of prostate cancer was publicised and patient confidentiality was not kept—to such an extent that somebody who met him in the street said, “Oh, have you now got the Archbishops’ disease?”, because Robert Runcie had died from the same condition. That was an embarrassing question. If a hospital like that goes out of its way, knowing that the only way it could protect my confidentiality was to designate my religion as unknown, you may say that that is going a bit too far. But, of course, in the Church we still have the seal of the confessional. If somebody comes and confesses, “I’m telling you this in confession that I’ve done this and I’ve done that”, in some quarters they will never ever tell anybody else. I remember asking Cardinal Basil Hume, “What do you do with the seal of the confessional?” He said, “If the state, the police or anybody else wants me to divulge what I know, I won’t—I’d rather go to prison”. So they took it far more seriously, probably, than within the Church of England.

title: Lobbying Transparency and Public Confidence
text: It was always a pleasure to work with the hon. Member and other hon. Members on important farming issues. It was about bringing expertise to this place so that hopefully decisions made here were better informed. Protecting the integrity of our democracy should not be a party political matter. It is about ensuring that the public have confidence in the decisions that are taken in this place. That confidence is under considerable strain. Ipsos polling commissioned by the Government found that 87% of people were concerned about the possibility of corruption among elected officials. More than three in five were not confident that the Government effectively maintained high ethical standards. We should certainly take that very seriously. The question is not whether reform is needed but how we deliver it and why the Government have been slow to do so. There is a particular point to this debate, given the controversies that have emerged under this Government. The Transparency of Lobbying, Non-Party Campaigning and Trade Union Administration Act, introduced under the coalition Government, established a statutory register of consultant lobbyists. That was an important step, but the framework still has significant gaps, as was alluded to in terms of in-house and incidental lobbying. I am not sure we will ever be able to capture incidental lobbying, because every time any of us meet businesses or individuals in our constituencies, that could be construed as lobbying. It is right that we meet as many people as possible to represent our constituents better. However, there is certainly a gap when it comes to in-house lobbying. We could look at those who have a clearly defined role in public affairs and lobbying. The previous Government committed to taking that further by developing a single database to collate and publish Departments’ transparency returns. It appears that the current Government have scrapped that plan. The events of the last two years have demonstrated even further why transparency gaps matter. We have seen the controversy surrounding ministerial gifts and hospitality, and serious questions raised by the Mandelson affair. The circumstances around his appointment as ambassador to Washington, and the questions about his commercial interests and connections, exposed serious weaknesses in the Government’s approach to transparency and the management of conflicts of interest. Those cases raise questions about whether the rules are sufficiently robust and whether the public can be confident that access to Government is being managed appropriately. The Government themselves acknowledge that the Mandelson affair raised serious concerns about standards and inflicted real damage on people’s trust in politics. I agree, and if the Government accept that public trust has been damaged, they must be prepared to do something meaningful to restore it. To their credit, the Government recognise that the existing framework needs examining, and in March they commissioned the Ethics and Integrity Commission to review the lobbying rules following the Mandelson affair. That is entirely welcome, and when Parliament considered the Lobbying Transparency (In-house Lobbyists) Bill in early July, the Government declined to commit to further action before the commission had reported. It was reasonable to await the findings of an independent review. The commission reported later in July and made recommendations for improving transparency and strengthening the existing arrangements. What has happened since? In September, the Parliamentary Secretary, Cabinet Office, the hon. Member for Gateshead Central and Whickham (Mark Ferguson), said that the Government were considering legislative reform. That is not necessarily a commitment. On 12 November, another Cabinet Office Minister, the hon. Member for Doncaster Central (Sally Jameson), said that the Prime Minister would respond “shortly”. title: Lobbying Transparency and Public Confidence
text: It is a pleasure to serve with you in the Chair, Sir Desmond. I warmly congratulate the hon. Member for Bolton West (Phil Brickell) on securing this important debate and opening it so well, as well as on his leadership role on the APPG on anti-corruption and responsible tax. As MPs, the decisions we make in Westminster have a direct impact on people’s lives. Every week, we make choices about how public money is spent, which contracts are awarded, what legislation is passed and which industries receive support. People have a right to know who was in the room when those decisions were made. At the moment, for the most part, they cannot find out. Lobbying, however, should not always be seen as a dirty word, as was very well explained by the hon. Member for Strangford (Jim Shannon). When a charity explains how a policy will affect the people it supports, a business sets out what a change will cost or a trade body provides technical knowledge that officials do not have, decisions get better. I always find it useful when people bring specialist knowledge and lived experience to a policy question, and Ministers should of course hear from a wide range of voices. The problem is the other kind of lobbying—the kind that relies on personal relationships and informal access. It happens over a private dinner or in a WhatsApp group, leaves no record and gets an outcome for a narrow interest at the public’s expense. Access to Government should be a democratic right. It should never be something that can be bought, but the current system does not protect that. The register of consultant lobbyists captures, at most, 4% to 6% of lobbying activity. In-house lobbyists—the people employed directly by large companies and trade associations to influence Government—are not covered at all. Contact with special advisers falls outside its scope, even though special advisers are lobbied precisely because they are close the Ministers. Whether someone has to register depends on whether they are VAT registered—a test with no connection to whether they are trying to influence policy. The punishment for breaking the rules is a fine of £7,500. For many organisations doing serious lobbying, that amount is negligible. Alongside the register sits the Government’s own transparency data. That tells us that meetings have happened, but it often does not tell us what was discussed. It is published quarterly, months after the event; it relies on Departments reporting on themselves; and it is spread across releases that are hard to search or compare. Anyone trying to build a full picture of who a single Minister has met and why will struggle. I made all those points when I gave evidence to the Ethics and Integrity Commission. In July, the commission published its “Lobbying, Business Appointment Rules and Disclosure” report, which found that the current system “fails to deliver the required level of transparency and…falls short of…the Nolan Principles.” The report calls for a comprehensive register covering all lobbying, for real-time publication of ministerial contracts, and for an end to the three exemptions that have hollowed out the register since 2014. This independent body has advised the Government that the current system does not work. Like the hon. Member for Bolton West, I am keen to hear from the Minister when the Government will respond and whether they will accept those recommendations. The Liberal Democrats want comprehensive reform. We would replace the narrow register with a single, accessible one covering all lobbying of Government, whoever is doing it. That should record who is lobbying, on whose behalf, who they are lobbying, about what, when and how. A register that cannot answer all those questions offers the appearance of transparency without actually providing it. Every contact with Ministers by any channel should be published, going beyond meetings to include who they receive emails, letters, phone calls and instant messages from. The covid inquiry

title: Health Bill
text: My Lords, I support Amendments 133 and 143A, in the name of my noble friend Lord Patel, to which I have added my name. Fundamentally, his amendments address the real tension that your Lordships’ House faces in considering Clause 52. On the one hand, there has been very strong support across the House for the principle of a single patient record, which will be a very powerful tool. We have heard how it will impact on improving clinical outcomes, driving patient safety and ensuring that valuable resources can be effectively applied where they are needed in the correct clinical care environment at the correct time. The single patient record is fundamental to the practice of modern medicine. It would be completely inappropriate, given that on repeated occasions your Lordships’ House has agreed that there must be a transition from hospital community care, and where care environments will now be dispersed, if those providing that continuity of care, and indeed acute care, are unable to access core and key clinical information in real time for the benefit of their patient. On the other hand, we have seen on repeated occasions in the past 20 years attempts to apply or to address that important commitment to providing continuity of patient data undermined because the proposed approach has failed to secure an appropriate social licence. We have not secured broad consent on and confidence in the way the state would deal with the collective and deeply sensitive nature of those data and make them broadly available and easily accessible. That is the fundamental question that needs to be addressed in looking at Clause 52 and the introduction of new Section 250E into the NHS Act 2006, which is the purpose of the clause.

title: Health Bill
text: My Lords, this incredibly important group of amendments goes absolutely to the heart of clinicians’ relationships with patients and how anything is recorded. How many of us as clinicians have been told by patients, “I’ve never told anyone this before”, who then disclose incredibly important but deeply sensitive information that they do not want shared even with the rest of the team, let alone being put down on a central record? As the noble Baroness, Lady Harding, said, trust by patients is essential, but there is another dimension, which is trust by staff. Last night, I was at a meeting where we heard about the problem of aggression and violence towards staff. Some 96% of emergency department workers have been subject in a two-month period to violence and aggression. The violence was not minor; some was life-threatening. Therefore, anything in this record must also be put there so that it will protect staff who may have to refer to it, at speed, in very difficult situations. There is then a fundamental question with the patient data included, namely: where does control sit? We have heard about the sensitivities—the things that people will not want on the record. How do they know and control what does and does not go on, and how are they supported in being able to determine what is relevant? I suggest that the complication and the complexities undermine why we need a super-affirmative procedure to be used for regulations—to avoid disasters happening. Confidentiality must be watertight for everyone or else trust will be lost, and once it is gone, it will be very difficult to get back. The recommendation from the committee on which I sit was that this section should be removed. I did not table an amendment to remove the whole clause because I felt that we had to discuss this in great detail, which is happening today. The list of safeguards is in there. However, the problem with lists is that they are often incomplete, so I would like a way that we could add to that list with great ease as things emerge. Our dependence on overseas technology, data storage outside our shores and procurement of updates, and a lack of clarity over security, legal interpretation, regulatory practice and technical standards, are concerns that affect care everywhere in the British Isles, hence Amendment 150 regarding the four nations, with annual reporting on the single patient record to Parliament. How will the bilingualism of Wales be managed in the single patient record, given that some patients have their record recorded in Welsh? For high-profile people, data security and the ability to opt out of some data uses can be critical for them, their families and possibly national security. Unauthorised access of a record is a breach of confidentiality, but in the situation of major trauma, where many different people at different grades are involved, it will be hard to determine exactly who is and is not authorised to view. Amendment 164 seeks to put the onus on the individual by inhibiting the temptation to have a peek. It aims to deter people from looking at patient records they have no reason to access. The offence would be knowing, unauthorised access, with a minimum of three months’ imprisonment or a fine on summary conviction, where “‘authorised’ means in the proper exercise of the person’s functions”. Overall, the public appear to favour the idea of a single patient record, and they want it supported by audit trails, transparency about access and clear consequences for misuse. But 44% worry about access by the wrong people, and for each individual the wrong people might be very different people. Amendment 146 would require a log of who accessed what, when they accessed it, and why. It would mean that a patient is shown their own log and would require an annual independent audit. Although the existing law in Section 170 of the Data Protection Act and Section 1 of the Computer Misuse Act could possibly be extended, can the Minister explain how that

title: Health Bill
text: My Lords, nobody in this House doubts the importance of an effective single patient record. Indeed, the NHS has been working towards this idea for decades because, while the idea is simple in theory, the implementation is incredibly difficult. Of course, there is the technical challenge, but as my noble friend Lady Harding reminded us, building trust is even harder. We have seen that from the care.data and GDPR attempts, which failed because patients and clinicians lost confidence in how their data would be used. I thank the Minister and the department for the extensive engagement that they offered us. As she candidly acknowledged in our previous debate, some of the questions asked do not have immediate answers. Indeed, there is a lot that we do not yet know and almost everything that we know comes from departmental assurances, not from Clause 52 itself. First, what is this? The department tells us that it will be a new clinical interface. Does that mean that it is view-only? If so, will that always be the case? Nothing in the Bill says so or would prevent the development of a different model later on. Secondly, how will privacy be protected? The letter from the Minister offers welcome assurances: role-based access, a detailed audit trail and clinicians able, we envisage, to restrict sensitive information. Yet this is only emerging thinking and none of it is in the Bill. Thirdly, who is liable when something goes wrong? We know that NHS organisations remain responsible for their source data, but if information in the SPR is displayed wrongly and a clinician acts on that inaccurate information, who is liable? The noble Baroness, Lady Finlay, and the noble Lord, Lord Scriven, both asked this question in the previous debate, but neither received a clear answer. Without clarity on liability, the department will find it very hard to win the support of clinicians, on whom this record will depend. Fourthly, what about research and planning? Clause 52 creates no new powers for secondary uses, but we know that the SPR could be used for planning and research, where there is a separate legal basis. That existing framework is itself changing, as the department considers proposals to modernise the control of patient information regulations and the Health Data Research Service prepares to give researchers a single point of access to national NHS data. How will all these pieces fit together? The Minister told us that this is not a “trust me” situation; it is just the reality of developing a system. With respect, trust is exactly what we are being asked for. We are being asked to have faith in not only this Secretary of State but every future one. The Minister will remind us that Parliament can debate and vote on future regulations, but as the noble Lord, Lord Patel, reminded us, we will not be able to amend them. Even then, the department told us that the regulations will be drafted to give flexibility. We are told that the aim of that is to avoid rigidly setting out processes that we expect to evolve, but the detail will not be in the Bill and it may not even be in regulation. The Minister explained that there must be a balance between a clear legal basis for the system and an agile approach to developing technology. Of course, I agree that a balance is needed. Nobody would advocate designing a single patient record by committee, even a committee as august as this one. However, I fear that the balance in Clause 52 is wrong, as does the Delegated Powers and Regulatory Reform Committee, which concluded that the clause is “not currently fit for purpose and, in the absence of significant amendments, should be removed from the Bill”. We need principles and guardrails in the Bill. They must give the Government the space that they need to iterate but also give the patients and clinicians the certainty that they need to proceed. title: Lobbying Transparency and Public Confidence
text: The hon. Member for Strangford (Jim Shannon) has actually pre-empted something I was about to say. I am going to talk about the defence industry, including small and medium-sized businesses and economic multipliers. I will come on to that in due course. Going back to my point, the claim that the UK lacks a national defence is a means to an end to try to boost and increase military spending. The lobbying companies are even trying to convince us that weapons manufacturing will be the route to economic revival and prosperity. But does military spending actually grow the economy? The Global Campaign on Military Spending says that it does not, finding that military spending, in fact, “has one of the lowest ‘employment multipliers’ of all economic categories. It ranks 70th in terms of the employment it generates, out of 100.” As such, my belief is that military spending will not bring the jobs that the industry claims it will. Furthermore, defence is not a UK-wide industry. It is very concentrated, going back to the point of the hon. Member for Strangford, in geographical pockets around the United Kingdom. It also does not help small and medium-sized businesses, which secure only about 5% of all orders. This prompts the question: if workers and small and medium-sized businesses do not benefit from military spending, who does? I looked through the Government’s strategic defence review, which has the goal of making the UK a defence industrial powerhouse, and it is obviously arms manufacturers and their shareholders who will benefit. These are the same organisations that consistently pop up in our inboxes, inviting us for a glass of wine and cheese on sticks. To me, the lobbying system that we are part of in this place is utterly broken and corrupt to its core—but that is what happens when money gets access.

title: Lobbying Transparency and Public Confidence
text: It is an honour and a pleasure to have you in the Chair, Sir Desmond. I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Bolton West (Phil Brickell) for bringing this debate to Westminster Hall. Given the ethos of this debate, I will draw everyone’s attention to my membership of Unite the union, the Community union, the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament and the Scottish CND. From the outset, I say to the Minister that my speech is not going to make any demands or ask any questions; I just want to get a couple of things off my chest, starting with the fact that money buys access. I want to focus primarily on the industry that has the most money and therefore the most access through its relentless lobbying: the arms industry. All parties are parroting pretty much the same thing at the moment: if we want peace, we have to prepare for war. I find the political passion for militarism that we see across both Chambers frankly terrifying. The defence industrial lobby has done some job of fuelling that war hysteria, and sometimes its lobbying goes beyond the canapés and lukewarm white wine at events somewhere in the bowels of this place. Investigative journalists at Declassified revealed how the all-party parliamentary group for defence technology had accepted donations from an arms company called RUK Advanced Systems Ltd. That company is directly controlled by the Israeli Government, meaning that a foreign power was part-funding a UK parliamentary group. To give hon. Members a flavour of what RUK does, some of its advertised products include missiles with “unprecedented” lethality and a defence system for tanks that has been tried and tested in combat “along Israel’s borders”. Let us be under no illusion: we all know what tried and tested means—it means murdered Palestinians. That is exactly the kind of foreign lobbying that we have been warned about in this place for years. I am relieved to say that the APPG was quickly disbanded after that fact was revealed. The intense lobbying from the wider arms industry is genuinely effective. We have the Defence Secretary saying that we should prepare for war in 1,000 days, and we should be stockpiling food and water. The other place along the corridor with the red Benches and red carpets is not immune to that ridiculous scaremongering either. On television last week, a Baroness said we must “be prepared” for Russia to invade the UK. Russian troops marching down British high streets—if anyone wants to know how utterly preposterous that take is, on the same programme, Richard Madeley was considered the voice of reason. The UK is represented in 145 military sites across 40 countries. Our military budget is bigger today in real terms than it was in 1980 at the height of the cold war. We have a nuclear arsenal with hundreds of warheads. The UK is not some small, vulnerable, isolated state like the military industrial lobby wants everyone to believe—like so many MPs in this place believe.

title: Health Bill
text: My Lords, before I refer to my own amendment, I say that I support the amendments from the noble Baronesses, Lady Harding and Lady Barker, for the very reasons that they mentioned. In my clinical practice, I was asked many times to keep information that I was given by mothers about their previous reproductive history confidential. That sometimes created a problem in managing their pregnancies, but we had to devise a way of coping with it. These are important issues to be considered for the single patient record. I too support strongly the development of longitudinal patient data in a single patient record, but I have serious concerns about Clause 52(2), which introduces new Section 250E(3). It says: “The regulations may provide that the processing of information in accordance with the regulations does not breach any obligation of confidence”— that is what we are talking about, the confidence and trust that patients can have— “owed by the person processing the information”. It removes the common law of patient confidentiality. This is fundamental. How can any legislation remove a law that has been in existence for many years and whose operation has been successful in addressing the issue of the confidentiality of patient information? Allowing for the removal of the common-law duty of confidentiality from the single patient record opens up a fundamental alteration of the patient-clinician relationship. It will establish new statutory legal gateways by removing the existing legal requirements for implied and, sometimes, explicit, consent. This risks significant scope creep beyond direct care because it allows access to the single patient record by anybody and everybody. It threatens a lack of trust, which could risk patient safety and outcomes due to care avoidance and incomplete medical records. New Section 250E(3), introduced by Clause 52(2), does not simply allow for removal of the duty of confidentiality as a right owed to patients; it removes an important legal deterrent to inappropriate access to patient records, and communicates the same to professionals. One of the primary mechanisms protecting patient well-being in healthcare is uninhibited, full and frank communication. If patients know that people using electronic records are no longer bound by a legal duty of confidentiality, their behaviour may change, subtly or otherwise, in ways that could directly harm their health. The Government’s position is that removing the duty of confidentiality from the SPR would not create a new legal gateway for accessing or sharing patient information. I disagree. Under the common law, confidential patient information can generally be used and shared for direct care on the basis of implied consent, provided that its use is within patients’ reasonable expectations. Where information is highly sensitive, explicit consent may still be required—we talked about sensitive issues in the amendment just discussed. If legislation removes the duty of confidentiality, clinicians and organisations will no longer need to rely on implied consent to justify processing covered by the regulations; the statutory provision itself in the Bill will supply the legal authority. In practical terms, removing an existing legal duty therefore creates a new legal gateway. This matters because implied consent is not merely a technical legal mechanism; it embeds the use of patient information in a framework of patient understanding and choice. Removing the obligation of confidentiality withdraws an important safeguard against uses of information outside these expectations by anybody and everybody. It overrides the legal requirement that users align with reasonable expectations, which underpins choice about how highly sensitive information is shared. Even if the SPR regulations are tightly confined to direct care as has been suggested, removing the duty of confidentiality would replace existing consent-based safeguards with a statutory permission to process informatio

title: Health Bill
text: My Lords, I will speak to Amendment 148 in the name of the noble Baroness, Lady Barker, to which I have added my name, and to other amendments in the group. As we heard from the noble Baroness, Lady Freeman, in her opening remarks on the group, and just now from my noble friend Lady Harding, the success of the single patient record will ultimately depend on trust. If patients trust the system, they will engage with it. If they do not, they may wish to withhold information from clinicians or, indeed, avoid seeking care altogether. That would undermine the very objectives that this reform is intended to achieve. Amendment 148 addresses one of the areas where trust is most fragile: sexual and reproductive healthcare. As I said at Second Reading, I am broadly very supportive of the SPR and recognise the significant benefits that better information sharing can bring, but my concern is that sexual and reproductive health information has always, rightly, been treated differently, as it is uniquely sensitive because disclosure can, in some circumstances, expose patients to real harm. That is particularly true for patients experiencing domestic abuse, coercive control or honour-based abuse. It may also affect young people seeking confidential advice and treatment. The Minister’s letter over the weekend acknowledges this concern. I welcome the Government’s recognition that some health information requires particular protection, and the assurance that there is no intention simply to make highly sensitive information widely available. The letter also points to role-based access controls, audit mechanisms and additional safeguards for sensitive records, and those commitments are important and welcome. However, Amendment 148 asks whether, for sexual and reproductive health information, we should go one step further and place a clear consent requirement in legislation. Not all women want or need this additional confidentiality, and the evidence shows that some women, though fewer than 50% in some cases, are happy for their GPs to know aspects of their care. However, the key aspect of this is consent and awareness. We started this group on Monday evening, when the noble Lord, Lord Weir, spoke specifically to Amendment 148 before it had been introduced. I agree with him on the importance of enshrining consent at the heart of the SPR and the need for consistency in this. I also agree on the importance of data for research, but there are ways to meet the goals of the Goldacre review without making sensitive data and individual records available where patients do not wish them to be. Amendment 148 seeks to preserve the patient choice over some of the most intimate information held about them and to maintain long-established expectations of confidentiality in these services. It is a small amendment but crucial to the welfare of patients. It is supported by the relevant medical professional bodies and, I believe, a reasonable and proportionate safeguard. I also support other amendments in this group. Amendment 135, in the name of my noble friend Lord Kamall and others, addresses the concerns I have laid out using a different approach. It is certainly worth considering as an alternative, although my preference would be to see these protections in the Bill. Amendment 130 would provide patients with a meaningful ability to opt out of having information included in the record, and Amendment 145 would allow patients to opt out of uses beyond direct care. Together, these amendments recognise that public confidence is strengthened when patients retain agency and control over how their information is used. Amendments 131 and 146 are also important for transparency and accountability, and I support Amendments 137A and 137B. As my noble friend Lady Harding set out, these would place key safeguards directly in the Bill. title: Lobbying Transparency and Public Confidence
text: Well, they are not here, but that is not a surprise. The DUP has consistently championed the highest standards of accountability and integrity in public life, whether through our support for robust registers of interest and strict rules on paid advocacy or by backing the Nolan principles. The hon. Member for Bolton West referred to the Nolan principles a number of times, and no doubt those who follow me will do likewise. We very much believe that openness is essential to maintaining trust between the electorate and those they send here to represent them. We all build up a relationship with our constituents over years. I am very fortunate, because this is my 41st year as an elected representative. I have been representing people since 1985 as a councillor, an MLA and now as an MP. When I walk down the high street in Newtownards, nearly everybody knows who I am. That is not built up by being there for a short period of time, but over years and years of involvement as a councillor, and MLA and a businessperson, and by chasing the issues that people bring to me. At the same time, we must recognise that legitimate engagement is a vital part of good lawmaking. That is how I develop my knowledge of issues that come up in this Chamber. It comes off the back of my engagement with my constituents. Every week, I meet farmers from the Ards peninsula, fishermen from Portavogie, local business owners, charity groups and community groups across Strangford. Those are the people on the coal quay, to use that terminology. They come to Westminster as well to share their lived experience and their practical expertise. That is not a sinister influence; it is democracy in action. That is what the I am referring to, as the hon. Member for Bolton West did and others. We must ensure that any reform of the lobbying rules, including the implementation of the recent recommendations by the Ethics and Integrity Commission, does not place heavy-handed, bureaucratic burdens on small businesses, voluntary organisations or grassroots community groups, because we know how important those organisations are. Transparency must shine a light on improper influence behind closed doors without locking ordinary citizens out of the democratic process. There is a difference; there is a line to be drawn. The focus of the hon. Gentleman’s debate is very important, but our role is to contact and engage with our constituents. However, when we are discussing transparency and public disclosure, we cannot ignore the very real question of safety. I am referring to Northern Ireland, as Members would expect. We know all too well that openness in public life has historically carried a severe personal cost. My hon. Friend the Member for East Londonderry has received threats for his public engagement and the role that he has played as an MP, an MLA and a councillor. He was under threat from the IRA, as I was in my role. But for the good police work, intelligence, response and protection of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, now the Police Service of Northern Ireland, perhaps neither of us would be sitting here today. Elected representatives, public servants and those who engage with our democratic institutions have faced intimidation, threats and violence simply for participating in the political process. Even today, the security threat level in Northern Ireland is a stark reality. Members of this House from across the wider United Kingdom, and those who work alongside us, face rising levels of online abuse, harassment and physical threat. I am amazed, sometimes overwhelmed, by the threats that MPs face—offices damaged and threats to their person. Two of our colleagues were murdered; we remember them. We think also of those who have been injured as a result of their roles as MPs. We are ever mindful not only of the importance of our role, but of the threats that hang over us because of it. title: Health Bill
text: My Lords, it is a pleasure to follow the noble Baroness, Lady Harding, and her discussion of the importance of trust. There are shared concerns addressed in slightly different ways between amendments in this group. In truth, data should be collected and shared only when there is a need to know, whether for clinical, administrative or research reasons. I am grateful to noble Lords who added their names to my Amendment 162, which is about the need to protect confidential psychological therapy records. I speak as a now retired psychiatrist and psychotherapist, and argue that detailed psychotherapy session narratives should be excluded from routine sharing by default. This should not mean that the whole record is then not shared; it is still essential that information about medication, allergies, risk to self or others, crisis plans and other information necessary for safe care remain available. In psychotherapy, confidentiality affects treatment itself. Patients need to be able to disclose difficult material—for example, feelings of anger and hate—and to trust that it will be held securely. I would particularly value the Minister’s consideration of whether the clinical consequences of routine narrative sharing have been assessed. A patient whom the Guardian calls “Rosanna” asked me to share her experience. I note that the noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, spoke briefly about her challenge to the London Care Record on Monday evening. We should learn what we can from this case. I will say a little more about Rosanna. She supports a single patient record. She wants a doctor treating her to see what medication she takes. What she did not expect, as she looked over her GP’s shoulder, was to see confidential material from a psychotherapy session where she had spoken about coping with loss. As she put it, “You can’t object to something if you don’t know it’s happening”. South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust told Rosanna that the entries shared on its clinical system can include key psychotherapy session content, and that its feed shares the 15 most recent eligible entries, including those from its children’s mental health and addiction services. That is not all. A requested audit of how often Rosanna’s record had been accessed revealed 27 occasions on which the psychotherapy section of her record had been opened outside the mental health trust. The service acknowledged that its confidentiality discussions did not specifically explain what would be shared. When she raised her concern, the trust blocked the whole record, although she wanted to keep sharing essential information. She simply wanted choice about what details from her therapy were appropriate to share. This loss of trust led her to pause treatment. She was subsequently discharged, pending a transfer to another specialist service. Amendment 162 would protect an informed choice about the routine disclosure of detailed confidential therapy through the single patient record with an exception for immediate risk. Would the Minister explain how, under the Government’s proposals, a patient like Rosanna could make that choice? How would she learn of this before she starts treatment? It is not sufficient to say that anyone accessing a person’s record must be engaged in the delivery of health or social care. More generally, in preparing the guidance, how decisions are to be made must come about as a result of consultation with patient groups as well as specialists.

title: Lobbying Transparency and Public Confidence
text: It is always a pleasure to serve under your chairship, Sir Desmond. I thank the hon. Member for Bolton West (Phil Brickell) for securing this timely and important debate in which we can participate, and for setting the scene so well. I had thought the attendance might have been better. Perhaps two late nights have made a call on people’s perseverance. There is no bother with our perseverance because we have managed to turn up—that is by the way and not a fair thing to say. Public confidence is the bedrock on which our parliamentary democracy rests. When constituents look at Westminster or Stormont for the Assembly back home, they expect to see decisions made transparently, fairly and solely in the public interest. All too often, even a hint of reticence can seem like cloaking. It is essential for constituents to trust the person elected to represent them, whether they voted for them or not. I have always stated when elected to Westminster that I am everyone’s MP. People may not agree with everything my party stands for or my stance on issues I take a personal interest in, but I am still their MP. I think back to the time when I was elected here in 2010. For three months, I was also an Ards borough councillor and a Member of the Legislative Assembly. I gave an undertaking that I would step away from those two positions over the summer. I was elected here in May and stepped away from the Assembly in August and from the council in September. I held three positions at one time, but they were complementary because they were all elected representative positions within the constituency of Strangford. I did the job of a councillor and an MLA, and I had a business too, which I gifted to my son. I am my party’s health spokesperson, so I meet bodies and companies that give me information all the time. I do not see it as lobbying, by the way; I see it as enriching my knowledge of health issues. That is how I have my meetings. They tell me about things that our Government here need to focus on, and that gives me knowledge and an interest. Questions in the Chamber on health issues and questions that I send to Ministers are opportunities to put forward ideas. That is how I see my role as my party’s health spokesperson. My hon. Friend the Member for East Londonderry (Mr Campbell) is here, and it is not often that I can say that the DUP is the second-largest party in Westminster Hall. We are beaten only by the Labour party—that is no reflection on the Conservatives or the Lib Dems.

title: Health Bill
text: My Lords, I will speak to my Amendments 137A and 137B. I thank my noble friend Lady Shawcross-Wolfson—who not only added her name to them but did most of the drafting—and the noble Lords, Lord Tarassenko and Lord Patel, who added their names as well. I am a big supporter of the concept of a single patient record. I saw at first hand what was possible during Covid, when we were genuinely able to join up all the data. There is much talk about how our NHS data is a great national competitive strength. The reality is that it is not, unless we actually join up the data. Except in extreme emergencies, we are not able to do that. We do not really have a whole-population longitudinal health dataset for our life sciences to use to identify new treatments and to improve both patient outcomes and our economic growth. It is just an illusion without a proper single-patient record, so I am a huge supporter. But—and this is a big but—we need to recognise quite how scary it is to so many people to create a single patient record. Just the words are scary. Previous attempts to join up NHS data have not worked, not because of the technology but because we have not built and maintained patient and citizen trust. Trust is really hard to build and very easily broken. Unfortunately, in this space, it has been broken multiple times, whether we are talking about care.data, NPfIT or the federated data platform—I could keep going. In each case, we have failed to build citizen trust in our potential single datasets. I promise I will be brief. My two amendments are designed to put in the Bill some of the things, although not all—they are definitely not complete—that we need to do to build trust in the process of creating the single patient record. I do not for a moment suggest that the Department of Health and Social Care does not intend to do this; it is just that it is not visible that it is doing it. In building trust, it is not enough to do things the right way; you have to be seen to be doing things the right way as well. That is why it is important to flesh out Clause 52 quite substantially, because it creates significant powers without visibility of how those powers will be implemented, which does not build trust. So my Amendment 137A specifies quite a long list of areas where safeguards are required. I very much expect that the Minister agrees that those safeguards are required. I am certain that my list is not exhaustive, but it is an attempt to put in the Bill a number of the most important areas where various parts of our society are scared that a single patient record could cause unintended harm. My Amendment 137B—they fit together—specifies who must be consulted. Again, this is not an exhaustive list, but it is an attempt to put in the Bill a broad, comprehensive set of stakeholders, particularly the most disfranchised and disconnected groups of society who are most scared of this single patient record. It is an attempt to require the Government to publish the response to the consultation before regulations are made. This is in part probing, but I very much hope that, through this process, we can have an active dialogue to put in the Bill both the areas where safeguards are required and who needs to be consulted and engaged before the regulations are laid.

title: Lobbying Transparency and Public Confidence
text: I thank the hon. Member for his contribution. He makes a very valid point, because comparative analysis shows that the number of registered lobbyists in the UK is far smaller the number registered in Brussels or Washington DC, which indicates that a great deal of activity is going on that is not formally registered. Are you an in-house lobbyist? If so, you are out of scope. Is your lobbying supposedly incidental to your primary work? Bingo: you are out of scope again. Is your organisation not registered for VAT in this country because you are a foreign-registered firm? You are out of scope. And do you message Ministers on WhatsApp or conduct your lobbying efforts through special advisers? Again, there is no need to make a declaration. Global Counsel, for example, did not have to register as a lobbyist in this country, despite having, quite legally and fairly under the current rules, lobbied former Ministers in the previous Government on behalf of the Qatar free zones. The reason is very simple: Global Counsel was not registered in the UK, so it did not have to pay VAT and was not required to sign up to the lobbying register. However, anyone looking at that in the real world would think it absurd. Global Counsel had about 100 employees and posted a revenue of more than £20 million, but was not captured in the current framework. It is patently clear that anyone so minded could drive a coach and horses through the 2014 Act. That takes me to the Ethics and Integrity Commission’s recommendations again, which I wholeheartedly endorse. Lobbyists should have to register if they lobby Ministers as well as permanent secretaries, special advisers, directors general, directors, non-executive directors, or any other Government advisers, paid or unpaid, equivalent to director general or director level. That is a much simpler activity-led approach that the Government should now carefully consider, because the public have a right to know who is being lobbied in government by whom, when, how, for what purpose and how often. That is not just my view; it is a view shared by industry representatives themselves. They include the Chartered Institute of Public Relations, which stated in its “No Rules Britannia” report: “Currently, the UK’s lobbying laws leave us languishing at the lower end of global governance rankings making it harder to promote our democratic values on the world stage.” There should be a level playing field here. If standards are effectively enforced, we should not fear greater transparency, and it is not just Government Ministers and senior civil servants who should be in scope of the regime. Front-Bench teams and spokespeople of all major political parties should be subject to some form of disclosure regime that is proportionate and reasonable. I would welcome the remarks of the other parties on that specific point. The hon. Member for Clacton (Nigel Farage), who I have informed I will mention, is seeking to become Prime Minister, but voters have absolutely no information about who Reform is meeting and who is feeding into Reform UK’s policy. Reform’s financial relationship with figures in the cryptocurrency industry is well documented, so voters deserve to know who Reform has been meeting. Has it been meeting with a balanced list of stakeholders to reach its policy conclusions, or have its meetings been solely with donors who would stand to benefit from relaxing the cryptocurrency rules? I put that challenge to the Opposition party spokespeople here today: would they welcome more transparency to benefit our democracy?
