That is why our Committee recommended comprehensive training and education alongside the introduction of the victims code, and I am proud that this Labour Government are strengthening the service justice system as part of our wider mission to halve violence against

title: Armed Forces Bill
text: This Armed Forces Bill makes a number of important changes that will strengthen our national defence and better support our men and women in uniform. Having spoken at a previous stage of the Bill’s passage, I am glad to see it come back to this House as it nears the end of its progress through Parliament. We are here to discuss a number of amendments, which I will come to shortly, but given the Bill’s important provisions, I hope we can reach agreement so that Ministers can crack on with implementing the vital measures it contains. Why is this Bill so important? As we all know, Parliament is required to renew the legislation every five years in order to maintain the armed forces. Ministers could simply have tabled a Bill to do that; instead, what we have in front of us is a genuinely ambitious set of changes to the law that will strengthen our defensive capabilities in a number of key areas. First, as Members across the House have mentioned, it puts the armed forces covenant into law to give much greater weight to the need to support our service personnel and their families in communities across the country. Secondly, it establishes the Defence Housing Service. I disagree with the right hon. Member for Rayleigh and Wickford (Mr Francois)—I think that service will provide clearer leadership, greater coherence and greater investment in military accommodation. In my previous speech on this Bill, I set out for Ministers more detailed thoughts on how that could best work. The Bill also improves our resilience by expanding our reserves pool, grows our whole-of-society approach, and expands life chances for young people by growing our cadet forces. Finally, it modernises the law to give service personnel much-needed new powers to tackle the threat from incursions and hostile surveillance by drones. On my visits to operational bases in this country and abroad as part of the armed forces parliamentary scheme, I have seen for myself just how much of a growing issue that is, and I am glad that the Government are making specific provision for it. Those measures, and the many others contained in the Bill, are very welcome, and I think they will make a real difference. Turning to the Lords amendments, Lords amendments 11 and 25 refer to the Government’s proposed change to the legal form and governance arrangements of the reserve forces’ and cadets’ associations. I followed with real interest the debates in the House of Lords on this issue. While there is clearly disagreement about the best future approach, it is important that we recognise that there is a lot of consensus. There is widespread agreement that our reserve forces and cadets play crucial roles and deserve the very best support. There is strong support for the strategic defence review recommendations that the strength of reserves and cadets be expanded. There is also recognition that activities to organise and promote reserves and cadets in local communities and to employers are central to their success. As we heard from the Minister, under the proposed new arrangements there is a clear, ongoing commitment to ensure regional and local work will be maintained by the establishment of regional councils across the UK. What remains in contention and is whether the new body will remain an unclassified arm’s length body with Crown status or will become, as we have heard, a non-departmental public body. My view is that the argument for the latter is relatively straightforward. In 2019, as the Minister set out, the Sullivan review recommended improvements to governance, financial reporting, audit and other arrangements relating to the reserve forces and cadets associations. We know that those issues still need to be addressed, because the National Audit Office and the Public Accounts Committee found inadequate arrangements for monitoring the financial performance of those bodies. title: Armed Forces Bill
text: Thank you for your kind words earlier, Madam Deputy Speaker. The Armed Forces Bill champions many new measures to strengthen our armed forces, which continue to have Liberal Democrat support. That includes the expansion of the armed forces covenant, action on defence housing and better support for victims of service offences. However, as the Bill returns to this House, we want to speak yet again in support of a better standard of housing for all serving armed forces personnel, both those in service family accommodation and those in single living accommodation. Every member of our armed forces deserves a decent standard of housing, but the Government continue to reject Liberal Democrat amendments to the Bill that would demand improvements to single living accommodation, just like the kind I lived in while serving in the Royal Air Force. Lords amendment 2 would require the Government to agree to a minimum housing standard for single living accommodation at least as good as the decent homes standard on behalf of more than 77,000 service personnel. That standard should cover everything from building safety to heating, plumbing and laundry facilities—a baseline to be agreed within six months of the Armed Forces Bill being given Royal Assent. The Lords amendment, from my noble friend Baroness Smith of Newnham, mirrors what the Liberal Democrats pushed for in this House during earlier readings of this Bill, and my hon. Friend the Member for Tunbridge Wells (Mike Martin) and I pushed for that again when the Bill was in Committee. The Elphicke Ross review into single living accommodation was published barely a fortnight ago, and it is completely clear about the need for a decent housing standard for military accommodation. Second only to emergency repairs, recommendation 2 of the review says that the Ministry of Defence “should introduce a new Decent SLA Standard”. Specifically, it says that military accommodation should be “safe”, “warm”, “clean”, “functional”, “secure” and “private”. It also says: “For too long, poor conditions have been institutionalised by an outdated accommodation grading system that compensates substandard living with discounted rent, rather than driving the necessary improvements”. It also warns of the disaster that happened when the last Government did not back words with actions: “In 2022 an attempt was made to address the poor state of Defence accommodation. The Defence Minimum Standard (DMS) was introduced to provide a baseline for acceptable accommodation. This attempt failed because there was no funding, no implementation plan, no timetable for improvement and no mechanism for enforcement.” This time last year, the former Secretary of State for Defence, when talking about improvements to defence housing, wanted to tell our armed forces: “We are on your side”, so it is disappointing to see that the Government have proposed to reject the Lords amendment entirely, letting single living accommodation fall behind. Can the Minister tell us whether the Government will make a separate commitment on this matter? If not, as my hon. Friend the Member for Lewes (James MacCleary) has already asked the Minister, how many of the 19 recommendations of the Elphicke Ross review will be either delayed or ignored? There are no doubt dozens of Labour Members with forces accommodation in their constituencies that house thousands of personnel. How will they answer that question? I urge them to think about the conversations they will have with young serving personnel in the future. The independent review says that the Ministry of Defence needs to move on from “fix on fail” building repairs to planned lifecycle maintenance and better accountability. Nor is this just about money. title: Armed Forces Bill
text: I rise briefly to address three matters of particular interest to the Defence Committee. First, Lords amendments 2 and 18 concern standards in military accommodation, particularly single living accommodation. This has been a long-standing concern of the Committee. We have seen the consequences of years of under-investment, poor maintenance and unacceptable living conditions for our service personnel. The Committee has not taken a view on whether the statutory military homes standard proposed by the Lords is the right legislative mechanism, but there should be no doubt about the standard we expect. Our service personnel should not be asked to live in accommodation that we would regard as unacceptable for anyone else. The Government have published the Elphicke Ross review, which recommends a new decent SLA standard across all permanent single living accommodation by 2032, overseen by a new office for military accommodation. Those commitments are welcome, but important questions remain. If the Government are asking this House to reject a statutory standard, will the Minister explain what status the new decent SLA standard will have, when it will be published, what interim milestones will apply before 2032, and how Parliament can hold the Government to account for meeting them? I turn next to Lords amendments 3 to 7 on the victims’ code for the service justice system. Through our work on women in the armed forces, the Committee has heard powerful evidence about the experiences of victims. I welcome the Government amendments requiring the code to be laid before Parliament and brought into force through secondary legislation, but the real test will be whether victims see a difference in practice, and whether they are properly supported, kept informed and treated with dignity throughout the justice process. The voices of victims must remain central as the code is developed and maintained. Finally, I welcome Lords amendment 1 on the armed forces covenant. The Defence Committee has supported the extension of the covenant duty, but we have stressed that much will depend on the accompanying statutory guidance. It is right that the Lords amendment preserves an appropriate degree of parliamentary scrutiny over the guidance. These changes matter to the daily lives of our service personnel and their families, and the Defence Committee will continue to scrutinise whether the improvements promised in the Bill are delivered in practice.

title: Armed Forces Bill
text: In which case, I should point out that the hon. Gentleman is an RAF veteran. I congratulate him on his appointment to the Front Bench. We look forward to his explaining how the amendment would work in practice and expanding on the details of the proposal, including whether the standards will apply to transit accommodation, of which the MOD has much, and what the implications might be for the rent charged to young, predominantly single soldiers if these standards were to apply. I am sure that he has thought that through. We will listen to that in a moment. For the record, I note that he is wearing a Royal College of Defence Studies tie. In summary, we commend the Government on doing the right thing by waiving visa fees for foreign and Commonwealth personnel who serve this country in uniform, and now for their loved ones, too. However, we continue to disagree with the Government on their attempts to replace the RFCAs with a national quango, and we are deeply unimpressed by Labour’s introduction, with great fanfare, of the Defence Housing Service through the Bill, only for it to breach its own ringfence and denude it of cash, having repeatedly promised for almost a year not to do precisely that. Our armed forces and their families really do deserve better than that.

title: Armed Forces Bill
text: I know that the hon. Lady speaks up strongly for her military community, so perhaps I could meet her halfway. I will absolutely believe what she tells me about what is going on in her constituency if, in return, she will believe that we are genuinely annoyed, because all the way through the Bill process, dating back to its Second Reading in January, the Opposition have been repeatedly promised that this money would be ringfenced, and would not be raided to meet short-term funding pressures. The permanent under-secretary, in his letter to the Chairman of the PAC—not to the hon. Lady, and not to me—admits that that has happened in this Parliament, to the tune of approximately £2 billion. I ask the hon. Lady to appreciate that this is not faux anger. We spent months asking this question, and we were told time and again that the Government would not do what we now know they have. We have it in writing. I turn briefly to amendment 2 in the name of the Liberal Democrats. We have considerable sympathy with what the drafters are trying to achieve by seeking to set minimum standards for both SFA and SLA. This matter was discussed during the earlier stages of the Bill, so I will listen carefully to the Lib Dem spokesman. I see a raft of Liberal Democrat Members in the Chamber, but I presume that the spokesman will be the hon. Member for North Devon (Ian Roome).

title: Armed Forces Bill
text: My hon. Friend is absolutely right to highlight the huge amount of work done by people with a huge passion for our reserve forces and cadets. I very much recognise the immense amount of work that they do and the importance of ensuring that their voices are represented. The findings of the National Audit Office and the Public Accounts Committee reinforce the case for establishing a single NDPB. Those successive independent reviews reached a consistent conclusion: the current structure does not provide the level of accountability, governance or financial assurance expected of a modern public body responsible for significant public expenditure. However, the Government very much recognise that the current RFCAs remain essential to Defence’s relationship with reservists, cadets, employers and local communities. That is why there must be the requirement that the RFCA establishes regional councils to maintain those connections. The Government have tabled amendments to strengthen those connections, and will ensure that the future NDPB retains a strong regional dimension and continues to benefit from the local knowledge, community connections and experience that have been the hallmarks of the associations over the years. The amendments will make several changes. First, they clarify the regional councils’ leadership and composition, providing for chairs and arrangements for appointing presidents and vice-presidents. Presidents will be appropriate lords lieutenant, where available, preserving the RFCA network’s constitutional, ceremonial and community links. Secondly, the amendments allow for a number of regional chairs to become representative members of the RFCA, ensuring that regional perspectives can be brought into discussions at the national level. Thirdly, they will establish a national council comprising regional council chairs, service representatives and others appointed by the RFCA. This formal forum will enable regional experience, advice and expertise to inform the organisation’s work and help to maintain strong links between the centre and regions. It is important to be clear that this reform is not about removing local engagement. Rather, it is about combining strong national governance with strong regional delivery, ensuring that local knowledge, employer engagement and cadet support, and community links remain central to the RFCA’s work. In conclusion, the choice is not between reform and tradition. The Government’s approach delivers both by preserving the regional connections, civic leadership and volunteer contributions that have been central to the RFCAs’ success, while introducing the accountability, transparency and assurance that are necessary for the future. I therefore urge the House to support the Government motion.

title: Armed Forces Bill
text: I, too, am very much looking forward to implementing our manifesto commitment. Lords amendments 19 to 24 are technical and consequential amendments. Amendments 19 and 20 clarify the Crown immunity provisions applying to the Defence Housing Service, while amendments 21 to 24 ensure that the transitional arrangements for the reserve forces operate as intended. The Government recognise the intent behind Lords amendments 2 and 18, and single living accommodation continues to be a priority for Defence. This is why the Government commissioned an independent review into single living accommodation, led by Natalie Elphicke Ross OBE. That review has now been published and, given the scale of change being proposed, it is essential that we take the time to get this right and put in place the foundations needed to deliver meaningful change for our people. However, recognising the need for change does not establish the case for the approach taken in Lords amendment 2. While the amendment allows for military-specific regulations, it would nevertheless make the civilian statutory requirements a mandatory minimum benchmark. The review expressly recognises that single living accommodation has a distinct function within service life and recognises operational requirements, cohesion, military culture and ethos as reasons why those arrangements can differ from civilian settings. As the Minister for Veterans and People set out in his written ministerial statement, we are already taking steps to drive this work forward. Air Marshal Sir Paul Lloyd, Deputy Chief of the Air Staff, will oversee this important work, supported by teams from across Defence. The Ministry of Defence is already looking at the review’s recommendations, and the immediate focus will be on how best to refresh the existing defence minimum standard to ensure that it better meets the needs of our people. I can speak of my own personal commitment to this issue, as someone who has experienced single living accommodation, and I take seriously the need to improve the standard of accommodation for people who work so hard in the defence of this country. Turning to Lords amendments 11 and 25, the Government strongly disagree with the other place’s decision to remove the provisions that establish the Reserve Forces and Cadets Association as a non-departmental public body. The RFCA provisions are in line with the 2019 Sullivan review, which recommended that the Council of Reserve Forces and Cadets Associations and the 13 reserve forces and cadets associations should be consolidated into a single executive NDPB with a national headquarters and strong regional structures.

title: Armed Forces Bill
text: The Government invite the House to agree with Lords amendment 1, 3 to 10, 12 to 17 and 19 to 24, which we tabled in the other place. We invite the House to disagree with Lords amendments 2 and 18, which were proposed by Baroness Smith of Newnham, and with Lords amendments 11 and 25, which were proposed by the Opposition. In disagreeing with Lords amendments 11 and 25, we will propose Government amendments to the restored Reserve Forces and Cadets Association provisions to the Bill. Lords amendments 1 and 3 to 7 respond to recommendations made by the Delegated Powers and Regulatory Reform Committee. The Government considered the Committee’s recommendations carefully, and the amendments simply ensure an appropriate level of parliamentary scrutiny for both the armed forces covenant statutory guidance and the code for victims in the service justice system. Lords amendments 8 and 9 ensure that the provisions enabling transfers between the regular and reserve forces operate as intended. Lords amendment 10 modernises the way in which reservists can be contacted by allowing call-out and recall notices to be served by email. Lords amendments 12 to 14, 16 and 17 make provision in relation to assaults against members of the service police and create an offence of impersonating a member of the service police. Lords amendment 15 concerns immigration fees for eligible armed forces personnel and their families. It requires regulations to provide for specified fee exemptions, which I confirm will be implemented before the end of September 2027.

title: Funeral Directors etc (Register)
text: I beg to move, That leave be given to bring in a Bill to require the Secretary of State to prepare and maintain a register of funeral directors, private mortuaries, direct cremation services and certain other persons who transport or hold the bodies of deceased persons; and for connected purposes. It has been three years since I first met Ministers to register my horror, because I had just discovered that anybody—no matter their background, expertise or resources—could set up business as a funeral director. Since then, there have been numerous meetings and numerous Ministers; the Government have said a lot and done almost nothing. The disturbing fact remains that in the funeral industry, there is no minimum qualification, no registration, no licensing, no inspection, no formal regulation and, crucially, no dedicated legislation to fall back on when things go wrong. In fact, the funeral sector is almost completely unregulated. Of course, this matter remains as pressing as ever. Last December, Gosport funeral directors Richard Elkin and Hayley Bell were convicted after a court heard they had kept 46 bodies on their business premises in an unrefrigerated room. Bailiffs entering the premises found two bodies stored without refrigeration in a dilapidated room with water leaking through the ceiling. One of those bodies—that of an elderly gentleman who had been left for 36 days—was badly decomposed. Elkin and Bell were brought to justice only by using a jigsaw of non-purpose-built legislation, including the offence of carrying on business with an attempt to defraud, causing a public nuisance, and a Victorian common-law offence of preventing a lawful burial that dates back to the times of the grave robbers. Imagine the hurt of those families who believed that the body of their loved one had been properly cared for, respectfully placed into a coffin and cremated with dignity, only to find that instead it had been left to rot on a rack at the back of the funeral parlour—it is almost unimaginable. We put enormous, unquestioning trust in those who care for the bodies of our loved ones when they die. There have been a number of high-profile cases across the UK, but in the case of Elkin and Bell, 46 grieving families were robbed of a proper grieving process because they had been left to worry about how their relatives’ bodies were mishandled. That is before we talk about those left wondering whether there were others besides those 46. I have therefore been calling for the Government to urgently bring forward proposals to establish a proper framework of regulation around the death pathway. The real horror is that this will not be an isolated case—it could be happening out there in our communities as I speak. Under the law as it stands today, anyone can set themselves up as a funeral director without any meaningful supervision. The Fuller inquiry, whose report was published in July last year, made five recommendations to the Government. Almost a year and a half later, the promised response has not arrived. Those recommendations were quite simple: first, that “The UK government should establish an independent statutory regulatory regime for funeral directors in England”; secondly, that “These regulations and standards should be considered within the overall care and journey of the deceased”; thirdly, that “mandatory information be given to customers by funeral directors to provide transparency about the care of the deceased”; fourthly, that “Direct cremation businesses should also be considered” as part of the reforms; and fifthly, that “the benefit to customers and the need for public confidence outweigh the difficulties that may be experienced by some businesses” in adjusting to a new regime. On 1 September, the Government took the meaningful step of committing formally to introducing legislation. title: COP31
text: Let me start with the point about us accounting for only 1% of emissions. The countries that account for 3% or less of emissions together account for 50% of global emissions, so we must all play our role, but the Father of the House is absolutely right to say that there is a balance. This is a transition, and Government’s responsibility is to get that transition right—to take the action that we need to take, in a way that protects our communities. The right hon. Gentleman talks about the acute cost of electricity. Our energy costs are some of the highest in Europe because we have an energy system that is not working and that is far too dependent on global fossil fuels. We must break that dependence. Critically, we have a privatised system that does not put affordability and the consumer—business or domestic—at its heart, and we are absolutely determined to change that. We care about our workers. For me, one of the travesties is that if we look at the North sea, we see that between 2016 and 2024, some 75,000 jobs were lost there. That happened on the Conservatives’ watch. We need to support a just transition, but that will not happen unless it is intentional. We are committed to doing the hard graft to support a balanced transition.

title: COP31
text: I share the hon. Lady’s concerns about our failure to reach a collective agreement. She must know that we and our negotiators did everything—for 36 hours at a stretch, with no sleep—to try to get a deal that was commensurate with what we believed was needed. We will continue to work and we will continue to fight. Progress was made, the action agenda moved forward, and commitments were made in the technical track. We are committed to playing our part in the coming year, working with our partners across the world, to deliver action, because we understand how important that is. On the hon. Lady’s point about replicating our domestic work internationally, I reassure her that we are absolutely resolute about climate action at home. This matters, because our communities are at the heart of this. We have seen the impact if we get this wrong. The first duty of Government is to protect our communities, as I have said, so we will ensure that we take action. We are governed by carbon budgets, which are legally binding limits for carbon emissions. Every decision we make is within the carbon budget. We will ensure that we take balanced action to drive carbon reduction while we protect our communities. I am proud that the UK has managed to reduce its emissions by 54% since 1990. We have done that at the same time as growing our economy by 85%, so it can be done. We will take that balanced approach. We will absolutely continue to drive the warm homes plan forward. Yes, there were cuts, but we have worked to ensure that we protect the schemes for low-income households. Alongside that, we have launched the warm homes loan. It has had record interest and support; we are now looking to scale it up, so there is a balance there. We are also looking to ramp up and scale up through devolved programmes. We are consulting on the ZEV mandate, but we are clear that the end destination of getting to zero emission vehicles by 2035 absolutely stays. Again, everything we do will be done in the context of maintaining our carbon budget, so that we are delivering on our climate commitments.

title: COP31
text: The failure to reach a final agreement at COP31 is a deeply concerning missed opportunity. I have worked for many years in some of the most climate-vulnerable islands and countries, and I know how desperately worrying this news will be for them. It is worrying for the vulnerable people at home in the UK, too, who face the consequences of our overshooting 1.5°C, such as heatwaves like the ones we had this summer, which led to a record-high 5,258 heat-related deaths in England. Heat-related deaths are avoidable deaths. Let that sink in. I respect the advances that were made at COP, and the country negotiators who drew a line in the sand. The UK was right to stand alongside the EU and refuse to accept a deal that made no mention of the need to phase out fossil fuels—the largest driver of climate change—or the commitment to keep 1.5°C within reach. But rejecting a bad deal is only half the battle; climate ambition and leadership means doing at home what we promise internationally. We Liberal Democrats are increasingly worried that this Government risk failing that test with some of their measures, such as cutting £2.5 billion from the warm homes plan; proposing to weaken the zero emission vehicle mandate; and considering approving Rosebank, in the face of our climate commitments to global science-based targets. At COP31, the Prime Minister promised “a new era of British leadership over the next decade.” Rowing back on climate action targets is the sort of thing we have come to expect from Conservative leadership; it is not what we in this House want to see. Will the Secretary of State turn the worry that many are feeling about the results of COP31 into hope, by agreeing to our calls for a national electrification strategy, with targets; by maintaining the zero emission vehicle mandate; by restoring the warm homes plan; and by ruling out Rosebank?

title: COP31
text: I am going to try to compose myself because I thought that was a shameful and shocking response. The hon. Member should hang his head in shame, because if against the backdrop of the science and overshoot, that is what he thinks is an appropriate response, he needs to think again. Let me answer the hon. Member’s specific questions. First, Britain has provided a model that other countries are following. We were the first country to put in place a Climate Change Act, and it has been replicated the world over. There was a time when the Conservatives agreed with us and there was consensus on the need for action. Businesses were at COP31 in force because they can see that this is a global economy—a sector growing to $3 trillion, with $2 trillion in clean energy last year alone. The UK can be at the forefront of that. China, which he mentions, is stealing a march. It is moving fast on this because it sees the opportunities at home and abroad. Even if the hon. Gentleman will not recognise the realities of climate change and the duty we all have to protect our communities, and therefore to act, he should look at the economic opportunity: £110 billion in clean energy alone has been unlocked by this Government in the last two years. There is a huge opportunity to build the industries of the future. That is why businesses are clamouring. The hon. Gentleman says that countries are not following. On the path to electrification, 80 countries signed the 35 by 35 pledge put forward by the Türkiye presidency. Country after country can see that this is not just a response to climate change. Critically, the dependence on global fossil fuel markets, which was compounded by the Conservatives when they were in government, has left us acutely exposed. We are experiencing a cost of living crisis today because we are too dependent on global fossil fuel markets. The response to that is clean energy and electrification. Whether we care about climate change—which we Government Members do—affordability, or investment in our businesses and communities, this is the way forward, which is why country after country is following suit. I end by quoting the shadow Secretary of State, the hon. Member for West Aberdeenshire and Kincardine (Andrew Bowie), from when he had a grip and some foresight and cared about the country: “We are not rowing back on anything. Net zero remains on the statute book, and we are going to smash the target.” That was in 2023. Something profoundly tragic has happened to the Conservative party. I ask Conservative Members to look at the evidence, the science, and what is happening in the world, and to join the side of the reasonable.

title: COP31
text: I thank the Secretary of State for advance sight of her statement. This Government told the British public that if we led the world on climate policy, the world would follow. Ministers have lectured industry, imposed extra burdens on households and sidelined concerns about competitiveness, all on the basis that Britain would provide the model that others would emulate, but even with 100 private jets touching down at Antalya, a British delegation of 255, and 92,000 people at the largest conference ever, the whole thing collapsed. After months of speeches, declarations and moral grandstanding, the outcome was failure. The truth is uncomfortable: while Britain has been busy making itself poorer in pursuit of climate leadership, the world’s major powers have been moving in a very different direction. The United States did not even send a delegation to the conference. Instead, it is pursuing what it openly calls “energy dominance” to win the race for artificial intelligence and future technologies. Does that not expose the central flaw in the Secretary of State’s approach? The rest of the world is focused on energy security and growth; meanwhile, this Government remain trapped in an ideological cage that assumes all nations share Britain’s priorities. It is obvious that they do not. Perhaps the most revealing moment of COP31 was when the proposed text omitted any reference whatsoever to fossil fuels. That is because everyone can see that the world has become more dangerous and our energy security is at risk. This so perfectly demonstrates why the Government’s approach is misguided. The Secretary of State believes that if Britain loses enough jobs, sacrifices enough investment and abandons enough industrial capacity, others will surely follow. I wonder what the GMB general secretary thinks of that. At COP31 we saw the reality: Russia, India, Saudi Arabia and other major producers of oil and gas are not following Britain. They are pursuing their own interests, and that means it is time for us to stand up for ours. I will ask the Secretary of State some basic questions. First, does she believe that other countries are following this Government’s example when it comes to energy security? Secondly, what assessment has she made of the impact on British competitiveness when countries such as the United States are explicitly pursuing energy expansion while we restrict our own domestic production? Thirdly, she made reference in her statement to maintaining “momentum behind forest finance”. Does that mean she is committing long-term to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility? Finally, what was the total cost to the British taxpayer of sending 255 people to COP31? The gap between Britain’s climate policy and the realities of international politics has never looked wider. The Prime Minister is still trying to govern on vibes alone, and while he may think he looks cool on TikTok, it makes him a laughing stock on the international stage. He flew all the way to COP for a three-minute speech, probably written by ChatGPT, in which his main point was to show the world that Britain would show leadership. But leadership is meaningful only if others follow—ask Keir Starmer. The events of the past week suggest that no one is following Britain. Showing leadership would be to fight for cheap energy at home, maintaining prosperity, competitiveness and energy security. The Energy Secretary could start by approving Rosebank rather than briefing against it. No one will be persuaded by her virtue signalling; they will be persuaded by innovation, growth and prosperity. After the collapse of COP31, it is the Energy Secretary’s duty to refocus on delivering that.

title: COP31
text: With permission, Madam Deputy Speaker, I would like to make a statement following the conclusion of the COP31 climate summit. This year’s climate conference sought to confront a hard truth: that the world is on course to exceed 1.5° of warming by around 2030. We all know what this will mean for communities at home and abroad. At around 1.4° of warming today, we are already seeing the impacts. Here in Britain, this summer brought record heatwaves, droughts and wildfires, and it was people’s homes, their livelihoods and the communities that they love that were impacted. And not just that: lives were lost, too. As my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care informed the House earlier, the UK Health Security Agency released data today showing that we saw a total of 5,258 heat-related deaths in the UK over 2026. We cannot stand by and let this be the new normal. Overseas, we saw the devastation on the Nepal-China border with heartbreaking scenes of communities destroyed. Around the world, communities on the frontline of the climate crisis are seeing their homes destroyed and their livelihoods threatened. Climate change is here, and as we overshoot 1.5°, the impacts will be felt in country after country, the world over. So I went to COP31 clear about the challenge we face, and about the urgency of taking climate action. The target of 1.5° remains the right target. As the UN Secretary-General has said, overshoot does not mean surrender; it means redoubling our efforts. We arrived in Antalya determined to work with our partners to reach consensus on the need for urgent, ambitious action. COP31 delivered important progress across the wider negotiations, especially through the action agenda, but as the House knows, parties were unable to reach consensus on the cover decision. After concerted negotiations and tireless efforts to up the ambition, the substance that was proposed in the final cover decision did not meet the moment and we were unwilling to support it. It moved us backwards on the science when we needed to move faster. It failed to reaffirm our existing collective commitment to transition away from fossil fuels and our commitment to keep 1.5° within reach. It compromised where we needed bold collective ambition, and I was immensely disappointed by this outcome. We were not alone in standing up for these issues. We stood alongside small island developing states and some of the least developed countries on the very frontline of this crisis, which could not accept this as an adequate outcome. Now we have a responsibility to uphold and protect the Paris agreement. We have a duty to protect communities here in the UK, across the Commonwealth and in the countries most vulnerable to climate shocks. Although we could not find consensus on the cover decision, COP31 saw success beyond this. We worked with partners around the world and made progress that was not reflected in the proposed cover text. The technical negotiations delivered progress on areas including the global goal on adaptation and just transition. Conferences of the parties are increasingly about turning commitments into action through the action agenda, which was a significant focus for the Turkish COP presidency. We saw the strongest ever backing for mobilising action, with 119 countries using the closing event to recognise the wider implementation that is happening. That is concrete progress, and it demonstrates the global momentum for the energy transition. I am proud of the UK’s role in this effort. More than ever, it has strengthened our commitment to multilateralism and our resolve to work with partners in every region of the world to drive action ahead of COP32. I want to thank the UK’s negotiating team, led by Kate Hughes, and everyone across the UK civil service, business and civil society who contributed to this effort. I have seen at first hand their dedication, hard work and determination to make progress. Together we focused our e

title: Timms Review: Final Report
text: I welcome the Minister’s statement, which is very welcome indeed. It is not surprising that there is not a single Back Bencher on the Tory Benches, because they left behind the scheme that we inherited, which is dehumanising, confrontational and has stigmatised tens of thousands of people. Going further back, it was Mrs Thatcher—the Tories’ heroine—who drove tens of thousands of unemployed mineworkers and others on to sick pay, because they were told that they would be left the rest of their lives without a job. It is true today that in my constituency there are still thousands of men who have not worked for 40 years who were instructed to go on to sick pay. That is a shameful record that we must reverse. I think this is a step in the right direction. I will make one further point. The employment rate under Thatcher meant that only two out of every three people who were available for work could get work. Now that figure is more than 75%, and it is increasing month on month. I urge the Minister to be careful not to fall into a moral panic and begin to cut things that might lead to destitution simply because there are loud voices on the Opposition Benches.

title: Timms Review: Final Report
text: Young disabled people in my constituency have been watching this process, and have been very worried about what it will mean for their dignity and their future, so I really want to thank the Minister for the approach that he has taken, through the report, and the consideration that has been put into coming to the House today to make these announcements. One of the biggest misconceptions is that PIP is an out-of-work benefit, so I appreciate the effort the Minister is making to take a more human approach to this. I am proud that the Scottish equivalent, the adult disability payment, has been described by the Resolution Foundation as “kinder”, but not more costly, and agree that this is the right objective. Can the Minister confirm with confidence that any changes that follow from Timms and Milburn will not remove crucial support for young people in Scotland? Will he continue to work positively with the Scottish Government on the quasi-devolved elements of welfare and employment, to ensure that we can all get this right for young people across Scotland?

title: Timms Review: Final Report
text: I thank the Minister for sharing his comments and the report in advance of today’s statement. It has been a very busy couple of weeks. There was very much a Mardi Gras feeling around the Milburn report, but it has been strangely quiet around the Timms report—it could even be seen as the “Tiny Timms report”, given the lack of media interest in it. [ Interruption. ] The reality is that we need to manage the benefit system appropriately, but PIP is there to support people to do things that many other people throughout the country take for granted. The fact of the matter is that people who are disabled are so much more likely to have high levels of deprivation, so it is very important to get this right. The Liberal Democrats welcome the fact that the Minister has worked really well with people with disabilities, and we want to make sure that that happens throughout the Department for Work and Pensions. It is very interesting to see how the two reports have taken a different approach to young people, which has led to uncertainty and anguish for them. It would be extremely helpful if the Government could get a grip on that. Some answers from the Minister would be really welcome. First, what conditions are included when he speaks about “severe” and “degenerative” conditions? Finally, will the final report apply to all claimants or just new ones?

title: Timms Review: Final Report
text: I congratulate my right hon. Friend, his co-chairs and all members of the steering group on coming up with this report. From what I have read so far, I think it is incredibly constructive. I particularly like the approach of framing future developments around the principles that he has set out. It is a personalised and positive approach rather than, as he has described it, the dehumanising system that was too often associated with the PIP process. As my right hon. Friend rightly explained, PIP contributes to, but does not wholly cover, the thousands of pounds in extra costs that disabled people have to pay by virtue of their being disabled. I have to say that I have been concerned about the conflation of PIP with out-of-work support. I am reassured by what my right hon. Friend says, but how can we ensure that, as we move forward—we will have the White Paper in the new year and legislation at the end of next year—the support provided by PIP is not lost? We need to have support for disabled people to cover their extra costs, and it should apply to everyone of all ages.

title: Timms Review: Final Report
text: I sympathise with the hon. Lady, who is feeling so lonely on the Opposition Benches because so few of her hon. Friends are present. I am grateful to my hon. Friends for being present in such large numbers and showing real interest in this work. Once again, she has set out her familiar attack on the system with which her party left us when it left office. Let me pick up some of the points that she has made. The need to reduce the costs of welfare has been spelt out very clearly by both the Prime Minister and the Chancellor. The Government want the welfare bill to come down, but the way to do that is not through crude cuts that then just show up somewhere else in the system—and the hon. Lady has delivered a list of the crudest kind of cuts. What we recommend in the review is an entirely new assessment focused on people’s needs and the costs arising from them, unlike the current assessment, which does not ask about people’s costs at all. We will set out the implications for the cost of the whole system in the White Paper that will be published in the new year. The hon. Lady asked whether I envisage a system in which it is easier to claim. I do not believe that claiming disability benefits needs to be dehumanising, which it currently is. We want a completely new approach to assessment that, unlike the current one, is not just about what someone cannot do. We can do a better job by asking about needs as well as costs. I do not believe that the assessment needs to be a traumatising experience, which it has been for too many people under the current system. The hon. Lady made a point about face-to-face assessments, and the review says that we want more of them. She will know that, for understandable reasons, face-to-face assessments were shut down during the pandemic, and the previous Government never really restarted them. It has been down to this Government to restart face-to-face assessments. We are now up to 20% of all PIP assessments being carried out face to face—a dramatic improvement on the woeful situation left behind by the last Government—and we will continue that process. The hon. Lady is wrong to say that we are tinkering with the system. This is a fundamentally new approach to the assessment for PIP, and I commend it to the House.

title: Timms Review: Final Report
text: I thank the Minister for advance sight of his statement. What a contrast this is with last week when we gathered for the statement on the Milburn review. It was a packed Chamber— [Interruption.] It’s your review! They do not like to hear it, Madam Deputy Speaker, but I remember well that, only a week ago, the Prime Minister and the Chancellor were both here to tell the country that they finally had some kind of plan for welfare, if only for the under-25s. Today we are here to talk about their plan for sickness benefits for everyone, but the Prime Minister does not seem to have made it. After the fanfare of Milburn, all the trumpets have been muted for Timms. It is almost as if the Government were hoping that no one would notice the Minister’s statement. The Timms review had a rather inauspicious start in life. It was set up to appease Labour Back Benchers after they had floored the Government’s last attempt at welfare reform, prohibited from making savings. The Minister himself has said that the spiralling costs of PIP are “not a great concern”. I respect the right hon. Gentleman, but I have to say to him that he may not be concerned about the cost of benefits, but people out there are. They can see the bill heading up and up. PIP alone will go up to £41 billion a year under this Government, and they know that they will be left footing the bill. Worse still, the Minister’s recommendations in the round make PIP easier to get; we will see more claims and an even higher bill, as the Institute for Fiscal Studies has warned. No wonder: we know that all Labour MPs ask is, “Who can we tax to pay more in benefits?” Of course Labour Back Benchers love welfare, but can the Minister not see that to a public struggling to make ends meet and sick of a welfare system that is out of control, a plan that refuses to make savings is simply a kick in the teeth? That said, it is not all bad. We agree that PIP looks too much at what people cannot do, not at what they can, and leads people to fear that working will make them worse off. We support fast-tracking PIP for people near the end of life, and reducing onerous reassessments for people with lifelong progressive conditions. Many who claim PIP do not have extra costs, and we welcome greater scrutiny, and yes, there should be more differentiation between awards for mild and severe conditions, but can the Minister tell me what evidence of their extra costs people will be required to provide? Will this be ongoing, or a one-off check with no accountability? Will the plan to move from cash to support have teeth, or will it be nothing more than optional, and enticing, Motability-style freebies? Why is there no proposal to tackle the extraordinary growth in the number of claims for mild conditions—for mental health and ADHD? Why is there no plan to require face-to-face assessment, or to crack down on those who are gaming the system? The review has taken over a year, but all we have is a report that tinkers around the edges of a failed system, with more spending, fewer checks, and a complete absence of substance. Of course, this is not the only review in town. Last week Alan Milburn also proposed changes to the disability benefit system, based on the plans that we have set out—shifting from cash to support for milder conditions, and reducing the total amount spent on sickness benefit. Two “landmark” reviews commissioned by the Government, landing one week apart, say completely different things. The Minister has tried to make out that they fit together, and that they have much in common. Pull the other one! They may have similar diagnoses, but their proposals are poles apart. What a mess. Which side is the Prime Minister going to pick: Team Milburn or Team Timms? Or will he freeze in the headlights and avoid the argument, refuse to choose, and create a two-tier system with one rule for under-25s and another for everyone else? This is no joke. Two hundred billion pounds—that is what the working-age welfa

title: Timms Review: Final Report
text: With permission, I would like to make a statement on the final report of the Timms review of the personal independence payment. PIP provides vital support to deaf and disabled people and people with long-term health conditions. It contributes to the additional costs they face, and aims to help them to live independently, to participate in their communities and often to work. PIP was introduced 13 years ago. Since then, lots has changed, but PIP has never been fully reviewed, and it has not kept pace, so the Timms review was launched in summer last year. The review was co-produced with disabled people, the organisations that represent them and other experts. It is the first time that the UK Government have co-produced a review of this scale. I express heartfelt thanks to my two co-chairs, Sharon Brennan and Dr Clenton Farquharson, and to the 12 steering group members, whom the three of us recruited from more than 340 applicants. The group has met for a full day on 15 occasions since January, with lots of other discussions in between. The whole group has shown exemplary commitment to the task. Each of the 15 members, including me, had one vote. Almost all 12 of the steering group members had lived experience of disability or long-term ill health, as well as a range of other expertise. The review heard from more than 40,000 people and organisations, including more than 38,000 responses to the call for evidence, 138 community workshops, and evidence from clinicians, charities, deaf and disabled people’s organisations, academics, frontline practitioners and international experts. I thank everyone who shared their expertise and their experiences—often very personal ones—with us. This was an ambitious review, and it asked big, complex questions. Co-production means that every participant does not necessarily agree on every detail, but we created the conditions for people with different perspectives to test the evidence and shape the outcome as equals. The review’s report has been submitted to my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State, and the Government will now consider its findings. I will turn to the review’s central conclusion: the system is no longer fit for purpose and requires a fundamental reset. The review is clear that PIP remains a vital source of support, but it finds that the system is failing in three fundamental respects. First, the assessment is not fit for purpose. It does not consider people’s needs, aspirations, barriers or extra costs—it is just about what someone cannot do. Many find it adversarial and dehumanising. It struggles to reflect fluctuating and cumulative conditions properly, and too often it leaves people fearing that work, health treatment or greater independence will count against them. Far from supporting independence, it can be a barrier to it. Secondly, awards do not consistently enable the right contribution towards the additional costs that people face. The areas of extra cost survey, reviewed by the steering group, showed that PIP does not always target the highest levels of support at those with the most severe needs. The future system should make the basis for support clearer, with decisions better reflecting individual circumstances. Thirdly, the system offers too little scope for personalised solutions. The review recommends that cash should remain central, but that people should have the choice to access practical services as part of the overall support they receive. That would allow the system to respond more flexibly to individual needs. The review reaches the view that we need a full system reform, not just some adjustment of the form or descriptors. It does not prescribe a final set of eligibility rules, because it recognises that decisions about eligibility criteria should sit with the elected Government, accountable to this House, but it does suggest principles on which those decisions should be made. Support should correspond more closely to genuine additional costs and needs. Cu

title: Civil Service Pension Scheme
text: I am sorry to say that I do not agree. The right hon. Gentleman should look at his own party and the last Government, which signed off the levers that this Government have available. The decision taken to hand the contract over at the time was— [ Interruption. ] It was the best option on the table at the time, because of yet another poor contract that was signed by the last Government. I accept that this is a terrible situation for all scheme members. I was a prison officer, and many of my own former colleagues get in touch with me about this issue, and it absolutely needs to be resolved. However, trying to throw the blame for this issue at the current Government and not acknowledging the role of the last Government or, frankly, just focusing on getting this situation better totally misses the point. The Cabinet Office and officials are working day in, day out to improve the situation. This Government are taking steps to ensure that this issue never happens again by looking at insourcing options for the future not just for Capita, but across Government.

title: Civil Service Pension Scheme
text: On insourcing, a new unit has been set up and is working with different Departments on insourcing strategies for contracts across Government. That work is ongoing, and I know the Minister for procurement will report back on that when he is ready to update the House. On bringing the Capita contract in-house, I sympathise with the hon. Member’s position—as someone who signed up to Labour’s 2024 manifesto commitment on insourcing, it is my ideological position as well—but I do not want to do anything that will lead to further or increased disruption for scheme members. We are seeing some improvements—I will not overstate them as it is not for me to defend Capita—on, for example, complex cases coming down, phone line answering and some of the business-as-usual non-complex cases. The improvements are not enough, and I continue to hold Capita’s feet to the fire to see further performance improvements, but the scheme members have to be our priority in the coming weeks and months, to get service up to a good standard, and then we can work on what comes next.

title: Civil Service Pension Scheme
text: The private sector does not always get it right, but neither does the public sector. In this case, the private sector has gone badly wrong and is causing huge financial hardship for my constituents and for people up and down the country. I congratulate the hon. Member for Boston and Skegness (Richard Tice) on securing this urgent question and thank you, Mr Speaker, for granting it. It is concerning that a company that is clearly failing has 80 Government contracts. That should be of severe and grave concern for the Government. When contracts like this are awarded to the private sector, there clearly needs to be more competition and more choice. We should look at where the contract is given and whether it should be in the public sector. If it should, I will support it. I am not ideological. What my constituents want is delivery and—to quote the Prime Minister—pragmatism. At the moment, constituents are spending hours on the phone—60 hours in one case—quotes are wrong when they come, and payments are severely delayed, causing many people financial hardship. I will reference one constituent, Mr Mark Churm of Apley, who has given consent for me to raise his case. Many people in my constituency are suffering right now, but would the Minister please look at his case at least?

title: Civil Service Pension Scheme
text: As I have said, the performance of Capita has been totally unacceptable, and it is nothing that any public servant or anyone in this House should expect; we would not accept it among ourselves. I have had a meeting with PCS and all the other unions that represent members who have been affected by this since I came to office, and I am happy to continue having those meetings, to keep people updated on where we are. We committed in our manifesto to the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation, and sitting next to me is the Minister for procurement, my hon. Friend the Member for Gateshead Central and Whickham (Mark Ferguson), who is working on this closely across Government. My priority at the minute, as I said, is ensuring that we get pension scheme members their money as quickly as possible, and I do not want to cause any further disruption to that. I am keen to ensure that this rectification plan works, and that Cabinet Office officials and our 150-person surge team remain working with Capita on the scheme to ensure improvement as soon as possible; and then, of course, we will continue to fulfil our manifesto commitments.

title: Civil Service Pension Scheme
text: May I thank the Minister for briefing my Committee properly, and the Government for changing the tax rules on lump-sum payments within a week of my raising it in the debate on the Budget? That will provide some reassurance to pensioners in the scheme. We are about to approach the 12-month anniversary of the scheme going live. Sadly, there have been some tragic and dreadful cases in that time. I heard of one poor lady who was living on benefits because she could not get the bereavement payments she needed after her sister’s death. I have heard of a member of parliamentary staff, not far from this Chamber, who is having to delay his retirement by a year because he cannot even get a statement from the scheme. If the rectification plan does not work, what further steps can the Minister take? For understandable reasons, she does not want to discuss that in the Chamber this afternoon, but if the worst happens and, for some reason or another, Capita cannot carry out the remainder of this contract, she must have a proper contingency plan in place.

title: Civil Service Pension Scheme
text: Capita has been open and transparent with the Government, and I was given information beforehand about the problems that it faced. That is in line with the agreements we have with Capita and all strategic suppliers on transparency in all Government contracts. It gave us and the permanent secretary pre-sight of that. As it stands, the rectification plan is still in place and will continue to run. We have been very clear with Capita that we expect the foot not to be taken off the pedal and that if we are to work to support it, it needs to continue to work on the rectification plan with Cabinet Office officials and the 150-strong surge team that we have put in place. I will continue to monitor that, as will officials, and if there is any change in the level of service, I will obviously address that with Capita and return to the House to set out the next steps. Capita still has significant resources from the Government, including the 150-strong surge team, the officials that are working on this every day and anything else that we can give the company to try to bring the service back up to a decent standard. As it stands, we believe that it has the resources it needs. We will continue to monitor the situation on a daily basis, and if there appears to be any change in its ability to deliver, or in the service that it is delivering, we will of course address that immediately. In relation to the 800 cases and the McCloud remedy, as I said in my recent statement, I will make sure that I update the House on McCloud before the end of the month, and that will happen very shortly. There has been a small improvement on the complex cases. I am happy to write to or meet the Opposition spokesperson to discuss the exact numbers, because I do not have them with me, but we are updating the dashboard on a fortnightly basis, and there is an explainer on the dashboard detailing the breakdown of which complex cases have and have not been dealt with. On debarment and procurement law, as I have said before in the Chamber, I am not in a position to say which companies, suppliers or contractors may or may not be considered for debarment, but as the whole House knows, that option is now available for the Government to consider in any circumstances, and general poor performance from suppliers is something that we can consider across Government when looking at issuing new contracts, in a way that we could not previously. On contingency planning, as I said in my initial response, we work with all strategic suppliers across Government and make sure that contingency planning is in place. Part of that is having transparency with suppliers—which, up to now, we have had with Capita—to allow us to put contingency plans in place. As I think I said in oral questions last week, we have been working on contingency in relation to the pension scheme, irrespective of the announcement that was made yesterday. For all the reasons that have been discussed in this Chamber many times, it would not be appropriate for me to go into the details of that, but it is being done in line with Government policy on having contingencies in place for all contracts of this nature.

title: Civil Service Pension Scheme
text: Will the Minister tell the House when she was informed of the resignation and what assurances she has received from Capita’s incoming chief executive that October’s recovery plan will not be derailed? Given Capita’s £85 million profit warning and £25 million in extra remediation costs, is the Minister still satisfied that it has the capacity and the resources that it will need to deliver the rectification plan? Last Thursday, I reminded the Minister that she had said five weeks ago that she expected to see visible improvements over the coming weeks. She replied that there had been “small” but insufficient improvements on some “complex cases”. Can she give the House any further update? Specifically, when will the 1,800 complex cases delayed for over a year, including bereavement payments and McCloud remedy cases, finally be cleared? What further contractual penalties or payment withholdings beyond the £10 million already retained will the Government impose? Why have the Government continued to hand Capita further contracts, such as Synergy, when it was already clear that it was failing in its existing commitments to pensioners? Will the Minister now use the powers introduced by the previous Government to consider whether Capita should be debarred from future contracts as a result of its failures? Finally, will the Minister now bring forward contingency plans for use if Capita is unable to fulfil its contract or if it becomes necessary to remove the contract because of its continued failure to deliver required improvements?

title: Civil Service Pension Scheme
text: The remedial report identified that Capita did not have ready what it said it had ready when it took over the scheme. It said that it was going to have the biggest AI-enabled pension scheme ever known, and that clearly was not the case. Its performance has been abysmal, as I have said a number of times in this Chamber. I am not here to make excuses for its performance or for the position that it is now in. In relation to the future of the scheme and bringing it back in-house, it is our manifesto commitment to have the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation, and we have not moved away from that at all. My priority at this point is making sure that the service is restored as quickly as possible and that members get the pension they deserve, so I think we need to do everything we can to deliver for scheme members, and then we will look at the future of the pension scheme. As I have said before, we have officials working up different options for its future, as we are with procurement across Government in order to fulfil our manifesto commitment.

title: Civil Service Pension Scheme
text: I thank the hon. Member for bringing this important issue to the House today and for the questions that he has raised. On what has changed compared with six months ago, following the report of the remedial adviser, Grant Thornton, a new rectification plan was set up in conjunction with the Cabinet Office. Previously, Cabinet Office officials did not even have access to the Capita data and could not see for themselves what the picture was. That is now different, and we have full access to the Capita operation so that we are able to see what is happening with the civil service pension scheme. The rectification plan was built on the back of that, so I think that Members can have more confidence that transparency is there in a way that it was not before, and that we are therefore able to tackle some of the root issues. We still have nearly 150 civil servants from the surge team working with Capita. That has not changed, and it will not change until the pension scheme scenario improves. On the wider issue of contingency, the Government routinely monitor the financial health of all their strategic suppliers, particularly ones as big as Capita, and we work across Government to ensure that relevant contingencies are in place. I am not in a position to discuss that in detail in the Chamber, but that is now routine and lessons were learnt on the back of what happened with Carillion to ensure that the Government do not find themselves in that position again. Capita has up to this point been transparent with the Government and let us know what its position is. While that continues, we will work with it, but it would not be appropriate for me to go into the intricate details of the contingency planning in the Chamber now.

title: Civil Service Pension Scheme
text: Thank you, Mr Speaker, for granting this urgent question on such a critical matter. The Minister speaks well about the supposed progress, but we have been here before. On 22 April, we discussed this matter and the then Minister, the right hon. Member for Torfaen (Nick Thomas-Symonds), said all the same warm words. The sad truth is that for the 1.7 million members of the pension scheme, the situation is getting worse, not better. When Capita took over the contract, there were about 86,000 outstanding cases; there are now almost 160,000. It is worse than at the beginning of October. I have constituents who are suffering. The number of MPs in the Chamber today indicates that many have constituents who are suffering. We will hear from them, I am sure. It is not good enough, and I warned of the problems. I warned in April that the company faced a financial crisis and that the Government needed a plan B. I said then that the market value of the company was £350 million. It had debts of £500 million. Yesterday, the share price collapsed by 70%. The market value is now £75 million. The chief executive has resigned. The company talks about a rights issue of £190 million. It will be lucky. That is the reality. This company is a critical supplier to the Government. It has over 80 contracts—some £7 billion-worth—running over many, many years. They include the Ministry of Defence’s Army recruitment, Royal Navy training, the Department for Work and Pensions and NHS England. This company is too big to fail. We cannot face an equivalent of Carillion plc, but that is where this is going, and I worry. It is all very well saying that we must rely on the commercial company and the shareholders, but there is no guarantee that the shareholders will pony up. This company could well go bust in the next three months. The reality is that the Government need to have a plan B, a plan C and a plan D. That might involve ensuring that Capita can merge with another outsourcing company or underwriting the share issue, or it might have to involve taking it in-house. I look forward to the Minister’s comments.

title: Civil Service Pension Scheme
text: Before I begin my response, I declare that I have a Capita pension from the Prison Service under the civil service pension scheme. We are aware of the announcement that Capita issued to the market yesterday, including on the appointment of its new chief executive officer, Pablo Andres. The Government routinely monitor the financial health of our strategic suppliers. It would not be appropriate for us to comment on the wider commercial position of Capita as a company, as that is a commercial matter for Capita and its shareholders. Capita’s performance on the pension scheme has had unacceptable impacts on people who have dedicated years of their working lives to serving this country, and they deserve better. We are using the most stringent commercial levers, including requiring deliverable plans and withholding payments under the contract that was signed under the last Government. To hold Capita to account, we mandated that it appoint an independent remedial adviser at its own expense. The report identified many weaknesses in Capita’s rectification planning, from technology implementation to its overall ambition, which fell well short of restoring the quality services that members deserve. To address that, I agreed with Capita executives that Cabinet Office officials would work with it to develop a credible, workable and realistic recovery plan for which Capita alone will be held to account. Cabinet Office officials now have full access to Capita’s systems and data to provide us with firmer assurance of the accuracy of the management information and to allow even stronger challenge on Capita’s direction and performance. I have put in place dedicated teams to work alongside Capita to agree priorities, improve quality and processes, and ensure that pensions are paid correctly. The new recovery plan is made up of five workstreams. They cover casework across every level of complexity, major statutory exercises, including the McCloud remedy, and the underlying technology and infrastructure needed to fix delivery. Rightly, we have required Capita to prioritise the oldest cases first, tackling the root causes in those legacy cases, and that is already unblocking similar queries across the system. That is why Capita is now issuing more quotes for complex cases that are less than three months old. Simultaneously, members with complex cases are now supported by a dedicated team and a specialist helpline. For non-complex cases, including retirement quotes, we have seen some improvement and, as I announced in my recent statement, there is now a fortnightly dashboard where members can view progress. Although that is some progress, there remains a lot more to do, and there are still too many people waiting on the pensions they are owed. I will continue to hold Capita’s management team to account and apply the strongest possible commercial levers under the contract to rectify the situation for those who still have not received the service that Capita should have already delivered.

title: Representation of the People Bill
text: My Lords, this has been an interesting debate. The Minister opened her remarks by saying, “Well, you know, electors come on the local register and the electoral registration officer can have a look at that”. But that is not the point. The point is that they may come on to the local register, but the ERO needs to have the power to see whether that person is on anybody else’s register. I am delighted that Professor James from my local university has written to the Minister, because he proposed that there should be a national check and an ability for EROs across the country to co-operate in some way. He proposed a national database. The Minister says, “Well, it’s too much significant work”. I do not accept that for a moment. There are only two software providers and only one Electoral Commission. It cannot be beyond the wit of man to sort this automatically by some JSON or XML interchange format. The Government are moving fast and breaking things in this Bill, and that is fine if you are a start-up company innovating in risky areas where no one is going to miss you when you are gone. But I was very taken by the comments of the noble Lord, Lord Pack, who said that the data in our electoral system is fragile and not robust. We heard the noble Baroness, Lady Lister, who is not in her place, give a strongly anecdotal approach that belies the integrity of the system. The Government are going at breakneck speed.
