title: Representation of the People Bill
text: My Lords, I will speak to Amendments 70 and 113 to start with. I thank the noble Lord, Lord Fuller, for these amendments that seek to identify duplicate registrations and identify anyone who has voted more than once. I recognise the importance of maintaining the integrity of the electoral system. I would say to the noble Lord that Professor James did write to me, but unfortunately, I got his letter only today, so I have not had time yet to properly respond to his email. For people who do not know, he is the co-director of the Electoral Integrity Project and Professor of Politics and Public Policy at the University of East Anglia. He certainly knows how to attract the attention of a Minister; he started off his email to me: “I would like to congratulate the Government on the important work made towards developing a historic Bill which will improve the quality of elections in the UK”. So, thank you, Professor James; I will be responding to his email. However, a number of aspects of the noble Lord’s amendment are either already in place as part of the Bill and existing legislation or currently not possible to achieve. The Bill already includes a measure which requires electoral registration officers to establish that a person is not already on their register before commencing the process of registering them without an application. Under existing legislation, EROs have legal duties to publish registers once a month and to keep their registers as accurate as possible. Electoral Commission guidance encourages EROs to take a proactive approach throughout the year and not just during canvass or election periods. Through the Bill and other work under way, we are exploring a range of further options to ensure that individuals are accurately registered. It is too early at this stage to legislate for any specific further approach to the issue of duplicate registrations as outlined by the noble Lord. Since there is currently no single register, there is also no straightforward way for an ERO to determine whether an individual is on another ERO’s register without creating unsustainable, significant additional work for EROs. The Government do not hold electoral registration data. Electoral registers are maintained by local authority electoral registration officers. There is no centrally held data on individuals’ voting patterns nor on specific electoral offences. Data on allegations and outcomes of electoral fraud is recorded by police forces across the UK and provided to the Electoral Commission. The Electoral Commission publishes this information annually on its website in the section titled “Research, reports and data”. Of course, the Government continue to work closely with the Electoral Commission, the police, and other partners to safeguard the integrity of elections and maintain public confidence in the democratic process. It is also important to state, as the noble Lord and others know, that individuals are entitled to register to vote at more than one address where they are resident at both addresses—the noble Lord gave the example of students entitled to register at a term-time address and a home address—but it remains a criminal offence to vote more than once in the same election; for example, in the UK parliamentary election or in a specific local election. The Government continue to work closely with the Electoral Commission, the police and others to safeguard the integrity of elections, and it is for those reasons that I would ask the noble Lord not to press his amendments. I thank the noble Lord, Lord Pack, for his Amendments 109, 110, 114, 115 and 116, which seek to amend Clause 50 so that the Electoral Commission may give directions requiring officers to provide information. The Government support the principle of making election information easier for the public to access and understand. While we are aligned on the objective of the amendment, I do not believe that it is necessary. The Government are working to ensure that r

title: Representation of the People Bill
text: My Lords, I thank noble Lords for their contributions to this debate, which has raised some important questions about the collection of electoral information, the integrity of our registers and the responsibilities of the Electoral Commission. I am grateful to the noble Lord, Lord Jackson of Peterborough, for raising the point that we may be somewhat more interested in the minutiae than the public are. The definition of “need” is an important one, so I will caveat my comments with that in the back of my mind. Amendments 70 and 113, tabled by my noble friend Lord Fuller, seek to strengthen the safeguards against duplicate registrations and multiple voting, both of which are important to maintaining the integrity of, and confidence in, our elections. Amendment 70 proposes a unique identification number for each voter registration. Amendment 113 seeks to identify electors who may have registered or voted more than once. These are legitimate concerns, particularly given the Government’s proposal for automatic voter registration. We on these Benches have consistently questioned whether automatic registration will produce sufficiently accurate electoral registers, particularly where individuals have moved address or are registered at more than one location. Can the Minister explain what mechanisms exist to identify duplicate registration across local authority boundaries? Have the Government assessed whether their proposals for automatic registration risk increasing inaccuracies? How would they distinguish between multiple registrations and unlawful multiple voting, intentional or otherwise? There are also concerns surrounding the safeguarding of data. I hope that the Government can explain how any additional collection of personal information would be appropriately protected. I turn to Amendment 111, tabled by the noble Lord, Lord Pack, my noble friend Lord Jackson of Peterborough and the noble Baroness, Lady Pinnock. I recognise the importance of the reliability of electoral statistics. However, much of the information covered by this amendment is already collected through existing electoral processes—although the noble Lord, Lord Pack, has just raised the point that it may be collected but may not be readily available. The two are not quite the same. Before creating further reporting requirements, we should establish what information is genuinely missing and whether additional obligations would improve electoral administration. Can the Minister clarify what information is not currently available to the Electoral Commission and whether the election officers have been consulted on the practical implications of collecting it? Amendment 112, in the names of the noble Lord, Lord Rennard, and the noble Baroness, Lady Pinnock, concerns postal voting information. I have a slight query on this. The amendment requests information on returns. I want to be clear that this also covers the sending of postal ballots and the timing of those postal ballots. I thought that was the case, but I wanted to check. As I said on group 1, there is a serious issue here, particularly for overseas electors. The Electoral Commission’s assessment of the 2024 general election found that only around half of overseas postal ballots were returned in time to be counted. That represents a genuine obstacle to democratic participation, yet this Bill does remarkably little to address it. Can the Minister explain how the proposed information would translate into practical improvements for overseas electors, rather than producing further statistics about an already well-established problem? Finally, Amendments 109, 110, 114 and 116, tabled by the noble Lord, Lord Pack, seek to replace the Secretary of State’s regulation-making powers with directions issued by the Electoral Commission. I have considerable reservations about this approach. The Electoral Commission performs an important independent role, but independence must be accompanied by proper accountability. We on t

title: Representation of the People Bill
text: My Lords, I will concentrate mainly on the amendments in my name in this group. As I have quite often disagreed with the noble Lord, Lord Fuller, so far in Committee, I should first acknowledge that his amendment and his speech just now make some very pertinent points, in particular the fact that there are, in effect, as I believe the noble Lord mentioned, only two suppliers of electoral management software to councils around the country. There is some scope to at least move in the right direction, even if not to get to the full data cross-checking nirvana that the noble Lord, Lord Fuller, set out for us. I will listen with interest to the Minister’s response on that. My Amendments 109 and 110 are really about the ability of the Electoral Commission and other internal organisations to provide information to the public about elections and to run helpful online services. As currently drafted, the Bill would use the statutory instrument process to enable the Electoral Commission to get the information it needs. But the statutory instrument process is relatively slow and clunky, as I have mentioned on other occasions. So, often, the reason that a statutory instrument does not come through sooner is that the Government explain what a lengthy process it is to get a statutory instrument through the whole process and what limited drafting capability there is. Therefore, there is a real risk that the statutory instrument process acts as a major bottleneck, particularly when there are changing requirements for data that the Electoral Commission may decide that it needs, perhaps particularly in the event of an unexpectedly early election. There is, though, an available model, which is in place and functioning successfully, that we can learn from: the model in use in Wales. Under the Elections and Elected Bodies (Wales) Act 2024, the Democracy and Boundary Commission Cymru has the power to issue directions to require returning officers to provide it with the analogous information, and that does not require secondary legislation. I hope the Government will see the merit of adapting that system to use in this Bill. As well as making the gathering of relevant data easier and more efficient, it would reduce the workload in the statutory instrument bottleneck, which would be a nice little bonus for the Whitehall policy machine. Amendment 111 would expand the data possibilities so that we can more easily ensure that some of the basic facts about how elections have been conducted and what the outcomes have been are properly gathered and preserved for the future. It is quite remarkable how quickly even relatively basic bits of information become fragmented and then lost from the historical record. You might think it is reasonable that it is difficult to figure out what the turnout was in, say, a particular council by-election way back in the 19th century, but actually one has to go back only a few years for those figures to often be quite difficult to unearth. We have a surprisingly fragile data record. Therefore, Amendment 111 and, indeed, Amendment 112—as my noble friend Lady Pinnock so eloquently set out—would ensure that more data is available and that it is more robust and more easily preserved for the future. Crucially, therefore, there will be a much stronger statistical and evidential base to underpin our debates on these Bills in the years and decades to come. In the end, while having better evidence cannot resolve all differences of opinion, it can certainly ensure that differences of opinion are expressed in more robust ways and lead to better decision-making in the end.

title: Representation of the People Bill
text: My Lords, Clause 50 is a positive change, as it enables evidence of engagement in the electoral process to be analysed and considered. Amendments 111 and 112 seek to expand the evidence collected to enable a deeper understanding of whether the election process is effective in a healthy democracy. I will speak largely on Amendment 112, in the name of my noble friend Lord Rennard, to which I added my name. It focuses on the administration and integrity of postal voting. As reliance on postal voting continues to grow, public confidence depends on complete visibility surrounding the dispatch, delivery and return of postal ballots. Amendment 112 would explicitly add key postal vote tracking metrics to the regulations in Clause 50, which include the total number of postal ballots issued; the number of postal ballots delivered before or on polling day versus those delivered after polling day; and detailed timing on when postal votes are provided and when postal vote arrangements expire. When voters request and return a postal ballot in good faith, they deserve to know that the administrative system is working efficiently. Tracking the precise volume of postal votes arriving after the polling deadline is essential for identifying postal bottlenecks and preventing voters being inadvertently disfranchised due to postal delivery delays. The reliance on Royal Mail for a significant proportion of votes cast is increasingly a potential problem—hence I have tabled an amendment in a later group to consider setting explicit days when postal ballots are sent to Royal Mail. In a recent election in my area, I received calls from concerned voters who had not received their ballot papers. In the end, the elections office travelled across the council district providing tendered ballots—an alternative type of ballot—which could be submitted on the day. It would counter the purpose of a postal vote, but at least it was an effort to ensure that people were not disfranchised. The unreliability of the postal service has resulted in elections officers sending the postal vote ballot papers to Royal Mail sometimes as much as three weeks before election day. This has a profound impact on candidates campaigning and creates a situation where there are, in effect, two polling days. The information in Amendment 112 is critical to understanding the effectiveness of the postal vote system, and I urge the Minister to accept it.

title: Representation of the People Bill
text: My Lords, like a number of my other amendments to the Bill, my Amendment 70 seeks to ensure the integrity of the electoral register by empowering the Electoral Commission with the statutory tools and data to identify two types of fraud—fraud that undermines the integrity of the elections upon which our democracy depends. I am concerned not only about intentional fraud but about innocent and accidental duplicates—people with more than one name, perhaps for all the right reasons. The ERO registers the same person twice, perhaps with the name Robert and again with the name Bob, or with a passport name rather than the commonly used name. My own father-in-law was known as Derek, but his given name was Clifford—that is just one example. For all the duplicates and additions, I do not see a reliable, practical mechanism to remove these artefacts when someone moves house and becomes ineligible, especially if they did not realise they had been added to the database in the first place. There will certainly be cases of duplication, but there is no method of practically identifying them for removal. That is why my amendment would require the voter registration process to be accompanied by a unique reference number, principally the national insurance number but regulations could also specify others, so that on a national basis we can conduct some sort of pre-match and post-match election analysis for duplicated entries on the register and for duplicate votes at a polling station. Do not misunderstand me: I am not suggesting that this unique number is presented, checked or validated at the polling station or on the postal vote ballot. There are other safeguards there, and I certainly do not—to go to the previous group—suggest that we have credit checks at the polling station either. I am not suggesting that the number should be part of any public register. But if we are concerned about the integrity of the register—and the Bill adds lots of opportunities for multiple and slightly different registrations of the same person, along with the temptation to use those twice—now is the time to legislate for the security, providing the powers and the data for the Electoral Commission to deduplicate. My Amendment 113 would permit and set the expectation that the Electoral Commission would conduct post-election research to determine how many unique individuals registered to vote more than once. More importantly, it would identify those who voted more than once when they were not entitled to. Multiple registrations are not a remote possibility. They are a certainty, made worse by hard-to-spell names or phonetic homophones. There are no controls at present to prevent somebody who is registered in two constituencies or two electoral registration areas—a district council, for example—voting twice in multiple locations, either by post or proxy in one or by travelling between the constituencies on election day. We know from social media that many students have performed this ruse. It is for Parliament to remove the temptation for students, who bragged about the fact that they voted twice in the 2017 election, particularly by using a postal or proxy form at the home address and then in person in the university constituency. I know this because, after that election, the Electoral Commission was forced to set out the offence, under Section 61(2)(a) of the Representation of the People Act 1983, for an elector to cast more than one vote on their own behalf in a UK parliamentary election or referendum. It reminded voters that the offence carries a fine, which is unlimited in England and Wales while not exceeding £5,000 in Scotland. In that post-election report, it regretted that there were no specific controls to prevent someone registered in two constituencies voting in each, because the electoral registers are held at the local level by the EROs appointed by each local authority in Great Britain, and by the Chief Electoral Officer for Northern Ireland. There is

title: Representation of the People Bill
text: The noble Lord should not worry about it. It has been another scintillating debate; it has taken us to 10 o’clock. We have been on this issue for over an hour now. I will get straight into it, on Amendment 68, which touches on the important issue of voter participation. The Government are committed to encouraging participation in our democracy and ensuring that every eligible elector is able to vote. This is why we are undertaking a broad programme of action to remove barriers to participation and support democratic engagement. We are investing £2.5 million through the democratic engagement fund in politically neutral, place-based projects, including work to understand our hardest-to-reach groups and communities that have historically participated less. Through this Bill, we are also laying the foundations for more automated voter registration to address the Electoral Commission’s estimate that between 7 million and 8 million eligible people are either incorrectly registered or missing from the register altogether. We are widening the forms of voter ID accepted at polling stations so that the proportion of people without accepted voter ID falls from between 2% and 4% to less than 1%. We are also extending the franchise to roughly 1.7 million 16 and 17 year-olds, improving democratic education and testing flexible voting options, such as early voting and central voting hubs. Taken together, these measures should significantly strengthen participation and engagement. It is important that we allow them to take effect and assess their impact before reaching conclusions about whether future measures might be required. For this reason, the Government believe that the proposals required by this amendment are premature, and I ask my noble friend to withdraw her amendment.

title: Representation of the People Bill
text: My Lords, this has been an interesting group, and I genuinely thank all noble Lords who have participated in it. I have certainly learned far more about statistical analysis of disproportionality and so forth than I knew when I started the day. I will start with Amendment 68 in the name of the noble Baroness, Lady Royall of Blaisdon. She will not be entirely surprised that I am not particularly supportive of compulsory voting. This is a fundamental issue of democracy. Democracy is the right to choose, and one of those rights to choose is the right to choose not to vote. I find myself in agreement on this with the noble Lord, Lord Wallace of Saltaire. I agree with him that you then need to think about the second order effects, such as registration. How many people will seek to not be registered simply because they do not want to receive a £10 fine, or whatever it ends up being? As my noble friend Lord Parkinson of Whitley Bay pointed out, I do not see non-voters as people to be ignored; I see them as fertile ground that we should actively go out and seek to convert to the right way, so to speak. I am sure other parties have their own version of the “right way”. We should not ignore non-voters, and I think most parties do not ignore them. It is a lot easier to convert somebody who has no opinion than one who has a very firm opinion that is contrary to one’s own. The very sensible amendment from my noble friend Lord Parkinson of Whitley Bay develops this concept of compulsory voting, because if we are going to have it for one form of democracy, surely we should have it for all forms of democracy. I do not need to go further on what my noble friend said, but compulsory voting would quite clearly make a little bit of a nonsense of the operation of both our Houses if it were to be the case all the time. It would stop many of us going out and doing many of the things that are so important, such as listening to our current or former voters—in my case, I will have voters until May, when I will stand down from my local council. This principle is very important. If we are going to impose compulsory voting on the public, surely we should be bound to it ourselves. I agree with the noble Baroness, Lady Fox—another person I agree with. Abstaining is a choice, and we need to inspire people. As the noble Lord, Lord Hayward, said, the last election had low turnout because of a negative opinion. We need to do more to give people a positive opinion of politics. I tend to disagree with Amendment 121 in the name of the noble Baroness, Lady Royall of Blaisdon. Having been at many counts, I find it quite interesting when we come to look at the spoiled ballot papers. Some noble Lords may know who my local MP was. I remember the last memorable occasion when she was elected, when she had to review a very large number of spoiled ballot papers. I certainly think she got the opinion of certain people within her constituency. I think that is important. It is always surprising to me, when I knock on doors and tell people that it is a really good thing to vote and that, if they do not like any of us, they have the option of spoiling their ballot paper—and, by the way, I will be one of the people who will be reviewing that spoiled ballot paper in my name, and I will see their opinion, even if I do not know who that opinion is from, obviously, because of confidentiality. Surprisingly, that enthuses quite a few people to come out and express their opinion. I cannot quite remember which Member mentioned pictorial diagrams, but I have seen one or two of those as well—not addressed to me, I hasten to add. I move on to Amendment 251—and I commend the noble Lord, Lord Pack, on how he has managed to squeeze a review of the electoral system into this Bill. I find myself agreeing with half of his proposals. I think that this Bill and its effects need a review; there needs to be a check to ensure that it has been thoroughly prepared and thought through, which, as the Min

title: Representation of the People Bill
text: Mindful of the time, I will not duplicate the wise words of my noble friend Lord Wallace in his genial scepticism about the merits of compulsory voting, but I want to put on record my admiration for the ingenuity of the amendment from the noble Lord, Lord Parkinson, on that topic. On the subject of “none of the above”, the ability to spoil your ballot paper is an important right that should be preserved. However, democracy—and indeed governing—is about having to choose between the options on offer, and not always wishing and thinking, “If I just put it off one more day, will some magic, perfect solution arise?” While I respect the ability of people, if they wish, to draw parts of the human anatomy on their ballot paper and spoil it, I think it would be a mistake to go further and positively encourage opting out of the choice between the available options that is an essential part of democracy. I am rather more enthusiastic, of course, about proportional representation. I am very tempted to rise to the request of the noble Lord, Lord Parkinson, for a detailed and lengthy lecture on the merits of the three different measures of disproportionality set out in the amendment in my name and the names of other noble Lords. I suspect, however, I may lose some noble Lords’ attention during that. I will therefore briefly say that, perhaps not surprisingly, I am especially attracted to the Sainte-Laguë method of measuring disproportionality, given the importance it places on disproportionality for very small parties. If you are a party that wins five seats but should have won 15, those missing 10 matter much more than if you are a party that, let us say, won a landslide with 400 and should have had 410. I am very happy to continue the discussion in more detail, perhaps over a cup of coffee in the Long Room, with the noble Lord. More generally, it is worth reflecting on how the last 15 or 20 years have seen first past the post fail to deliver even what its own supporters have argued as being its important merits. We have not seen repeated stable Governments and clear election results; we have repeatedly seen the exact opposite of that. First past the post is not delivering on its own professed merits. The noble Baroness, Lady Pinnock, made some very similar apposite points about how first past the post is failing to work well at local government level, and she picked up the example of a council ward result in which the winner polled under 20%. I always feel a little sorry for the winner, Councillor Steven Webb, who is the most amazing individual. At 18, he had a horrible and tragic accident in a swimming pool that left him paralysed. The number of things he has achieved in life since then, including becoming mayor of his local town and carrying out a 500-mile charity fundraising drive, means I always feel a little sorry for him when he is acknowledged only as being a person who won a remarkably low share of the vote. He has achieved so much in life, and I want to put that on record. Returning to this question about electoral systems, the Prime Minister, with his promise of a national commission and a national conversation on electoral reform, has, to his credit, recognised that our electoral systems are not working in the way we need them to work. However, so far all we have had are some fairly scattered and, at times, contradictory press briefings by unnamed individuals as to when the national commission might happen and what its remit and membership might be. I hope this amendment provides an opportunity to get a little bit of a move on, because, after all, the Prime Minister is understandably talking up the merits of growth in every postcode. Perhaps we should also have a competitive democracy in every postcode.

title: Representation of the People Bill
text: My Lords, I will just make one or two quick observations. A number of noble Lords have commented on turnout. I quote again from the Electoral Commission’s report on the general election in 2024, released this year: “Turnout fell significantly at this election … While this can be due to several factors, we continue to find that negative perceptions of party politics and politicians contribute to people’s decisions not to vote”. There is a very clear message there to all of us and to the Members of the other Chamber: that is what drove the substantial decline in turnout. It is not the sole factor, as the Electoral Commission identified, but we have to be honest about where we are in British politics. My other brief observation is in relation to all the alternative systems. We could debate these for hours, days or weeks probably. The one thing I would say to people is: please, do not be perceived as changing the voting system to stop one particular political party being represented in either Chamber. If there is one thing that will guarantee the sorts of things the noble Baroness, Lady Fox, referred to, it is telling the disenfranchised that they will be continuously disenfranchised. That is the worst possible message we can send to anybody.

title: Representation of the People Bill
text: My Lords, I am delighted to follow the noble Baroness, Lady Lawlor. She made some excellent points and I agree with her completely in respecting the aims of the amendments looking at voting systems, both on compulsory voting and on PR voting. I have a lot of regard for the notion of better political engagement and making voting more meaningful. That is what is at the heart of the Bill and what I think the Government are trying to get at. That is far more positive, at least in spirit, than a rather more regressive contemporary trend, which is to put caveats on certain types of people voting. I draw the Committee’s attention to a shocking report that came out this week, What Britain’s New Establishment Thinks A nd Why I t Matters , in which 1,000 higher professionals were polled. Half of them think that the general public should pass a civic responsibility test before getting a vote; mind you, 61% of the same group think that important decisions should be made by experts rather than elected politicians. That would probably be popular here but not with the public, so there we go. It reminded me, though, of those grim days post 2016, when a particular type of remainer—a sore loser, to say the least—started to complain that leave voters were uneducated, stupid or ignorant and did not have enough qualifications to be trusted ever again. I remember those days bitterly. The slurs, smears and insults were aimed largely at working-class voters—indeed, many millions of Labour voters—who were demonised by elite politicians from all parties for voting the wrong way. This top-down contempt for democratic engagement is ironic, because it came when we had just seen the greatest and most vibrant display of engagement. The specific proposals on compulsory voting are supported by some heavy hitters—the noble Baroness, Lady Royall, and the noble Lords, Lord Foulkes, Lord Kinnock and Lord Blunkett. While I want to support the spirit of all this and better engagement, I do not think this will solve the situation. It will not work and will have the opposite effect. It is worth noting that voting has historically been a hard-won right, if maybe not for 16 and 17 year-olds. To turn it into a compelled legal duty really would undermine individual autonomy and liberty. When compulsory voting is presented as a way of increasing political engagement, it assumes that not voting is an expression of apathy or a lack of engagement. Instead, the freedom to abstain can sometimes be an active political statement of dissatisfaction at the state of political parties on offer. All that compulsory voting would do is mask rather than solve problems of engagement or reasons for a lack of legitimacy expressed by a low turnout. I think that issues such as first past the post voting, the safe seats issue, tactical voting against rather than for certain parties, et cetera, can make citizens feel disenfranchised, so much so that they conclude, “What’s the point in voting?” In that sense, the discussion around the proportional representation amendments cannot be dismissed and needs to be considered. It is ironic, in this week of all weeks, that we are discussing the problems of turnout and engagement, because there was an example of a huge turnout in 2016: for the referendum about whether to remain in or to leave the EU. Voters were assured, for that hugely important constitutional decision, that historic moment, that, for once, each and every vote would count—that is why first past the post is problematic for me. Millions of ordinary people rose to that challenge. They were involved in debates and discussions. There was huge engagement everywhere you went. Democratic life really took off during that time. As we know, it led to the largest democratic exercise in the UK’s history. For those who want to increase engagement, I would take lessons from that. The answer is not to force people to put an X on a ballot paper or to reduce it to something technocratic; it is to inspir

title: Representation of the People Bill
text: My Lords, Amendment 68 from the noble Baroness, Lady Royall, would require the Secretary of State to introduce compulsory voting. I understand that the aim—which noble Lords on the other side of the Committee have explained—is to combat inequality, increase participation and all kinds of things that are good aims in themselves, but it raises a problem about the secrecy of the ballot. Compulsory voting would need enforcement. I understand that the other amendment in the noble Baroness’s name suggests that one could have an option saying “none of these options”, but that does not combat the problem of enforcing. How does one enforce whether a vote was made if there is to be secrecy of the ballot? There must be some way of tracing if we are to enforce a requirement to vote that is compulsory under law. It also raises other problems—questions of choice, tradition and freedom in a democracy, particularly characterised in this democracy. As my noble friend has said, people may have other interests. Indeed, the Minister almost defined some of us who stay up late to watch election results as political geeks—almost as a group outside the mainstream. That is a legitimate choice that people make. They may have no interest in elections; they may be busy or working late; they may miss the polling; they may choose to get their job finished before they get home. All these things happen—or they may simply not be interested in what is on offer. Even with the dramatic win of the party opposite in 2024, we cannot forget that in terms of attracting a wide turnout, only 59.7% of the electorate turned out. It is not fair to oblige the rest of the electorate to come out to vote if they are not enthusiastic about what is on offer. Maybe we should be talking about how to interest voters and make what we offer in a manifesto relevant and important to the things that matter to them, whether it is the cost of living, rising immigration or all kinds of other things that upset voters. I close by simply saying that we should pay attention to some of the great characteristics of this democracy. It has endured and been persistent when other democracies in states as old as ours—unitary democracies, such as France—have suffered interruption and invasion. Britain’s democracy has survived on the basis that whatever the problems of the day, there was choice, the freedom to vote—not the compulsion—and a respect for people’s wishes.

title: Representation of the People Bill
text: My Lords, I cannot resist arguing against Amendment 269, which I oppose in every sense of the word. As somebody who has worked in the City of London for much of my life, I have never been involved with the governance of the City of London, but I have worked there, I have seen it and I know how it operates. I just do not think that the noble Baroness, Lady Bennett of Manor Castle, has a full appreciation that this is not a local authority like other local authorities; it is something utterly different. On national economic security, it serves as a police authority. It plays a national lead in tackling fraud, cyber crime and economic crime. This sort of work has to be done by somebody, and much of it is funded by the businesses in the City of London. For example, insurance fraud enforcement is funded largely by the insurance industry. The dedicated card and payment crime unit is paid for largely by the banks. Furthermore, through the business rate premium, businesses in the City make an additional contribution towards policing and security within the square mile, which welcomes millions of international workers and tourists annually. Does the Minister agree that these voting businesses have a legitimate interest in the governance of the institution to which they make such a nationally significant and valuable contribution, and that the national economic security of the United Kingdom is good enough reason alone to protect and maintain the status quo? Secondly, noble Lords should understand that, on international trade and investment, the City today continues to be the driver and engine of economic growth nationally, especially when it comes to attracting inward investment and championing British commercial interest. Each year, the City generates over £113 billion of economic output. The corporation’s close relationship with the businesses of the square mile is central to the work. I put it to your Lordships that, however well intended this amendment, to vote in favour of it would be to significantly undermine our national economic and growth interests. It is also worth highlighting that the corporation collects £1.6 billion in business rates, the vast majority of which is passed to the Treasury for redistribution under the national funding arrangements. The success of businesses in the City therefore makes a significant contribution to public services right across the country. In addition, the corporation pays for the London Port Health Authority, the Heathrow Animal Reception Centre and the Central Criminal Court—the Old Bailey. These massive institutions are funded by an organisation that is not like any other local authority. The amendment also fails to grasp the fact that this exceptional institution has an exceptional and significant national responsibility, and that needs to be recognised.

title: Representation of the People Bill
text: My Lords, I will speak mainly to Amendment 251 in the names of my noble friends Lord Pack and Lord Wallace, which asks the Government to think about the efficacy of the different voting systems that are already in use across the nations of the UK. So far, the debate has focused entirely on parliamentary elections, but local elections are also affected by this Bill. As noble Lords know, the four nations of the UK use different voting systems in their local elections. Scotland and Northern Ireland use single transferable vote, and England and Wales retain the first past the post system. First past the post worked reasonably well when there were three, sometimes just two, political parties contesting elections. But, as more political parties are joining the fray, so there are frequently five or even six or seven candidates—a local election in Kirklees last May had eight nominated candidates—it suddenly becomes more of a lottery. For example, in the 2025 local elections, a candidate in Truro won the election with just 18.9% of the votes cast. In the same year, none of the winners of the mayoral elections, which were being held under first past the post, recorded more than 50% of the vote. The Mayor of the West of England was elected with just 25% of the votes cast. First past the post is at breaking point in local elections, if it has not already broken. Five years ago, just over 60% of winning candidates in local elections had an overall majority. In 2025, it was just 16%. That is a reflection of the greater number of candidates in each election. That is one of the reasons that voters feel that their voice is not being heard, and apathy then ensues. The fall in turnout in elections generally, particularly in general elections, is a cause for concern. A healthy democracy depends on good turnout. Amendment 68, in the name of the noble Baroness, Lady Royall, proposes compulsory voting as an answer. I am not convinced by that solution. Voters need a reason to vote. Part of the solution is to adopt a voting system that gives individual voters a realistic expectation that their vote will make a difference to the outcome of an election. That is why a move away from first past the post is important. Just as important, though, is that voters have justified reasons to expect change. In local elections, local flexibility has been largely removed. The tight budgets of councils spent mainly on statutory services have reduced the scope for local initiatives. The cabinet system, enabling just 10 councillors or fewer to make all the decisions on behalf of the whole council, means that half or more of councillors’ views are never taken into account when decisions are made. For a healthier local democracy, issues of local flexibility need to be urgently addressed. The recent planning changes, which I debated with the Minister, will result in even controversial applications being decided not by those elected to make decisions but by planning officers. This will remove a significant area of local voice in decisions which affect neighbourhoods. A vibrant, healthy democracy depends on an expectation by voters that their vote can have an impact. The current voting system, with a plethora of political parties, cannot deliver that for voters. Equally, much more needs to be done to remove the centralised grip on councils to enable them to have the flexibility to respond to local needs.

title: Representation of the People Bill
text: My Lords, it is a great pleasure to follow the noble Lord, Lord Wallace, and point out to him that people have been saying for a long time that proportional representation is never going to happen, but I think it is now closer than ever before. It is a pleasure to take part in this really interesting and important group. I have to begin by telling the noble Lord to my right—the noble Lord, Lord Parkinson—that every Green Party election already delivers what he is asking for in his amendment. We do not call it “none of the above”; we have RON—reopen nominations. That is on every Green Party ballot paper, and I think it is a good idea. It is generally known as RON, and lots of jokes are made about the character of RON. I have seen RON win once or twice, but not very often. Talking about votes in your Lordships’ House, if the noble Lord would like to talk to me later about the idea of approaching the powers that be about a provision for recording a deliberate abstention, that would actually be a useful provision that would add to the democracy of the House—indeed, I would suggest the other place as well. Briefly, the noble Baroness, Lady Royall, talked about compulsory voting. My accent gives away the fact that I have some experience of this. However, my personal view is that I am not in favour of compulsory voting, because I do not believe that the problem with our current system is the voters. The problem is the system, as the noble Lord, Lord Wallace, outlined, with 33% of the vote delivering a massive majority in the Commons, and the nature of politics that people have been offered. That relates to the voting system, as people vote for the party they dislike second-most to stop the people they dislike most getting in. I will focus on my Amendment 269. I am starting here a mirror image of the debate we had on day 1 in Committee on Amendment 5, in the name of the noble Lord, Lord Frost, which sought to standardise all franchise arrangements on these islands, with the exception of the City of London Corporation. This amendment seeks to regularise and democratise just the City of London franchise, which is a one-off standout unlike any other on these islands, and to deliver, very belatedly, one person, one vote for the City, and to finally, after centuries of incremental and occasionally sweeping electoral reform, rid the country of its last rotten borough. I declare a kind of interest, in that I am working with the APPG on Investment Fraud and Fairer Financial Services on a public survey asking the simple question: should the corporation be left as it is, fundamentally reformed or abolished? That is an unbiased survey open to all, but I in no way hide my own long-held position, which is that this last rotten borough should be done away with. Electoral reforms finished in 1948 in abolishing all forms of plural and business voting, except for the City of London Corporation. Under the Attlee Government, the City also stopped having its own MP, which it had up until then; until 1885, it was four MPs. For the parliamentary elections then, the City was merged into the seat of the Cities of London and Westminster. Here are some facts not very widely known, including to many of the people affected. The City has a two-chambered structure with aldermen elected in ones and twos throughout the year, and a common council elected every four years in mid-March; the latest election was in 2025. There are also lord mayor and sheriff elections for which the franchise is the Common Hall Register of Liverymen. I understand if your Lordships’ Committee feels that it has gone back five or six centuries in a time machine, but I will park those for the moment as they are not covered by the amendment.

title: Russia's own figures show it has lost nearly 500,000 people in Ukraine war
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East US & Canada Russia's own figures show it has lost nearly 500,000 people in Ukraine war Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Russia does not provide numbers of its fallen soldiers At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC. The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old. BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow. Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday that only Russia's defence ministry could officially report data on losses: "I suggest no other data be taken into account." The defence ministry has not released any official casualty figures for several years. Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records. Military experts estimate that the BBC's list of 290,012 deaths, gleaned from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll, which would range from 527,295 to 644,471. The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict. The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000. During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there. Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses. For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army were accounted for in the Rosstat files. Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count. Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952. The Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death. We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army. Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations. text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East US & Canada My family were killed in Ukraine. My mum blamed Zelensky's troops - the truth is complicated To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Watch: BBC reporter investigates deaths of family members in Russia-Ukraine war I am sitting on my balcony in Kyiv looking at a photo of a garden in the village I grew up in, in eastern Ukraine. The plot is overgrown with thick grass, and two wooden stakes are planted in the ground. Despite the warm sunshine, I find myself shivering. The woman who sent me the photo says the stakes mark the graves of my grandparents, killed as the Ukrainian-Russian front line reached our little community. Not far away, in another garden in the village, the body of my father, Serezha, is buried in a greenhouse. Image caption, The photo Anastasiya was sent of her grandparents' graves I cover the Russia-Ukraine war for the BBC World Service, but found myself in the middle of that story in February last year when my mother sent me a devastating text message. "Granny, grandad and Serezha are gone. Now there is no-one left," it said. Because not only had I lost three beloved family members, my mother blamed Ukraine for their deaths - the country where I was born and have lived for most of my life. Mum was born in Siberia. From the moment Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, she had supported Russia in the conflict. Image source, Gribanova family handout Image caption, Anastasiya (bottom left) with her father (top left) and grandparents (right) before the war Backing Moscow is not that unusual in the Donbas region - the predominantly Russian-speaking part of eastern Ukraine where my village Dachne is located. After pro-Russian forces captured large parts of the Donbas in 2014, many of those who stayed supported Moscow over Kyiv, a stance cemented by exposure to Russian state TV. Now the Russians occupy almost 80% of Donetsk - the part of the Donbas where my village is. Over the past nearly five years, since Russia's full-scale invasion, entire towns and cities have been razed to the ground , external . Image source, Ukraine's 33rd Mechanised Brigade Image caption, The remains of Anastasiya's family home are circled in a frame of a video, filmed by Ukraine's 33rd Mechanised Brigade on 27 January 2025 I had already fallen out with my sister Sasha, who had been living in Moscow with her young family when the war broke out. She refused to take sides - I felt hurt and cut her off. But earlier this year, around the first anniversary of dad's death, Sasha unexpectedly texted me. We started talking over text about our childhood - the way things used to be. I realised I was not angry with her anymore. She too was grieving, missing dad just as much as I was. Image source, Aleksandra Gribanova Image caption, Anastasiya's father Serezha - he stayed in Dachne to look after his elderly parents I told her I wanted to make a documentary about dad and she was very supportive. I knew then that I had an ally on my journey. But we decided not to tell our mum just yet. I started looking for witnesses to the events in Dachne that took place in January 2025, the month dad is believed to have been killed. It was not easy. title: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Business New Tech Economy Technology of Business Artificial Intelligence Africa Business Paths to Success US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation. Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about US President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback. Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Asked several times on Tuesday whether the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about." Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged spy who previously ran Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia. Trump has said he would consider pardoning Huang for any potential criminal activity, though he does not think it will come to that. "It's always an option, I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary," Trump told the New York Post in an interview published on Tuesday. With Huang rescue, Trump riskily ties his political fortunes to Nvidia Published 13 hours ago The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The commerce and justice departments said last week that they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations" . But Blanche told reporters on Tuesday that the latter had "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time. "So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said. Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with inquiries into whether it or Huang knew about chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen. "Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people. While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading. The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return. Huang reportedly apologised to Nvidia employees on Tuesday, the day after returning to the company as chief executive, saying he had made "terrible mistakes" and was now receiving daily 90-minute therapy sessions. title: Close-up images to be revealed of asteroid deliberately hit to test ability to protect Earth
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Science Close-up images to be revealed of asteroid deliberately hit to test ability to protect Earth Image source, ESA Image caption, The Hera spacecraft will study the 150m-wide (490ft) asteroid called Dimorphos Pictures will be released later of damage to an asteroid that was deliberately hit with a spacecraft four years ago as part of a test of Earth's defences. In what may sound like the plot of a disaster movie, Nasa's Dart spacecraft smashed into the space rock in 2022 to knock it slightly off course. The Nasa craft was obliterated on impact. Now, a European Space Agency (ESA) mission called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision - with the first images set to be released later on Wednesday. The asteroid poses no threat. Instead, this was the first ever test of our planetary defences to see what action we could take if a space rock were heading for our planet. "Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact," said Patrick Michel, principal investigator of ESA's Hera mission. Image source, NASA/Johns Hopkins APL Image caption, This was the last image from Dart before it crashed into Dimorphos in 2022 The crash test focussed on a pair of asteroids: a larger one called Didymos - about 730m (2,400ft) wide - which is orbited by a smaller rock called Dimorphos, about 150m wide. The Dart spacecraft targeted Dimorphos, hurtling into the rock at 22,000km/h (14,000mph). Images beamed back showed the asteroid's rocky surface coming ever closer until the feed cut out upon impact. It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 10,000km long (6,200 miles), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space. The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid. Before the collision, it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the Dart crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes. But the arrival of the second spacecraft, Hera, will help scientists answer many more questions. "Dart exploded in the asteroid and therefore we don't have the information of what is its final state," explained Michel. "The impact could have left a crater - and if it is the case, we need to understand the size and the depth. Or [the impact] may have entirely reshaped the asteroid." Image source, NASA/Hubble Space Telescope Image caption, A 10,000km-long (6,200 miles) debris trail was spotted by the Hubble Space Telescope The Hera mission will spend the next year studying Dimorphos and will look at Didymos too. The spacecraft is packed with instruments and has two small shoe-boxed sized satellites onboard, which can study the impact site up close, and then later land on the asteroid. A key task is to measure the mass of Dimorphos to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was. This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth. "It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," said Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team. "We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'." title: Thomas Markle charged in US for possessing child sex abuse images
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East US & Canada Thomas Markle charged in US for possessing child sex abuse images Image source, Pinellas County Sheriff's Office By Sareen Habeshian Reporting from Los Angeles Published 24 November 2026 Updated 25 November 2026 01:40 GMT Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex has been charged by a federal grand jury in Los Angeles with possessing child sex abuse images. Markle, who remains in custody in Florida, allegedly possessed materials that include at least one image involving a prepubescent minor and a minor under 12 years old, court documents filed in California show. The 82-year-old has denied possessing images of child sex abuse. Last week, a judge in Florida declared Prince Harry's father-in-law mentally competent to stand trial. The FBI arrested Markle on 6 November at an elderly care home in Florida on a single federal charge of possessing child sexual abuse material. He now faces two counts. US attorney Bill Essayli said Markle faces a maximum of 20 years in prison on each count if convicted. His arrest came after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles for almost two decades uncovered the abuse material. Markle was initially released on conditional bail but was then ordered to stay in jail pending trial after allegedly removing a location monitoring device. To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Watch: Thomas Markle's charges over child sexual abuse material In the indictment, filed by the US Attorney's Office in the Central District of California, Markle is accused of knowingly possessing 35mm film negatives on 30 October and 4 November that contained child sexual abuse materials. The US Attorney's Office said that during both instances Markle allegedly knew the images contained such materials. Inside the storage units, federal agents found two images that depict an adult man - whom a witness identified as Markle - with an underage child, the US attorney's office said. They also alleged that a third image appears to depict a child in a room believed to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines. Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and he lived in Cebu until May. "The affidavit also describes additional photographs that appear to show Markle with children in various stages of undress," prosecutors said. title: Colombian police storm supermarket to free 20 held hostage for 17 hours
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East US & Canada Colombian police storm supermarket to free 20 held hostage for 17 hours Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, Relatives of those being held hostage spent anxious hours as the situation unfolded Colombian security forces have freed around 20 shoppers and employees who had been held hostage for about 17 hours at a supermarket in the city of Cartagena. Gunmen had stormed into the building at 08:00 (13:00 GMT) on Tuesday after what Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella said was a failed attempt at robbing an armoured car carrying money. They held those inside at gunpoint while trying to negotiate their getaway. With the situation becoming ever more intense as the day progressed, De la Espriella gave the green light for special forces and police to launch a daring operation to free the hostages, in which one gunman was killed. Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, Around 20 people were still being held hostage when the security forces moved in Residents living near the supermarket reported hearing explosions as the security forces moved into the building. Police later confirmed that officers had used stun grenades to overpower the hostage takers. One was killed in the operation and four have been arrested. De la Espriella described it as "an extraordinary joint operation", which he said had been carried out "flawlessly". He flew into the northern city to oversee the operation. In footage released since then, he can be seen, with a handgun strapped to his belt, flanked by the commanders of the operation. Speaking after the successful rescue of the hostages, he said that the gunmen had been given the chance to hand themselves in, which they had refused. Earlier in the day, the assailants had freed 10 of their hostages, among them elderly women. But they continued to hold around 20, even as a police helicopter hovered above and special forces teams prepared to enter the building, which is located in a popular shopping mall. Local media said that as well as asking for safe passage out of the supermarket, the gunmen also demanded nearly $2m (£1.5m) and armoured vehicles. According to President De la Espriella, they had no political affiliations but had taken the hostages once their plan to rob an armoured car carrying money had been foiled. "It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping - no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out, and then kidnapped a group of people," he said. Photos taken during the rescue operation show armed soldiers inside the building as people are kneeling with their hands behind their heads. It is not clear from the photos whether those kneeling are hostages or the hostage-takers. Local media are reporting that the authorities feared that some of the gunmen may have tried to pass themselves off as hostages as the rescue mission unfolded. The identities of the four arrested have not yet been released. The hostages are being reunited with their families after being checked over by medical teams, according to the mayor of Cartagena. Many anxious relatives had spent hours waiting for news outside the perimeter place around the supermarket by security forces. A woman called Sandra told news site Caracol that her 76-year-old mother was one of those being held hostage. Sandra's mother - among a group of elderly people released after six hours - was reunited with her daughters and grandchildren. title: Huawei found guilty of stealing US trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Business New Tech Economy Technology of Business Artificial Intelligence Africa Business Paths to Success Huawei found guilty of stealing US trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering Image source, REUTERS/Jane Rosenberg Image caption, Defence lawyer Brian Heberlig makes closing arguments at the Huawei Technologies trial at Brooklyn federal court on November 17. Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US. In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage. Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation. Huawei said , external the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis", adding that it would "take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests". Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions. However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise. Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada. Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors. During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge. "For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in statement , external . "Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable." The Chinese government hit out at what it called the US "suppression" of Chinese companies and said it supports Chinese firms protecting their interests. Defence attorney Brian Heberlig said it was by dint of hard work that Huawei's business had expanded with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff. Following the verdict, Heberlig told the BBC that Huawei was gratified that the jury had rejected the racketeering charge. "The RICO [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act] count that alleged that Huawei was a corrupt organisation, with a corporate culture and policy of committing crime. That was, in our view, a significant overreach, and the jury soundly rejected it," he said. "Of course, we have mixed emotions about the rest of the verdict ... [we] thought that Huawei was deserving of acquittals across the board." Sentencing is planned for September 2027. Heberlig said there will be "significant advocacy" to achieve the lowest sentence possible. Following that, he said he fully expects Huawei to appeal. "If I know Huawei, that fight will continue, and the company's not going to rest until it's pursued every last argument it can through appeal, and hopefully, ultimately toward vindication," he said. title: Veteran Nigerian Nollywood actor Pete Edochie dies aged 79
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East US & Canada Veteran Nigerian Nollywood actor Pete Edochie dies aged 79 Image source, peteedochie/Instagram Image caption, Pete Edochie was one of Africa's most celebrated film stars Veteran Nigerian actor Pete Edochie, one of Africa's most celebrated film stars, has died at the age of 79, his family has announced. Known for his deep voice, commanding screen presence and memorable use of African proverbs, Edochie became a household name across Africa, often portraying powerful traditional rulers, wealthy businessmen and family patriarchs. In a statement, his family said Edochie died in the early hours of Wednesday in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer. Tributes are pouring in from fans and fellow actors, remembering him as a Nollywood legend who helped shape Nigeria's film industry. Edochie began his career as a broadcaster in 1967 before turning to acting. He rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart. His portrayal of Okonkwo, the proud but troubled Igbo warrior in Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart, earned him international recognition helping establish him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors. The television series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life. He went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has since grown into one of the world's largest film industries. Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals, Billionaire's Club and the 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart. His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON). He also received several other accolades during his career, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards. In recent years, his distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films found a new generation of admirers through viral social media memes. "As we mourn this painful loss, we pray that Almighty God grants his gentle soul eternal rest and gives the entire family the fortitude to bear this irreparable loss," a statement shared on Instagram by his son Leo said. Enugu State Governor Peter Mbah said Edochie's death was a huge loss to Nigeria, praising the actor for introducing international audiences to Igbo traditions and inspiring younger performers. "Pete Edochie was more than an accomplished actor, he was an institution," Mbah said. The Actors Guild of Nigeria (AGN) president, Abubakar Yakubu, described Edochie as a "father figure" in the entertainment industry, saying his influence would be felt for generations to come. Edochie had spoken publicly about his deteriorating health during a visit to Ghana in October, saying he was struggling to walk and experiencing swelling in parts of his body. He is survived by his wife, Josephine, and their six children, including fellow Nollywood actors Yul and Linc Edochie. title: Two children among six dead after plane crash off Mississippi coast
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East US & Canada Two children among six dead after plane crash off Mississippi coast Image source, Getty Images By Harriet Whitehead Published 7 hours ago Six people, including two children, have been found dead after a plane crashed off the coast of Mississippi on Tuesday, the US Coast Guard says. The Cessna 210 was on its way from New Orleans to Fort Myers, Florida, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware. Air traffic control lost touch with it at about 15:45 (21:45 GMT) and it later went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula and Horn Island, officials said. Divers found the bodies of four adults and two boys, aged 8 and 10, in the fuselage, said Coast Guard spokesperson Juan Ros. Rescuers spent hours searching for the group and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane's cabin floating on the water, he said. Cmdr Trevor Blount, the Coast Guard rescue mission co-ordinator, said: "While this is not the outcome any of us had hoped for, we are grateful for the strong interagency co-ordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families."
