title: South Africa's Ramaphosa wins court battle over impeachment threat
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East US & Canada South Africa's Ramaphosa wins court battle over impeachment threat Image source, Gallo via Getty Images Image caption, President Cyril Ramaphosa has faced calls to resign over his handling of the "Farmgate" scandal South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has won a legal battle to overturn a report that found he may have a case to answer over the theft of large sums of cash from his private farm. In 2022, an independent panel said Ramaphosa may have committed serious misconduct relating to the theft of $580,000 (£443,000), hidden in a sofa, at his Phala Phala game farm in the Limpopo province. He denied any wrongdoing. Ramaphosa challenged the findings of the report in court after the Constitutional Court ruled that parliament had violated the constitution by blocking moves to impeach him. The Western Cape high court ruled that the panel's report was unlawful and set it aside "in its entirety". In its judgment, the court said the panel, appointed by parliament to investigate the allegations against Ramaphosa, had "misconstrued its function, the nature of the inquiry it was to conduct and the recommendation it was required to make". "It went beyond its lawful remit ... and made several material errors of law. [Therefore] the report of the independent panel ... is declared unlawful and is reviewed and set aside in its entirety," Judge Nolwazi Mabindla-Boqwana said. The court also declared unlawful the steps taken by parliament in relation to the report. Political analyst Khanyi Magubane said the court ruling was a victory for Ramaphosa as it gave him "political and constitutional credibility". She made it clear that the ruling was not a criminal finding on possible improper conduct at the farm but rather an indictment at the independent panel's report. "[So] he does get significant reprieve ... but there will always be the shadow of the Phala Phala report," Magubane said. The ruling effectively removes the basis for the parliamentary impeachment process against Ramaphosa, although opposition parties have indicated they intend to challenge the decision. The scandal, dubbed "Farmgate" by local media, has has dogged Ramaphosa since it emerged in 2022, when former spy chief Arthur Fraser reported the matter to police in a dossier. Fraser, an ally of former President Jacob Zuma, accused Ramaphosa of concealing the theft from the police and tax authorities. The break-in took place in 2020, when thieves allegedly stole bundles of US dollar bills hidden inside a sofa at the farm. Image source, Gallo via Getty Images Image caption, Opposition parties, pictured above, have been vocal in their call for the president to account for his role in the saga Earlier this month, two people were found guilty of the theft. Ramaphosa confirmed that a robbery had taken place but said the money had been from the legitimate sale of buffalo from his livestock business. Several investigations cleared him of any wrongdoing, but parliament began an impeachment proceedings in 2022 and appointed an independent panel to investigate the allegations. The panel made a series of damaging findings, including that there was "substantial doubt about the legitimacy of the source of the currency that was stolen". It also concluded that Ramaphosa "has a case to answer". Ramaphosa initially challenged the report in court but withdrew his application after parliament voted against adopting its findings. title: Solomon Islands ends controversial security pact with China for Australian treaty
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East US & Canada Solomon Islands ends controversial security pact with China for Australian treaty Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Australia and the Solomon Islands have signed a new treaty on security and economics The Solomon Islands has signed a "historic" treaty with Australia, after reportedly telling China it was ending a controversial security pact signed in 2022. At a press conference in Canberra on Wednesday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale said the new treaty would ensure that Australia was the Pacific nation's "security partner of choice". In 2022 the Solomon Islands, then under the leadership of now-Opposition Leader Manasseh Sogavare, signed a security and policing pact with Beijing . There were fears the pact gave China a crucial military and strategic foothold in the Pacific amid a battle for influence in the region with the US. On Tuesday, Australian media outlets reported that Honiara had told Beijing it would not renew the pact, understood to be expiring in April 2027. Wale told reporters on Wednesday there were "ongoing discussions" with China but he was "unable to talk about" the pact, because of a non-disclosure agreement. He said the treaty with Australia provided a reset after several years in which the Solomon Islands had been a point of "uncertainty and doubt in the region". Albanese said the treaty would strengthen the two countries' security partnership. "Backing our Pacific neighbours is an investment in Australia's own security and our own prosperity." "We'll do that in a way that completely respects Solomon Islands sovereignty and its right to make its own decisions." On Tuesday China's foreign ministry spokesman, Guo Jiukan, did not confirm or deny that the pact had been terminated. "There is no element of geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation in cooperation between China and Pacific island countries, including the Solomon Islands," Guo said. The pact was never publicly released, but leaked excerpts revealed it gave China extensive involvement in security and policing including deploying its own officers to the Solomon Islands, and allowed it to establish a quasi military base. It was a "massive coup" for Beijing, said Lowy Institute Research Fellow, Dr Connor Graham, but its unprecedented scale sparked alarm in the Pacific and the West. Wednesday's treaty had delivered "an enormous win for Canberra", and "closes the loop" on a series of security deals Canberra signed with Pacific nations in the wake of the Solomons-China pact. "That [China pact] was the thing that put fear in the hearts of diplomats in Washington and Canberra," he told the BBC. William Yang, the International Crisis Group's Senior Analyst for North East Asia, said the end of China's "flagship" Pacific deal and the signing of the new treaty also reaffirmed the Pacific's "longstanding consensus-based decision-making model, especially in the security space". Under the new treaty, the Solomon Islands commits to prior consultation with Australia on critical infrastructure and to ensure any security cooperations are with Pacific Islands Forum members. China is a dialogue partner but not a member of the forum. Honiara also commits to its sensitive infrastructure remaining "free from militarisation, any form of foreign interference or unauthorised access", and to not permit its territory to be used for any foreign military or security base. title: Zimbabwe issues arrest warrant for Robert Mugabe's son over missed court date
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East US & Canada Zimbabwe issues arrest warrant for Robert Mugabe's son over missed court date Image source, Gallo Images via Getty Images Image caption, Bellarmine Chatunga is the youngest son of Robert Mugabe and his second wife, Grace Mugabe A Zimbabwean court has issued an arrest warrant for Bellarmine Chatunga Mugabe, the youngest son of the country's late former president Robert Mugabe, after he failed to appear in court. Mugabe was arrested earlier this month alongside four others over assault allegations on a police officer during an investigation into the suspected smuggling of luxury vehicles. The group subsequently faced charges of robbery and malicious damage to property. They have yet to enter pleas. They were granted bail on 6 November and were due back in court on Tuesday. However, Mugabe failed to attend. His co-accused, an aide and three security guards appeared and were remanded until 10 December. Prosecutors allege that Mugabe and the others assaulted an investigating officer using their hands and broomsticks. The officer's phone was allegedly taken and smashed on the ground, while one of the accused is said to have seized the officer's loaded pistol. Bellarmine Chatunga is the youngest son of Robert Mugabe and his second wife, Grace Mugabe. Robert Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe for 37 years before being forced from power in 2017, aged 93, following a military intervention. He died in 2019. His son has attracted public attention in recent years over a series of legal troubles and his high-profile lifestyle. Last month, he admitted to drug-related charges involving the possession of cannabis. In April, he was deported from neighbouring South Africa after pleading guilty to pointing a firearm and being in the country illegally. He had been arrested following the shooting of a 23-year-old man at his home. In 2023, he was arrested in Harare, Zimbabwe's capital, over allegations that he damaged property and spat at a police officer during a party. He was later freed after reaching an out-of-court settlement with the complainant, who was a friend. title: Kilmar Ábrego García arrives in Spain, ending Trump deportation battle
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East US & Canada Kilmar Ábrego García arrives in Spain, ending Trump deportation battle Image source, Reuters Image caption, It is unclear how long Kilmar Ábrego García will stay in Spain for Kilmar Ábrego García, whose deportation last year to El Salvador sparked a bitter legal battle, has arrived in Spain from the US. He took a commercial flight to the country on Tuesday. His lawyer said the relocation was temporary while Ábrego García sought to eventually return to the US. After the US government admitted it had wrongfully sent Ábrego García to his home country, he was returned to face human trafficking charges that were later dropped. The administration then continued its attempts to deport him to other countries, including Uganda and Ghana. His deportation and return became a flashpoint in the debate over US President Donald Trump's immigration agenda. Ábrego García, who is married to a US citizen and lived in Maryland, came to the US illegally from El Salvador as a teenager. Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, visited Ábrego García while he was in the notorious Cecot prison in El Salvador in 2025 and advocated for his release. "A year and a half ago, the Trump administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego García to rot in a Salvadoran gulag," Van Hollen said in a statement on Tuesday. "Today, Kilmar is travelling to a country of his choice, a free man - unharmed and with dignity." Ábrego García's lawyer said in a statement that his departure was "temporary" as he had "many options to return to the United States". "We don't expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritise reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland," the statement said. "Where he goes from here, where he chooses to settle for the next two years while he waits out the end of this administration, will be his choice, not the administration's choice." The BBC has contacted the US Department of Homeland Security for comment. Ábrego García was arrested in 2019 alongside three other men and detained by federal immigration authorities. A judge granted him protection from deportation to El Salvador at the time, citing the risk of persecution by one of the country's criminal gangs. In March 2025, the Trump administration deported him to El Salvador, where he was held in Cecot, a prison known for its harsh conditions. The US Supreme Court then ordered the government to facilitate his return. The administration admitted that he was deported in error and brought him back to the US, where he was set to face human trafficking charges. A federal judge dismissed the case, saying Ábrego García had been charged for political reasons. For months, he was locked in a battle with the government over further efforts to deport him. Ábrego García had repeatedly said he would be willing to be deported to Costa Rica, while the Costa Rican government had agreed to accept him as a refugee and provide him with legal status. After reports emerged that the administration was considering sending him to Uganda, a judge barred the government from deporting Ábrego García to a third country. At one point, the Trump administration requested that the judge lift the order so that Ábrego García could be deported to Liberia, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner. title: Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East US & Canada Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza Image source, Reuters Image caption, A funeral was held earlier in southern Gaza for three Palestinians killed in an Israeli strike At least seven Palestinians, including a senior Hamas security official, have been killed in Israeli air strikes in the Gaza Strip, health officials and first responders say. Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service, was targeted in western Gaza City, Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry said. The 50-year-old had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid by Israeli special forces . Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz announced that Abu Nahel was "eliminated" by the Israeli military. The six other people were killed in two earlier air strikes elsewhere in Gaza. Three people, including a teenage boy, were killed in the Wadi Gaza area, south of Gaza City, according to the health officials and first responders. The other three were killed at a police station in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis, they added. Gaza's police force, which operates under the interior ministry, said two of its officers were among those who died in the second attack. It also accused Israel of "an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos" in the territory. The Israeli military said it struck "military operatives" in both areas. Witnesses said an Israeli drone targeted Naeem Abu Nahel as he was walking on a side street near a tent camp for displaced people in Gaza City. Several other people were reportedly seriously injured in the strike. The Israeli military said Abu Nahel had "possessed extensive institutional knowledge" about Hamas's internal security service - which is responsible for enforcing discipline, protecting infrastructure and rooting out informants - and that his death constituted "a blow to the apparatus's management capabilities". It also alleged that he had advanced attacks on Israeli troops and civilians during the war and that it killed him "to remove the threat he posed". Gaza's interior ministry said Abu Nahel's killing followed what it described as the internal security service's "important achievements in combating gangs collaborating with the occupation [Israel] and operating in areas under the control of its military". Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Gaza's health ministry warned that there was a rapid rise in cases of meningitis in October Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced. At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period. The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to thousands of shelters for displaced families. The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases. This video can not be played Watch: India's government is 'scared', cockroach movement leader says after travel ban One of the leaders of India's "cockroach" movement has said the Delhi government has "completely lost the plot" after he was stopped from leaving the country for the UK. Saurav Das said he was meant to board a flight on Tuesday morning but was told by immigration officers his passport had been "flagged" because of discrepancies involving his date of birth. In an interview with the BBC, Das said there were no discrepancies in his documents, accusing the Indian government of using cheap tactics to stop activists from travelling and speaking on issues that matter to young people. The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment. Saurav told the BBC World Service's Newshour programme the incident showed the government was "scared". "They are scared of the cockroach movement. They're scared of young people asking them questions because they have never had to deal with a generation that wants to ask questions so head on. So that jitters them." By not allowing him to travel, he said the government had lowered India's stature in the world. "It's international news that I am unable to travel to the UK," he said. "And this shows Prime Minister Modi in such poor light. "It's a way to harass, to target activists, young voices in India by the Modi government." Das said he had been invited by the Oxford Union, as well as universities including Cambridge and Edinburgh, to speak about the movement. Ratna Singh, another leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), wrote: "The manner in which Saurav was not allowed to board today raises deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country." On Tuesday, the London School of Economics Student Union's Amnesty International Unit, a student-led charity group, shared a post on Instagram saying that an event featuring Das had been "indefinitely postponed". Image source, EPA Image caption, Saurav Das (L) speaking following the resignation of India's education minister in July Das, a former journalist, became one of the faces of the CJP - a Gen Z-led movement that began as satire but has since emerged as a youth-led pressure group. In July, protests spearheaded by the CJP over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan . In October, CJP leaders including Das were among thousands detained by the police for trying to hold protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing. The same month, Das and Ashutosh Ranka, another CJP leader, were jailed for seven days after being arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi. title: Land mine casualties soar in Syria, two years after war
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East US & Canada Land mine casualties soar in Syria, two years after war Image source, PA Image caption, Syrians coming back after the war are falling victim to mines and other explosives Eleven-year-old Alaa was tending her family's goats with her siblings in a field behind their home in Umm Khuzaym, north-west Syria, on Sunday when there was a flash and a deafening bang. "Then we heard people screaming," Alaa's father, Walid Mohammed Al-Ghafar, told the BBC. Walid ran outside to find his daughter lying face down, killed, and her 10-year-old brother, Mahmoud, seriously injured. Unwittingly, the children had triggered a landmine. The incident and others this week bring to nearly 1,000 the number of children killed or injured by explosive ordnance in Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, according to the UN Mine Action Service (Unmas). The village is one of many where families have returned to homes and farmland that were once on the front lines of Syria's 13-year civil war. Alaa's father said demining teams had visited several times to clear the fields. He and other residents believed it was safe for farmers and children to move around. But mines and other explosives can lie far beyond former battle lines, making it difficult to establish which areas are safe. "Remnants of war from today's conflicts are often very widely and broadly scattered, often without patterns, which makes it extremely difficult to do clearance," Katrin Atkins, research lead at Landmine Monitor, a global mine monitoring initiative, told the BBC. The dangers are reflected in a sharp rise in casualties across Syria. A total of 1,602 people were killed or injured by landmines and explosive remnants of war in 2025 alone, an increase of more than 50% on the previous year, according to the Landmine Monitor report, published by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines on Tuesday. Only Myanmar, with 1,891 casualties, recorded more. The report attributes the rise in Syria partly to the large-scale return of refugees and internally displaced people following Assad's overthrow. "When you look at population movement, a couple of months later you see an increase of incidents in these areas, because that's exactly where people go and start to use the fields again," Atkins said. More than 60% of casualties recorded by the world's largest landmine clearance charity, the Halo Trust, involve farming, agriculture or shepherding, according to its Syria programme manager, Simon Jackson. "They're not going to wait for the government or for organisations like us to come and tell them that everything is safe and clear," he told the BBC. "People are taking risks out of desperation." Since Assad's fall on 8 December 2024, Unmas has recorded at least 1,556 incidents in Syria involving explosive ordnance. They have caused 2,701 casualties: 935 people killed and 1,766 injured. Children account for 995 of those victims, or about 37%. But the toll is likely to be higher, with experts estimating that overall casualties could be under-reported by 25-50%. title: Trump's rescue of Nvidia's Huang brings political risks
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East US & Canada Trump's rescue of Nvidia's Huang brings political risks To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Trump boosts Nvidia boss return but are US politicians on board? After the AI chipmaker Nvidia announced it was bringing back embattled former head Jensen Huang and the company's stock shot up like a bullet, President Donald Trump took a very public victory lap. "I made the deal," he said during a lengthy phone interview with cable business news channel CNBC. Trump followed that with an AI-generated image posted to his social media platform that riffed on the famous photograph taken moments after the 2024 attempt on his life in Pennsylvania. But instead of Trump in the image, Huang was the one surrounded by Secret Service guards. It depicted him in front of an Nvidia banner - with a raised fist clenching a red bra. The post was classic Trump – potentially offensive, yet still a bit opaque. Was Trump suggesting Huang survived a scandal – one that includes allegations of recklessly jeopardising US national security by consorting with a suspected Chinese spy – the way he had survived an assassin's bullet? Was the bra a celebration Huang's reported extramarital affairs? By replacing the US flag with an Nvidia standard, was he claiming that America and one of its largest, most powerful companies are one and the same? At the very least, the image underscores how inextricably linked Huang and Trump now are, with the fate of the former hinging on the successes and failures of the latter. Image source, Getty Images And with that comes significant risks for the American president and for Republicans, including Vice-President JD Vance, who played a key part in his efforts to rescue Huang. While Trump has said that a "very thorough investigation" by federal officials "exonerated" Huang and his reinstatement poses no national security threat, that is far from the final word on the matter. "Every time you have a Chinese woman that's good looking or beautiful, they say she's a spy," Trump told CNBC, adding that "with Jensen, I don't believe that's true". Democrats and some concerned Republicans in Congress have a different view. They are promising to launch their own oversight of Huang and Nvidia, with subpoenas and compelled witness testimony, in order to assess whether they violated laws by allowing China to access sophisticated microchip technology. State governments could also launch their own investigations. Any new revelations could further damage the company's standing – and, by association, Trump himself. "I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," Republican Senator Tom Cotton posted on X. Even if he is free from any criminal liability, the tech mogul is about to be in a much harsher spotlight than he has ever experienced. Trump also appears to be on the wrong side of public opinion when it comes to AI writ large. title: These North Koreans say they were spied on, beaten and jailed for being Christian
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Asia China India These North Koreans say they were spied on, beaten and jailed for being Christian Image source, KCNA via Getty Images Image caption, Kim Jong Un's communist regime is accused of brutal crackdowns on religious freedom in a new report Living in North Korea, Kim Bo-bin got used to praying with her eyes open. She found ingenious ways to keep her Christian faith a secret in the Communist dictatorship, which tightly controls how and where its citizens worship. Unauthorised displays of faith could land people in prison, she tells the BBC. So Kim would silently mouth hymns and clap with just two of her fingers. "In North Korea, if there are three people in a room, you are being spied on. So I would only close my eyes [and pray] when I lay on the floor." Now 44, Kim lives just outside the South Korean capital Seoul, where she fled 15 years ago. Her testimony - of how she prayed in secret for years, and was jailed and beaten for her faith - is part of a new report , external documenting the experiences of 570 North Korean escapees, most of whom say they experienced or witnessed anti-Christian persecution. Spanning five years and featuring interviews with defectors from across the country, the report by British human rights group Korea Future accuses Kim Jong Un's regime of repeatedly violating religious freedom through a system of surveillance, fear and violence. It suggests little has changed after sustained international pressure, with multiple incidents of suspected Christians being beaten and tortured as recently as last year. North Korea maintains that it allows religious freedom in spite of years of evidence heard by rights groups and the United Nations. While churches exist in Pyongyang, they are controlled by the state and widely seen as projecting an illusion of religious liberty. "The North Korean leader's authority is god-like," says Kang Dong-wan, professor at Dong-a University. "So they cannot allow gods whose authority is above him." Pyongyang fears that religious freedom may threaten the regime itself, he adds. Image source, Courtesy Kim Bo-bin Image caption, Kim Bo-bin has been living in South Korea for 15 years now First established in Korea in the late 1700s, Christianity exploded across the north after Protestant missionaries arrived in the 1880s. North Korea provides no figures on its Christian population but the UN has referred to estimates of 200,000 to 400,000 of them practising secretly, some of whom are detained in camps. Surveillance and control over religion, like many other aspects of North Korean life, intensified under Kim Jong Un, who succeeded his father in 2011. Three South Korean missionaries operating in the Chinese border region were arrested between 2013-2014 and sentenced to life in prison on charges of espionage and plotting a coup. It's not clear if they are still alive, as Seoul says Pyongyang has refused to share any information about the detainees. Pyongyang has also been cracking down on smuggled memory sticks containing South Korean-made videos of Christian sermons. In 2020, it passed a law - on Rejecting Reactionary Ideology and Culture - to block so-called "foreign influence". Owning Bibles and hosting services can now result in imprisonment, while distributing religious books or videos is punishable by death. Lessons against religion begin as early as kindergarten for most North Koreans. Children must attend "self-criticism" sessions at school in which they are warned against "superstitions", widely understood to refer to Christianity and other faiths. title: Is China behind a wave of AI fake videos targeting Taiwan?
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat BBC Verify Is China behind a wave of AI fake videos targeting Taiwan? By Sam Howarth and Matt Murphy , BBC Verify Published 24 November 2026 Taiwan's ruling party is being repeatedly targeted with AI videos spreading false claims about its leader and other key members ahead of crucial local elections, BBC Verify has found. A China-linked network has pumped out more than 500 fake videos about the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in the past year, which experts suggest is part of a long-running campaign to influence the outcome of the elections. The videos appear to try to smear President Lai Ching-te by claiming he holds a US green card - and would abandon Taiwan if war broke out with China - which Taiwan's presidential office says is completely false. Deepfakes also appear to show Puma Shen, who is running to be the mayor of capital Taipei, using drugs, which he denies. Others seek to undermine or ridicule the politicians by showing them in children's clothing or as popular film characters. The Taipei mayoralty has traditionally served as a springboard to the presidency. Experts say this has made Shen, who has been openly critical of Beijing, an obvious target for disinformation campaigns. The current mayor, Chiang Wan-an, is part of Taiwan's Kuomintang (KMT) party, which favours closer ties with China. Taiwan is a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory. Beijing and Taipei have long observed an uneasy status quo under which Taiwan, backed by the US, neither formally declares independence nor unites with China. But tensions have risen since the DPP came to power in 2016. Beijing has repeatedly accused the party of pursuing independence while China's leader Xi Jinping, who has said "reunification" with Taiwan is a key goal, has stepped up pressure against the party with increased military activity around the island. Experts believe the current disinformation activity is part of a broader campaign against Taiwan designed to undermine trust in its democratic process. Image caption, The campaign has targeted Taiwan's President Lai (top) and his predecessor Tsai (bottom) "The account operators are trying to make people distrust the DPP politicians so that they will not believe whatever they say," Austin Horng-En Wang, an expert in cognitive warfare at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, told BBC Verify. "If you don't trust that candidate then you will not listen to what they say," he added. The videos, many of which were shared from an account called "noxparable" or carried a watermark with the same name, have been viewed tens of millions of times across several social media platforms since May 2025. More than half of those views were tracked in the past four months as the activity has ramped up ahead of the elections. Many of the accounts involved in spreading disinformation listed their locations on social media as mainland China and Hong Kong, while a number of the clips carried labels showing they were generated with AI. Many people who engaged with the videos were often seen repeating the false claims or attacking DPP figures in the comments, while others appeared to treat the clips as entertainment. One of the most widely shared videos targeted Shen by superimposing his face onto a man who is seen holding a lighter and exhaling smoke alongside claims he is smoking drugs. The video appears to build on accusations from Taiwan's opposition party that he supports drugs decriminalisation, which Shen denies, and was debunked by a local news network. Shen has taken legal action against people sharing deepfakes, local media

title: Lies, a disguise and surfboard bags: How a jealous Sydney policeman tried to cover up double murder
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East US & Canada Lies, a disguise and surfboard bags: How a jealous Sydney policeman tried to cover up double murder To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Watch: The CCTV that helped convict a Sydney policeman of double murder It was just after 09:00 on a warm February morning when CCTV picked up a man dressed as an UberEats rider hovering on a sidewalk in one of Sydney's wealthiest neighbourhoods. He dawdled for around 20 minutes, "steeling himself for what he was about to do" prosecutors say, before disappearing out of sight. Minutes later another CCTV camera captured the sound of gunshots ringing out. Former police officer Beau Lamarre, 31, was on Wednesday found guilty of murdering his former partner Jesse Baird, a TV presenter, and Luke Davies, Baird's new partner, with his work-issued gun. In February 2024, the bloodied belongings of Baird and Davies were found in a skip in the suburb of Cronulla, sparking a frantic search for the couple. It culminated in the discovery of their bodies on a rural property, partially buried beneath sticks and debris. Image source, Supplied: Jesse Baird Image caption, Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird had been dating only months when they were gunned down During a two-month trial filled with at-times extraordinary testimony and a wealth of CCTV evidence, the court heard Lamarre had planned his crime over months. Jurors watched CCTV of the then police officer purchasing a surfboard bag in which to put Baird's body, after casually sizing it up against a friend in the shop, and heard from a stream of former friends and colleagues who testified that Lamarre asked them for advice about everything from mobile phone signals to where he could buy a gun. One recounted the chilling moment Lamarre told her that if he were ever to murder someone, he would leave their belongings in a dumpster and hide the body in bushland where they would never be found. "What would you do if I told you I killed somebody? Would you help me hide the body?" he asked, according to her testimony. Later, Lamarre asked for help in covering up the killings; his friends - none of whom have been implicated - say they began receiving panicked calls and odd requests from him. One told the court Lamarre persuaded her to go for a drive in the country, during which he tried to dispose of the bodies at the family farm of a man he'd met on a dating app. Over the speakers, he played Taylor Swift's No Body, No Crime. Baird, 26, and Lamarre - a one-time celebrity blogger who also had his own swimwear line on the side of his police work - met in a nightclub in October 2022. For Lamarre, it quickly became an infatuation, but for Baird, an AFL referee and former Network Ten presenter, the relationship appeared to be casual. After discovering in April 2023 that Lamarre had gone through messages on his phone, and unfollowed other men on his Instagram account, Baird broke it off. But Lamarre's obsession only grew. He watched Baird having sex with another man through his bedroom window, broke into his house multiple times, deleting contacts on his phone and turning on location settings so that he could engineer meetings with the TV presenter. On one occasion Baird woke up to find Lamarre in his bedroom; not realising who it was, he chased him down the street. title: The rising cost of putting food on the table in India
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Asia China India The rising cost of putting food on the table in India Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images Image caption, As food inflation rises, vegetables are becoming an increasingly expensive part of the household budget India correspondent Published 25 November 2026, 01:02 GMT India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices. The latest government data , external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September. But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%. The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas. In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation. Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists. With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall , external , India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production. Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty Images Image caption, Onion prices have surged, adding to the pressure on household food budgets A survey by polling agency LocalCircles found that six in 10 consumers say household essentials cost them over 20% more each month than a year ago, prompting calls for government intervention. Rising prices are also forcing cutbacks: 74% are curbing discretionary spending on eating out, shopping and entertainment, while half are buying smaller quantities of essentials. Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences. In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation. That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items. Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment. "Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food. Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty Images Image caption, Rising food prices hurt the poor the most According to calculations by Dharmakirti Joshi, chief economist at analytics firm Crisil, the bottom 20% of rural households faced inflation of 6.9% in October, against 6.5% for the richest 20%. In urban India, the corresponding rates were 6.1% and 5.3%. The pressure is visible even in the cost of a simple meal. Crisil's Roti Rice Rate analysis , external found that the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali - a meal platter - rose 12% year-on-year in October, driven by higher prices of onions, tomatoes, vegetables, edible oil, rice and cooking gas. A non-vegetarian thali became 9% more expensive. Rice prices were up about 10% year-on-year, pulses 8%, edible oil 13% and LPG 10%, according to Pushan Sharma, director of intelligence at Crisil. title: Clashing political visions reflect a divided Spain ahead of election
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East US & Canada Clashing political visions reflect a divided Spain ahead of election Image source, EPA Image caption, Pedro Sánchez has won praise from the left for standing up to Donald Trump and promoting progressive causes Speaking in a wrestling ring on the island of Tenerife as he campaigned ahead of Sunday's general election, Spain's Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez cautioned those listening about the spread of right-wing governments. "What good has President [Donald] Trump done the United States and, by extension, the world - was he a change or a step backwards?" he asked supporters, before invoking the administrations of Brazil's former leader, Jair Bolsonaro, and Argentinian President Javier Milei. "If we don't want that for the world, why would we want it for our own country?" said Sánchez. He issued his warning as Spain's conservative People's Party (PP) leads most of the polls and appears poised to form a governing coalition with the hard-right Vox. The election comes amid a deeply polarised political atmosphere in which both left and right have warned about their opponents' ability to undermine democracy. In a Europe dominated by right-leaning governments, Sánchez has gained a reputation as the continent's most outspoken and uncompromising left-wing prime minister. His strident rhetoric defending feminism, immigration and green energy, along with his condemnation of Israel's military action in Gaza and verbal clashes with Trump, has fostered this image. Having overseen consistent economic growth in recent years, his stock is high among the international left. Yet in Spain, Sánchez has become a hate figure for the right, who see him as an autocrat with little regard for the separation of state powers, obsessed with clinging on to power and surrounded by a corrupt cabal. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Alberto Núñez Feijóo's right-wing People's Party (PP) is currently ahead in the polls In a bullring in Valencia, the same day that Sánchez was staging his rally, PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo told supporters that the last few years of Socialist-led government had been "insulting and even humiliating for a lot of people". He added: "We know them, they are capable of anything." A couple of days earlier, Ignacio Garriga, spokesman for Vox, had gone further, describing Sánchez as "a very dangerous psychopath". Both the PP and Vox have cast doubt on the neutrality of postal votes and votes cast by Spaniards abroad ahead of the election, suggesting that government manipulation could sway them in its favour. "This is a campaign that is overwhelmingly ideological," said Cristina Monge, a political scientist at the Complutense University. "That means that it is not so much about voters rewarding or punishing a government's performance or the proposals being made, but about belonging to one or other ideological bloc." Much of the hostility to Sánchez stems from his reliance on hard-left and separatist parties. Ahead of the 2023 general election, he faced fierce criticism from the right for his reliance on the pro-independence EH Bildu coalition, which had links to the defunct Basque armed group ETA. After that vote, he was able to form a new administration with the support of another separatist party, Together for Catalonia (Junts), in exchange for an amnesty for all Catalans facing legal action for their role in a failed 2017 bid for independence. title: Shot in the face at 15: The lives shattered by Cameroon's decade of conflict
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East US & Canada Shot in the face at 15: The lives shattered by Cameroon's decade of conflict Image source, Michel Mvondo/BBC Image caption, Median Bah was shot several times in the face by unknown gunmen Median Bah was just 15 when her life changed forever. She remembers the date vividly - 7 April 2018. She was ill and confined to her bed. Armed men stormed her family's compound in Cameroon's Southwest region, one of the country's two English-speaking areas at the centre of a separatist conflict. Median, now 23, says she was fast asleep when her brother woke her, panicked by the approach of a group of armed men who were shooting indiscriminately. He escaped through a window. But for Median, fleeing was not so easy. "Since I was sick, I had no strength to jump through the window with him, so I had to pass through the door," she tells the BBC. She says she came face to face with two of the attackers in the backyard, who opened fire at her. They first shot her in the thigh before firing several more rounds, which severely damaged her face. "I kept pleading with them not to kill me, that I wasn't feeling well. However, I found myself on the floor," she recalls. Everything went dark. She lost consciousness and could neither see nor speak. The attack left her with devastating facial injuries. Her jawbone was damaged, most of her teeth destroyed and much of her mouth severely injured. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The Anglophone crisis began in 2016, when English-speaking Cameroonians took up arms over alleged marginalisation by the French-speaking government (file photo) Over the past eight years, she has undergone at least four reconstructive surgeries in Cameroon, Ghana and India, with more procedures expected next year. Parts of her face have been reconstructed using tissue taken from other parts of her body. She also lost the ability to breathe normally through her nose and mouth. She underwent a tracheostomy, a surgical procedure that creates an opening in the neck to allow air into the windpipe. For eight years, she relied on a tube to breathe. It was only recently removed, allowing her to breathe normally again. A teenager left with devastating facial injuries, a mother forced to flee her home and a student whose education was disrupted. Nearly a decade of fighting in Cameroon has left countless lives shattered. The crisis began in October 2016, when lawyers and teachers in Cameroon's English-speaking regions went on strike over the alleged marginalisation of Anglophone communities by the Francophone-dominated government. They were concerned about the appointment of French-speaking judges and teachers to courts and schools in the English-speaking Northwest and Southwest regions. Initially, the protest was peaceful, with thousands demanding greater recognition of the English-speaking minority. But human rights groups accused security forces of using excessive force to suppress the protests. The crackdown, critics say, helped fuel an armed separatist movement. By 2017, a dozen armed groups had emerged, according to the International Crisis Group, seeking independence for the two English-speaking regions and the creation of a breakaway state known as Ambazonia. Since then, separatist fighters have engaged in a prolonged and often brutal conflict with government forces. Rights groups have documented serious abuses by both sides. Separatist fighters have been accused of targeted killings, kidnappings for ransom, torture and attacks on schools and other public and private facilitie

title: Energy bills to rise by 26% from January after gas prices surge
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Business New Tech Economy Technology of Business Artificial Intelligence Africa Business Paths to Success Energy bills to rise by 26% from January after gas prices surge Image source, Getty Images By Kevin Peachey Cost of living correspondent Published 25 November 2026, 00:03 GMT Updated 53 minutes ago Energy bills will soar by 26% for millions of households in January after a surge in gas prices sparked by the Iran war. A typical bill will increase by about £37 a month in the first three months of the new year, although the price will depend on how much energy a household uses, so it could be closer to £60 extra a month in winter. A household using a typical amount of energy in England, Scotland and Wales and paying by direct debit, would see their annual bill rise from £1,723 to £2,166 if the increase was sustained for a year, said regulator Ofgem. The government will pay millions of households £100 from 4 January to help cover winter costs on top of an existing VAT cut on electricity. Charities and suppliers expect debt to rise and a wave of people to need emergency support. Ofgem said the rise had been driven entirely by higher wholesale costs faced by suppliers owing, primarily, to the Iran war. Wholesale gas prices , paid by suppliers, were up 33% in the last three months, the period used to set the January to March cap. They have more than doubled since late 2025. The warm home discount will take £150 off bills for six million households on benefits this winter. There have been calls for this support, funded through everyone's bill, to be extended. "We are staring down the barrel of a brutal winter," said Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice. Neil Kenward, Ofgem's director general for markets, said it wrote to energy suppliers "reminding them of their responsibilities" to customers this winter. They have been told to identify people who need help early, make support easy to access and ensure repayment plans are affordable and sustainable. Campaign Groups Friends of the Earth and Global Witness said major oil and energy companies are making huge profits because of spiralling oil costs, hurting households. Energy UK, which represents suppliers, said the firms which send your bill, have profits capped on a percentage basis and do not see the same benefit as international energy generating companies. However, higher bills will mean higher profits in nominal cash terms. The increase is the biggest since Russia's invasion of Ukraine drove up prices. It comes at a tough time of year, when the weather is at its coldest. People on prepayment meters will be hit as their spending comes when energy is needed, rather than the cost being spread over the year as with direct debits. The cap sets a maximum price for each unit of energy, not the total bill. Those on fixed deals are unaffected until the end of their term, but for those on variable tariffs it means: For electricity, average unit prices will go up on 1 January from 26.32p per kilowatt-hour to 32.69p. The electricity price is often pegged to gas, owing to gas-fired generation. Gas will increase from 7.97p per kilowatt-hour to 10.96p, higher than in the wake of the invasion of Ukraine. Daily standing charges will be 54.77p for electricity and 29.65p for gas. The cap is set every three months, based on the costs faced by suppliers as well as the cost of running the energy system. It is based on a three-month period that ends about six weeks before the new cap comes into force. A fall in international wholesale prices in recent days will not be reflected in January's cap, but

title: Two men charged with trying to steal cufflinks and clock from Royal home
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat England Regions Norfolk Two men charged with trying to steal cufflinks and clock from Royal home Image source, Getty Images Image caption, William and Catherine use the estate as a country retreat during the holidays Two men charged with trespassing at the Prince and Princess of Wales's country home are accused of trying to steal cufflinks and a clock. Police were called to Anmer Hall, on the Sandringham estate in Norfolk, shortly before 18:00 GMT on Monday after reports of suspicious activity. Mirgen Doku, 34, of Courtfield Gardens, London, and Arilen Ndoci, 32, of no fixed address, have both been charged with entering a dwelling with intent to steal and trespassing on a protected site. Both appeared at Norwich Magistrates' Court earlier and have been remanded in custody until a hearing on Monday. Prosecutors said a third suspect remained at large. The men, who appeared in court in black sweatshirts, are accused of stealing six pairs of cufflinks and a clock. Both spoke through an Albanian interpreter, but did not enter pleas. The court heard one of the pairs of cufflinks were described as "the Duke of Edinburgh cufflinks". Image source, Reuters Image caption, Police said Anmer Hall was not occupied by the Royal couple at the time of the incident William and Catherine do not live at Anmer Hall full-time, but use the estate as a country retreat during the holidays. The property was unoccupied at the time of the incident, police added. On Monday, Kensington Palace said it did not comment on security matters. Dogs, drones and a helicopter were used to search the area before two men were arrested within the estate's grounds. Anmer Hall is located on the private estate and is about two miles (3km) east from Sandringham House, one of the King's private residences. title: EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Politics Parliaments Brexit EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme Image source, Getty Images By Chris Mason Political editor Published 3 hours ago The UK could be included in the EU's proposed scheme to protect car manufacturing in Europe without Britain having to impose import taxes on Chinese electric cars, under draft plans. The proposal has been drawn up by Ireland, which currently holds the EU's rotating presidency, and will be discussed by European ambassadors later on Wednesday. It comes after previous suggestions the EU would demand the UK align its tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles as a condition of joining the scheme. Senior figures in the British government have been talking increasingly positively about the potential to join on terms London would be willing to sign up to, and are cautiously optimistic about this latest move. The "Made in Europe" scheme, known formally as the Industrial Accelerator Act, aims to protect EU manufacturing with restrictions on goods from outside countries, with a particular focus on both China and the car industry. The idea is potentially dangerous to the UK, as being outside the EU would mean being exposed to restrictions principally intended for others. Alignment with higher EU tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles would increase their price in the UK, at a time when they have become increasingly popular. It also raises the prospect of a potential Chinese retaliation with its own tariffs imposed on cars made in the UK. Now Ireland, as first reported by the Financial Times , external , is suggesting the UK could join Made in Europe without the need to match the EU's tariffs. The argument made in favour of this is the UK and EU car industries are so heavily integrated and interdependent. The proposal, which would also apply to Switzerland and countries in the European Economic Area (EEA) such as Norway, would depend on the non-EU countries granting the EU access to their subsidy and procurement schemes. However, the idea is still at its early stages. After Wednesday's meeting of EU ambassadors, it will be discussed again by competition ministers from the EU's member states at a meeting before Christmas. The proposal would also have to be accepted by the European Commission and the European Parliament. After last week's EU-UK summit in Brussels, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Made in Europe had become a "source of real concern across the British economy, particularly for our car makers". "It will come as a relief to workers that the UK and EU committed in Brussels to avoid measures that would harm each other's industries," he added. This video can not be played Watch: Moment Raheem Sterling arrested after car crash Former England footballer Raheem Sterling has been given a suspended sentence after admitting dangerously driving his Lamborghini while inhaling nitrous oxide from a balloon on a motorway. The 31-year-old, from Berkshire, who later crashed into a metal gate during rush hour, gave no reaction as he was handed a 12-month jail term, suspended for 18 months, at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court. Sterling had pleaded guilty to dangerous driving of a Lamborghini Urus and possessing nitrous oxide on the M25, the M3, the A327 and Minley Road on 28 May. The judge said Sterling's use of the Class C drug had became a "maladaptive coping mechanism during a difficult period" in his career. Sterling, who left the court without making any comment, was ordered to complete 100 hours unpaid work and was banned from driving for 24 months. He was arrested after crashing near the M3 in Hampshire. Raheem Sterling - from national icon to suspended jail sentence Published 1 hour ago District judge Kirsty Allman told the court on Wednesday that Sterling was seen at 01:10 BST at a McDonald's in Hayes driving "erratically and at speed" while inhaling from a pink balloon. She went on: "At 7.45am, having not slept, you made a deliberate and entirely selfish decision, to drive your vehicle without adequate sleep and whilst consuming a Class C drug, nitrous oxide." She said this exposed a "large number of road users to a significant risk of serious harm by the manner of your driving on two motorways and in peak travel time that morning". During the September hearing, prosecutor Simon Jones said a number of calls were made between 07:45 and 08:52 BST about a black sports car and the manner it was being driven. To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Footage was released of the footballer driving dangerously Witness Christopher Jennings called 999 after driving alongside Sterling's car on the M25, and "he was shocked by what he saw", Jones said, and made clear "he sighted the defendant inhaling from the balloon". Fiona Jennings – driving on the southbound M3 – described the driving as "absolutely horrendous" and "swerving in and out of lanes", the court heard. The court heard Sterling strayed into the central reservation of the M3, exited at junction 4A, and veered off the A327, crashing into a metal gate near a layby. His vehicle sustained "substantial damage to the tyres and bodywork and was no longer capable of being driven", the court heard. Sterling was taken to Basingstoke police investigation centre by officers, where he disclosed he had a "problem with nitrous oxide", said Jones. The substance is legally sold for catering, medical and industrial purposes but is frequently used as a recreational drug, commonly known as laughing gas. Sterling complied with an impairment test, but for a blood sample, Sterling asked to obtain legal advice before making a decision. In the police sergeant's view "he was deliberately failing to provide a clear answer". Sterling was later interviewed by police with legal representation present where he accepted he had been the driver and provided no comment answers about the driving. title: Man and daughter who dumped body in canal jailed
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat England Regions Birmingham & Black Country Man and daughter who dumped body in canal jailed Image source, Family Image caption, Chereiss Bailey was described by her family as having a "beautiful heart" A man and his daughter who disposed of a woman's body in a canal, after she was murdered in a "brutal" attack by the father, have been jailed. Chereiss Bailey was found dead near a waterway off Ryders Green Road in West Bromwich, West Midlands, in October last year. John Anslow, 65, assaulted the 36-year-old victim at his home before he and Hayley-Marie Ferguson, 42, moved her body in a wheelchair and used a washing line with paving slabs attached to submerge it in the water. Anslow was jailed for life for murder with a minimum term of 26 years while Ferguson, who was convicted of assisting an offender and preventing a lawful and decent burial, was given six years in prison. Warning: This story contains details which some people may find distressing The court heard how Anslow had previous convictions for rape of children under the age of 16, both of them at knifepoint, and was previously jailed for life in 2003. He was on life licence when he attacked and killed Chereiss. The court also heard how how "trophy" pictures had been taken by Ferguson of the victim's dead body in the wheelchair, a "prop" used by Anslow even though he appeared to be "strong, fit and able". Ferguson, of Herenville Road, also made several visits to the canal to check Chereiss's body remained undiscovered, and to throw further items of building material on her. Anslow refused to attend court for the sentencing with Judge Simon Drew KC saying he had no power to make him attend. Chereiss Bailey was the mother of a young child who was six months when she died, the court heard. "We will make sure he grows up knowing exactly who she was, how much she adored him and how fiercely she was loved," the family said in a statement. Image source, West Midlands Police Image caption, John Anslow and his daughter Hayley-Marie Ferguson used John's wheelchair to move the body of Chereiss Bailey to the canal Chereiss was last seen on the afternoon of 27 September 2025. Police said CCTV footage revealed she had entered Anslow's home on Stour Street in West Bromwich on that day, after the pair met on Great Bridge Street. Anslow was "the only person left alive" who knew what happened but he refused to tell police and did not give evidence at his trial, the judge said. There was "no evidence" as to why Chereiss had been in Anslow's flat. "Nobody knows if it was a planned meeting. Chereiss was a sex worker, there was no other obvious explanation as to why she would have gone back to your flat, other than to provide you with sexual services," the judge said. He told the court Anslow had a history of luring females to isolated places and then using sexual violence against them. His victim's jaw had been broken in a "ferocious" attack and injuries inflicted on her private parts before she was killed. The following morning, Anslow cancelled his community carers and called his daughter for help. Ferguson travelled to her father's address in a taxi with slabs and claimed she was helping him with his garden, the court heard. She returned in the early hours of 29 September when the pair were caught on CCTV as they moved the body in Anslow's wheelchair. The father and daughter then stripped Chereiss and dumped her body in the canal known locally as "eight locks". title: Burnham defends inviting influencers into No 10 in PMQs row with Badenoch
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Politics Parliaments Brexit Burnham defends inviting influencers into No 10 in PMQs row with Badenoch Image source, House of Commons By Brian Wheeler , Political reporter and Emilia Belli , Political reporter Published 25 November 2026, 11:46 GMT Updated 1 hour ago Andy Burnham has defended his use of social media influencers to get the government's message across to young people in angry exchanges with Kemi Badenoch at Prime Minister's Questions. The Conservative leader called on the prime minister to apologise for "debasing his office" by allowing a content creator to record a video on the steps of Number 10, which included "vile" and "obscene" comments about women. Burnham said the video had been taken down and its creator had "rightly apologised" for it. But he said he would not apologise for engaging with influencers who "young people themselves are looking to for their information" and accused Badenoch of "sneering" at TikTokers. Image source, YouTube/@max_balegde Image caption, Max Balegde has 3.6m followers on TikTok and 640,000 on Instagram About 60 content creators were invited to a Downing Street reception last month, with videos from the event, including of Burnham DJing, subsequently emerging online. In one video, Max Balegde, whose real name is Max Trobe, mouths the words "bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets", using audio from a meme that is trending online. Badenoch said the words used were "so offensive that I will not repeat them in this House". "Disgusting and pejorative comments about women's private parts, obscene language that referred to white women as cheap meat. "This is grotesque. Labour MPs constantly tell us about their commitment to fighting violence against women and girls. Those MPs were silent yesterday, I won't be." Burnham said the Tory leader was "right to call out that, because it was not acceptable" but he would "not apologise" for engaging with young people. "She sneers at TikTokers, she sneers at influencers," he added, accusing Badenoch of "having nothing positive to say to the country" and of "constantly talking it down". The two leaders continued the argument throughout their weekly Commons clash, with Burnham saying "it's true I have spoken to influencers, and then I have to come to this House, with the opposite of influencers". Badenoch said the PM preferred to "take questions to people dancing around Downing Street", a reference to a video of another content creator dancing through Number 10 and down the stairs in an attempt to recreate a scene from the film Love, Actually. This prompted Burnham to make a jibe about "lockdown parties" in Downing Street during the Covid pandemic. Responding to the row about his now-deleted TikTok video in an Instagram post on Tuesday, Balegde said: "My content is always meant to be silly, fun, and light-hearted. "If anybody was offended by that video, I sincerely apologise." But he said "nobody was offended for weeks until revolting right-wing people tried to put this disgusting narrative on it". "And if anybody then looks at the video and is offended, I get that. So hence why I took it down because I think that is disgusting." Attendees at the event have confirmed they had to hand personal devices in and were given a phone and a camera to film with, with the footage they recorded sent to them after the event. title: NHS Grampian surgeon operated on patient while recovering from endoscopy
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Scotland Scotland Politics Scotland Business Edinburgh, Fife & East Glasgow & West Highlands & Islands NE, Orkney & Shetland South Tayside & Central NHS Grampian surgeon operated on patient while recovering from endoscopy Image caption, The unnamed surgeon took over the knee surgery from a colleague at Dr Gray's in Elgin An NHS Grampian surgeon took over a knee operation while he was recovering from a medical procedure and under the influence of drugs, the BBC has learned. The doctor, who had to be driven to Dr Gray's hospital in Elgin, allegedly stepped in because a colleague felt unable to complete the surgery. In a separate incident in the same department, it is alleged that a surgeon had a physical altercation with a registrar who suggested they were about to replace the wrong hip of a patient who was lying unconscious on the operating table. NHS Grampian said both matters were addressed at the time through the appropriate governance and employment processes, and immediate action had been taken. The allegations, first reported in The Times , external newspaper, have emerged less than two weeks after the watchdog Healthcare Improvement Scotland (HIS) published a damning report identifying serious shortcomings with NHS Grampian's leadership. 'Dramatic action' needed after NHS Grampian leaders criticised in damning report - Swinney Published 12 November The BBC has verified the first allegation involving the surgeon who was recovering from an endoscopy - a procedure where a tube with a camera attached is inserted into the body. Patients are often given a sedative for this. He took over the knee operation after being driven from his home to the hospital, because he felt he could not drive himself. A senior member of NHS Grampian's management team learned what was happening and removed him from the operating theatre. The BBC has asked NHS Grampian whether the patient had been informed of the incident. The allegations, including the claim about a separate physical altercation, were brought to the attention of former MSP Douglas Ross by a whistleblower last year. Ross then raised both incidents with NHS Grampian chief executive, Laura Skaife-Knight, at the end of October by email. The following week, Skaife-Knight replied that the health board "cannot respond to the specific issues" due to duty of care to individual employees. Ross told her the response was "unacceptable" and repeatedly asked whether NHS Grampian had been "100% open, honest and transparent" with the press and public - which Skaife-Knight declines to answer. NHS Grampian's chief officer of acute services, Geraldine Fraser, said the health board takes concerns about patient and staff safety "extremely seriously". She said: "The matters referred to were addressed at the time through the appropriate governance and employment processes, with immediate and appropriate action taken. "The organisation sought external support as part of its response and there has been continuing oversight of the service since, including to address workforce challenges relating to this service. "It would be inappropriate to comment further on any employment matters about individual staff." Speaking to the BBC, Ross said it was one of the most serious cases he had received about care in the NHS - and said Skaife-Knight had "stonewalled" him. He said: "I was surprised, it looked like they were just building up a defensive wall. They didn't want to get to the root of the problem, they just didn't want this problem being exposed.
