title: Third of young Brits have never had sex, but many are sexting and watching porn
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Health Third of young Brits have never had sex, but many are sexting and watching porn Image source, Getty Images Published 24 November 2026 By Michelle Roberts Digital health editor British people, particularly teens and young adults, are having less or no sex compared to past generations, but lots are watching porn and sexting, a major study reveals. It is the first time The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles' ( Natsal , external ) research into general public sex lives has asked about online behaviours. Half of people aged 16 to 24 have sent or received sexual images on their phone in the last year, while one in two young women and almost nine in 10 young men say they have viewed pornography. But a third of this age group have never had sex, up from a fifth in the last study 12 years ago. Adults under 45 are having less sex too, doing it twice a month, on average, down from once a week in 1990. More than one in three (37%) women said they had watched porn in the past year. Among the 16-24 year-olds, half of women and most young men (86%) said they watched it. Porn use and masturbation were less common among people who had never had sex, which the authors say suggests solo and online activity is not simply replacing in-person sex, although they cannot be sure. They didn't ask about AI or virtual relationships with romantic chatbots, but say they probably should next time. Soazig Clifton, one of the Natsal team and from University College London, said: "When we did our fieldwork in 2022-24 that seemed a little bit sci-fi. "In the future we might be looking at the impact of AI on people's sexual behaviour and on their relationships, thinking about things like AI companions." Co-researcher Prof Wendy Macdowall, from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM), says while it may be tempting to blame screen time for less sex, it's likely many other factors are involved, "especially for young people." Young people are drinking less alcohol than past generations and more live at home with their parents, for example. Rising rates of mental health conditions might also be involved, along with the Covid pandemic that stopped people going out. She says more open discussion of consent could also mean young people feel better able to decide whether and when to have sex. One in seven women (14%) reported ongoing upset with others about things done to them in their sexual past. The same proportion of men reported feeling shame about some of their sexual thoughts and desires. This fourth Natsal survey reveals trends, but cannot fully explain them. The previous one, in 2010, suggested having sex too soon was the biggest regret of young people losing their virginity. Almost two in five young women (38%) and more than one in four young men (28%) now report never having had sex. That is up from around one in five in the earlier surveys of 1990, 2000 and 2010. And among all adults who are having sex, most are doing it less often. The average used to be once a week. Now, it's fortnightly. title: Hundreds complain about I'm A Celebrity after Mariella Frostrup called AJ Odudu 'aggressive'
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Entertainment & Arts Hundreds complain about I'm A Celebrity after Mariella Frostrup called AJ Odudu 'aggressive' Image source, ITV Image caption, AJ Odudu said being called aggressive was "very harsh" and it was "an insane word" to use about her More than 800 people have complained to the media regulator about an episode of ITV reality show I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! in which Mariella Frostrup accused her campmate AJ Odudu of being "aggressive". Ofcom said 887 people had filed complaints about Sunday's episode in relation to "alleged bullying behaviour" by Frostrup towards Odudu. An Ofcom spokesperson told BBC News: "We are assessing the complaints against our rules, but are yet to decide whether or not to investigate." The pair were seen clearing the air on Tuesday, with broadcaster Frostrup saying she was "sorry for calling you aggressive" and Odudu telling her it is "a strong word to use in casual scenarios, particularly towards black women". Image source, ITV/Shutterstock Image caption, Wayne Rooney tried to repair relations between AJ Odudu (left) and Mariella Frostrup on Sunday Relations between the pair became fractious when Odudu attempted to help Frostrup cook on Saturday's episode. Tensions flared further as they and other campmates discussed their friction and the cooking arrangements the following morning. After fellow celebrities Wayne Rooney and Claire Sweeney tried to smooth the strained relationship in Sunday's episode, Frostrup told Odudu she was "making a drama out of a crisis" and that she had been "thrilled there was another person" who said they could cook. Odudu responded: "You have a funny way of showing it, that's all," before Frostrup replied: "You see, that's just aggressive and that's what keeps happening." Odudu said she felt being called aggressive was "very harsh". Both women later had tearful conversations with other campmates, with Odudu saying "aggressive" was "an insane word" to use about her, while Frostrup said the pressure in the camp was "too much". They included former BBC Radio 1 DJ Clara Amfo, who said: "Calling a black woman 'aggressive' when she is being anything else but is a classic microaggression." Singer Beverley Knight wrote: "The word 'aggressive' feeds directly into the 'angry Black woman' trope. It IS hurtful and offensive." Speaking on spin-off show I'm A Celebrity... Unpacked on Sunday, former campmate Jordan Banjo said Frostrup had handled the situation "poorly", but urged people to "give a bit of grace to Mariella, and everyone in the camp" because "you can't judge an abnormal situation by normal standards". It is "a really weird situation that every single person's in, and I'm not sure if people go at stuff with the clearest head", he said, explaining: "You get these weird breakdowns, and I think that's what we're seeing." Image source, ITV Image caption, Mariella Frostrup risked further tension when she told Odudu that "you don't take an apology well" Frostrup apologised during an amicable conversation in Tuesday's episode. Odudu told her being called "aggressive" was "triggering because in this world, navigating it as a person who looks like me can be difficult sometimes because my experience is that my emotions and my intent are completely misconstrued". She added: "In same way that you are allowed to express yourself, I can't express myself in the same way. We're not granted the same freedom. title: Fury vs Joshua fight to go ahead despite objections over 3am finish
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Wales Wales Politics Wales Business North West North East Mid South West South East Cymru Local News Fury vs Joshua fight to go ahead despite objections over 3am finish Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The all-British heavyweight fight is due to take place on 11 December Councillors have approved plans allowing December's highly anticipated Tyson Fury v Anthony Joshua fight in Cardiff to finish in the early hours. Fans in hospitality boxes at the Principality Stadium will be allowed to drink alcohol until 03:00, with the venue closing at 03:30, to align with prime time viewing in the US. Members of Cardiff Council's Licensing Sub Committee were told 130 police officers would help maintain order at the event on 11 December, with twice the number of stewards present compared to a regular sports event. A handful of residents had objected to the proposed late finish , raising concerns over noise, antisocial behaviour and public safety, but none came to the meeting. Councillors were told the event was a "big deal for the city" and would boost the Welsh capital , in terms of "revenue" and "profile." Huw Thomas, chief inspector with South Wales Police, said the challenge for officers was the length of the programme, compared with other events in the stadium, saying the fight was begin viewed by the force as a "three-day event". On Wednesday, the council meeting was told 450 out of the 1600 stewards present on the night would be dedicated to fans seated on the pitch area of the stadium. Mark Williams, Stadium Director at the Principality Stadium, said the ring walk would take place at 01:00 GMT on 12 December, with the fight expected to start at 01:30. Motson, who died in 2023, was the main commentator for BBC Sport for decades - and performed the same role for the video game series during the 90s and 00s. It is the first time the hit series, formerly known as Fifa, has featured a deceased commentator. With the permission of his widow and his son, Motson's voice has been synthesised using a combination of old recording sessions and generative AI. It will become available in FC 27 on 26 November. The legendary commentator died aged 77 in February 2023 - several months after the launch of ChatGPT and the massive growth of AI it set in train. Fred Motson told the BBC it "means an awful lot" to have his dad's voice in EA Sports FC once again. "I grew up with Fifa," he said. "I always used to tell my parents that I needed the latest console for Christmas because otherwise dad couldn't see how the game worked." Electronic Arts, which was bought for $55bn (£42bn) in August , told the BBC it paid Motson's family for the rights to use his likeness and recreate his voice, but would not disclose the financial terms of the deal. This video can not be played Watch: 'The truth will have its own power,' Burnham says Andy Burnham has told nuclear test veterans they will get "the full truth" as he confirmed plans for an investigation into the health legacy of Britain's Cold War-era atomic programme. The prime minister has ordered an independent panel to assess the potential impact of testing exercises in the 1950s and 1960s. Burnham told veterans and their families that the government would treat the process with the "utmost seriousness", later telling the Commons an interim report would be published by the 75th anniversary of the first test, in October next year. The Ministry of Defence (MoD) has for decades denied it covered up the impact of radiation on troops ordered to carry out nuclear weapons tests. A BBC Newsnight special programme heard reaction from veterans, including John Morris, a laundry operator at a nuclear test site who went on to develop cancer and lost a four-month-old son. He believes both were linked to radiation exposure. He said: "Seventy-two years ago I was an 18-year-old, sent to Christmas Island, totally unaware of what I was being led into. "I am here today and I am looking for, and sincerely hope we will get, justice." Victoria Derbyshire speaks to veterans as an independent panel is announced into health impacts Veterans who were involved in the tests, predominantly carried out in Australia and the South Pacific, have long called for a full investigation into the long-term health effects it had on them and their children. Many of the surviving veterans say they were more likely to develop a range of illnesses in the years that followed, while their descendants say they have suffered an increased risk of hereditary illnesses and fertility problems. Veterans have recounted being ordered to fly through radioactive clouds without protection, witnessing atomic explosions with nothing to shield them from the fallout, and living on sand they believe was contaminated with nuclear material. The announcement of an independent panel is the culmination of years of campaigning by the Labrats (Legacy of the Atomic Bomb: Recognition for Atomic Test Survivors) group and others, and comes 14 years after a legal challenge at the UK Supreme Court failed. Many veterans have died in the decades since the tests, but some of those still alive shared their stories with Newsnight on Tuesday. Brian Unthank says he witnessed three hydrogen bomb explosions in the Pacific without protective equipment and went to on develop multiple skin cancers. He said: "I've always wanted to get a prime minister... to stand up in Parliament and make a total, abject apology for the total mess-up of the way they treated us veterans and the families through this 74 years. "Next year is our 75th year of misery. Let's get it done today." To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. At his peak, the four-time Premier League winner was earning £325,000 a week at Chelsea . "Raheem is a huge player with a huge influence in the last few years in English football," said then Blues boss Thomas Tuchel when he signed a 27-year-old Sterling in a £50m deal in 2022. "He is at the perfect age to take responsibility around the younger players that we have and be an example. "He just needs to do what he did over the last few years and he will be a huge asset for us." Sterling enjoyed a 10-year England career, also played for Liverpool , Manchester City and Arsenal , and commanded combined transfer fees of about £100m. But his career at the top level looks to be in the balance at the age of 31 after he was handed a 12-month prison sentence, suspended for 18 months, for dangerous driving. Sterling has also been disqualified from driving for two years and ordered to carry out 100 hours of unpaid work. At an earlier hearing in September, Sterling admitted dangerous driving on a motorway before crashing a Lamborghini on 28 May. The crash caused "substantial" damage to his car and all four wheels, which prevented him from driving further, the court heard. Sterling also admitted possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, and failing to provide a specimen for analysis. To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played How Sterling went from England star to court appearance Sterling's life was touched by tragedy at a young age. Born in Kingston, Jamaica, he was just two when his father was shot dead. His mother, Nadine, was determined to give her children a safer environment to live in. She moved to England to lay a path for Sterling and his sister to join her once she had found a home and finished her education, while cleaning bathrooms and changing bedsheets in hotels to earn extra money. Sterling grew up on a housing estate in Neasden, north-west London, and spent part of his education at Vernon House, where teachers attempted to help the football-obsessed youngster with behavioural problems. In an interview with the Players' Tribune , external in 2018, Sterling said: "I was so naughty that they kicked me out of primary school. I just didn't like to listen to anyone but my mum. That was my problem." He was 10 when teacher Chris Beschi told him: "If you carry on the way you're going, by the time you're 17 you'll either be playing for England or in prison." title: Three reasons why your energy bill is so high
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat BBC Verify Three reasons why your energy bill is so high By Ben Chu , Policy and analysis correspondent and Mark Poynting , BBC Verify Published 21 July 2026 Updated 4 hours ago Bills are set to rise for millions of households, after Ofgem announced that the energy price cap will rise by 26% in January. The main reason for the increase is international gas prices, Ofgem says, but UK energy prices - particularly for electricity - have been high for some time. The price energy suppliers pay for electricity is often determined by a bidding process, with each generating company saying what it would be willing to accept to produce one unit of electricity. Once built, the cost of generating power from renewables like wind and solar is relatively low, so these typically come in with the cheapest bid. Nuclear might come next. Gas generators often have high costs because they have to buy fuel to generate electricity as well as paying a "carbon price" - a charge for emissions. The wholesale market price is set by the most expensive unit of electricity needed to meet demand. This means that even if gas only generates a small proportion of electricity at a given time it can set the overall market price. So when gas costs spike - as has happened following the wars in Ukraine and Iran - electricity prices do too. Not all electricity generation is directly priced in this way. For example, newer wind and solar farms are typically guaranteed a fixed price, irrespective of the wholesale price, while some generators enter into direct contracts with suppliers. In the first quarter of 2027, the contribution of wholesale energy costs to a typical annual household bill in Great Britain will be £1,216 - up from £604 in the first quarter of 2026 and up from £373 in the winter of 2019-20. These figures account for both electricity and gas. Northern Ireland operates on a separate system to the rest of the UK, being part of the Single Electricity Market with the Republic of Ireland. 2. Other countries have a different energy mix Analysts say that one of the reasons why energy prices are relatively high in the UK is because of the country's reliance on natural gas - leaving households exposed to gas price spikes. While renewables are generating more electricity than a decade ago, a relatively high share still comes from natural gas. In 2025 31% of the UK's electricity was produced in that way. This compares with just 3% in France, which generated the majority of its electricity - 69% - from nuclear power. The US has a higher share of natural gas in its electricity generation mix than the UK - 40% - but American wholesale gas prices are considerably lower thanks to the shale gas production boom of the past 20 years. Most UK homes also rely on gas for heating, for example, so are directly hit when gas prices rise - as well as those who use electricity. Another reason energy bills have risen in recent years is down to the cost of expanding and modernising the UK's energy networks. Those investments are partly to upgrade an ageing gas grid but also to accommodate new wind and solar farms and transmit their power to homes and businesses. The network costs contribution to a typical annual energy bill will be £417 in the first quarter of 2027, an increase of £197 from £220 in the winter of 2019-20. "We've probably underinvested in the last decade and now we're trying to catch up so there's quite a lot of spending," says Frankie Mayo, an energy analyst from Ember Energy. title: A question of trust in the NHS could be Swinney's most dangerous political moment
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Scotland Scotland Politics Scotland Business Edinburgh, Fife & East Glasgow & West Highlands & Islands NE, Orkney & Shetland South Tayside & Central A question of trust in the NHS could be Swinney's most dangerous political moment Image source, Press Association Image caption, John Swinney has asked the government's top civil servant to review how correspondence is handled Scotland political editor Published 24 November 2026 Updated 8 hours ago At its heart this is a story about trust. Trust in doctors and other health professionals at NHS Grampian to provide the highest standards of treatment and care. Trust in their managers to effectively deal with problems when they arise. And trust in the Scottish government to step in if that does not happen. What we have learned about the operation of NHS Grampian in the last two weeks raises huge questions in all of these areas. First we had a scathing report by the watchdog Healthcare Improvement Scotland, which found serious shortcomings with NHS Grampian's leadership and oversight of clinical governance. There was particular concern about patterns of repeated and avoidable harm, and the board's ability to learn from serious adverse events. Does Scotland's NHS have a revolving door problem with senior managers? Published 1 day ago Surgeon calls for corporate homicide probe over claims patients unnecessarily bled to death Published 5 days ago Man who nearly died during liver surgery at Aberdeen hospital says mistakes were made Published 4 days ago The Scottish government has sent in a support team to help the current management at NHS Grampian make improvements. Questions have been raised about the suitability of some of those appointed to carry out this work given problems they have faced in their own areas of responsibility . The watchdog's report was followed by a powerful intervention from a surgeon-turned-whistleblower who works at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary. Dr Mohammed Habib said he had been raising serious concerns about liver and pancreatic services at the hospital for 10 years. He released a previously unpublished review from 2022 that looked at 45 patients in the care of this specialist unit over the previous seven years. It said that 31 had died, and 19 of them were considered to have died of avoidable consequences of surgery or intervention. Nineteen people died and their deaths were potentially avoidable. This finding was not made public by NHS Grampian or those in the Scottish government who knew about it. This is where this story becomes political - because Dr Habib tried to get the attention of ministers. He raised his concerns with the Scottish government including, he said, writing to the first minister on three occasions. At Holyrood question time, John Swinney acknowledged that the issues raised were of the "gravest concern". He said Dr Habib's messages had received "appropriate responses" from officials. It seems they directed him to a national whistleblowing service and to the police. Image caption, Dr Habib said he wrote to the first minister on three occasions This is what, in my view, makes this potentially the most dangerous political moment for John Swinney since he took over as first minister in 2024. A surgeon writes to him because 19 people may have died unnecessarily as a result of how they were treated by the NHS and nothing seems to happen. We have since been told that Swinney's office did not make him personally aware of this correspondence. title: 'I only use the washing machine on a Sunday' - how we're keeping our energy bills down
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Business New Tech Economy Technology of Business Artificial Intelligence Africa Business Paths to Success 'I only use the washing machine on a Sunday' - how we're keeping our energy bills down By Daniel Thomas and Anuk Weerawardana , Business reporters Published 25 November 2026, 00:30 GMT Updated 2 hours ago Domestic energy prices will soar by 26% in January under the regulator Ofgem's new price cap, pushing up bills for millions of households across England, Scotland and Wales. With household budgets already under pressure, finding ways to reduce gas and electricity costs has become increasingly important. But how much difference can simple changes really make? The BBC spoke to three people about what they're doing to keep their energy costs down. Image source, Kelly Anne Harvey Image caption, Kelly Anne Harvey uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators in some rooms to save on the central heating Like many people, Kelly Anne Harvey, a building surveyor from Cleveleys near Blackpool, is worried about her energy bill going up next year. The 44-year-old, who is married with a five-year-old son, has a combined household income of £60,000. She currently pays about £154 a month for gas and electricity on a standard variable rate with Octopus, but is looking for a fixed-rate deal to offset the rise. The family fell into arrears on their energy bills a few years ago and Kelly says she won't let it happen again. To control her costs she pays by direct debit, which spreads her payments and is typically £138 cheaper a year than paying on receipt of a bill . The family uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators in some rooms so they don't have to turn the central heating on as often. They also take part in Octopus's energy saving scheme, which rewards customers who use less electricity at peak times, such as early evenings, with a free hour of energy at the weekend. "On Sunday we'll turn on the dishwasher, tumble drier, washing machine and maybe even charge our electric cars," says Kelly. Image source, Supplied Image caption, Stacey says she keeps the curtains closed "to keep the heat in" and her daughters wear thermal clothing Stacey, 40, a single mother from Bristol, says dealing with rising energy costs has felt like a "battle" recently and she's worried about 2027. The office worker, whose daughters are aged 10 and 12, is on a fixed-term tracker tariff with E.On Next, which charges rates set below the quarterly Ofgem price cap. She expects to pay £1,800 for energy this year, up £400 on last year. Stacey, who is part of the Changing Realities project at Glasgow University, which documents life for people on low incomes, has tried a number of things to control her energy costs. She's turned her central heating down from 22C to 19.5C, bought electric blankets and pays her bills by direct debit. She also leaves her curtains shut to "keep the heat in", while her daughters wear thermal clothing if it gets chilly in the house. The family is also using less hot water. "I've got girls and they're growing up and they want to spend loads of time in the shower [but] it's just not possible." title: Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Business New Tech Economy Technology of Business Artificial Intelligence Africa Business Paths to Success Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it? Image source, Getty Images By Mitchell Labiak Business reporter Published 28 October 2026 Updated 24 November 2026 Up to 20 million households in England will get a £100 payment to help with their energy bills this winter, Chancellor John Healey has announced in his Budget. For many people, the £100 on offer is a lot of money, but it's worth considering the context. A typical energy bill is forecast to jump by £443 a year from January , according to consultants Cornwall Insight. Therefore many people will still feel worse off despite the payment. Those living in properties which are in council tax bands A to D in England will get the payment, the government has said. As such, it's worth checking which council tax band your home is in , external . If you live in England, you can use the search function by typing your postcode into the box. If you get a paper council tax bill, your band will also be printed on there. The chancellor said the policy was for England but that funding would be given to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to make the payment as well. The Scottish and Welsh governments have confirmed they will use the funding to introduce equivalent or similar payment schemes. The Northern Irish government does not have the legal authority to make the £100 payments unless it agrees its budget, which it has failed to do since the start of this financial year. Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you Published 29 October How do I get the money? Will I get it if I'm a student or don't pay council tax? If you pay your council tax by direct debit, the money will be paid directly into your bank account. Those who don't pay by direct debit will be contacted by their council and given the choice to receive the £100 directly into their bank account or as credit on their council tax bill. The government will ask councils to make payments from 4 January, and the scheme will be open until the end of May. Students living in halls will not get the payment because student halls are not in council tax bands A to D. However, if you're a student living in a property that is in council tax bands A to D, as in a private home or flat let out by a landlord, then you will get the payment. Students do not pay council tax so the local authority will be responsible for finding a way to give them the payments. This is also the case for those who do not pay council tax because of another kind of exemption, or if you do pay council tax but you do it by cash or some other way. The government said it would give councils guidance on how local authorities should do this in due course. The government has said the support is to help households with the cost of energy. But the money will appear directly in people's bank accounts so you could choose to spend it on something else, while some people may choose to receive the £100 as a credit on their council tax bill. The chancellor said the money for the £100 cash payments is coming from a tax rise on banks. The surcharge on banks' corporation tax will rise from 3% to 6% for 15 months from 1 January 2027 to 31 March 2028. title: Energy bills will soar - here's how you can ease the pain
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Business New Tech Economy Technology of Business Artificial Intelligence Africa Business Paths to Success Energy bills will soar - here's how you can ease the pain Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Keeping yourself warm by wearing thick clothes, using blankets and having hot drinks can help reduce heating bills Cost of living correspondent Published 27 August 2025 Updated 3 hours ago Energy bills will soar by 26% in the new year as the war in Iran pushes up wholesale prices. Typical household bills will rise by £37 per month as Ofgem's latest price cap comes into force from January to March, but experts say it is possible to keep rising bills in check. Here are four areas to consider ahead of the increase. Ofgem's price cap, as well as suppliers' fixed deals, set a limit on the price of each unit of energy, not the total bill. So, you pay for what you use. Millions of people have cut back on their energy consumption during years of relatively high prices. With the unit price of gas, in particular, set to soar, experts say you should take a fresh look at your energy use and renew good habits. turning down the flow temperature on a combi boiler - usually indicated by a radiator icon, to make it operate more efficiently turning off the pre-heat facility on some combi boilers, which would have kept some water heated up when not in use turning down the thermostat one degree, although 18C is the recommended minimum lowering radiator valves outside of the living room These are small changes but - alongside washing clothes at 30C, blocking draughts and batch cooking - they can reduce energy use and bills. Ofgem says about five million people still pay their bill when it arrives every three months, rather than receive a monthly bill often initially based on an estimate. Taking regular meter readings, or having a smart meter, while paying by monthly direct debit solves that problem. Paying by direct debit costs significantly less than by so-called standard credit - typically £138 cheaper a year. Customers on prepayment schemes - usually people on low incomes struggling to pay bills - used to pay a higher rate than others, but now they pay slightly less than the capped direct debit variable rate. Various deals may rely on paying by direct debit or having a smart meter. Moving to a fixed energy tariff means the price you are charged per unit of gas or electricity does not change every three months, although the total bill will still vary depending on how much energy you use. The trouble is that it is very difficult to work out whether a fixed deal is a good deal at the moment, for those renewing fixed deals or looking for one for the first time. Some fixed deals are available at unit prices below the next forecast price cap level. But should energy prices fall sharply then a longer-term fix might not seem such good value compared with the price cap. So consumer group Which? also recommends paying close attention to any exit fees when picking a fixed deal. If variable prices fall below your fixed rate and you want to get out of it before the end of your agreement period, you may have to pay a hefty sum. Before you fix, consumer website MoneySavingExpert advises you look at all the deals available , not just what your own supplier is offering. The government will give a £100 payment to millions of homes to help cover winter energy costs. It will go to homes in council tax bands A to D in England, with the equivalent expected in Scotland and Wales. title: What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills?
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Business New Tech Economy Technology of Business Artificial Intelligence Africa Business Paths to Success What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills? Image source, Getty Images Published 6 August 2021 Updated 4 hours ago Energy bills are to soar in January, as prices governed by regulator Ofgem's cap rise at the coldest time of the year. The cap affects millions of people in England, Scotland and Wales, and reflects higher wholesale gas costs which have been pushed up by the US-Israel war with Iran. It means people on variable tariffs should give an accurate meter reading, ensure they are receiving all the support to which they are entitled, and take care over energy use. The energy cap fixes the maximum amount which customers on standard variable tariffs can be charged for each unit of gas and electricity used. It covers more than 20 million households in England, Wales and Scotland and is set by the regulator Ofgem every three months , external . It affects those paying by direct debit, by standard credit (they pay when they get a bill), or prepayment meters in slightly different ways. Most of the increase in the energy price cap has, and will be, driven by higher gas prices. The government's decision to temporarily remove VAT from domestic electricity bills has cut about £45 a year from a typical bill. Meanwhile, millions of households will receive a £100 automatic payment to help cover winter costs. Customers' actual bills depend on the amount of energy they use and how they pay for it. For electricity, average unit prices will go up on 1 January from 26.32p per kilowatt-hour to 32.69p Gas will increase from 7.97p per kilowatt-hour to 10.96p, higher than in the wake of the invasion of Ukraine Daily standing charges will be 54.77p for electricity and 29.65p for gas The roughly 11 million households on fixed tariffs will not see their prices change until the end of their fixed term. Ofgem regulates the energy market in England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland has a separate system. As well as how much energy you use and how you pay for it, where you live, the type of property you have, how energy efficient it is, how many people live there, and the weather all make a difference. The Ofgem cap is illustrated using "typical" household energy use in a year with a single bill for gas and electricity settled by direct debit. The vast majority of people pay their bill this way to help spread payments across the year. In July, Ofgem reduced what it believes to be a "typical" level of energy use, because many homes have cut back due to high prices in recent years while energy efficiency has improved. Its new estimate is 9,500 kWh of gas and 2,500 kWh of electricity a year. Should I take a meter reading when the energy cap changes? Submitting a meter reading when the cap changes means you are not charged for estimated usage at the wrong rate. Customers with working smart meters do not need to submit a reading as their bill is calculated automatically. Ofgem also controls standing charges, which are a fixed daily fee to cover the costs of connecting households to gas and electricity supplies. These vary slightly by region , external and payment method. title: Why tiny cars are taking off across Europe
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Business New Tech Economy Technology of Business Artificial Intelligence Africa Business Paths to Success Why tiny cars are taking off across Europe Image source, John Laurenson Image caption, Selena uses her car to get to school Selena Buse, 16, reverses her Citroën Ami out of a parking space and heads off past the school playground. Heads turn. The Ami looks pretty remarkable. Futurist or like-a-toaster depending on your point of view. But it's changed her life. "I got it because I really needed it to get to school. And I use it to visit friends on the weekends. It's indispensable in rural areas like where I live," she says. In France, you can drive a car like this from the age of 14 with a road safety certificate and eight hours training. In Italy too. In Germany and Spain it's 15, in the UK 16 , external . Because they are classed as motorised quadri-cycles. Four-wheel mopeds in other words. Registrations have risen from about 13,000 in 2019 to around 25,000 last year in France. In Europe, sales have gone from 30,000 to 60,000 in the past five years. And the Ami, launched in 2020, has really changed the image, with teenagers who now account for a quarter of all mini-car sales. In Selena's very small Citroën, we are soon rolling along at the top speed of 45km/h (28mph). For other road users, no-licence cars like this can seem like mobile traffic calming. "When I'm on faster roads and there's a lot of traffic the cars behind me sometimes honk their horns but I can't go any quicker!" Selena says. Image source, John Laurenson Image caption, Daniel Laprès says the Aixam car was "the exact solution to our problem" Another local Daniel Laprès, who drives a micro-car made by French firm and market-leader Aixam, tells me he actually pulls over to let the cars behind pass. He and his wife moved from Paris to this country village two years ago. Of Canadian nationality, he didn't swap his foreign licence for a French one in time and lost the right to drive. That didn't matter much when he was in Paris. Like many Parisians he didn't need a car. He used public transport. But that's not possible here. "We tried living off of taxis and it was in the end a disaster. Then we heard about how you could drive without having to have a licence, and it was the exact solution to our problem. Cheap, inexpensive to operate, basically no administrative formalities, you get insurance." However, Laprès feels less safe in his small car. "They're little more than tin cans on wheels, right? I mean, you're not going to be driving fast, but someone else could be." These cars are forbidden on motorways. But even on medium-fast roads, being considerably slower than the average vehicle can be a problem. "You go on national highways at your risk and peril. I did it once and I will never, ever do it again. On those roads (speed limit 110km/h), everybody is passing you, including the biggest trucks. And they come at you very fast from the rear, so it's scary," Laprès says. Daniel is 77 so fits in with the long-established market for these cars: older people living in the countryside. Traditionally the market also included quite a few people who'd lost their licences, often because of drink-driving offences. But the launch of the electric Citroën Ami in 2020 changed the customer profile and the product. "The launch of the Ami was the beginning of the transformation of the sector, with more and more electric models coming on to the market. In 2026, more than 67% of new licence-free cars are electric," says Marie-Laure Nivot, market analyst at AAA Data. Image source, AFP via Getty Im

title: Zoe Kleinman: Nobody is irreplaceable - unless you're Jensen Huang
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Tech Zoe Kleinman: Nobody is irreplaceable - unless you're Jensen Huang Image source, Getty Images By Zoe Kleinman Technology & AI editor Published 4 hours ago Remember the tech boss and his head of HR, both married to other people, who were caught on camera at a Coldplay concert with their arms wrapped around each other? Their horrified reaction went viral, and the pair both resigned . Astronomer, the firm where they both worked, said their actions had fallen short of its standards. Compared with the scandal which has engulfed Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang in recent weeks, that Coldplay kiss cam moment now feels rather tame. Huang admitted to having had an affair, reportedly with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. There were suggestions that she may have been involved in smuggling Nvidia chips into China, in breach of a US export ban. Concerns about national security had reached the desk of US President Donald Trump. There were other stories about some of Huang's relationships with female colleagues. For most of us, that would without question amount to instant, and irreversible, dismissal. But while Huang briefly left the company, he was just as swiftly reinstated, and welcomed back with open arms. As I watched footage of him being greeted with cheers, applause, high fives and a big hug back at the company's HQ on Monday, I wondered how many disgraced bosses would kill to be in his shoes. "Imagine being that Coldplay CEO reading all the comments on here about how it's OK if you're actually a good enough CEO," quipped menswear writer Derek Guy on X , external . To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO Huang has blown out of the water the old adage that nobody is irreplaceable. Despite names of potential permanent replacements being bandied around, Nvidia's board evidently reached the same conclusion - interim chief executive Colette Kress was in for less than two weeks. Well firstly, Huang is the boss of a company that has manoeuvred itself into a uniquely powerful position. Nvidia's computer chips are considered the best in the business for driving AI. Demand for its latest tech is through the roof and the firm sets its prices accordingly: Its Rubin and Vera GPUs sell for tens of thousands of dollars each, and one data centre might contain hundreds of them. So, the US AI sector relies on Nvidia, Trump is determined that the American AI industry needs to be the best in the world, and Huang is the only leader the company has ever known. He's been at the helm for 33 years and he's a computer scientist himself, renowned for being very hands-on with the development process. (Whether the boss's input is always wanted is another matter, but it's always there.) Long hours are normal and negative feedback is often given in front of everyone else. When he wants something to happen, he doesn't stop until it does: one of his early ideas was to halve the chip production cycle, in order to get one step ahead of the competition with their longer lead times for orders. Lots of experts told him it couldn't be done. Until eventually, they did it. Not only does Huang have technical expertise, he's also a charismatic figurehead, representing Nvidia at events around the world in his trademark leather jacket, rubbing shoulders with world leaders, royalty, and fellow tech bosses. For many, he's become something of a cult figure. Nvidia sometimes sells limited edition clothing at conference pop up stalls. A jumper featuring a cartoon image of Huang

title: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Business New Tech Economy Technology of Business Artificial Intelligence Africa Business Paths to Success US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Tariffs are a signature policy of Trump's office The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy. The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of country's biggest trading partners, with China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions. The move comes after the White House's investigation into the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal . China is facing the highest rate of "up to 40%", followed by Vietnam at up to 35% and then others facing either 20% or 25%. Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. The economies subjected to the so-called "Section 301" investigations were: China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India. Section 301 investigations cover the behaviour and policies of foreign governments and whether they unfairly affect US businesses, workers and consumers. Trump has repeatedly threatened or imposed tariffs during his second term, arguing the policy will boost American manufacturing and create jobs. But economists have warned import taxes can fuel inflation and push prices up for consumers and dampen global trade. title: Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Business New Tech Economy Technology of Business Artificial Intelligence Africa Business Paths to Success Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away Image source, Getty Images By Faisal Islam Economics editor Published 24 November 2026 As the market bell rang out at the Nasdaq today, the Nvidia super-bounce faded. Its shares slid and are down almost 30% over the past six months, well before the scandal involving Jensen Huang emerged earlier this month. The legitimate fears about the staying power of the tech boom pre-dated Huang's exit. They have not gone away with his return. Investors are jittery. Already Anthropic is now trading notably lower than last week's stock market flotation. The firm is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, and is being seen as a big test for continued investor appetite for the technology. President Trump's extraordinary phone call to CNBC taking credit for telling the board to reinstate Huang showed the extent of the operation - of some in Silicon Valley and within the US administration - to get him back at the helm. Among the truly astonishing reflections from President Trump was a suggestion that a two-day investigation of allegations was done and had cleared Huang of national security concerns. The President said his remarkable move to intervene was because Huang is a "national treasure" who has the next generation of AI chips "in his head". Trump says this is why he needed to act. In markets, those sceptical about the AI boom say they have never seen an operation to prop up a stock market boom like this. The bond vigilantes and short sellers are now up against Silicon Valley and the White House. Investors are trading not revenue numbers but levels of political support at a time when US voters have just delivered a backlash against AI data centres. Against this backdrop, the recovery of the central cash-generating foundation of the tech boom - Nvidia and its $400bn (£304bn) annual sales of advanced chips - looks politically fragile. This worsens other uncertainties and risks, such as Nvidia's central role in the web of financing, borrowing and cross-ownership to support every corner of the build out of data centres. The brief interim Nvidia chief executive Colette Kress had already signalled a rowing back from elements of this strategy last week. Where is that now? The fall back in Anthropic's share price also raises questions about OpenAI's planned listing on the stock exchange. Ultimately these two companies might be the most critical part of all this. They remain valuable companies with phenomenal technology relied on by the world's biggest companies. The real question is whether that reliance eases, as corporations eschew expensive frontier models for cheaper generic models offered by China. In turn, all this could be affected by the political backlash, to which the Nvidia psychodrama now contributes. It is simply not normal to have trillion dollar swings in the value of individual companies. The extraordinary volatility shows the fragile mood of investors. title: Trump faces backlash after saying he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Business New Tech Economy Technology of Business Artificial Intelligence Africa Business Paths to Success Trump faces backlash after saying he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia Jensen Huang has been reinstated as the boss of Nvidia less than two weeks after he was forced to resign following the revelations of extra marital affairs, one of which was with a suspected Chinese spy. The AI chipmaker handed its co-founder his job back, despite rejecting his initial offer to return, after pressure from US President Donald Trump. Trump said he "made the deal" with the tech giant's board to get Huang his job back, but both the president and Nvidia are facing backlash from lawmakers. But his comeback added almost $1 trillion to Nvidia's market value as its share price jumped 31%, ending ended a streak of losses on the US stock market. Nvidia's gains helped boost shares in other tech companies and financial markets in Asia while European markets were flat. However, despite Huang's return, Nvidia's share price remains down over the past month amid investor concerns about the wider AI industry and future development. But it is a dramatic return for the man dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech" to the company at the centre of the AI spending boom. Attention will soon turn to Huang's appearance before Congress next week, where the Nvidia boss will be questioned over his relationship with Alice Huang, alleged to be a spy for China, due to national security concerns. On Monday, the US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang (no relation) was chief executive. China has denied the spying allegations. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's reinstatement after originally resigning on 12 November was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers". The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk. Last Tuesday, the board explicitly said it did not intend to reinstate him following calls to do so and Huang himself stating he would be open to returning. Asia markets jump as Nvidia boss Jensen Huang reinstated after spy scandal How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy? Published 1 day ago The U-turn suggests Nvidia's board believe Huang is irreplaceable. The 63-year-old, who co-founded the company in 1993, transformed it from a chipmaker for video and computer games to the semiconductor powerhouse it is today, making the chips used in AI systems. It is now one the most valuable firms in the world. Some believed Huang's departure risked not only the future of Nvidia, but the wider AI industry given the position the company, under Huang, has in the financing of other tech firms. "They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot." "People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president added. The president was asked whether Nvidia stock

title: World Cup drove profits surge, says Marston's
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat World Cup drove profits surge, says Marston's Image source, Marston's Image caption, The New Spires in Coventry was one of the busiest Marston's pubs in the country during this summer's World Cup Pub company Marston's has said an "excellent World Cup" helped drive stronger trading as annual profits rose by nearly a fifth, despite reporting a dip in sales . The Wolverhampton-based firm, which operates more than 1,300 pubs across the UK, reported underlying pre-tax profits of £85.4m for the year to 26 September, up 18.4% from a year earlier. The company said trading was improved by new-look pubs, strong trade during this summer's football World Cup, and a partnership with Jeremy Clarkson's Hawkstone drinks brand. "For the third year running, profit is significantly up, cash flow is strong and margins have improved," said chief executive Justin Platt. The pub chain also said bookings for Christmas events were 9% ahead of the same point last year. Marston's has invested heavily in refurbishing pubs into new formats, including its sports-focused "Grandstand" venues. It plans at least 100 more conversions in the new financial year, in a bid to accelerate sales growth further. One of the busiest locals during the World Cup was The New Spires in Coventry, which reopened in March following a £400,000 makeover. Image source, Marston's Image caption, The New Spires in Coventry reopened in March following a £400,000 conversion to a "Grandstand" venue The World Cup had been "very full on," said pub partner Pip Sullivan, explaining that on one match night alone they took more than £25,000 over the bar. Marston's said it had selected the venue for investment because of its involvement with local sports teams, community groups, and charities. "We've got two football teams, four darts teams and a dominoes team," explained Sullivan, all of which had also helped bolster sales. But she recognised not all businesses were thriving. "It's been a difficult year for a lot of pubs and we have empathised as they've lost a lot of trade," she said. But investment by the company had brought the pub "back to life", she continued. "We've managed to keep as much custom as we possibly can and seen new custom." Image source, Marston's Image caption, A partnership with Jeremy Clarkson also helped drive profits, said the company Marston's also pointed to events and promotions, including darts champion Luke Humphries' darts nights and the partnership with Clarkson. "Guest satisfaction levels have improved again, thanks to the amazing work of our pub teams, whose passion and commitment keep our pubs at the heart of every local community they serve," added Platt. "Our new pub formats are performing especially well and are now a proven growth engine for the business, giving us real confidence to accelerate our investment plans in 2027." title: The shake-up facing renters as a new kind of landlord emerges
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat The shake-up facing renters as a new kind of landlord emerges By Mitch Labiak On Christmas Eve 2021, there was a knock on the door of Lexi Levens' rented flat. It was a letter sent by special delivery from the NHS nurse's landlord saying she, her husband, and four children had two months to move out. "The kids all thought it was a present arriving," she recalls. Lexi's landlord had used something known then as a Section 21 notice to evict her family without needing to give a reason. Lexi, along with the housing charity Shelter, went on to lobby the government to improve rights for renters. The Renters' Rights Act, which came into force in May this year, banned Section 21 evictions and also made it illegal to refuse to rent to people based on their status as a family with children. The landlords Lexi had been renting from at that time were typical of the English housing market - individuals who owned one or a handful of properties. Image source, Sarah Brick/Prima Magazine Image caption, Lexi Levens received a letter on Christmas Eve 2021 telling her that her family had to move out Many of these small landlords say the Renters' Rights Act has left them feeling squeezed. They also say rising interest rates, new regulations and tax changes (including some in the most recent Budget) are making things harder. Some say they are selling up. Meanwhile, according to Savills estate agents, 2026 is likely to be another record year for investment from large institutions in what is known in the property industry as build to rent (BTR). This is when big developers build blocks of flats or family housing to rent out, something that is commonplace in parts of Europe and the US. It means that rather than dealing with an individual landlord or letting agent, tenants are instead renting from larger, typically corporate, entities. So does the shift, as some believe, represent a welcome professionalisation of the UK rental sector? Or will renters increasingly miss the positive elements of the personal touch that small landlords can provide? According to the latest government survey of private landlords in England, 83% of English landlords own four properties or fewer, representing 51% of tenancies. And according to 2024 research by real estate agency Savills, around 40% rental homes in the US and Germany are owned by large institutions - be they private firms, listed companies, pension funds, or co-operatives. For the UK, Savills calculated that figure was just 3%. But the rental market is changing. The trend is most visible in England, where BTR has boomed in large cities and where regulations like the Renters' Rights Act apply, but there are BTR developments in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland too and the devolved nations are also seeing increased regulation on landlords, such as with Scotland's rent controls. Lexi is pleased with the idea of a sector with stricter rules for landlords and more professional institutions getting involved. "Anything that takes away from landlords having personal preferences [around choosing who they are or not prepared to rent to]… is a good thing," she says, adding that she believes large, corporate landlords would be less likely to act that way. Not everyone is convinced BTR landlords are better, though. Clint Stevenson, a 44-year-old magician for weddings and events, has been renting his one-bedroom flat in Ramsgate for £550 a month for two years. He says he has "the most amazing landlady" - an older woman who he regularly chats to. He sometimes walks her dog and does her shopping as well. He says he had considered renting fr

title: BBC secret filming shows dog breeder selling sick puppies for £2k each
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat BBC secret filming shows dog breeder selling sick puppies for £2k each To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played BBC secret filming shows dog breeder selling sick puppies for £2k each When Katie Thornton paid £2,000 for a nine-week-old puppy for her son, she knew it was a premium price - but was happy to be doing business with a "legit", council-approved breeder. But Ozzy the Dobermann pup started coughing in the car on the way home, and within 48 hours he was in a veterinary hospital receiving urgent treatment for pneumonia. Since then, his ongoing health problems mean Katie has racked up more than £5,000 in vet bills. A BBC investigation has found the breeder had been stripped of his five-star rating two months before selling several sick puppies, but continued to advertise as five-star. We have also found at least 15 other breeders in England advertising puppies alongside claims their star rating is higher than it really is. An expert reviewing our findings - including undercover footage we recorded at the breeder's home - said the investigation exposes a nationwide "wild west" of dog licensing, making it "easy for consumers to be scammed". The breeder has not responded to our request for comment. Image source, Katie Thornton Image caption, Katie Thornton has spent more than £5,000 on vet bills since buying Ozzy earlier this year When Katie visited the premises of Mikjulora Dobermanns in Whitby, North Yorkshire, she said the puppies' mother "didn't look very well" and was "skinny" and "shaking". But she felt the breeder, Michael Estill, was "pushing me to buy Ozzy" so she paid for him and took him home on the spot. Katie defended her decision because she had done extensive research to check the business was "legit". The mother-of-one, from Harrogate, said she had checked his licence number and read through his website and online adverts, which said he had decades of experience and a "five-star" breeding licence. In England, local councils grant breeders in their area a licence and star rating dependent on welfare standards. Vet reports for North Yorkshire Council from August and December 2025, seen by the BBC, cited dozens of concerns with Estill's business, including: "Poor" living conditions "akin to a prison", with dogs kept in cages, stacked on top of each other, that were too small for them to turn around in Puppies for sale not matching descriptions - "in other words it is a scam" Prospective buyers "very vulnerable to unsuspectingly purchasing unhealthy puppies" The business was "more or less a puppy farm masquerading as an honest and conscientious breeder. This must stop" Estill "bullied" a local vet to perform an "unnecessary" Caesarean section on one of his dogs, to reduce the time he would have to spend monitoring her His "demanding" behaviour led the practice to give him several doses of a powerful stimulant which he gave to one of his dogs at home - which the vet considered to be "negligent" He had a three-year-old dog euthanised because he suspected her to have a neurological condition, despite the vet encouraging him to get diagnostic tests and specialist treatment first. Following the reports, which concluded that the business was "functioning outside the law", the council renewed Estill's licence in January but downgraded his rating from five-star (the highest standards) to one-star (minor failings). title: Nvidia value climbs by almost $1tn and tech stocks rally after Jensen Huang returns
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Business New Tech Economy Technology of Business Artificial Intelligence Africa Business Paths to Success Nvidia value climbs by almost $1tn and tech stocks rally after Jensen Huang returns To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia Nvidia's market value rose by nearly $1 trillion as its share price skyrocketed after the tech firm reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive with immediate effect. His shock reinstatement comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned after admitting an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy, a period in which shares in the chipmaker have also fallen significantly. Nvidia shares rose by more than 31% which also lifted stock markets, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq climbing by 6.5% and the S&P 500 also rose 4.75%. Tech stocks more broadly have also rallied following large falls on Friday , with much of the rally starting in pre-market trading before Huang's return was announced. Other chipmakers experienced large increases following Monday's announcement from the Nvidia board. Shares in Micron Technology jumped 19%, while AMD shares rose nearly 7%. Tesla shares also lept up by nearly 11.5%, while other tech gains were more muted by comparison: Amazon shares were up nearly 3.5%, and Apple and Microsoft rose by less than 2%. While the surge in Nvidia shares was large and drove its market value back towards $4tn, the firm's share price remains about 21% down from a month ago. A sharp drop occurred on 4 November, after the Democrat's midterm election victory sparked fears of tougher AI regulation to come led to a broad tech stock sell-off. On Friday alone, Nvidia shares fell by 13.7% as tech stocks more broadly fell, and as Reuters reported - unconfirmed by the BBC - that the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) over its accounting practices. Nvidia is a key firm at the core of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, with the chips it makes central to the industry. Nvidia's board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate the firm's co-founder following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him, the company said - but US President Donald Trump has claimed he "convinced" the board to reinstate Huang. Kathleen Brooks, research director at brokerage firm XTB, said Huang's return showed Huang was the "godfather" of AI, and "has a talismanic influence over the sector". "Barely two weeks ago this man was ousted from the company that he founded due to serious misconduct and potential national security issues," she said. "Even though Huang did not hold special voting shares on the board, Nvidia's directors cannot see a future for the company without him." Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said Huang's reinstatement was an astonishing about-turn for Nvidia, particularly given reports of an as-yet unconfirmed SEC investigation. "This is the biggest corporate U-turn in living memory. To go from being embroiled in a spy scandal to being reinstated as the head of one of the world's most valuable companies in less than a fortnight is nothing short of remarkable," he said. "Today's stock market rebound represents a massive sigh of relief by investors. However, one cannot rule out a more conservative approach by Huang going forward. "His every move will be scrutinised by the market, and he may wish to tread more carefully to protect his integrity and ensure that Nvidia is being run responsibly." title: How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Business New Tech Economy Technology of Business Artificial Intelligence Africa Business Paths to Success How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy? Image source, Getty Images By Michael Race Business reporter Published 18 November 2026 Updated 23 November 2026 Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom. No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology. That central position prompted questions, in the aftermath of Huang's departure over revelations of extramarital affairs, over how important he was to the wider AI industry and US economy. The fact he has been handed his job back after just 11 days in a U-turn by Nvidia's board implies the top brass believe Huang is irreplaceable. Shares in the company have surged on the news of Huang's shock return, following a period of sharp declines. While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years. The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders. Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market. It is now one the most valuable firms in the world and its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier. Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on it, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him. Some suggested his departure, which was sparked by the emergence that Huang had an affair with a woman alleged to have been a spy for China, posed a risk to the wider AI industry. That was because it was unclear whether Nvidia would change strategy and potentially rein in spending - a move could have had wider implications for the US economy, but which looks unlikely now Huang has returned. The fears were sparked due to Nvidia being a key source of finance for many firms, as well as being a microchip supplier. On its journey to the top of the AI industry, it has, through Huang, created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing". Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly. The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy? That risk was perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, had called for Huang's reinstatement. Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, and backed a campaign, along with shareholders and supporters, to "Bring Jensen Back". title: I pay £250 a month for someone else to do my life admin - it's worth it
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Business New Tech Economy Technology of Business Artificial Intelligence Africa Business Paths to Success I pay £250 a month for someone else to do my life admin - it's worth it Image source, Maxine Dillon Image caption, Maxine Dillon says she needed help to get through her to-do list Maxine Dillon, a busy 44-year-old mum of two, was struggling with her life admin – the never-ending to-do list of household and personal chores. Everything from arranging for a handyman to fix something, to posting her clothing returns on Vinted, she wasn't getting around to it. "I felt like all the little jobs that I didn't have time for were mounting up," says Maxine, who is self-employed helping businesses with their use of social media. Then last year, Maxine, who lives in Mansfield in Nottinghamshire, discovered a new company called Life Laundry. Launched in 2025 by two women based in Wakefield, Yorkshire, you can pay them to do all your admin jobs for you. Such companies are known as life personal assistants, and in recent years a growing number have sprung up on both sides of the Atlantic. Maxine, who earns £32,000 a year, doesn't have a massive amount of disposable income, but she decided to start spending £250 a month for five hours' work and thinks it is worth it as it also helps reduce her "mental load" . The owners of Life Laundry, Alicia Papachristou and Jane Forbes, now look after a host of things for Maxine. Other jobs they take care of include arranging insurance, sending school emails, and managing online subscriptions. Much of the work they can do remotely, but once a month they travel to Mansfield to do the jobs that require them to be physically present. "If someone asks us what we do, we say we're life PAs [personal assistants], and we ease your overwhelm," says Forbes. Image source, Amanda Sims Nichols Image caption, Amanda says she and her husband made a conscious decision to spend more quality time with their family With such companies also increasingly available in the US, another busy working mother, Amanda Sims Nichols in Austin, Texas, has also employed a firm to look after her life admin. Amanda, who is a business consultant, has three children with her attorney husband, and decided to start paying for help with life admin after moving house, away from her family support network. She pays $2,250 (£1,750) a month for 25 hours, and says she relishes offloading regular chores including the weekly food shop and clothes washing. "Money cannot buy you everything, but it can buy you back some of your time," says the 45-year-old. The company she uses, Queen of To Do, was founded by Kate Ginsberg in 2011. She says that interest has greatly increased since the pandemic. The business now has more than 50 active users. Meanwhile, Life Laundry has 25 customers. Both companies say demand is growing for their services as people's lives become increasingly frantic. Ginsberg says that the work they do for clients can be very diverse, with no task too big or too small. Some of the larger tasks her team has faced over the years include flying from Austin to New York City to buy a desperately needed Christmas gift, and finding a new wedding location for a client with just three days' notice due to an incoming hurricane.
