title: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Business New Tech Economy Technology of Business Artificial Intelligence Africa Business Paths to Success San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing Image source, San Francisco Travel Association Image caption, The city of San Francisco is the heart of the AI sector Lauren Goldboss is busy. The owner of a small San Francisco dog-walking company, she has been hiring staff and buying vans. Fuelling the growth is her new office dog-walking service Paw Perk, popular with some local AI start-ups. Her business is an example of how the AI boom in San Francisco is benefiting other sectors. The city saw an exodus of residents during the pandemic and its downtown was weakened by remote work, but it's now enjoying a rejuvenation, with AI being the major driver. Image source, Lauren Goldboss Image caption, Lauren Goldboss walks dogs for AI workers Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange. Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up , external in San Francisco. Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts. But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn , external that this was a possibility. Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (£49bn). Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting? Published 6 days ago The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal Published 1 day ago Wealthy AI workers send San Francisco house prices soaring Published 9 July Follow the money: Who pays for the AI boom now? What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco – no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles – be preparing for a possible crash? One AI worker employed in the city is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come down… and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name. He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China. But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?" Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible". Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity. "In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great." If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south. title: Should AI be judging our credit worthiness?
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Should AI be judging our credit worthiness? Image source, Sophie Hope Image caption, Sophie Hope's credit score was hit by identity fraud Getting approval for a mortgage, a car loan or even a mobile phone contract can rest on a credit score. Sophie Hope was on the sharp end of just such a decision. "When I first checked my credit score, it was excellent. But then my mortgage application was suddenly denied by the lender because of my credit report. It was a massive shock as I'd never had bad credit. When I looked into it, my score had gone to 'very poor'," she says. It turns out, the Brighton-based nail technician and content creator, had been the victim of identity fraud. "Someone had opened accounts in my name across various catalogue sites and ordered multiple items, including a PlayStation 4 and Nike socks," she says. "Without me knowing, the debt was transferred to a secondary finance company. It spent three to four years accumulating in the background. It was only when I went to apply for a mortgage that I discovered how severely it had dragged down my credit score," she says. Image source, Donna Ford Image caption, Credit scores are "backward looking" says Funmi Olufunwa Hope's experience shows how crucial a credit score can be, but, as in her case, it does not tell the full story. "As a nation, we are overly obsessed with credit scores," says Funmi Olufunwa, a consumer finance lawyer and founder of financial education business, Hoops Finance. Three firms - Experian, Equifax and TransUnion - produce credit scores in the UK, and they all work from roughly the same data. "A credit score is backward looking. It's looking at what has happened in the past, which doesn't necessarily predict the future," says Olufunwa. "But when somebody's looking to lend you money, they're looking at what actually is affordable," she says. Traditional credit scoring systems also disadvantage "thin-file applicants" - young people and recent immigrants to the UK who won't have built up a credit history. But with more financial data available than ever before - and a growing appetite for AI to make sense of it - could artificial intelligence help lenders work out who is safe to lend to? In the US lending decisions will often hinge on a credit score from a company called FICO, which uses data from the big three credit assessment firms. But AI-powered lending firms, Upstart and Zest AI have both built businesses which offer lenders an extra option when it comes to assessing a client's credit worthiness. "Thanks to our machine-learning models that look at more than 2,500 variables, we believe we can make significantly more loans at low prices to borrowers from every demographic group," Upstart said in statement. Mortgage expert and founder and CEO of The Mortgage Mum, Sarah Tucker says: "AI has the potential to help lenders analyse much broader sets of information, identify patterns more quickly and build a more individual picture of someone's affordability and risk." If technology allows lenders to understand so-called thin-file applicants better, rather than simply applying increasingly rigid rules, Tucker believes there is "a real opportunity to improve financial inclusion". But like with many other applications of AI into everyday life, there are concerns. "Consumers need to understand what information is being used to make decisions about them, and they need to be able to challenge something when it is wrong," Tucker explains. title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Photonic chips use light instead of electrons to process data "Photonic chips are on the verge of a breakthrough," says Ton van Mol of the Dutch research institute TNO. If van Mol is right – and TNO, the European Union and the Dutch government are backing the idea with millions of euros - then the technology could be a gamechanger. The chips which run today's society, from your phone and TV, to the vast data centres meeting our insatiable desire for AI, are mostly electrical. They process data by shunting electrons around tiny circuits – a single microchip produced today can contain billions of transistors, and sizes are measured in nanometres (one nanometre is a billionth of a metre). Because they use light instead of electricity, photonic chips are faster, use less energy and generate less heat than traditional computer chips. Van Mol hopes for an acceleration in photonics similar to the one seen in electrical chips since the 1970s. "With optical chips, you are now where electronic chips were maybe 40 [or] 50 years ago." American, Taiwanese and Chinese firms dominate the computer chip industry, but Europe sees the emergence of photonic chips as a fresh opportunity to lead, on what could be, a key future technology. Which is why the European Union has committed €400m ($450m; £330m) to a project called PIX Europe , external , with the stated goal of making the continent "a global leader in emerging technology for Photonic Integrated Chips". "Europe said 'we need to have our own manufacturing in-house'," says van Mol, who is leading a key part of the programme. "We cannot depend like in the past that everything is manufactured in the US or China - that's not wise, so the [European] Chips Act was called into life, and one of the parts of the act is to build pilot lines to really bring the technology, which is now in labs, to the next stage - manufacturing." Electronic and photonic chips are produced on wafers made up of hundreds of individual chips. Factories with machines that can handle bigger wafers can churn out chips more efficiently. "[Photonic chip] manufacturing worldwide is [currently] done on wafers which are four inches (10cm) in size, and the next step is to scale-up production to a six-inch wafer," says van Mol. His team are already building a 10,000 sq m factory to produce six-inch indium phosphide wafers on the High Tech Campus in the Dutch city of Eindhoven. It's due to fully open in 2030 and will be a major step forward, not just for photonics in Europe, but around the world, according to van Mol. "That's the development TNO is going to do, in a pilot line which is really serious. "In 2030, we hope that we have a stable, reproducible, high-yield process, and then the intention is that the pilot line [opens] to industrial parties who can make commercial production out of it." Image source, ASML Image caption, Netherland's based ASML is a crucial supplier of chip-making equipment Europe does have one crucial player in the current computer chip industry - ASML. The Netherlands-based tech giant is the only company in the world able to build the machines needed to make the most sophisticated semiconductors. Which is why ASML products will sit at the heart of the pilot line in Eindhoven - it's no coincidence that van Mol's project is based around the corner from ASML's headquarters. title: How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Business New Tech Economy Technology of Business Artificial Intelligence Africa Business Paths to Success How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security? New York business correspondent Published 13 November 2026 How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang? The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US president. He had met Trump repeatedly, travelled with him to Britain and, in May, joined him on Air Force One for his trip to China. Jensen Huang wasn't just another tech billionaire seeking the president's ear. He had become an important voice in one of the biggest arguments inside the administration: how much of America's most advanced technology should be allowed to reach China. Nvidia makes the chips that power the AI revolution. Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China since 2022, believing they could help Beijing develop its military and technological capabilities. But enforcing those restrictions is difficult. Chips can be bought legally by customers in countries such as Singapore and Malaysia and then diverted to China. Chinese companies can also rent access to computing power through data centres outside the country. Jensen Huang has long argued that the restrictions are counterproductive. They shut Nvidia out of a huge market and encourage Chinese companies to develop their own alternatives. Trump appeared sympathetic to this view, allowing Nvidia to resume sales of certain chips to China last year in return for a share of the revenue, although its most advanced Blackwell chips remain off limits. But that relationship now looks rather more complicated. The allegations surrounding Jensen Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, of no relation but a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, have raised the possibility that a foreign intelligence operation was targeting not just a powerful businessman, but someone with unusually close access to the American president. US intelligence reportedly suspects Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. But the affair has opened up a much bigger question: what did the administration in Washington know, and what did it do about it? That question leads directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. His department was responsible for controlling exports of sensitive American technology. It was also being pressed to act on concerns about Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. On Thursday, Megaspeed chief executive, Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan, said the company "takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously" and is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". He said the company had co-operated with US Commerce Department inspections. A highly classified memo was shared with Lutnick about the concerns surrounding Alice Huang and Megaspeed. He resisted taking action against the company, a decision that is now under scrutiny. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was among those who reportedly questioned why Megaspeed had not been placed on the Commerce Department's blacklist. title: Robot vessels take on the dangerous work of mine hunting
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Tech Robot vessels take on the dangerous work of mine hunting Image source, Reuters Image caption, This South Korean vessel is among the ships damaged in the Strait of Hormuz Traversing the Strait of Hormuz remains one of the most dangerous trips a vessel can take. Despite assistance from the US Navy, ships are still being attacked . "To transit the Strait of Hormuz you need agreement between the captain and the crew to take the risk. You need war risk insurance. And the captain has to make the final decision," says Steve Cameron, a former merchant navy officer and maritime consultant. Missiles and drones are a threat from the air, but under the surface mines may also be lurking. "If you're a captain, you'd like to see evidence mines aren't present," Cameron adds. Modern mines rest on the seabed and detonate when they detect an acoustic or magnetic signal, triggering a pressure wave that will break the keel of a passing vessel. Others can rise through shallow waters or float, or be powered towards a target. The technology itself is not difficult or costly, but the mere threat can stop a tanker fleet from sailing. Ian McFarlane of French defence group Thales is a naval architect who knows mine warfare well. "Mines are a very cheap way of waging a naval war, as the Royal Navy is acutely aware," he says. Finding sea mines has traditionally been the job of specialist mine-hunting vessels, with crews of around 80 sailors. To keep humans out of harm's way, an increasing amount of the work is done by systems that are autonomous and monitored from the shore. They might only need 20 personnel, working in shifts on land. With the recruitment and retention challenges facing Nato navies these highly-portable robot systems are very attractive. During the 2003 Iraq war the US Navy poked around the seabed looking for mines with a torpedo-shaped robot called the Remus 100. Pinging around with sonar these little machines operated down to around 100ft depth and spared divers a difficult and dangerous task. Image source, IRGC / WANA via Reuters Image caption, Iran's military published this picture of a US submersible captured in the Gulf The latest conflict in the Gulf is testing much more capable systems. The US military is sparing with details about their mine-hunting craft, but we have seen glimpses of them. Iranian forces hauled an uncrewed US autonomous sub , external out of the waters of the Strait of Hormuz in early September. The Pentagon claimed this robot, an Extra Large Uncrewed Underwater Vehicle (XLUUV) from US autonomous defence tech venture Anduril, was a malfunctioning older device with no classified equipment on-board. Whatever its mission, no sailors were imperilled. That, says William Lupton, a naval analyst with Shephard Group, "was a drop in the ocean compared to having prisoners taken", and part of the point of uncrewed vessels. What if an uncrewed vessel is captured? Nato navies are reluctant to go into details, but computer drives can be wiped or destroyed remotely by various means. This may have taken place inside the humming circuit boards of the XLUUV seized by Iran. Cooperation between Thales, the Royal Navy, and France's Marine Nationale has produced a robot motor launch. title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Tech The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe' Image source, Rolls-Royce Image caption, A jet engine will have hundreds of turbine blades Every time you fly, an extraordinary feat of endurance occurs inside the aircraft's engines. Hidden from view inside the sleek outer nacelle are hundreds of little turbine blades that can shrug off enormous mechanical stresses and temperatures exceeding 1,500C. It is a true engineering marvel. And these hardy blades are not sculpted or cut from their material – they are grown. During the 1960s, engineers worked out how to take a molten metal alloy, cast it into the shape of a turbine blade, and then cool it very carefully from one end to the other over a matter of hours. A single crystal or grain of metal alloy forms during this process of gradual, delicate solidification. Like turning a cup of water into one big snowflake, of your own design, rather than a mini blizzard of many smaller snowflakes. "It's about as complicated as manufacturing gets," says Ben Fifoot, manufacturing engineer at Rolls-Royce, which makes turbine blades in the UK. "It's a real motivator to get out of bed in the morning." Only a handful of companies around the world can produce these single crystal turbine blades, and the process has been perfected end-to-end in just five countries, including the US and UK. Engine-makers continually vie for access to the technology. Rolls-Royce, GE and France's Safran are among the few firms that have perfected the process. In September, GE Aerospace announced , external it would acquire its turbine blade supplier for $11.75bn (£8.78bn). Neither company responded to BBC News' requests for comment but the move has been described as an effort to ensure supply of these critical components. Separately, in March, Rolls-Royce said it would invest more than £19m in its Rotherham blade casting facility. Turbine blade specialists continue to work on improving the capabilities of this little-known technology. All the while, China is desperate to prove that its engineers can produce turbine blades of the same quality as those in the West. Who will come out on top? "Demand for [turbine blades] is huge. So few companies have managed to do it, which does give it this kind of magical aura," says Bill Sweetman, an aviation industry writer and consultant. He suspects GE Aerospace's recent move is about securing reliability and predictability in the notoriously volatile aircraft manufacturing supply chain. Image source, Rolls-Royce Image caption, The casts play a crucial part in the cooling process But why is the single crystal casting process, which has been around for decades now, still so specialist? To grow one of these blades, asserts Fifoot, is to "fight the laws of the universe". This is because each molten blade would naturally cool into a solid object consisting of many small grains of metal alloy, all jumbled together. But you don't want a crumbly sugar cube, you want a perfect diamond. Getting a single crystal to grow into the shape of the blade instead isn't just a matter of cooling the molten version down slowly, the process also uses a bizarre trick called a pigtail. The pigtail is a small spiral at one end of the blade. Fifoot says that, at the beginning of the cooling process, this spiral "chokes" the flow of solidifying crystals so that just one takes over. A bit like a hairpin corner in an F1 race right before the finish line – one driver can take the lead here and go on to win. title: Graduates are managing AI - but are they learning much else?
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Tech Graduates are managing AI - but are they learning much else? Image source, Lotte Underwood Image caption, Managing AI agents is a big part of Lotte Underwood's job Recent university graduate Lotte Underwood is a public relations executive with a twist - she spends more time using AI than actually doing PR. Underwood, 25, joined London-based PR agency Fight or Flight in November last year, in the new role of "AI associate" after completing a degree and then a masters in marketing. She's part of a recently established, dedicated AI team that has built around 30 AI agents. Specific tasks include industry research, client reporting, media interview preparation, helping clients create clearer briefs, and image generation. A big part of Underwood's job is to manage those agents, check their outputs and feed those to the team members who are dealing directly with clients and the media. Another key responsibility of hers is to monitor how clients appear in the responses from AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and others. "A huge part is being in client meetings and calls to work out what is actually going to be most helpful from these agents," says Underwood. AI is seen as one of the main factors behind graduate job cuts , but companies are also creating dedicated AI-specific graduate roles like Underwood's. Dillan Patel, for example, joined engineering software company Stride 18 months ago as an intern. A business management graduate, he was put to work developing an internal chatbot designed to capture the knowledge of a senior staff member transitioning into retirement. Patel, 24, is now an AI automation analyst, tasked with developing further internal agents to provide specific information to individual teams, while also identifying which manual or repetitive tasks across the company could be done by AI. "My role focuses on finding practical ways to use technology, automation, data and AI to improve how we operate," says Coventry-based Patel. Image source, ArvatoConnect Image caption, Debra Maxwell is looking for "AI disruptors" Such AI savvy graduates are also in demand from companies like ArvatoConnect, an outsourced contact centre company. CEO Debra Maxwell says the company's usual graduate intake is on hold this year, but she plans to resume it next year with a bigger focus on AI. "We would be looking for more AI-disruptor type roles, where you can challenge us as an organisation to think more holistically about where AI can be applied and where we could grow our business from," says London-based Maxwell. "We see our graduates as not filling administrative roles, but actually adding value to the organisation in a different way." Maxwell adds: "For example, one of our recent graduates is using AI to do deep dives on specific markets, and provide more information for when we're bidding [for new contracts]. It's basically giving him a more rounded role." title: Salon owner's chore woes prompt idea for new app
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat England Regions Gloucestershire Salon owner's chore woes prompt idea for new app Image source, Marie King Image caption, Marie King says TradeOff now has 300 registered users who are exchanging all manner of services A salon owner says she was inspired to set up a skill-swapping app after she and her clients spent time "moaning" about chores and admin. Marie King, who owns Finishing Touches Beauty, in Leckhampton, Cheltenham, set up Trade Off UK after some of her clients expressed concerns they could no longer afford to get their nails done, and so they began exchanging tasks like cooking for beauty treatments. "I'd be more than happy to spend an extra hour in the salon doing somebody's nails, rather than going home and cooking a lasagne for my kids," she said. Rebecca O'Meegan, who exchanged skills with King and other app users, said: "It felt good to be useful and it was lovely for it to be reciprocated". Published 8 hours ago 'Hope' as Black Friday ad ban launches in UK first Published 8 hours ago 'Deep-seated cultural issues' within police force Published 20 hours ago King said that with the cost-of-living crisis, luxuries, like beauty treatments, were often "the first thing" those finding it difficult would drop. "I was like, 'Oh, that's a bit of a shame', and then in the next sentence, I'd be saying things like, 'I've got to bake a birthday cake tonight, which I am terrible at'," she said. "It was just a conversation, and then [the client] said, 'I'll bake the cake for you, and then you do my nails'." King said the app, which launched in June, now has 300 registered users, with a "community" of people offering everything from catering and baking to PT sessions and dog walking. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Nail technician services are among the skills being offered out to TradeOff users, along with gardening, weeding, sewing, and filling out forms "A lot of people will say, 'I don't have any skills', and then you start talking to them and then they say about their hobbies," King said, adding things like sewing, gardening and weeding are all skills. "I'm not very good at sewing, it would take me probably three times the amount of time to actually do it, where if I just gave it to someone, it'd probably take them half an hour. "You're making valuable time for yourself by giving that job to somebody." O'Meegan, a former operations manager, said she wanted to help King and offered to do a report for King in exchange for getting her nails done, but it "grew into so much more". "It was something that came easily to me, I was really happy to help, and then when Marie said, 'I'll exchange it for your nails', which I was having done once a month, it seemed like such an obvious thing to do," O'Meegan said. "I've dog sat, I've mowed a lawn, and I've offered decluttering services." However, anyone wanting to take part in such service exchanges are still subject to tax rules, according to HMRC. King confirmed HMRC's rules still applied to her bartering and exchanging services, even when no money changed hands, but the £1,000 annual trading allowance might apply to individuals. She also said exchanged skills could be a hobby or an interest and not related to someone's business, which could exempt them. A HMRC spokesperson said: "Businesses exchanging goods or services may still have income tax, VAT and record-keeping obligations and should check the rules that apply to them on GOV.UK." title: Badenoch challenges Burnham over university fees for EU students
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Politics Parliaments Brexit Badenoch challenges Burnham over university fees for EU students Image source, UK Parliament By Becky Morton Political reporter Published 17 minutes ago Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has challenged Andy Burnham over whether EU students in the UK could pay lower university tuition fees as part of his deal with the bloc. The prime minister insisted the issue of tuition fees was "a separate deal", with discussions on this continuing. Asked whether he could rule out EU students paying the same fees as British students, Burnham said this was "the European negotiating position" and "won't be put on the table". At a UK-EU summit last Friday, the two sides agreed a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth travel scheme . A joint statement said they would also work towards a "supplementing" agreement on tuition fees for EU students in the UK and British students in the EU, with negotiations concluding within six months. EU sources had earlier suggested the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students. But the UK has insisted the wider deal will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can reach an agreement on tuition fees. Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says Published 4 days ago What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start? Published 4 days ago At the moment, EU students at UK universities generally pay the same fees as international students, ranging from £11,400 to £38,000. For British undergraduate students tuition fees are currently capped at £9,790 a year. Universities have raised concerns that capping EU student fees at the same level could cost hundreds of millions a year, at a time when the sector is struggling financially. At Prime Minister's Questions, Badenoch asked Burnham who would pick up the bill if EU and British students paid the same fees, "cash-strapped universities or cash-strapped taxpayers?" In response, the PM said "the deal on tuition fees is not done", adding: "We will take that conversation forward always rightfully mindful of the challenges faced by higher education." Pressed over whether the EU would still sign his wider deal if he refused to cut fees for European students, Burnham said legislation introduced in Parliament on Thursday would set a date for the implementation of deals on food, emissions and a youth experience scheme. He added: "We will continue discussions with the European Union on the question of tuition fees." Asked if he would rule out EU students paying the same tuition fees as British students, Burnham replied: "She is referring to the European negotiating position, which is not the British negotiating position. "That has not been put on the table. It won't be put on the table." However, the prime minister's response leaves open the possibility that tuition fees could still be reduced for EU students, even if they are not capped at the same level as for British students. title: None of UK government's £2.5bn steel package spent in Wales, figures show
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Wales Wales Politics Wales Business North West North East Mid South West South East Cymru Local News None of UK government's £2.5bn steel package spent in Wales, figures show Image source, Getty Images/Matthew Horwood Image caption, A new electric furnace is due to be up and running at Port Talbot by the end of 2027 Wales has not received any money from the UK government's £2.5bn steel industry investment plan announced in February 2025, according to figures obtained through a Freedom of Information (FOI) request. The UK's Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade confirmed that "the government has not spent, nor allocated, nor committed any money under the £2.5bn commitment in Wales". The FOI was obtained by the Liberal Democrats, whose Welsh leader David Chadwick said that Welsh Labour MPs needed to "demand a fair share for Welsh steel now, before their own government spends the rest". The UK government said it had "invested extensively to secure steelmaking" in Port Talbot. The department's FOI response noted that £751m had been invested in the nationalised British Steel site in Scunthorpe and another £172m spent stepping in to save Specialist Steel UK in south Yorkshire and the West Midlands. Wales is home to Port Talbot's Tata Steel site, the largest steelworks in the UK, which closed its last blast furnace in September 2024 . A new electric furnace is due to be up and running at the site by the end of 2027, but there are concerns it could now be delayed due to grid connection issues . Speaking on 24 February 2025, following the announcement of the new steel investment plan, the then-Labour energy minister Sarah Jones said the £2.5bn "could benefit regions across the UK - like Scunthorpe, Rotherham, Redcar, Yorkshire and Port Talbot - which have a strong history of steel production". She added the money would be "spent on initiatives that would give the industry a long future - such as supporting the transition to electric arc furnaces or other improvements in UK capabilities". As of October, the UK government had spent £751m on sustaining British Steel in Scunthorpe, since ministers took it into full public ownership in July 2025. But the National Audit Office warned in March that spending on the site could exceed £1.5bn by 2028 , external . The £172m spent on Specialist Steel UK has funded things such as ongoing site safety and wages, since the company entered liquidation in August 2026. In September the UK government announced plans to nationalise the business , which has sites in south Yorkshire and the West Midlands. In September 2024, Tata Steel in Port Talbot was promised a £500m subsidy from the UK government towards a new electric arc furnace, alongside a commitment by Tata Steel to invest £700m of its own money . That investment was a conditional grant, not part of the £2.5bn steel industry investment fund announced in 2025. title: Ministers ask public for views on changing age of consent
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Politics Parliaments Brexit Ministers ask public for views on changing age of consent Image source, Getty Images By Kate Whannel Political reporter Published 24 November 2026 Updated 4 hours ago The UK government is inviting the public to share its views as ministers consider whether or not to stagger the age of consent. Currently adults of any age are legally able to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds, however some campaigners have argued that different limits should apply, depending on the age gap between the people involved. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted survivors, parents, young people, victim support services and the wider public "to share their experiences and inform this process". The government is also announcing that new limits on non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) will come into force months earlier than originally planned. The measures, which will now become law in January 2027, invalidate confidentiality clauses in new NDAs if they prevent employees from talking about harassment or discrimination or victims from reporting criminal conduct. The changes will also cover NDAs signed outside of the workplace and mean that even if victims of crime have signed an NDA, it would not stop them from speaking to anyone, including the media, about what had happened. Zelda Perkins, founder of the group Can't Buy My Silence, said the laws would "uphold the integrity of a legal system that must never be used to protect perpetrators at the expense of victims". Perkins has previously said she felt forced to sign an NDA, which prevented her talking about abuse carried out by her former boss, the film producer Harvey Weinstein. In 2017, she told the BBC she had tried to speak out about Weinstein's behaviour towards a co-worker but was told by lawyers she "didn't have a chance" due to signing an NDA. Writing in the Guardian, , external Burnham said: "NDAs should protect sensitive business information or commercial interests. They should not protect powerful men who have abused, harassed or discriminated against women." He added he would "keep working to make sure NDAs can't be used to silence others, including freelancers employees and fans who experience abuse". The government has also said it is actively looking at whether to change the law on the age of consent and that it will ask members of the public for their opinions in the new year. Burnham said: "I not only want to make sure victims can speak out about their own abuse, but also have the opportunity to challenge the status quo." The Close the Consent Gap campaign is proposing that 16-year-olds would not be able to have a sexual relationship with anyone older than 19, and that someone aged 17 would be prohibited from a relationship with anyone older than 20. Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Equalities Minister Bridget Phillipson said there is a question about what is considered "appropriate" for 16 and 17-year-olds. She said: "I think some of the cases that we've seen where you have a huge age difference and often where you've got a much older adult man, who is in a position of authority, having a relationship with a 16 or 17-year-old makes me feel deeply uncomfortable." She added: "I think we do need to look at that, but it's complex, we want to look at all of the options and we'll be setting out more and making sure survivors, women's groups and others are involved in that so we can get this right." title: Disability benefit review calls for closer link with claimant costs
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Politics Parliaments Brexit Disability benefit review calls for closer link with claimant costs Image source, Getty Images By Becky Morton Political reporter Published 24 November 2026 The main disability benefit in England and Wales should be more closely linked to the additional costs claimants face, a government-commissioned review has recommended. The review on personal independence payment (Pip) led by Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms said the current system was "not appropriate" for claimants who do not have any extra costs arising from their condition. The government has committed to some of its recommendations, including fast-track payments for people with severe conditions, but will not respond fully to the plans until early next year. The Conservatives said the year-long review was a "compete farce" and showed a "complete absence of substance". Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately added: "All we have is a report that tinkers around the edges of a failed system". Pip is available to people with long-term physical or mental health conditions who have difficulty doing every day tasks, regardless of whether they work, and it is not linked to income or savings. The number of people claiming Pip in England and Wales has roughly doubled since 2019 to around four million. The Timms review was set up last year by Sir Keir Starmer's government after his aborted attempt to cut welfare spending, which was derailed by the threat of a rebellion by Labour MPs. It was co-produced with groups representing disabled people, who had a role in drafting the report. Key takeaways from the Timms review into Pip disability benefit Published 1 day ago Giving a statement in the House of Commons, Sir Stephen said Pip "remains a vital source of support" but the system was "no longer fit for purpose". He told MPs the current assessment process was "dehumanising" and focused on "what somebody cannot do", rather than "supporting independence". The government has committed to a recommendation that people receiving end-of-life care or with "serious, well-evidenced conditions" would receive payments without a full assessment. It has also agreed to reduce "unnecessary" reviews for people whose conditions are lifelong or unlikely to improve. Under the report's proposals, cash payments would remain alongside better support to signpost people into education or employment, although claimants could choose to exchange part of their payment for practical services instead. In the longer-term, the report recommends changes to the assessment process that look at someone's real-life additional costs and individual needs, focusing on "how people can live the life they want to live, rather than what they cannot do". It proposes "improved" questions to understand the extra costs people face, although claimants would not be asked to calculate their costs or provide receipts. Currently eligibility for Pip is based on how difficult people find carrying out everyday tasks, with two levels of payment available. But the review suggests future payment options could include bands more closely linked to extra costs. The report says its approach is likely to lead to a "rebalancing" of payments, indicating that some claimants could lose out under a new system, either receiving less than they do currently or not qualifying for payments at all. "Those with the highest additional costs, and so the most significant needs, should receive the most support," it says. title: Tory plan to sell off London's Victorian jails to raise £1.4bn
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Politics Parliaments Brexit Tory plan to sell off London's Victorian jails to raise £1.4bn Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Wandsworth prison, in south London, is among those that would be closed by the Conservatives London's Victorian jails should be closed down and the land sold off to property developers, the Conservatives have said, as they launched a plan to massively increase prison places in England and Wales. Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy said the move could raise £1.4bn to help fund the construction of "modern, purpose-built prisons elsewhere". He claimed a Tory government would create 50,000 extra prison places within "six or seven years" and end Labour's early release scheme in its first term in office. Labour said nobody would believe the Tory plan "given they only added a dismal 500 places while in government". Speaking at a press conference in Westminster, Timothy said it was "fair" to highlight the previous Conservartive government's failure to significantly increase prison places. But he insisted "this is a different generation of Conservative politicians under Kemi [Badenoch]'s leadership, and we are making different choices". Unlike previous Tory-led administrations, they were being "explicit" about which departmental budgets they would cut - international aid, culture and the Cabinet Office - to fund new prisons, he added. Under the Tory plans, an extra £2bn a year would go to the Ministry of Justice to pay for what Timothy called "the largest prison-building programme in modern history". "It will let us end Labour's early release schemes once and for all, and bring back shorter sentences to lock up criminals like shoplifters," he added. He told the audience "prison works" because it kept criminals off the street and he was "deeply sceptical about talk of rehabilitation". The Conservatives are setting up a commission, chaired by former minister Sir Simon Clarke, to work out how to speed up the building of new prisons by removing obstacles in the planning, procurement and judicial systems. The review would also look at "how to get out of the old Victorian prison estate, starting in London," Timothy said in his speech. Prisons such as Wormwood Scrubs, Brixton, Wandsworth and Pentonville "sit on some of the most valuable land in the world," he added. "Getting out of these sites is not only a good idea in itself. It will free up land for residential use in London, where our housing shortage is most acute." He said the Tories would "strip back regulations, like affordable housing quotas and listed status, to give the land its highest realisable value," but it would only sell off the land when "market conditions are favourable to the taxpayer". This could raise more than £1.4bn which would go towards building new prisons "in addition to" the 50,000 places the party has already pledged to build , he added. The previous Conservative government set out plans to sell off London's Victorian jails, but this was ditched by Boris Johnson's administration in 2019 because of the shortage of prison places. A Labour spokesperson said: "When it comes to leaving the prisons estate on the verge of collapse, the Tories are guilty as charged. "They should be apologising to victims of crime who they badly let down rather than spending time lecturing others who are fixing the mess they left behind." The Labour government was "delivering the largest prison building programme since the Victorian era so victims of crime get the justice they deserve," they added. title: Reform bid to oust presiding officer fails after its Senedd boycott ends
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Wales Wales Politics Wales Business North West North East Mid South West South East Cymru Local News Reform bid to oust presiding officer fails after its Senedd boycott ends Image source, Senedd Cymru Image caption, Huw Irranca-Davies gave a passionate speech to the Senedd in defence of his role An attempt by Reform UK to remove the Senedd's presiding officer has failed, following a passionate speech to the Welsh Parliament by Huw Irranca-Davies. Members of the Senedd (MSs) rejected Reform's motion by 55 votes to 29. Earlier the party ended a two-week boycott of most proceedings in the chamber after one of them, Joe Martin, was banned from speaking and told to apologise for remarks about immigration. Irranca-Davies, whose title is Llywydd, said his duty was to "apply the rules fairly and impartially". Reform's Llyr Powell said: "If you had a problem with what Joe Martin said, debate him, don't shut him down." A source close to Irranca-Davies had "wholly refuted" Reform's accusations he had changed his mind during negotiations about Martin returning to the debating chamber. Irranca-Davies had ruled that a claim by Martin - that white people were being "replaced" - broke the rules because it was "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive". Responding to Reform's attempt to remove him on Tuesday evening, the presiding office gave a long and passionate speech in defence of his role, which prompted a standing ovation from the other Cardiff Bay parties. "The duty of the chair is not to please, it is not to flatter, not to avoid controversy, it is to apply the rules fairly and impartially, irrespective of pressure, of popularity or of political consequence," he said. "Parliamentary privilege has never meant that anything goes, it has never meant speech without standards, it has never meant rights without responsibilities. "Without rules, eventually it is only the loudest voices that are heard, without rules intimidation begins to replace persuasion, without rules scrutiny deteriorates into shouting." After losing the vote, which Reform had no realistic prospect of winning, its Welsh leader Helen Jenner said it was "now clear that the establishment parties are content to see a Member of this Senedd silenced". "We will continue to fight for the rights of elected members to represent their constituents as they see fit," she said. To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Reform MSs walked into the debating chamber together ahead of First Minister's Questions on Tuesday afternoon At the start of the afternoon session, without announcing an end to their protest, Reform MSs walked into the debating chamber together ahead of First Minister's Questions on Tuesday afternoon. Martin was not among them. Jenner began her contribution by asking Senedd members: "Did you miss us? "It's been a little bit duller without us in here." In an answer to a question from her, First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said "it's good of her to turn up today", and later accused her party of "chucking their toys out of the pram". Reform is the biggest opposition group in the Senedd, but its members have stayed away from plenary sessions - full meetings in the debating chamber - since 11 November . The party said it had left its seats empty during debates and questions to Welsh government ministers because it was standing up for free speech. The boycott began after Irranca-Davies told Martin his comments had broken the Senedd's rules, and he would not be called to speak until he apologised. Image source, Senedd Cymru Image ca

title: Prince William meets Burnham on first Downing Street visit
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat UK England N. Ireland Scotland Wales Isle of Man Guernsey Jersey Politics Local News Prince William meets Burnham on first Downing Street visit To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Prince William meets Burnham in first visit to Downing Street Royal correspondent , Reporting from Downing Street Published 24 November 2026 The Prince of Wales walked up Downing Street for the first time, as he visited Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Behind the black door of No 10, Prince William is expected to talk to Burnham about issues including homelessness, with both the prime minister and the prince committed to tackling the problem. The two men have met before, such as the Omani state visit last month, where they both attended the state banquets at Windsor Castle. But this is the first visit that Prince William has made to meet a serving prime minister in Downing Street - and the first senior royal to visit No 10 since the late Queen Elizabeth II came here in 2012. Image caption, Prince William and Andy Burnham are expected to discuss homelessness Burnham has a weekly meeting with the prince's father, the King, and they are said to have developed a friendly relationship. By convention, the Prince of Wales is meant to meet the prime minister once a year, but not necessarily at Downing Street. He met Sir Keir Starmer last year at Kensington Palace. Prince William's appearance on a chilly morning will be seen as another step in his apprenticeship as a future king and head of state. And it's expected that next year the prince will be carrying out more diplomatic visits at the request of the government. The two men have a shared interest in addressing homelessness, which is expected to be among the topics under discussion. Prince William has his Homewards project, which is testing ideas to reduce homelessness in six areas of the UK. Burnham has pledged to give rough sleepers in England support to get off the streets by Christmas. The prince and Andy Burnham have been active supporters of the Big Issue magazine which supports the homeless. Both of the men have a reputation for being relaxed communicators in public, with Prince William recently getting plaudits for his unpompous appearance on the Graham Norton Show. It's a relatively rare sight to see a royal in the prime minister's domain. The late Queen Elizabeth II visited in 1985 to commemorate the 250th anniversary of Downing Street and was here in 2012, when David Cameron was prime minister. But there were no royal visitors during the intervening years, when Theresa May, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss, Rishi Sunak and Keir Starmer were prime ministers. The then Prince Charles and Princess Diana visited 10 Downing Street in November 1989, for a dinner hosted by then then prime minister, Margaret Thatcher. title: State failing to keep public safe, warns victims' commissioner
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Politics Parliaments Brexit State failing to keep public safe, warns victims' commissioner Image caption, Claire Waxman said the state was failing in its duty to keep the public safe The victims' commissioner for England and Wales has said the state is failing to keep the public safe, as she urged Andy Burnham to put the justice system at the heart of his 10-year plan for government. Claire Waxman told the BBC that she would press the prime minister to commit to reforms in the decade-long blueprint, which he is set to unveil next month. She warned that the early release of prisoners to ease overcrowding in jails, along with long waits in the courts, had eroded the trust of crime victims to come forward. It comes as the commissioner's latest annual survey of victims, to be published on Tuesday, found many had experienced long waits for justice. Nearly half of respondents whose case went to a crown court had seen their trial postponed, with over a quarter reporting the trial had taken place more than a year after it was originally scheduled. Almost half of the respondents to the survey also said they were dissatisfied with communication from the police. Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast, Waxman said the results showed victims were being failed "at every point". The commissioner, who said she was due to meet Burnham in the coming weeks, said she wanted him to put a "real commitment to reforming our criminal justice system" as part of his 10-year plan. "It's been under-invested and mismanaged for so many years. That's why we're in the state that we're in," she added. She warned: "It can't continue. Otherwise I will be in a position as the victims' commissioner to have to be very honest and open with victims publicly to say there's no point coming forward and reporting." Asked whether the state was failing in its duty to keep the public safe, she replied: "It is failing", adding that the early release of prisoners could lead to the potentially risky offenders being supervised by a probation service "on its knees". Waxman also criticised the government's handling of the scheme, saying that victims needed further reassurance that they would be kept safe when offenders are let out under the programme to ease overcrowding in jails. Around 5,000 prisoners are scheduled to eventually be released under the latest version of the scheme , the need for which Labour has blamed on a lack of investment in prisons under the Conservatives. Waxman said that letters sent over the summer to warn victims ahead of releases had been "very poor" and lacked detail on how offenders were going to be risk-assessed prior to being let out early. She said she was "still waiting to see" data about the impact of releases on the ground, adding it had been around a year since the last meeting of the National Criminal Justice Board, an oversight body for the justice system. As part of the latest survey, the commissioner is recommending that all crime victims should receive a victim identifier number to track their progress through the criminal justice system. The survey report will argue this would improve coordination between different agencies, as well as allowing victims to monitor when they will access the various legal rights they have under the Victims' Code. It will also call for an "end-to-end" review of how victims navigate the system, similar to recent reviews that have focused on sentencing or the courts. title: My approach to EU is pragmatic, says Burnham
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Politics Parliaments Brexit My approach to EU is pragmatic, says Burnham Image source, House of Commons Image caption, Burnham made the comments while addressing MPs in parliament on Monday The prime minister has said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything", as he outlined his agreement with the bloc to MPs. Andy Burnham told the Commons there was "no fixed destination" on talks to explore closer ties with the European Union, adding it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum. After several former prime ministers urged him to not reopen the Brexit debate, Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" - and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour. Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015". At a summit on Friday, Burnham agreed a new deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. He also finalised the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU and said both sides will "brainstorm" options for their long-term relationship. He has previously suggested potential options for the future could include rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership. However, he has ruled out major changes to the UK-EU relationship before the next general election, saying he will stick to Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement. Speaking in the Commons on Monday, Conservative MP Sir Edward Leigh said the "reset" with the EU is "a prelude to the prime minister's sincere desire to rejoin the EU and have another referendum" and risked leading to another Scottish independence referendum. Burnham replied to the Gainsborough MP: "It's not a prelude to anything. It's a pragmatic approach and it will continue to be a pragmatic approach. "If it's in Britain's national interest, I will recommend it to this House. If it is not, then I won't. There is no fixed opinion here. There is no fixed destination. "Europe could change again in the next year, 18 months, and we'll have to obviously watch how life changes. But where Britain can make progress, surely we should make progress." The prime minister also told MPs the government's forthcoming 10-year plan for the country will consider the "range of options for our long-term relationship with our largest market" - the EU. MPs heard the "plan for Britain" will be published next month and the results of the "informal exchanges of ideas" with the EU will be presented around the time of their next joint summit. To laughter from the opposition benches, Burnham said: "So there will be no banging on about Europe from this side or a running commentary." The words echoed those used by Conservative former Prime Minister Lord Cameron in 2006 . Burnham went on to say there would be a "calm, constructive and pragmatic consideration of what is in Britain's interests in the long-term", adding "always the British people will be the boss and they will decide what comes next". Conservative MP Sir Bernard Jenkin asked Burnham to "give a clear and unequivocal statement that it would be unthinkable for any prime minister to try and take the UK back into the EU without a referendum". Burnham replied to the Harwich and North Essex MP : "Yes, it would be unthinkable." Theresa May 'aghast' at Burnham's EU plans and says 'Brexit is done' Published 3 days ago 'Move on!' title: Welsh Greens back plan to separate from English party
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Wales Wales Politics Wales Business North West North East Mid South West South East Cymru Local News Welsh Greens back plan to separate from English party Image source, Press Association Image caption, Welsh Greens leader Anthony Slaughter says the decision to part from Zack Polanski's party is a "positive step" Members of the Green Party in Wales have backed plans to split from their colleagues in England and form their own independent party. The Welsh Green conference in Bangor on Sunday supported a motion setting out a timetable to split by 2035, subject to a further vote of party members. BBC Wales was told the changes were endorsed by a large majority of members who attended. Welsh party leader Anthony Slaughter said the move was a "positive step" at a "transformational time" for Welsh Greens. A Green Party spokesperson said there would be no short-term changes. Whether the Welsh Greens should start their own party, as the Scottish Greens did in 1990, has been on the agenda for some time. While the Welsh section is referred to as a "party", it is legally part of the same organisation as the Greens in England. Slaughter, who will stand down as the party's Welsh leader later this year , previously described the formation of a separate party as "inevitable". The decision comes six months after the Greens won their first ever seats in the Welsh Parliament, winning one each in Caerdydd Penarth and Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf. Slaughter said that "devolved decision-making has always been at the heart of our party values, with decisions being made closest to those affected as is practical". "With two new members of the Senedd, and membership that has tripled over the last 18 months, this decision is a positive step at a transformational time for Welsh Greens. "The motion sets out a detailed process for member engagement on the shape of an independent Welsh party, which will be subject to a final vote of members," he added. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Paul Rock and Anthony Slaughter won the Greens' first two seats at a Welsh Parliament election in May Monmouthshire council Green cabinet member, Ian Chandler, said: "We believe in being a more independent party that can be more focused on Welsh issues. "It will help us to grow even further as a movement in Wales and as an electoral force." The party is in the midst of a Welsh leadership contest, as Slaughter has come to the end of the period of time that he is able to stand. The party confirmed Ian Chandler and Debra Cooper were the candidates for the leadership contest, with the vote expected to close in December. A Green Party spokesperson said: "This was a decision for the members of the Wales Green Party, and has been part of an ongoing conversation over many years. We are a party that believes in devolved decision-making, so that decisions can be made closest to those affected as is practical. "There will be no short-term changes as the proposal voted for today sets out a process to 2035 for transition to independence, that will still be subject to a final vote of members." title: Burnham does not view Wales as an equal nation, claims first minister
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Wales Wales Politics Wales Business North West North East Mid South West South East Cymru Local News Burnham does not view Wales as an equal nation, claims first minister Image source, Reuters Image caption, Andy Burnham says he is "not persuaded" by the case for more powers The first minister says he wants an urgent meeting with the prime minister after Andy Burnham rejected calls to give more powers to the Welsh government. Rhun ap Iorwerth said he was "deeply disappointed" and that Burnham "does not view Wales as an equal nation". Meanwhile, Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates urged Burnham to "negotiate around a table" with ap Iorwerth. In a letter to ap Iorwerth last week, the prime minister said he was "not persuaded" by the case to devolve policing and justice , the Crown Estate and rail infrastructure to Wales. Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock said the UK government believed "devolution must be about more than transferring powers from one government to another". Trade union body TUC Cymru said it was disappointing calls for further devolution had been "dismissed without any discussion". In a written statement to Senedd members, the first minister said: "The refusal to even explore the devolution of the crown estate, justice and policing, and rail infrastructure proves that the prime minister does not view Wales as an equal nation. "The case in favour of Wales having control over these areas of responsibility - just like Scotland - is compelling. Several commissions have argued for the devolution of justice and policing, yet the UK government seemingly prefers to put unionist ideology before hard evidence. "This government is not interested in more powers for power's sake. The current settlement is unfair, unjust and unsustainable." Image source, Matthew Horwood/Press Association Image caption, Rhun ap Iorwerth is Plaid Cymru leader and first minister of Wales In a letter to the prime minister, ap Iorwerth asked the prime minister to reconsider the work of previous reports on the issue. He said he would "welcome an urgent meeting with you to discuss the evidence and agree a substantive way forward". Meanwhile, Skates called on the Welsh and UK governments to continue talks on the devolution of powers. He called for "greater detail" on why further devolution of policing was not happening, and said he will be meeting with Burnham himself. Welsh Labour has not dropped calls for the devolution of justice, the Crown Estate and rail investment. "You negotiate around a table," he said. "And you don't walk away when work needs to continue. Devolution is a process, not an event and Welsh Labour's position remains clear that we support further devolution to and within Wales." Skates continued: "Devolution of employment support is vital in getting to grips with the crisis of youth unemployment. The devolution of innovation funding will help strengthen the economy. "Devolution of youth justice will lead to better integration of youth services and social services and the justice system. "We need action as fast as possible in bringing these powers to Wales and in ensuring they go to the right people and places. "On policing, progress is being made, but I want greater detail over why full devolution is not happening as part of the current reforms." Meanwhile, TUC Cymru's general secretary, Laura Doel, said: "Our focus is on securing the powers and resources needed to improve outcomes for working people. That must include fair funding for Wales. title: Theresa May 'aghast' at Burnham's EU plans and says 'Brexit is done'
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Politics Parliaments Brexit Theresa May 'aghast' at Burnham's EU plans and says 'Brexit is done' To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Watch: Theresa May says Burnham must 'accept Brexit and move on' Political editor Published 22 November 2026 Former Prime Minister Theresa May has warned Andy Burnham he should "move on" from Brexit, telling the BBC she is "aghast" the prime minister could be considering rejoining the EU. At the Brussels summit this week the PM said he wanted to "brainstorm" options for the future relationship between Britain and the trading bloc. In an exclusive interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Baroness May, who spent three years negotiating an EU exit deal, said: "Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on." May claimed Burnham "wants to pat people on the head" by suggesting: "Remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn't you. So have another go and come out with the right answer." May, who was prime minister between 2016 and 2019 urged Burnham to "just get on with" today's challenges rather than re-opening the conversation around being in the European Union. Before becoming PM she had campaigned to stay in the EU, but when in No 10 she presided over three years of tortuous negotiations. The deal she concluded was rejected by MPs. She was forced to quit and was replaced by Boris Johnson in 2019. Telling Burnham to "move on", she said: "What I saw was that the extent of those negotiations, the hours that have to be put in - it's across the whole of government. "It's not just prime ministerial time, cabinet ministers' time, officials' time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations. Because you have to negotiate hard in order to make sure that you're getting out what you want. "And that's one of the reasons why I look slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham is talking about, further negotiations of going into the EU. And also we, as a country, we voted for Brexit. "When I was prime minister I was very clear, we should deliver on that vote. So I'm afraid my message to him really is, you know, people voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on." Warning against another vote, May told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "I almost think this is what Andy Burnham is saying to the British people, sort of patting them on the head. "He wants to pat them on their head and say, you know what, remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn't you? So have another go and come out with the right answer. "Or what he thinks is the right answer. But as I say, let's just get on with making sure the UK is as strong economically, in security terms, and in terms of opportunities for people as it can be." Speaking to the BBC back in 2023 , she said the UK "would have been better off if MPs had backed her deal to leave the European Union". Her deal had included the prospect of a vote on holding a second referendum, and a vote on a temporary customs union, as well as promises on workers' rights and environmental protection. May claimed her plan was thwarted by "hardline" Brexit-supporting MPs and those who wanted to remain in the EU. 'Move on!' Former PMs pile in with advice for Andy Burnham, but will he listen? title: Tories would scrap Burnham's deal with EU, deputy leader says
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Politics Parliaments Brexit Tories would scrap Burnham's deal with EU, deputy leader says Image source, PA Media Image caption, Conservative deputy leader Alex Burghart says the deal will not lead to lower prices in shops Conservative deputy leader Alex Burghart has said his party would scrap the deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday, if the Tories win the next general election. The agreement signed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham covers a youth travel scheme, emissions trading and British food exports. The government has argued scrapping most checks on British food exports will cut costs for businesses and could bring down prices for shoppers. Burghart told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme the deal was "a dog's dinner", which would not lead to lower prices in the shops and would mean the UK "gives up our ability to set our own rules". Under the agreement, the UK will also have to follow some EU regulations. Burghart acknowledged the deal would reduce some trade "friction" but he said it would put a "massive additional burden on the 90% of farmers that don't do any trade with the EU". Pressed over whether the Conservatives were committed to scrapping the deal if the party wins the next general election, Burghart said: "I don't think that there will be positive outcomes, and yes, we would scrap it." He added: "I also don't think it is a good idea for a country like Britain to hand over control of its rules to another power and have no say over how those rules are created right into the future." Food retailers have welcomed the deal, saying it will cut costs, reduce bureaucracy and remove barriers to trade. However, they have not committed to cutting prices as a direct result of the changes. The British Retail Consortium has said it does not expect prices on supermarket shelves to fall in response to the deal. It has said upward pressures on prices remain and will not be alleviated by the agreement. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband insisted the deal "reduces pressure on trading costs", adding: "They're the things that go into prices." "It will reduce the costs that the retailers face, all of that Brexit red tape, millions of forms that they were having to fill in, frankly pointlessly, as a result of the bad deal that we had," he told the BBC. Challenged that the UK was also giving up some powers to set regulations itself, Miliband argued businesses were already "rule takers" from Brussels if they wanted to sell into the European market. "So they have to abide by the rules of the European Union. But at the same time, because we are not integrated into that market for food and agricultural products, they have to fill in a whole bunch of forms... to confirm that they're observing the right standards, which is frankly crackers," he said.
