title: UK should only rejoin EU if it innovates on technology, Blair warns
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Politics Parliaments Brexit UK should only rejoin EU if it innovates on technology, Blair warns Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Tony Blair, a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, has said "Brexit was a real mistake" Former prime minister Sir Tony Blair has said Britain should only rejoin the European Union if it reforms - and allows more innovation on technology. Speaking to The Sunday Times , external , Sir Tony said: "I was painted as saying Britain should just go back and rejoin - I'm not saying that - it's heavily conditioned." Sir Tony was a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, and told the paper: "I do think Brexit was a real mistake." But he added the debate was different now than it was in 2016. Referencing the need for technology innovation, he said Europe could and "probably are" moving in the wrong direction. He said: "The problem if we go back and join Europe is that; I can't say that the technology revolution is the single biggest thing, and then if Europe moves in the wrong direction on technology innovation, which they might do and presently probably are doing, that it's a good idea for Britain to rejoin. That's what's changed in this last ten years." He argued Britain should have an ambition to reform the EU. But he added that we have to be "prepared to walk away from that negotiation" and need to make our own economy and tech sector strong. Prime Minister Andy Burnham this week agreed what he called a "win-win" deal with the EU. The agreement covered British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also announced that the trading bloc and the UK are launching a digital partnership, including areas like artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum technology. The EU and Britain "have enormous potential to innovate together", she added. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, PM Andy Burnham met EU chief Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa in Brussels on Friday On artificial intelligence, Sir Tony said that "AI is like fire - it can cook your food and burn your house down". Sir Tony said the risks of AI are "very considerable" and that tech "can be used for good or bad". He added other countries are "coming up and rising and there is a dynamism and energy in them" and he fears the UK is "not as dynamic and energetic as we need to be". Burnham was in Brussels on Friday to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU - which originally began under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer. European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK. The prime minister added that beyond the deal "we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship". He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are. He fell short of discussing whether the UK could rejoin the EU. title: Capita shares plunge 70% as boss quits after civil service pensions failure
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Business New Tech Economy Technology of Business Artificial Intelligence Africa Business Paths to Success Capita shares plunge 70% as boss quits after civil service pensions failure Image source, Getty Images Published 23 November 2026 Shares in outsourcing business Capita have sunk 70% after its boss stepped down as the saga over public sector pensions drags on. Chief executive Adolfo Hernandez has agreed with the firm's board to leave with "immediate effect", admitting that the company had "not delivered" for members of the UK's Civil Service pension scheme. The scheme, which manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK, has been mired in controversy, with tens of thousands of retiring civil servants having faced delays receiving their pension payments. Capita has cut its profit forecast, partly due to the problems surrounding the scheme, and says it plans to raise £190m to bolster its finances. Capita took over the administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme in December last year. One Cabinet Office minister last month labelled the company's progress in improving how it runs the scheme as "abysmal". Hernandez, who will be replaced by current chief financial officer Pablo Andres, said: "I am proud of the groundwork we have laid and the progress we have made under my leadership. "Of course, within that I recognise that we have not delivered the service that members of the Civil Service pension scheme deserve." Bereaved families will not face tax bill over pension delays under new rules Published 29 October Capita said it was now expecting its underlying operating profit for 2027 to be hit by between £85m and £95m, having previously expected a reduction of up to £40m. This comes from the extra cost of the recovery plan, as well the loss of two other "major" contracts in the defence and pension solutions divisions. Capita said it was planning an equity raise of £190m in the first half of next year, in order for the company to "move forward from a more stable foundation". The backlog of payments from the civil service pension scheme has been described as "hell" by people who have failed to receive money, some of whom retired early owing to ill health. BBC Radio 4's Money Box programme has been hearing from people caught up in the saga , and left in financial hardship. Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs the Public Accounts Committee of MPs, said: "The mishandling of the civil service pension scheme has caused severe hardship for some scheme members, particularly considerably delayed bereavement payments. "The PAC will continue to pursue this dreadful matter and we can only hope that the new acting Chief Executive, Pablo Andres, will be able to get a grip on this whole affair." Until the end of November 2025, the scheme was administered by a company called MyCSP. The contract was taken over by Capita on 1 December, in a seven-year deal worth £239m. "Capita inherited an enormous backlog of cases which needed addressing and failed to deliver on the promised automation, AI and digital tools needed to manage the 1.7 million members," said Russ Mould, investment director at investment platform AJ Bell. "Efforts to fix the problems failed and government deadlines came and went, leading to the withholding of milestone payments, with the National Audit Office probing the contract. "Capita needs to steady the ship quickly, and hope that the modest recent improvements in service levels on the civil service scheme can be built upon." Ireland Scotland Wales Isle of Man Guernsey Jersey Politics Local News MP criticises company ownership register plans Image source, Reuters Image caption, MP Sir Andrew Mitchell has campaigned for publicly accessible registers of who owns companies in British Overseas Territories and Crown Dependencies Plans to improve transparency over company ownership in Guernsey and Jersey have come under criticism from a Westminster MP, who says they "do not go nearly far enough". The comments come after Guernsey , external and Jersey , external set out plans to allow approved applicants access to information about who owns or controls companies when investigating suspected financial crime. Sir Andrew Mitchell, who has campaigned for greater scrutiny of company ownership, said there were "immediate indications" the proposals would fall short. He said limits on access to the information could mean "national security threats may remain entirely invisible to investigators". The plans follow a joint commitment made by Guernsey, Jersey and the Isle of Man in December 2023 to increase transparency around company ownership and help tackle money laundering, terrorist financing and other financial crime. Currently, information about who ultimately owns or controls companies is generally only available to law enforcement agencies, regulators and certain regulated businesses carrying out anti-money laundering checks. The new proposals would allow journalists, academics and other applicants with a legitimate interest to apply for access. Sir Andrew said investigators could face a "catch-22" because they may need access to the register to prove wrongdoing in the first place. He also said he understood applicants would have to show they had been unable to find the information elsewhere, arguing: "This entirely defeats the object of a register." Jersey's consultation response says applicants would be expected to show that "all reasonable alternative sources have been exhausted" before access was granted. Guernsey's published response does not explicitly set out the same requirement. He said: "Access should be open to those from other jurisdictions, for example those in the global south from whom much of the world's dirty money was stolen in the first place." Sir Andrew also questioned whether users would have to pay to access the information, saying: "This information should be free at the point of access." He said the proposals should eventually lead to fully public registers. Both the governments of Guernsey and Jersey rejected Sir Andrew's criticism and said they continue to meet international standards in tackling financial crime. A Government of Jersey spokesperson said the concerns raised by him "do not accurately reflect what is in Jersey's consultation response paper". They said the policy was intended to help Jersey meet its international commitments while maintaining "a fair, proportionate, and effective transparency framework". They added: "Jersey continues to meet international standards for transparency and countering money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing." Deputy Andrew Niles, from Guernsey's Policy & Resources Committee, rejected Sir Andrew's criticism and pointed to a positive 2025 assessment of the island's efforts to tackle financial crime , external . title: Staff gagging clauses lifted ahead of probe into culture at data watchdog

Ministers are expected to publish the details of how an independent review of the working environment at the Information Commission will be carried out next week. It follows the departure of the watchdog's boss five months ago amid allegations of sexually inappropriate behaviour. A government spokesperson confirmed that NDAs, known as "gagging clauses", would not be enforced by the Information Commission, saying the regulator "will not use the terms of any agreement to prevent people from participating in the review". The government "will set out further details on the review, including its terms of reference and the independent reviewer, shortly", they added. The Information Commission is one of the UK's most high-profile regulators charged with the crucial task of regulating AI, data protection and Freedom of Information requests. It recently won a court battle with TikTok after it fined the social media platform £12.7m for misusing children's data, and has penalised bodies including the Ministry of Defence after an email blunder exposed the details of interpreters fleeing Afghanistan. But it has been without permanent leadership since Information Commissioner John Edwards resigned earlier this year . It came after an independent investigation found a "case to answer" over reports of alleged inappropriate behaviour towards staff including claims of sexual harassment. The Information Commission said the investigation found Edwards' behaviour "fell short of the conduct expected from a public official". In a resignation statement posted on his LinkedIn page in June, Edwards said he disagreed with how the investigation had been carried out but accepted his position had "become untenable". The statement continued: "I have accepted that there have been occasions where I exercised poor judgement and made attempts at humour that were inappropriate and caused offence." Freedom of Information requests have found that since the start of Edwards' tenure in 2022 to the present, 16 current and former employees have signed non-disclosure or confidentiality clauses costing more than £354,000. Nine of those , external included a "non-derogatory clause" which legally prevents employees from making negative comments publicly. While this is a small proportion of the more than 1,000 staff employed by the commissioner, government advice stipulates that public bodies should only use confidentiality clauses "when necessary" and that they should "not seek to stifle or discourage staff from raising concerns". Since 2025, new laws also mean they cannot be used to silence employees subjected to harassment or abuse. After Edwards' departure, the government announced a review , external into the Commission's culture and governance, with the then-Secretary of State for Science, Innovation and Technology Liz Kendall telling a committee of MPs she was "absolutely appalled at what the independent investigator found - sexual harassment and bullying". Five months later, the investigation has not begun. In recent weeks, the two major civil service unions, the PCS and FDA, have pushed for an external examination of the events leading up to Edwards' resignation in meetings with government officials. title: Spitting Image co-creator Peter Fluck dies aged 85
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Entertainment & Arts Spitting Image co-creator Peter Fluck dies aged 85 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Peter Fluck alongside a satirical puppet of Margaret Thatcher that he created, pictured in 1992 Peter Fluck, co-creator of award-winning satirical puppet show Spitting Image, has died aged 85. His family said he died in the early hours of Saturday at home in Cornwall, following a recent illness. Spitting Image was immensely popular and sometimes controversial, running from 1984-1996 across 18 seasons, and featured puppet caricatures of celebrities, politicians and royals, including former Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother. "The spirit that Spitting Image brought to the country was epoch defining," a family statement said. "With Roger Law ('Luck and Flaw'), he brought a unique cutting edge to caricaturing that later evolved into a production company that created the TV series Spitting Image," it added. "Peter's creative life continued after the series for many years from his studio in Cornwall. He was a private man who eschewed fame and attention." The show won several awards, including one Bafta TV award and two Emmys and at its peak drew an audience of 15 million. Fluck was born in Cambridge in 1941, and created the show alongside childhood friend Roger Law, who he met while studying at Cambridge School of Art. Following school, both Fluck and Law moved to London and set up as freelance illustrators, and in 1976 set up their partnership 'Luck and Flaw' back in Cambridge. Image source, Dunsmore/Express/Hulton Archive/Getty Images Image caption, Peter Fluck (left) and Roger Law in 1984 "You could say we took the traditional newspaper editorial cartoon and put it on the screen," Fluck told ArtCornwall in an interview , external in 2006. He described the show as being shown "at the difficult time of 10 o'clock on a Sunday night when all politicians should have been in bed". Many of the characters included parodies of Thatcher's cabinet, with Douglas Hurd depicted with "Mr Whippy ice cream" hair, and her successor John Major caricatured as a dull, grey puppet with a penchant for peas. "We did get quite a lot of approaches from politicians for their puppet to be made, because if you didn't appear as a puppet on Spitting Image you hadn't made it as a politician," Fluck said in an interview in 2011. , external It was eventually axed by ITV because of declining audience numbers. In a statement, the broadcaster said Fluck's "creative contribution to TV satire is simply unrivalled... his cutting edge puppetry and caricature skills, alongside the show's sharp and always shrewdly observed humour, became a defining part of the cultural zeitgeist. "Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with his family and friends at this very sad time." When he stepped away from the show, Fluck moved to Cornwall and focused his art on ceramics, printmaking and mobiles. In 2018, Law donated his entire archive of Spitting Images to Cambridge University. The collection - including original scripts, puppet moulds, drawings and recordings - was conserved and held in the library. text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat UK England N. Ireland Scotland Wales Isle of Man Guernsey Jersey Politics Local News Scouts say they face £1m tourist tax cost for overnight trips Image source, Press Association By Henry Moore Published 21 November 2026 Scout groups are warning they could face an additional annual bill of £1m as a result of the government's proposed tourist tax for England. The overnight levy would allow councils and regional authorities to charge visitors an additional fee for their accommodation, including campsites, raising money to be spent on local services. The increased cost from the Visitors Levy could price some young people out of joining Scout camps and other trips, the group said. Dwayne Fields, the UK's Chief Scout, has called for youth groups to be exempted and said the charity - which sees more than 1.4m overnight stays a year - would be "firmly opposed to any proposal that would see local mayors tax Scouts and other voluntary youth organisations". The Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government told the BBC that local leaders who introduce the levy "will have the option to exempt certain types of accommodation in their areas, including accommodation which is often used for trips by youth groups like Scouts and Girl Guides - such as camping pitches". They added money raised from the levy will "stay local and be invested in the visitor experience and local growth including in high streets, parks and events". Labour mayors have indicated they would cap the levy at 5% but the legislation contains no maximum limit. In a statement, the Scout Association said the tax, if set at 5% across the country, could cost the charity £1.04m a year and force volunteers to deal with onerous paperwork. They worked this out by assuming the levy would be set at 5% for all the 1,423,344 annual overnight stays across Squirrels, Beavers, Cubs, Scouts, Explorers and volunteers. In a statement, Fields said: "We strongly support investment being made available to strengthen local communities. Well-crafted legislation can unlock that opportunity. "But we are firmly opposed to any proposal that would see local mayors tax Scouts and other voluntary youth organisations for camping trips that equip young people with skills for life, while burdening volunteers with the role of unpaid government tax collectors." Image source, Simon Carter Image caption, Manchester Scout volunteer Chris Taylor called the proposals "madness" Chris Taylor, lead volunteer for Greater Manchester East Scout County, called the levy a "tent tax" and branded it "madness". Referring to the levy being applied to the Linnet Clough campsite run by his group in Stockport, he said: "Our members spent nearly 25,000 nights away from home last year, and a 5% levy would add over £11,000 a year to the cost of their camps and sleepovers." He added: "On top of that, and as a charity, we'd have to employ someone just to collect the tax and send returns to the Mayor's office. That's another £7,000 a year, and that's just one campsite - there are plenty more across Manchester." Labour MP Gareth Snell, who challenged ministers when the levy was debated in the House of Commons , said Scouts "provide some of the most memorable experiences for young people up and down the country." The Stoke-on-Trent Central MP called on the government to take the decision out of mayors' hands and ensure Scout camps are exempted from the bill. title: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Politics Parliaments Brexit UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham Image source, EPA/Shutterstock Image caption, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Council President Antonio Costa join hands at the end of a press conference during the EU-UK summit in Brussels Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year. European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people". Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week. Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer. The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028. The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker. To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played Watch: What the new UK-EU deal could mean for European relations The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe. The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030. A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block. There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU. On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data. Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel". The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028. title: First minister 'gobsmacked' by Burnham's devolution calls rejection
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Wales Wales Politics Wales Business North West North East Mid South West South East Cymru Local News First minister 'gobsmacked' by Burnham's devolution calls rejection Image source, Matthew Horwood/Getty Images Image caption, Rhun ap Iorwerth says the decision shows Westminster is disregarding the views of the people of Wales Wales political correspondent Published 20 November 2026 Updated 21 November 2026 Wales' First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth has declared he is "gobsmacked" after calls for powers to be handed from Westminster to Cardiff were snubbed. In a letter to ap Iorwerth, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was "not persuaded" by the case to devolve responsibilities over policing and justice, the Crown Estate and rail infrastructure to Wales. The first minister told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast that "this is about Westminster saying, we decide, it doesn't matter what the people of Wales think". Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock said the changes would have led to "destabilisation and fragmentation and disintegration". The first minister said what Kinnock said was there had been a lot of engagement across the departments of the UK government in Whitehall, and not with Wales, and they "then decided that they didn't want Wales to be empowered on policing injustice in the Crown Estates and on rail". He added: "I'm pretty gobsmacked by that, but at least one positive here is that we are seeing very clearly now that this is about Westminster saying, 'we decide, it doesn't matter what the people of Wales think'. "We heard the secretary of state there saying that there's a variety of views on devolution. "Yes, those views in Wales on one side and those in Westminster and Whitehall on the other." Kinnock said there was "a bold and ambitious offer on the table there to work with the first minister on a whole range of issues around devolving fiscal powers, employment support, reindustrialisation, innovation and regional empowerment". This was "to get power and growth closer to regional areas of Wales and local areas and communities", he said. Former First Minister Mark Drakeford, said he was "disappointed" by Burnham's decision. He said: "I don't think he quite understands how different things are when you talk about a country, with the Senedd. "We'll just have to keep going within the Labour party internally to make the cause, to persuade people." Ap Iorwerth earlier accused Burnham of "turning his back on devolution" and not viewing Wales as an "equal nation" after he decided against devolving the powers. Burnham's position is also at odds with Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates who reiterated his position at a party conference last weekend that policing and the Crown Estate should be devolved. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Andy Burnham said he wanted to see "one Labour team" at the Welsh Labour Conference The letter, seen by BBC Wales, follows what had been seen as positive talks between the prime minister and first minister in Glasgow last month. Asked about the prime minister's position on devolving policing following that meeting, ap Iorwerth said: "I think instinctively the prime minister wants to go there." Burnham had also previously said he was "open" to the idea. However, in his letter on Friday, Burnham said he was "not persuaded" by the case. "The integrated England and Wales policing system is essential to maintaining interoperability, enabling seamless cross-border working and ensuring forces in Wales can draw on national and specialist capabilities," Burnham said. title: Fine Gael leader wants border poll criteria talks with London
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat World Africa Asia Australia Europe Latin America Middle East US & Canada Fine Gael leader wants border poll criteria talks with London Image source, PA Image caption, Simon Harris is due to become taoiseach in November 2027 The leader of Fine Gael, Simon Harris, has said that a conversation between the British and Irish governments over the criteria for a border poll would be "useful". Harris, who is the tánaiste (Irish deputy prime minister), said he and the Taoiseach (Irish PM) Micheál Martin are "aligned" on the issue. He said there could be joint Irish government proposals on Irish unity preparation "by the end of the year". It comes after the Northern Ireland Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said that it is his job to decide when to bring forward a border poll and that he does not "detect a mood" for it. Harris said that it would be good if the British and Irish governments "could at least have a shared understanding as to what criteria may be considered". "At a point in time Dublin and London having a conversation about criteria is useful and is also just good governance," he said Speaking on BBC News NI's The View programme, he added: "British Irish relations have never been better". Under the Good Friday Agreement, Bryant as the NI Secretary of State, decides whether to call a border poll or not. On Thursday morning Sir Chris told RTÉ's Morning Ireland programme , external he would "only bring forward a border poll at such time" as he thinks the people of Northern Ireland would want to join a united Ireland "I don't detect that that is the situation now," he added. Asked what criteria he will use to decide if the mood to join a united Ireland appears likely, he said "when it appears likely". Image source, PA Image caption, Under the Good Friday Agreement, Bryant as the NI Secretary of State decides whether to call a border poll or not When asked why the Irish government should not have a role, Sir Chris said that the Good Friday Agreement is very clear that it's a matter for the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland and that is agreed by the two governments as co-guarantors. In response, the tánaiste said that "the commitment in the Good Friday Agreement is exactly as Chris Bryant read out, there's no disputing of that. But the application of that is something that would be good to have a greater understanding". Simon Harris sent a letter to some party leaders in Northern Ireland asking for their views after his party, Fine Gael, published proposals on how to prepare for Irish unity . The "blueprint" on Irish unity came days after the taoiseach, leader of Fianna Fáil, circulated a document to his parliamentary party laying out his own thoughts on how to prepare for a united Ireland . He proposed setting up a new "initiative" on the constitutional future of the island of Ireland. The two parties are both in a coalition government, supported by a number of Independent TDs (members of the Irish parliament) in Dublin. Simon Harris is due to become taoiseach in November 2027, under the coalition's rotating taoiseach agreement. He added that he had already had discussions with the Taoiseach Micheál Martin. Harris said that people don't need to agree with the outcome to wish to partake in discussions on Irish unity. "We no longer live on an island where one constitutional view has greater value than the other. We left that behind us as a people when we voted for the Good Friday Agreement,"he said. title: Key takeaways from the Timms review into Pip disability benefit
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat UK England N. Ireland Scotland Wales Isle of Man Guernsey Jersey Politics Local News Key takeaways from the Timms review into Pip disability benefit Image source, Getty Images By Michael Buchanan Social affairs correspondent Published 24 November 2026 A review of the main disability benefit has recommended an overhaul of the system to allow disabled people to "achieve better health, higher living standards and greater independence". The report proposes both short and long terms changes to the personal independence payment (Pip) for claimants in England and Wales. The benefit is claimed by four million people and is available to people whether they are in work or unemployed. Its aim is to help with the additional costs of being disabled. Pip benefit system 'not fit for purpose' and 'dehumanising' assessments should change, review finds - follow live This is the first review of the benefit since it was introduced in 2013. More than 40,000 disabled people engaged with the process with more than 90% of them saying they'd had a negative experience while applying for Pip, describing it as stressful, dehumanising or psychologically damaging. The review concludes the Pip process is "not fit for purpose" and calls for a fundamental redesign. While the review was chaired by Sir Stephen Timms, the disability minister, the experience of disabled people is clear throughout the review. A fast-track process should be introduced for two types of claimants. Those with terminal illnesses should get the fastest route to an award to ensure their lives are as comfortable as possible. Those who have severe conditions that are well-evidenced and unlikely to change over time, and whose impact on daily living is clear, should also receive the benefit without a full assessment. Any subsequent review should avoid unnecessary reassessments. Other claimants will have to go through an updated initial assessment. This will examine how a person's condition affects their daily life – functions, barriers, and needs that are currently not being met. This assessment will determine entitlement to the benefit. It will also decide the level of cash award, which will remain the bedrock of the benefit. Optional referrals to support services should also be offered but this will be voluntary and a refusal to engage with them should not affect the benefit level. A new set of questions should be developed to better understand the extra costs a person faces, but will not ask them to calculate costs or provide receipts. The system should recognise fluctuating and cumulative needs and produce decisions that are consistent and be robust against misuse. The 28-day hospitalisation rule – which sees Pip payments suspended if someone spends more than 28 days as an inpatient – should also be reviewed as claimants find it can cause unnecessary stress and can delay discharges from hospitals. The inquiry was not set up to find savings in the system despite the fact that spending on Pip is forecast to cost more than £40bn by 2030. In the year before the Covid pandemic, Pip cost £16.3bn when adjusted for inflation to today's prices. The report acknowledges that since the benefit was introduced, the number of people receiving disability benefits has increased across every age group for both men and women. Most of the increase has happened between 2019 and 2024, with the sharpest increases among young people aged 16-19, people in their 30s and women, whose rates of benefit receipt have risen faster than men's. title: No 10 North will face greater scrutiny as Burnham's 10-year plan looms
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Politics Parliaments Brexit No 10 North will face greater scrutiny as Burnham's 10-year plan looms By Jack Fenwick Political correspondent Published 24 November 2026 The work of Andy Burnham's new Number 10 North office in Manchester has been kept largely away from the headlines since it opened in July. But the officials based there are mainly focused on two soon-to-be-published documents that could go on to define his time as prime minister. The first is Burnham's 10-year plan, which is due next month, and which the prime minister says will lay out a path "to where I believe we all want Britain to be". The second is the 'rewiring the state' white paper, a detailed policy document that will follow in the new year and should give the clearest indication yet of what power Burnham hopes to move away from Westminster to other parts of the country. But despite Burnham insisting his new Manchester team will be the "engine room" of change, others in government question how much difference they can really make. There's talk among Labour MPs that the 10-year plan, which has also had significant input from Westminster departments, will not go as far as the prime minister had hoped. But one official who has seen elements of the plan said it will be "pretty weighty" and include "quite a lot of radicalism". Number 10 North has been focused on how the plan can deliver on Burnham's pledge to achieve "growth in every postcode". One major theme is expected to be reindustrialisation, with advisers exploring how to attract businesses to less prosperous towns and cities. Staff in Manchester are also said to be looking at what parts of the country may not see growth through reindustrialisation – such as some rural and coastal areas – and what the alternative offer for those places could be. Eyebrows were raised in Whitehall this summer when a government statement said that "local economic growth policy" would be transferred "from HM Treasury directly into No 10 North". Some saw that as an attempt to disempower the Treasury, but sources there insist that no serious decisions on growth can be made without the department's involvement and approval. Burnham's Number 10 North goes on multi-million pound hiring spree Published 30 October 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy Published 21 October When Burnham first announced plans for the Manchester base, he singled out housing as an issue on which it would take the lead. In a speech last month Number 10 North's deputy director highlighted health, transport and education as other areas it was focused on. While it's understood the 10-year plan is likely to include long-term ambitions for social care, skills training and council housebuilding, there are doubts within government departments about exactly how involved Number 10 North will eventually be in those areas. One Whitehall official said "most things" that have been announced as Number 10 North priorities have in practice "stayed with other departments". They said Number 10 North is "not doing delivery" because it "doesn't have its own resource" and is "underpowered compared to departments" in London. A recent hiring spree will see around 120 officials and advisers working from Number 10 North when it moves into its permanent premises next spring. That is almost half of the around 280 staff members that work for "Number 10 South", a term some advisers are now using for Downing Street. title: Chris Mason: Can Burnham turn volume down on EU debate?
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Politics Parliaments Brexit Can Burnham turn volume down on EU debate? Image source, Getty Images By Chris Mason Political editor Published 24 November 2026 When the prime minister told MPs "there will be no banging on about Europe" from him, my mind flashed back 20 years. It is 2006 and a fresh faced David Cameron had just taken over as the Conservative leader , promising, yes you guessed it, to stop "banging on" about Europe. And we all know how that turned out: a decade later as prime minister, he held and lost a referendum on whether the UK should stay in the European Union, as he advocated, or leave. Andy Burnham's address to the Commons, after Friday's EU-UK Summit in Brussels, felt like an attempt by a man who chose to turn the Europe conversation up to full blast this autumn, to try to turn the volume back down again. All of this prompts two big questions: whether he will be able to do that and what, in the end, Labour promises at the next general election. Asked if that could include seeking a mandate for another in/out referendum at that election, he didn't rule that out. "If it's in Britain's national interest, I will recommend it to this House. If it is not, then I won't," he said. But he very carefully left his options open: "There is no fixed opinion here. There is no fixed destination." Published 1 day ago He also suggested the frequency of his public utterances on the subject may be limited, insisting there would be no "running commentary," offering instead what he called "a calm, constructive and pragmatic consideration of what is in Britain's interest in the long term." Plus, he said Europe could change in the coming years. A nod, without naming her, that Marine Le Pen could become president of France, for instance. How might that shift the debate? Burnham's willingness to repeatedly talk about the European question in the last few months has, inevitably, spawned quite the reaction. A campaign group, Stay Out, has got itself up and running to argue exactly that. And the European Movement is helping launch a rival outfit called, again, you guessed it, Get In. It is a reminder that that the EU question has a knack of getting under the skin of British politics, often to the exclusion of other things, sometimes to the exclusion of seemingly everything. Can the prime minister successfully manage the volume switch so the topic is background hubbub in 2027, rather than a deafening din? Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images Image caption, Ursula von der Leyen, Andy Burnham and António Costa at the EU-UK Summit in Brussels last week. Meanwhile, what does the European Union itself make of all of this? EU sources see Andy Burnham's desire to "brainstorm" with them what the future relationship might look like as "normal diplomacy" as one figure put it, adding: "I don't think there are many options. And they are clear. The status quo. The customs union. The single market. And full membership." They mirror his expectation that "brainstorming" won't involve additional meetings, let alone a structured set of bespoke talks arriving at a conclusion. "We don't need a template. It will be part of the regular discussion," is how it was put to me. On Thursday, the government will publish its European Partnerships Bill, the legislation needed to enact, at the UK end, the agreements reached at the summit. Also later this week, the legal text of those agreements is due to be published – the small print of which will be pored over. title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Politics Parliaments Brexit Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more Image source, EPA By Henry Zeffman Chief Political Correspondent Published 20 November 2026 Andy Burnham has hailed his deal with the EU as a "good day for Britain" and a "good day for Europe". In the hours before the prime minister spoke, it had become, if nothing else, a confusing day. That confusion was unleashed by an EU official who briefed reporters in the morning that implementing the new arrangements on youth mobility, food exports and carbon emissions would be contingent on the government agreeing within six months to cut university tuition fees for Europeans studying in Britain. That was later qualified by others in the EU - and straightforwardly disputed by the British government. And for all that it dominated the morning, it did not ultimately dominate or particularly overshadow what was a warm press conference between the prime minister and his EU counterparts, Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa. The settled position appears to be that negotiations on student fees will continue into the next six months but on a separate track, or a "different sheet of paper" as von der Leyen put it. This still carries some degree of political risk for Burnham, because if Britain agrees to reduce, let alone equalise, university fees that would be an economic hit for universities which would presumably end up being covered by the government. And it may still be possible, though probably unlikely, that a deterioration in those negotiations could pollute the progress of today's agreements. Conversely, expect Burnham and his ministers to talk up another area where negotiations will continue - on the UK not being affected by the EU's "Made in Europe" plans, an attempt by the bloc to protect its industries from Chinese competition. Today's achievements and hiccups alike may quickly pale into insignificance anyway. Over the subsequent two months it has at times been a bit unclear how exactly he envisages that playing out and quite how far he is willing to go. But focusing on the process risks obscuring the most important development, which is that the prime minister and the government are now unambiguously committed to Britain not only getting closer, but getting much closer to the EU. There were two significant moments at today's summit in that regard. First, Burnham said that the government had got as far as it could go with incremental deals with the EU, at least this side of a general election. In other words, he has got as far as he believes is possible with the strategy he inherited from Sir Keir Starmer of getting closer to the EU within the confines of the post-Brexit architecture set out by Theresa May all those years ago, of Britain remaining outside the single market and the customs union. That suggests that after two years of this, there will not be a third annual summit to unveil specific agreements designed to smooth post-Brexit issues affecting specific sectors. title: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Business New Tech Economy Technology of Business Artificial Intelligence Africa Business Paths to Success Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow Image source, Getty Images By Faisal Islam Economics editor Published 20 November 2026 The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times. In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports. And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move. The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers". Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow". Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK? This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout. Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East. It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers. This is not the first time Labour has sought to reduce the weekly shop costs. Sir Keir Starmer's administration floated the idea that supermarkets might even offer some form of branded discounts, a suggestion that was met with collective bemusement by those in the industry. However, there will be less paperwork, checks and red tape on food imports too, but they were already lightly enforced. No longer will hundreds of pages of documents be required. No longer will perishable goods lose valuable hours or days at border checks. No longer will the incorrect colour of ink or Latin name for a meat disallow a shipment of British exports. Some, though not all of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, could be regained by a bonfire of this red tape. In particular, smaller exporters of food will be able to return to the large EU market. But the extra benefit here is unclear, and there could be extra checks and costs required instead on non-EU food imports. The government's own assessment is that the economy will gain £5bn through this, or 0.14% by 2040. Critics point out that this benefit does not include the quid pro quo - having to align with EU laws. Farmers have pointed to compliance with pesticides and fungicide regulation. The classic example of the benefits of post-Brexit autonomy has been the development of precision-bred foodstuffs, such as Vitamin D-enhanced tomatoes. The producer of this technology has, however, backed the deal after the government negotiated an "exception period" for ongoing UK sale. Professor Cristobal Uauy of the John Innes Centre said that "aligning with the EU market will bring our science to a greater number of people". title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Politics Parliaments Brexit What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start? Image source, Getty Images By Kate Whannel Political reporter Published 20 November 2026 The UK and EU have agreed a youth experience scheme which will allow a limited number of 18 to 31-year-olds to work, study or travel in the European Union for up to three years. Every year, 100,000 Britons will be able to participate in the scheme, with a reciprocal arrangement for 100,000 EU citizens. A joint EU-UK statement says the scheme is due to launch no later than January 2030. The numbers for both those coming to and from the EU will be allocated among the member nations according to each country's population. UK participants will initially be able to apply to travel to one particular EU country but can later switch to a different one, staying in a total of three countries during their three-year stay. However, they must spend 12 months in one country before switching. Visas issued by the EU or the UK will initially be valid for two years, with an option to extend for one more year. Neither UK nor EU citizens will be able to access benefits while abroad or bring dependants such as children. Participants will need to pay an application fee and prove they have enough money to support themselves during their stay. There are currently no details on what application fees UK citizens will have to pay, but the EU currently charges €90 (£75) for short-term visas. Numbers vary between countries for longer-term stays. The UK charges £340 for its other youth mobility schemes, in addition to a £776 annual health surcharge. The UK government has not said how much money an EU or UK national needs to have access to in order to take part but for similar schemes the figure is £2,530. There are no details yet on how places on the scheme will be allocated if it is oversubscribed; however previous schemes have used either a first-come, first-served basis or a random ballot system. The UK already has youth mobility schemes in place with other countries, including 45,000 places for Australians, 8,500 for New Zealanders and 1,000 for Icelanders. In 2024, 24,400 out of a possible total of 81,100 youth mobility scheme visas were issued by the UK. Speaking at a joint press conference with EU leaders, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "These opportunities open horizons, and they create friendships that will last a lifetime. "So it's a very emotional moment because these are the young people that will shape our future." One sticking point in the negotiations had been tuition fees and the EU's request that Europeans studying at UK universities should pay the same as British students. A typical undergraduate degree in the UK (excluding Scotland) costs up to £9,790 a year for a domestic student, while the cost for international students, including those from the EU, can vary from around £11,000 to £38,000. If the UK did agree to reduce fees for EU students, British higher education institutions could lose out financially. British students at European institutions pay non-EU rates, but these tend to be lower than in the UK, ranging from €1,000 to €20,000 per year. The UK and EU have not reached an agreement on the issue, but the joint statement says the two sides will continue working towards a deal and conclude negotiations by May 2027. The two sides have also agreed to continue discussions about the UK's participation in the Erasmus + programme. The initiative provides funding for students, teachers, youth workers and sports professionals to study or do work experience in the EU. The U

title: The Brexit debate is back – and there are nerves about what happens next
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Politics Parliaments Brexit The Brexit debate is back – and there are nerves about what happens next Image source, EPA/Shutterstock By Nick Eardley , Political correspondent , Henry Zeffman , Chief political correspondent and Chris Mason , Political editor Published 19 November 2026 "Stop Me If You Think You've Heard This One Before" sang Morrissey, as part of The Smiths in 1987, shortly before the band's acrimonious divorce. It's a lyric Brexit veterans might be humming to themselves this week. Maybe even the prime minister, who is an avid fan of the Manchester band. Some of the names - and arguments - that defined the Brexit period inside and outside Parliament are starting to emerge again, as the debate about the UK's relationship with the EU returns. "It's like déjà vu with knobs on," said one veteran of the Leave campaign to us. A new group called Stay Out has been set up, backed by figures who were part of the official Leave campaign in 2016. Boris Johnson has been back in the headlines, saying he still thinks Britons would choose to be outside the bloc. Pro-EU groups such as the European Movement are raising their voices, pointing to the range of politicians, diplomats and academics they have supporting their argument. And a steady stream of Labour figures are now emerging to say they want to rejoin. The former Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy made the argument on the BBC on Wednesday , saying Labour should go into the next election backing renegotiating membership of the EU and then putting that to people in another referendum. He joins a list of cabinet ministers under Sir Keir Starmer who want to revisit EU membership; a list that includes former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, former Business Secretary Peter Kyle and former Welsh Secretary Jo Stevens. Others who served around Sir Keir's cabinet table think the same privately. That is significant. Yes, they all backed Remain in 2016. But these are figures who were part of a government elected on a manifesto saying it was important to make Brexit work. They set red lines in that manifesto because they thought the public had moved on. But they have now decided to say - most of them very publicly - that they think the picture has changed and the UK needs to think again. The prime minister has opened the door to all options, from single market membership to rejoining the customs union to a referendum on full membership. But in recent days, his language has softened a little from the clear commitment in his party conference speech that around the time of this Friday's summit he would "lay out to the country" the different options for Britain's long-term relationship with Brussels. After some confusion about when this would take place, the government now says this will happen around the time that Burnham presents his 10-year plan, right before Parliament's Christmas break. Burnham's allies say this will allow him to tie his EU policy more closely to his domestic agenda, arguing that a different arrangement with Europe would help with his other priorities such as the cost of living and re-industrialisation. Others worry that the all-consuming nature of the EU debate means that it will drown out the other parts of the 10-year plan. To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. title: The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left By Katya Adler Europe editor "Opening the door to uncontrolled immigration," is how Reform UK described it. "Dragging us into the European Union via the back door," was the charge levelled by the Conservatives. You could be forgiven for expecting drastic change come Friday's EU-UK summit in Brussels judging by some of the criticism levelled by opponents of the Labour government. Instead, what's on the table is a limited youth work and mobility scheme (the source of Reform's ire), agreement on cross-channel carbon emissions pricing and a deal to ease food trade. There's also talk of reducing tuition fees for EU students at British universities (something EU member states, like Germany, really want) in exchange for the UK being admitted to an EU manufacturing scheme (which is important to the Burnham government). Even in these limited areas, I'm told, not all details will be ironed out by the time of Friday's meeting. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham admitted last week this is all a "step" towards a closer working relationship with Europe. It's certainly not a leap, and definitely not a matter of rejoining the bloc at this stage. Other "steps" under immediate discussion are the UK rejoining the EU's electricity market, and the UK trying again to join an EU-backed defence loan scheme. "Small steps… to make both sides stronger," is how the EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas describes this process. She also warns: "We have in Europe a lot of trauma from Britain leaving [the EU], so things will not be easy." Image source, Stefan Rousseau - WPA Pool/Getty Images Image caption, At this week's summit, the UK and EU are expected to discuss a limited youth mobility scheme, cross-channel carbon emissions pricing, and a deal to ease food trade Bigger, potentially more politically explosive EU-UK questions look likely to follow after Friday's summit. It's thought Burnham may propose rejoining the EU's customs union and/or the single market. There are suggestions he could eventually table a new referendum on rejoining the EU. None of this before the next general election, though. On this side of the Channel, the debate is very much focused on what Britain might want. Burnham's plan is bold, belated or completely barmy - depending on your political perspective. But there's been little discussion about the EU point of view, and less still on how the EU has changed since Britain left it. Just how different is the EU in 2026 from the bloc Britain turned its back on a decade ago? And with the UK still mired in arguments over its relationship with Europe, does the EU even want GB back in the fold or would Brussels now rather avoid more drama? Since 2016, a series of international shocks have fundamentally changed the EU. The Covid crisis collapsed international supply chains. Europe became aware just how dependent it was on China for medical supplies, for example. Then, Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine showed the EU how utterly reliant many members were on energy supplies from Moscow. Big EU beasts like Germany and Italy were particularly affected. The Ukraine war, the continent's biggest active conflict since World War Two, has persuaded the EU that Europe's domestic defence industry and industrial policy needs a boost and far better coordination. Donald Trump's two stints as US president convinced the EU that it can never again fully rely on the US to be Europe's best friend abroad, either in trade or security terms. title: Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs?
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Business New Tech Economy Technology of Business Artificial Intelligence Africa Business Paths to Success Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs? Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Some British sausages have faced barriers to being exported to the EU In Boston, Lincolnshire, a supplier of ready meals to Marks & Spencer (M&S) manufactures thousands of portions of spaghetti bolognese to be sent to the retailer's shops in the Republic of Ireland. Every plastic pallet is meticulously individually tagged with a green-grey label “Eire”. Every truck full of food sent to European Union countries requires hundreds of pages of forms, checks by vets, expense and delays. It has cost M&S millions of pounds and is part of that reason the British business shut down 11 French stores in 2021. Many smaller exporters stopped sending their goods to the EU entirely. Some produce, including sausages and certain types of seafood, were entirely stopped. All this was the predictable consequence of former Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s 2020 deal prioritising regulatory freedom over freeflowing goods trade. That will end with a Brexit "reset" that Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to sign with the EU on Friday. The government claims it could boost the economy to the tune of £5bn a year and cut the cost of food for households. But will the agreement mean a return to frictionless trade for food with the EU or are there trade-offs and quid pro quos the UK will have to make? EU affairs minister Hamish Falconer, who is a key negotiator with the bloc, acknowledged a “choice” is being made. In exchange for being able to export produce such as Lincolnshire sausages to the 27 countries, the flipside is the extent to which the UK will be able to influence EU food policies. The UK will have a "voice in the room", said Falconer, but no vote. Critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker", not a rule maker. But Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules. A Brexit reset would not involve any upfront payments, said Falconer, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment. He said this was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements. Both parties have said they would if they were in power. "The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said. The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit. Image source, Getty Images The prime minister has said he believes there is a "win-win" deal to be had with the EU. Speaking at a Marks & Spencer food court in central London, Falconer said reducing the cost of importing food "will mean less cost for supermarkets, and I hope that less cost then turns into cheaper produce on the shelves". He said companies have to currently deal with "pages and pages" of form-filling. Some exports are rejected for having the wrong colour of ink on forms, or an inaccurate Latin name for cooked meats. The reset could also mean "tearing up" checks that were introduced on goods flowing from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, following Brexit, he said, as well as separate "Not for EU" labelling. The whole deal to be signed on Friday is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP. title: Chris Mason: Milburn may have gifted Labour MPs a moral argument for welfare reform
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Politics Parliaments Brexit Chris Mason: Milburn may have gifted Labour MPs a moral argument for welfare reform Image source, Press Association Image caption, Alan Milburn's proposals to help young people who are neither learning nor earning would reduce benefits for some young people but aim to get them jobs in the long run Political editor Published 18 November 2026 The prime minister describes Alan Milburn's report on jobs, training and benefits for young people as a "watershed moment". In so doing, he is accepting Milburn's case for change and taking on the task of delivering it. Were ministers to actually manage that, it would amount to one of the most significant shake-ups of the welfare state in its history. But the proposed timeframe for this stretches to a decade, which is another geological era in political terms, at least two general elections away. Milburn is a deft operator. From a round of morning television and radio interviews, to addressing the cabinet, to releasing his report into the wild, he was still out and about on Tuesday evening in Westminster persuading, charming and cajoling those possibly in need of all three. And this former MP, still every inch the politician, has an ongoing role - appointed the chairman of the government's new Youth Opportunities Unit. The new job, which will report directly to Andy Burnham, is about tying together the myriad different aspects of change he is suggesting, involving multiple government departments. And yes, it does mean a 68-year-old bloke becomes an early beneficiary of new employment prospects for the young. But that glib observation apart, there is a hope that Milburn has gifted Labour MPs a moral argument for welfare reforms they can endorse. Or, to put it more bluntly, one not grounded in a specific objective to make benefits cuts to make the sums add up elsewhere. Plus, him hanging around perhaps means he can be a useful lightning conductor for any forthcoming angst on Labour's benches – as having persuaded them of the big picture mission, the gritty reality of implementing it begins to take shape. Published 7 days ago Watch: What's in the Milburn review? Published 17 November At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report Published 17 November The young people caught up in Britain's Neets crisis Published 17 November As the prime minister puts it in an interview in the Times , external , the government wants to offer "a new social contract" for "the let-down generation". And he tells the newspaper that the initial upfront cost of around £500m, for employment support in 2027-28, will come from existing government budgets, which will mean cuts to other things elsewhere in government. Crucially, if you are in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland, many of the decisions around whether or not to press ahead with these ideas will be up to the devolved governments in Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast. From the government at Westminster's perspective, the focus now will be drawing up the specific plans for implementing Milburn's ideas, having accepted the broad thrust of his argument. A white paper will follow in the new year, and then legislation. What we don't know yet and will be crucial to the next stage of this debate, is precisely who will be the perceived winners and losers, at least in the short term, of the proposed changes. Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told me that "those with the most severe and lifelong disabilities where work is not a realistic prospect" should, as Milburn suggests, "get more support than they receive at the moment". To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. This video can not be played 'It felt like I was dying’: Why some teenagers don’t go to school The stories of Eva and Mali - which you can watch in the video above - and the many teenagers like them who don't go to school, either regularly or at all, strike to the heart of one of the many big challenges the Milburn Review is seeking to address. The government-commissioned work, led by former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, is looking into how to solve the problem of nearly one million young people not being in employment, education or training, or Neet. A key challenge is addressing the issue of school absence. The government believes around a third of young people who are persistently absent in Years 10 and 11 in England go on to be Neet, compared with 10% of those who are not persistently absent. Persistent absence almost doubles between Years 7 and 9, reaching around one in four children by Year 9. Image caption, Eva, 13, stopped going to school after struggling with the transition to secondary school Thirteen-year-old Eva hadn't been to school for 15 months before September. She described how she used to get up every morning, try to get ready for school and get stuck by the front door. Mali, 18, stopped attending school three years ago when she was in year 10. We shared their stories with the decision makers and those who want to be our decision makers – in other words, those in government and those who would like to be. It offers an insight into the political arguments to come. Labour reckons the Conservatives' education reforms of the last decade and a half served academic high achievers very well but created what one source described as an an "endless treadmill of failure" for some - and so let them down. A government spokesperson said: "When children feel they belong at school, they show up, and when they show up, they achieve." Therefore, the spokesperson added, "the education secretary is driving ambitious reforms to boost attendance" and "intervene earlier when children need support". The Liberal Democrats also sought to pin the blame on the Tories. Munira Wilson, who speaks for the party on education, said "the Conservatives failed to give them the support they needed after lockdown, and years of underinvestment in their recovery are now showing up in rising mental health figures". She added that "every young person should feel they belong". These reactions prompt some of the big questions that arise from Eva and Mali's experiences. Where should responsibility for their situations lie? The individual, the parents, the rules in the pandemic, schools, colleges, mental health provision? Perhaps a combination of all of these things in some instances and other things besides. The Conservatives have pushed back strongly against the criticism from Labour and the Liberal Democrats. Shadow education secretary Laura Trott told the BBC: "We mustn't give up on any child, every day a child misses school sets them back. "Schools are doing great work to bring absence down. Those children who have special education needs or are struggling to leave home, need specialist support and in some cases specialist schools." And she added: "High academic standards lift everyone up. It is insulting to suggest that not all children are capable of good academic outcomes. Too much maths and English are not making young people Neet." Former Co

title: Burnham's push for closer EU ties causes ripples in his party and others
text: BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health In Pictures More BBC Verify Newsbeat Politics Parliaments Brexit Burnham's push for closer EU ties causes ripples in his party and others Image source, Phototek via Getty Images By Harry Farley , Political correspondent , Henry Zeffman , Chief political correspondent and Jack Fenwick , Political correspondent Published 12 November 2026 There is renewed attention on the prime minister's push for closer relations with Europe - and that is causing ripples in his own party and others. Andy Burnham told his Cabinet earlier this week: "I firmly believe we have ended up with a harder Brexit than people voted for… no sensible person thinks the deal negotiated by the Tories is working for the country." It comes ahead of a week which will focus minds on the UK's relationship with the bloc. On Thursday, at a gathering of European leaders in Dublin, Burnham will for the first time meet those who could prove pivotal as he sells his vision for Britain's future in the bloc. And next week, he will deliver a speech on foreign policy, in which – for Burnham – Europe is a central plank. He will then travel to Brussels for a UK-EU summit to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility. Talking about the new deal to be signed at the summit, Burnham said to ministers: "We will take opportunities that make people in this country better off. Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, says Burnham Published 30 September UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports Published 3 November This lies behind the prime minister's decision to open the door to the argument about rejoining the EU single market - along with the freedom of movement that would bring - and even the EU altogether. But that longer-term ambition is dividing his cabinet and his party. Some welcome his approach, including those with formerly Brexit-backing constituencies. Angela Rayner, for example, is understood to have been pushing former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer to be bolder on Brexit since at least autumn 2022. The housing secretary is said to have been insistent that Labour needs to stick to its manifesto red lines – not to return to the EU single market, customs union, or freedom of movement – but is open minded to changing those at the next election. Another cabinet minister said: "The best thing you can do in politics is tell the truth. And the truth is that Brexit has been hugely damaging to Britain. "We are not leading a public conversation here, we are racing to catch up with the public." But others are watching nervously at a strategy one former minister described as "high risk". Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, for example, has struck a more cautious tone warning about the "costs and consequences" of rejoining the EU as well as staying out. Jonathan Reynolds, the Business and Trade Secretary, is supportive of getting closer to the EU and discussing the UK's long term relationship. But he has previously warned against joining the EU's customs union and is also unsure about the prospect of rejoining the EU, highlighting the uncertainty of what terms the UK would face, and what the bloc could look like in years to come with nationalist parties in the ascendancy in several European countries. A voice from the past has a different set of concerns. Lord Cameron told Bloomberg's Mishal Husain that starting a conversation about rejoining would be "very long and painful". The former prime minister warned "flirting with rejoining" could also harm Burnham's attempts to renegotiate the Conservative's Brexit deal.
