We present Hesperos & Eosphoros, a forced-photometry operator and a forward model that, respectively, perform and model the spectrophotometric measurement of the Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization, and Ices Explorer (SPHEREx). Implemented as GPU-accelerated, differentiable JAX programs, the two may be directly composed to measure the response of a downstream product (e.g., the galaxy density field) with respect to a modeled systematic or perturbation through the full measurement pipeline. We describe their design and demonstrate the composition on the response of an astrometric perturbation, and demonstrate how these may be used to generate direct measurement/pipeline response templates $\partial({\rm reconstructed\ density})/\partial({\rm systematic\ amplitude})$ for known image-level effects. Hesperos achieves a factor of $\sim700\times$ increased throughput per node-hour at production scale compared to the prior CPU-based Tractor measurement, previously the limiting step in the experiment's data processing, and propagates automatic derivatives through the full production measurement operator. We validate the measurement operator Hesperos against the public SPHEREx fork of The Tractor, and the forward model Eosphoros against the SPHEREx Sky Simulator and the renders themselves independently against GalSim. Taken together, this represents a powerful increase in capability for scaling, iterating, and optimizing galaxy clustering measurement pipelines.

title: A model colloidal gel former for the measurement of inter-particle forces
text: A model colloidal gel former for the measurement of inter-particle forces. Tracking of particle coordinates in colloidal model systems is an established technique. Recently, an emulsion system has been introduced where not only the coordinates, but also contacts and compressive forces between the droplets can be determined [Dong et al. J. Chem. Phys. 156 214907 (2022). Here we develop this system to control both the density mismatch and refractive index contrast between the emulsion droplets and the solvent. The former is important in minimizing sedimentation due to gravity and the latter is necessary for 3d imaging with confocal microscopy. By mapping our system carefully to computer simulation, we quantify interdroplet forces and packing geometries in depletion gels and probe the relationship between local structure and compressive stress. The simulations also provide ensemble measurements of the attractive part of the force between droplets and related quantities such as the stress tensor. Finally, we implement an improved measure of local stress in our experiments, which can be directly compared with the corresponding quantity in simulations. We find that locally rigid minimum energy clusters are associated with regions of higher stress in the gel network.

title: Signatures of Kitaev quantum spin liquid states in $α$-RuCl$_3$ revealed by nitrogen-vacancy spin-noise spectroscopy
text: Signatures of Kitaev quantum spin liquid states in $α$-RuCl$_3$ revealed by nitrogen-vacancy spin-noise spectroscopy. Bond-dependent magnetic interactions, strong spin-orbit coupling, and quantum fluctuations in $α$-RuCl$_3$ make it an archetypical candidate for exotic Kitaev quantum spin liquid (QSL) states. While electronic transport, neutron scattering, optical and tunneling spectroscopies were used to probe global QSL signatures in large scale $α$-RuCl$_3$ samples, nanoscale evidence of local QSL behavior via a non-invasive experimental probe is still missing. Here, we use diamond nitrogen-vacancy (NV) spin-noise spectroscopy to probe QSL states in α-RuCl3 nanoflakes with thicknesses ranging from 8 to 150 nm over a temperature range of 4.3-250 K. Our measurements reveal a pronounced decrease in the NV spin-lattice relaxation time ($T_{1}$) below ~100 K in proximity to the $α$-RuCl$_3$ flakes, indicating enhanced GHz-frequency magnetic fluctuations. This temperature scale is consistent with the energy scale associated with Kitaev interactions (~8 meV) and the emergence of low-energy fractionalized excitations. Below 50 K, thicker (> 90 nm) flakes exhibit a distinct bi-exponential $T_{1}$ decay, unlike the single-exponential behavior observed for off-flake and thinner (8 nm) flake measurements, suggesting an increasingly heterogeneous magnetic noise environment. These results establish NV spin-noise spectroscopy as a local, non-invasive probe of low-energy spin dynamics in $α$-RuCl$_3$ nanoflakes and open a route to testing predicted noise signatures of fractionalized excitations in atomically thin QSL candidates.

title: Initial Conditions and Wave-Phase Resolution for Scalar-Field Dark Matter Simulations
text: Initial Conditions and Wave-Phase Resolution for Scalar-Field Dark Matter Simulations. Wave-based cosmological simulations of scalar-field dark matter (SFDM) require accurate initialization of both density and complex-wavefunction phase. We develop and validate a matched $Λ$CDM--SFDM initialization framework connecting CLASS-SFDM, MUSIC, and AxioNyx. For quadratic SFDM with $m_φ=3.1623\times10^{-22}\,\mathrm{eV}$ at $z_{\rm ini}=120$, the scalar-component half-power scale is $k_{50}^φ\simeq10.54\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$. An independent AxiECAMB comparison gives a normalized RMS deviation of $0.328\%$ in the synchronous-gauge SFDM velocity divergence over $0.20944\leq k\leq13.4\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$. A $256^3$ MUSIC realization reproduces the CLASS density power spectrum over $8\leq k\leq13.404\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ with a median ratio of $1.00131$ and an RMS fractional deviation of $0.138\%$. Despite this agreement, full-volume phase diagnostics show that the fraction of velocity-implied phase increments violating the Nyquist criterion decreases from $46.7\%$ at $256^3$ to $13.685\%$ at $512^3$ and $0.124060\%$ at $1024^3$. A separately generated realization yields $13.7299\%$ and $0.124983\%$ at $512^3$ and $1024^3$, respectively, with relative differences below $1\%$. In a common-parent $512^3$--$1024^3$ comparison, the central-plane density fields remain strongly correlated ($r_δ=0.9989$). The median absolute circular phase difference is $0.264$ rad without masking and $0.246$ rad for $86.6\%$ of blocks satisfying $R\geq0.5$, with 90th percentiles $0.826$ and $0.753$ rad. These results demonstrate that accurate linear density recovery does not guarantee adequate wave-phase resolution and provide validation criteria for SFDM initial conditions prior to nonlinear evolution.

title: Holographic ensembles and giant gravitons at the Leigh--Strassler fixed point
text: Holographic ensembles and giant gravitons at the Leigh--Strassler fixed point. Finite-rank observables in holographic quantum field theories provide stringent tests of string and M-theory, but remain challenging to compute when supersymmetry is non-maximal. In this paper, we study the finite rank partition function of the $\mathcal N=1$ Leigh-Strassler CFT, which admits an interacting Fermi-gas description. We compute the partition function explicitly in two ensembles: the canonical ensemble at fixed rank $N$, and the grand canonical ensemble, where $N$ is summed over while its conjugate chemical potential $μ$ is held fixed. In line with recent proposals, we find that the perturbative large-$N$ and large-$μ$ expansions in both ensembles are reproduced by the on-shell action and one-loop determinant over Kaluza--Klein modes of type IIB supergravity, with appropriate ensemble-dependent boundary terms. Furthermore, the one-loop partition function of a D3-brane giant graviton precisely matches the leading nonperturbative correction to the boundary partition functions.

title: Finite-Temperature Superradiant Criticality and Thermal Emission in the Open Dicke Model
text: Finite-Temperature Superradiant Criticality and Thermal Emission in the Open Dicke Model. Near the superradiant phase transition of the Dicke model, the lowest-frequency excitation softens and its losses can no longer be treated as a weak perturbation. We develop a finite-temperature theory of this transition in the open system, with no restriction on the strength of the system-bath coupling. The cavity mode and the atomic ensemble are coupled to independent reservoirs, the first at zero temperature and the second at temperature $T$, and we assume that the spins remain thermalized with their reservoir. We find that the reservoirs do not shift the temperature-dependent critical coupling for a broad class of spectral densities, while the polariton becomes overdamped in a finite interval of couplings around it. As expected, raising the temperature moves the transition to stronger couplings, and in the superradiant phase we find a faster decoupling of light and matter. The theoretical framework developed here yields the reflection and thermal emission spectra for arbitrary parameters in both the normal and the superradiant phase, and provides a basis for comparison with experiments on systems displaying ground-state condensation. We also identify conditions under which the system behaves, at specific frequencies, as both a perfect absorber and a perfect emitter.

title: Class-resolved sifting for quantum key distribution with photon pairs hyperentangled in polarization and transverse spatial variables
text: Class-resolved sifting for quantum key distribution with photon pairs hyperentangled in polarization and transverse spatial variables. Photon pairs hyperentangled in polarization and transverse spatial variables can carry two key bits per pair in entanglement-based quantum key distribution. We develop class-resolved sifting for such sources: every detected pair is assigned to a class according to which degrees of freedom were measured in compatible bases, and error and key rates are estimated separately in each class. Applied to previously reported data from a two-crystal spontaneous parametric down-conversion source read out in intermediate fractional-Fourier planes, the method recovers the key yield of independent sifting and turns the comparison between classes into a quantitative consistency test for cross-dependencies between the two degrees of freedom. The measured dependence lies below the spatial-polarization coupling predicted for the source, at the edge of the present statistical sensitivity. Resolving the data by polarization-analyzer setting, we find an approximately twofold dependence of the spatial error on the polarization setting in one readout arm, attributable to the measurement apparatus rather than to the source and relevant to basis-dependent side channels. We compare the hyperentangled protocol with a single 4-dimensional system measured in two mutually unbiased bases. Fundamentally, both yield the same key per detected pair and obey the same entropic bound, but they differ in their tensor-product structure: hyperentanglement factors the bases into separate two-outcome measurements, which are simpler to implement and allow errors to be attributed to each degree of freedom, whereas a single variable gives access to non-product bases that can increase the noise tolerance. For the present source, whose polarization coherence is limited by partial which-crystal erasure, a single-variable spatial encoding would yield more key only if its four-outcome readout kept the symbol error within a few percent.

title: Scalar-tensor interactions selected through their first-order thermodynamic dynamics
text: Scalar-tensor interactions selected through their first-order thermodynamic dynamics. We investigate the restrictive capability of first-order thermodynamics on scalar-tensor gravity. Starting from a general action containing nonlinear curvature dependence, an Einstein-tensor-Hessian coupling, and independent quadratic and cubic scalar-Hessian interactions, we derive the complete effective-fluid quantities. Simultaneously imposing Eckart's heat-conduction and shear-viscosity equations, while accounting for cancellations between interactions, substantially reduces the original operator basis and determines the geometric shear viscosity. Retaining the complete heat-conduction law, we establish an integrability condition that constrains the nonlinear Hessian interactions without prescribing the temperature and thermal conductivity. We construct explicit constitutive pairs and derive the associated thermal evolution, revealing contributions beyond the usual acceleration-aligned description. Remarkably, the thermodynamic integrability condition simplifies the scalar-metric kinetic structure such that imposing covariant degeneracy excludes the remaining nonlinear interactions, recovering the established luminal Horndeski subclass. Nonlinear thermodynamically compatible interactions nevertheless survive when degeneracy is restricted to the scalar-unitary gauge. These results establish a connection between thermodynamic integrability and dynamical degeneracy, demonstrating the potential of first-order thermodynamics as an independent and complementary criterion for selecting gravitational interactions.

title: Polynomial Master Equations of Open Quantum Systems and an Analysis on the Critical Solutions
text: Polynomial Master Equations of Open Quantum Systems and an Analysis on the Critical Solutions. The dynamics of open quantum systems exhibits in general a non-Markovian behavior, lying typically beyond the description of first-order differential equations. Traditional methods commonly turned to first-order integro-differential equations, which allowed for the standard interpretation of non-Markovianity as having its origin in the global history of the system evolution. We examine the possibility of an alternative, locally deterministic interpretation [arXiv:2607.09651] of the working of its dynamical hysteresis, where the evolution of a system is determined by its local behavior alone. The present work elaborates on our systematic method in deriving non-Markovian linear differential equations associated with matrix polynomials of higher order. Our methods will be demonstrated with exact analyses on two illustrative examples: one built upon the simplest non-trivial model concerning a two-qubit system, and another involving an unbounded Hamiltonian defined on an infinite-dimensional quantum system. We also analyze the critical parameters at which qualitative changes are observed in the system dynamics, and reveal how our polynomial equations account for the phenomena.

title: Z-Boson Production in Proton-Lead Collisions with MRW Nuclear TMDs
text: Z-Boson Production in Proton-Lead Collisions with MRW Nuclear TMDs. The production of dileptons in proton-lead collisions probes the transverse-momentum structure of partons in a nuclear environment. We summarize a $k_t$-factorization study of $Z$ boson production at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=8.16\,\mathrm{TeV}$, comparing transverse-momentum-dependent (TMD) distributions constructed with leading-order and Next-to-leading-order Martin-Ryskin-Watt (LO-MRW and NLO-MRW) prescriptions. Parton-level predictions obtained with \textsc{KaTie} are confronted with the CMS measurements in two invariant-mass regions, using the dilepton transverse momentum, $φ^*_η$ and center-of-mass rapidity. The models describe the overall trends near the $Z$ resonance, while the virtuality constraint in NLO-MRW changes the high-transverse-momentum behavior. At lower dilepton masses, both prescriptions underestimate parts of the data, particularly the NLO-MRW result. These comparisons illustrate both the potential and the limitations of last-step-evolution nuclear TMD models for $Z$ boson production in proton-nucleus collisions.

title: Iterative Petz Protocols for Quantum State Recovery
text: Iterative Petz Protocols for Quantum State Recovery. Noise is omnipresent in quantum systems, and thus, approximately reversing this noise is a central challenge towards quantum technologies. The Petz map provides a physically admissible recovery channel, but its performance depends critically on the choice of reference state. Here, we introduce and investigate the iterative Petz recovery (IPR) protocol, an adaptive multicopy strategy that begins from an unbiased reference state and uses each recovered output to construct the Petz map for the next iteration. We establish the stability of the protocol and develop a tomography-assisted finite-copy implementation with explicit control of error propagation and fidelity loss. For qubit depolarizing noise, we derive an exact recurrence for the fidelity of every pure input. For single-axis Pauli noise, we derive an exact recurrence for the six-state Pauli average and compare it numerically with the Haar average. We further benchmark finite-copy IPR against measure-and-prepare strategies based on local and collective measurements, revealing the associated finite-resource tradeoffs.

title: The Cosmological Constant as a Clock and the Vilenkin Wavefunction as a Resonance
text: The Cosmological Constant as a Clock and the Vilenkin Wavefunction as a Resonance. We address the problem of time in quantum gravity using a covariant formulation of unimodular gravity. As a result, the cosmological constant is canonically conjugate to a global four-volume variable, which serves as a clock and leads to a time-dependent Wheeler--DeWitt equation. We construct exact, background-independent solutions related to the full Chern--Simons--Kodama state and demonstrate unitary evolution in minisuperspace. The Chern--Simons functional also provides an intrinsic gravitational clock. These solutions reveal that the Vilenkin wavefunction is a gravitational Gamow resonance, in which its non-normalizability follows from the outgoing boundary condition. The tunneling probability into the expanding branch increases with the positive cosmological constant. These results give a dynamical interpretation of the wavefunction of the universe and clarify the role of its boundary conditions.

title: Quantum-Inspired Tensor Train Spectral Solver for High-Resolution PDEs with Non-Periodic Boundary Conditions
text: Quantum-Inspired Tensor Train Spectral Solver for High-Resolution PDEs with Non-Periodic Boundary Conditions. Tensor train (TT) methods enable high-resolution computational mechanics simulations by exploiting low-rank structure in discretized fields and operators. While the superfast Fourier transform (SFFT) has enabled efficient TT-based spectral solvers for periodic problems, corresponding representations for non-periodic boundary conditions remain underexplored. We introduce the superfast cosine and sine transforms (SFCT and SFST), extending the TT spectral framework to homogeneous Neumann and Dirichlet boundary conditions, respectively. Building on a quantum-circuit construction of the discrete cosine and sine transforms, we derive both transforms from a shared TT operator representation and prove that their TT ranks are bounded by $6r_S$, independently of the discretization order, where $r_S$ is the rank of the SFFT at the prescribed accuracy. The measured ranks plateau near 32 for grid sizes up to $2^{26}$ points. For Rayleigh-Bénard convection, spectral pressure projection achieves up to a 7-fold speedup in the Poisson solve relative to a preconditioned physical-space TT solver while maintaining comparable accuracy. Three-dimensional computational homogenization achieves a 2-6-fold speedup and a 4-7-fold reduction in memory consumption compared with the existing TT-based approach. The results establish an efficient TT framework for spectral PDE solvers with non-periodic boundary conditions.

title: Anomalous front propagation in many-body quantum transport with memory-dependent resetting
text: Anomalous front propagation in many-body quantum transport with memory-dependent resetting. We introduce an exactly solvable framework for non-Markovian quantum many-body dynamics based on stochastic resetting with memory. Applicable to arbitrary time-independent Hamiltonians, including interacting systems, our framework provides an exact representation of the dynamics with memory in terms of the corresponding reset-free evolution, which can be accessed either analytically or numerically. We demonstrate the power of this approach by studying domain-wall melting in a one-dimensional chain of noninteracting fermions, obtaining exact analytical results for the density profile, the local structure of the front edge, the extreme-value statistics of the rightmost fermion, and the integrated current. Remarkably, memory transforms ballistic transport into logarithmically slow propagation without arresting spreading. While the macroscopic density profile retains its original scaling function, the front edge broadens as $\sqrt{\ln t}$ rather than $t^{1/3}$ at late times and develops a qualitatively different edge structure. Furthermore, the extreme-value statistics change from Tracy--Widom to Gaussian, while both the mean and variance of the integrated current grow logarithmically in time. Our predictions are in excellent agreement with numerical simulations. These results reveal how memory can fundamentally alter quantum many-body transport and its fluctuations.

title: Quantum kernels on breast data: concentration, surrogates, and two ways an advantage gets manufactured
text: Quantum kernels on breast data: concentration, surrogates, and two ways an advantage gets manufactured. Quantum-kernel advantage claims on breast data are usually a single number: one quantum arm, one comparator, one test split. We asked what that number measures once the full comparator set and selection history are visible. We report three active benchmarks, all exact classical statevector simulations of 8-qubit fidelity kernels with no quantum component in the inference path: a sample-efficiency sweep on Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer at ten training-set sizes; raw-versus-processed arms on 1,200 M-SYNTH simulated mammograms with a matched closed-form dequantisation surrogate, five classical methods at the same input and eleven kernel families; and a 30-seed selection-inflation measurement on BreastMNIST. A CMMD D1 clinical arm is withdrawn as a result arm because its frozen splits leak the label through patient serial order, a defect reported in a separate study; it is retained only as a worked example. All three active arms are negative. On M-SYNTH raw an apparent +0.1736 (p = 5.2e-06) against a tuned RBF-SVM falls to +0.0019 (p = 0.937) against a random forest at the same input, and a Laplacian kernel wins on validation. On WDBC, with model selection confined to training data, the quantum kernel is below the selected classical arm at every training-set size, with 2 of 200 paired subsamples ahead. Best-of-30 seed selection adds +0.0210 on BreastMNIST. One result does not fit: at bandwidth 2pi the matched closed-form Gaussian surrogate failed to reproduce the M-SYNTH raw kernel (0.5410 against 0.7045, p = 6.3e-06). Comparator choice and selection each produce effects larger than any quantum-classical difference we measured; we give a reporting standard that removes both.

title: Entanglement Asymmetry and the Quantum Mpemba Effect in Inhomogeneous Quenches
text: Entanglement Asymmetry and the Quantum Mpemba Effect in Inhomogeneous Quenches. Entanglement asymmetry is a powerful probe of symmetry breaking and its dynamical restoration following quantum quenches. While extensively studied for homogeneous initial states, its evolution from inhomogeneous initial configurations remains largely unexplored. We investigate a spin-$1/2$ XX chain whose two halves are initially prepared in tilted ferromagnetic states with different tilt angles. Combining generalized hydrodynamics (GHD) and the quasiparticle picture with exact fermionic correlation-matrix calculations, we study the dynamics of entanglement asymmetry. We find good agreement between the two approaches for generic initial configurations and observe the quantum Mpemba effect, whereby states with stronger initial symmetry breaking can restore the symmetry faster. This effect now depends on the subsystem position: while the homogeneous behavior is recovered when the subsystem lies entirely within one of the initially tilted halves, the entanglement-asymmetry curves for subsystems straddling the interface can exhibit multiple crossings or no crossings at all. A notable exception occurs for subsystems entirely within an initially non-tilted half. In this case, GHD predicts vanishing asymmetry, but the exact dynamics generates a small, nonzero asymmetry that can develop a plateau before decaying toward zero. This feature reveals contributions beyond the leading-order hydrodynamic description.

title: Multi-Component Axion Dark Matter Revisited and the Role of Ultralight ALPs
text: Multi-Component Axion Dark Matter Revisited and the Role of Ultralight ALPs. In this work, we revisit the multi-component axion dark matter (DM) scenario and explore the role of ultralight axion-like particles (ALPs). After briefly reviewing maximal axion mixing, we incorporate a stochastic axion mixing mechanism that generalizes it by relaxing the requirement of a uniform hierarchy among the axion decay constants. We find that, depending on the parameters, either the QCD axion or an ALP can dominate the DM abundance after mixing; once axion mass contributions are included, the heaviest ALPs tend to prevail. In a two-component framework, stochastic mixing significantly enlarges the allowed parameter space for the QCD axion decay constant, enabling the QCD axion to constitute the entirety of cold DM. The corresponding ALP mass range remains largely unconstrained by current experiments and is within reach of future searches. In the multi-component case, a larger ALP population leads to the emergence of more ultralight ALPs with large decay constants. These ultralight ALPs represent compelling targets for upcoming axion searches.

title: Theory-Informed Quantum Error Mitigation for Shor Order Finding with Fourier Neural Operators
text: Theory-Informed Quantum Error Mitigation for Shor Order Finding with Fourier Neural Operators. Quantum noise distorts the distribution of circuit measurement outcomes, often leaving enough information to infer the algorithm's correct result. To recover this latent information from the noisy distribution in Shor order finding, we introduce a theory-informed quantum error mitigation method. We model how circuit errors shift, broaden, or weaken peaks in the output distribution. These models guide both the generation of synthetic training data and the design of a Fourier neural operator with a learned gain that attenuates or amplifies higher retained Fourier modes. We score each candidate order by averaging the correlations between its ideal distribution and the distributions measured in three circuit executions. The network adjusts these scores to guide the order estimate and determine the weights of a normalized mixture of the ideal distributions. On 1,351 simulated test cases for general modular exponentiation, held out by circuit configuration, exact order recovery rises from 19% to 34%, and the median Jensen-Shannon divergence from the ideal distribution falls by 50%, from 0.64 to 0.32. On 101 Mersenne rotation circuits executed across five IBM quantum processors, a separate model trained and calibrated in simulation increases the number of correct order estimates from 35 to 53. Algorithmic structure can remain recoverable even when noise makes it barely visible.

title: Dirac Propagation for Simulating Fermionic Observables under Particle-Number-Conserving Unitaries
text: Dirac Propagation for Simulating Fermionic Observables under Particle-Number-Conserving Unitaries. Simulating the dynamics of interacting fermions remains a central computational challenge across physics and chemistry. We introduce Dirac propagation, a classical method that simulates local observables in fermionic systems subject to particle-number-conserving unitaries. We show that, in the operator expansion, strings with weights above the total particle number can be discarded without incurring any error in the final expectation value. This exact cutoff bounds the number of retained strings polynomially in the number of modes at fixed particle number, including for interacting dynamics. The formalism combines a compact representation with explicit expressions for interacting gates and exact treatment of number-conserving fermionic Gaussian and Clifford unitaries. This framework offers an approach to simulating fermionic many-body dynamics and classically benchmarking fermionic quantum circuits.

title: Fisher information in the flux landscape
text: Fisher information in the flux landscape. We quantify the fine-tuning of the flux superpotential in Type IIB Calabi-Yau orientifold compactifications using the Fisher Information Metric. Treating the background fluxes as model parameters and the magnitude of the superpotential as the physical observable, we show that the Fisher matrix admits a unique non-zero eigenvalue that bounds the superpotential from above and factorises into axio-dilaton, complex structure components and a bounded factor depending on both moduli and the phase of the superpotential. In the canonical duality frame and over the full flux lattice, this eigenvalue grows linearly with the inverse string coupling and cubically with the complex structure saxions. Specialising to a two modulus orientifold of the degree 18 hypersurface in $\mathbb{P}^4(1,1,1,6,9)$ at large complex structure, we combine the flux integrality with the D3-brane tadpole condition to show that several flux components, including the one driving this growth, are forced to vanish across deep moduli space patches, truncating the twelve-dimensional flux lattice to an eight-dimensional sublattice. The Fisher eigenvalue restricted to these admissible flux directions either approaches a constant or grows at most linearly, much more slowly than over the full lattice.

title: Trotterized hybrid qubit-boson simulation of the Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard model
text: Trotterized hybrid qubit-boson simulation of the Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard model. The Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard (JCH) model describes the interaction of light and matter in coupled optical cavities and provides a framework for studying their quantum dynamics. In this work, we design a Trotterized quantum circuit to investigate the real-time dynamics of the JCH model using Bosonic Qiskit and a Matrix Product State (MPS) backend. We simulate single-polariton transport and benchmark site occupations against exact diagonalization results. We then extend the simulations to the two-excitation sector under a hard-core photon constraint, examining excitation transport and symmetry properties. Finally, we study the dependence of bipartite entanglement entropy on the inter-cavity photon-hopping strength. The results illustrate how hybrid qubit-boson circuits, simulated with matrix product states, can be used to study light-matter lattice dynamics. This work provides a numerical benchmark for extending hybrid simulation approaches to more complex interacting and open light-matter systems.

title: Lensing ratios as a geometric probe of dark energy in the LSST and Simons Observatory era
text: Lensing ratios as a geometric probe of dark energy in the LSST and Simons Observatory era. Ratios of galaxy-CMB and galaxy-galaxy lensing around the same foreground galaxies probe relative distances extending to recombination without a standard candle or ruler. For sufficiently narrow foreground redshift distributions, and with intrinsic alignments and lens magnification controlled, these lensing ratios (LRs) become geometrical. Here we characterize the geometrical limit and develop an end-to-end optimized framework for the probe with LSST Y10 and Simons Observatory uncertainties. In our forecast for LSST Y10, the individual ratios are measured to a median precision of 1.0%, with a total signal-to-noise ratio of 360. We then study the complementarity of LRs as an additional geometrical probe to constrain dark energy and curvature. We find that LRs improve the $w_0$-$w_a$ figure of merit of the combined CMB, Type Ia supernova, and baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) data by 15%, after marginalizing over systematic uncertainties. As an independent geometric probe, they also enable competitive leave-one-out tests, in which one of the probes is dropped, and we find they are most effective at replacing the BAO: adding LRs to CMB+supernova raises the figure of merit from 33% to 66% of that of the full CMB+supernova+BAO combination. We also find LRs are especially valuable in extended model spaces constrained with minimal assumptions: in a seven-bin reconstruction of the dark-energy density, they reduce per-bin uncertainties by up to 16% at $z>1$, and by up to 50% when freeing curvature and dropping the non-geometrical part of the CMB likelihood (i.e. keeping the acoustic angular scale part), where they are able to break the degeneracy between curvature and dark energy.

title: Modified recombination or dynamical dark energy (or both)?
text: Modified recombination or dynamical dark energy (or both)?. Several recent analyses report a hint of modified recombination when the latest cosmic microwave background (CMB) and baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) data are jointly analysed. We examine whether this preference persists when allowing for departures in the late-time expansion history of the Universe. We fit a seven-parameter reconstruction of the free-electron fraction and a $w_0w_a$ dark-energy model, separately and jointly, to DESI DR2 BAO, a $5\times2$pt combination of galaxy clustering and CMB lensing, and three CMB likelihoods: P-ACT, Planck PR4 and Planck 2018. With a cosmological constant, our baseline data combination favours early recombination near last scattering, agreeing with previous analyses. Allowing for dynamical dark energy (DDE) removes this preference, while the constraints on $w_0$ and $w_a$ change little when the recombination history is marginalised over. DDE has the lowest Akaike information criterion of the models we consider for every data combination, and adding recombination freedom to it raises the AIC by $5.1$--$11.7$ and is disfavoured by the Bayesian evidence. We interpret these results in terms of CMB predictions for the BAO distances: earlier recombination and DDE both shift these predictions towards the measurements, but only DDE also changes the redshift dependence of the late-time expansion, which anisotropic BAO measurements constrain. We support these conclusions using noiseless mock data, finding that fitting modified recombination to a mock Universe generated with DDE reproduces the apparent preference for modified recombination, whereas DDE cannot similarly reproduce the signatures of modified recombination. The preference for modified recombination found with a cosmological constant therefore reflects the discrepancy between the CMB and BAO, rather than independent evidence for departures from standard recombination physics.

title: The Four-Loop Ladder Integral Family for the QED Electron Self-Energy
text: The Four-Loop Ladder Integral Family for the QED Electron Self-Energy. We compute the complete set of master integrals of the four-loop ladder integral family contributing to the electron self-energy in Quantum Electrodynamics. We obtain the results through canonical differential equations and write them as iterated integrals over integration kernels related to different parametrizations of the sunrise elliptic curve and a Calabi-Yau threefold. The rich structure of geometries and couplings between them requires the introduction of a large number of extra transcendental functions to reach $ε$-factorization. We discuss explicitly how to find a canonical basis for a selection of particularly interesting sectors. Additionally, we compute local series expansions and numerical boundary constants at $p^2=\infty$ and $p^2=m^2$ up to weight seven, and for the polylogarithmic constants we find analytical representations by numerical matching. The on-shell boundary values of this single family already span all non-polylogarithmic constants entering the planar contribution to the four-loop result for the anomalous magnetic moment $(g-2)$ of the electron. We obtain precise numerical results across all values of $p^2$ using numerical transport.

title: Strong hyperbolicity of puncture-gauge formulations of gravitational theories with second order equations of motion
text: Strong hyperbolicity of puncture-gauge formulations of gravitational theories with second order equations of motion. We prove that the modified CCZ4 (mCCZ4) formulation, used in nonlinear puncture-gauge simulations of (d+1)-dimensional Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity and four-derivative scalar-tensor theory in four dimensions, is strongly hyperbolic for both theories at sufficiently weak coupling, provided that the gauge parameters are chosen to satisfy a cone-separation condition. The proof applies to the full principal symbol of the theories, extending previous analyses based on first-order perturbation theory about the Einstein limit. We establish strong hyperbolicity by recasting the mCCZ4 equations into a formally equivalent second-order system whose derivative structure resembles that of the modified harmonic formulation of Kovács and Reall. This allows us to adapt their covariant characteristic analysis and continuity argument, without assuming that individual eigenvalues or eigenvectors depend analytically on the coupling. We also show that standard CCZ4 in general relativity is strongly hyperbolic in puncture gauge away from two defective degeneracies.

title: Perturbative unitarity bounds from qubit entanglement in scalar scattering and QED
text: Perturbative unitarity bounds from qubit entanglement in scalar scattering and QED. In the framework of $2\to 2$ relativistic scattering described by the perturbative $S$-matrix, we perform a comprehensive analysis of the properties of quantum channels obtained by tracing out the momentum from the scattered state. We work in two distinct scenarios with qubit degrees of freedom: flavored scalar contact interactions and QED, focusing in particular on initial-state leptons with transverse polarization. We identify the conditions that make the quantum channel unitary, calculate the entanglement of the qubits through the concurrence, and use its maximally allowed value to extract perturbativity upper bounds on the coupling constants. We find that the limits are often more constraining than the corresponding partial-wave expansion bounds, and that they allow us to bypass some of the obstacles associated in the latter with the singular behavior of forward scattering.

title: Cosmological Constant Screening from Quantum Horizon Chaos
text: Cosmological Constant Screening from Quantum Horizon Chaos. We propose a microscopic mechanism for screening the cosmological constant through quantum chaos of the horizon degrees of freedom. We show that in a recently proposed quantum-horizon matrix model arXiv:2406.01466, the Schwarzschild--de Sitter junction completion arXiv:2608.21178 supports a gravitationally dressed soft mode that approaches the massless minimally coupled scalar of de Sitter gravity. Interactions among the microscopic horizon degrees of freedom provide a mechanism for force relaxation. Assuming a finite-memory force spectrum with nonzero regular low-frequency weight, the gravitationally dressed soft mode undergoes Brownian diffusion after momentum relaxation. The resulting bosonic coarse-grained entropy supplements the background entropy arising from fermionic parton microstates. We propose that their sum defines the total thermodynamic entropy, which can be identified with the Gibbons--Hawking entropy of the backreacted causal horizon. Entropy generation during the diffusion regime then leads to infrared screening of the effective cosmological constant, with a universal entropy--variance coefficient agreeing with that of Kitazawa and collaborators. Radiative lifting of the soft mode provides a possible mechanism for terminating the screening regime.

title: Exploiting SU(2) Symmetry for Efficient Quantum State Preparation of Matrix Product States
text: Exploiting SU(2) Symmetry for Efficient Quantum State Preparation of Matrix Product States. Quantum computing offers a promising route to simulating strongly correlated systems, particularly for dynamical and spectral quantities whose classical computation can become prohibitively expensive. Fault-tolerant algorithms for these tasks, including real-time dynamics and phase estimation, assume efficient preparation of the initial many-body state, making state preparation an important bottleneck. Matrix product states obtained classically with the density matrix renormalization group can be compiled sequentially into fault-tolerant circuits. We exploit non-Abelian spin SU(2) symmetry in this compilation. By the Wigner-Eckart theorem, only the reduced tensors, which carry the variational information, need generic unitary synthesis. The magnetic structure is restored by Clebsch-Gordan transformations with analytically known angles. We benchmark the method on representative strongly correlated models, including the one-dimensional Hubbard model, quasi-one-dimensional Hubbard geometries, and Anderson impurity models, and perform fault-tolerant resource estimates using the Toffoli count as the primary cost metric. Across the systems considered, exploiting non-Abelian SU(2) symmetry reduces the Toffoli cost roughly threefold relative to U(1)-adapted compilation and by more than an order of magnitude relative to the standard dense compilation method. These results demonstrate how non-Abelian symmetries can substantially reduce the cost of transferring classically tractable many-body ground states to quantum computers, facilitating their use in quantum dynamics and energy estimation.

title: Large-Scale Streaming Portfolio Optimization with Pauli Correlation Encoding
text: Large-Scale Streaming Portfolio Optimization with Pauli Correlation Encoding. Classical portfolio construction over large asset universes is a combinatorial selection problem that existing heuristics do not solve well at scale. Pauli Correlation Encoding (PCE) addresses this by representing the underlying clustering problem with far fewer qubits than one per asset, and a prior study showed it is competitive with classical methods on a single historical snapshot. This paper moves beyond that static test to a streaming deployment, in which the correlation structure and the portfolio are both re-estimated on a rolling basis, as a live rebalancing system would actually operate. We introduce two streaming variants -- PCE itself and a joint multi-cut variant, dPCE -- and evaluate both against a Buy & Hold baseline across window lengths, portfolio sizes up to several thousand assets, risk-aversion and transaction-cost settings, and measurement-shot budgets. Streaming PCE and dPCE consistently outperform the passive baseline, including during a market downturn where both lose money but PCE loses markedly less -- evidence that the method's value is not confined to rising markets. PCE also proves the more practical choice at scale, since dPCE's resource requirements and its sensitivity to rebalancing frequency both grow faster with portfolio size. We further report which operational choices -- rebalancing cadence, shot budget, and transaction-cost awareness -- matter most for a real deployment, and which matter less than commonly assumed.

title: Programmable multipartite entanglement analogues
text: Programmable multipartite entanglement analogues. Quantum entanglement underpins the quantum information science. Its multipartite forms distribute coherence across several subsystems, but controlling their composition and order is increasingly difficult as more subsystems participate. Classical nonseparable waves provide accessible analogues of these structures, although existing implementations largely fix the participating degrees of freedom through their generating architectures. Here we overcome this constraint by making multipartiteness itself programmable in electromagnetic fields. A spatiotemporal metasurface reconfigures the identity and number of coherently linked state spaces independently across polarization, frequency, orbital angular momentum, wavevector direction, and orthogonal envelope modes. We realize complete Bell-like and Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger-like families from bipartite to five-partite order and exchange constituents at fixed order. To our knowledge, the five-partite state has the highest multipartite order experimentally realized in classical electromagnetic fields. These results establish the distribution of coherence across physical state spaces as a programmable property of classical waves and provide a platform for studying selected structures of multipartite quantum states without invoking quantum entanglement or nonlocality.

title: Classical sampling of verifiable graph-state quantum advantage experiments
text: Classical sampling of verifiable graph-state quantum advantage experiments. Quantum computers are expected to outperform classical ones on some tasks, but a convincing demonstration must be both hard to reproduce classically and verifiable. A recent proposal achieves verifiability by preparing graph states with built-in error detection, so that the quality of the experiment can be certified without simulating it; hardness is added by measuring in a non-Clifford basis or by inserting T gates. We show that the two instances posted to demonstrate this proposal on IBM hardware can be sampled classically on eight graphics processing units, with higher quality than the hardware in comparable or shorter time. For the 70-qubit instance our samples are drawn from the ideal output distribution; for the 64-qubit instance with 314 T gates they come with a certified fidelity of at least 0.908, against 0.349 for the hardware. The reason lies in verification itself: T gates can only be placed where the error detection cannot see them, which pushes them towards the end of the circuit, where they add little classical cost. Our results identify the features that future verifiable advantage experiments must control.

title: Multiscale Zoom-in Lattice Simulation for Inflation
text: Multiscale Zoom-in Lattice Simulation for Inflation. Lattice simulations are a powerful tool for studying the nonlinear evolution of inflationary fluctuations. The exponential expansion, however, makes it challenging to cover a broad range of scales relevant for the dynamics, limiting how many e-folds a single fixed grid can follow. We develop a three-dimensional zoom-in lattice method to follow inflationary fluctuations over a broad range of scales from the adiabatic subhorizon regime through horizon crossing. Every few e-folds, the grid is refined into one or more subgrids, with small-scale power injected and large-scale fluctuations inherited from previous generations. Each zoom shifts the resolved band while keeping its dynamic range fixed. This extends the duration over which lattice simulations can follow inflationary fluctuations from a few e-folds to tens of e-folds. In a Starobinsky benchmark evolved for 50 e-folds, the curvature power spectrum agrees with linear theory. In a model with an oscillatory feature, the zoom-in simulations recover the peak seen in a high-resolution fixed-grid run and show scale-dependent non-Gaussianity.

title: Baker-Akhiezer functions for Koornwinder-van Diejen integrable system
text: Baker-Akhiezer functions for Koornwinder-van Diejen integrable system. The Koornwinder-van Diejen integrable system is a counterpart of the trigonometric Ruijsenaars integrable system (associated with the root system $A_n$) for the root system $(C_n^\vee, C_n)$. It depends on the standard Macdonald parameters $q$ and $t$ as well as the Koornwinder (Askey-Wilson) parameters $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$. Different specializations of the parameters connect it to the other classical root systems from the $(C_n^\vee, C_n)$ family. The eigenfunctions of the Koornwinder-van Diejen integrable system are the symmetric Koornwinder polynomials; for certain values of the parameters $t$, $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ they coincide with the sum over the Weyl group of the Baker-Akhiezer functions introduced by O.A.\,Chalykh for the classical root system $BC_n$. The main idea behind this paper is to elucidate Chalykh's formalism and apply it to other affine root systems. We define Baker-Akhiezer functions for all root systems in the $(C_n^\vee, C_n)$ family. We also present some explicit expressions for Baker-Akhiezer functions.

title: Quantum Community Detection for Data Analysis
text: Quantum Community Detection for Data Analysis. Community detection offers an alternative to conventional methods for data analysis tasks such as feature selection and clustering, and detecting communities with quantum algorithms is a promising avenue for quantum speedup. We investigate quantum spectral community detectors, such as the modularity-matrix algorithm deteQt, in pipelines for both tasks. We first generalise deteQt to multiple communities by recursive bisection, and show that it recovers planted communities, and hence redundant features, in synthetic and small datasets. We then propose projeQt, which applies a spectral filter to the encoded modularity matrix through the quantum singular value transformation, retaining higher-order eigenvectors that deteQt does not use. projeQt acts on the generalised modularity matrix and extracts several communities at once, without recursion, by k-means clustering of a Gram matrix built from quantum state overlaps. On MNIST we demonstrate both pipelines, selecting informative pixels and classifying images directly by clustering, and find them competitive with standard community detectors.

title: A Gauge Pathway to an Ultralight Axion through a Hidden Portal
text: A Gauge Pathway to an Ultralight Axion through a Hidden Portal. We study a gauge realization of an ultralight axion with a hidden $SU(2)$ interaction, an Abelian vector portal, a charged Higgs and a Stückelberg field. The vector absorbs one scalar combination and leaves a physical phase. Its normalization is fixed by the Higgs and Stückelberg scales, while hidden confinement generates its mass. Keeping this phase ultralight requires an additional symmetry: the displayed gauge charges alone allow large phase-dependent scalar interactions. We quantify the suppression required of these interactions. Pure-$SU(2)$ lattice results relate the susceptibility to physical confinement scales; one- and two-loop running illustrate the dependence on the chosen high-energy coupling. We derive the coherent radiation-era density and exhibit an initial angle giving the reference dark-matter abundance for $F_χ\simeq10^{17}\,\GeV$ and zero-temperature mass $m_{χ,0}=3\times10^{-20}\,\eV$. We follow the confined population through number-changing and number-conserving limits and bound its energy contribution. An illustrative inflaton background satisfies the stated vacuum and isocurvature tests, conditional on control of a large portal correction to its potential. Its cold hidden history requires a hidden-to-visible reheating fraction near $5\times10^{-12}$, whose microscopic origin remains an input. A second, gauge-anomaly-free model gives the same physical phase scale using two charged Higgs singlets. These constructions specify conditional cosmological examples and the additional protection and reheating mechanisms needed to complete them.

title: Intrinsic longitudinal Hall effect in ferroaxial metals with high-order rotation axes
text: Intrinsic longitudinal Hall effect in ferroaxial metals with high-order rotation axes. The low-field Hall resistivity of non-magnetic metals has an intrinsic quantum contribution that derives from the field-corrected Berry curvature and intrinsic magnetic moment of the Bloch states near the Fermi surface. However, its effect is usually overshadowed by the classical Lorentz-force contribution. Here we show that for the longitudinal Hall effect, which occurs in ferroaxial crystals when the applied magnetic field lies in the Hall plane, the Lorentz force contribution vanishes for the eight ferroaxial groups with a 3,4 or 6-fold rotation axis. This provides an opportunity to measure the quantum correction in isolation, but so far all measured instances of the effect fall in the remaining five ferroaxial groups of lower symmetry, where the Lorentz force dominates the signal. We compile a list of candidate ferroaxial metals with such high-order rotation axis and compute the Hall effect from first principles for representative candidates, identifying Ni$_3$P with $σ^{\rm H}_{xzx} = 28.4$ S/m/T as a promising material to unambiguously measure the intrinsic longitudinal Hall effect.

title: Krylov dynamics of deformed oscillator chains: localization, ballistic spreading, and indeterminacy
text: Krylov dynamics of deformed oscillator chains: localization, ballistic spreading, and indeterminacy. Krylov and spread complexity map quantum dynamics onto a quantum walk on a half-line whose hopping amplitudes are the Lanczos coefficients, so that Krylov dynamics is the theory of orthogonal polynomials and Jacobi operators. We use this correspondence to study Krylov chains generated by the two-parameter $(p,q)$-deformed oscillator, which interpolates between the Heisenberg--Weyl chain, the $q$-oscillator chain of double-scaled SYK, and chains with exponentially growing Lanczos coefficients. For the deformed displacement chain the spread complexity is the mean excitation number, its rate is the deformed momentum quadrature, and its acceleration is $\ddot C_K=2ω^2\langle[a,a^\dagger]\rangle$, so the deformed commutator acts as a force along the Krylov chain and the mean deformation controls early-time growth. The deformation parameters separate four regimes. For $\max(p,q) 1$ the Jacobi operator is not essentially self-adjoint, the moment problem is indeterminate, and the Lanczos coefficients no longer determine the dynamics. Even and odd truncations converge to two different evolutions, the two reflection-symmetric N-extremal solutions of the moment problem, the odd one carrying a zero-energy atom of closed-form weight; the self-adjoint extensions yield a family of complexity curves that coincide at early times and separate once the Krylov wavefront reaches infinity. Krylov complexity in this regime is thus defined only once a boundary condition at infinite Krylov index is specified. The orthogonal-polynomial procedure and its checks on exactly solvable chains are given in the appendices.

title: Bayesian Learning of Spatially Heterogeneous Causal Structure in Spatial Transcriptomics
text: Bayesian Learning of Spatially Heterogeneous Causal Structure in Spatial Transcriptomics. Spatial transcriptomics preserves the location of each expression profile, making it possible to study how gene regulatory networks differ within a tissue. Across regions of a tissue, regulatory relationships may vary and even reverse direction, so identifying the causal relationships in a specific pathological region can provide insight into therapeutic targets. We propose SpaDAG, a Bayesian method for learning spatially varying causal directed acyclic graphs. By defining the graphs on a triangulation of the tissue, SpaDAG allows each edge to have its own spatial pattern and even to reverse direction across regions. We show that the graphs nonetheless remain fully identifiable, and develop an MCMC sampler that explores them efficiently by reversing an edge over an entire connected region in a single move. SpaDAG outperforms competing methods in simulations with and without direction reversals. In a section spanning a renal cell carcinoma and the adjacent kidney, SpaDAG finds largely different relationships in the two tissues, with those in the tumor concentrated on genes associated with therapeutic targets. Between two of these genes, it identifies a relationship whose direction reverses across the tumor boundary, generating hypotheses about their region-specific coupling. Supplementary materials and code for this article are available online.

title: Pragmatic Deeply Debiased ML
text: Pragmatic Deeply Debiased ML. Debiased machine learning (DML) combines a fitted outcome regression with weighted residuals to remove first-order regularization bias when estimating parameters such as average treatment effects, yet a second-order bias remains whenever regression and weighting errors align. For linear regression functionals, we target this second-order bias by training a strong learner to predict first-stage residuals from many covariates, yielding a one-dimensional (or low-dimensional) working model whose bias contribution is estimated on an independent sample. To complement this targeted search, we also analyze general kernel-based corrections, including covariate partitions and smoothers. We prove that deeply debiased ML is algebraically identical to ordinary DML evaluated with a post-hoc regression update that adjusts each scored observation using kernel-weighted residuals from the remaining evaluation observations. In our empirical and simulation studies, strong initial DML learners often leave the second-order correction small relative to sampling uncertainty, in which case the correction serves as a diagnostic check alongside sensitivity bounds for any remaining misspecification bias.

title: Certifying total-variation contamination by betting on trimmed kernel witnesses
text: Certifying total-variation contamination by betting on trimmed kernel witnesses. Two laws share a common component after each discards a fraction $α$ of its mass, a trimming, exactly when their total variation is at most $α$, so the contamination level $α^\star = \mathrm{TV} (P,Q)$ is the share of each population without counterpart in the other. We bound it from below from two samples on any space with a bounded characteristic kernel. The kernel mean embeddings of all such trimmings of a law form a convex region, the regions of two laws first touch at $α^\star$, and in every direction a region reaches as far as a trimmed mean. The difference of their closest points, the witness, selects the trimming. We fit a ramp of the witness on part of the data and bet on the rest, at each level of a grid. The bound is valid at every sample size. The cut points of the tested level carry most of its finite-sample gain over an untrimmed witness, while refitting the witness at that level makes it consistent, gives its rates and returns the trimming. When a function of the kernel's Hilbert space separates the parts of the two laws without counterpart, the bound is within order $(n\wedge m)^{-1/2}$ of $α^\star$ on a grid of that mesh, which is minimax over such pairs. When these parts touch, a margin condition guarantees a polynomial rate for Sobolev kernels and a logarithmic rate for the Gaussian kernel. For the Laplace kernel on the line this guarantee is not sharp: the witness stays between its two cut points, and for densities that cross once, with a likelihood ratio bounded away from one off the crossing, the error on such a grid is again of that order up to logarithmic factors. No informative upper bound exists without assumptions. On the Right Heart Catheterization data, with confidence $0.95$, each arm must lose more than a fraction $0.35$ of its patients, if both lose the same fraction, before their covariate distributions can coincide.

title: Online V-Learning with Adaptive Longitudinal Data
text: Online V-Learning with Adaptive Longitudinal Data. Reinforcement learning methods for estimating optimal dynamic treatment regimes are increasingly applied in mobile health (mHealth), where treatment decisions are made continually. Luckett et al. (2020) proposed V-learning, which estimates an optimal policy from offline trajectories. In practice, mHealth policies are updated online. Batch updating, in which the policy is re-estimated after each block of new data, is a tractable middle ground between offline learning and updating after every observation. However, because each batch's treatment policy is estimated from data pooled across patients in earlier batches, the resulting data are adaptively collected and patient trajectories are dependent, a setting that offline theory does not address. We develop statistical theory for V-learning in this setting with varying, deterministic batch sizes. For each fixed batch, as the number of patients grows, we establish uniform consistency of the estimated value function, consistency of the estimated policy, a functional central limit theorem over the policy class, asymptotic normality of the estimated value of the learned policy, and a consistent variance estimator. To first order, the online procedure performs as well as an oracle that deploys the optimal policy after the first batch. With the number of patients fixed and the number of batches growing, the estimated value function and policy remain consistent under a persistent identifiability condition. In simulations, as the number of patients grows with the number of batches fixed, confidence intervals attain near-nominal coverage under adaptive assignment and the online procedure closely matches the oracle. With a small cohort followed over many batches, the learned policies improve steadily.

title: PHM-ensemble: Scalable and Stable Probabilistic Multiresolution Clustering via Ensemble Density Estimation
text: PHM-ensemble: Scalable and Stable Probabilistic Multiresolution Clustering via Ensemble Density Estimation. Clustering is a foundational tool for exploratory data analysis across the sciences. We argue that clustering methods should be evaluated along four dimensions: fidelity to the data's underlying structure, interpretability of the recovered groups, stability under data perturbations and algorithmic randomness, and scalability to modern scientific datasets. Yet existing methods rarely satisfy all four criteria. To address this gap, we introduce PHM-ensemble, a general probabilistic framework for multiresolution clustering that estimates the underlying data density by pooling mixture models from an ensemble of fits and subsequently constructs a clustering hierarchy through hierarchical merging of the mixture components. On simulated datasets and the MNIST benchmark, PHM-ensemble matches or outperforms widely used clustering algorithms in agreement with ground truth, produces more stable results across runs, and reveals complex underlying structures. Applied to 1.82 million peripheral blood cells from the Human Immune Health Atlas, PHM-ensemble achieves higher agreement with expert-curated major cell-type annotations than the Leiden clustering used in the original study (adjusted Rand index 0.965 versus 0.789), while requiring only half the computing time. Beyond identifying major immune lineages, it reveals biologically coherent relationships among cell types and resolves finer structure within individual lineages, uncovering subtypes and cellular states consistent with known biology.

title: Statistical Process Monitoring of Functional Linear Models
text: Statistical Process Monitoring of Functional Linear Models. Monitoring the stability over time of the relationship between a functional response and multiple functional covariates is important in many industrial applications, either because the relationship itself is the quality characteristic of interest or because it underpins a predictive model whose validity must be verified as the process evolves. Existing methods either assume the model estimated in Phase I to be stable and monitor the resulting residuals, or re-estimate its coefficients at each sampling stage, which requires several observations to be available at a time. In this article, we propose the regression coefficient function (RCF) control chart to monitor functional linear models (FLMs) in which, at each sampling stage, an individual observation of the functional response and an arbitrary number of functional covariates become available. The proposed method employs an exponentially weighted moving loss to sequentially update estimates of the regression coefficient functions and the intercept function, which are monitored through Hotelling's $T^2$ and squared prediction error (SPE) control charts. A post-signal diagnostic procedure is also provided to support the identification of the source of the detected change. A Monte Carlo simulation study demonstrates that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly against small and persistent shifts, and a case study on monitoring the relationship between the air/fuel ratio and engine state variables in an automotive after-treatment system illustrates its practical applicability.

title: Efficient inferential models and their fiducial connections
text: Efficient inferential models and their fiducial connections. Valid inferential models (IMs) provide frequentist calibration guarantees, but validity alone does not determine which construction is most informative. We study finite-sample efficiency through concentration risk, the expected volume under a possibility contour. For a smooth, fully identified association and a specified parameter-volume measure, a weighted Neyman--Pearson argument identifies the generalized fiducial density as the optimal score for minimizing cut volume subject to fixed-data auxiliary compatibility. The resulting maximum-specificity transform gives an explicit volume interpretation of the fiducial efficiency ceiling, which need not itself be sampling valid. We develop two approaches to valid construction. The first minimizes design-averaged concentration risk among single, data-independent auxiliary-compatible contours. The design measure prioritizes efficiency without requiring prior beliefs or restricting validity. The second localizes the parameter-volume score to candidate-specific contours, yielding a normalized, valid IM equivalent to sampling validification of the relative fiducial likelihood. A parallel sample-space construction recovers the ordinary likelihood-ratio IM; direct validification of the ceiling provides another repair. For the same association, exact, data-independent predictive contours share a common fiducial distribution as a saturating inner probability, while generating different calibrated confidence-region geometries. Design averaging thus selects an efficient member without changing the underlying fiducial law. Examples in a two-component measurement model and an exponential scale model illustrate the efficiency gains and show that sampling-valid repair can improve on the raw ceiling by leaving the fixed-data auxiliary-compatible class over which it is optimal.

title: Generalizing Couple-Randomized Trials Under Limited Overlap and Missing Partner Linkage
text: Generalizing Couple-Randomized Trials Under Limited Overlap and Missing Partner Linkage. We study how to generalize couple-randomized trials when some couple types are absent from the trial and the target survey reports partner characteristics without linking spouses. Under an additive effect model with unrestricted partner-profile terms, the target average effect is identified exactly when the wife and husband margins assign equal mass to each connected component of the trial support graph. A specified interaction is identified when its alternating contrast around at least one cycle is nonzero. Without linkage, we obtain sharp bounds by optimizing over pairings consistent with the survey margins. A spousal odds ratio can narrow the bounds for a binary interaction. We derive joint bounds for an index-patient design, quantify bias from common shortcuts, and estimate effects and bounds using Bayesian dyadic multilevel regression and poststratification. In a worked example based on 3,826 Health and Retirement Study couples and simulated trial outcomes, an index-patient trial and an unlinked survey yielded a 2.93 mmHg wide identified set for the couple-average effect. Linking the survey narrowed it to 2.38 mmHg. Adding 300 couples without diabetes narrowed the unlinked set to 0.28 mmHg and yielded point identification with linkage under the fitted model.

title: Regression calibration for logistic regression with correlated measurement error and multiple misclassification in covariates
text: Regression calibration for logistic regression with correlated measurement error and multiple misclassification in covariates. Epidemiological analyses often suffer from covariate data quality issues: measurement error in continuous predictors and misclassification of categorical variables. Existing logistic regression correction methods mostly handle only one error type or a single misclassified variable, with limited tools for multiple misclassified categorical exposures together with correlated measurement error in continuous covariates. To address this gap, we extend regression calibration for logistic regression to jointly accommodate multiple continuous covariates with correlated additive measurement error and two or more misclassified categorical predictors. We build a unified framework integrating additive measurement error models and misclassification transition matrices, deriving the regression calibration estimator (RCE) using Kronecker product algebra. This computationally feasible approach extends naturally to more than two misclassified categorical variables. We evaluate RCE via simulations across varied misclassification rates, error magnitudes, sample sizes and effect sizes, comparing it with the naive estimator that ignores measurement error. We apply RCE to the EPIC-InterAct male case-cohort data to adjust for correlated error in protein and energy intake, plus misclassification in binary physical activity and three-category alcohol consumption. Results show that neglecting these error sources produces substantial bias and misleading inference for main and interaction effects in nutritional epidemiology. While the RCE is a practical correction tool, it treats validation nuisance parameters as known and does not account for their estimation uncertainty.

title: Accuracy of Noise Ceiling Estimators for Brain Scores
text: Accuracy of Noise Ceiling Estimators for Brain Scores. The internal activations of modern machine learning models align surprisingly well with the activities recorded in real brains. In the last five years, the alignment between encoding models and brain activities, often called brain scores, has steadily increased. Because brain recordings are noisy, there exists an upper bound to the brain scores that any model can achieve. This bound, called the noise ceiling, is crucial for two reasons: it determines whether further improvements in model performance are possible, and it enables meaningful comparisons of brain scores across benchmarks. The field has developed multiple approaches to estimate noise ceilings, but the statistical properties of existing estimators remain poorly understood, leaving it unclear in which experimental settings they provide reliable estimates. Here, we introduce a unified mathematical framework for brain recordings, use it to derive closed-form expressions for four commonly used noise ceiling estimators, and provide theoretical predictions for the behavior of each estimator. We validate the theoretical predictions with simulations that we compare to noise ceiling estimates in existing fMRI and EEG datasets. We find that the existing methods underestimate the true noise ceiling in different settings. We conclude with recommendations for best practice in different situations.

title: SGD with Large Learning Rates: General Analysis & Improved Rates
text: SGD with Large Learning Rates: General Analysis & Improved Rates. Stochastic Gradient Descent lies at the core of modern machine learning. However its classical analysis typically restricts the stepsize to be below a curvature-dependent stability threshold. Recent developments in deterministic optimization have challenged this paradigm, showing that suitably chosen large stepsizes can not only preserve convergence, but also accelerate Gradient Descent (GD). Whether this phenomenon persists in the presence of stochastic gradient noise has remained an open question (Wu et al., 2024). In this work, we answer this question affirmatively for the cross-entropy loss with linear predictors and two-layer neural networks, establishing an accelerated $\mathcal{O}(T^{-2})$ convergence rate. At the core of our analysis is a fine-grained characterization of the stochastic large-stepsize dynamics. This sharper control of the trajectory further yields tight convergence guarantees within the stable regime, improving existing bounds even in the deterministic setting. Taken together, our results show that the acceleration mechanism induced by large stepsizes survives stochasticity and extends beyond linear models. Numerical experiments demonstrate the benefits of large learning rates in practice.

title: Model-Based Clustering of Longitudinal Functional Data with Hidden Semi-Markov Models
text: Model-Based Clustering of Longitudinal Functional Data with Hidden Semi-Markov Models. Model-based clustering of longitudinal functional data must account both for heterogeneity among curves and for temporal dependence in their latent group memberships. Functional mixture models typically treat curves as exchangeable, while temporal approaches may restrict regime persistence or ignore state-specific functional variation. We propose hidden semi-Markov models for ordered sequences of multivariate functional observations in which each latent regime has a parsimonious, state-specific functional principal subspace, extending functional high-dimensional data clustering (funHDDC) to longitudinal settings. Gaussian, contaminated-Gaussian and multivariate-$t$ emissions accommodate atypical observations, and explicit state-specific sojourn distributions govern regime persistence, with hidden Markov models as the geometric special case. Estimation uses expectation-maximization (EM) and expectation/conditional-maximization (ECM) algorithms with segmental forward-backward recursions, and identifiability is established up to label permutations and spectral indeterminacies. In simulations, temporal dependence yields the largest gains when single curves are weakly informative; with robust emissions, state-specific subspaces outperform a global functional principal component representation; and explicit durations add smaller gains when regimes overlap and sojourns are non-geometric. Applications to air-quality profiles and smartphone activity recordings, evaluated on held-out years and subjects, show improved predictive fit and illustrate how apparent duration effects can reflect time-varying transitions.

title: Adaptive Multi-kernel Correntropy Kalman Filter: A Variational Bayesian Approach
text: Adaptive Multi-kernel Correntropy Kalman Filter: A Variational Bayesian Approach. This paper proposes an adaptive multi-kernel correntropy Kalman filter (AMCKF) for robust state estimation in the presence of heavy-tailed measurement noises and outliers. The multi-kernel correntropy loss is reformulated via half-quadratic (HQ) duality into a quadratic form with auxiliary weights, enabling efficient Kalman-like recursions. We establish a rigorous variational Bayesian framework under the mean-field assumption, deriving closed-form coordinate ascent variational inference updates for joint state and kernel width estimation. To enable online implementation, AMCKF is then proposed as an efficient single-pass approximation of the exact coordinate ascent variational inference (CAVI), where the state and auxiliary variables are updated iteratively via IRLS, followed by a closed-form kernel width update. A forgetting mechanism is designed to prevent over-confidence and ensure long-term adaptability. Simulations on target tracking and IMU attitude estimation demonstrate that the proposed AMCKF significantly outperforms standard KF, VBKF, Student's t-based KF, and fixed-kernel MKCKF in scenarios with sparse outliers, heavy-tailed noise, and mixed disturbances, while maintaining optimal performance under Gaussian conditions.

title: Partial Identification under Imperfect Compliance via Cross-World Correlation Restriction
text: Partial Identification under Imperfect Compliance via Cross-World Correlation Restriction. This article develops a unified partial identification approach for the average treatment effect (ATE) and the local average treatment effect (LATE) in randomized experiments with imperfect compliance, incorporating the cross-world correlation between potential treatment statuses. Even under random assignment and exclusion restriction, the correlation is unidentified. However, given the two identified marginals, it uniquely determines the relative proportions of the four principal strata, with monotonicity corresponding to a special case. We derive explicit sharp bounds for both the ATE and LATE at a fixed correlation and extend the results to prespecified correlation ranges, providing a sensitivity analysis that incorporates substantive information about compliance behavior. For the ATE, the lower bound decreases and the upper bound increases with the correlation. Although imposing monotonicity does not tighten the conventional Balke--Pearl bounds, we show that restricting the correlation can yield tighter bounds, even when defiers remain possible. For the LATE, the sharp bounds may not vary monotonically with the correlation, and we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for point identification of the LATE at any feasible correlation value, with the conventional Wald ratio identification result under monotonicity as a special case. In addition, we derive a breakdown point for the correlation that determines when the Wald ratio falls outside the sharp identified set for the LATE. Applications to four empirical studies illustrate how cross-world correlation restrictions tighten the sharp bounds for the ATE and LATE and assess the breakdown of the Wald ratio.

title: Cross-Order Information-Guided Estimation for Non-Uniform Hypergraphs
text: Cross-Order Information-Guided Estimation for Non-Uniform Hypergraphs. Many real-world interactions involve groups of nodes rather than pairs. A non-uniform hypergraph records such interactions as hyperedges of different orders, where the order counts the nodes in a hyperedge. Full estimation evaluates every candidate hyperedge, whose number grows exponentially with the order, and classical remedies sacrifice higher-order information or aggravate computation. The orders are not isolated: the lower orders, cheap to compute and rich in information, reveal where higher-order hyperedges are likely to occur. We propose CINE (Cross-order Information-guided Negative-sampling Estimation) under a latent space model in which all orders share latent positions. Starting from order two, CINE climbs one order at a time. At each higher order, CINE keeps all present hyperedges, samples a small subset of negative examples guided by lower-order scores, and corrects for the known inclusion probabilities to preserve the target of full estimation.
