CINE thereby lets users choose the trade-off between computation time and estimation accuracy: the retained orders and the sampling budget set the time, and the retained information provably approaches full-data information as the sampling budget grows. In simulations, CINE approaches the accuracy of full estimation at a small fraction of its computation time, and larger teams in MADStat reveal research associations.

title: High-throughput light-sheet 3D microscopy of whole rodent brain microstructure for integration with MRI
text: High-throughput light-sheet 3D microscopy of whole rodent brain microstructure for integration with MRI. Whole-brain cellular mapping is essential for understanding how differences in cellular architecture shape brain organisation and function. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) provides whole-brain coverage in humans and animal models but is only indirectly sensitive to cellular features. Integrating MRI with whole-brain microscopy is therefore critical for interpreting existing microstructural MRI measures and developing more specific ones. Here, we present a scalable cross-resolution framework integrating 3D light-sheet microscopy (LSM) of intact rodent brains with diffusion MRI (dMRI). By combining active tissue clearing and immunolabelling with accelerated LSM acquisitions, we achieve multiplexed whole-brain mapping of neuronal and glial populations on timescales comparable to conventional histology and 2D microscopy. This throughput enables LSM and MRI integration at scale, linking macroscopic MRI contrasts to spatially-matched microscopic cellular features within the same tissue. We apply this framework across eight genetically diverse mouse strains to develop predictive models of 3D microscopy-derived cellular features from dMRI contrasts. We demonstrate that data-driven combinations of state-of-the-art multi-shell dMRI measures predict neuronal and astrocytic features better than individual contrasts, across all animals. Our approach enables 3D microscopy to guide the development and interpretation of biologically-specific microstructural MRI measures, with the potential for translation to the living human brain.

title: Interconnected reservoirs of multidrug-resistant bacteria and plasmids within hospital plumbing infrastructure
text: Interconnected reservoirs of multidrug-resistant bacteria and plasmids within hospital plumbing infrastructure. Hospital sinks and wastewater streams are hotspots for contamination and colonization with multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria (MDR-GNB). While hospital water systems may facilitate MDR-GNB transmission during outbreaks, longitudinal population dynamics of environmental MDR-GNB and their long-term relationship with patient isolates remain unclear. Here we aimed to characterize the diversity and abundance of MDR-GNB within the hospital built environment and evaluate their relationship with clinical isolates. We performed nanopore sequencing on MDR-GNB cultured from sink drains (n=523) and wastewater (n=146) at a New York City hospital between March-August 2023. We assessed spatial and longitudinal genomic strain and plasmid dynamics and quantified relatedness to historical clinical isolates from the same hospital (n=602). Sink drains (54-73%) and wastewater (100%) demonstrated widespread, longitudinal colonization with MDR-GNB, driven primarily by carbapenem-resistant GNB including opportunistic organisms and Enterobacterales encoding blaKPC. While bacterial colonization differed across environmental niches, we identified both MDR-GNB strains and resistance plasmids that were shared between clinical and environmental sources, as well a distinct interplay between clinical and wastewater versus sink drain samples. This study supports the role of hospital plumbing as an important reservoir for clinically relevant MDR-GNB, but highlights differences across environmental sources, which may impact surveillance approaches.

title: Molecular Modulation of the SAM-I Riboswitch Drives Global Dynamical Shifts
text: Molecular Modulation of the SAM-I Riboswitch Drives Global Dynamical Shifts. A surge in antimicrobial resistance in recent years has made protein-targeting antibiotics less effective against key pathogens. It is possible to expand the range of therapeutic targets by using RNA-based therapies, but it remains necessary to improve the molecular-level understanding of interactions between RNA and known and potential binders. The SAM-I riboswitch, which controls the transcriptional termination of gene expression involved in sulfur metabolism in most bacteria, is an excellent ligand target. Thus, understanding its behavior with and without ligand complexes would be helpful for drug design. Here, we studied the interactions between the SAM-I riboswitch and its natural ligand, SAM, which controls riboswitch function, and compared those to its interactions with the similar small molecule SAH, which does not control riboswitch function, and to its interactions with a potential binder JS4, identified via virtual screening. From our simulations, we deepen understanding of small molecule interactions with the SAM-I riboswitch on both a local and a distal level. The results reveal how differently ligands (SAM, SAH and JS4) can bind to and potentially induce conformational changes in the riboswitch. Our findings offer valuable insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying riboswitch RNA-ligand interactions for the design of more effective RNA-targeting therapeutics.

title: Hybrid RY-mers increase aDNA alignment sensitivity
text: Hybrid RY-mers increase aDNA alignment sensitivity. One of the key steps in ancient DNA data analysis is the accurate identification of endogenous short reads that originate from the ancient genome. Currently, this step is performed using general-purpose sequence aligners, such as BWA-aln, with parameter settings optimized for sensitivity. This approach results in increased runtime, even relative to standard DNA alignment workflows, and is not sufficient for aligning samples that are highly divergent from a reference database. We introduce hybrid RY-mers, a seed construct designed to incorporate aDNA-specific sequence damage. We adapt hybrid RY-mers to the existing concept of multi-context seeds and implement them in the read aligner strobealign. On simulated genomic and metagenomic datasets, we show that hybrid RY-mers result in higher mapping accuracy, while also reducing runtime by 4-6 times compared to the state-of-the-art aDNA alignment method BWA-aln. Furthermore, substituting aDNA aligner MALT in the metagenomic tool-suite aMeta with our new alignment approach demonstrated that aMeta gave a faster and less memory consuming detection of ancient taxa present in the samples.

title: Implicit Hierarchical Tensor Decomposition of Single-Cell Four-Omics Data Reveals Cell-Type-Linked Candidate Enhancer--Promoter-Associated Programs
text: Implicit Hierarchical Tensor Decomposition of Single-Cell Four-Omics Data Reveals Cell-Type-Linked Candidate Enhancer--Promoter-Associated Programs. Single-cell multi-omics provides complementary views of gene regulation, but integrating modalities with natural features comprising enhancers, genes, and three-dimensional (3D) genomic loci remains challenging. This study developed an implicit hierarchical tensor decomposition framework and applied it to the CHARM single-cell four-omics mouse brain data (GSE303006) by jointly analyzing ATAC, H3K27ac, RNA, and reconstructed 3D enhancer--promoter (E--P) distances. After quality control, 730,969 E--P pairs, 42,669 enhancers, 16,239 genes, 391,435 20-kb bin pairs, and 4,258 cells were retained. Each modality was independently reduced to 20 components and mapped to an implicit 730,969x4{,}258x20x4 tensor, which was decomposed without materializing the full array. In a joint model, cell type explained more variance than biological replicate for all 12 distinct cell components represented among the 100 largest Tucker core elements. A representative core linked the Inh_Ndnf/Lamp5--Ex_L3/4_IT cell axis to contrasting presynaptic-transmission and developmental/morphogenetic candidate E--P-associated programs. Its E--P and cell factors were recovered when the whole analysis was repeated independently on each pair of replicates, and the E--P pairs it prioritized agreed in direction with the cell-type-resolved enhancer--gene links of the original CHARM study. No single modality reproduced the program, which required the combination of accessibility, chromatin contact, and expression. Backprojection showed reproducible ATAC, H3K27ac, and 3D effects across three biological replicates; RNA differed clearly for the developmental module but not for the presynaptic module. The framework thus identifies regulatory structure that is shared across molecular modalities and is not recoverable from any single modality.

title: Simple models outperform single-cell foundation models on downstream benchmarks
text: Simple models outperform single-cell foundation models on downstream benchmarks. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data exhibit strong and reproducible statistical structure. This has motivated the development of large-scale foundation models, such as TranscriptFormer, that use transformer-based architectures to learn a generative model for gene expression by embedding genes into a latent vector space. These embeddings have been used to obtain state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on downstream tasks such as cell-type classification, disease-state prediction, and cross-species learning. Here, we ask whether similar performance can be achieved without utilizing computationally intensive deep learning-based representations. Using simple, interpretable pipelines that rely on careful normalization and linear methods, we obtain SOTA or near SOTA performance across multiple benchmarks commonly used to evaluate single-cell foundation models, including outperforming foundation models on out-of-distribution tasks involving novel cell types and organisms absent from the training data. Our findings highlight the need for rigorous benchmarking and suggest that the biology of cell identity can be captured by simple linear representations of single cell gene expression data.

title: Large seed size accompanying GmSDP1 suppression is linked to cellular remodeling and phytohormone regulation
text: Large seed size accompanying GmSDP1 suppression is linked to cellular remodeling and phytohormone regulation. Soybean (Glycine max) seeds contain approximately 20% oil and 40% protein and are important for food, feed, and biofuel. Improving soybean productivity and seed quality requires optimizing carbon partitioning during seed development. Previously, seed-specific suppression of the lipase-encoding gene Sugar-Dependent 1 (SDP1) increased seed oil content by approximately 5% while slightly reducing raffinose family oligosaccharides without compromising protein content. Seed-specific SDP1 suppression also increased seed size by 18-25% without affecting seed number, resulting in greater seed biomass per plant. To determine the developmental basis of the increased seed size, we investigated the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying this phenotype. Microscopy and biochemical analyses showed that larger seeds were associated with increased seed cell size and enhanced lignocellulosic cell wall accumulation. Temporal biochemical and transcriptomic analyses further revealed coordinated changes in hormone homeostasis, including altered levels of abscisic acid, 12-oxo-phytodienoic acid, and jasmonoyl-isoleucine, together with differential expression of F-box and RING/U-box family genes. The results indicate that the enhanced seed size resulting from SDP1 suppression is associated with coordinated changes in cellular development, cell wall accumulation, hormone homeostasis, and regulation of gene expression during seed development. Developmental and metabolic changes associated with the increased seed size phenotype support SDP1 manipulation as a potential strategy for improving soybean seed yield and quality.

title: A Proteome-Wide Gain-of-Function Atlas Mapping the Landscape of Chemotherapy Response
text: A Proteome-Wide Gain-of-Function Atlas Mapping the Landscape of Chemotherapy Response. Background: Conventional chemotherapies remain the core therapeutic backbone of cancer treatment, yet the rapid emergence of chemoresistance often compromises their clinical efficacy. Although large-scale functional genomics has transformed precision oncology, existing reference maps rely predominantly on loss-of-function paradigms and lack systematic data on gain-of-function (GOF) events that commonly drive clinical resistance. Methods: To address this gap, we engineered a site-specific Bxb1 integrase landing-pad system in HeLa cells, enabling single-copy integration of a human proteome-wide library [18,388 open reading frames (ORFs)] at the AAVS1 locus under a uniform EF1 promoter. We systematically profiled cellular fitness across 16 chemotherapeutics. We integrated this GOF perturbation screen with bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing, FACS-based lysosomal functional screening, clinical cohort survival analyses, and preclinical xenograft modeling. Results: Stratified modeling of over 230,000 gene-drug interactions defined distinct functional categories that are strongly enriched for clinical cancer biomarkers and prognostic relevance. Global network analysis and organelle-specific lysosomal functional screening uncovered that chemotherapeutic agents, most prominently the nucleoside analog TAS-102 (Lonsurf), converge upon a shared survival hub centered on the BCL-2 family-associated autophagy-endolysosomal network. Mechanistically, TAS-102 triggered lysosomal activation as an adaptive survival response. Co-treatment with the BCL-2 family inhibitor ABT-263 (Navitoclax) attenuated this TAS-102-induced lysosomal response and synergistically reversed TAS-102 resistance across colorectal and pancreatic cancer models in vitro and in colorectal cell line- and patient-derived xenograft (CDX, PDX) models in vivo. Conclusions: Our study establishes an open-access, proteome-wide GOF reference atlas that systematically maps chemotherapeutic responses, recapitulates canonical resistance biology, and nominates rational drug combinations. This systems-genomics resource bridges massive-scale perturbation mapping with actionable target discovery, providing a translational framework to overcome therapeutic resistance and reprogram cancer drug responses.

title: Shared experimental materials inflate and reorder cross-participant decoding benchmarks
text: Shared experimental materials inflate and reorder cross-participant decoding benchmarks. Decoding mental states from brain activity underpins brain-computer interfaces and cognitive neuroscience. Decoders are judged by how well they generalize to people left out of training, taken as evidence that they capture what transfers between brains. However, most benchmarks present the same experimental materials to every participant, so held-out participants are tested on materials the model has already seen. Here we show, across 15 EEG, fMRI and eye-tracking datasets and 318 matched comparisons, that shared materials inflate cross-participant accuracy by up to 46 percentage points. They also reorder methods, reversing the advantage of foundation models over handcrafted features on the largest emotion EEG benchmark. The inflation tracks cross-participant item identifiability and, in sealed prospective tests, vanished where items could not be identified. Adding training items improved new-material accuracy more reliably than adding participants. These findings call for reporting new-material accuracy alongside conventional scores and for measuring item identifiability first.

title: Widespread oscillatory suppression in autism persists in the absence of psychotropic medication.
text: Widespread oscillatory suppression in autism persists in the absence of psychotropic medication.. Purpose: Investigate the neural oscillatory activity associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) using electroencephalographic (EEG) recordings in children and adolescents. Compare the corresponding oscillatory power between ASD patients taking psychotropic medication with a drug-naive group. Methods: ASD diagnosis was done using DSM-IV and CARS (Childhood Autism Rating Scale). EEG recordings employed 22 scalp electrodes (10/20 system). ASD vs. neurotypical groups were matched for sex and age (5 females; average age: ~10 years old). We analyzed the resting state (eyes open) EEG power spectrum during ~2-minute recordings. The multitaper FFT method was used to estimate spectral power for the delta, theta, alpha, beta and gamma frequency bands. We pooled together data from several electrodes to compute comprehensive power spectra and assess the oscillatory behavior of macro brain regions. Results: We observed widespread (~4Hz - 20Hz) oscillatory suppression comprising the theta, alpha and beta frequency bands. The most widespread and robust ASD-associated power suppression was in the high theta and alpha bands. Delta and gamma bands showed no significant power change for any of the brain regions studied. Results from a subgroup of patients (N = 9) who never used psychotropics confirmed these findings, indicating that they are not an artifact of medication. Conclusion: Suppression in theta, alpha and beta oscillations may offer insights into the neurophysiological underpinnings of autism and could be used as an accessible and comprehensive tool in ASD diagnosis, regardless of the patients being or not on medication.

title: Accessing Mesoscale Functional Organization from Standard Functional MRI Leveraging AI-Based Super-Resolution
text: Accessing Mesoscale Functional Organization from Standard Functional MRI Leveraging AI-Based Super-Resolution. Access to the fine-scale functional organization of the human brain is essential for understanding cognition and neurological disorders yet remains beyond the reach of conventional functional MRI (fMRI) because of its limited spatial resolution and contrast-to-noise ratio. To overcome this limitation, we developed f-LENNS (functional Localization Enhancement via Neural-Net-Sharpening), an artificial intelligence (AI)-based framework that enhances the effective spatial resolution of reconstructed fMRI magnitude images. The model was trained exclusively on high-resolution synthetic MRI data using extensive domain randomization and no adversarial or generative components. This approach enables robust out-of-the-box generalization (without retraining) to experimental datasets obtained with diverse acquisitions, while effectively curbing hallucination. Our experiments show that our publicly available model substantially improves the spatial fidelity of functional activation maps across multiple imaging paradigms and generalizes to a cohort of individuals with atypical brain function caused by amblyopia (lazy eye). F-LENNS consistently outperforms conventional resolution enhancement approaches, including interpolation-based upsampling and sharpening methods. These findings demonstrate that AI-driven super-resolution combined with domain randomization can overcome domain shifts arising from differences in MRI acquisition, enabling scalable, fine-scale functional brain mapping with widely available MRI hardware.

title: Rab10 and Arhgef7 interact to promote axon extension by linking vesicle supply and exocytosis
text: Rab10 and Arhgef7 interact to promote axon extension by linking vesicle supply and exocytosis. The formation of functional neural circuits begins with the extension of a single axon by immature neurons. Axon elongation requires an expansion of the plasma membrane that depends on the polarization of vesicle trafficking and exocytosis. It is not completely understood how the increased transport of vesicles into the growing axon is linked to their subsequent insertion into the plasma membrane. An analysis of early stages of neuronal differentiation indicates that an asymmetry in neurite length precedes axon specification and the accumulation of PPVs in the nascent axon. We show that increasing the transport of vesicles in unpolarized neurons is sufficient to promote the extension of additional axons. This effect indicates that an increased supply of vesicles stimulates their subsequent insertion into the membrane to allow neurite growth. The link between vesicle transport and exocytosis is mediated by the interaction of Rab10 with Arhgef7. Rab10 stimulates Arhgef7 activity on PPVs as a GEF for Cdc42b to promote axon extension through exocyst-dependent exocytosis, suggesting that their interaction links the increased supply of PPVs to their exocytosis.

title: Geometric Kinematics of Human Eyes
text: Geometric Kinematics of Human Eyes. In previous studies by the author on binocular vision with the asymmetric eye (AE), which models a healthy human eye with misaligned optical components, the results were primarily presented in the Rodrigues' vector (RV) framework and supported by simulations and 3D visualizations in GeoGebra's dynamic geometry environment. In this paper, the novel geometric kinematics of the human eye, that is, the eye with misaligned optics, and simplified assumptions about the eye rotations (the eye's translational movements are disregarded), are developed within the framework of rigid-body rotations. The originality of the analysis lies in a precise geometric decomposition of a full rotation of the eye's posture into a torsion-free rotation (the geodesic part) and a torsional rotation (the non-geodesic extension of the geodesic part). This decomposition is extended to the corresponding decomposition of the angular velocity. A novel derivation of the eye's angular velocity from the RV formulation of the eye kinematics is proposed.

title: SPOUT: An open-source hardware and software platform to study decision making while manipulating and recording from neural activity
text: SPOUT: An open-source hardware and software platform to study decision making while manipulating and recording from neural activity. Recording and manipulating brain activity during behavior is critical to understanding the underlying mechanisms of decision-making. Linking neural activity to behavior requires behavioral hardware and software tightly integrated with recording and perturbation systems on a shared clock. We built SPOUT (State-machine Platform for Operant Uni/dual-spout Tasks), an open-source, Teensy-driven state-machine platform with a MATLAB interface that runs 10 unique decision-making tasks (with dozens of variations available through user-friendly settings) to study behavior in head-restrained mice. The platform is built on several custom hardware devices: a dual-lick detector, headplate designs for optogenetics and two-photon calcium imaging, a three-axis motorized spout manipulator, and an optogenetics power modulator. The firmware differentiates between one and two lick spout tasks and can be controlled by a user-friendly interface. Task settings can be selected through the interface or by loading predefined settings files. We validated the clock speed and lick detection against an independent, external acquisition system and identified highly precise, sub-millisecond detection of single licks. Using a pseudo-random synchronization pulse generated by SPOUT, we corrected for missing data due to glitches in the acquisition system and clock drift. We showcase the versatility of SPOUT by training mice on an uninstructed lick-left/lick-right task in which the rewarded side switches unexpectedly and found that mice use history-dependent action-outcome associations to guide future behavior. Transiently inhibiting the anterior lateral motor cortex (ALM) during cue presentation induced contralateral deficits, without affecting ipsilateral trials. Finally, two-photon imaging of ALM neurons revealed stronger population responses during contralateral choice licks compared to ipsilateral ones. Together, SPOUT offers an open-source, affordable platform to study decision-making in head-restrained mice while combining neural recordings and manipulations.

title: Sex differences in astrocytic reactivity and its association with cognitive decline in cognitively unimpaired older adults
text: Sex differences in astrocytic reactivity and its association with cognitive decline in cognitively unimpaired older adults. INTRODUCTION: Astrocyte reactivity may contribute to increased Alzheimers disease (AD) risk in women. Although plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) levels have been reported to be higher in women than in men, few studies have examined sex-specific associations with other plasma AD biomarkers and cognition. METHODS: Participants were enrolled in the Memory Education and Research Initiative, a longitudinal community-based cohort, and underwent evaluation including blood biomarker sampling. The Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) was included as a replication cohort. RESULTS: Females had higher plasma GFAP levels than males in MERI (N{equiv}584), a finding that was replicated in ADNI. In MERI, higher baseline GFAP was associated with lower A{beta}42/40 and higher p-Tau231 and NfL levels. Higher baseline GFAP was also associated with steeper longitudinal decline in global cognition and episodic memory; however, GFAP x sex x time interactions were not significant. In ADNI, higher baseline GFAP was associated with higher p-Tau217 and NfL levels and with steeper longitudinal decline in global cognition and selected executive and semantic measures, without consistent evidence of sex-specific longitudinal effects. DISCUSSION: Plasma GFAP levels were consistently higher in females across two independent cohorts. GFAP was associated with AD-related blood biomarkers and longitudinal cognitive decline, but sex did not consistently modify these associations. These findings support a role for astrocytic reactivity in early AD-related processes while underscoring the need for further replication of sex-specific effects.

title: Using wearable EEG to examine age trends in sleep macro- and micro-architecture across adolescence
text: Using wearable EEG to examine age trends in sleep macro- and micro-architecture across adolescence. Adolescence is a period of distinct maturational changes in sleep physiology. Age-related trends in sleep physiology have been captured using laboratory-based polysomnography, a method limited by logistical burden and high cost. We tested the ability of the Dreem3 sleep EEG headband to replicate established age effects in sleep physiology from late childhood through early adulthood. Typically developing youth (N=100, 9-26 years) completed 3-4 consecutive nights of at-home sleep recording. We estimated age-related trends across eight macro-architecture and 15 micro-architecture variables with known age effects and conducted exploratory analyses of 24 additional variables. The Dreem3 replicated some established age trends, including increases in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) stage 2%, and decreases in N3%, time in bed, NREM delta and theta power with increasing age. Although not all expected age-related associations reached statistical significance, like total sleep time and sleep efficiency, effect estimates were largely in the expected direction. These findings highlight the promise of wearable EEG devices for characterizing developmental sleep physiology while underscoring the need for further validation across sleep measures and age groups.

title: BenchRep-T: A Systematic Evaluation of T-Cell Repertoire-Based Disease Diagnostics
text: BenchRep-T: A Systematic Evaluation of T-Cell Repertoire-Based Disease Diagnostics. Adaptive immune receptor repertoire sequencing data has emerged as a promising potential modality for disease diagnosis, relying on computational methods to analyze T-cell receptor (TCR) sequences from an individual's blood sample. Published methods rely on different cohorts, data preprocessing pipelines, and evaluation metrics, making direct comparison across methods challenging. We present BenchRep-T, a unified benchmark that standardizes multiple publicly available TCR repertoire datasets and evaluates nine computational approaches, spanning statistical enrichment of shared sequences, feature-engineered ensembles, deep learning, and sequence clustering. BenchRep-T evaluates methods on four tasks: disease classification across conditions, performance scaling under restricted sequence-sampling depth, recovery of known antigen-specific driver sequences, and evaluation of sensitivity to demographic confounding. Under controlled evaluation, simple baselines prove competitive, with tree-based models trained on V- and J-gene usage and short sequence motifs approaching the classification performance of more complex methods. Our findings underscore the complexity of modeling TCR repertoire data, and show that no single method dominates across all tasks. BenchRep-T provides a framework for rigorous and reproducible evaluation of TCR repertoire classification methods to accelerate the development of immune repertoire-based diagnostics.

title: Systemic TLR7 agonism moderates disease severity in acute DSS-induced colitis in mice
text: Systemic TLR7 agonism moderates disease severity in acute DSS-induced colitis in mice. Toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7) is an endosomal sensor of single-stranded RNA, studied for its antiviral and pro-inflammatory functions. Its role in intestinal inflammation is undefined, and no approved or clinical-stage therapy for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) engages this pathway. Here we report that systemic administration of the reference TLR7 agonist GS-9620 (vesatolimod) moderates disease severity in acute dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)-induced colitis in mice. GS-9620-treated mice lost less weight, had lower Disease Activity Index scores, and were protected from DSS-induced colon shortening. Immunophenotyping of the spleen showed reduced Th17 and Tr17 populations and an increased proportion of regulatory T cells. These findings indicate that pharmacological TLR7 agonism is not merely tolerated in the inflamed intestine but is associated with a shift of the systemic immune compartment toward a regulatory phenotype. The results identify TLR7 as a candidate disease-moderating target in IBD and motivate direct tests of causality, route and chronic-disease relevance.

title: Metagenomic Insights into the Fecal Microbiome, Resistome, and Mobilome of Beef Cattle in Cow-Calf Operations in Florida, United States
text: Metagenomic Insights into the Fecal Microbiome, Resistome, and Mobilome of Beef Cattle in Cow-Calf Operations in Florida, United States. Food-producing animals are a focus of One Health approaches to antimicrobial resistance (AMR) as reservoirs of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria (ARB) and antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs). We hypothesized that microbial composition, ARGs profiles, and mobile genetic element (MGE) profiles would differ by operation size and animal age group. Fecal samples from 162 cows and calves were combined into 54 composite samples, each comprising three animals of the same age group. Across operation sizes, Bacillota (51.4-64.9%), Bacteroidota (12.0-17.3%), Pseudomonadota (10.3-16.5%), and Actinomycetota (3.3-10.9%) were predominant phyla. Alpha diversity did not differ among operation sizes; however, cows exhibited greater observed richness, Shannon diversity, and Simpson diversity than calves (all P < 0.001). Microbial composition did not differ significantly among operation sizes (PERMANOVA, R{superscript 2} = 0.065, P = 0.609) but differed significantly between cows and calves (R{superscript 2} = 0.200, P < 0.001). Seventy-five ARGs representing 14 resistance classes were identified. Normalized ARG hit rates were higher in small operations (0.444) than in medium (0.278) and large operations (0.222; P = 0.088), whereas calves exhibited a higher estimated marginal mean normalized ARG hit rate than cows (0.383 vs. 0.247 hits/million reads; P < 0.001). Of 1,054 curated ARG hits, 23.9% occurred on predicted plasmid contigs, 0.9% on predicted viral contigs, and 7.1% on contigs containing insertion sequences. Overall findings demonstrate differences in fecal microbiome diversity and ARG abundance between cows and calves and indicate that predicted plasmids are associated with a notable proportion of ARG hits in Florida beef cow-calf operations.

title: Structural basis of virion assembly in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis-infecting mycobacteriophage SWU1
text: Structural basis of virion assembly in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis-infecting mycobacteriophage SWU1. The rising threat of drug-resistant tuberculosis has renewed interest in bacteriophage therapy as an urgently needed alternative. Rational engineering of these viruses, however, requires an atomic-level understanding of virion architecture. Mycobacteriophage SWU1 belongs to subcluster A2, one of the few mycobacteriophage lineages known to infect Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tuberculosis). Using single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), we resolved essentially the entire SWU1 virion architecture by localized reconstruction of four modules, the capsid, portal vertex, tail and baseplate, at resolutions of 3.62 [A], 3.51 [A], 3.70 [A] and 3.22 [A], respectively. The T=7 capsid comprises 415 copies of an HK97-fold major capsid protein and lacks any decoration protein in density. The 12-fold portal reconciles its C5-C12 mismatch with the capsid vertex through defined, non-equivalent subunit contacts. The baseplate carries a 13-fold tail-fiber ring on a 6-fold hub, a geometry without precedent among characterized phages, established here by symmetry-free reconstruction. These findings provide the critical insights into the assembly and infection of SWU1, laying a structural foundation for the future optimization of phage-based anti-TB therapeutics.

title: Novel viral diversity and geographic structuring in the New Zealand West Coast blackfly (Austrosimulium ungulatum)
text: Novel viral diversity and geographic structuring in the New Zealand West Coast blackfly (Austrosimulium ungulatum). Background Vector-borne diseases represent a major global public health burden, with climate change, land-use change and increasing human activity altering arthropod vector distributions and creating opportunities for infectious disease emergence. In Aotearoa New Zealand, insects commonly referred to as "sandflies" are blackflies belonging to the family Simuliidae. The West Coast blackfly, Austrosimulium ungulatum, is an endemic, human-biting species abundant throughout the South Island, yet its associated viral diversity remains largely unexplored. Methods Here, we used metatranscriptomic sequencing to characterise the virome of the West Coast blackfly and investigate patterns of viral diversity and community composition across geographical and environmental gradients. A total of 425 blackflies were collected from 19 locations spanning approximately 187 km. Results We identified 94 viral sequences across 16 orders and six phyla, all of which were putatively novel viruses. These included divergent lineages within families containing recognised vertebrate and arthropod pathogens, such as the Rhabdoviridae and Orthomyxoviridae. Viral community composition varied among sampling locations, but no significant associations were detected between land-use categories and viral diversity or community composition. In contrast, we revealed a weak but significant positive correlation between geographical distance and viral community dissimilarity, suggesting some degree of spatial structuring across the sampling range. Conclusions This study provides the first metatranscriptomic characterisation of the virome associated with the endemic West Coast blackfly, revealing substantial previously undescribed viral diversity and providing insights into the geographical distribution of arthropod-associated viral communities.

title: Metabolism of bilirubin to urobilinogen by human gut bacteria occurs by a branched, multi-enzyme pathway
text: Metabolism of bilirubin to urobilinogen by human gut bacteria occurs by a branched, multi-enzyme pathway. Bilirubin, the predominant product of heme catabolism in mammals, enters the intestine via the hepatobiliary system and subsequently is metabolized by the gut microbiome into multiple downstream derivatives, such as urobilinogen and stercobilinogen. Variation in levels of bilirubin and its derivatives are associated with inflammatory and metabolic disorders, but the microbial species and enzymes that metabolize bilirubin have remained largely unknown, which has precluded causal and mechanistic studies. Here, we demonstrate that metabolism of bilirubin to urobilinogen requires multiple distinct reactions carried out by separate enzymes. We find that bilirubin reductase (BilR), an enzyme that was recently discovered and proposed to convert bilirubin to urobilinogen, is specific for reducing the methine bridges of bilinoids, converting bilirubin to the previously uncharacterized intermediate divinylurobilinogen and mesobilirubin to urobilinogen. We identify bilinoid vinyl reductase (BilV), a flavin-dependent oxidoreductase of the Old Yellow Enzyme (OYE) superfamily, as the enzyme responsible for reducing the vinyl groups of bilirubin and divinylurobilinogen. Both BilR and BilV are capable of acting on multiple bilinoids, such that the reductions required to convert bilirubin to urobilinogen can proceed in multiple orders through a branched network of intermediates. BilV is widespread in human gut metagenomes and is broadly distributed across gut bacteria in a manner that overlaps with but does not mirror the distribution of BilR. These findings establish the identities of novel factors in bacterial bilirubin metabolism, delineate the branched architecture of the pathway, and enable defined studies to interrogate how such branched metabolism contributes to human health and disease.

title: Characterization of Lactobacillus rhamnosus-Derived Extracellular Vesicles and Their Cellular Cytoprotective Effects Against Trimethylamine-Induced Oxidative St
text: Characterization of Lactobacillus rhamnosus-Derived Extracellular Vesicles and Their Cellular Cytoprotective Effects Against Trimethylamine-Induced Oxidative Stress in Caco-2 Cells. Dietary trimethylamine (TMA) underwent gut microbiota-mediated catabolism and subsequent hepatic oxidation to generate trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), a key metabolic factor linked to vascular and colorectal diseases. While the systemic effects of circulating TMAO were heavily investigated, the direct localized cellular interactions of its precursor, TMA, at the intestinal epithelial level required further elucidation. This study characterized extracellular vesicles isolated from Lactobacillus rhamnosus (Lr-EVs) and evaluated their cytoprotective potential in an in vitro human intestinal Caco-2 cell model under TMA-induced stress. Exposure to a high concentration of TMA (20 mM) significantly reduced Caco-2 viability to 78.8%, triggered intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, and compromised tight junction integrity as observed via the disruption of Zonula Occludens-1 (ZO-1) alignment. Co-treatment with Lr-EVs (100-300 g/mL) counteracted this cellular toxicity, enhancing cell survival up to 172%. Quantitative PCR analysis revealed that Lr-EVs suppressed the transcriptional upregulation of the pro-inflammatory gene IL-1{beta}, restored the expression of the metabolic regulator SIRT1, and stabilized transcript levels of key mitochondrial-encoded electron transport chain genes (ND6, CYTB, CO1, and ATP6). Additionally, Lr-EVs exhibited intrinsic radical scavenging activities in cell-free ABTS and DPPH assays. These preliminary in vitro findings demonstrated that Lr-EVs mitigated TMA-induced cellular injury, oxidative stress, and junctional disruption at the transcriptomic level, supporting further investigation of probiotic-derived EVs as prospective cell-free functional ingredients.

title: Viral replication and host response in airway epithelial cells predicts coronavirus pathogenicity and identifies HCoV-229E as an atypical seasonal coronavirus
text: Viral replication and host response in airway epithelial cells predicts coronavirus pathogenicity and identifies HCoV-229E as an atypical seasonal coronavirus. Human coronaviruses (HCoVs) range from mild seasonal strains to pathogenic viruses that cause severe pneumonia. The virological and host determinants that distinguish pathogenic coronaviruses (MERS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2) from seasonal strains (HCoV-229E, HCoV-NL63 and HCoV-OC43) remain poorly defined. To identify determinants of pathogenicity, we systematically compared replication, cellular tropism, innate responses and cytopathogenicity of pathogenic compared with seasonal HCoVs across nasal, bronchial, small airway and embryonic stem cell derived alveolar type II (AT2) epithelial cell cultures. All HCoVs preferentially infected ciliated cells in the upper airway, but only pathogenic viruses replicated to high titres in AT2 cells. Pathogenic HCoVs reprogrammed AT2 function and suppressed key innate immune signatures, consistent with distal lung epithelial dysfunction. In contrast, seasonal HCoVs were associated with limited alveolar replication and milder disruption of AT2 homeostasis. Strikingly, despite modest replication in all cell types, HCoV-229E induced pronounced epithelial injury, cilia loss and strong interferon stimulated gene expression, as well as induction of cellular stress/death programmes resembling those induced by MERS-CoV. These findings highlight the striking differences in cellular responses throughout the airways and between distinct HCoV strains and emphasizes the importance of assessing distal lung tropism and epithelial host responses to evaluate emergent coronaviruses to inform pandemic preparedness strategies.

title: Chromosome-scale CRISPR screening reveals secretory pathway genes as drivers of aneuploidy-mediated antifungal tolerance
text: Chromosome-scale CRISPR screening reveals secretory pathway genes as drivers of aneuploidy-mediated antifungal tolerance. The gain or loss of chromosomes in eukaryotes often drives aberrant phenotypes by altering the expression levels of hundreds or thousands of genes. In the case of beneficial aneuploidies, the genetic basis of fitness improvement has rarely been pinpointed, and identifying the causal genes remains a major challenge in engineering biology. The leading cause of human fungal infections, Candida albicans, frequently acquires extra copies of chromosome R (ChrR) following exposure to azole antifungal drugs, resulting in heightened antifungal tolerance. Despite this, why this aneuploidy frequently emerges following azole exposure and how it promotes antifungal tolerance remain unknown. Here, we combine RNA-seq with parallel chromosome-wide CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) and CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) screens to systematically profile the ChrR genes contributing to azole tolerance. Using multiplexed CRISPR-dCas12a tools, we further characterize the combinatorial effects of candidate genes and uncover a central role for post-Golgi secretory trafficking in antifungal tolerance. Specifically, we demonstrate that the secretory pathway regulators SEC4 and YPT31 are both necessary and sufficient for ChrR-mediated azole tolerance, and drive increased ergosterol content in the cell membrane. By leveraging a large-scale CRISPRa screen in a fungal pathogen, our work functionally dissects one of the most common aneuploidies observed in C. albicans, provides mechanistic insight into the molecular basis of antifungal tolerance, and establishes a generalizable framework for studying aneuploidy-mediated phenotypes across eukaryotic organisms.

title: Nuclear retention and RNA editing safeguard self-tolerance to immunogenic intron lariats
text: Nuclear retention and RNA editing safeguard self-tolerance to immunogenic intron lariats. Introns are excised as lariats and rapidly degraded upon linearization, leaving their post-splicing role unclear. Here, we investigate their immunoregulatory potential by analyzing the intron lariat landscape upon inhibition of the debranching enzyme DBR1. We find that lariats harboring transposable elements (TEs), especially inverted Alu repeats (IRAlus), elicit cell cycle-dependent activation of protein kinase R (PKR), but only in cells harboring a high burden, such as breast cancer. These immunogenic lariats are initially retained in the nucleus, but upon cytosolic release, they drive PKR activation and apoptosis. Exploiting this, we combine DBR1 depletion with anti-mitotic chemotherapy to enhance lariat-PKR interactions and promote cancer cell death in vitro and in vivo. We further show that A-to-I editing of IRAlus-containing lariats weakens their interaction with PKR and suppresses PKR activation. Our findings highlight two parallel molecular mechanisms to sustain self-tolerance to repeat-rich introns, revealing a vulnerability exploitable for anti-tumor therapy.

title: LOca-1: A minimal calcium-activated arginyl-specific orthocaspase from the Loki's Castle hydrothermal vent field
text: LOca-1: A minimal calcium-activated arginyl-specific orthocaspase from the Loki's Castle hydrothermal vent field. Orthocaspases are prokaryotic homologs of metacaspases within the C14 family of cysteine proteases, yet their biochemical properties and cellular roles remain poorly understood. Here, we report the discovery and comprehensive characterization of LOca-1, a metagenome-derived orthocaspase from the Loki's Castle hydrothermal vent field. LOca-1 consists primarily of a single, conserved p20 catalytic domain and undergoes calcium-dependent activation through cleavage at a conserved arginine residue. Once activated, LOca-1 displays strict arginyl-specific proteolytic activity and strong selectivity for residues surrounding the cleavage site. The enzyme is both thermoactive and thermostable, exhibiting maximal activity at 65 {degrees}C and a melting temperature of approximately 72 {degrees}C. Structural modelling revealed conservation of the catalytic core relative to plant metacaspases despite substantial sequence divergence. To our knowledge, LOca-1 is only the second biochemically characterized orthocaspase and the first reported from a deep-sea hydrothermal vent environment. LOca-1 expands the known biochemical diversity of prokaryotic metacaspase homologs and provides insights into the properties of a minimal p20-domain orthocaspase. Together, our findings establish LOca-1 as a thermostable, calcium-activated arginyl-specific orthocaspase and provide a foundation for future studies of orthocaspase function in prokaryotes.

title: A TMEM175 Mutation Disrupts the Lysosomal-Mitochondrial Axis Causing Short QT Syndrome and Sudden Cardiac Death
text: A TMEM175 Mutation Disrupts the Lysosomal-Mitochondrial Axis Causing Short QT Syndrome and Sudden Cardiac Death. Short QT Syndrome (SQTS) is a rare cardiac channelopathy characterized by abnormally short QTc intervals and increased sudden cardiac death (SCD) risk. Only 20-30% of SQTS cases have been linked to genetic mutations, typi-cally in surface membrane ion channels. We identified a novel lysosomal TMEM175 gene mutation (p.Arg377His) in 7 patients in a family with SQTS and SCD. Genetic analyses, including whole exome sequencing in the family and rare-variant burden testing in [~]118,000 UK Biobank participants, sug-gested an association between TMEM175 rare variants and QT interval short-ening. Functional studies in CRISPR-engineered mice and patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs) revealed that TMEM175R377H causes shortened QT intervals and hastened repolariza-tion, respectively, as well an increased arrhythmia susceptibility. Isolated TMEM175R377H cardiomyocytes showed action potential duration (APD) abbre-viation, confirmed in whole TMEM175R377H mouse hearts and patient-specific iPSC-CM monolayers. In silico and electron microscopy studies showed that TMEM175R377H disrupts lysosomal-mitochondrial interactions, leading to mito-chondrial dysfunction, as evidenced by the reduced maximal respiration and spare respiratory capacity, with reduced ATP production, IKATP activation, and APD shortening. This mutation represents the first non-sarcolemmal ion chan-nel defect associated with SQTS and high SCD risk, potentially expanding the genetic landscape of the disease.

title: Deep Vein Thrombosis-primed neutrophils reshape the brain microenvironment to promote brain metastasis
text: Deep Vein Thrombosis-primed neutrophils reshape the brain microenvironment to promote brain metastasis. Brain metastasis (BrM) is a devastating complication of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), yet how host macroenvironmental conditions influence brain metastatic susceptibility remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the impact of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), a common complication in patients with cancer, on TNBC brain metastasis. Analysis of a large clinical cohort identified DVT as an independent risk factor for BrM in patients with metastatic breast cancer. Using two syngeneic TNBC models, we demonstrated that DVT selectively enhanced brain metastasis without significantly affecting primary tumor growth or lung metastasis. Mechanistically, DVT increased neutrophil accumulation in the brain metastatic microenvironment, and neutrophil depletion completely abrogated the metastasis-promoting effect of DVT. Single-cell RNA sequencing of CD45+ cells in peripheral blood revealed that DVT reprogrammed circulating neutrophils toward migratory and inflammatory transcriptomic profiles characterized by neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation. DVT increased CXCR2 expression on circulating neutrophils and enhanced neutrophil recruitment in brain. Moreover, DVT significantly increased circulating NETs. Collectively, our findings identify DVT as a systemic driver of TNBC brain metastasis and reveal that DVT primes circulating neutrophils toward enhanced vascular recruitment and NET formation, providing a mechanistic link between cancer-associated thrombosis and brain metastatic susceptibility.

title: A LOV-domain photoreceptor mediates phototaxis in brown algae
text: A LOV-domain photoreceptor mediates phototaxis in brown algae. Phototaxis enables motile cells to navigate light environments and plays a critical role in survival and reproduction across diverse eukaryotic lineages. This ability has evolved independently through distinct photoreceptor systems. Yet, the molecular mechanisms underlying phototaxis remain poorly understood in many major eukaryotic lineages, including stramenopiles. Here, combining functional genetics, cell biology and evolutionary analyses, we identify Helmchrome (HELM), a LOV-domain protein required for phototaxis in the brown alga Ectocarpus. HELM localizes to the posterior flagellum and is responsible for the characteristic flavin-associated fluorescence of brown algal gametes. Loss of HELM abolishes phototactic accumulation and directional orientation without affecting basal motility or fertilization, demonstrating its specific requirement for light-directed movement. Phylogenetic analyses reveal that HELM-like proteins are distributed across diverse stramenopile lineages and that their domain architecture evolved through repeated duplication of an ancestral RGS-LOV module. Our findings identify HELM as a key component of the light-sensing machinery in brown algae, provide a molecular explanation for the long-standing observation of flagellar flavin fluorescence, and reveal a distinct phototaxis system that expands the known diversity of eukaryotic light-sensing mechanisms.

title: Multiplexed Targeted iprm-PASEF Assays for MALDI Mass Spectrometry Imaging of Lipids, NAD+ 2 , and Related Metabolites in CD38 Knockout Mice
text: Multiplexed Targeted iprm-PASEF Assays for MALDI Mass Spectrometry Imaging of Lipids, NAD+ 2 , and Related Metabolites in CD38 Knockout Mice. Mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) maps the molecular landscape of tissues; however, confident in situ identification and accurate quantification of analytes by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization (MALDI)-MSI remain challenging. We present a new targeted imaging methodology, imaging parallel reaction monitoring parallel accumulation-serial fragmentation (iprm-PASEF), which utilizes trapped ion mobility spectrometry (TIMS) and MALDI for assessment of metabolites and lipids on the fragment ion level in tissue. We investigated liver tissues from wild-type and CD38 knockout (CD38-/-) mice, as CD38 contributes to age-related nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) decline and direct detection of NAD+ within tissue remains challenging. The iprm-PASEF workflow enabled confident differentiation of lipid isomers, resolving phosphatidylinositols at m/z 857.52 and confirming the presence of PI 36:4(16:0/20:4) and absence of PI 36:4(14:0/22:4) at the fragment ion level. We confirmed a more than 2-fold increase in NAD+ in CD38-/- liver tissues of male and female animals (n = 3 per genotype and sex) and decreased adenosine diphosphate ribose (ADPR) through relative quantification of characteristic fragment ions, confirming alteration of NAD metabolism in these animals. This approach provided confident and specific MS2-based identification and relative quantification of fragment ions in MSI experiments, with consistent fold changes across multiple characteristic fragment ions and biological replicates.

title: Replication stress links Geminin depletion to centrosome amplification
text: Replication stress links Geminin depletion to centrosome amplification. The timing of DNA replication and centrosome duplication is tightly regulated with cell cycle progression to ensure the faithful duplication of the genome during cell division. Both DNA and centrosomes are licensed for replication in late telophase/early G1, replicated in S phase and segregated during mitosis; yet how defects in DNA replication licensing are coupled to centrosome homeostasis remains poorly understood. Here, we show that depletion of the replication licensing inhibitor Geminin in proliferating mouse embryonic fibroblasts induces robust centrosome amplification together with impaired primary cilium assembly. Rather than promoting whole-genome reduplication, knockdown of Geminin triggers a replication stress response, characterized by DNA damage accumulation throughout the cycle, and activation of an ATR-dependent DNA damage response. Mechanistically, Geminin depletion-induced replication stress activates the ATR-Chk1-Wee1 checkpoint axis prolonging G2 and leading to premature centriole disengagement and centrosome amplification. These findings identify replication stress as the signaling module that couples defective DNA replication licensing to centrosome amplification.

title: Kinetochore-microtubule attachments are strengthened by Cnn1 stabilization of Stu2
text: Kinetochore-microtubule attachments are strengthened by Cnn1 stabilization of Stu2. Accurate chromosome segregation requires kinetochores to form robust, load-bearing attachments to dynamic spindle microtubules, mediated primarily by the Ndc80 complex. Two receptors, Dsn1 and Cnn1 (CENP-T), recruit multiple copies of Ndc80c to the kinetochore. We previously demonstrated that kinetochore components co-purifying with the yeast Dsn1 protein can maintain persistent load-bearing attachments that track with microtubule tip growth and shortening, but the properties of the Cnn1 receptor have not been explored. Using an optical trapping-based assay, we show here that Cnn1 purifications also sustain dynamic microtubule attachments under load. Mutation of a conserved region within the disordered N-terminal tail of Cnn1 weakened attachment strength in vitro and caused a growth defect when Dsn1 function was impaired. The Cnn1 mutation reduced Stu2 kinetochore levels without altering other kinetochore proteins. Restoring Stu2, either by direct addition in vitro or by tethering it to Ndc80c in vivo, rescued both attachment strength and cellular viability. These findings reveal a biophysical role for Cnn1 in enabling Stu2-dependent stabilization of kinetochore-microtubule attachments.

title: High-content screening identifies FDA-approved activators of mitophagy
text: High-content screening identifies FDA-approved activators of mitophagy. Mitochondrial diseases are highly heterogeneous disorders caused by defects in oxidative phosphorylation, for which only limited therapeutic options are available. The elimination of dysfunctional mitochondria via mitophagy activation is an attractive strategy to treat several mitochondrial diseases, irrespective of the underlying genetic defect. To identify pharmacological activators of this pathway, we performed a high-content screening of 1,971 FDA-approved compounds using cellular reporters of TFEB nuclear translocation and mitophagy. This screening identified 294 compounds that promoted TFEB translocation, nine of which increased the number of mitolysosomes without compromising cell viability or damaging mitochondria. Among the selected compounds, Meptazinol and Ponatinib emerged as the top-ranked mitophagy inducers in fibroblasts from patients with complex I and IV deficiency, respectively, and were prioritised for further characterisation. However, they did not rescue the bioenergetic defect, suggesting that the stimulation of mitophagy per se is not sufficient to ameliorate the OXPHOS defect in mitochondrial diseases. Overall, our findings establish a scalable platform for the identification of pharmacological activators of TFEB and identify candidate compounds for therapeutic modulation of mitophagy.

title: Receptor-proximal phosphoform organization precedes β2 integrin activation
text: Receptor-proximal phosphoform organization precedes β2 integrin activation. Receptor signaling is often framed as protein recruitment after stimulation, but whether receptor-proximal environments are organized in composition and phosphorylation state beforehand remains unclear. We used CD18-APEX2 proximity labeling and a spatial membrane reference to quantify proteins and phosphosites near leukocyte {beta}2 integrins. At rest, receptors, adaptors and Rap GTPases were preferentially represented relative to several catalytic classes. Parent-protein correction revealed spatial phosphoform organization, with 32% of 4,564 phosphosites deviating significantly from the distribution center and 56% of proteins with multiple quantified sites showing divergence beyond measurement error. Sustained activation altered 31% of phosphosites while 95.9% of proteins remained equivalent within {+/-}0.5 log2 and spatial phosphoform organization largely persisted. Most phosphorylation responses were shared across both labeling environments, whereas receptor-preferential changes were dominated by phosphosites. These findings suggest that receptor signaling can regulate pre-existing molecular states without extensive protein redistribution.

title: Host availability, climate and pupal-stage ecology shape the predicted environmental suitability of the New World screwworm across Central and South America
text: Host availability, climate and pupal-stage ecology shape the predicted environmental suitability of the New World screwworm across Central and South America. Background: The New World screwworm, Cochliomyia hominivorax, causes primary myiasis in warm-blooded vertebrates. Its recent resurgence in Central America has renewed the need for spatial tools that identify environmentally suitable areas and surveillance gaps. Most previous distribution models have emphasized climate and livestock, whereas ecological constraints acting during the free-living pupal stage have rarely been incorporated. Methods: We compiled 2,461 georeferenced occurrence reports from the literature across Central and South America and linked them to climate, livestock density, forest cover and superficial soil predictors. Four sequential (nested) logistic models quantified the incremental contribution of predictor blocks, compared using likelihood-ratio tests, AIC and discrimination metrics. Logistic regression and Random Forest were then compared using five-fold spatial block cross-validation, which we treat as the primary measure of generalisation, and an independent municipality-level 70:30 train-test split. Variable importance was assessed using Random Forest Mean Decrease Accuracy together with partial-dependence profiles. Because presence and pseudo-absence classes were balanced before fitting, model outputs are interpreted as relative environmental suitability rather than absolute probability of occurrence. Results: The literature database represented 2,589 infected hosts, dominated by cattle, pigs, dogs and humans. Across the sequential models, AUC increased from 0.780 for climate alone to 0.898 with livestock density, 0.908 with forest cover and 0.918 with superficial soil properties; the increment attributable to the soil block ({Delta}AUC = 0.010) was smaller than the between-fold variability observed under spatial cross-validation (SD 0.049) and is therefore reported as suggestive rather than established. Sheep and horse density and cold-quarter soil temperature showed the highest Mean Decrease Accuracy values, while silt texture ranked above cattle density and forest cover. Under spatial block cross-validation Random Forest was markedly more stable than the GLM (mean AUC 0.926 {+/-} 0.049 versus 0.814 {+/-} 0.157) and was retained as the final model. On the independent municipality-level test set it achieved AUC 0.981, TSS 0.824, sensitivity 0.850 and specificity 0.972, values we regard as optimistic relative to the spatially blocked estimates. Predicted suitability was highest across Central America and parts of northern and tropical South America. Conclusions: C. hominivorax occurrence was associated with interacting climatic, host and landscape conditions. Superficial soil variables added a small, biologically interpretable signal consistent with constraints acting during pupation, but one that lies within the uncertainty of our spatial validation and requires confirmation with independent data. The maps estimate relative environmental suitability rather than infection incidence, and are intended to identify areas where surveillance could be strengthened rather than to guide control operations directly.

title: Protein sequence evolution underlies interspecies incompatibility of a cell fate determinant
text: Protein sequence evolution underlies interspecies incompatibility of a cell fate determinant. Novel and rapidly evolving genes can integrate into conserved gene networks and play critical roles in development. Understanding how sequence variation in the orthologs of such genes influences functional interactions with the molecular products of older, more conserved genes requires investigation at the level of protein function. Here, we ask this question using the oskar gene as a case study. oskar is essential for primordial germ cell specification and embryonic patterning in fruit flies. Previous work showed functional incompatibility between oskar orthologs from the congeneric fruit fly species Drosophila melanogaster and Drosophila virilis. However, the region(s) of Oskar in which protein-coding sequence evolution led to this incompatibility, and the molecular mechanisms underlying it, remained unknown. To address these questions, we generated chimeric versions of oskar comprising different combinations of Oskar protein domains from each species, expressed these chimeric oskar sequences in D. melanogaster, and quantified their ability to assemble functional germ line and abdominal patterning determinants (germ plasm). We found that a specific portion of D. virilis Oskar, namely the OSK domain, was primarily responsible for the cross-species incompatibility of Oskar. In the absence of endogenous D. melanogaster Oskar, chimeras containing the D. virilis OSK domain could not localize posterior germ plasm well enough to generate primordial germ cells, but were sufficient to specify the anteroposterior axis. We also found that the D. virilis OSK domain had dominant-negative effects on D. melanogaster Oskar's ability to localize germ plasm mRNAs, resulting in severe axial patterning defects. Both in vivo and in silico analyses support the hypothesis that evolved changes in the ability of the OSK domain to interact with conserved germ plasm mRNAs played a significant role in the evolution of interspecies incompatibility of Oskar. Under this hypothesis, an essential germ line determinant evolved to be incompatible across species of the same genus in less than 50 million years, while retaining functional within-species molecular interactions. Thus, by investigating in vivo protein function, we link genomic and molecular evolution with phenotypic variation and fitness at higher scales.

title: An elongated lifespan is associated with higher oxidative protection of flight tissue in Heliconiini butterflies
text: An elongated lifespan is associated with higher oxidative protection of flight tissue in Heliconiini butterflies. Evolutionary theories of ageing often invoke trade-offs in resource allocation between somatic maintenance and other important physiological functions. One proposed mechanistic mediator of these trade-offs is oxidative stress, which arises from an imbalance between an organism's production of reactive oxygen species and its ability to detoxify them. Accordingly, many long-lived species across the animal kingdom show evidence for resistance to oxidative stress. However, it can be difficult to associate lifespan differences with oxidative phenotypes when comparing species across wide taxonomic distances, which may also show large differences in physiology. Butterflies in the long-lived Heliconius genus show a 3-fold lifespan extension and slowed ageing in comparison with their close relatives in the Heliconiini tribe, to whom they are phylogenetically, ecologically, and physiologically similar. However, proximate explanations for this extended longevity are currently lacking. Here, we leverage the neat comparative framework between Heliconius hecale and Dryas iulia, a shorter-lived Heliconiini outgroup, to test whether the observed lifespan differences between the two species are associated with differences in oxidative physiology. Our findings suggest superior oxidative protection of thoracic tissue in the longer-lived H. hecale compared to D. iulia, as evidenced by increased superoxide dismutase activity, increased total antioxidant capacity, and a corresponding reduction in lipid peroxidation in this tissue. Considering the metabolic demands of insect flight, we suggest that this oxidative phenotype may contribute to the extended longevity of Heliconius by enhancing protection of thoracic tissues against oxidative damage, representing a plausible proximate pro-longevity mechanism in this genus.

title: Measuring the strength of selection and pollen limitation on flower colour along an urban rural cline in Hesperis matronalis
text: Measuring the strength of selection and pollen limitation on flower colour along an urban rural cline in Hesperis matronalis. Closely located urban and rural environments can differ in temperature, water availability, species diversity, and more. As a result, organisms in urban environments may experience different selection than those in rural environments. We investigated whether differences in selection might explain a previously identified urban-rural cline in the flower colour of Hesperis matronalis (dame's rocket). To explore whether plants in urban and rural environments are impacted by possible differences in pollinator availability or behavior, we performed a pollen supplementation experiment. We did not detect an effect of pollen supplementation on seed production in either setting (urban or rural), indicating that there is limited opportunity for any differences in pollinator availability or visitation to explain the cline in flower colour. We also measured the strength of selection acting on flower colour to investigate if it differed between urban and rural populations. In all but one population, we failed to detect significant linear or non-linear selection on flower colour, suggesting that selection on flower colour does not differ between urban and rural populations. Our results suggest that the urban-rural flower colour cline is likely not caused by differences in selection or pollen-limitation and may be due to stochastic forces.

title: Diploidy alters the path of fluconazole adaptation in Candida glabrata
text: Diploidy alters the path of fluconazole adaptation in Candida glabrata. Candida glabrata (syn. Nakaseomyces glabratus) is a major fungal pathogen, typically isolated as a haploid. We isolated a spontaneous diploid variant of the type strain CBS138 and performed experimental evolution under fluconazole. At physiologically relevant concentrations of fluconazole, we found that haploids and diploids both acquired PDR1 mutations, as is commonly observed in C. glabrata; diploids additionally acquired heterozygous ERG11 and ERG25 mutations and were more likely to acquire aneuploidies. Despite an ancestral fitness advantage for haploids, after ~200 generations the highest-fitness clones, as measured in competitive assays with and without fluconazole, were diploid double heterozygotes having nonsynonymous mutations to PDR1 and ERG11 or PDR1 and ERG25. Diploid clones also had higher minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) to fluconazole. These results suggest, in this particular context, an evolvability advantage for diploids. In a follow-up experiment in which we rapidly increased the fluconazole concentration to a very high concentration, haploids and diploids adapted via entirely distinct routes: haploids via co-mutation in ERG3 and CgOSH3, a previously unreported path to fluconazole resistance, and diploids via heterozygous mutation in ERG25 coupled with trisomies of chrF, chrG, and chrI in all sampled clones, and chrC in most sampled clones.

title: Comparative phylogenomics reveals multilevel genomic differentiation between annual and perennial Hordeum species
text: Comparative phylogenomics reveals multilevel genomic differentiation between annual and perennial Hordeum species. Annual plants complete their life cycle with a single reproductive episode, whereas perennials must balance reproduction with the maintenance of tissues that sustain future growth. Despite the fundamental importance of this distinction, the genomic differences associated with these contrasting life histories remain poorly understood. Here, we utilize independent occurrences of annuality in the grass genus Hordeum to identify recurrent differences between annual and perennial species. Combining transcriptomes from 82 accessions with recently published reference genomes, we compared protein-coding sequence evolution, gene copy number, gene expression and co-expression while accounting for evolutionary non-independence. We found widespread genomic differentiation, with several consistent patterns. Genes involved in cell division and genome maintenance showed evidence of stronger evolutionary constraint in perennials, while gene families associated with developmental regulation and senescence were more frequently retained in higher copy numbers in perennials. Differences in gene expression and coordination were particularly pronounced during reproduction, when perennials showed higher expression of genes involved in cell division, cytoskeletal organisation, cell-wall formation and resource transport, together with extensive reorganisation of gene co-expression relationships. Across these complementary analyses, processes involved in cellular proliferation, developmental regulation and tissue maintenance repeatedly distinguished the two life histories. Our findings suggest that annual-perennial differentiation extends beyond individual flowering regulators to broader genomic differences associated with a more complex coordination of processes balancing growth and senescence in perennials. By identifying these recurrent patterns across evolutionary lineages, this study provides a comparative framework for understanding the genomic differentiation underlying contrasting plant life histories.

title: A population-scale isoform atlas enables isoform-based trait association and regulatory analysis in lettuce
text: A population-scale isoform atlas enables isoform-based trait association and regulatory analysis in lettuce. Genomic variation shapes phenotypic diversity, yet how genetic variation contributes to transcript isoform diversity remains poorly understood at the population scale. Here, we integrated transcriptomic data from 240 lettuce accessions with a lettuce pangenome to construct a comprehensive pan isoform atlas comprising 531,657 isoforms from 49,729 transcribed loci. Isoform presence absence variation (iPAV) captured extensive transcript diversification during domestication and horticultural differentiation, providing additional resolution beyond locus-level analyses, particularly within loci shared across the population. To facilitate the systematic analysis of isoform trait associations, we developed ISONET-GWAS, a computational framework that integrates isoform-based association mapping, functional annotation, and network-based candidate prioritization. ISONET-GWAS recovered the known chlorophyll regulator LsGLK, identified 455 metabolite isoform associations across 77 metabolites, and prioritized candidate regulators of chlorophyll metabolism supported by functional validation. Genome-wide splicing quantitative trait locus (sQTL) mapping identified 10,498 sQTL associations, revealing widespread distal genetic associations with alternative splicing and candidate trans-sQTL hotspots. Notably, we identified a trans-sQTL hotspot overlapping LsPPR, which encodes a pentatricopeptide repeat RNA-binding protein. Perturbation of LsPPR resulted in widespread changes in alternative splicing of floweing-related genes, accompanied by delayed bolting and flowering and altered splicing of flowering-related genes. Together, our study establishes a population-scale pan-isoform resource and a broadly applicable analytical strategy for isoform-level trait association, candidate prioritization, and complementary analysis of the genetic regulation of alternative splicing in crops.

title: Functional genomics reveals mediators of beta cell survival in ER stress and type 2 diabetes risk
text: Functional genomics reveals mediators of beta cell survival in ER stress and type 2 diabetes risk. Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress in pancreatic beta cells contributes to impaired function and type 2 diabetes (T2D). In this study we performed genome-wide perturbation screens and genomic profiling in beta cells to identify novel mediators of ER stress responses and diabetes risk. We defined gene regulatory networks in beta cells and identified specific beta cell networks enriched for T2D risk variants with altered expression in ER stress. We performed a loss-of-function CRISPR screen for survival under ER stress in EndoC-bH1 cells, which identified 167 pro-survival and 47 pro-death genes involved in processes related to insulin secretion, mitochondrial transport and protein ubiquitination. Beta cell survival genes collectively had limited genomic change in stress yet showed significant, independent enrichment for T2D risk variants, including novel T2D candidate gene DTNB which we validated protects against beta cell death during stress. Overall, our results revealed mediators of ER stress responses in beta cells and identified novel therapeutic targets to preserve beta cells in diabetes pathogenesis.

title: Shared brain transcriptome signatures of social evolution and plasticity in shell-dwelling cichlid fishes
text: Shared brain transcriptome signatures of social evolution and plasticity in shell-dwelling cichlid fishes. Inter-individual variability in phenotypic traits is widespread in nature both across and within species, with similar patterns of variation often occurring between and within species. Given that these two types of variation are generated by evolutionary and plasticity processes respectively, it raises the question to what extent the causal mechanisms underlying such variability at these two different levels are shared or not. To address this question, we studied the variation in brain transcriptomes in Tanganyikan cichlids that exhibit both intra- and interspecific variation in social behavior. We compared two facultatively social cichlid species, each containing naturally occurring solitary and social-living individuals, with a closely related obligatory solitary resembling the ancestral state. Differential gene expression and Gene Set Enrichment Analyses were performed in the telencephalon and diencephalon transcriptomes to investigate the molecular basis of both behavioral plasticity and the evolution of sociality. Behavioral plasticity involved few differentially expressed genes but extensive changes in biological pathways, supporting a highly polygenic architecture of social behavior. Across both species, social-living individuals consistently upregulated pathways involved in translation, protein homeostasis, and energy metabolism, whereas solitary individuals showed enrichment of neuronal morphogenesis, cell adhesion, and structural plasticity. Remarkably, these same functional programs were associated with the independent evolution of sociality, revealing a strong overlap between evolutionary and plastic transcriptional responses. This convergence was largely restricted to the telencephalon, while the diencephalon showed limited and inconsistent functional signatures. Together, our results support the repeated recruitment of gene regulatory programs during the evolution of sociality and demonstrate that behavioral plasticity and evolutionary transitions share common neurogenomic responses, consistent with a conserved genetic toolkit for social behavior.

title: Multimodal temporal modeling of behavioral reorganization across threat learning and extinction in rats
text: Multimodal temporal modeling of behavioral reorganization across threat learning and extinction in rats. After threat disrupts a learned activity, does engagement return as defensive responding later declines? Tri-reference-point theory describes decisions under risk relative to a minimum requirement, the status quo and a goal; we extended this logic to defense and engagement. We followed freezing, 22-kHz and 50-kHz calls, and food-reinforced lever responses across conditioning, extinction, delayed retesting and context changes in 29 male rats (45,300 five-second windows). A hidden Markov model described recurring response combinations, or configurations, and their persistence. For every animal, it predicted behavioral sequences excluded from fitting better than a matched model that ignored temporal order. Among models with two to eight configurations, eight predicted best; four provided a coarser description.
