This coarser model separated relatively brief press-active patterns from more persistent vocal-active and low-output patterns. Low-output patterns contained few calls and lever responses, but could involve either little or substantial freezing. In the repeated-session comparison, the estimated share of time in press-active patterns increased on average in the full extinction group (n=9) and decreased in cue-free context controls (n=8), from different first-session levels. These descriptive trajectories included renewed instrumental engagement alongside continued defensive immobility. We separately tested whether configuration summaries added predictive value beyond the measured behaviors for later responding or whole-recording fecal-pellet counts, finding no consistent benefit. Tracking how behavioral combinations change and persist provides a computational framework for evaluating functional adaptation beyond defensive decline.

title: EngA adopts multiple distinct conformational states during ribosome assembly
text: EngA adopts multiple distinct conformational states during ribosome assembly. Ribosome assembly, a highly coordinated and crucial cellular process, is assisted by various assembly factors, including GTPases. EngA, an essential P-loop GTPase, is involved in late-stage assembly of the 50S ribosomal subunit. The structures of 50S ribosome in complex with EngA-bound GMPPNP, and EngA-bound GDP alone, without 50S subunit, have been reported previously. However, the molecular mechanism of EngA GTP hydrolysis-assisted 50S maturation remains poorly understood, and structures of the 50S ribosome in complex with EngA-bound GDP have yet to be deciphered. We have reported cryo- EM structures of the Mycobacterium smegmatis 50S ribosome in complex with EngA-bound GTP{gamma}S or GDP at 2.8 - 3.5 [A] resolution. Structural analysis revealed that EngA and 50S subunit undergo a coordinated structural rearrangement, and an assembly intermediate is formed in which the stem-loop of H80 makes base-pair interactions with the junction of H89 and H90, forming a unique stem-loop-junction (SLJ) motif. EngA-bound GDP adopts distinctly different conformations in its ribosome-bound and unbound states. In summary, this study proposed a multi-state conformational model for EngA-assisted ribosome assembly.

title: Disentangled generative modeling of single-cell perturbation responses across dynamic cellular states
text: Disentangled generative modeling of single-cell perturbation responses across dynamic cellular states. Single-cell perturbation studies are increasingly conducted across complex, multi-condition biolog-ical systems, offering a powerful lens into how interventions reshape cell states and molecular pro-grams. However, standard computational models compress single-cell profiles into unified repre-sentations where treatment effects are obscured by cell division, lineage progression, donor varia-tion, and cellular stress. Here, we present Disentangled Variational Inference for Perturbation Re-sponse (PertVI), a deep generative model that separates baseline mitotic phase, cellular state, and batch effects from treatment-induced shifts while isolating aberrant off-manifold responses in or-thogonal anomaly space. This structured design tackles two intertwined tasks: (1) quantifying treatment-induced changes in cell-state composition, and (2) inferring state-gated transcriptional changes in response to treatment. Across simulated benchmarks, PertVI accurately disentangles coupled biological axes and recovers weak treatment signatures. In conditional chemical and genet-ic screens of primary human CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, PertVI separates memory-precursor adju-vants from toxic phenocopies, resolves co-clustered regulators into directional kinetic trajectories and biphasic rebounders obscured by standard workflows, and reveals that treatment-induced phe-notypic shifting is decoupled from broad transcriptional perturbation responses and instead gov-erned by state-specific impulses. Altogether, PertVI brings unique mechanistic granularity to sin-gle-cell perturbation response modeling, serving as a proof of principle for biology-informed, struc-ture-guided variance disentanglement in dynamic cellular systems.

title: KLONE: An Imbalance-Robust k-NN Ensemble for Cross-Modal Single-Cell Clone Assignment
text: KLONE: An Imbalance-Robust k-NN Ensemble for Cross-Modal Single-Cell Clone Assignment. Single-cell DNA sequencing (scDNA-seq) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enable the inference of copy number clones and transcriptional states in tumor studies. However, these two assays usually profile different cells of the same tumor, requiring computational assignment of unpaired scRNA-seq cells to clones identified by scDNA-seq to link clonal genotypes with transcriptional profiles. This task is challenging because the only connection between the two modalities is a weak, gene-dependent dosage effect, and the absence of clone labels for RNA cells precludes supervised learning of this relationship. Moreover, clonal distributions may differ between the two modalities because the cells are profiled independently, while the inherent clonal imbalance of real tumors can leave minority subclones underrepresented, further compromising assignment accuracy. To address these challenges, we present KLONE, a per-clone $k$-nearest-neighbor ($k$-NN) ensemble that assigns RNA cells directly to copy-number clones based on cross-modal Pearson similarity, without the need for a parametric model or clone labels for RNA cells. To ensure a fair assessment of each clone's compatibility with a given RNA cell, KLONE allocates an identical neighborhood budget to every clone, preventing majority clones from dominating the affinity assessment solely through their greater abundance. We compare KLONE with six existing methods on three colorectal cancer patients, using cells profiled in both modalities as ground truth. KLONE is the most accurate method and recalls minority clones at 100\%. Despite discrepancies in clonal distribution between the two modalities, KLONE recovers the clonal distribution of RNA cells almost perfectly ($\rho = 0.99$).

title: ASD Neuro Agentic (ANA): An Agentic Framework for Feature Discovery and Cross Site Generalization in Autism fMRI Classification
text: ASD Neuro Agentic (ANA): An Agentic Framework for Feature Discovery and Cross Site Generalization in Autism fMRI Classification. Classifiers of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) from resting state functional MRI rarely generalize across sites, and many reported accuracies are inflated by data leakage.We show that an agentic artificial intelligence framework, ASD Neuro Agentic (ANA), whose language model agents propose features from the literature and researcher input while fixed tools perform every calculation, can search auditably for site independent classifiers while controlling the leakage. In 1,028 participants from 17 ABIDE I centers, ANA tested 71 pipelines and selected a ComBat harmonized ensemble of tangent space connectivity models from six parcellations and 98 public connectivity derivatives. In leave one center out testing, the ensemble reached an area under the curve of 0.814 (95% CI, 0.773 to 0.841), outperforming ASD DiagNet and ASD SAENet. Predictive connectivity was mainly reduced in ASD. Agentic AI offers a systematic and efficient approach to exploring, evaluating, and identifying pipelines as model selection grows complex.

title: Joint protein-DNA language modeling enables prediction and engineering of DNA recognition specificity
text: Joint protein-DNA language modeling enables prediction and engineering of DNA recognition specificity. Protein-DNA recognition specificity underlies transcriptional regulation, DNA replication, chromatin remodeling and genome editing. Protein-DNA recognition depends on both interacting sequences, yet language models that learn this cross-molecular dependence explicitly during pretraining remain limited. Here, we developed the Protein-DNA Language Models (PDLMs), interaction-aware language models that jointly represent protein and DNA sequences. PDLMs were built by continued pretraining from ESM2 with masked language modeling on paired protein-DNA sequences. A shared encoder places amino acids and nucleotides in the same molecular context, enabling conditional sequence scoring and transferable pair representations. We further introduced a domain-aware masking strategy that increased masking probability within DNA-binding domains to strengthen learning of interaction-relevant regions. Across downstream tasks, PDLMs improved protein-DNA pair classification relative to independent-encoder baselines and supported prediction of mutation-associated binding changes. Zero-shot scoring recovered known changes in DNA-recognition specificity and prioritized variants with higher editing activity. Learned representations also supported cross-study prediction of base editor activity. After fine-tuning on transcription factor binding data, PDLMs predicted DNA motifs directly from protein sequences. Together, PDLMs provide a framework for interaction-aware biomolecular language modeling, with potential applications in protein engineering and genome editing.

        p = self.construct_fast(self.c.copy(), self.x, self.extrapolate)

        for axis, n in enumerate(nu):
            p._derivative_inplace(n, axis)

        p._ensure_c_contiguous()
        return p

    def antiderivative(self, nu):
        p = self.construct_fast(self.c.copy(), self.x, self.extrapolate)

        for axis, n in enumerate(nu):
            p._antiderivative_inplace(n, axis)

        p._ensure_c_contiguous()
        return p

    def integrate_1d(self, a, b, axis, extrapolate=None):
        if extrapolate is None:
            extrapolate = self.extrapolate
        else:
            extrapolate = bool(extrapolate)

        ndim = len(self.x)
        axis = int(axis) % ndim

        # reuse 1-D integration routines
        c = self.c
        swap = list(range(c.ndim))
        swap.insert(0, swap[axis])
        del swap[axis + 1]
        swap.insert(1, swap[ndim + axis])
        del swap[ndim + axis + 1]

        c = c.transpose(swap)
        p = _PPoly.construct_fast(c.reshape(c.shape[0], c.shape[1], -1),
                                  self.x[axis],
                                  extrapolate=extrapolate)
        out = p.integrate(a, b, extrapolate=extrapolate)

        # Construct result
        if ndim == 1:
            return out.reshape(c.shape[2:])
        else:
            c = out.reshape(c.shape[2:])
            x = self.x[:axis] + self.x[axis+1:]
            return self.construct_fast(c, x, extrapolate=extrapolate)

    def integrate(self, ranges, extrapolate=None):
        ndim = len(self.x)

        if extrapolate is None:
            extrapolate = self.extrapolate
        else:
            extrapolate = bool(extrapolate)

        if not hasattr(ranges, '__len__') or len(ranges) != ndim:
            raise ValueError("Range not a sequence of correct length")

        self._ensure_c_contiguous()

        # Reuse 1D integration routine
        c = self.c
        for n, (a, b) in enumerate(ranges):
            swap = list(range(c.ndim))
            swap.insert(1, swap[ndim - n])
            del swap[ndim - n + 1]

            c = c.transpose(swap)

            p = _PPoly.construct_fast(c, self.x[n], extrapolate=extrapolate)
            out = p.integrate(a, b, extrapolate=extrapolate)
            c = out.reshape(c.shape[2:])

        return c


@functools.lru_cache(16)
def _get_xp_ndppoly_cls(xp):
    """Returns ndppoly class to delegate to for xp along with internal namespace.

    Parameters
    ----------
    xp : module

    Returns
    -------
    cls : type
        The ndppoly class to delegate to for namespace `xp`.
    namespace : module
        The internal namespace that calculations are performed with
        (may differ from `xp`, e.g. numpy delegation for torch on CPU).
    """
    if is_numpy(xp):
        return _NdPPoly, xp
    spx = scipy_namespace_for(xp)
    cls = getattr(getattr(spx, "interpolate", None), "NdPPoly", None)
    if cls is not None:
        return cls, xp
    return _NdPPoly, np

# 3.2 Check the approximate Armijo condition, i.e. the first inequality
                # of Eq. 4.1 of Hager & Zhang (2005) "A New Conjugate Gradient Method
                # with Guaranteed Descent and an Efficient Line Search":
                #   phi'(alpha) <= (2 * sigma - 1) * phi'(0)
                # (our sigma is their delta, 3.1 is their Eq. 4.2). It is the Armijo
                # condition with phi replaced by its quadratic interpolant, and
                # phi'(alpha) can be computed much more precisely than differences of
                # phi.
                # With an L1 penalty, phi is not differentiable. We then interpolate
                # only the smooth part of phi and use the convexity of the L1 norm,
                # ||w + alpha * d||_1 - ||w||_1 <= alpha * (||w + d||_1 - ||w||_1).
                # This gives the same condition as above with phi'(alpha) replaced by
                #   gradient(alpha) @ coef_newton + l1_term
                # which equals armijo_term / sigma for alpha = 0.
                if armijo_term < 0:
                    phi_prime = self.gradient.ravel() @ self.coef_newton.ravel()
                    phi_prime += l1_term
                    phi_prime_max = (2 * sigma - 1) * armijo_term / sigma
                    check = phi_prime <= phi_prime_max
                    if is_verbose:
                        print(
                            "      check gradient @ newton step <= (2 * sigma - 1) *"
                            " gradient_old @ newton step: "
                            f"{phi_prime} <= {phi_prime_max} {check}"
                        )
                    if check:
                        ls_converged = True
                        break

#ifndef NUMPY_CORE_SRC_COMMON_NPY_FLOAT_TO_INT_H_
#define NUMPY_CORE_SRC_COMMON_NPY_FLOAT_TO_INT_H_

#include "numpy/npy_math.h"

/* Whether a float is in [min, max + 1); evaluates value more than once. */
#define NPY_FLOAT_IN_INT_RANGE(value, min, max) \
    (npy_isfinite(value) && (value) >= (double)(min) && \
            (value) < 2.0 * ((max) / 2 + 1))

/* Truncate toward zero; on failure return -1 and leave *out unchanged. */
#define NPY_DEFINE_DOUBLE_TO_INT(name, type, min, max) \
    static inline int \
    npy_double_to_##name(double value, type *out) \
    { \
        value = npy_trunc(value); \
        if (!NPY_FLOAT_IN_INT_RANGE(value, min, max)) { \
            return -1; \
        } \
        *out = (type)value; \
        return 0; \
    }

NPY_DEFINE_DOUBLE_TO_INT(int, int, INT_MIN, INT_MAX)
NPY_DEFINE_DOUBLE_TO_INT(intp, npy_intp, NPY_MIN_INTP, NPY_MAX_INTP)
NPY_DEFINE_DOUBLE_TO_INT(int64, npy_int64, NPY_MIN_INT64, NPY_MAX_INT64)
#undef NPY_DEFINE_DOUBLE_TO_INT

#endif  /* NUMPY_CORE_SRC_COMMON_NPY_FLOAT_TO_INT_H_ */

/* Representation of a dict as implemented in this file. The numbers are for
 * 64-bit builds: on 32-bit builds a bucket has 12 slots of 4 bytes instead of
 * 7 slots of 8 bytes. In the diagrams a bucket is written as [k0 k1 -- ...],
 * where "--" is an empty slot and "*" is the pointer to a child bucket.
 *
 * DICT STRUCTURE
 * --------------
 * A dict has two hash tables. Normally only ht_table[0] is used; ht_table[1]
 * exists only while the dict is resized (see INCREMENTAL REHASHING). A table
 * is an array of 2^ht_size_exp buckets of 64 bytes, one cache line each, and
 * a bucket holds up to 7 entries. The low bits of a key's hash pick its
 * bucket (hash & mask). When that bucket is full, its last slot becomes a
 * pointer to a child bucket, so every top-level bucket is the head of a
 * chain of zero or more child buckets:
 *
 *   struct dict             ht_table[0]: 2^ht_size_exp[0] buckets
 *   +------------------+
 *   | type             |    +----------+----------+----------+----------+
 *   | ht_table[0] -----+--->| bucket 0 | bucket 1 | bucket 2 | bucket 3 |
 *   | ht_table[1]      |    +----------+----------+-----+----+----------+
 *   | ht_used[2]       |                                |
 *   | child_buckets[2] |                                v
 *   | rehashidx        |                          +----------+
 *   | pauserehash      |                          |  child   |
 *   | ht_size_exp[2]   |                          +-----+----+
 *   | pauseAutoResize  |                                |
 *   | metadata[]       |                                v
 *   +------------------+                          +----------+
 *                                                 |  child   |  last bucket
 *                                                 +----------+
 *
 * A key is either in its top-level bucket or in one of that bucket's child
 * buckets, in no particular order. ht_used[] counts the entries of each table
 * and child_buckets[] its child buckets. The capacity used by the resize
 * rules is the number of slots of the top-level buckets; child buckets don't
 * count.
 *
 * BUCKET LAYOUT
 * -------------
 * A bucket keeps in a single cache line everything needed to find a key in
 * it, except the keys themselves:
 *
 *    byte 0   bytes 1..7             bytes 8..63
 *   +-------+----------------------+--------+--------+-----+--------+
 *   | c   p | h0 h1 h2 h3 h4 h5 h6 | slot 0 | slot 1 | ... | slot 6 |
 *   +-------+----------------------+--------+--------+-----+--------+
 *
 *   c       chained bit: slot 6 holds the pointer to a child bucket instead
 *           of an entry, so a chained bucket holds at most 6 entries.
 *   p       presence bits, one per slot: bit i is set if slot i holds an
 *           entry. A delete clears only the bit, so an empty slot and its
 *           tag may keep stale bytes.
 *   h0..h6  the tag of the entry in each slot: the top byte of its hash.
 *   slot i  an entry (see ENTRIES), or the child pointer in slot 6.
 *
 * ENTRIES
 * -------
 * A no_value dict (e.g. a set, or the keyspace whose kvobj holds both the key
 * and the value) stores the key pointer itself in the slot and allocates
 * nothing per entry. Any other dict stores a pointer to a 16-byte dictEntry
 * holding the key and the value. The low 3 bits of the slot tell the two
 * apart (see the pointer tagging notes in dict.h)

    By default, this checks that the types and shapes of the arrays are
    consistent with calling the same estimator with numpy arrays.

    Parameters
    ----------
    name : str
        The name of the estimator. Used in error messages but ignored here.

    estimator_orig : estimator
        Original (uncloned) estimator instance.

    X_ns_and_device : NamedTuple
        Namespace and device of reference array API input: `X` as "everything
        follows X".

        Namespace and device of other array API inputs. Used for `y` and
        `sample_weight`.

    dtype_name : str, default=None
        The name of the data type to use for all arrays. If `None`,

        Whether to check the values of attributes, method outputs (including
        `inverse_transform`) obtained with array API inputs match that of all-NumPy

    check_sample_weight : bool, default=False

        Whether to expect non-array outputs such as sparse data structures and lists.

        outputs are skipped and only a smoke test is performed for `inverse_transform`.

        when it is yielded as a partial. Not used by the check itself.

						 * enabled, changing to 'log' drops the conflict log
						 * table, which can be blocked forever if a prepared
						 * transaction of the subscription holds a lock on it.
						 * So allow it only when the subscription is disabled,
						 * no worker is running, and there are no prepared
						 * transactions.
						 *
						 * XXX Another option would be to allow this on an
						 * enabled subscription by restarting its workers. We
						 * chose to require the subscription to be disabled
						 * instead, following the precedent of existing
						 * options such as two_phase and retain_dead_tuples
						 * (see CheckAlterSubOption()).
						 */
						if (CONFLICTS_LOGGED_TO_TABLE(old_dest) &&
							!CONFLICTS_LOGGED_TO_TABLE(opts.conflictlogdest) &&
							sub->twophasestate != LOGICALREP_TWOPHASE_STATE_DISABLED)
						{
							CheckAlterSubOption(sub, "conflict_log_destination",
												false, isTopLevel);

							/*
							 * Note that workers may still survive even if the
							 * subscription has been disabled.
							 *
							 * Ensure workers have already exited to avoid
							 * getting prepared transactions while we are
							 * dropping the conflict log table.

/*
	 * Disallow dropping a subscription that has a conflict log table while it
	 * has a prepared transaction, as we cannot tell whether that transaction
	 * holds a lock on the table. If it does, dropping the table would wait
	 * for the lock, but only an apply worker can finish the prepared
	 * transaction and none can run while we hold the subscription lock. The
	 * lock manager cannot detect this wait cycle, so the DROP would hang
	 * until canceled or until the prepared transaction is resolved manually.
	 */
	if (OidIsValid(subconflictlogrelid) &&
		subtwophasestate != LOGICALREP_TWOPHASE_STATE_DISABLED &&
		LookupGXactBySubid(subid))
		ereport(ERROR,
				errcode(ERRCODE_OBJECT_NOT_IN_PREREQUISITE_STATE),
				errmsg("cannot drop subscription \"%s\" when prepared transactions exist",
					   subname),
				errdetail("A prepared transaction of the subscription may hold a lock on the subscription's conflict log table."),
				errhint("Resolve these transactions and try again."));

Parameters
    ----------
    message_consumer : callable
        A one-argument function, `message_consumer(message)`, that processes an
        incoming message to update the callback's state. This callable may be called
        from multiple different threads, and must therefore behave in a thread-safe
        manner. In particular, it must not be a bound method of the callback.
    """

    # Class attributes so that a copy unpickled in a worker starts out without
    # connection and consumer, and opens its own connection on first send.
    _connection = None
    _message_consumer = None

    def __init__(self, message_consumer):
        self._message_consumer = message_consumer
        self._lock = Lock()
        self._listener_address, self._authkey = open_listener(message_consumer)
        weakref.finalize(self, close_listener, self._listener_address)

    def __getstate__(self):
        # Exclude the message consumer, the connection and the lock. Without a consumer,
        # a copy takes the cross-process path of `send` instead of the in-process fast
        # path. A worker that is itself pickling this channel should not share its live
        # client, and the copy opens its own connection and lock when unpickled.
        return {"_listener_address": self._listener_address, "_authkey": self._authkey}

    def __setstate__(self, state):
        self.__dict__.update(state)
        self._lock = Lock()

    def send(self, message):
        """Deliver `message` to whoever is listening on the other end.

        There are two possible delivery paths:

        - In-process fast path: `send` is called on the instance that created the
          channel. The message consumer can directly be called without any serialization
          overhead.

        - Cross-process path: `send` is called from an unpickled copy of the channel.
          It connects to the listener on first use and reuses that connection for the
          following messages. `send` then waits for an acknowledgement from the main
          process so that, by the time it returns, the message has actually been
          processed by the consumer. Access to the connection is serialized with a lock
          because nested thread parallelism inside a worker process shares the same
          unpickled channel across threads.

        If the exchange fails, the connection is dropped and the error is re-raised, so
        that the next `send` reconnects instead of reusing a connection that may be out
        of sync. This happens when the message consumer in the main process raises,
        which makes its handler close the connection without acknowledging the message,
        and when the connection breaks, e.g. because the main process went away. It also
        covers interruptions such as `KeyboardInterrupt` in the middle of the exchange,
        which can leave a message unacknowledged. Dropping the connection is
        conservative when the message cannot be pickled, since nothing has been written
        in that case.
        """
        if self._message_consumer is not None:  # fast path
            self._message_consumer(message)
            return

        with self._lock:
            if self._connection is None:
                self._connection = Client(self._listener_address, authkey=self._authkey)

def make_lineage_task_id(
    operator_id: OperatorId, task_index: TaskIndex
) -> LineageTaskId:
    """The lineage task ID of ``operator_id``'s task first submitted as ``task_index``."""
    return f"{operator_id}:{task_index}"


def parse_lineage_task_id(
    lineage_task_id: LineageTaskId,
) -> Tuple[OperatorId, TaskIndex]:
    """Split a lineage task ID into ``(operator_id, task_index)``.

    The inverse of ``make_lineage_task_id``.

    Args:
        lineage_task_id: The ID to split.

    Returns:
        The ID of the operator that owns the task, and the task's index.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If ``lineage_task_id`` isn't ``"{operator_id}:{task_index}"``
            with a non-empty operator ID and a non-negative integer index.
    """
    operator_id, sep, task_index = lineage_task_id.rpartition(":")
    if not sep or not operator_id or not task_index.isdigit():
        raise ValueError(
            f"Malformed lineage task ID {lineage_task_id!r}: expected "
            "'{operator_id}:{task_index}'."
        )
    return operator_id, int(task_index)

def _task_index_of(self, lineage_task_id: LineageTaskId) -> TaskIndex:
        """The task index in one of this operator's lineage task IDs. The inverse of
        ``_lineage_task_id_for``.

        Args:
            lineage_task_id: A lineage task ID of one of this operator's tasks.

        Returns:
            The index the task was first submitted under.

        Raises:
            ValueError: If ``lineage_task_id`` is malformed or belongs to another
                operator.
        """
        operator_id, task_index = parse_lineage_task_id(lineage_task_id)
        if operator_id != self.id:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Lineage task ID {lineage_task_id!r} belongs to operator "
                f"{operator_id!r}, not {self.id!r}."
            )
        return task_index

    def owns_data_task(self, lineage_task_id: LineageTaskId) -> bool:
        """Whether this operator owns the data task with the given lineage task ID.

        A malformed ID belongs to no operator.
        """
        try:
            operator_id, _ = parse_lineage_task_id(lineage_task_id)
        except ValueError:
            return False
        return operator_id == self.id

# NVFP4 K/V converted to FP8 (rows of [K | V]): workspace shared by the decode
# and prefill conversions; one launch converts as many rows as fit.
_NVFP4_FAST_WORKSPACE_BYTES = 512 << 20
# Decode batches of at least this many requests that verify drafts convert
# each request's selected keys once (compact_nvfp4_kv_cache); smaller ones
# convert each row's (gather_nvfp4_kv_cache_by_position, one launch).
_NVFP4_UNION_MIN_DECODES = 16
# Most row groups (requests, or parts of a long prefill) per compaction launch;
# sizes its key bitmap (a bit per key of max_model_len per group).
_NVFP4_MAX_GROUPS = 256
# Rows per trtllm-gen launch over the converted K/V: 32 (decode) and 256
# (prefill), the launches of the earlier per-row conversion. trtllm-gen picks
# its kernel (split-KV or not, hence the summation order) by the launch's rows,
# so these keep the outputs bit-identical to it.
_NVFP4_DECODE_FMHA_ROWS = 32
_NVFP4_PREFILL_FMHA_ROWS = 256
# Conversion launch tuning (tokens per program, warps); no numerical effect.
_NVFP4_CONVERT_TOKENS = 16
_NVFP4_CONVERT_WARPS = 4


def _nvfp4_prefill_launches(
    query_lens: tuple[int, ...],
    context_lens: tuple[int, ...],
    top_k: int,
    region_rows: int,
    max_rows: int,
    max_groups: int,
) -> tuple[list[tuple[int, int, int, int, int]], np.ndarray]:
    """Split prefill requests' tokens into compaction groups and launches.

    A group is a run of one request's tokens whose selected keys get one
    region of the FP8 workspace: all its tokens when the region fits, else
    runs of region_rows // top_k tokens. A group is dense (its region holds
    every key up to its context, by position) when its rows select at least
    as many keys as its context holds, else a union (its region holds each
    selected key once; at most rows * top_k of them). Launches take whole
    groups while their regions fit region_rows, their tokens max_rows and
    they number at most max_groups.

    Returns the launches as (first group, end group, first token, end token,
    largest region), and per group (request, first token, tokens, region
    offset in its launch, dense).

    >>> launches, groups = _nvfp4_prefill_launches(
    ...     (2816, 50), (200_000, 150_000), 2048, 1 << 20, 65535, 256
    ... )
    >>> launches
    [(0, 2, 0, 2866, 200000)]
    >>> groups.tolist()
    [[0, 0, 2816, 0, 1], [1, 2816, 50, 200000, 0]]
    >>> launches, _ = _nvfp4_prefill_launches(
    ...     (3000,), (900_000,), 2048, 300_000, 65535, 256
    ... )
    >>> len(launches), launches[0], launches[-1]
    (21, (0, 1, 0, 146, 299008), (20, 21, 2920, 3000, 163840))
    """
    groups = []
    token = 0
    for request, (tokens, context) in enumerate(zip(query_lens, context_lens)):
        if min(tokens * top_k, context) <= region_rows:
            run = tokens
        else:
            run = max(1, region_rows // top_k)
        run = max(1, min(run, max_rows))
        for first in range(0, tokens, run):
            count = min(run, tokens - first)
            dense = context <= count * top_k
            region = context if dense else count * top_k
            groups.append([request, token + first, count, region, int(dense)])
        token += tokens
    launches, begin, used, rows = [], 0, 0, 0
    for index, group in enumerate(groups):
        count, region = group[2], group[3]
        if index > begin and (
            used + region > region_rows
            or rows + count > max_rows
            or index - begin >= max_groups

def _fused_shared_expert_kwargs(
        self,
        fuser: MoEBlockFuser,
        moe_block: nn.Module,
        prefix: str,
        intermediate_size: int,
        fused_layers: dict[tuple[str, str], set[int]],
    ) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
        """`FusedMoE` kwargs running the block's shared expert as extra routed
        experts (ROCm AITER), if it can.

        Records the layer index in `fused_layers` under the block's
        `(shared expert, experts)` names, relative to the layer."""
        name = fuser.shared_name
        if name is None or fuser.scoring_func is None:
            return None
        shared = getattr(moe_block, name)
        if not _fusable_shared_expert(
            shared, intermediate_size, self.num_shared_experts
        ):
            return None
        # Checkpoint weights are matched to layers by their only index
        parts = prefix.split(".")
        indices = [i for i, part in enumerate(parts) if part.isdigit()]
        if len(indices) != 1:
            return None
        if not resolve_layer_fused_shared_expert(self.quant_config, prefix, name):
            return None
        idx = indices[0]
        block = ".".join(parts[idx + 1 :])
        key = (maybe_prefix(block, name), maybe_prefix(block, "experts"))
        fused_layers.setdefault(key, set()).add(int(parts[idx]))
        setattr(moe_block, name, None)
        moe_block.is_fused_shared_expert_enabled = True
        return dict(
            n_shared_experts=self.num_shared_experts,
            fuse_shared_experts=True,
            shared_expert_prefix=f"{prefix}.{name}",
            shared_expert_gate=fuser.shared_expert_gate(moe_block, prefix),
        )

def iter_batches(self, batch_size=65536, stripes=None, columns=None):
        """Read streaming batches from the file or selected stripes.

        Parameters
        ----------
        batch_size : int, default 65536
            Maximum number of rows per batch. Must be positive.
        stripes : sequence of int, optional
            Zero-based stripe indices, read in the supplied order. Repeated
            indices repeat the corresponding rows. None reads the entire file;
            an empty sequence produces no batches.
        columns : list, optional
            Column names, nested field paths, or top-level integer indices,
            using the same selection syntax as read_stripe. Names and integer
            indices cannot be mixed.
            Output follows the file's column order. None
            reads all columns; an empty list reads no columns but preserves
            the number of rows.

        Yields
        ------
        pyarrow.RecordBatch
            A batch containing at most batch_size rows. Stripe boundaries may
            produce smaller batches.

        Notes
        -----
        Reading starts when the iterator is consumed. Call its close() method
        to release the reader when stopping early. This does not close a source
        supplied by the caller. Returned batches remain valid after closing.

        Batches are decoded incrementally, without first constructing an Arrow
        batch for the entire stripe. batch_size limits rows, not bytes or total
        process memory: ORC dictionaries and decompression buffers may still
        depend on the stripe size.
        """
        batch_size = operator.index(batch_size)
        if batch_size <= 0:
            raise ValueError("batch_size must be greater than zero")
        if stripes is not None:
            stripes = tuple(operator.index(stripe) for stripe in stripes)
            for stripe in stripes:
                if not 0 <= stripe < self.nstripes:
                    raise ValueError(f"Out of bounds stripe: {stripe}")
        columns = self._select_names(columns)
        return self.reader.iter_batches(batch_size, stripes, columns)

"""
Score items against a query with SGLang and Ray Data LLM.

Requires SGLang with FlashInfer for multi-item scoring.
"""

# __sglang_score_example_start__
import ray
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
from ray.data.llm import SGLangEngineProcessorConfig, build_processor

model = "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model)
# With apply_softmax=True, each item's scores are normalized over Yes and No.
label_token_ids = [
    tokenizer.encode(word, add_special_tokens=False)[0] for word in ("Yes", "No")
]

config = SGLangEngineProcessorConfig(
    model_source=model,
    task_type="score",
    # Multi-item scoring scores all items of a row in one forward pass.
    engine_kwargs=dict(enable_mis=True, attention_backend="flashinfer"),
    task_kwargs=dict(label_token_ids=label_token_ids, apply_softmax=True),
    batch_size=16,
    concurrency=1,
)
processor = build_processor(config)

ds = ray.data.from_items(
    [
        {
            "query": "Is this city the capital of France? ",
            "items": ["Paris", "London", "Berlin"],
        }
    ]
)

for row in processor(ds).take_all():
    # One [p_yes, p_no] list per item, in item order.
    print(row["items"], row["scores"])
# __sglang_score_example_end__

"""Tokenize stage for the SGLang score task."""

from typing import Any, AsyncIterator, Dict, List, Optional, Type

from ray.llm._internal.batch.stages.base import (
    StatefulStage,
    StatefulStageUDF,
)
from ray.llm._internal.batch.stages.common import is_missing
from ray.llm._internal.batch.stages.tokenize_stage import TokenizeUDF


class SGLangScoreTokenizeUDF(TokenizeUDF):
    def __init__(
        self,
        data_column: str,
        expected_input_keys: List[str],
        model: str,
        trust_remote_code: bool = False,
        enable_mis: bool = False,
        item_first: bool = False,
        score_extraction_token_id: Optional[int] = None,
    ):
        """Tokenize the `query` and `items` text columns of score rows.

        The token IDs match what SGLang's `Engine.score` builds from the same
        text:

        - With multi-item scoring, or with embedding overrides in the row, the
          query is tokenized on its own with special tokens, and each item
          without.
        - Otherwise, each `query + item` text (`item + query` with
          `item_first`) is tokenized as one sequence with special tokens, and
          `query_token_ids` is empty, because the engine concatenates the two.
          With score extraction, a query containing the extraction token is
          rejected, as SGLang does, since its tokens would be scored as part
          of an item.

        Args:
            data_column: The data column name.
            expected_input_keys: The expected input keys of the stage.
            model: The model to use for tokenization.
            trust_remote_code: Whether to trust remote code when loading the model.
            enable_mis: Whether the engine runs multi-item scoring.
            item_first: Whether each item goes before the query.
            score_extraction_token_id: The score extraction token ID, if set.
        """
        super().__init__(data_column, expected_input_keys, model, trust_remote_code)
        self.enable_mis = enable_mis
        self.item_first = item_first
        self.score_extraction_token_id = score_extraction_token_id

    async def udf(self, batch: List[Dict[str, Any]]) -> AsyncIterator[Dict[str, Any]]:
        """Tokenize a batch of score rows.

        Args:
            batch: A list of rows to tokenize.

        Yields:
            Dict[str, Any]: Rows with `query_token_ids` and `item_token_ids`.
        """
        # Texts tokenized with and without special tokens, each in one call.
        special_texts: List[str] = []
        plain_texts: List[str] = []
        # Per row: whether the query is tokenized on its own, and the items.
        plans = []
        # Queries to check for the extraction token before concatenation.
        queries_to_check: List[str] = []
        for row in batch:
            query = _as_text(row["query"], "query")
            items = [_as_text(item, "items") for item in _as_text_list(row["items"])]
            separate = self.enable_mis or _has_embed_overrides(row)
            if separate:
                special_texts.append(query)
                plain_texts.extend(items)
            else:
                if self.score_extraction_token_id is not None and query:
                    queries_to_check.append(query)
                special_texts.extend(
                    f"{item}{query}" if self.item_first else f"{query}{item}"
                    for item in items
                )
            plans.append((separate, len(items))

1903 NSWAFL season
text: The 1903 NSWAFL season was the inaugural season of the New South Wales Australian Football League (NSWAFL), the highest-level Australian rules football competition in Sydney. Eleven clubs participated in the inaugural season: Alexandria Ashfield Balmain East Sydney Newtown North Shore Paddington Redfern Sydney West Sydney Y.M.C.A. East Sydney won the inaugural NSWAFL premiership, defeating North Shore by 18 points in the 1903 NSWAFL Grand Final. Ladder Source: Finals Grand Final Grand final replay Under rules of the time, East Sydney, as minor premiers, reserved the right to challenge North Shore for a re-match of the Grand Final. Season Notes Round 4 of the 1903 VFL season featured a match between Collingwood and Fitzroy played at the Sydney Cricket Ground, between rounds 1 and 2 of the NSWAFL season. The £605 raised from admission fees was given the NSWAFL. The round 2 game between Balmain and Sydney at Birchgrove Oval on 30 May 1903 was the first game between Sydney-based clubs to use a Sherrin football. Balmain supplied the ball, and won 5.12 (42) to 6.4 (40). Alexandria's round 9 loss to East Sydney, with a final score of 33.23 (221) to 1.1 (7), was the first recorded game of Australian rules in Sydney with a score exceeding 200 points. Balmain's Qualifying Final against North Shore, played at North Sydney Oval, was awarded to North Shore after Balmain abandoned the field due to player safety concerns. References

title: 1902 Nobel Prize in Physics
text: The 1902 Nobel Prize in Physics was presented in a ceremony in Stockholm, Sweden to the joint laureates, Netherlanders Hendrik Antoon Lorentz and his former pupil Pieter Zeeman, "in recognition of the extraordinary service they rendered by their researches into the influence of magnetism upon radiation phenomena", namely, light. It was the second of its kind and the first joint award resulting from the 1895 will of Swedish chemist Alfred Nobel to recognize "the person who made the most important discovery or invention in the field of physics". Laureates Hendrik Lorentz Hendrik Lorentz (1853–1928) was a professor at the Leiden University when he received the Nobel Prize. His central work was to refine James Clerk Maxwell's unified theory of electricity and magnetism with respect to how matter interacts with the electromagnetic field. To do so, Lorentz formulated the existence of "charged particles", on which the field exerts a force. This theory allowed him to explain a number of phenomena, including anomalous dispersion and the reflection and refraction of light. Such successes, together with the 1897 empirical discovery of the electron by J. J. Thomson, meant that by 1900, Lorentz was "Europe's foremost physical theorist" and "the world's leading spirit." However, certain phenomena could not be explained by Lorentz's theory, including the photoelectric effect. Furthermore, his theory presumed a luminiferous aether, the existence of which was questioned after the Michelson–Morley and other experiments. Through the 1900s, Lorentz devised calculations to try and prove his theory by explaining the movement of objects relative to the aether with the Lorentz contraction and Lorentz transformations. Both ideas would be fundamentally reinterpreted in Albert Einstein's theory of special relativity that rejected the aether and attributed the phenomena as reflecting the physical structure of spacetime. Einstein, who was personally and intellectually close with Lorentz, received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921, especially for discovering "the law of the photoelectric effect", which remains definitive. Pieter Zeeman Pieter Zeeman (1865–1943) was a professor at the Municipal University of Amsterdam when he received the Nobel Prize. He was a pupil of Lorentz's at Leiden. An experimental physicist specialising in optical phenomena, in 1896, Zeeman discovered in a namesake effect that an atom's distinctive spectral line may split in the presence of a magnetic field. Together, Lorentz and Zeeman interpreted this phenomenon as experimentally confirming Lorentz's theory. The demonstration of the particles' negative nature and high charge-to-mass ratio provided important evidence for Thomson in confirming he had discovered the electron the following year. Later experimentation determined exceptional cases of the Zeeman effect which Lorentz's theory could not explain—modern quantum mechanics resolves them with such concepts as spin and orbital motion. Thomson himself received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1906. Deliberations The Nobel Prize in Physics is awarded by an absolute majority vote of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences from among the persons given valid nominations by scientists and/or Academy members qualified to do so. Within the academy, there is a specialist Nobel Committee for Physics, usually composed of Swedes, who issue their own proposals and judgement. The committee's membership in 1902 follows: The academy held a plenary session on 11 November to vote, with the secretary being Swedish chemist Wilhelm Palmær. There is no record of either votes or proceedings to comply with standards on secrecy. Lorentz received six valid nominations from among the 24 nominators. Members of the academy are denoted with an asterisk (*) in the table below. Only one member of the Nobel Committee for Physics within the academy nominated a candidate: Svante Arrhenius, who gave Zeeman his sole nomination. Arrhenius is denoted with a dagger (†). P

title: 2026 Indonesian vice-presidential election
text: The 2026 Indonesian vice-presidential election is scheduled to take place on Friday, 11 December 2026, during a plenary session of the People's Consultative Assembly (MPR). The election will determine the successor to Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, who submitted his resignation on 12 November 2026, leaving the vice-presidential position vacant for the remainder of the 2024–2029 presidential term. The vacancy followed months of controversy surrounding Gibran's educational qualifications and his eligibility to hold public office, which centres on the validity of the educational documentation he submitted when registering as a vice-presidential candidate in the 2024 Indonesian presidential election. Following legal challenges and subsequent court rulings, Gibran resigned from office, citing his intention to prevent the controversy from becoming prolonged. Under Article 8(2) of the Constitution of Indonesia, the People's Consultative Assembly (MPR) is responsible for electing a successor from two candidates nominated by the president. On 23 November 2026, President Prabowo Subianto submitted the nominations of Amran Sulaiman, Minister of Agriculture, and Sugiono, Coordinating Minister for Human Development and Cultural Affairs and Secretary General of the Gerindra Party, to the MPR. The successful candidate will serve the remainder of the 2024–2029 presidential term. Notes References

title: /04 (Ryuichi Sakamoto album)
text: /04 is a studio album by Jananese musician and composer Ryuichi Sakamoto. The record was released on November 24, 2004 via Warner Music Japan. The album features deep minimalism, intimate sound, and acoustic piano synthesis with ambient electronic textures and field recordings. Background The album's name /04 refers to year 2004, the time of its creation and release. The composer used the slash symbol (/) to indicate a pause, break, and separation that occurred in his life. It is a collection of self-covers featuring piano-driven performances of his classic tracks, including film theme songs, solo works, and YMO songs. Reception Mark Deming of AllMusic wrote: "Ryuichi Sakamoto, one of the pioneering figures of Japanese electronic music, demonstrates his versatility on this change-of-pace album. Released in 2004, 04 is dominated by Sakamoto's prowess on the acoustic piano, and features excerpts from several of his scores for motion pictures." title: 2018 National Premier Leagues Tasmania
text: The 2018 National Premier Leagues Tasmania was the sixth season of the National Premier Leagues Tasmania, the top-tier men's association football competition in Tasmania. The season began on 16 March and concluded on 1 September 2018. Eight clubs contested the competition, each playing 21 matches in a triple round-robin format, for a total of 84 matches. Devonport City won the title with 50 points, three ahead of runners-up South Hobart, and qualified for the national NPL finals. Devonport's striker Brayden Mann won the Mitsubishi Medal and Golden Boot, while teammate Michael Holden won the Players' Most Valuable Player award. Northern Rangers withdrew from the competition following the season and returned to the Northern Championship in 2019. The eight-team 2018 competition was intended to expand for 2019 following the promotion of clubs from the northern and southern championships. title: 1st Czechoslovak Brigade Jan Žižka
text: The 1st Czechoslovak Brigade Jan Žižka (full name: 1st Czechoslovak Brigade of the National Liberation Army "Jan Žižka of Trocnov", also known as the 1st Independent Czechoslovak Brigade of Jan Žižka of Trocnov) was a military unit during World War II that conducted partisan warfare in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. It was established on 26 October 1943 near the village of Bučje and consisted of three battalions: the 1st was entirely Czech, while the 2nd and 3rd were mixed. Approximately 3,500 men and women of Czech, Slovak, Serbian, Croatian and other nationalities served in the brigade. Around 700 fighters were killed and more than 800 wounded. In total, approximately 3,000 Czech and Slovak compatriots served in the brigade, of whom nearly 300 were killed and several hundred wounded. History From 1941 onwards, approximately 2,200 Czechs and Slovaks joined partisan units in the region of Slavonia, in the territories of the former districts of Daruvar, Slavonska Požega, Kutina, Grubišno Polje, Našice, Novska, Pakrac, Nova Gradiška, Garešnica, Đakovo, Virovitica and Bjelovar. These units later formed the basis of the brigade. The area of operations was extensive, but was concentrated mainly in Slavonia, between the Drava and Sava rivers. As the unit, and later the brigade, operated in an area with a substantial Czech and Slovak minority until the end of the war, it was able to replenish its numbers continuously. On 3 May 1943, the 1st Czechoslovak Battalion of the Third Operational Zone (1st Czechoslovak Battalion) was formed in the small village of Cikoty, in the Papuk mountain range. It had 150 members, including 23 women. Its command structure followed the model of the Czechoslovak Army of the First Czechoslovak Republic. Czech was spoken in the unit, which had its own flag. Its members wore two crossed Czechoslovak flags above a five-pointed star on their caps. The battalion took part both in internal conflicts within Yugoslavia, including clashes with Croatian Ustaše and Serbian Chetniks, and in battles against the German Army. The brigade was established by Order No. 16 of the VI Corps staff, issued on 26 October 1943. At the time of its formation, it had 590 men and women. Of these, 289 were Czechs and Slovaks, 201 Serbs, 69 Croats and 20 members of other nationalities. According to a statistical report dated 21 December 1943, the brigade consisted of 571 men and 29 women. By the end of 1944, it had more than 1,000 soldiers, of whom 915 were Czechs and Slovaks. On 24 April 1945, shortly before the end of the war, the brigade was incorporated into the newly forming Yugoslav Army. In September 1945, its members were decorated in Old Town Square in Prague by Minister of National Defence Ludvík Svoboda, receiving the highest military decorations of Czechoslovakia. Brigade commanders Antonín Doležal (died 29 January 1945 in combat) Josef Růžička (1919, Otkopi – died 7 February 1945, Končenica, in combat) He was posthumously declared a People's Hero of Yugoslavia. The Czech-language primary school in his birthplace of Končenica was named after him. Josef Vojáček, code-named Taras, an official of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia.

title: 1929–30 American Basketball League season
text: The 1929–30 ABL season was the fifth and penultimate season of the original rendition of the original American Basketball League (ABL). This would also officially be the first season where the ABL would be significantly affected by the Great Depression, as that worldwide event would officially occur by late October 1929, while the regular season would begin ten days after the infamous Wall Street crash of 1929 occurred. The ABL would originally start their season out with eight teams in their league, with two of them being the return of the fabled New York Original Celtics and an expansion team known as the Syracuse All-Americans, but both of those teams in question would go defunct before the first half of the season would conclude properly (with the Celtics' record being stricken from the ABL's record books officially and the All-Americans having their final four games in the first half of the season become forfeited matches won by other surviving teams in the league) to have six teams remaining in their league by the end of the season (including the rebranded Paterson Crescents). In any case, while it would currently be unknown as to when the regular season would begin or end this time around (or even when the first half of the season would end and when the second half of the season would begin), due to the ABL utilizing the split season formatting for their competitive operations once again, they would see the Cleveland Rosenblums and the Rochester Centrals be the two teams that would win their respective half-seasons of play this time around. While Rochester would win the first game played in the best-of-seven World Series championship series, Cleveland would win the rest of the games played not long afterward to repeat as champions once again with a 4–1 series victory under a low-scoring championship series. Teams Following the season's conclusion, Jim Furey (the owner of the Original Celtics franchise) would revive his New York Original Celtics franchise following his completion of his prison sentence for embezzlement involving a business he was involved with and having them essentially replace the New York Hakoahs for the season. In addition to them, the Trenton Royal Bengals (alternatively referred to as just the Trenton Bengals) would decide to withdraw their franchise from the ABL entirely (potentially due to them still deciding to utilize a cage for their home games when other teams wouldn't be doing that with the ABL being an established league by this point in time) and the Paterson Whirlwinds would decide to rebrand themselves as the Paterson Crescents for essentially the rest of their existence going forward (though at least one place would still refer to them to as the Paterson Whirlwinds for the season instead of their more common Paterson Crescents name). Not only that, but former ABL player Vic Hanson would create his own team to compete against the rest of the league in the Syracuse All-Americans to have eight competing teams to start out the season. However, due in part to the early effects of the Great Depression, the ABL would end their season with only six teams remaining by the end of the season due to the (technically) two new teams of the season withdrawing their operations from the league before the start of the second half of the season. Preseason Originally, when the ABL planned on starting their new season out, they had anticipated on it being more or less being similar to the previous season, only with the replacement of the veteran-based Trenton Royal Bengals (alternatively referred to as just the Trenton Bengals) with the newly added Syracuse All-Americans expansion team created by former ABL player Vic Hanson and the temporary New York Hakoahs team surprisingly being replaced by the revived edition of the New York Original Celtics, who would have team owner Jim Furey back as their proper team owner once again after he previously completed his prison sentence from the Sing Sing Correctional F

title: 1928–29 American Basketball League season
text: The 1928–29 ABL season was the fourth season of the original rendition of the American Basketball League (ABL). After dealing with mixed results from the previous season, the ABL would decide to return to the split season formatting that was used from the previous two seasons of play for the rest of the original iteration of the ABL's existence going forward. Not only that, but the sheer dominance of the Original Celtics under both their previous Brooklyn Celtics name and their New York Original Celtics name from the previous season would result in the ABL breaking up the franchise entirely (though they would end up distributing the Celtics' players rather poorly on their ends by comparison) and replacing them with the New York Hakoahs for this season only, with the ABL replacing president and treasurer Joseph Carr (who would also work with the NFL during this same period of time) with former Metropolitan Basketball League president and founder John O'Brien for the rest of the league's existence going forward. Furthermore, the eight teams that competed in the ABL this season would be the first and only season in the original rendition of the original version of the ABL where the teams that started out a season in the ABL would remain in the league by the end of the season. While it would currently be unknown as to when the regular season would begin or end this time around (or even when the first half of the season would end and when the second half of the season would begin), due to the ABL returning to utilizing the split season formatting for their competitive operations once again, they would see the Cleveland Rosenblums and the Fort Wayne Hoosiers be the two teams that would win their respective half-seasons of play. Despite there being much hype over the upcoming World Series championship series (which would become a best-of-seven series this time around instead of a prior best-of-five series that used to have it around in the previous three seasons of play) due to the way those two teams remained competitive throughout the entire season, the championship series would ultimately end up disappointing the league due to the Rosenblums winning another championship with a now 4–0 sweep to their name instead of having it feel more competitive as a whole for the league's sake. Teams Before the previous season concluded, five teams would already be confirmed to return for the season in the Brooklyn Visitations, Chicago Bruins, Cleveland Rosenblums, Fort Wayne Hoosiers, and the now two-time defending champion New York Original Celtics (with questions regarding whether the Rochester Centrals would return alongside the Philadelphia Warriors), though multiple reporters at the time expressed concerns regarding the league's stability by this point in time due to a combination of the Original Celtics' own success as a team and the way fans felt less interested in attending games that wouldn't involve the Celtics in particular. (While Rochester would end up deciding to stay with the ABL for another season, the Philadelphia Warriors would end up not only leaving the ABL, but also decide to return to their original Philadelphia SPHAs for essentially the rest of their existence going forward and briefly competed in the revived (minor) Philadelphia Basket Ball League before going independent for the rest of that season due to them losing $60,000 in their two seasons with the ABL as the Quakers turned Warriors, which gave most of the league pause for concern when Eddie Gottlieb thought he couldn't succeed in the ABL as it was at the time not too long after George Preston Marshall from Washington D.C. had done the same thing himself.) However, due to concerns on both the league's long-term and financial success, new league President John O'Brien would allow for the New York Original Celtics to be broken up and replaced by the New York Hakoahs for this season, with their players being planned to be given out by a new expansion team in Baltimor

title: 1892 Holborn by-election
text: The 1892 Holborn by-election was a Parliamentary by-election held on 12 August 1892 for the UK House of Commons constituency of Holborn. The constituency returned one Member of Parliament (MP) to the House of Commons of the United Kingdom, elected by the first past the post voting system. Vacancy The seat had become vacant following the appointment of the incumbent Conservative MP, Gainsford Bruce QC, as a Judge of the Queen's Bench division of the High Court of Justice on 18 July 1892. Bruce had been Member of Parliament for the constituency since an 1888 by-election. Previous result Candidates Conservative It was thought the vacancy had been created to allow Charles Thomson Ritchie, the outgoing President of the Local Government Board a route back into the House of Commons. Ritchie had been Member of Parliament for Tower Hamlets from 1874 to 1885 United Kingdom general election, and then MP for the St George division of Tower Hamlets until his defeat at the general election held that July. Some newspapers reported Ritchie had been invited to contest the seat, but these reports were contradicted. Ritchie himself was said not to be anxious to return immediately to the House of Commons. At a meeting of the executive committee of the Holborn Conservative Association held on the evening of Monday 18 July, Sir Charles Hall QC was unanimously selected as the Conservative candidate. At a meeting of the members of the Association on Friday 29 July, the selection of Hall was “enthusiastically approved”. Hall had been the Member of Parliament for Chesterton from the 1885 general election until his defeat at the general election held in July. Hall was a barrister who had been appointed Recorder of London in February that year. Liberal George Bateman, the Lib-Lab candidate who stood in the recent general election, suggested that he might stand again in a humorous article written for The Star of Tuesday 12 July, but his comments alienated some Liberal supporters, and he was later thought unlikely to stand. The General Council of the Holborn Liberal and Radical Association met on the evening of Wednesday 20 July and decided to fight the seat. They sounded out seven candidates, including: Some newspapers reported that F. O’Connor Prince had been selected, but these reports were premature. However, meeting at the National Schools, Bury Street, Bloomsbury on the evening of Thursday 4 August, the General Council of the Association decided by an overwhelming majority not to contest the seat. Result The writ for the by-election was issued on Monday 8 August. The date for nominations was set for Friday 12 August and polling day for Monday 15 August. As only one candidate was nominated, there was no poll. References

title: 1888 Holborn by-election
text: The 1888 Holborn by-election was a Parliamentary by-election held on 29 November 1888 for the UK House of Commons constituency of Holborn. The constituency returned one Member of Parliament (MP) to the House of Commons of the United Kingdom, elected by the first past the post voting system. Vacancy The seat had become vacant following the death of the incumbent Conservative MP, Francis Duncan on Friday 16 November. Duncan had been Member of Parliament for the constituency since the 1885 general election. Previous result Candidates Conservative The Holborn Conservative Association met on the evening of Monday 19 November, and agreed to defer the selection of a candidate until after the funeral of Duncan, which took place the next day. A meeting was held at the Conservative Club, Red Lion Square, on the evening of Tuesday 20 November where Gainsford Bruce QC was selected as the Conservative candidate. Bruce was a barrister from Newcastle upon Tyne who had previously been an unsuccessful candidate for Gateshead in 1880, Newcastle in an 1883 by-election, Tyneside in 1885 and Barrow in an 1886 by-election. Liberal At a meeting of the Holborn Liberal and Radical Association, held at the Holborn Gladstonian Club on the evening of Tuesday 20 November, Earl Compton, the heir to the Marquess of Northampton was unanimously selected as the Liberal candidate. Compton had been the Member of Parliament for Stratford-on-Avon from the 1885 general election until his defeat at the 1886 general election. He had contested South Warwickshire at an 1884 by-election. Campaign On Saturday 24 November at Holborn Town Hall Catherine Gladstone, wife of the Leader of the Opposition William Ewart Gladstone, chaired and addressed a meeting of ladies who supported Compton. Both candidates were actively engaged in canvassing voters the day before polling. Process The writ for the by-election was issued on Wednesday 21 November. The date for nominations was set for Monday 26 November and polling day for Thursday 29 November. On nomination day at Holborn Town Hall, Compton’s original nomination paper was rejected. An amended nomination paper was later submitted. Result Aftermath Speaking at Edinburgh on Friday 30 November, the Conservative Prime Minister Lord Salisbury sought to explain the reduced majority for Bruce on the basis that the Liberal candidate in 1886 had been a "black man": But then Colonel Duncan was opposed to a black man, and, however great the progress of mankind has been, and however far we have advanced in overcoming prejudices, I doubt if we have yet got to the point where a British constituency will elect a black man to represent them.... I am speaking roughly and using language in its colloquial sense, because I imagine the colour is not exactly black, but at all events, he was a man of another race. The "black man" was Dadabhai Naoroji, an Indian Parsi. Salisbury's comments were criticised by the Queen and by Liberals who believed that Salisbury had suggested that only white Britons could represent a British constituency. Three weeks later, Salisbury delivered a speech at Scarborough, where he denied that "the word "black" necessarily implies any contemptuous denunciation: "Such a doctrine seems to be a scathing insult to a very large proportion of the human race... The people whom we have been fighting at Suakin, and whom we have happily conquered, are among the finest tribes in the world, and many of them are as black as my hat". Furthermore, "such candidatures are incongruous and unwise. The British House of Commons, with its traditions... is a machine too peculiar and too delicate to be managed by any but those who have been born within these isles". Naoroji was elected for Finsbury in 1892 and Salisbury invited him to become a Governor of the Imperial Institute, which he accepted. title: 2026 CME Group Tour Championship
text: The 2026 CME Group Tour Championship was the 16th CME Group Tour Championship, a women's professional golf tournament and the season-ending event of the 2026 LPGA Tour. It was held November 19–22, 2026, on the Gold Course of Tiburón Golf Club in Naples, Florida, with a 60-player field competing over 72 holes without a cut. The purse was US$11 million, including a $4 million first prize. Jeeno Thitikul of Thailand won the championship for the third consecutive year, finishing at 24-under-par 264, two strokes ahead of Japan's Akie Iwai. Thitikul closed with a seven-under-par 65 and earned $4 million. The victory, her fifth of the 2026 season and 12th LPGA Tour title, moved her ahead of Annika Sörenstam on the tour's all-time official career money list. Format Qualification The championship was the final event in the season-long Race to the CME Globe, with the top 60 LPGA Tour members and ties on the points list after the final regular-season tournament, The ANNIKA, qualifying. The event was a 72-hole stroke-play competition with no 36-hole cut; all qualifiers started at even par, and the tournament winner was named the Race to the CME Globe champion. A victory in an earlier LPGA tournament did not, by itself, guarantee entry. Field The following 60 players qualified for the tournament. Players are listed alphabetically with their position in the final pre-championship Race to the CME Globe standings in parentheses. Tournament summary First round Thursday, November 19, 2026 Defending champion Jeeno Thitikul, A Lim Kim and Australian Karis Davidson shared the first-round lead after each shot seven-under-par 65. Thitikul birdied five consecutive holes, from the 13th through the 17th, while Davidson began with four consecutive birdies in her first appearance at the course. Haeran Ryu was among the players a stroke behind after a bogey-free 66. Second round Friday, November 20, 2026 Kim made a hole in one at the par-three 16th during an eight-under-par 64, taking the outright lead at 15-under 129, three strokes ahead of Thitikul. Thitikul recovered from an even-par front nine to birdie five of her final eight holes and post a 67. Kim's ace came with a seven-iron from 168 yards. Third round Saturday, November 21, 2026 Kim maintained the lead with a three-under-par 69, reaching 18-under 198 after 54 holes. Thitikul followed with a 67 to move within one stroke at 17-under, while Nelly Korda shot a seven-under 65 to reach 16-under and move into third place, two shots behind Kim. Kim's lead was reduced after two bogeys late in the round. Final round Sunday, November 22, 2026 Thitikul began the final round one shot behind Kim, but eagled the opening par-five hole as Kim made a double bogey. Iwai challenged for the lead with a final-round 65, drawing level with Thitikul at the tenth hole before the Thai player answered with a birdie. Thitikul added birdies at the 14th and 17th, finishing with a bogey-free 65 and a 24-under-par total of 264. Iwai finished second at 22-under 266 and Korda third at 20-under 268. Kim, who shot an even-par 72, finished in a three-way tie for seventh. The victory gave Thitikul three consecutive wins in the event (2024–2026), the first three-year winning streak at one LPGA Tour tournament since Inbee Park won the Women's PGA Championship from 2013 to 2015. Her $4 million prize increased her official LPGA Tour career earnings to $24,292,858, surpassing Sörenstam's previous record of $22,583,693. Korda also passed Sörenstam's career total by finishing third and earning $550,000. Final leaderboard Sunday, November 22, 2026 Source:

title: 2026 Co-op Live incident
text: On 22 November 2026, an unidentified substance was released into the audience during a concert by American rapper Don Toliver at Co-op Live in Manchester, England. The incident occurred at approximately 22:00 GMT, near the end of the performance, and prompted reports of eye irritation, coughing, breathing difficulties and a burning sensation in the throat among attendees. Greater Manchester Police (GMP) declared a major incident at 22:25 GMT. Police initially believed the substance may have been tear gas, but later said its identity and origin had not been established. More than 12,000 people were safely evacuated from the arena. North West Ambulance Service assessed 88 people at the scene for symptoms believed to be linked to the substance, while one person was taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further treatment. The major incident was lifted at around 04:00 GMT on 23 November. Police said there was no wider risk to the public and began an investigation into the nature and origin of the substance, as well as whether any criminal offence had been committed. Background Co-op Live opened on 14 May 2024 and is located on the Etihad Campus in Manchester, adjacent to the Etihad Stadium. It has a maximum capacity of 23,500, making it the largest indoor arena in the United Kingdom by capacity. Don Toliver was performing in Manchester as part of the second leg of his Nitrous – Octane World Tour. The tour supported his fifth studio album, Octane, released earlier in 2026. He had been scheduled to perform at The O2 Arena in London on 23 November and at OVO Arena Wembley on 24 November, the final date of the tour. Following the Manchester incident, the O2 Arena concert was postponed to 15 December 2026. Promoters attributed the postponement to production delays because Don Toliver's stage and production equipment remained at Co-op Live and could not be moved in time for the London show. The OVO Arena Wembley concert was also postponed, moving from 24 November to 14 December 2026. The venue said that the rescheduling was necessary because the production equipment could not be transported from Manchester in time. Incident GMP said that a major incident was declared shortly after 22:00 on 22 November 2026, following reports that people in the crowd were suffering from the effects of some unknown substance, which police initially thought to be tear gas. Footage shared on social media appeared to show concertgoers coughing and covering their mouths as they left the venue. Police later referred to an "unknown substance" rather than tear gas. In a statement issued shortly after 02:00 on 23 November, GMP said attendees have been safely evacuated. Assistant Chief Constable Steph Parker said that more than 12,000 people had been evacuated and that declaring a major incident allowed emergency services and partner agencies agencies to coordinate their response quickly. Casualties and response The North West Ambulance Service (NWAS) said that more than 50 people were assessed by clinicians, some with eye and respiratory symptoms. NWAS deployed several crews, including its Hazardous Area Response Team, and said "decontamination" was being carried out as a precaution. One patient was taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment. NWAS and GMP advised anyone who had attended and subsequently became unwell to seek medical advice. Investigation Greater Manchester Police Assistant Chief Constable Steph Parker, the incident's Gold Commander, said that officers would investigate what the substance was, where it had come from and how the incident had occurred. She also advised anyone who had attended the concert and subsequently felt unwell to seek medical advice. Co-op Live said that it was working closely with Greater Manchester Police to identify the cause of the incident and take appropriate action.
