title: Calva of Čáslav
text: Calva of Čáslav (Czech: Čáslavská kalva) is the upper part of a human skull discovered on November 21, 1910 during renovation work in the Church of Saints Peter and Paul in Čáslav. It is traditionally considered to be the remains of the Hussite military commander Jan Žižka, whose remains were transferred to Čáslav according to some historical sources. The discovery has been repeatedly subjected to anthropological and other scientific investigations. Although some findings support the possibility of its association with Žižka, the identity of the remains has not been conclusively established. Historical background According to an entry in the Old Czech Annals, after his death in 1424, Jan Žižka's body was buried in the Church of the Holy Spirit in Hradec Králové and later transferred to Čáslav. However, medieval chroniclers' accounts of Žižka's burial differ. Some historians, including Josef Šimák, Rudolf Urbánek and Karel Guth, questioned whether the remains had been transferred to Čáslav. Other historians, by contrast, maintained that the Hussite commander had been buried only in Čáslav and that the reported burial in Hradec Králové was a hoax. If the transfer of the body did take place, it probably occurred no earlier than the second half of the 15th century. The Chronicle of Jan Žižka (Kronika velmi pěkná o Janu Žižkovi), which is dated to approximately this period, states: "And they buried him (Žižka) in Hradec Králové, and there he lies." Some versions (R and G) of the Old Czech Annals indicate that their authors were already aware of the transfer of the remains after 1471. The reason for the exhumation remains unknown. Evidence supporting the transfer from Hradec Králové to Čáslav includes repeated references in chronicles to a chest containing the remains, reports of the existence of a stone cenotaph and accounts of visits by prominent figures to the memorial. Four accounts are also known of the destruction of the tombstone and attempts to find and destroy all memorials to Jan Žižka in Čáslav. These actions were attributed to the post-1620 Catholic Counter-Reformation. Its supporters initially believed that Žižka's bones were kept in the cenotaph, but it was empty. After this failure, they attempted to find them inside the Church of Saints Peter and Paul in Čáslav. In 1741, they probably discovered several skeletal remains there, which they had publicly burned by an executioner in the town square. Further attempts to locate Žižka's final resting place followed in 1801, 1875, 1880 and 1901. Discovery in 1910 An unexpected breakthrough came on 21 November 1910, when renovation work inside the church revealed a recess measuring 115 cm in height and 84 cm in both width and depth. According to architect Kamil Hilbert, the recess had been built into the church wall during the construction of the tower around 1450. At the bottom of the recess were two crossed thigh bones, a damaged calva and a piece of an earthenware bowl. Other remains of skull bones and a skeleton, two wooden tablets and a clump of decayed fabric were arranged around the crossed bones. Experts from the Archaeological Commission of the Academy of Sciences and Arts in Prague were invited to secure and examine the site. In January 1911, Professor Jindřich Matiegka presented a report on the discovery and declared the bones to be the remains of Jan Žižka. He based his conclusion on the morphological characteristics of the bones, particularly the apparent loss of one eye, the circumstances of the discovery and comparisons with the earliest depictions of the Hussite commander. The entire investigation was, however, accompanied by a degree of mistrust. This stemmed from the activities of local patriots in Čáslav, who, in an attempt to provide historical support for the discovery, placed an inscription on the pages of an old book in a recess on the opposite side of the tower. It read: "The bones of the famous Czech leader Jan Žižka are secretly kept in the opposite w

title: Fiona Drouet
text: Fiona Drouet MBE is the British Chief executive officer of EmilyTest. She and the EmilyTest have campaigned to increase the safeguards to support victims of gender based violence following the death of her daughter Emily Drouet. Life Drouet was born in Bellshill in the 1960s. She married Germain and they had children including a daughter, Emily Drouet, in about 1998. Emily went on to study law at Aberdeen University in 2015. She stayed in the university's halls of residence. In 2016, her daughter took her own life after suffering abuse by her boyfriend. He was not given a custodial sentence although he admitted assaulting her. Her parents took out a civil case against the daughters former boyfriend and abuser because of their loss, and disappointment that he had only been given community service as a punishment. The case was rejected, but Emily's siblings were allowed to start a similar case. Fiona was of the opinion that her daughter's life might not have been lost if she had received better support from Aberdeen University. Her daughter had asked for help from her university. In 2021 the university announced an Emily Drouet Award that would be given every year for five years and that an intern would be funded to support student services. She founded a charity called EmilyTest that campaigns for universities to improve their procedures. Seven universities of colleges were engaged by 2022. In 2024 she raised a petition to make non-fatal strangulation an offence. She met the Scottish First Minister John Swinney who said it would be considered although he noted that the existing laws allowed for life-imprisonment as a punishment. Awards In 2022 Princess Anne made awards to people associated with campaigning against domestic violence. Fiona received the award with others including the former Spice Girl Mel B. Drouet was given honorary doctorates and degrees including by the Open University, Aberdeen University and Strathclyde University. References

title: Daniel Friebe
text: Daniel Friebe is a British cycling journalist, author and podcaster. Friebe is a co-founder and presenter of The Cycling Podcast, which he established with Lionel Birnie and Richard Moore in 2013. He has also worked as an on-the-ground reporter for ITV Sport's cycling coverage. He was formerly features editor of Procycling magazine, and has written for publications including The Daily Telegraph, The Sunday Telegraph and FourFourTwo. His books include biographies of Eddy Merckx and Jan Ullrich, as well as books written with Mark Cavendish and photographer Pete Goding. Bibliography Friebe, Daniel (2012). Eddy Merckx: The Cannibal. title: Chathuranga Kodithuwakku
text: Kodithuwakku Arachchilage Lakshan Chathuranga Kodithuwakku, (born 16 August 1995), is an actor in Sri Lankan cinema and television and also a photographer and model. He is best known for the roles "Nimesh" in "Hadawathe Kathawa" and "Aadesh" in soapie "Ron Soya". Personal life He was born on 16 August 1995 in Homagama, Sri Lanka. His father is Mahinda Kodithuwakku is a machine operator at State Printing Corporation and mother is Mallika Alwis Jayasinghe, who is a housewife. Chathuranga made his primary education from Subharathi Mahamathya Maha Vidyalaya, Godagama. Then he completed his secondary education from D. S. Senanayake College, Colombo. During school times, he was excelled in sports as well as an active school's media society. In 2013, he won the award for the Best upcoming photographer in school awards. After school life, he studied at Sri Lanka Media Training Institute (SLMTI). He is married to fellow actress Dusheni Silva, where they celebrated the wedding in 2026. Career Chathuranga started his photography career at very young age, where he was the chief photographer of Let me know.lk. Then on 12 February 2014, he started the modeling career. In 2018, he appeared in the music video Agarajini sung by Harshana Wijesinghe amd later in the song Facebook Love by Randhir Vithana ft. RapZilla. In 2019, he appeared in another popular music video As Gawa by Nehara Pieris. During the same time, he joined as a contestant for the reality show Derana Thathvika season 1. In 2019, Chathuranga made his television debut with a main role "Nimesh" in the serial Hadawathe Kathawa telecast in Swarnavahini. His role got high publicity where he got the opportunity to act another lead role in the serial Lan Wee in 2022. Since then, he acted many lead and supporting roles in the television serials such as LBW, Divithura, Jaanu, Juraliya, See You, Unmadini, Veeduru Thira and currently in Ron Soya and Jahuta. In 2025, he made his film debut with the sports drama film Mother Lanka. In 2025, Chathuranga won the award for the Most Popular Upcoming Actor for his role in the serial Veeduru Thira at the Popular Awards. Then for the same role, he won Upcoming Actor of the Year award at Puravesi Abhiman Awards, Pinnacle Awards and Sumathi Awards, all in 2025. In 2026, he won several awards including Most Popular Teledrama Actor at the Raigam Tele'es, Global Synergy Awards, Asia Miracle Awards and Popular Awards. Meanwile, he along with fellow actress Michelle Dilhara won the most popular on-screen couple of the year at the Popular Awards. title: Sapindus emarginatus
text: Sapindus emarginatus, commonly known as the soapnut tree or South Indian soapnut, is a species of flowering deciduous tree in the family Sapindaceae native to South Asia. In India, it is primarily found in the southern regions, alongside the northern species Sapindus mukorossi. Description Sapindus emarginatus is a medium-sized deciduous tree growing to a height of 10 to 18 m (33 to 59 ft). The bark is grey to dark brown and covered with rough scales. The leaves are pinnately compound, each bearing two to three pairs of opposite leaflets; the leaflet tips are characteristically notched or slightly emarginate. Small greenish-white flowers are borne in terminal panicles. The fruit is a three-lobed drupe that turns wrinkled and brown upon maturity, enclosing a hard, round, black seed. Phytochemistry The outer fleshy pericarp of the fruit contains high concentrations of saponin, a natural glycoside. When dissolved in water, saponin lowers surface tension to produce a natural lather. Biologically, saponins act as a chemical defence mechanism protecting the seeds from insects, microbes, and fungi. Uses Due to the surfactant properties of the saponins present in the pericarp, the dried fruit pulp has traditionally been used in South India as a natural cleanser, detergent, and hair wash. title: Nanjing Museum Mile
text: Nanjing Museum Mile (Chinese: 南京长江路文博街区、南京博物馆大道) is a cultural, museum, commercial and tourism district located along Changjiang Road in Xuanwu District, Nanjing, Jiangsu Province, China. Stretching approximately 1,800 metres through central Nanjing, the corridor connects museums, historic sites, galleries and commercial venues. Cultural and commercial venues Major sites include Nanjing Library, the Presidential Palace, which houses the Museum of Modern Chinese History, Jiangsu Art Museum and its exhibition hall, the Nanjing Culture and Art Center, the Jiangning Imperial Silk Manufacturing Museum, the Six Dynasties Museum, and the Memorial Hall of the Chinese Communist Party Delegation in Meiyuan Xincun. Other institutions in the district include Deji Art Museum and the Nanjing Museum of Modern Architecture. The cultural institutions represent different periods of Nanjing's history. The Six Dynasties Museum preserves archaeological remains associated with Jiankang, the city that served as a capital during the Six Dynasties period. The Jiangning Imperial Silk Manufacturing Museum occupies the former site of the Qing-dynasty imperial silk manufacturing establishment and presents the history of Nanjing yunjin brocade. The Presidential Palace preserves buildings associated with Qing dynasty, Taiping Heavenly Kingdom and the Republic of China. Jiangsu Art Museum and Nanjing Library provide spaces for art exhibitions, historical collections and public cultural activities. Commercial and leisure establishments are concentrated particularly toward the western end of the corridor, where Changjiang Road connects with the Xinjiekou shopping district. They include Deji Plaza, IST Mall and nearby hotel and retail developments. The Nanjing Museum, located outside the main Changjiang Road corridor, also participates in the district's joint ticketing and cultural programmes, connecting it with museums and heritage institutions along the street. History During the Six Dynasties period, parts of the present corridor lay within the imperial city of Jiankang. Archaeological remains of the former palace complex, including rammed-earth foundations and other structures, have been preserved and displayed within museums along the route. The area subsequently developed around government buildings, residential compounds and commercial streets during Ming and Qing dynasties. Parts of the present road were historically known as Dacangyuan, a name associated with storage facilities established during the Ming dynasty. Following the establishment of Nanjing as the capital of the Nationalist government, the road was widened and named Guofu Road (国府路) in 1930. It was later renamed Linsen Road (林森路), in memory of Lin Sen, the former president of the Nationalist Government. After 1949, the road got its present name, Changjiang Road, referring to Yangtze River. In 2026, Xuanwu District undertook an urban renewal project along Changjiang Road. The Nanjing Culture and Art Center removed approximately 120 metres of perimeter walls and outdated display structures, creating an open forecourt with seating and facilities for small performances. Jiangsu Art Museum removed sections of its northern boundary and reorganised an existing sunken plaza into a stepped public space. Other works included adjustments to pedestrian routes, bicycle parking, landscaping and nighttime lighting.

title: Kumano (album)
text: Kumano is a 1980 album by Canadian group Kumano. It contains the dance hit, "I'll Cry for You". Background The main part of the ensemble was keyboardist, vocalist Randy Kumano and vocalist, bassist Stuart Peterson. Producer Kumano worked with engineers Gerry Lester and Dan Lanois to record the album at Grant Avenue Studios in Hamilton. The single "I'll Cry for You" was a hit on the Billboard Disco Top 100 chart where it spent fifteen weeks on the chart, peaking at No. 24. It also made the Record World Disco Top 50 chart where it peaked at No. 30. The album was re-released on the Unidisc label in 2010. Reception In the 5 April issue of Record World, Brian Chin praised the song "I'll Cry for You" and also wrote that it may have been a lucky accident that Kumano came up with such a fusion of accessible styles and due to the fact that they didn't have a pat formula made their album so fresh and cliche free. Barry Lederer of in his Disco Mix column of the 24 April issue of Billboard referred to the five tracks on the album as riveting. The album was reviewed in the 21 June 1980 issue of RPM Weekly. The reviewer called it a tight smooth dance-oriented album with strong material and that Peterson's voice was a particular strength. Chart UK In May 1980, the album was on the Sounds Disco chart. title: Shaoyang North Pagoda
text: The Shaoyang North Pagoda (simplified Chinese: 邵阳北塔; traditional Chinese: 邵陽北塔; pinyin: Shàoyáng Běitǎ) is a Ming dynasty pagoda in Beita District, Shaoyang, Hunan, China. It stands on the northern bank of the Zi River, near its confluence with the Shao River. Constructed between 1573 and 1582. History In 1570, the retired official Gao Gangfeng (高冈凤) initiated the project with support from provincial official Wu Dui (吴兑) and Baoqing prefect Wei Yuankang (蔚元康). Gao's family organised public fundraising, and construction commenced in 1573, the first year of the Wanli Emperor's reign. Financial shortages halted work after the completion of the first three storeys. In 1582, the newly appointed prefect Hu Pian (胡楩) secured further contributions and completed the remaining four storeys by the end of the year. The pagoda subsequently became a navigational landmark for boats travelling along the Zi River. The establishment of Beita District in 1997 perpetuated the pagoda's name. The structure sustained damage during the Second Sino-Japanese War, leaving impact marks on its masonry and dislodging an iron component of its finial. Restoration work in 2001 uncovered a small seated Buddha figure inside the finial. In 2001, the Chinese government included the pagoda in the fifth batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level. Architecture The North Pagoda is a seven-storey. A stone platform supports the progressively narrowing tower. The fourth national cultural relics survey recorded an overall height of 31.43 m (103.1 ft), including the finial, and a foundation width of 18.56 m (60.9 ft). An arched entrance on the southern face opens into a spacious ground-floor chamber. An internal passage ascends anticlockwise to the uppermost chamber. Windows and doorways punctuate the brick exterior, while projecting eaves divide the tower into distinct storeys. References

title: Khirbet Marjameh
text: Khirbet Marjameh is an archaeological site and a tell located in the eastern Samarian hills of the modern-day West Bank. The remains indicate Bronze Age activity (including Early and Late Bronze remains) and a major fortified Israelite town from the Iron Age II, which was occupied up until the Assyrian conquest. Name In Arabic, Khirbet Marjameh means "the ruin of the rock piles", apparently referring to the remains of Iron Age II houses that cover the site's slopes. Geography Khirbet Marjameh lies at an elevation of 450 metres (1,480 ft), in a narrow, dry transitional belt between the Jordan Valley and the central Ephraim highlands. It lies near the perennial spring of Ein Samiya, whose waters were used in antiquity to irrigate the adjacent valley. This fertile valley appears to have supported settlement at the site throughout its history. Nearby sites include the ridge of Dhahr Mirzbaneh, which was settled during the Bronze Age, and Khirbet Samiyeh, a site inhabited during the Roman and Byzantine periods that may also have been occupied during the early Islamic period. The nearby site of Khirbet el-Bayadir was occupied up until the Crusader period. The Palestinian village of Kafr Malik lies approximately 2 kilometres (1.2 mi) to the west. Research history The site was first surveyed by William F. Albright in 1922. He documented a "megalithic monument" on the summit, which he interpreted as a possible cultic site. In 1964, Lapp conducted a further survey, reporting that most of the pottery dated to Iron Age II. He also noted sherds from the Early and Middle Bronze Ages, Iron Age I, and the Roman–Byzantine periods. In a 1968 survey conducted by Zecharia Kallai, Late Bronze Age potsherds were also recorded. In 1975 and 1978, Amihai Mazar excavated the summit on behalf of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and the Staff Officer for Archaeology, uncovering city fortifications dating to Iron Age II. In 1980, M. Zohar conducted a salvage excavation on the site's southern slope, which had been damaged during construction of the Ein Samiya pumping station. In 2015, the site was surveyed again as part of the New South Samaria survey. Archaeology The site was a fortified Israelite city that Amihai Mazar estimates covered about 30 dunams (7.5 acres) during the Monarchic period (Iron Age II). According to Mazar, "Kh. Marjameh is the only urban site with continuous settlement from the Bronze Age to the period of the Monarchy in this semi-arid region at the eastern fringe of the Hills of Ephraim, and one of few such sites in the entire Land of Ephraim." Its fortifications made use of the local topography. Mazar's excavations concentrated on the upper part of the site and on its Iron Age II fortifications. Above the western cliff, a rubble-stone wall about 4 metres wide was uncovered, with rooms added along its inner face at a later stage. To the north, the excavators exposed a rectangular tower measuring about 14.4 metres (47 ft) by 20 metres (66 ft), rounded on its western side. It occupies the highest point of the site and covers the northwest approach, and at least two rooms of a house were built against its southeast wall. Mazar considered the tower "one of the largest and most impressive remains of urban fortifications from the period of the Monarchy in the entire country." Pottery from Building 10 and the city wall at Khirbet Marjameh has been dated by Mazar based on parallels to the 8th century BCE, probably to the time of the Assyrian conquest of the kingdom of Israel in 722 BCE. The assemblage features a combination of Judahite and northern Israelite characteristics; kraters, pithoi and lamps resemble Judahite forms, while storage jars with ridged rims are typical of the north. Red slip and burnishing are scarce, and Samaria ware is absent, possibly because it was not distributed this far south. Mazar regarded the assemblage as reflecting a ceramic tradition that combined elements of Judahite pottery with those characteristic of ce

title: David A. Baldwin (political scientist)
text: David Allen Baldwin is an American political scientist who specializes in international political economy, international relations theory, and American foreign policy. Education Baldwin received an A.B. in economics from Indiana University in 1958 and graduated with highest honors. He undertook graduate study in political science at the University of Michigan from 1958 to 1959. He then studied at Princeton University from 1959 to 1961 and from 1963 to 1964. He received his M.A. in 1961 and a Ph.D. in 1965. Career Baldwin began his academic career at Dartmouth College, where he was an assistant professor of government from 1965 to 1970 and associate professor of government from 1970 to 1975. He became professor of government in 1975 and held the John Sloan Dickey professorship in the Social sciences from 1975 to 1980. He remained associated with Dartmouth until 1985. In 1980, he was appointed as a visiting professor in the Department of International Relations at the London School of Economics and Political Science. In 1985, he joined Columbia University as professor of Political science until 2004. He was the Director of the Institute of War and Peace Studies from 1987 to 1994 and held the Wallach professorship of World Order studies from 1989 to 2004. Baldwin returned to Princeton University in 2005 as a Senior Political Scientist at the Princeton School of Public and International Affairs, formerly known as the Woodrow Wilson School of Public and International Affairs. He also holds the title of Wallach Professor of Political Science Emeritus at Columbia University and is affiliated with Columbia's Arnold A. Saltzman Institute of War and Peace Studies (SIWPS). His other academic appointments have included a research fellowship at the Brookings Institution. Research Baldwin's research interests include international political economy, international relations theory, political power, and geoeconomics. He has authored 5 books, edited over 10, and published articles in academic journals, including American Political Science Review, Journal of Politics, World Politics, International Organization, Journal of Conflict Resolution, Journal of Political Power, International Security, Review of International Studies, and International Studies Quarterly. His publications include Economic Statecraft (Princeton University Press, 1985), Power and International Relations (2016), and a new edition of Economic Statecraft (2020). His 1985 book Economic Statecraft received the Gladys M. Kammerer Award from the American Political Science Association for the best political science publication of 1985 on U.S. national policy. His contributions to Sage Publications' International Encyclopedia of Political Science (2011) also formed the basis of his contributions to Encyclopædia Britannica. Honor and awards Baldwin's honors and awards include election to Phi Beta Kappa and the Moffat Prize in Economics at Indiana University in 1958. He received Danforth Foundation and Woodrow Wilson fellowships for the periods 1958-1964 and 1958–1959. The Helsinki Geoeconomics Society established the David A. Baldwin Prize in Geoeconomics to recognize his contributions in geoeconomics. In 2001, he was named a Distinguished Scholar Honoree by the International Political Economy section of the International Studies Association (ISA) at its annual convention. Professional affiliations and Service Baldwin is a member of the Council on Foreign Relations, the American Political Science Association, the International Political Science Association (IPSA), and the International Studies Association. He has also been associated with the British International Studies Association (BISA). His professional service includes membership on the Governing Board of the International Studies Association, New England, from 1972 to 1976. His service consisted of multiple positions, resulting in his presidency from 1975 to 1976. In 1976, he joined the International Studies Association's Tra

title: Josh Blake (actor)
text: Josh Buxbaum (born January 7, 1975) is an American film, stage and television actor. He is best known for playing the recurring role of Jake Ochmonek in the American science fiction sitcom television series ALF. Life and career Blake was born in New York on January 7, 1975, the son of Fred, a podiatrist, and Liz Buxbaum. He began his stage career in 1984, appearing in the stage play The Human Comedy, playing Ulysses Macauley. He then began his screen career in 1985, appearing in the television film The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus. In 1986, he appeared in the stage play Rags, playing David Hershkowitz. Later in his career, in 1989, Blake starred as Aristotle Zakalokis, the title character's brother, in the CBS sitcom television series The Famous Teddy Z, starring along with Jon Cryer, Alex Rocco, Tom LaGrua, Milton Selzer, Jane Sibbett and Erica Yohn. After the series ended in 1990, he guest-starred in television programs including The Wonder Years, Home Improvement, Full House, Sabrina the Teenage Witch, Married... with Children and JAG, and played the recurring role of Jake Ochmonek in the NBC science fiction sitcom television series ALF. He also appeared in films such as Fat Guy Goes Nutzoid, Going Down and Just for Kicks.

title: Raghunath Singh (ruler)
text: Raghunath Singh (1860 – 9 January 1896) was Thakur of Bagli from January 1869 until his death in 1896. Early life, family, and education Singh was born in 1860 into a family that was related to the ruling family of Bagli. As Subhag Singh, the Thakur of Bagli, had no sons of his own, he adopted Singh as his son. He was educated at the Rajkumar College in Indore. He married and had two sons, Ranjit Singh and Sajjan Singh. He was a Rathore. Reign Following the death of his adoptive father in June 1866, he claimed his adoptive father's title, rank and dignity. However, Jayajirao Scindia, the Maharaja of Gwalior, disputed the validity of his adoption and refused to recognise him as the deceased's successor. The dispute between him and Scindia resulted in the Bagli succession case, which continued from 1868 to 1869 and was heard by the Government of India. The Government ultimately ruled in his favour and declared his adoption to be legal and valid and binding upon Scindia. Following the decision, he paid a nazarana (transl. tribute) to the Scindia amounting to one-fourth of the net revenue of the fourteen guaranteed villages. In January 1869, his succession as Thakur of Bagli was formally recognised by the Government. In 1870, he entered into an agreement in which he acknowledged the Scindia of Gwalior as his suzerain, both on his own behalf and on behalf of his heirs, and undertook to render service to him in accordance with custom. In the same year, the Scindia increased the annual jama (transl. revenue; rental; rent roll) on the 69 remaining unguaranteed villages in Singh's estate from Rs. 7,251 to Rs. 10,001. Death He died on 9 January 1896, and his son Ranjit Singh succeeded to his title, rank and dignity. References

title: Adam Rosenberg (entrepreneur)
text: Adam Rosenberg is an American entrepreneur and cannabis policy advocate. Since 2025 he has chaired the board of the National Cannabis Industry Association (NCIA), a trade association for the cannabis industry. He is also a partner and board member at Vlasic Bioscience, a cannabinoid company, and co-founder and president of the nutrition company Vegan Minerals. Biography Rosenberg grew up in Birmingham, Michigan. In 2017, as a sophomore at the University of Michigan's Ross School of Business, he started Green Wolverine, an organization for students interested in the business side of cannabis. Public radio station WEMU called it the first group of its kind in the United States. The club went on to become a nonprofit with chapters at other universities, and it helped start the university's first course on medicinal cannabis. Rosenberg started investing at the Arcview Group, an investor network, and then at the venture capital firm Tress Capital. He later became the first president and chief financial officer of Vlasic Bioscience, a company started by members of the family behind Vlasic pickles. Rosenberg joined the NCIA board in January 2025, and a month later the board voted unanimously to make him chairman. Cultivated noted that he was the youngest person ever to hold the post. When founding CEO Aaron Smith stepped down later that year, the board took over his leadership duties under Rosenberg's direction. Rosenberg has commented on cannabis policy in The Wall Street Journal, on NPR, and in STAT. References

title: Kuusisaari (Laukaa)
text: Kuusisaari is a 1.7-square-kilometer (0.66 sq mi) island in the northern part of lake Leppävesi in Laukaa, Finland, in the village of Vuontee. The island has been connected to the mainland by a causeway since 1994. Geography Kuusisaari is located in the northern part of Leppävesi, west of the village center of Vuontee. The Poudanlahti bay divides the island's northern part into two peninsulas, Kiviniemi in the west and Jorpakanniemi in the east. In the south, the Likosalmi strait separates Kuusisaari from the island of Pernasaari. Kuusisaari has an area of about 1.7 square kilometers (0.66 sq mi). The average elevation of Kuusisaari is 88.2 meters (289 ft). The surface level of Leppävesi is 81 meters (266 ft), while the highest point on the island, the Kurkivuori hill on Jorpakanniemi, reaches an elevation of 110.8 meters (364 ft). The island consists of two rocky moraine ridges and flat depressions between them that were formed as the Fennoscandian ice sheet retreated from the area, with the modern shape of the island being a result of the following post-glacial rebound. Around 5,000 BC, only the highest point of modern Kuusisaari was visible above water as a 100–200 m (330–660 ft) long islet, with the rest of the island gradually emerging later. The most common rock type on the island is porphyritic granodiorite, but porphyritic biotite granite is also found in its northern part. There are no significant outcrops on the island. Kuusisaari is connected to the mainland via a causeway, and the road leading to the island branches off from the highway 640 (Saviontie). The causeway restricts flow between the shallow Vihtalahti bay and the rest of the lake, as a result of which the bay has become somewhat overgrown. As of January 2026, there were two permanently inhabited houses and ten seasonal homes on the island. In 2022, the municipality of Laukaa made plans to re-zone the island to allow for the construction of more houses. Nature Most of Kuusisaari is covered by managed forest, while 34.5 hectares (85 acres) or 21 percent of it is farmland. Protected areas make up 6.5 hectares (16 acres) of the island. The forest on the moraine ridges is dominated by pines, while the low-lying areas are covered mainly by monocultural spruce forest, though larches have also been planted in some sections. Patches of older, more natural forest are found on the Kurkivuori hill (including a protected area) and at the end of the Poudanlahti bay. There are naturally occurring littleleaf lindens on the island not far from the northern limit of their range, including many old trees; the largest measured linden on the island has a diameter at breast height of about 80 centimeters (31 in). The trees are concentrated in fertile sections of spruce forest, where other more demanding plants such as Lonicera xylosteum, Actaea spicata, Lathyrus vernus, Viburnum opulus, Equisetum pratense, Milium effusum, Scrophularia nodosa and Paris quadrifolia also grow. On the western shore of Kiviniemi, there is a boulder field with a length of 100 meters (330 ft) and a maximum width of about 30 meters (98 ft). The boulders are covered mainly by low-growing lichens in addition to some Cladonia and Stereocaulon lichens. A section of birch-dominated flooded forest is found around the Likosalmi strait. Notable birds found on Kuusisaari include willow tits (endangered in Finland), crested tits, reed buntings, hazel grouse and Eurasian wigeons. A regionally important resting stop for migratory birds is located east of the island. Protected animals living on or near the island include northern bats and whiskered bats, moor frogs, and two species of dragonfly: Leucorrhinia caudalis and Leucorrhinia pectoralis. History Kuusisaari was first mentioned in 1553 as Kusysalo [sic] (Kuusisalo), when it was settled by Olavi Pekanpoika Nyppyläinen. title: Burnett baronets of Leys (1626)
text: The Burnett baronetcy, of Leys in the County of Kincardine, was created in the Baronetage of Nova Scotia on 21 April 1626 for the politician Thomas Burnett, a leading Covenanter. He was the brother of Robert Burnet, Lord Crimond, and uncle of Gilbert Burnet, Bishop of Salisbury. The 3rd Baronet was one of the Scottish representatives to the 1st Parliament of Great Britain. The 8th, 10th and 12th Baronets all served as Lord Lieutenant of Kincardineshire. The 13th Baronet was a major general in the British Army. The Official Roll marks the title "dormant", as it has been since the death of the 14th Baronet in 1959. Burnett baronets, of Leys (1626) Sir Thomas Burnett, 1st Baronet (died 1653) Sir Alexander Burnett, 2nd Baronet (died 1663) Sir Thomas Burnett, 3rd Baronet (died 1714) Sir Alexander Burnett, 4th Baronet (died 1758) Sir Robert Burnett, 5th Baronet (died 1759) Sir Thomas Burnett, 6th Baronet (died 1783) Sir Robert Burnett, 7th Baronet (1755–1837) Sir Thomas Burnett, 8th Baronet (1778–1849) Sir Alexander Burnett, 9th Baronet (1789–1856) Sir James Horn Burnett, 10th Baronet (1801–1876) Sir Robert Burnett, 11th Baronet (1833–1894) Sir Thomas Burnett, 12th Baronet (1840–1926) Sir James Lauderdale Gilbert Burnett, 13th Baronet (1880–1953) Sir Alexander Edwin Burnett, 14th Baronet (1881–1959) died unmarried. Extended family The 6th Baronet married Catherine, sister and heiress of the 6th and last of the Ramsay baronets of Balmain (first creation, 1625). Their second son Alexander Burnett succeeded to the Ramsay estates on his uncle's death in 1806 and assumed the surname of Ramsay; the same year the baronetcy of Balmain was revived in his favour. Sir Alexander Burnett Ramsay, 6th Baronet (1903–1965), of the Ramsay baronets of Balmain (second creation, 1806), was heir presumptive to the title, but did not claim it on the death of the 14th Baronet. His son Sir Alexander William Burnett Ramsay, 7th Baronet (born 1938), presumed holder of the title, has not claimed it. This Burnett family line succeeded to the Ramsay estates and changed surname by royal licence. After the 13th Baronet's two sons, Alexander and Roger, both died as young men, the estate passed through his daughter Elizabeth Rohays Mary Burnett to her son James Comyn Amherst Cecil (born 1941) by her first marriage to Henry Kerr Auchmuty Cecil, elder brother of Henry Cecil. He changed his surname to Burnett in 1966 in the Court of the Lord Lyon, in order to succeed to it. Notes

title: Len Ashby
text: Leonard James "Buck" Ashby (16 September 1902, Ridleyton North, South Australia – 5 July 1986, South Australia) was an Australian rules football player for West Torrens, and coach for the Eagles, Port Adelaide and South Adelaide. Playing career The son of Harold "Wharfie" Ashby who played for Port Adelaide between 1902 and 1911, his father wished him to play for the Magpies but he was zoned to West Torrens. Ashby began his senior career in 1921 after advancing from Torrens' successful "B" grade team. He became a regular member of the eighteen the following season, and established himself as a very solid and reliable player, either in defence or as a follower, who was always noted for putting his whole effort into a game. Ashby played in Torrens' 1924 premiership team, where he was a typically reliable defender in the Grand Final. He would gain state selection in the 1927 Melbourne Carnival and play all four South Australia games there, and during the 1928 season Ashby would receive a testimonial of £50 from the blue and golds upon completing his one hundredth game. However, Ashby's career would suffer a massive setback very soon after when he was reported for striking an umpire against West Adelaide at Thebarton and suspended for three years. Like West Adelaide goalsneak Bennetts, Ashby would serve his full sentence. After his sentence ended, Ashby would initially play for the second team, but would be recalled to the senior team at the age of thirty midway through the 1932 season. He would then become the only player to play in both Torrens' 1924 and 1933 premiership teams, before retiring as a player after the defeat of Norwood. He would return as a player for two matches late in 1936, when coaching a struggling side. Coaching career West Torrens Although Ashby was disqualified from playing at the time, he would be appointed to coach Torrens for the 1930 season; however, Torrens would win only three of seventeen matches and finish last for the first time in its history. He would also coach the club's Association team through the full three seasons of his suspension, during which time it would finish fourth twice and then win a premiership in 1931. After his stint at Port, Ashby would be re-appointed to coach his former club for the 1936 season. However, expectations of a strong combination were not realised and the blue and golds won just five matches for the season to finish ahead of only the persistently weak Glenelg and West Adelaide. Ashby was nonetheless made a life member of the club in January 1937. Port Adelaide In April 1934, Ashby was appointed coach of traditional powerhouse Port Adelaide, who in 1933 had missed the major round for the first time in a decade. In his two seasons as coach, Ashby would lead the Magpies to two minor premierships, but they would unexpectedly be beaten narrowly beaten by traditional stragglers Glenelg in 1934 and South Adelaide in 1935, and Ashby wanted to return to his original club after that season. Nonetheless, by the time his stint at Alberton ended, Ashby was already viewed as one of the best coaches in South Australian football. South Adelaide After Vic Johnson announced a move into the media during the off-season, Ashby was appointed coach of a South Adelaide team, who, via-then-innovative country recruiting, had risen from just 30 wins in 164 games over the decade from 1925 to 1934, to their first premiership in 36 years in 1935 and a semi-final berth in 1936. Under Ashby, South would reach their second Grand Final in three years in 1937, and sweep all before them in 1938, losing only two games all season and swamping Ashby's former club Port with a thirteen-goal third quarter in the Grand Final. Ashby would also be appointed South Australian state coach that winter, and he retained the position for 1939. title: Croydon-Ferntree Gully Football League
text: The Croydon-Ferntree Gully Football League was the final name of an Australian rules football competition based in the eastern suburbs of Melbourne. The League was previously known by the following names: 1927-1934: Ringwood District Football Association 1935-1941: Ringwood District Football League 1945-1947: Croydon Mail Football League 1948-1949: Croydon District Football League History The Ringwood District Football Association was formed in 1927 as a breakaway from the Reporter District Football Association. The inaugural season featured ex-RDFA clubs Blackburn, Doncaster, Ringwood and Vermont as well as Yarra Valley FA club Croydon, Diamond Valley FA club Warrandyte and new club Kilsyth, all clubs which had previously competed in the Reporter District FA. The RDFA folded after 1927 which saw Mitcham and Tunstall join the Ringwood District FA along with Templestowe from the DVFA. The 1928 grand final was originally won by Blackburn, however the premiership was awarded to Doncaster after it was determined that Blackburn played a suspended player, L. Stainsby, in the game. By 1930 the RDFA had expanded to 12 teams with the additions of Bayswater and Ringwood East. Templestowe returned to the DVFA in 1931 and Mitcham merged with Vermont in 1932 owing to the effects of the Great Depression. 1934 saw a second grade competition introduced for the first time, although it would only last a further two seasons in its initial form. The Eastern Suburban FL began to poach clubs from the west of the RDFL's territory, including Blackburn, Doncaster, Mitcham and Vermont by 1938 and Ringwood after WWII. The RDFL looked further east for more clubs, a move which saw Olinda, Monbulk, Boronia and Lilydale all join the League during the late 1930s. The RDFL entered recess in 1942 due to WWII, but returned in 1945 as the Croydon Mail Football League. A further name change to Croydon District Football League occurred in 1948, followed by a final change to Croydon-Ferntree Gully Football League in 1950. The 1950s were dominated by Kilsyth, East Ringwood and Ringwood, who returned to the competition in 1955. All but two of the grand finals during this decade featured two of these three clubs. Kilsyth won three premierships in a row between 1950 and 1952, a feat equalled by Ringwood between 1955 and 1957. The growth of the eastern suburbs and subsequently the League itself saw the second grade reintroduced in 1947 and a third grade competition in 1952. Clubs from the Eastern Suburban FL joined the CFGFL in large numbers during the 1950s and by 1961 it was clear that a unified league for the East was desired, culminating in the reorganization of the CFGFL into the Eastern Districts Football League. title: Static (Israeli singer)
text: Liraz Russo (Hebrew: לירז רוסו; born 8 December 1990), known professionally as Static (סטטיק), is an Israeli singer, songwriter and rapper. From 2015 to 2022 he was one half of the pop duo Static & Ben El Tavori, which had a string of number-one hits in Israel, including "Tudo Bom", signed a ten-year deal with Capitol Records in 2018 and released English-language singles with Pitbull, the Black Eyed Peas and Snoop Dogg. After the duo split, he began a solo career, releasing the albums Liraz (2023) and Leharim (2024). Early life Russo was adopted as an infant by Moshe and Nitza Russo, who raised him in Haifa. He has said that his childhood family story is a central part of his identity. He began learning piano at the age of three and later took up guitar, and as a teenager he trained in freestyle rap and performed with the Haifa rap group Unique T. His stage name came from a childhood friend, who said he was as sharp and unpredictable as static electricity. He served in the Israel Defense Forces as an officer in the Manpower Directorate, and left the army before completing his full term of service. Career Early career After his military service, Russo began working with producer Omri Segal, and later collaborated with rapper Ron Nesher and producer Mor Sagiv. His first breakthrough came as a featured artist on Alon De Loco's hit "Loco Vine". In 2015, he and DJ Gal Malka released "Ba La Lirkod", which entered the Galgalatz playlist. Static & Ben El Tavori (2015–2022) Russo's work on Ron Nesher's viral 2015 single "#DubiGal" brought him together with singer Ben El Tavori and producer Yarden Peleg (Jordi), and the three began recording together as Static & Ben El, starting with the single "Barbie". The duo's hits included "Kvish HaHof", "Silsulim", "Zahav" and "Tudo Bom", and Russo has been described as the mastermind behind the duo's hits. In March 2018, the duo signed a ten-year deal with Capitol Records, brokered by Haim Saban, to produce English-language albums. Their English-language collaborations included "Further Up (Na, Na, Na, Na, Na)" with Pitbull, which reached the US Billboard Latin chart, and singles with the Black Eyed Peas, J Balvin and Snoop Dogg. Static and Ben El were also judges on the reality show HaKokhav HaBa and on the Israeli version of The Masked Singer. In August 2022, amid controversy over recordings of Tavori published by Israel Hayom, the duo announced that they had "reached the end of our musical project" and would pursue separate careers. Solo career (2023–present) In February 2023, Russo released his first solo album, Liraz, with 12 songs. He wrote it during a month-long creative retreat in Caesarea with Jordi and other Israeli producers and songwriters, and the album was accompanied by a documentary. He said the title reflected a side of himself that the public had not yet seen. Maariv reviewed the album on its release. His second solo album, Leharim, with 12 songs, followed on 9 April 2024. His later singles have included "Atalef", "Chik Chak", "Federer" and "Pokemon", a duet with Adi Biti. In January 2025, he staged a large-scale solo show at Expo Tel Aviv, and in late 2025 he released the mini-album Kaakuim. Personal life Russo became engaged to his longtime girlfriend, Sarit Polak, in 2019, and they married in 2021. The couple divorced in November 2022. He has said that the breakup of his marriage and of the duo affected him deeply, and that he stepped back for a time before returning to music. In a 2026 interview, Russo said that he does not perform or work on Shabbat, puts on tefillin, observes kashrut and recites blessings before eating. title: Okoia railway station
text: Okoia railway station was a railway station serving the rural locality of Okoia, near Whanganui, New Zealand, on the Marton–New Plymouth line. It opened on 17 May 1877, with goods traffic listed from 12 July 1878, and closed to all traffic on 1 August 1971. The Okoia–Turakina deviation ran south from Okoia along the Matarawa Valley, sharing the original alignment as far as the site of Matarawa station, south of which the two routes diverge. History Opening and early sidings (1877–1900) Authority for £700 for road filling to a siding at Okoia was sought in April 1878. In October 1881 Messrs Newberry & Millard wrote asking for a tramway crossing over the line and siding at the station, and a record of the same month says they would contribute £100 towards a siding. A siding was granted to them in 1882 and an agreement for a private siding was recorded in May of that year, and in March 1885 they were recorded as its present holders. A listing of July 1896 records a shelter shed, a passenger platform and two loops holding 14 and 9 wagons, and by September 1897 the larger loop held 18. In May 1900 it was reported that T. Higgie said the similarity of the names of the Okoia and Okehu railway stations caused much inconvenience, and suggested that Okoia be renamed after the road district, Kaukatea. He was asked to obtain a petition from Okoia residents for presentation to the Government. In September 1900 it was recorded that a public siding lay on one side of the line and a private siding serving a brickyard on the other, platform, side. Standing room in the loop was 18 wagons (14 with an engine and van), and an extension to hold about 35 was proposed. Records between 1878 and 1944 give the station's position by mileage, but the datum is not always stated and the figures differ. Facilities and local use (1900–1915) In July 1903 two local men, Buchanan and Neilson, put the case for better loading and unloading facilities to the district railway engineer during a visit to the station. It was reported that everything had to be carried across the main line and a side line, that Neilson had had several narrow escapes from passing trains while unloading, and that Buchanan's output over the previous three months, put at £1,800, had nearly all passed through the station. The correspondent added that cream from a public creamery and a large private one also had to be carried across both lines and loaded some distance from the station, and that the department was said to intend spending about £200 on alterations contemplated for two years. In August 1903 authority was recorded for £100 for improvements, including a cart approach and lengthening the crossing siding and goods shed loop. A listing of 1904 records a shelter shed, a passenger platform on the left side of the line, a cart approach, sheep yards and fixed signals, with loops holding 41 and 10 wagons. Okoia was also used as an excursion stop. A picnic at Waikupa in November 1905, on land lent by Tucker Brothers, was advertised with the train stopping at the station, about 300 yards from the grounds across a paddock whose owner had allowed access. A King's Birthday picnic organised by the T.Y.M.I. was held at the same grounds in November 1907, described as almost alongside the station, with a train leaving town at 9.35 am and tickets, including admission, at 2s for adults and 1s for children. In late 1907 the platform was recorded as about 100 feet (30 m) long, instructions were issued to raise the ground in line with it to rail level for that distance, and a porter's cottage is recorded. A lamp was requested in November 1908. In June 1910 representatives of the Kaukatea Road Board asked the Minister that the Railway Department contribute to maintaining a culvert at the station, made necessary when the department diverted creeks while building the line. The Minister instructed the engineer to have a concrete culvert built. In February 1911 the board resolved to ask the Railway Departmen

title: Benghazi attacks 2026
text: The Benghazi naval attacks were a series of military attacks targeting Russian ships near the Port of Benghazi in Libya during November 2026, attributed to Ukraine in the context of the Russo-Ukrainian War. The attacks involved the use of unmanned boats and resulted in damage to vessels belonging to Russia, including the warship Merkury. The incident attracted widespread international attention because it took place within Libyan waters and had political and security implications, in addition to concerns about the extension of the Russo-Ukrainian War into Libyan territory. Attack summary An explosion occurred in the early hours of 22 November 2026 inside the Benghazi Naval Base, targeting a Russian ship that was docked at the port. At the time, the Libyan government announced that the preliminary investigation results suggested that the ship had been attacked using unmanned vehicles. It also indicated that the ship had been停 at the port to refuel and take on provisions while returning to Russia, under the cooperation agreements and naval facilities arrangements between the two countries. Satellite images published by Vantor showed that the targeted ship was Merkury, a war cruiser belonging to the Russian Navy. The images showed most of the ship sinking, with its bow remaining visible above the water's surface, alongside rising smoke and debris near the pier. Medical sources reported that ten Russian and Libyan people had sustained minor injuries in the incident. The General Command of the Libyan Arab Armed Forces also announced the deaths of the two martyrs: 1. R.A.W. / Al-Taher Abdullah Al-Sadiq 2. Lieutenant / Ali Mohammed Al-Sayed Both were members of the General Staff of the Libyan Navy. They died on Tuesday, 24 November 2026, from wounds sustained during the attack at dawn on Sunday, 22 November 2026, and the subsequent explosions caused by the targeted ship. Other attacks A commercial ship flying the flag of Malta was attacked by an unmanned boat off the coast of Benghazi later on the same day. The Libyan Navy managed to rescue the ship's crew, while the Ministry of Health reported that several crew members had sustained minor injuries. Military sources also stated that the naval and air forces intercepted more than twenty unmanned boats off the city's coast during those events. Claim of responsibility On 23 November 2026, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced his country's responsibility for the attack, describing the operation as a "typical Ukrainian operation" in response to the Russo-Ukrainian War. He explained that Ukrainian forces had used seven Ukrainian-made naval drones, which managed to target and sink the Russian cruiser Merkury in the Port of Benghazi. They also targeted the Russian cargo ship MV Angara, which he said was being used to transport weapons. The Ukrainian presidency published video footage of the operation, showing the unmanned boats approaching the targeted ships and carrying out the attacks. The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) confirmed its participation in the operation in coordination with the Ukrainian Defense Forces, stating that the seven boats had been launched from a mothership at sea. It also announced the destruction of a Russian Ka-27 military helicopter that was aboard the cruiser. References

title: Intentions (Hikaru Utada song)
text: "Intentions" is a song recorded by Japanese-American singer-songwriter Hikaru Utada, released on November 25, 2026, via Epic Records Japan. Background and release In August 2026, the Central Japan Railway Company aired a new commercial marketing their "Supreme Class Cabin", which launched in October. Starring in the commercial was Hikaru Utada, depicting them enjoying a ride on a bullet train. An un-released song by Utada, "Intentions", served as the image song for the commercial. On November 1, Utada's staff announced "Intentions" would be released digitally on November 25, 2026. A 60-second version of "Intentions" was released to social media services Instagram, YouTube and TikTok later that day. Promotion Following two of Utada's songs, "Anata" and "Michi", gaining traction on TikTok, their staff held a live stream on the platform on October 21, 2026. The stream consisted of 60 minutes of tour footage from Utada's 2018 Laughter in the Dark Tour. Five different Sony stores in Ginza, Sapporo, Nagoya, Osaka, and Fukuoka held listening sessions of the full song. A pre-add campaign was held by Epic Japan through November 25. Participants that pre-added or pre-ordered "Intentions" were entered into a lottery, with 100 winners receiving a handkerchief. title: Bunny (Pakistani singer)
text: Mohsin Raza Khan (c. 1952 – 23 November 2026), professionally known by his stage name Bunny, was a Pakistani pop singer, composer, and recording studio owner. A prominent figure in Pakistan's pop music scene during the late 1980s and 1990s, he was best known for his signature baritone voice and his breakthrough hit "Dil Mein Tum". Early life and background Mohsin Raza Khan was born around 1952. During his childhood, his father nicknamed him "Bunny" due to his prominent front teeth and the popularity of the animated character Bugs Bunny—a moniker that stayed with him throughout his personal life and musical career. Musical career Early beginnings and European tour (1973–1988) Bunny began his musical career in Lahore in 1973, performing as part of a local band. Over the following decade, he performed at major hotels and toured across several European countries to showcase his music before returning to Pakistan to record and release his debut solo material. Breakthrough and 1990s stardom (1989–1999) In late 1989, Bunny gained national prominence with the release of his signature track "Dil Mein Tum", issued under EMI Pakistan. Featuring a prominent bassline, upbeat rhythm, and his distinctive baritone vocals, the song became a commercial success and made him a regular feature on Pakistani television pop programs, notably Music Channel Charts. Following his breakthrough, Bunny released subsequent albums including The Exciting Crooner (Bunny) (1992) and delivered several well-received singles that blended romantic pop melodies with bhangra rhythms. Notable songs from this era included "Deewane" (also cited as "Deewana"), "Raasta Naya", "Zakhmi Jigar", "Pehla Pyar", "Bhangra Is King", "Aa Bhi Ja", and "Nasheeli". Mentorship and later years (2000–2026) Beyond his own recordings, Bunny operated a recording studio near Tariq Road in Karachi that served as an informal creative hub for aspiring musicians. He mentored and supported emerging Pakistani artists—including members of the band Mizaan—by allowing them to rehearse and record at his studio free of charge. In 2011, his signature hit "Dil Mein Tum" experienced a resurgence among younger audiences when Lahore-based rock band Roxen and vocalist Mustafa Zahid collaborated on a rock rendition of the track. Although Bunny stepped back from releasing new commercial albums in his later decades, he remained an enduring figure in retrospectives on the 1990s era of Pakistani pop music. Personal life, illness, and death Bunny resided primarily in Karachi and had been diagnosed with tongue cancer roughly three decades prior to his death. In his later years, he lived quietly in Karachi with close support from his neighbors, while his son resided in London. On 23 November 2026, Bunny died at his residence in Karachi early in the morning before Fajr prayers at the age of 74. He was taken to Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre, where doctors pronounced him dead on arrival. His passing was confirmed to the press by his close friend Dr. Shafqat Ali and actor Khaled Anam, prompting tributes from across Pakistan's entertainment industry. title: Western Breakaway Movement
text: The Western Breakaway Movement was an autonomist movement that emerged in the Western District (today Western Province and Choiseul Province) of the British Solomon Islands Protectorate. The district was created in the early 20th century, laying a common administrative structure over the area, which subsequently developed a distinct regional identity. When the protectorate was being moved towards independence, Western concerns about their position within an independent Solomon Islands led to a movement for local autonomy. While this movement had no single leader, the Western Council provided a focal point for its activities. The council called for the district to be given constitutionally guaranteed "state government", possibly within a wider federal system. This was unsuccessful, and the movement quietened after independence. However, a desire for more autonomy remained, being most prominently revived during the tensions at the turn of the century. Federalism remains subject to ongoing political discussion within Solomon Islands to this day. The Southwest Pacific Ocean became an area of colonial competition in the late 19th century. What is now Solomon Islands was subject to influence from both Germany and the United Kingdom, which negotiated their respective spheres of influence. The eventual border divided what became Western District from nearby Bougainville, to which the islands that became the Western District were connected through trade and familial links. While British administration of the district remained weak, existing connections were deepened due to shared missionary activities, which brought with them both religious commonality and shared lingua franca. Cultural, economic, ethnic, and religious differences with other islands in the protectorate, especially with people from Malaita, were brought into view following internal migration into Western District, reinforcing a growing regional identity. In the 1970s the United Kingdom suddenly shifted from viewing Solomon independence as unviable to actively seeking the protectorate's independence. Western District was the most economically developed part of the protectorate. However, Westerners made up only a fifth of the total population, leaving Western politicians concerned about a loss of local control following independence. While some individuals advocated for complete independence, along the lines of Tuvalu, the Western Council came to a collective position advocating for provincial autonomy to be enshrined in the constitution. This campaign was influenced by events in and individuals from Bougainville, which at the time had its own secessionist movement, although the Western movement remained within the confines of politics. The movement also gained some external support, such as from Guadalcanal, whose leaders had similar concerns about internal migration. The central government was able to avoid giving extensive concessions to the Western movement, and sought to assuage concerns by changes to funding formulas and bringing Westerners into the central government. Western politicians boycotted independence celebrations in 1978, although relations improved in later years. While the movement largely ended after independence, devolution remained a political topic that prime ministers had to engage with. The issue regained prominence at the turn of the century, when the tensions led to a loss of central government control over security and an accompanying economic crisis. Many provinces took unilateral steps towards autonomy, and leaders from Western Province and Choiseul Province declared an intention to form a joint state. The end of the crisis brought with it a national agreement to move towards a federal system. However, resulting draft constitutional changes underwent a series of revisions and none have been implemented, although they have remained a regular topic of political discussion. title: Vicente Victoria
text: Vicente Victoria Gastaldo, also known as Vittoria (13 August 1650 – 22 May 1709), was a Spanish priest, painter, printmaker, art collector and scholar. While in Rome, he came into contact with Carlo Maratta, under whom he completed his artistic training. He wrote treatises on painting, amassed a collection of prints and drawings, and worked in fresco and oil, producing portraits and trompe-l'œil paintings. He also practised etching, creating original compositions as well as reproductions of works by Raphael and Maratta. Biography The son of an Italian merchant and of a Spanish woman, Victoria studied grammar, philosophy, and theology at the University of Valencia, where he began his artistic training. In 1679, he moved to Rome to pursue an ecclesiastical career. Through his religious connections, he was able to obtain the financial support of Cosimo III de' Medici and went to Rome to study painting under Carlo Maratta. According to Antonio Palomino, who knew Victoria personally, he devoted himself intensely to portrait painting, demonstrating a keen understanding of symmetry and anatomy. After being appointed a canon in Xàtiva, Victoria returned to Valencia in 1688. He collaborated with Palomino on a fresco for the dome of the Chapel of St. Peter in Valencia Cathedral; Vitoria is considered one of those who brought Palomino to Valencia. Records also indicate his involvement in fresco decorations for other churches and convents in the region of Valencia, though all of these works have since been lost. During his ten years in the Kingdom of Valencia, Victoria wrote his main work, Academia de Pintura del Señor Carlos Maratti (composed 1688–1694), whose original manuscript is held in the Corsini Library in Rome (MS 660). The work is an adaptation of Vasari's Vite in dialogue form that was intended to be supplemented with contributions regarding seventeenth-century artists. The most interesting part of the manuscript, which deals with the life of Joan de Joanes, has been published in modern times. Around 1698, Victoria returned to Rome and became a member of the Academy of Arcadia. According to Palomino, who claimed to have seen the official documentation, Victoria was appointed court painter to the Grand Duke of Tuscany and antiquarian to the Pope in recognition of his scholarly pursuits. A devoted admirer of Raphael, Victoria assembled a collection of around 600 prints reproducing the artist's work. Based on this collection, he compiled the first catalogue raisonné of Raphael prints produced in Europe, the Indice dell'opere di Raffaello Sanzio d'Urbino (Rome, 1703), an autograph manuscript of 314 pages, known from two identical copies in the Royal Library at Windsor and the Kunsthistorisches Institut in Florence, and dedicated to Pope Clement XI. He also amassed a notable collection of drawings. One volume of copies after antique paintings, mostly by Pietro Santi Bartoli, is now at Windsor Castle; a volume of landscape drawings by Giovan Francesco Grimaldi is in the British Museum, and a third album, with copies of his small antique sculptures and objects, was acquired by the Getty Museum. The other albums were dismembered in the 18th century by their next owner, the banker Pierre Crozat. In the last years of his life, Victoria devoted himself to scholarship and earned distinction as an art theorist and a staunch supporter of classicism. He died in Rome on 22 May 1709. In 1923, the art historian Elías Tormo dismissed Vitoria as «desmayadísimo italianizante» ("a most faint-hearted Italianiser") and «demasiado famoso" ("too famous"), a judgement that Bassegoda says damaged his historiographical reputation. Work In his biography of Victoria, Antonio Palomino describes some trompe l'œil paintings that he saw in his studio, noting that he initially mistook them for real objects. He describes a canvas on which various papers, drawings and other trinkets appeared to hang. He admits that it fooled him. The same was true of a painted sect

title: Halstead (house)
text: Halstead is a heritage-listed villa with former stables and garden, located at 23 Bambra Road in Caulfield North, in the City of Glen Eira, in the inner eastern suburbs of Melbourne, in Victoria, Australia. The villa was built from 1857 and is believed to be the oldest extant suburban farm villa in the Caulfield area. Built on the traditional lands of the Bunurong people, the villa was added to the Victorian Heritage Register on 29 August 1979 in recognition of its architectural significance; and was also added to non-statutory lists by the Victorian branch of the National Trust on 19 July 1973 and the now defunct Register of the National Estate on 14 May 1991. History During the 1850s the discovery of gold brought great wealth to Melbourne, and Caulfield became a wealthy locality on the periphery of an expanding Melbourne; and Caulfield North became a desirable residential location. A number of large villas and mansions were built on substantial acreages by Melbourne's gentry until the financial crash of the 1890s. In addition to Halstead, other surviving examples include Rosecraddock (c. 1857), Nithsdale (1858), Kynaston (1889), Rosemont (1868), Clarence Lodge, as well as ornate boom era examples such as Labassa (1873–1890) and Myoora (1887). The villa was built on the outskirts of Melbourne, then a ten-kilometre (six-mile) journey by horse. Villas and mansions were often developed with towers, like the substantial three-storey structure at Halstead, which symbolised the owners’ wealth and status. Stables were necessary because of the reliance on horse travel, and gardens afforded privacy and shade within a larger acreage cleared for agriculture and grazing. Halstead, a detached villa with stables and garden, was built in c. 1857 by wealthy pastoralist, Dr James Dickson, who had extensive pastoral interests in South Australia and the Riverina. James Dickson lived at Halstead until his death in 1880 when his son George became the owner. George also owned Uabba and Maahope Stations in the Lachlan district of New South Wales and Uranaway Station in South Australia. In 1885, James' widow, Ellen, was listed in the rate book as the owner of Halstead. She died there in 1893. By the late 1890s, George Dickson was again named as the owner in the rate books, the house having a series of tenants in that and the next decade. In 1910 further subdivisions of Halstead were advertised for sale. The blocks comprised 54 ‘fine villa sites’ and ‘the recently renovated Halstead residence’. In 1911 Mr and Mrs SJ Plain purchased the residential block, which had been reduced to 0.23 hectares (0.57 acres), and they converted the former servants' quarters/services wing to a billiards rooms, attached to the house. After the death of Mr and Mrs Plain, the property passed to their daughter Mrs Ercil White. In 1977 after her death, it was sold to three development companies: Resco Nominees, Pty Ltd, Kathandra Pty Ltd, Camarda Pty Ltd. The occupying tenant was architect Vladmir Chernov. Set on 2,760 square metres (29,700 sq ft), the property with swimming pool, tennis courts, and the former stables that were converted into a one-bedroom self-contained unit, was listed for sale in 2019. The new owners extensively renovated the house. Description In 1858 the Halstead Estate comprised a brick residence on 6 hectares (14 acres). The house had six rooms with kitchen, servants’ rooms, stables and outbuildings. By the early 1890s, Halstead had been subdivided and the house block comprised one hectare (two acres) and a nine-roomed residence. A plan by the Melbourne & Metropolitan Board of Works of 1905 showed Halstead with its long verandah facing Bambra Road. At the time, there was a large front garden area, a building variously described in the 1970s as either servants' quarters or a services wing, and rear stables. title: Rapaport Group
text: Rapaport Group is a company that provides diamond pricing information, trading services, auctions and market analysis. It publishes the Rapaport Diamond Report, a diamond industry standard for pricing of diamonds. Overview Rapaport Group was founded in New York in 1976 by diamond dealer Martin Rapaport. In 1978, it began publishing the Rapaport Diamond Report, also known as the Rapaport Price List, which provides reference asking prices for polished diamonds based on carat weight, color and clarity. Diamond dealers use the list as a pricing benchmark. Changes to the Rapaport Price List have occasionally drawn criticism from diamond dealers. In 1996, Rapaport Group launched the Internet Diamond Exchange (INDEX), an online diamond trading platform later known as RapNet. The platform expanded to include jewelry in 2019 and colored gemstones in 2025. In 2026, RapNet was renamed Rapaport Trade. The group introduced diamond auctions through its service Rapaport Auctions in 2007. In 2017, it handled the sale of Sierra Leone's 709-carat Peace Diamond. In 2023, Rapaport Auctions began conducting natural pearl auctions in partnership with the Bahrain Institute of Pearls and Gemstones (DANAT). The company banned diamonds originating from Zimbabwe's Marange diamond fields from its trading platform in 2009 due to reports of human rights abuses. In May 2022, following sanctions imposed over Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the platform banned diamonds sourced from Russia. The company publishes diamond and jewelry industry news through Rapaport News and Rapaport Magazine. It also publishes market research through the monthly Rapaport Intelligence Report. References

title: Roland Castonguay
text: Roland Castonguay (15 January 1913 – 28 April 1989) was a Canadian soccer forward. He was notably a 1934 Dominion of Canada Football Championship winner with Verdun Park FC and then a 1940 National Soccer League winner with Montréal Carsteel FC. He was posthumously honoured by the Canada Soccer Hall of Fame in 2013. He started his senior career with Montréal CPR in 1932 in the Montréal League, then joined Verdun Park FC in the National League the following year. In 1934, he helped Verdun Park FC beat the Prince Albert City Reds in a best-of-three series to win the Dominion of Canada Football Championship for the Challenge Trophy. Verdun Park FC folded before the 1935 season, so Castonguay then signed with Montréal Aldred FC, but then just a few weeks later he joined Montréal CNR. He joined Montréal Notre Dame in 1936 and then Montréal Wanderers in 1937, then found his way to Montréal Carsteel FC. With Carsteel FC, Roland was joined by his younger brother Paul-Émile in 1938, then another younger brother Marcel in 1939. The Castonguay trio helped Carsteel win the National Soccer League Québec Section and also reach the 1939 Dominion of Canada Football Championship. Carsteel lost the Canadian Final to the Vancouver Radials. In 1940, Castonguay helped Carsteel FC win the National Soccer League Championship for the Lord Atholstan Trophy. He was posthumously honoured by the Québec Sports Hall of Fame alongside his brothers Paul-Émile and Marcel in 2011. The three brothers were honoured by the Canada Soccer Hall of Fame two years later in 2013. In 2026, Québec City named Parc des Frères-Castonguay, in Beauport, in honour of the three brothers.

title: Melissa Núñez
text: Melissa Núñez is a Dominican model and beauty pageant titleholder who won Miss Dominican Republic 2026. She represented the Dominican Republic at Miss Universe 2026, where she finished as first runner-up. Early life and education Núñez was born in La Vega, Dominican Republic. She studied in the United States, where she earned a degree in Medical Sciences and Psychology from The City College of New York. She also studied medicine in the Dominican Republic before continuing her education in the United States. Career Núñez has worked as an international model and has been associated with fashion brands and beauty campaigns. Her modeling work has included collaborations with fashion houses such as Moschino, Michael Kors and Alberta Ferretti, as well as beauty brands including Maybelline, NARS and L'Oréal. She has also worked in the mental health field in New York, including professional experience involving patients with substance-use disorders. In addition, she has participated in initiatives with Dress for Success, an organization supporting women's professional development and employment opportunities. Pageantry Núñez competed in Miss República Dominicana Universo 2024, representing the Dominican Community in the United States. She finished as the first runner-up to winner Celinee Santos. On 30 July 2026, Núñez was crowned Miss República Dominicana Universo 2026 at the Eduardo Brito National Theater in Santo Domingo. She represented Concepción de La Vega and succeeded Jennifer Ventura. The first runner-up was Valentina Campión, representing Samaná, while Floralba Caba of Monseñor Nouel finished as second runner-up. Following her victory, Núñez represented the Dominican Republic at Miss Universe 2026, where she finished as first runner-up. References

title: Marcel Castonguay
text: Marcel Castonguay (1919 – 15 September 1969) was a Canadian soccer forward. He was notably a 1948 Dominion of Canada Football Championship and National Soccer League winner with Montréal Carsteel FC. He was posthumously honoured by the Canada Soccer Hall of Fame in 2013. He was the third Castonguay brother to star in the Montréal Leagues in the 1930s and 1940s. After playing for Rosemount Athletics and then Royal Victoria Hospital, he joined Carsteel FC in July 1939 where he played alongside his brothers Roland and Paul-Émile. The trio helped Carsteel win the National Soccer League Québec Section and also reach the 1939 Dominion of Canada Football Championship. Carsteel lost the Canadian Final to the Vancouver Radials. From 1941 to 1947, the young Castonguay played for Montréal Wings / Canadian Vickers United, Canadair Falcons FC, (briefly) Carsteel FC, (briefly) Hungária SC, and (once again) Canadair Falcons FC. In 1948, Marcel rejoined Carsteel FC where he won the Dominion of Canada Football Championship, the National Soccer League Québec, and the National Soccer League Championship for the Atholstan Trophy. He scored the winning goal in the last match of the Dominion of Canada Football Championship. He was posthumously honoured by the Québec Sports Hall of Fame alongside his brothers Roland and Paul-Émile in 2011. The three brothers were honoured by the Canada Soccer Hall of Fame two years later in 2013. In 2026, Québec City named Parc des Frères-Castonguay, in Beauport, in honour of the three brothers.

title: Mississippi Half-Step Uptown Toodeloo
text: "Mississippi Half-Step Uptown Toodeloo" is a song by the American rock band the Grateful Dead, released as the opening track on the band's sixth studio album Wake of the Flood (1973). Overview Echoing both the title and music of Duke Ellington's "East St. Louis Toodle-Oo", "Mississippi Half-Step Uptown Toodeloo" includes very distinct sections, which mention a nameless adventurer going on a journey, with lyrics from lyricist Robert Hunter that, according to Benjy Eisen of Rolling Stone, are of "philosophical advice, personal liberty, card games, hard liquor, and come-hell-or-high-water determination". Jerry Garcia reportedly saw issue with Hunter using the word "styrofoam" in the song's lyrics, as he feared it would date back to "post-war America". According to Hunter, Garcia told him "This is so uncharacteristic of your work, to put something as time-dated as the word "Styrofoam" into it." Its lyrics tell of a cheating gambler who is always on the run. Although there exist 16 marked takes, only five of them are complete, according to the Good Ol' Grateful Deadcast, an official podcast which discusses the Grateful Dead. Release and reception In a retrospective review of Wake of the Flood, Ultimate Classic Rock critic Nick DeRiso believes it "incorporates the band's penchant for old-timey jug-band sounds". Blair Jackson called it a "playful country-flavored song that felt like an old-time fiddle tune with a dash of early jazz throw in". In a ranking of band's 20 best songs, Paste magazine critic Matt Mitchell placed it a number 17 and called it a "hell of a hoppin' romp", noting its arrangement "takes a turn towards an old rag-time jaunt packed with nautical absurdity." Live performance history "Mississippi Half-Step Uptown Toodeloo" was first performed live on July 16, 1972. A video recording of the band's performance on June 28, 1991, at Denver's Mile High Stadium was uploaded to the band's YouTube channel on January 25, 2024. A May 7, 1977 performance at the Boston Garden was highlighted by Pitchfork in that "Garcia's voice is sweet and strong", noting that "Keith Godchaux brings the Dixieland piano [while] Bob Weir expertly places his rhythm arpeggios snugly alongside Garcia’s crisp and clear leads [as t]he drummers press hard as Garcia fans power chords in the lead-up to the song’s refrain".
