title: Peace.Love.Rindu
text: Peace.Love.Rindu is the tenth studio album by Malaysian singer, Ella, released on 21 September 2017 by Universal Music Malaysia and EMI Music Malaysia. It is her first studio album in 10 years since Rama-Rama (2007), marking the longest gap between studio albums in her career. The album is also her first studio album with Universal Music after previously having been signed to EMI, and the first album to be produced by M. Nasir since Ella USA from 1994. Production After the release of her tenth and last studio album with EMI Music Malaysia, Rama-Rama, in 2007, Ella decided to take a long break from recorded and released any studio albums. During that period, she came up with more compilation albums. However, Ella announced in February 2017 that she will be releasing her tenth album as early as September. The album was then announced as being titled Peace.Love.Rindu, and according to Ella, it carries a deeper meaning for herself. She said of the album's title: "Peace means peace that must always be maintained, love for the fans who never stop supporting and rindu (longing) because I have been harboring feelings to produce a song after so long". For the album, she decided to stick with modern pop ballads, rock ballads and rock & roll influences while retained pop rock sounds. The album's recording session began in 2015 and took two years to completed. Of all 158 songs in her catalogue, only eight of them make the final cut as she believes that these songs "are the best for inclusion on the album", and reflected that not all songs in the album received radio airplay. She said: "In terms of the production process alone, it took us two years because we wanted to find a song that not only suited my abilities and current tastes, but also had to be in line with the latest image,". Ella had recorded a song, also bearing the album's title and composed by her longtime collaborator Lokman "Lord" Idris, which specially dedicated to her husband, Azhar Ghazali, whom she married in 2012. She said the song's composer, Lord, wanted the concepts of "humanity, peace, love and pray". On the album, Ella provided vocals and was accompanied several professional musicians including Hanafi Hamdan and Jamie Wilson on guitars, Kelly on bass, and Ujang on drums as well as Mu'azam Shah on keyboards. Backing vocals were provided by Izzad Izzudin, Baby Akma, Nurdianah Shamsuddin and Zuliana Eusoff. Songwriting was handled by M. Nasir, who composed three songs, and Lord composed two songs. Ella stated that the album's songwriting process was very different from her previous albums. Release and reception Prior to the album's release two years later, "Istimewah" was released as a standalone single on 30 April 2015. To promote the single, its music video was produced and filmed in London, England. The album was released on 21 September 2017 to commemorate the World Peace Day and was well received. It yielded two singles: the title track and "Ku Sedia". The music video for "Ku Sedia" was filmed at Jogjakarta, Indonesia. Ella followed the release of Peace.Love.Rindu with a concert tour involving seven locations in Malaysia including SACC Mall in Shah Alam, Selangor, and Kuching Waterfront in Kuching, Sarawak from 27 October to 4 November 2017. title: Lukkus-kaxa
text: The lukkus-kaxa (also known as lukus qaxa, literal meaning: "shell-bead garment") is a distinctive element of Atayal attire. In the Atayal language, the term signifies a "precious garment" or "golden garment." Historically, the right to wear such a long garment was reserved exclusively for headhunting warriors, chieftains, tribal leaders, and the women skilled enough to weave them. Within traditional Atayal culture, the shell-bead garment serves not only as a symbol of high social status but also functions as a medium of exchange, a bridal gift, and a form of restitution to settle conflicts—embodying profound social and cultural significance. The weaving culture of the Atayal people in Taiwan suffered a severe blow following Japanese colonial rule. Japanese anthropologists observed that when Atayal women wove together for their respective families, it fostered cohesion within the kinship group and strengthened its collective power. Consequently, the Japanese colonial government sought to suppress this practice, discouraging the people from weaving by claiming that "those who only weave instead of working are lazy". This fundamentally altered the lifestyle of Atayal women. The Japanese authorities even sent the most skilled weavers from the tribes to sericulture facilities for training, or instructed them in the use of hand-operated looms, effectively compelling them to abandon their traditional weaving tools. Appearance and Characteristics These garments are crafted by attaching white shell beads—made from Tridacninae (also known as giant clam shells)—onto a base of woven hemp fabric, with the beads arranged in aligned rows. In terms of construction, the traditional long shell-bead garment is a collarless, sleeveless, open-front coat with symmetrical front panels, no buttons, and seams at the underarms. The hemp fabric is adorned with strings of shell beads and woven with brown hemp threads, as well as blue and red wool yarns. A single long garment requires tens of thousands of shell beads (sometimes as many as 120,000) typically weighing around three to four kilograms, though the heaviest examples can reach six to seven kilograms. Although these items take the form of clothing, their substantial weight means they are rarely worn as everyday attire; instead, they primarily serve functions related to currency, trade, and bridewealth. The craft of creating these shell-bead garments is known as "shell-bead weaving". In addition to the traditional long coat, shell-bead attire also encompasses items such as caps, skirts, chest coverings, leg wraps, necklaces, wristbands, and leg ornaments. References

title: Glenfern (house)
text: Glenfern is a house located at 417 Inkerman Road, at the corner of Hotham Street, in St Kilda East, in the City of Glen Eira, in the inner eastern suburbs of Melbourne, in Victoria, Australia. Glenfern was built on spacious grounds in two main stages in 1857 and 1876. From 1876 to 1984 Glenfern had only two owners, including the Boyd family, a well-known Australian family of artists. The property was bequeathed to the Victorian branch of the National Trust in 1984, and they have retained ownership. Built on the traditional lands of the Bunurong people, the house was added to the Victorian Heritage Register on 9 October 1974 in recognition of its historical and architectural significance; and was also added to non-statutory lists by the Victorian branch of the National Trust on an unknown date and the now defunct Register of the National Estate on 21 March 1978. History The original Glenfern allotment was bought by John Bakewell in 1856 and sold the following year to Francis McDonnell, a prominent Melbourne investor. By 1858, the house, originally intended to be situated in East Melbourne, rated as the most valuable in Caulfield, had been built on the site. Due to financial difficulties, McDonnell offered a number of properties for sale in 1860, including Glenfern. It was not sold at this stage, but subsequently mortgaged in 1862. In 1866 Thomas Watson purchased the property and lived there until 1876 when it was sold to Captain John Theodore Thomas Boyd and his wife, Lucy, founders of the Boyd dynasty of artists, musicians, writers and architects. The Boyd family, including twelve children, lived there until 1907, with Lucy Boyd retaining ownership after her husband's death in 1891. In 1907 the property was subdivided and the greatly reduced Glenfern portion was purchased by the Ostberg family, who lived there from 1915. In the latter years of Boyd family ownership and the Ostberg ownership, Glenfern had several tenants and was run as a school on two occasions. The Ostberg family occupancy continued until the death of Miss Amy Ostberg in 1984. From 1929 the property was listed as Glenfern Flats, necessitating various internal alterations over a period of time. Ownership of Glenfern passed to the National Trust of Australia (Victoria) in 1984 and in 2002 transformation of the property into a Centre for the Arts and Culture commenced. This began with the establishment of an Artist-in-residence program, followed by the Glenfern Writers Centre, run jointly with Writers Victoria. Restoration and renovation of the building was completed in 2006, funded by Arts Victoria and the Pratt Foundation, and Glenfern accommodated writers until 2022, when the Trust took over sole management of the property for their own use. Description Designed by Charles Laing in 1857, and extended according to plans by M. Hennessy in 1876, Glenfern is a two-storey and an unusually intact and rare example of a picturesque domestic Gothic Revival house. Built of stuccoed brick with steep, gabled slate roofs, elaborate bargeboards, and chimneys of conjoined stacks set diagonally, the original, asymmetrically planned L-shaped house, containing the principal rooms and a rear wing, was designed with two main facades facing north and west. The north facade contains an unusual recessed pointed arch bay formed between twin chimney flues. Internally cedar joinery includes an unusual set of double doors between the drawing room and parlour, the centre pair of which fold back and then slide into the walls. The 1876 extensions, during the Boyd family's ownership, comprised the addition of a two-storey wing to the south of the existing house, and the bargeboards, chimneys, and western verandah copied the style of the original house. The stables were built in 1884 by the architects Smith and Johnson and other outbuildings, since removed, were recorded on the site. title: 2028 United States House of Representatives elections in Alabama
text: The 2028 United States House of Representatives elections in Alabama will be held on November 7, 2028, to elect the seven U.S. representatives from the state of Alabama, one from each of the state's congressional districts. The elections will coincide with other elections to the House of Representatives, the presidential election, elections to the United States Senate, and various state and local elections. District 1 The 1st district encompasses the southwestern part of the state near the Gulf of Mexico, including all of Baldwin, Mobile, Escambia, and Covington counties. title: Live from The Great Divide
text: Live from The Great Divide is the second live album by American singer-songwriter Noah Kahan, following 2024's Live from Fenway Park. It documents the live tour supporting his fourth studio album, The Great Divide (April 2026), which served as the follow-up to his commercial breakthrough Stick Season (2022) and debuted at number one on the US Billboard 200. Background Whereas Stick Season centered largely on Kahan's upbringing and nostalgia for New England, The Great Divide expanded into his diagnosis of obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD), intrusive thoughts, impostor syndrome, and the strain placed on his relationships with family and friends following his rise to fame. To support the album, Kahan embarked on The Great Divide World Tour in 2026, selling out stadium dates across North America alongside arena shows in Europe, the United Kingdom, Australia, and New Zealand. The 16 tracks on Live from The Great Divide were recorded across 16 different North American stadium stops during the summer 2026 leg, preceded by the live single and video for "Orbiter", filmed at Citi Field in New York City. Release The album was announced on November 24, 2026, alongside the release of "Orbiter" recorded live from Metlife Stadium. It will be released on December 11, 2026. Track listing References

title: Fazemos
text: Fazemos (trans. We Do) is a Portuguese political party project promoted by Isaltino Morais, the mayor of Oeiras, announced in November 2026. The project seeks to establish a political force positioned in the centre of the Portuguese political spectrum, between the Socialist Party (PS) and the Social Democratic Party (PSD), with a proposed ideological orientation based on modern social democracy, reformism and regionalism. The initiative was publicly announced by Morais in November 2026, following contacts with individuals associated with different political parties. The name Fazemos, meaning "We Do" in Portuguese, was subsequently associated with the project. Its public presentation was scheduled for 28 November 2026 at the Faculty of Law of the University of Lisbon. As of November 2026, the organisation had not been registered as a political party with the Constitutional Court of Portugal, and its complete political programme, internal structure and leadership had not yet been made public. History Origins and announcement The initiative emerged during the autumn of 2026, following discussions about the creation of a new moderate political force in Portugal. On 6 November 2026, Isaltino Morais, who had been elected mayor of Oeiras with the support of his independent movement, Isaltino Inovar Oeiras, acknowledged that he had been approached by individuals associated with the PS, PSD and the Democratic and Social Centre – People's Party (CDS-PP) regarding the establishment of a new political party. Morais argued that the Portuguese political system lacked an adequate political alternative for moderate voters, particularly those dissatisfied with the established parties. He described the proposed organisation as pragmatic, reformist and social-democratic, and expressed support for regionalisation. On 13 November, Morais confirmed his intention to proceed with the creation of the new party in an interview with Expresso. He described the initiative as an irreversible project and indicated that it would seek to occupy political space between the PS and PSD. Although he initially did not formally confirm the name Fazemos, he referred to the expression as an appropriate description of the project's political purpose. The proposed name was subsequently reported by several Portuguese news organisations. On 17 November, the publication idealista/news reported that the organisation would use the name Fazemos and that a visual identity featuring the letter F and an olive branch was being considered. On 23 November, Morais announced the public presentation of Fazemos for 28 November at the Faculty of Law of the University of Lisbon. The invitation described the initiative as the creation of a new political project by Morais and a wider group of participants, under the slogan Há momentos em que não basta querer mudar, é preciso fazer ("There are moments when wanting change is not enough, it is necessary to act"). Proposed political positioning Fazemos is intended to occupy the political centre, between the Socialist Party and the Social Democratic Party. Morais has described its proposed political orientation as a form of modern social democracy, combining state intervention in certain areas of public policy with the role of private enterprise and economic initiative. The project has also been described as reformist and regionalist. Morais argued that a new political organisation should promote cooperation between the main political parties, particularly the PS and PSD, in order to develop long-term policies that would survive changes of government. According to Morais, the initiative is particularly intended to appeal to moderate voters who consider themselves insufficiently represented by existing political parties. He has also identified younger generations as an intended audience for the new organisation. Political positions As of 25 November 2026, the organisation's complete political programme had not been published. Its publicly repor

title: Maria Dońska
text: Maria Ludwika Dońska (3 September 1912 – 20 December 1996), known in Britain as Maria Donska, was a Polish-born British pianist and piano teacher. She studied in Berlin with Artur Schnabel and received a diploma of honour at the II International Chopin Piano Competition in Warsaw in 1932. After settling in London in 1934 to escape antisemitism in Germany, she became a British citizen, played in the wartime lunchtime concerts at the National Gallery, and taught at the Royal College of Music from 1943 to 1946 and again from 1960 to 1980. She was best known as an interpreter of Beethoven and gave two complete cycles of his piano sonatas. Early life and training Donska was born in 1912 in Łódź, then part of Congress Poland in the Russian Empire, to an Ashkenazi Jewish family as the daughter of a philologist and engineer. She began to play the piano at the age of four and was described as a child prodigy. The family moved to Gdańsk, where her father arranged a shipbuilding contract, and she performed her first concert there at age seven. She made her debut with an orchestra at the age of eleven, in 1923. In 1926, she went to Berlin to study with Schnabel, and there she met a fellow pupil, Leonora ("Baba") Speyer, the daughter of the violinist Leonora Speyer. In 1929, Schnabel took her to London, where Samuel Courtauld had invited him to give a series of Mozart and Schubert recitals. She continued to study with Schnabel until 1933, and during those years she made her Berlin debut with Carl Maria von Weber's Konzertstück in F minor. In March 1932, she entered the second edition of the International Chopin Piano Competition in Warsaw and was awarded a diploma of honour. She then spent a short period in Poland working for Polskie Radio, and The Times linked her return from Germany in 1933 to Hitler's rise to power and growing antisemitism in the country. Career in Britain Studies and the war years In 1934, Donska travelled to London, where she settled and successfully applied for British citizenship. The BBC, learning of her experience in radio, asked her to make recordings, and she lived in St John's Wood with Speyer. She entered the Royal College of Music in 1936 and studied with Arthur Alexander. There she won the Hopkinson Gold Medal in 1936, the Chappell Gold Medal, the college's highest award, in 1937, and the Clement Exhibition in 1938. Binns considered the choice of teacher unusual, because Alexander was a pupil of Tobias Matthay, and Matthay's pupils regarded Schnabel's own teacher, Theodor Leschetizky, with some suspicion. During the Second World War, Donska toured for the Council for the Encouragement of Music and the Arts and played Brahms's second piano concerto on tour. A severe breakdown, worsened by anxiety over her family in occupied Poland, kept her from public performance for a time. In 1943, she returned to the BBC, played at the National Gallery concerts organised by Myra Hess and at Wigmore Hall, and began teaching at the Royal College of Music, where she stayed until 1946. A thesis on the reception of women pianists in London lists her among the pianists who appeared at the Gallery between 1939 and 1946. Postwar career From 1948, Donska took part in the Bryanston Summer School each year, and she continued when it moved to Darlington in 1951 and throughout the 1950s. In 1955, she gave recitals of the complete Beethoven sonatas at the Royal Festival Hall. Binns writes that she presented two complete cycles of the 32 sonatas in the 1950s and 1960s, at the South Bank and at Wigmore Hall. She also played Brahms's second concerto at The Proms, worked in partnership with the pianist Alan Rowlands, and appeared in recitals broadcast live and recorded by the BBC. In 1960, Donska returned to the Royal College of Music as a teacher and remained there until 1980. Her students included Malcolm Binns, who later recalled that she made him justify his interpretive choices, and British tenor Ian Partridge, who recalled her exhort

title: Jack Campbell (offensive lineman)
text: John "Jack" Carter Campbell (born December 16, 1958) is an American former professional football player who was an offensive tackle for the Seattle Seahawks of the National Football League (NFL). He played college football for the USC Trojans and Utah Utes. Early life Campbell was born on December 16, 1958, in Los Angeles, California. He attended West High School in Torrance, California. As a senior, Campbell earned all-state honors. College career Campbell played college football for the USC Trojans from 1977 to 1978 and Utah Utes from 1979 to 1981. After he redshirted his freshman year, he lettered in 1978 and earned a national championship. Campbell then transferred to the University of Utah and sat out the 1979 season. In 1980, he earned second-team All-WAC honors in his first year at Utah. As a senior, Campbell was named to the first-team All-WAC team. Professional career Seattle Seahawks Campbell was selected in the sixth round, with the 144th overall selection, by the Seattle Seahawks in the 1982 NFL draft. He played in one game his rookie season after he battled with an ankle injury and the flu. On August 29, 1983, Campbell was waived by the team. Los Angeles Express On January 14, 19894, Campbell signed with the Los Angeles Express of the United States Football League (USFL). On February 14, he was released. BC Lions On March 11, 1987, Campbell was signed by the BC Lions of the Canadian Football League (CFL). On June 17, he was released. Calgary Stampeders On June 21, 1987, the Calgary Stampeders signed Campbell to the practice roster. On July 1, he was elevated to the active roster. Campbell played in one game before he was released on July 13. References

title: Ranjit Singh of Bagli
text: Ranjit Singh (23 July 1882 – 1923) was Thakur of Bagli from 9 January 1896 until his death in 1923. Early life, family, and education Singh was born on 23 July 1882 to Raghunath Singh and received his education at Daly College in Indore. He claimed descent from Gokul Das and was a Rathore. Reign Following his father's death on 9 January 1896, he succeeded him as Thakur of Bagli. As he was then only thirteen years old and therefore a minor, the administration of Baagli was entrusted to a superintendent, who acted under the general supervision of the First Assistant to the Agent to the Governor-General in Central India. He was formally installed on the throne in 1897 by L. S. Newmarch. Upon attaining his majority, he was invested with administrative powers in June 1908. From that time onwards, he himself oversaw the affairs of his estate. During World War I, he contributed 1,500 rupees to the Gwalior Imperial Indian Relief Fund. On 30 January 1915, he contributed 4,000 rupees for providing comforts to Indian troops serving at the front. On 3 April 1915, he contributed 1,000 rupees to provide sweets to Indian troops serving at the front. Death Singh died in 1923, upon which his stepbrother, Sajjan Singh, succeeded to his title, rank and dignity. Honours During his lifetime, Singh served as an honorary aide-de-camp to Madho Rao Scindia, the Maharaja of Gwalior, and held the honorary rank of captain in the 1st Maharani Sakhya Raja's Own Gwalior Infantry. He also attended the Delhi Durbar of 1911 with Madho Rao Scindia. References

title: Guilherme Almor de Alpoim Calvão
text: Guilherme Almor de Alpoim Calvão (6 January 1937 – 30 September 2014) was a Portuguese naval officer who served in the Portuguese Navy during the Portuguese Colonial War. He became particularly associated with the Portuguese military campaign in Portuguese Guinea, where he commanded the Special Marines Detachment No. 8 and participated in several major operations. He is best known for planning and commanding Operation Green Sea (Operação Mar Verde), the Portuguese amphibious raid on Conakry, the capital of the Republic of Guinea, on 22 November 1970. Following the Carnation Revolution of April 1974, Calvão became involved in the political and military opposition to the revolutionary process. He participated in the failed 11 March 1975 coup attempt and subsequently became one of the principal operational figures of the clandestine Movement for the Democratic Liberation of Portugal (MDLP), an organisation associated with General António de Spínola. In a 1994 interview, he acknowledged responsibility for ordering bomb attacks carried out in the name of the organisation before 25 November 1975. He was expelled from the armed forces in March 1975, reinstated in April 1978, and eventually retired in 1990 with the rank of captain at sea. He died in Cascais in September 2014, aged 77. Early life and education Guilherme Almor de Alpoim Calvão was born in Chaves, in northern Portugal, on 6 January 1937. He moved with his parents to Mozambique when he was approximately one year old, growing up in the former Portuguese colony. He later returned to Portugal to pursue a military career. According to the Portuguese Navy's archival biographical record, Calvão entered military service on 15 October 1953 and was transferred to the Navy on 19 October 1954. He attended the Escola Naval, completing his naval course on 31 December 1957, according to an account published by a fellow officer who had trained alongside him. During his early naval career, he specialised in submarine operations and underwater activities. His qualifications included submarine specialisation, the ninth Special Marines course (Curso de Fuzileiro Especial), a Shallow Water Driver course and the Naval War Course (Curso Naval de Guerra). Naval career Submarine service and transfer to the Marines Calvão initially served in the submarine branch of the Portuguese Navy. Following the outbreak of the Portuguese Colonial War in Angola in 1961, he sought a transfer to the Navy's Marine Corps (Fuzileiros). According to his 2014 obituary in Correio da Manhã, he believed that remaining in the submarine service would make deployment to the colonial conflict less likely. He subsequently volunteered for the Special Marines, a force employed in amphibious operations, riverine warfare and operations in difficult terrain. He chose Portuguese Guinea as his principal theatre of operations. His first commission there lasted from 1963 to 1965, and his second from 1969 to 1971. During the first commission, he commanded the Special Marines Detachment No. 8 (Destacamento de Fuzileiros Especiais n.º 8, DFE 8). Operation Trident In January 1964, Calvão commanded DFE 8 during Operation Trident (Operação Tridente), a major Portuguese military campaign on Como Island in southern Portuguese Guinea. The operation was launched after the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC) had established positions on the island. Portuguese forces sought to dislodge the guerrillas and restore government control over the area. The campaign lasted approximately 70 days. The Portuguese Navy's retrospective account describes it as an important experience in developing the operational capabilities of DFE 8, whereas military historian Fernando Policarpo characterises the operation as a strategic failure: Portuguese forces suffered substantial casualties and failed to dislodge PAIGC fighters or retake the island. Policarpo specifically identifies Calvão as the commander of DFE 8 during the campaign.

title: Romance of Alisaunder
text: The Romance of Alisaunder (also called Alexander of Macedon or Alexander A) is a Middle English alliterative poem about Alexander the Great. The text is fragmentary. It begins with an account of Alexander's grandfather, King Amyntas III of Macedon; describes how Alexander was conceived by Pharaoh Nectanebo II and how he unknowingly murdered his father; skips over Alexander's birth and youth; describes the taming of Bucephalus; and ends abruptly while covering the siege of Byzantium by Philip II. It runs to 1247 lines before breaking off, perhaps because the scribe of the sole surviving copy lost interest. The complete poem, if ever it was completed, must have been huge. The Romance was composed around 1340–1370, probably in Gloucestershire or the South West Midlands. It is based on the J2 recension of the Historia de preliis—a Latin translation and elaboration of the Greek Alexander Romance—with additions from Orosius' Historia adversus paganos. For his information, Orosius was using Justin's epitome of the Philippic History of Pompeius Trogus. Since the author elaborates on his source and had direct access only to Orosius, he sometimes diverges from Justin. In recounting the siege of Methone, he has Philip fly into a rage at the loss of an eye, although Justin has Philip reacted with equanimity. The Romance is known only from an incomplete copy in school notebook from around 1600, now Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Greaves 60, where it bears the title þe Gestes of þe Worþie King and Emperour, Alisaunder of Macedoine. The exemplar from which the scribe worked was probably copied in northern England. The scribe was intrigued by the language of the text. Many words no longer current in the English of his day are underlined and others are glossed, although in some cases the scribe has updated the word in the text and provided the original as a gloss. The name 'Alexander A' was coined by Walter William Skeat for his edition. The standard edition is by Francis Peabody Magoun. The exact relationship of the poem to the fragmentary Alexander and Dindimus (or Alexander B) is uncertain, but they are probably not by the same author. They are two of three alliterative Alexander poems in Middle English, the third being the Wars of Alexander or Alexander C.

title: Bloody Tennis
text: Bloody Tennis is a 2026 sports horror drama film written and directed by Nikias Chryssos. Its cast includes Sandra Guldberg Kampp, Elina Löwensohn, Tracy Gotoas, Helena Zengel, Lucie Zhang, and Zlatko Burić. Premise Sophie is a teenager with aspirations of becoming a successful tennis player. She is sent to an esteemed but remote tennis academy in rural Spain. The instructors there guarantee results for students who give the training their all. Cast Sandra Guldberg Kampp as Sophie Elina Löwensohn as Mary Tracy Gotoas as Bana Lily Taïeb as Nelly Juliana Vieira-Guerra as Frida Helena Zengel as Heidi Lucie Zhang as Xue Vincent Romeo as Fred Zlatko Burić as Stavkos Ambre Olive as Erin Release Bloody Tennis was released in Germany on October 30, 2026, as part of the Film Festival Cologne. It is distributed in the United States by Shudder. Critical reception On the review aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes, 64% of 14 critics' reviews are positive. Leo Barraclough of Variety reported that the film "takes the world of elite sports to disturbing new extremes, filled with brutal ambition, blood-sucking leeches, and hard-hitting serves." Rob Hunter of Bloody Disgusting called the film "an uneven matchup between sports thrills and horror chills", but ultimately praised it as "an entertaining and icky entry in the sport horror subgenre." Martin Kudlac of ScreenAnarchy commented that the film "works best when it embraces its vintage slasher core, shedding its pretensions as a mysterious occult thriller and turning into an unexpected yet bizarrely funny session of family therapy." Brian Orndorf of blu-ray.com said that the film "has its moments of intensity and unpleasantness, making for a decent sit."

title: Morrisonnepa
text: Morrisonnepa is an extinct genus of nepomorph hemipteran from the Upper Jurassic Morrison Formation. It belongs to the infraorder Nepomorpha (Family unknown) and contains only one species: M. jurassica. Discovery and naming The only known specimen and its counterpart were discovered in the Jurassic Salad Bar locality (Upper Brushy Basin Member) of the Morrison Formation, southeastern Utah. The fossil was discovered in the finely laminated silty shale with rich organic matters, alongside abundant plant macrofossils. The holotype (FHPR 17299) includes partial body fossil icluding thoracic and abdominal segments, forewing, clavus and possible head are preserved. Generic name derives from the Morrison Formation and -nepa, a standard suffix used for the superfamily Nepoidea. Characteristics and classification Total body length of Morrisonnepa (from scutellum to forewing tip) is 25.37 mm long. Size of abdomen suggests this specimen was macropterous and taphonomically flattened. Combinations of features on forewing (shape, venation pattern, large membrane, long claval furrow) and big and robust abdomen suggests this taxon could be distinguished from previously reported fossil belostomatids and nepomorphs. Lara et al. (2020) suggested Morrisonnepa is placed under nepomorpha based on following characters: Well-developed and folding flat on the abdomen, abdomen with oval shape of typical of aquatic hemipterans and presence of pair short appendaces similar to respiratory processes observed in aquatic hemipterans. Despite they didn't give a further decision due to the poor preservation of Morrisonnepa, they suggested a possible affinity with Belostomatidae based on well-developted hemelytra, distinctive venation patterns on forewing, membrane on forewing with numerous irregular vein cells, total body length (25 mm in Morrisonnepa, falling within the range of extant belostomatids and nepids), robust and flatterned abdomen, color pattern resembling the light or dark brown color observed in modern belostomatids, and a pair of short and tubular processes close to the scutellum. Paleoecology and paleoenviornment Based on finely laminated mudstone with abundant organics from the Jurassic Salad Bar locality, Morrison Formation, it is suggested to be the site where yields Morrisonnepa represents oxbow lake or less likely a small pond or marsh settings. Large and robust abdomen suggested to be this taxon was predatory, as shown in modern belostomatids. Presence of pair of appendages probably served as respiration under freshwater. In the Jurassic Salad Bar locality, plant fossils including ginkgophyte Czekanowskia, Ginkgoites, conifer Brachyphyllum and the fern Coniopteris have been discovered, while animal fossils including spinicaudatan carapaces, fish scales and regurgitalite from a fish, which contains frog and salamander bones. title: Marie Eline Madsen
text: Marie Eline Madsen (born 2004) is a Danish professional golfer and LPGA Tour player. Amateur career Madsen was born in Viborg, Denmark. She was runner-up at the 2023 Danish National Stroke Play Championship behind Emma Kaisa Dalgaard Bunch. In 2024, the two teamed up to win the 2024 Spirit International Amateur in Texas. Madsen became a member of the National Team and represented Denmark at the 2024 European Nations Cup – Copa Sotogrande, the 2025 Espirito Santo Trophy, and at the European Ladies' Team Championship four times, becoming stroke play champion individually in both 2024 and 2026. Those performances helped her qualify to represent Europe at the Vagliano Trophy in the Netherlands and Patsy Hankins Trophy in the United Arab Emirates. Madsen performed well at The Women's Amateur Championship, reaching the semi-finals in 2024 at Nairn Golf Club, and the quarter-finals in 2025 at Muirfield. She was tied 6th at the 2024 European Ladies Amateur in Finland and 7th at the 2026 event in Sweden, six strokes behind winner Charlotte Naughton. She reached a career-high of 19th in the World Amateur Golf Ranking. College career Madsen enrolled at North Carolina State University in 2024 and started playing for the NC State Wolfpack women's golf team. She broke the school record for lowest scoring average in a season (71.23) and won twice as a freshman, including the NCAA Charlottesville Regional, earning a spot to the 2025 NCAA Division I women's golf championship. As a sophomore, she set a new school record with a 70.88 scoring average, won three times, and earned All-ACC Women's Team and WGCA All-America Second Team honors for a second time. She helped secure an international victory at the 2026 Arnold Palmer Cup in Ireland, earning a win in the final round for a final score of 301⁄2–291⁄2 at Tralee Golf Club. Professional career Madsen left N.C. State after a little over two seasons and turned professional during Q-Series in 2026. She made it through the three rounds of Q-School to earn her 2027 LPGA Tour card by finishing tied 15th in LPGA Q-Series Final Qualifying, following a final round 64. title: Fourth Siege of Philadelphia
text: In the middle of 1335, the Byzantine city of Philadelphia was subjected to a siege by the Aydinids of Emir Umur. After a failed assault and subsequent sortie, the citizens of Philadelphia agreed to pay tribute. However, during a diplomatic meeting with John Kantakouzenos that followed right after the siege, Umur renounced the tribute and instead allied himself with Byzantium. Background Collapse of the Anatolian frontier In the late 13th and early 14th centuries, Turkoman nomads began penetrating into Byzantine Anatolia, raiding and sacking the cities of the region, while forming their own independent beyliks. Multiple attempts were made by Emperors Michael VIII, Andronikos II, and Andronikos III to reverse the situation and reestablish order in Asia Minor, from the campaigns of Alexios Philanthropenos in the Meander Valley, to the attempted reforms of John Tarchaneiotes, to the exploits of the Catalan Company. However, by 1329, the last major attempt at the Battle of Pelekanon ended in failure. Prusa fell in 1326, followed by Nicaea in 1331, while Nicomedia was still under siege. The situation in Philadelphia As central authority in Asia Minor collapsed within a few decades, Philadelphia was unsuccessfully besieged three times by the Germiyanids and the Aydinids, under the overall command of Bey Yakub I. In 1304, the city was successfully defended by Metropolitan Theoleptos, until the Catalan Company of Roger de Flor defeated the Turks in battle. In the winter of 1310/11, it was defended by strategos Manuel Tagaris. The last attempt in 1322–1324 was thwarted due to the intervention of the blind Alexios Philanthropenos, after he was pardoned by Andronikos II. In 1327, the Mongol viceroy of Anatolia Timurtash arrived in Philadelphia, supporting the city's independence against the Germiyanids and Aydinids, while upholding the Byzantine–Mongol alliance. However, after the Ilkhanids collapsed in 1335, and while Byzantine Bithynia was being overrun by the Ottomans, Philadelphia was left with no external allies, and was thus vulnerable to a renewed Aydinid attack. Siege In 1335, after a piratical raid against Monemvasia, Messenia, and Mystras in the Peloponnese, the Aydinids under Umur attacked Philadelphia. The emir besieged the fortified city, launching an assault, but only 30 of his men managed to climb over Philadelphia's walls before the ladder was broken. The Philadelphians in return attempted a sortie, but they were driven back by the Aydinids. According to Byzantinist Paul Lemerle: The siege dragged on, the situation of the besieged became increasingly difficult, the besiegers despaired of breaching the walls, and negotiations were initiated. The Greek governor left the city, met with Umur, and concluded an agreement with him, following which the emir lifted the siege and returned to Birgi. According to an interpretation of the writings of the Ottoman historian Enveri, the siege ended in a victory for Umur, who placed a garrison within the city. However, according to another interpretation of the same source by Paul Lemerle, also favoured by historian Clive Foss, the Aydinids did not enter the city, nor took any prisoners, but they did obtain money and perhaps goods in kind, and demanded an annual payments of tribute from the Philadelphians. Aftermath Diplomatic arrangements Following the siege, Umur met with Megas Domestikos John Kantakouzenos at Klazomenai. There, they formed an alliance and also became friends. Kantakouzenos convinced the emir to "change his attitude towards the inhabitants of Philadelphia, to become their ally rather than their enemy, and to renounce the collection of the tribute that the Philadelphians were required to pay". It is possible that after this agreement, a mosque was built within the city named after Umur, since he returned to the Philadelphians the tribute he had imposed, and had also agreed to protect the city from neighbouring beyliks instead of being its enemy. The alliance was confirmed

title: William Mills Todd
text: William Mills Todd III (born August 15, 1944) is an American literary scholar and Slavist who is the Harry Tuchman Levin Professor of Literature, emeritus, at Harvard University. His research focused on Russian literature from the eighteenth to the twentieth centuries, with particular attention to Alexander Pushkin, Fyodor Dostoevsky, and the sociology of literature. He began his career at Stanford University, and from 1997 to 2000 he served as Harvard's dean of undergraduate education. He has been a senior fellow at the Harvard Society of Fellows since 1992. Todd is the author of The Familiar Letter as a Literary Genre in the Age of Pushkin (1976) and Fiction and Society in the Age of Pushkin (1986), both of which have been translated into Russian. He received the Medal of Pushkin from the Russian government in 2003 and awards from the American Association of Teachers of Slavic and East European Languages (AATSEEL) for outstanding contribution to scholarship on literature. Early life and education Todd was born on August 15, 1944, in Newport News, Virginia, the son of Jeanette (née Hofman) and William Mills Todd Jr., a businessman. He earned a Bachelor of Arts from Dartmouth College in 1966 before attending the University of Oxford, where he earned a bachelor's and Master of Arts degree in 1968. He earned a doctorate from Columbia University in 1973. Career Stanford In 1972, Todd joined the Department of Slavic Languages at Stanford University as an assistant professor of Russian literature. At Stanford, he served on the Faculty Senate and on a curriculum development committee. During the 1986 to 1987 academic year, he was a Richard W. Lyman Fellow at the Stanford Humanities Center. Harvard Todd moved to Harvard in the late 1980s, where he held the Curt Hugo Reisinger Professorship of Slavic Languages and Literatures and was also a professor of comparative literature. In the 1990 to 1991 academic year, he joined the Faculty Council on behalf of a colleague who was on leave. By 1996, he was chair of the Department of Slavic Languages and Literatures and a member of the Board of Syndics of Harvard University Press. Todd sat on selection committees for the International Research & Exchanges Board (IREX), the National Endowment for the Humanities, the Social Science Research Council, and the Guggenheim Foundation. In March 1996, Dean of the Faculty of Arts and Sciences Jeremy Knowles chose Todd as dean of undergraduate education, with a three-year term set to begin in July 1997 after a sabbatical year. His time in the office coincided with a growth in the number of Core curriculum courses, a review of departmental concentration requirements, and the introduction of a foreign-language citation, first awarded in 1999. He returned to teaching and research full time on July 1, 2000, when the historian Susan Pedersen succeeded him. In 2002, Todd was named a Harvard College Professor, a five-year appointment given for excellence in teaching. He later became the Harry Tuchman Levin Professor of Literature and is now emeritus, with the title of research professor. Scholarship Todd's faculty profile lists his interests as narrative and cultural studies, literary sociology, and semiotics, along with Russian, English, and French literature from the eighteenth to the twentieth centuries. His first book, The Familiar Letter as a Literary Genre in the Age of Pushkin, was published by Princeton University Press in 1976. In 1978, Stanford University Press published Literature and Society in Imperial Russia, 1800–1914, a volume he edited. Fiction and Society in the Age of Pushkin: Ideology, Institutions, and Narrative appeared from Harvard University Press in 1986. A Russian edition of his Pushkin-era work was issued in 1996 in the series "Contemporary Western Rusistika." Todd also wrote the introduction to Michael R. title: Đào Hồng Lan
text: Đào Hồng Lan (born 23 July 1971) is a Vietnamese politician and economist. She has been serving as Minister of Health of Vietnam since 2022 and member of the National Assembly since 2021. Early life and education Lan was born on 23 July 1971 in a village of the Hải Dương province, then North Vietnam. She graduated in industrial production and business management and a master's degree in economics. Career She began her professional career in 1993 at the Hanoi Youth Employment Promotion Centre. She joined the Communist Party of Vietnam in 2001. Between 1995 and 2018, she worked at the Ministry of Labour, Invalids and Social Affairs, where she held various positions, including Director of the Cabinet between 2009 and 2014, and Deputy Minister between 2014 and 2018. Lan has been a member of the Communist Party's 12th and 13th Central Committees, and is a member of the National Assembly. She previously served as deputy secretary of the Party Committee at Bắc Ninh province in 2019 and was its secretary between 2020 and 2022. During her term, she served as chairwoman of the province's Steering Committee for the Prevention and Control of COVID-19. On 15 July 2022, she was appointed acting Minister of Health by Prime Minister Phạm Minh Chính in place of Nguyễn Thanh Long, who was dismissed for his involvement in the Viet A COVID-19 test kit scandal. Lan became the first Minister of Health not to come from the healthcare or pharmaceutical sector. In October 2022, she was appointed as the formal Minister of Health and was re-appointed in 2026. title: Elsternwick Union Church
text: The Elsternwick Union Church is a former Uniting church building, located at 84–86 Orrong Road in Elsternwick, in the City of Glen Eira, in the inner eastern suburbs of Melbourne, in Victoria, Australia. Established in 1889 as a church for use by both the Congregationalists and the Baptists, it was acquired by the Congregationalists in 1894. The congregation joined the Uniting Church in 1977 and merged with St John's Church, Elsternwick in 1990, after which the building was sold. The former church was added to the Victorian Heritage Register on 5 October 1988 in recognition of its historical and architectural significance; and was also added to non-statutory lists by the Victorian branch of the National Trust on 20 November 1975 and the now defunct Register of the National Estate on 27 October 1998. History The former Union Church was designed by the architect George de Lacy Evans and erected between 1889 and 1890 by McMurtie, McNaughton and Stewart. Although the church is not one of the oldest buildings in the area, it is contemporaneous with the extensive suburbanisation of the district from the late 1880s and is one of the earliest non-residential buildings in the district. Baptists and Congregationalists both believed in the autonomy of individual congregations and both refused to enforce subscription to formal creeds or confessions of faith. Both were also strictly voluntaryist. Their common beliefs enabled the two groups to cooperate by forming several Union churches, one in Hawthorn, Elsternwick, and possibly a few in country areas. The history of the church dates from the 1850s when members of various denominations met together in private homes and later a makeshift chapel in Caulfield. A building was erected near the south-east corner of Orrong and Glen Eira roads. When this building was destroyed by fire in 1889, a decision was made to abandon this site and to rebuild on the present site near the expanding Elsternwick township. The new church building included a baptistery suitable for total immersion, according to the practice of the Baptists' Union. During the depression years of the 1890s, the financial situation of the Union Church was precarious. In 1894, the Congregationalists acquired the building and it continued as the Elsternwick Congregational Church until the formation of the Uniting Church in 1977. The building is believed to be a rare, possibly unique, surviving example of a church building erected for dual use by the Congregationalists and Baptists. In 1987, the Orrong Road parish merged with the St John's Uniting Church, Elsternwick – a former Presbyterian church – to form the Elsternwick–Caulfield South Parish, and the Union Church became redundant. The final service was held on 2 December 1990. The former church was sold in 1989 and subsequently used as a Rabbinical college by the Ripponlea College of Jewish Education, and later repurposed for use as a campus of the Adass Israel School, an ultra-Orthodox Jewish day school. Another former Uniting Church building, located at 64–66 Orrong Road, was sold by the church and redeveloped as luxury housing in 2017. Description The church building is a rare and well-developed example of the early French Gothic manner as popularised through the muscular Victorian re-interpretation of English architect William Burges, which in turn were derived from the publications of Eugène Viollet-le-Duc. Other Victorian cases of detailing derived from Viollet-le-Duc include Barwon Park (1868), the Presbyterian Church, Skipton (1871), the Bourke Street West Police Station by Bindley and Brittingham that dated from 1888 to 1889, and the Trinity Lutheran Manse, East Melbourne by John A. B. Koch (1890). However, none of these buildings related closely in form to the Union Church. The only building which has been identified as closely comparable is the Bairnsdale Courthouse by A. J. Macdonald, that dated from 1892. The former Union Church is a red-brick building with Oamaru ston

title: Amy Racine-Poon
text: Amy H. K. Racine-Poon is a retired Bayesian statistician and pharmacometrician known for her work in the agrochemical and biopharmaceutical industry. Originally from Hong Kong, and educated in the United States, she worked for many years for Ciba-Geigy and Novartis in Switzerland. Education and career Racine-Poon is originally from Hong Kong, one of four children of a middle-class family. Growing up in Hong Kong, she spoke Cantonese with her family, and English in school; she also learned Mandarin and German at university, and Italian later in life. She was an undergraduate mathematics student at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, in Chung Chi College, where she received a bachelor's degree with upper honours in 1970; mathematician Shing-Tung Yau was a classmate. Intimidated by his brilliance, she decided to go into applied rather than pure mathematics. Because her only job option after graduation was to become a schoolteacher, she "applied for graduate school to postpone the job decision". Her application was successful and she continued her studies in statistics at the University of California, Berkeley. She completed her Ph.D. in 1977, under the name "Amy Poon Davis". Her doctoral dissertation, Robust Measures of Association, was supervised by Erich Leo Lehmann. During her time at UC Berkeley, she also worked as a lecturer in statistics from 1975 to 1977. Next, from 1977 to 1980, she was a statistician in the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, in its Biometry Branch. There, she met her future husband, Swiss geneticist Robert Racine, who was visiting the institute as a postdoctoral researcher. After starting a family with him, they returned to Switzerland so that their son could be raised there. From 1981 until her retirement in 2023, she worked for Ciba-Geigy and Novartis in Basel, Switzerland. Until the mid-1980s, her work as a statistician involved robust and frequentist statistics, and the design of experiments. She shifted her interests to Bayesian methods under pressure from her work to find methods that would produce usable inferences from smaller samples, and under the influence of Adrian Smith, who worked as a consultant for Novartis. Her work concerned statistics, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamic modeling, at all stages of the drug development process. She has also held visiting faculty positions at several universities in the UK, and volunteered as a statistical consultant for the Gates Foundation from 2015 to 2019, on "a public health project on child growth in low- and middle-income countries". Recognition Racine-Poon was the 1995 recipient of the Greenfield Medal of the Royal Statistical Society, "for the innovative use of Bayesian approaches to complex non-linear problems in the chemical-pharmaceutical industry, including radioimmunoassay, non-linear calibration and population kinetics". She was named as a Fellow of the American Statistical Association, in the 1998 class of fellows, and as a Novartis Distinguished Scientist in 1999. Novartis honored her for "recommending and driving the implementation of innovative pharmacometrics approaches that led to better clinical trial designs and more efficient use of available data in the company’s clinical development programs". The American Statistical Association gave her their 2020 Youden Interlaboratory Research Award, and the American Society for Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics gave her their 2024 Sheiner–Beal Pharmacometrics Award.

title: Hay Football Association
text: The Hay Football Association was an Australian rules football competition based around the town of Hay in south-west New South Wales. History Australian rules football has existed in Hay longer than any other location in New South Wales, with the original Hay club being established on the 24th of May 1876 - ten days before the Albury Football Club was formed. The first 16 years of football consisted of scratch matches between members of the club until 1892, when the first organized Association was formed to provide a premiership competition. Hay and Half-Holiday were the initial clubs and competed in a 3-match season for the premiership. Trades United joined to form a 3-team competition in 1893. This season would end in a farcical manner after the Half-Holiday club was disqualified from the competition, resulting in Trades withdrawing from the competition and Hay as the only remaining club declining to accept the Premiership. Trades did not rejoin the HFA in 1894 and Hay and Half-Holiday would remain the only clubs in the Association until 1899, when Federals replaced Hay. A year later Imperials would replace Half-Holiday. The Gymnasium club was formed in 1902 and took the place of Imperials. They would go on an extended run of dominance, winning 6 premierships in a row between 1902-1907 and another in 1909. The HFA expanded to a three-team competition in 1906 with the addition of Suburban. In 1910 an interesting situation developed when each club won four games each, tying the premiership three ways. Unusually it was decided to simply declare all three clubs premiers rather than implement any form of tiebreaker. Suburban, once cellar-dwellers, had become the dominant club by 1912 to the point where the Association was forced into recess due to an apathetic attitude from the other clubs towards forming up and attempting to beat them. This recess continued through World War I. Football in Hay was re-established in 1919 with Suburban and Federals competing, however a lack of players forced the competition to disband before completion and no premiership was awarded. Gymnasium returned in 1920, strengthening the competition along with the return of players from the War and population growth in Hay. Another three-way tie occurred in 1925 and again all three clubs were declared premiers. This decision was not popular and calls for a percentage system of sorts to be implemented were made. Federals folded during the 1927 season and an inability of the Association to obtain a quorum at the next year's AGM saw the HFA enter recess in 1928. 1929 saw two new clubs - Imperial and Wanderers - join the HFA in place of Federals and Gymnasium. A play-off system was implemented for the first time in the HFA's history, with Wanderers winning the grand final at their first attempt. Rovers replaced Wanderers in 1931. This season was not completed due to the failure of the Imperials to contest the grand final against Suburban, after which the Subs withdrew from the Association. The 1932 season was suspended in May due to the Hay Municipal Council barring the Association from using the public recreation reserve for its games. The dispute was resolved before 1933, allowing football to return. Gymnasium re-joined the competition in place of Rovers in 1933. The Association lapsed in 1936, with "passive attitude" towards the "decadence" of Australian rules in Hay lamented as the reason for football's demise. In 1937 the Hay Football Club was established and, although not joining any existing competitions due to the isolation of Hay from other population centres, played challenge matches against a number of surrounding clubs in the years leading up to World War II. The Hay FC continued to serve as the primary Australian rules football club in Hay post-war, however the HFA was re-established in 1947 to provide a game for players who were unable to play in the Hay side. title: Thomas Ninigret
text: Thomas Ninigret (1736 – November 12, 1769), also called King Tom, was the hereditary sachem of the Narragansett in the colony of Rhode Island from 1746 until his death. He was sent to England for his education. Thomas succeeded his father, George Augustus Ninigret, at the age of ten. He inherited the debts from his father and his own spending increased them. To pay his debts he sold a large portion of tribe's reservation in Charlestown. In response, a group led by the minister Samuel Niles and the Shattock family asked the Rhode Island General Assembly and Sir William Johnson, the British superintendent of Indian affairs, to stop the sales. In April 1766 his opponents attempted to depose him, citing his marriage without the tribe's approval and his sales of its land. He refused to step down, and the Assembly continued to deal with him as sachem. From 1767 the Assembly barred him from selling land and put his debts in the hands of a committee. Thomas set up a school for the tribe's children. A deed drawn up in his name in 1768 said they should be taught English and arithmetic and, if they wished, Greek and Latin. The school stayed in use until 1880. He died in 1769, still deeply in debt, and was succeeded by his sister Esther. His lands continued to be sold to pay his creditors until 1773. After the death of Esther's son George, the last hereditary sachem, around 1779, an elected council became the tribe's governing body. Early life and inherited lawsuits Thomas Ninigret was born in 1736, the son of the sachem George Augustus Ninigret and his wife, Sarah Sachem. He had a brother, George, and a sister, Esther. He was a great-grandson of Ninigret, the 17th-century sachem of the Niantics, whose descendants governed the combined Niantic and Narragansett tribe from its reservation in Charlestown. His father had become sachem in 1735 after the death of his brother, Charles Augustus Ninigret, over the rival claim of Charles Augustus's infant son, Charles, whose mother, Kate, contested George's authority in the colonial courts. The litigation left George in debt; in 1741 the Assembly allowed him to sell land to pay his debts, and in 1745 he asked again for permission to sell land to cover the costs of the suits. George died in 1745 or 1746, and on June 21, 1746, Thomas, then ten years old, was "chosen Sachem by the unanimous Voice of the Tribe". The succession was contested again on behalf of his cousin Charles, but Thomas's lawyers prevailed in court. During his youth his mother Sarah acted as his guardian, together with eight councillors chosen by the tribe. In 1746 the General Assembly had appointed five trustees to collect the rents of the sachem's lands, much of which was leased to English farmers. In June 1747 Sarah and the councillors, among them Samuel Niles and John Shattock, protested that the trustees had been appointed without their consent and had leased away the cornfields, woodland and cedar swamp on which the tribe depended. In August the Assembly recorded that the young sachem had received none of his rents "and indeed must have suffered had it not been for the charitable Assistance of some of his Friends". His mother Sarah had won a suit against one of his tenants in both the inferior and superior courts, but the trustees had appealed to the King in Council. The Assembly ordered the appeal stopped. The appeal nevertheless remained before the Privy Council in England until November 1755, when Thomas successfully petitioned through his guardian Jonathan Nichols of Newport for its dismissal; by his own later account it was dismissed with costs. His cousin Charles brought further suits, in which Thomas said he won "upwards of twenty verdicts of jury", until Charles enlisted for the expedition against Canada in the French and Indian War and Thomas paid him £500 sterling for a quitclaim of his rights. title: Sohel Khan
text: Sohel Khan (Bengali: সোহেল খান; 1960 – 24 November 2026) was a Bangladeshi television and film actor. He first gained public recognition for his appearance in a television commercial for Banglalink, directed by Mostofa Sarwar Farooki. He later became well known to audiences for playing the character Bishu in the television series 420, also directed by Farooki. Throughout his career, he acted in standalone television dramas, series, telefilms and various feature films. Career Khan began his acting career by appearing in a Banglalink commercial directed by Mostofa Sarwar Farooki. Subsequently, he worked in standalone dramas, series, and telefilms. Among his television roles, 420 remains particularly notable. Khan portrayed a wide range of characters, including several comedic roles. His notable film credits include Noy Number Bipod Sanket (2007), Daruchini Dwip (2007), Bouer Jala (2007), Khoj: The Search (2010), Projapoti: The Mysterious Bird (2011), Common Gender (2012), Lal Tip (2012), Inchi Inchi Prem (2013), Onek Sadher Moyna (2014), Desha: The Leader (2014), Porobashinee (2017), Bir (2020), Kemne Ki! (2021), Prio Komola (2021), Shaan (2022), and Jongli (2025). Death On 19 November 2026, Khan went to Bogura to participate in the filming of the movie Nosib. Five days later, on the morning of 24 November 2026, while in Bogura for a film shoot, he fell ill. Khan was found unwell in his hotel room while preparing for a shoot. He was taken to the TMSS Medical College & Rafatullah Community Hospital, where he was pronounced dead by attending physicians. Khan was 66. The hospital's death certificate cited cardiac arrest as the cause of death. His death was confirmed to the media by Rashed Mamun Apu, General Secretary of the Actors' Association (Abhinay Shilpi Sanga), and producer Arshad Adnan. After Khan's death, at 4:00 pm, his body was brought to his home in Rajapur village, located in the Dhamrai Upazila of Dhaka District. His funeral prayer (janaza) was held that evening at the Rajapur Eidgah ground, following the Maghrib prayers. He was later laid to rest at the Rajapur graveyard.

title: Judy. London. 1969
text: Judy. London. 1969 is a live album by American singer and actress Judy Garland, released by Juno Records. Recorded during her final London engagement in 1969, it documents her last live performance and final recording. The album received reviews from several music publications, which commented on its significance as Garland's final recording. It peaked at No. 10 on Record World's "LP's Coming Up" chart and was reported to be a consistent seller for Juno Records. Background The album was the first major release by Juno Records. Mickey Deans, Judy Garland's husband at the time, personally taped the performance at a London club in 1969 for their personal use, and agreed to share the recording to other fans after Garland's death. Bernard Gurtman, of Gurtman-Brown Associates, was appointed publicist for the album, he worked alongside Ben Arrigo, the label's national sales representative. Gamma Records in Montreal acquired the Canadian distribution rights for the album. Critical reception Billboard described the album as "a potent collector's item", since it contained Garland's "last recorded performance". RPM wrote that the recording contained "an abundance of Garland happiness but also a measure of sadness". Cash Box described the album as "a nostalgic package that could see nice sales". Record World called it a "happy coincidence" that Garland's final performance had been recorded, although she "isn't in great voice, but she's Judy. For the last time". Accolades Rex Reed was nominated for the Grammy Award for Best Album Notes at the 13th Annual Grammy Awards in 1971. The award went to Chris Albertson for Bessie Smith's album The World's Greatest Blues Singer. Commercial performance The album peaked at No. 10 on Record World's "LP's Coming Up" chart. It was reported to be a consistent seller for Juno Records, with distributor Argus Record Distributors noting strong Christmas orders for its catalog. title: 2025 New Zealand Formula Ford Championship
text: The 2025 New Zealand Formula Ford Championship (known for commercial reasons as the 2025 NAPA Auto Parts New Zealand Formula Ford Championship) was a motor racing championship for drivers of Formula Ford racing cars. It was the 54th national series for Formula Fords to be held in New Zealand. The season began at Timaru International Motor Raceway on 25 January and concluded at Manfeild: Circuit Chris Amon on 6 April. The season was largely dominated by Blake Dowdall who won seven races and won the championship with one race remaining. As part of winning the title, Dowdall received a private test with Rodin Motorsport at their Mount Lyford facility as part of the Formula Ford to Formula 1, powered by Rodin Cars initiative and subsequently tested Formula 4 machinery in Britain later that year. In the regional championships, Toby McCormack won the North Island Formula Ford Championship while William Neale claimed the South Island Formula Ford Championship. Calendar The schedule for the 2025 New Zealand Formula Ford season was announced in September 2024. Results and standings Season summary Championship standings References

title: USCGC Coho
text: USCGC Coho (WPB-87321) is an 87-foot (27 m) Marine Protector-class of the United States Coast Guard. Commissioned in 2000, it was based at Panama City, Florida, in the late 2000s. In April 2010 it was one of the cutters sent to search for survivors of the Deepwater Horizon explosion. It later served from Corpus Christi and then New London, Connecticut. In 2024 it searched off Georgia for two missing sailors, and in April 2026 it enforced security zones offshore during the launch of Artemis II. Design Coho is one of the Marine Protector-class coastal patrol boats built for the Coast Guard by Bollinger Shipyards of Lockport, Louisiana, under a contract first awarded on March 13, 1996. The class replaced the older 82-foot Point-class cutters. Coho was launched on April 4, 2000, and entered service in a special commissioning on June 13, 2000. Service history Panama City In August 2009 the crew of the offshore supply vessel Fighting Chicken reported that a recreational boat had capsized in the Gulf of Mexico. The Coast Guard sent Coho along with a helicopter and an HC-144 Ocean Sentry patrol aircraft. The supply vessel rescued four people and transferred them to Coho, and the helicopter rescued two more from a nearby oil rig. Coho and a Sea Tow boat then righted the capsized boat and found the body of a seventh person in its pilothouse. On April 20, 2010, the drilling rig Deepwater Horizon exploded and caught fire about 42 miles (68 km) southeast of Venice, Louisiana, leaving 11 crew members missing. Coho, then homeported in Panama City, and Pelican were sent to join the search, which Cobia and the patrol ship Zephyr had carried on overnight. Southeast coast In November 2024 a mariner reported a capsized 50-foot (15 m) catamaran about 65 miles (105 km) east of Brunswick, Georgia. Two men who had been sailing it from Connecticut to Florida were missing. Coast Guard Sector Charleston searched with Coho and Kingfisher along with aircraft from several air stations. The search was suspended on November 27 after about 77 hours and more than 9,140 square miles (23,700 km2). On April 1, 2026, Coho's crew enforced limited access areas offshore of Port Canaveral during the launch of NASA's Artemis II mission from Kennedy Space Center. The areas included a security zone, a regulated navigation area and a safety zone.

title: Mabushi
text: Mabushi (also spelled Mabuchi) is an urban village and informal settlement in the Mabushi District of Abuja, Nigeria. Location and history Mabushi District lies to the north-west of Wuse, near Utako. A 2012 study for the Woodrow Wilson Center described it as a settlement of about 5,000 people on roughly 10 hectares, led by a district head. According to the study, residents had been compensated and moved to a resettlement site, but later returned, and continued to live in fear of eviction. Living conditions Mabushi is densely populated. Reporting by Daily Trust described poor sanitation and a two-room clinic serving the community, with no standard hospital nearby; residents told the paper they feared demolition and wanted to be resettled on a permanent site. In 2023 ThisDay reported deteriorating roads and streets that flooded during heavy rain, and residents' appeals to the new Federal Capital Territory minister for government attention. Demolitions In October 2023 the FCT minister, Nyesom Wike, ordered the demolition of a scavengers' settlement along a road in Mabushi, describing it as a security risk.

title: 2021–22 Persib Bandung season
text: The 2021–22 season was the 62nd season in the history of Persib Bandung, and the club's 25th consecutive season in the top-flight of Indonesian football since it became fully professional. In their third season under head coach Robert Alberts, Persib finished second in Liga 1 with 69 points, six points behind back-to-back league champions Bali United. title: Brida (TV series)
text: Brida is a Brazilian telenovela produced and broadcast by Rede Manchete, from 11 August to 23 October 1998, in a total of 54 episodes, replacing Mandacaru and being replaced by the rerun of Pantanal. It was Manchete's final new telenovela, before the network declared itself bankrupt. Based on Paulo Coelho's eponymous novel, it was adapted by Jayme Camargo, with collaboration from Ana Fadigas, Angélica Lopes, Samy Wurman and Sônia Mota, directed by Luiz Antônio Pilar and Sérgio Mattar and general direction of Walter Avancini. In its main roles, the actor roster included Carolina Kasting, Leonardo Vieira, Rubens de Falco, Othon Bastos, Edney Giovenazzi, Bete Mendes, Guilhermina Guinle and Manuela Dias. Production Brida is based on Paulo Coelho's novel of the same name, which sold 800,000 copies in Brazil and a total of eight million copies in 36 countries, where both Portuguese and Spanish-speaking versions were released. The contract where Paulo Coelho ceded the rights of the book to Rede Manchete stated that he could not interfere in the adaptation. Manchete hoped to see Brida exported abroad, since, at the time filming began, the book was sold in over 40 countries. Manchete invested approximately R$45,000 in each of the 180 episodes it was expected to have. Before Carolina Kasting was selected for the role of the main character, Christine Fernandes, Drica Moraes and Teresa Seiblitz were also mooted. Christine Fernandes did not agree with the nude scenes, and Carolina Kasting, initially set to be the role of Inês, got the title role. The first scenes were shot on 23 June 1998, a Tuesday, in Rio de Janeiro; the first day of shooting ended ahead of schedules, as the team wanted to watch the match between Brazil and Norway for the 1998 FIFA World Cup (where Norway won 2–1), to which Avancini questioned about what was happening, saying "did you forget that I am here?", to absolute silence. Shooting took place at Gávea Pequena Road, in Alto da Boa Vista, Rio de Janeiro, and was directed by Walter Avancini. The director and the team embarked to Ireland on 1 August, to record some scenes. A team of 18 people went to Dublin, including Carolina Kasting, Guilhermina Guinle, Rubens de Falco, Wanessa Bonelli, Fabiana Amorim and Manuela Dias. The scenes shot there were set in the fourteenth century, according to Paulo Coelho's book. Among the scenery, the team chose a medieval castle in Limerick. All the equipment, consisting of cameras, cables, costumes and wigs, came to Ireland via a cargo flight. From episode 14, airing on 28 August, Avancini changed scriptwriter Walter Avancini with romancist Sônia Mota, daughter of Nelson Rodrigues, and Angélica Lopes, who worked with the director on Tocaia Grande, to provide "a story focusing more on the female interior universe", which, according to Avancini, Camargo was not doing well, as he gave a more male view to the story, and was exploiting external actions of the characters. The change provided the series with a "more intimist", feminine story. After changing the scriptwriter, Avancini decided to add actors who were already known with the viewers, under the justification that these would help increase its ratings. He chose Victor Wagner and Carla Regina, both in their fourth consecutive telenovela on Manchete, after Tocaia Grande, Xica da Silva and Mandacaru. In addition, Tânia Alves, of Tocaia Grande and Mandacaru, Anselmo Vasconcelos, of Mandacaru and Alexia Deschamps, of Mandacaru, e Xica da Silva also joined. For the first time on the network, actresses Rosane Gofman and Fafy Siqueira, went on board with the goal of "making the people laugh". Avancini said that it was not the solution he wanted for the problem of the storylines, but that he could do that given the circumstances at the time of production and with the resources he had.
