title: Yudai Shimamoto
text: Yudai Shimamoto (嶋本悠大, Shimamoto Yudai; born 26 October 2006) is a Japanese professional footballer who plays as a midfielder for J1 League club Shimizu S-Pulse. He has represented Japan at youth level, winning the 2026 AFC U-23 Asian Cup and finishing as runner-up at the 2026 Asian Games. Youth career Shimamoto played for Blaze Kumamoto and then Kumamoto Prefectural Otsu High School, who won the 2024 Prince Takamado U-18 Premier League for the first time in the school's history. He scored 12 goals in 22 appearances during the campaign. Club career Shimizu S-Pulse Shimizu S-Pulse announced in September 2024 that Shimamoto would join the J1 League club ahead of the 2025 J1 League season. He made his professional debut in February 2025, coming on as a substitute in Shimizu's season opener against Tokyo Verdy. Manager Tadahiro Akiba described him as an exceptionally promising 18-year-old. He made his first start the following month, in a 1–0 league defeat to Gamba Osaka. He finished his debut season with 16 appearances in all competitions. In April 2026, Shimamoto scored his first professional goal in a 3–0 win over V-Varen Nagasaki in the J1 100 Year Vision League. He scored two more goals in his next four appearances and finished the competition with three goals in 12 appearances. In the 2026–27 J1 League, Shimamoto won the Young Player of the Month award for September. International career Shimamoto has represented Japan at U-18, U-20, U-21, U-22 and U-23 levels. In 2024, Shimamoto represented the U-18s in the SBS Cup and captained the team in a 4–1 friendly victory over Sweden. In October 2024, he played two friendly fixtures for the U-19s, scoring in a 3–2 victory over United States. He was part of the U-23 team that won the 2026 AFC U-23 Asian Cup in January 2026. He played in all of Japan's matches and came on as a substitute in the final, a 4–0 win over China. As part of the Mirabror Usmanov Memorial Cup in July 2025, Shimamoto scored for the U-22s in a 2–0 win over Uzbekistan. In July 2026, he was named in the U-21 squad for the 2026 Asian Games. He scored twice in a 7–0 group stage win over Kyrgyzstan. Shimamoto started the final, which Japan lost 1–0 to South Korea. In November 2026, he was called up to the U-21 squad for a tour of Spain and Egypt. Style of play Shimamoto plays primarily as a central midfielder. Shimizu manager Takayuki Yoshida has praised his ball control and work rate. Career statistics Club As of 23 November 2026. Honours Japan U-21 Asian Games silver medal: 2026 Japan U-23 AFC U-23 Asian Cup: 2026 Individual J1 League Young Player of the Month: September 2026

title: Julie Kegels
text: Julie Kegels is a Belgian fashion designer and the founder of the Antwerp-based womenswear label Julie Kegels. She won the 2026 LVMH Prize, which included a grant of €400,000 and a year of mentorship. Early life and education Kegels grew up in Antwerp, where she read books about couture and learned dressmaking techniques from a local seamstress after school. She studied fashion at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts (Antwerp) from 2018 to 2021, when Walter Van Beirendonck was head of the fashion department. Her 2021 graduate collection, "Supper Club", was inspired by Judy Chicago's installation The Dinner Party and included garments designed to double as table decorations. Career After freelance work and a short internship with Meryll Rogge, Kegels moved to Paris in 2021 for a year-long internship at Alaïa under Pieter Mulier. She launched her label in Antwerp in 2024 after obtaining private investment from family and industry contacts. Her debut collection, "50/50", was presented as a tableau vivant in a Paris shop window and included a suit with a formal front and shorts at the back, and a hybrid knit-and-denim skirt. Her second collection, "A Pool Will Do", imagined a romance between a bourgeois Parisian woman and a Los Angeles surfer. Presented beside a pool in Paris in September 2024, the Spring 2025 collection combined tweed tailoring with board-short details, bikini bandeaus, and beach towels. For Fall 2025, "Dresscode" took Judith Price's 1980 book Executive Style: Achieving Success Through Good Taste and Design as its starting point. The collection included office tailoring, upholstery-inspired accessories, and a full-length dress made from wood. Kegels presented "Quick Change" for Spring 2026 beneath a metro bridge in Paris, where models used magicians' techniques to transform garments, including a wedding gown that became a slip and a bubble skirt. By September 2025, the label had 29 stockists, including Nordstrom and H Lorenzo, and two employees. It manufactured in Belgium, Portugal, and Romania, while its largest regional sales shares were in Asia-Pacific and the United States. For Fall 2026, Kegels examined appearance and transformation in a show on Boulevard des Invalides in Paris. The collection included leather face masks, jewelry made from chandelier parts, and projections of shadows that did not always match the models' movements. For Spring 2027, presented on September 28, 2026, she explored gravity and falling through dresses and trousers that appeared to slip downward. As the models walked, organza garments released pigment that colored their shoes. Design approach Kegels has described her collections as studies of female archetypes and the different roles a woman may occupy during one day. She has said that she looks for a balance between beauty and the "off-kilter", using contrasts in silhouette, material, and narrative. Her process often begins with cutting apart vintage clothing to study its construction; for "Dresscode", she also studied sofa construction. Awards On September 4, 2026, Kegels won the LVMH Prize at the Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris, receiving €400,000 and a year of mentorship from LVMH experts. She received the award from actress Jennifer Lawrence. WWD reported that she was selected from 2,400 applicants and that her label was carried by 38 points of sale at the time of the award.

title: Spexin
text: Spexin (SPX, Neuropeptide Q, NPQ) is an endogenous neuropeptide 14 amino acids in length, with the sequence NWTPQAMLYLKGAQ-NH2 or Asn-Trp-Thr-Pro-Gln-Ala-Met-Leu-Tyr-Leu-Lys-Gly-Ala-Gln-NH2. It is produced by cleavage of the larger protein pre-pro-spexin along with another neuropeptide spexin-2. Spexin is related to other neuropeptides such as galanin and kisspeptin and is both a reproductive hormone as well as being involved in regulation of appetite, lipid metabolism, and glucose homeostasis. Spexin levels are decreased in people with obesity or type 2 diabetes, but are increased by regular exercise. It has an appetite suppressing activity and also has anxiolytic, antidepressant, analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects. Spexin binds to the galanin receptors GALR2 and GALR3, and has also been identified as a possible endogenous ligand for the orphan receptor GPR161. Using spexin directly or modulating its release has been suggested as being potentially beneficial in the treatment of obesity and diabetes, but since it was discovered relatively recently, research in this area is still ongoing.

title: Penstemon dolius
text: Penstemon dolius, Jones' penstemon, is a small species from Utah and Nevada in the western United States. It is part of the veronica family and has blue-violet flowers. Description Jones' penstemons are herbaceous plants that grow flowering stems that can rest on the ground, grow along the ground before turning upwards at the ends, or lean out from the base of the plant and then grow upwards. Usually the stems near the edge of the plant partly or totally on the ground. They reach lengths of 2 to 20 centimeters (1–8 in), but are usually less than 14 cm (5.5 in) long. The stems are often reddish-purple and always have a dense covering of stiff, backwards pointing hairs giving an ashy appearance. Plants have both basal and stem leaves that are not leathery, have smooth edges without teeth, and are covered in the same retrorse hairs that give the stems their appearance. The basal leaves and the lowest ones on the stems have leaf stalks and generally are 1–4 cm (0.5–1.5 in) long, but can be as short as 0.5 cm or as long as 5.5 cm (2 in), and are just 0.4–1.4 cm wide. They are spatulate to oblanceolate in shape with a blunt to narrow point. Each stem will have two to six leaves attached to opposite sides in pairs with the uppermost leaves directly attached by the main stem. The upper leaves will be 1.2–3.8 cm (0.5–1.5 in) long and just 0.3–0.7 cm wide with an oblanceolate shape. The flowers are largely blue, but are violet at the base; though the color can range from light blue to blue-purple and usually have faint blue or reddish-purple floral guide lines, though can lack them at times. They measure 1.3–2.1 cm long and are covered on the outside with glandular hairs while the lower surface of the interior is sparsely covered in long white hairs. The three lobes of the lower lip spread downwards while the two lobes of the upper lip project forwards. It is very similar to the dwarf penstemon (Penstemon nanus), but that species has horseshoe shaped anthers and glandular hairs on the inflorescence portion of the flowering stem. In contrast Jones' penstemons have widely spreading pollen sacs that split the full length and an inflorescence that is covered in ashy hairs that are not glandular. Taxonomy The botanist Marcus E. Jones published the scientific description of Penstemon dolius in 1920. It is classified in the Penstemon genus as part of the Plantaginaceae. The species has no accepted synonyms or varieties according to Plants of the World Online, however Penstemon duchesnensis was initially described as a variety of P. dolius in 1979 before being described as a species in 1986. As late as 1999 botanists such as John T. Kartesz continued to accept P. duchesnensis as a variety and this is the classification used by NatureServe. Names The species name, dolius, means barrel-shaped in Botanical Latin. It is known by the common names Jones' penstemon or Jones' beardtongue. Range and habitat Jones' penstemon is native to a limited area of east-central Nevada and west-central Utah. In Nevada the species grows in three counties, eastern Elko, White Pine, and northeastern Nye. The range in Utah includes Beaver, Millard, Sanpete, Juab, and Tooele counties. It is found at elevations of 1,195 to 1,985 meters (3,921 to 6,512 ft).

title: Gerardo Vargas Varela
text: Gerardo Vargas Varela (born 12 September 1960) is a Costa Rican former Catholic priest and politician. He represented Limón in the Legislative Assembly of Costa Rica, as a member of the Broad Front party. Early Life He attended primary school at the Palomo School in Santa Teresita and secondary school at the Presbítero Enrique Menzel School, both in Turrialba, before entering the Major Seminary of Paso Ancho. He also obtained a bachelor's degree in theology from the Catholic University of Costa Rica. He served as a priest in the Diocese of Limón from 1987 to 2009. Political Career In 2010 Vargas Varela left religious life and started his political career, joining the Frente Amplio political party, and ran in the 2010 elections. In the 2014 elections he was elected to the legistlative assembly, and served from 2014 to 2018. During that time he was also parliamentary advisor to deputy José María Villalta. Views and poistions Vargas Varela often campaigned on issues related to finances, social affairs, human rights, and the environment. In 20 he justified his refusal to back Gonzalo Ramírez and Óscar Andrés López Arias as candidates to preside over the legistlative assembly, citing their conservatice Evangelical views such as refusing to accept gay civil unions which Vargas Varela supports. title: CEMA Chile
text: CEMA Chile (Mother Centers or Centros de Madres in Spanish) was a Chilean foundation created in 1954 mission of helping low income women work in to improve their family's material and moral conditions. CEMA became well known during the Pinochet Dictatorship (1973–1990), when Augusto Pinochet's wife Lucía Hiriart de Pinochet served as its director. Under Hiriart's direction, CEMA Chile focused on recruiting middle-class women - many of them military wives - who taught classes on home economics and domestic skills to poor women, emphasizing their Catholic moral obligations as housewives. Hiriart remained the head of CEMA Chile until it closed in 2016. History In 1957, during the second term of President Carlos Ibáñez del Campo, his wife first lady Graciela Letelier Velasco brought together several organizations designed to provide support for impoverished women. In the 1960s, these women's groups were mainly groups of lower-class women who met in their neighbor's homes to support each other and organize for collective social action. In their research, historian Teresa Valdés and others found that in the 1970s, Chile had 25,000 of these women's centers and nearly half of adult women in Chile participated. In 1971, the state recognized first lady Hortensia Bussias the official "Coordinadora de Centros de Madres (COCEMA)" - "Coordinator of Mother's Centers." Pinochet Dictatorship Conservative women had played an important public role in opposing President Salvador Allende's government through "March of the Pots and Pans" protests that capitalized on their political roles as mothers and housewives fighting for their families amid food shortages. After Augusto Pinochet took power in 1973, the dictatorship encouraged Chilean women stop their public political activism and return to their household roles. In 1974, Decree N° 226 officially created CEMA Chile as a private organization. Under the direction of first lady Lucía Hiriart de Pinochet, Chilean women's centers were re-purposed as an opportunity for conservative indoctrination of the wives and female family member of the Chilean working classes. The Centers became more hierarchical, with greater centralized control over their work. Classes were taught by military wives or wives of Pinochet administration officials, with a focus on giving lower-class women instruction to foster their moral, physical, and intellectual development. Candidates wanting to join a local center had to be nominated by an older member. Women over age 18, married women, and/or mothers were eligible for membership. Post Dictatorship On November 22, 1989, a few months before the end of the dictatorship, Lucía Hiriart changed the statutes governing CEMA Chile that named the first lady as automatic head of the organization. This change was designed to impede Leonor Oyarzún, the wife of president elect Patricio Aylwin, from becoming the new CEMA president when she assumed her role as first lady of Chile. Instead, Hiriart changed the statue to make the new CEMA foundation president be the wife of the head of the armed forces, a position she herself would occupy because Pinochet remained head of the armed forces even after Aylwin assumed the presidency in 1990. Up until 2005, CEMA Chile, by law, still received funding from the Chilean lottery, estimated at more than US$280 million. In May 2006, the Chilean congress passed a lay that suspended the use of public funds for CEMA, instead directing them to other charitable functions. In December 2018, the Chilean government's Minister of National Assets sought the return of all public lands transferred to CEMA during the Pinochet Dictatorship with a total value of at least $6.5 million US dollars. title: The Political Lives of Dead Bodies: Reburial and Postsocialist Change
text: The Political Lives of Dead Bodies: Reburial and Postsocialist Change is a 1999 book by the American anthropologist Katherine Verdery. The book as a project started with lectures the author gave at Columbia University's Harriman Institute in December 1997. Verdery asks why the exhumation, repatriation and reburial of corpses (along with the toppling of statues) became so widespread in Eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union after the end of communist rule. She argues that corpses, concrete objects open to many readings, served to rewrite national histories and to press claims to property, territory and moral authority. After a survey of cases and a theoretical chapter, the book presents two case studies: the 1997 reburial in Blaj, Romania, of the eighteenth-century Greek Catholic bishop Inochentie Micu-Klein, and the exhumation and reburial of anonymous dead in the former Yugoslavia. A Romanian translation titled "Viața politică a trupurilor moarte. Înhumare și schimbare postsocialistă" and translated by Liviu Chelcea was published in 2006. Summary The book is short, made up of an introduction and three chapters, and is illustrated with photographs of toppled statues, reburials and exhumations. Verdey starts with a question: why the postsocialist period has "been accompanied by so much activity around dead bodies, and what does the politics concerning them signify?" The introduction, “Corpses on the Move”, assembles what Verdery calls “a parade of dead bodies”. She starts with statues, which to her are bodies in bronze and stone: the Lenin taken down from its pedestal in Bucharest, the statue of Felix Dzerzhinsky hoisted by crane in Moscow, the monuments gathered in Budapest's Statue Park, and a Lenin statue that crowds in Yerevan drove around the central square as if in an open coffin. Most of the bodies she discusses are real, though, and many of them famous. Émigrés were brought home: the composer Béla Bartók from New York, the generals Władysław Sikorski and Tadeusz Bór-Komorowski from Britain. About a quarter of a million people watched Imre Nagy reburied in Budapest in June 1989. Russians argued over whether to bury Lenin's embalmed body, and over the remains of Nicholas II and his family. Before the 600th anniversary of the Battle of Kosovo, the bones of the medieval Serbian Prince Lazar were carried through monasteries in lands claimed for Serbia. The rest are anonymous: victims of communist prisons and labour camps, the Polish officers killed at Katyn, and the skeletons taken from limestone caves in Yugoslavia. Verdery sets these cases beside those of Oedipus, Dante, Eva Perón and Ferdinand Marcos. She says at the outset that she will offer no single explanation for them. Corpses, Verdery argues, make effective political symbols because they combine material presence with ambiguity: “Dead people come with a curriculum vitae or résumé—several possible résumés, depending on which aspect of their life is being considered.” They cannot contradict the words put in their mouths, and they evoke the sacred and the questions death raises about the order of the universe. She cites Susan Gal, who found five rival readings of Nagy's reburial. Verdery calls the end of party rule a “reordering of people’s entire meaningful worlds”, and corpses did part of that work. They made authority sacred and assigned blame and compensation. They also changed what places and dates meant, and helped redefine national identity. Drawing on Meyer Fortes, Edmund Leach and Benedict Anderson, she argues that nationalism is “a kind of ancestor worship”, a patrilineal kinship system in which national heroes take the place of clan elders. She connects reburial to beliefs in the region about proper burial, including the restless dead and vampires, and to the worldwide movement to repatriate “cultural treasures”. title: United Nations General Assembly Resolution 76/262
text: United Nations General Assembly Resolution 76/262 is a resolution adopted by consensus (without a formal vote) by the UN General Assembly on 26 April 2022. It was introduced by Liechtenstein and co-sponsored by 83 member states. It establishes a permanent, mandatory mechanism that triggers a debate in the General Assembly whenever a permanent member of the UN Security Council exercises its veto power. The document was first proposed more than two years prior to its adoption. The proposal's revival has been linked to Russia's use of veto power in the context of the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Provisions Resolution 76/262 consists of an eight-paragraph preamble and a five-paragraph operative part. The document stipulates that the General Assembly will be required "to hold a debate on the situation" that sparks a veto in the Security Council within 10 working days. Precedence will be given on the list of speakers to the permanent member having cast a veto. Analysis Although the resolution does not explicitly impose an obligation on the permanent member or members that have exercised their right of veto, the decision is nonetheless a way of imposing greater accountability for veto use. title: The Piano Factory
text: The Piano Factory, also known as 454 W 46th Street, is a six-story residential co-op building in the Hell's Kitchen, Manhattan neighborhood of New York City. It is named after the Wessell, Nickel & Gross factory, which had occupied 457 W 45th Street beginning in 1874 and gradually expanded to adjacent buildings thereafter. History In its heyday, the Wessell, Nickel & Gross factory was one of the largest manufacturers of piano actions in the United States. (The current building's name is thus a misnomer, as no whole pianos were ever manufactured in the building; however, the building was commonly referred to as "the piano factory" by neighborhood residents prior to conversion.) The company began as a partnership among Otto Wessell, Adam Nickel, and Rudolph Gross, one American and two German immigrants, respectively, who had worked at the Steinway & Sons piano factory. Their factories occupied four lots (at 455, 457, 459, 461) on West 45th Street, two lots (636, 638) on 10th Avenue, and four more (452, 454, 456, 458) on West 46th Street. The office was located in the original building at 457 West 45th Street. The factory also maintained lumber yards at 446, 447, 449, 451, 453 West 45th Street and 533, 535, 537 West 48th Street. Some of the lumber yard properties were sold off in the 1940s, and none are associated with the modern residential building. The current West 46th Street building was constructed in 1888, on the site of what had been a German Baptist Church. The Great Depression was hard on the piano market. In December 1932, Wessell, Nickel & Gross contributed $100 to a New York City emergency unemployment relief fund. Unable to pay bills, Wessell, Nickel, & Gross entered into bankruptcy, and much of their action-making equipment was purchased from the bankruptcy court by the Aeolian Piano Corporation. Aeolian effectively absorbed the Wessell, Nickel, & Gross name and reputation, while relocating production to Rochester, New York. The name "Wessell, Nickel, and Gross" was acquired in 1953 by two brothers, Kirk and Gary Burgett, and the company now exists in Sacramento, California. Co-op Renovation In the late 1970s, the 70,000 square foot site was purchased by Richard A. Klein and Charles P. West, two former bankers. They divided the 60,000 square feet of usable space into 49 apartments, 48 of which were listed in 1981 for between $92,000 and $230,000, with one retained for a live-in superintendent. Ceiling heights vary by floor, between 9 and 14 feet, and the developers retained the building's original nineteenth-century oak and maple floors. Appliances were included, but there were no medicine cabinets in the original design. West told the New York Times, "Our option was for big mirrors instead." At the time of conversion, the neighborhood was considered "marginal," which impacted the original development financing. Klein and West were able to get construction financing for a project that had a total cash offering of $6.1 million from an investment subsidiary of the Bank of Credit and Commerce International, based in London, which served as a vehicle for Middle Eastern Capital, a limited partner venture. In 1981, the building was the largest market-rate offering in the neighborhood. It was also one of the few at that time to be converted under Clinton Preservation District code, designed to promote the creation of larger, family-friendly units by stipulating that any multiple dwelling must have the same number of bedrooms as apartments. title: Richmond Library
text: Richmond Library is a library on Little Green in Richmond, London. Its main building, completed in 1881, is Grade II listed. Since 1987, it has housed only the lending library, while the reference library is in the Old Town Hall. Background Precursors A small library had existed from 1838, opened for the Richmond Mechanics' Institute on Church Walk. In 1843, plans were put forward for the opening of a theatre in Richmond to host concerts and performances which had until then been held in various venues. The site of the former town pond was chosen, with construction and completion later that year of what is now known as the Dome Buildings. Provision was made to house a new museum and the Mechanics' Institute library; however, following an inability for the institute to pay off its debt, it was disbanded. The building then held the Richmond Baths until 1863. Rev. Harry Dupuis, vicar of Richmond, held a meeting in 1855 for the creation of a Parochial Reading Room. It was opened in the National Schools (today the Christ's School) on the corner of Eton Street and Paradise Road. By 1878 the National Schools suggested the library vacate their premises as they were needed fro use by the school. The reading room was therefore moved to 2 The Quadrant, and coexisted for some time with the Richmond public Library, with operations finally ceasing by 1888. Origins of the public Library The Public Libraries Act 1850 (13 & 14 Vict. c. 65) and the subsequent Public Libraries Act 1855 (18 & 19 Vict. c. 70) first gave local authorities the abilities to create free public libraries. London's outer boroughs were generally slow to adopt the act, with Richmond being one of the first following the encouragement of Edward King who published a supportive leader in the Richmond and Twickenham Times. Its library was therefore described by Nikolaus Pevsner as "the first library in outer London". History and description The building, erected on an unoccupied site facing onto Richmond Green, was designed by F. S. Brunton in a Gothic Revival style. The newly completed library was opened in 1881 by Frances Russell, Countess Russell. It is of a red-brick frontage with sandstone dressings and has a pointed arch entranceway. The library was an immediate success and required expansion, first in 1886 with an extension opened by Princess Mary Adelaide with her husband Francis, Duke of Teck and daughter Mary of Teck present. It was expanded again in 1905 with the incorporation of "The Cottage", a house to the north. The current Richmond Theatre was built next door in 1899. For 30 years Albert Barkas, a prominent local historian, served as the Librarian. From early on there were suggestions that a museum be built on the grounds of the library, although no such plan ever materialised. The current Museum of Richmond was opened in 1988 in the old Richmond Town Hall building. The library was Grade II listed in 2003 for its historical and architectural significance; Historic England's listing entry describes it as the "earliest public library in London still in use as such". Refurbishments and restoration works were carried out in 1976, 1978 and in 2021 when the building was closed for renovation including repairs resulting from Second World War bomb damage. The local studies section was moved in the 1980s to join the borough's central reference library in the Old Town Hall, housed with the Museum of Richmond.

title: Joel Bichsel
text: Joel Bichsel (born 4 March 2002) is a Swiss professional footballer who plays as a centre back for FC Lugano. Club career Born in Olten in the Canton of Solothurn, Bichsel joined the youth ranks of BSC Young Boys in 2015. On 4 August 2023, he was loaned to SC Freiburg II in the German 3. Liga. On 27 August 2024, Bichsel signed on a contract of undisclosed length with 1. FC Saarbrücken, also in Germany's third tier. He played 34 games in his first season, and scored on 22 October 2024 to open a 2–0 win at home to FC Hansa Rostock; his team reached the promotion/relegation playoff with the 2. Bundesliga but lost in extra time to Eintracht Braunschweig. In 2025–26, the club won the Saarland Cup; he scored in an 8–0 win away to FC Kandil in the quarter-finals, and played in the 4–2 final win over FC 08 Homburg in the final on 23 May. Bichsel returned to Switzerland on 2 June 2026, signing a three-year deal at Swiss Super League club FC Lugano. International career In 2023, Bichsel played one match for the Switzerland national under-20 team and four matches for the under-21 team. Personal life Bichsel's younger brother Lian Bichsel is a professional ice hockey player for the Dallas Stars of the National Hockey League. References

title: 2028 United States House of Representatives elections in Georgia
text: The 2028 United States House of Representatives elections in Georgia will be held on November 7, 2028, to elect the 14 U.S. representatives from the state of Georgia, one from each of the state's congressional districts. The elections will coincide with other elections to the House of Representatives, the presidential election, elections to the United States Senate, and various state and local elections. The primary elections are to be determined. District 1 The 1st district is based in the southeast corner of the state, encompassing Savannah. title: Symplocos paucistaminea
text: Symplocos paucistaminea is a species of plant in the family Symplocaceae, native to New Guinea and northeast Queensland, Australia. It is a rainforest tree, first described in 1890, and has a conservation status of least concern. Description Symplocos paucistaminea is a tree up to 18 m (59 ft) tall. The leaf-bearing twigs petioles are covered in long, rusty-brown hairs. The leaves are simple and may be toothed. They measure up to 28 cm (11 in) long and 10 cm (3.9 in) wide, and are hairy on both sides. The inflorescence is a spike up to 5 cm (2.0 in) long, carrying small flowers about 3 mm (0.12 in) long, which have five cream or white petals. The fruit is a purple or blue drupe about 7 mm (0.3 in) long and 6 mm (0.2 in) wide, containing a single brown seed. Distribution and habitat This species grows in mature rainforest from Mount Bellenden Ker to the area near Millaa Millaa, where it occurs as an understory shrub or tree. The altitudinal range is from 500 to 1,075 m (1,640 to 3,527 ft). Taxonomy It was first described by botanists Ferdinand von Mueller and Frederick Manson Bailey in supplement three to the book A synopsis of the Queensland flora; containing both the phaenogamous and cryptogamous plants. They based the description on material collected during an earlier expedition to Mount Bellenden Ker. Conservation status This species was assessed by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) in 2018 and found to be of least concern. It is also rated as least concern by the Queensland Government under its Nature Conservation Act. In its statement, the IUCN cites the species' wide distribution and the lack of any perceived threats to it, as the basis for the assessment. The WildNet database does not provide any explanations for its assessments.

title: Technopolis (Japan)
text: The Technopolis program was a regional development plan and policy in Japan. The term 'technopolis' was coined in Japan. It was conceptualized in the eighth chapter of a report by the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI). Technopolises were "high-technology-oriented industrial complexes" that would be established in and around existing "mother" cities with at least 150,000 residents. Site selection criteria also included the ability to utilize existing physical infrastructure, therefore requiring minimal new public investment to improve it. Technopolis cities were also expected to have a university or college in the region for collaboration with industry. The program was implemented from the 1980s to the 1990s. Although guided by MITI, it relied on local governments. The plan's focus was on facility construction rather than research and development itself. History In 1980, MITI proposed Technopolis as a concept for demonstration in limited key cities. However, a majority of the prefectures' governments submitted proposals, leading to a rapid expansion of the pilot project. Versions of the plan were developed in 1981 and 1982. The Law for Accelerating Regional Development Based Upon High-Technology Industrial Complexes (Technopolis Law) was passed in 1983. Formal Technopolis construction began in 1984. The plan's target date for creating the new regional centers was 1990. The Technopolis program was discontinued in 1998. Structure The plan largely depended on private or local government funding. In the first few years, MITI's annual budget for the Technopolis program was less than 10 million dollars. Regional governments had to develop implementation plans, which would then have to be approved by MITI. Once the 'technopolis' designation was granted, MITI would assist regional governments with planning, management, and limited financial incentives. The program did not provide opportunities for technology transfers. So rather than pursuing the "endogenous development" of local enterprises, most Technopolis regions would invite "outside enterprises" to build facilities. Target industries The following eight "high-tech" industries were targeted in the Technopolis Plan: pharmaceuticals telecommunications and related equipment computers and related equipment electronic application devices electric measuring instruments electronics and telecommunication parts medical equipment and supplies optical instruments and lenses References

title: Crown and Anchor, Llanidloes
text: The Crown and Anchor is a Grade II listed public house on Long Bridge Street in Llanidloes, a town in Powys, Wales. Incorporating a 17th-century structure behind an early 19th-century frontage, it is recognised by the Campaign for Real Ale (CAMRA) for its historic interior, which is included on the National Inventory of Historic Pub Interiors with a three-star rating. Following its closure in 2022, the pub was acquired by new owners in 2025, who announced plans to restore and reopen it. History The building has an early 19th-century frontage incorporating a 17th-century two-storey structure. One of the pub's rooms formerly served as a haberdashery and remained in that use until around 1948, when it was incorporated into the licensed premises. The pub is locally known as "Ruby's" after a long-serving landlady who retired in 2018. It had remained in the same family for more than 200 years. On 10 April 1989, the Crown and Anchor was designated a Grade II listed building. It is regarded by the Campaign for Real Ale (CAMRA) as having an interior of "outstanding national historic importance" and is rated three stars on its National Inventory of Historic Pub Interiors. The Crown and Anchor closed in 2022, with rising operating costs cited as a contributing factor. In October 2025, the pub was purchased by new owners, bringing to an end a community campaign to acquire the building through the Crown and Anchor Community Benefit Society. The new owners subsequently announced plans to restore and reopen the pub independently, and repair works were carried out ahead of a proposed reopening in 2026. Architecture Exterior The building is a two-storey structure with a late Georgian three-window rendered frontage and a slate roof. The front elevation retains sash windows at first-floor level, while the ground floor includes a tripartite window and a large former bar window flanking the main entrance. To the right is a long range constructed of rubble stone with later projecting sections and a varied slate and corrugated roof. Exposed timber framing survives at the rear above a covered passageway. Interior The interior is arranged as five small rooms separated by a corridor with half-height panelling. The former public bar retains a bar counter dating from the early 20th century, historic mirrored bar-back shelving, fixed bench seating and a glazed screen with surviving lettering. Elsewhere, timber-and-glass partitions retain small service hatches and sliding ventilation windows, while historic features include original wall panelling, advertising mirrors and a tiled fireplace dating from the 1950s. Although much of the interior has been modernised, some historic timber beams survive. A large fireplace and an opening leading to a bread oven in the cellar also remain, suggesting that part of the building may formerly have been used as a kitchen.

title: Waldemar Roszkiewicz
text: Waldemar Cezary Roszkiewicz (24 February 1957 – 1 November 2026) was a Polish dentist and politician. Life and career Roszkiewicz graduated from the Medical Academy in Łódź, before completing a postgraduate MBA studies at the Leon Koźmiński Academy in Warsaw, as well as Postgraduate Management Studies for Public Administration at the Faculty of Management of the University of Warsaw. From 1982 to 1987, he was the head of the Garrison Dental Outpatient Clinic in Trzebiatów, and from 1987 to 1997, senior assistant at the Maxillofacial Surgery Clinic of the Military Medical Academy Dentistry Institute. From 1997 to 2003, he ran a dental office, and from 2003 to 2004, he was the director of the Provincial Dental Center in Warsaw. Since 1994, he was a supernumerary of Opus Dei. From 2004 to 2005, he was a member of the board of the Masovian Voivodeship; from 2005 to 2006, he served as deputy marshal of the voivodeship; after the 2006 elections, he again took the position of board member, a position he held until 2010. He then became the liquidator of the Provincial Dental Center in Warsaw, and later became deputy mayor of Ożarów Mazowiecki. Until 2006, he was affiliated with the League of Polish Families, but formally he was not a member. He unsuccessfully ran for the Sejm in 2005 and for the Masovian Voivodeship assembly in 2006. In 2006, he joined the Polish People's Party. From 2008 to 2010, he was a member of the party's provincial board. He ran from the PSL list for the European Parliament in 2009 and 2014, for the Masovian regional assembly in 2010, and in 2011 for the Sejm. Roszkiewicz died on 1 November 2026, at the age of 69. title: Bystrytsa, Astravyets district
text: Bystrytsa (Belarusian: Быстрыца, romanized: Bystryca; Russian: Быстрица, romanized: Bystritsa; Lithuanian: Bistryčia) is an agrotown in Astravyets District, Grodno Region, Belarus. It was established at least in the 14th century and is one of the oldest settlements in the Astravyets District. History Bystrytsa developed near a river rapid of the same name. The settlement is mentioned as early as 1390 as a possession of Jogaila, King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania. At that time, the first Catholic church was built, and an Augustinians Monastery was established. Historically, river tolls were collected at Bystrytsa, and overland routes to Buivydžiai passed through the settlement. It is one of the oldest settlements in the Astravyets District. In 1760–1761, the Vilnian Baroque style Catholic Church of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, designed by renowned architect Johann Christoph Glaubitz, was constructed in Bystrytsa. At the beginning of the 19th century, a significant number of Lithuanians still lived in Bystrytsa, and the village belonged to the Zavileyka Powiat. By the end of the 19th century, it had become a small town and the centre of the Bystrytsa Volost within the Vilna Governorate. In 2010, Bystrytsa had 154 inhabitants. References

title: Kimberly Harmon
text: Kimberly G. Harmon is an American sports medicine physician and academic. She is the Chief Medical Officer of the National Hockey League (NHL), a post she has held since July 2026; she previously served as the league's deputy chief medical officer. She is a professor in the Departments of Family Medicine and Orthopaedics and Sports Medicine at the University of Washington (UW), where she heads the sports medicine section and has been the head team physician for the Washington Huskies football team since 2012. Her research on sudden cardiac death, sickle cell trait and concussion in athletes has informed policy in college sport. She was president of the American Medical Society for Sports Medicine (AMSSM) from 2009 to 2010. Early life and education Harmon attended the University of Notre Dame, where she played on the women's basketball team in 1986–87 and worked as a student athletic trainer from 1986 to 1989. She was then head athletic trainer at Saint Mary's College from 1989 to 1991. She earned her medical degree from the Indiana University School of Medicine. She completed a family medicine residency at Memorial Hospital in South Bend, Indiana, and a sports medicine fellowship at Ball Memorial Hospital in Muncie, Indiana. She is board certified in family medicine with added qualification in sports medicine. Career University of Washington Harmon joined the University of Washington in 1998. She is a professor in the Departments of Family Medicine and Orthopedics and Sports Medicine and head of the sports medicine section. She directed the UW sports medicine fellowship from 2004 to 2014. At UW she has been a team physician for football, women's basketball, women's volleyball, track and field, cross country, softball, baseball and swimming. She became head football physician in 2012. Oregon State University described her as the second woman to serve as a football physician in a Power Five conference. Collegiate athletics Harmon served on the NCAA Committee on Competitive Safeguards and Medical Aspects of Sports from 2003 to 2007. She later joined NCAA task forces and its Concussion Advisory Group, and developed the UW NCAA Athlete Death Database. From 2015 to 2020 she represented UW on the Pac-12 Student-Athlete Health and Well-Being Board, which she chaired from 2017 to 2019. In that role she guided a conference-wide injury and illness surveillance system covering more than 6,000 athletes at 12 universities. She became the Pac-12's research development director in 2020, overseeing grants for student-athlete health research. Oregon State put the total funding at $18 million. She is also a member of the Knight Commission on Intercollegiate Athletics. Professional sports and other advisory roles Harmon was a medical advisor to the National Basketball Players Association from 2014 to 2019. She sits on the NFL's Head, Neck and Spine Committee. By early 2025 she was deputy chief medical officer of the National Hockey League. She became the league's chief medical officer in July 2026. She serves on the medical advisory boards of the Nick of Time Foundation, Parent Heart Watch and Who We Play For. Research Sudden cardiac death With Jonathan Drezner and others, Harmon studied sudden cardiac death (SCD) in NCAA athletes. A 2011 study in Circulation identified deaths from 2004 to 2008 using an NCAA database, media searches and insurance claims. It estimated an annual SCD rate of about 1 in 43,770 athletes, higher than earlier estimates, with greater risk for Black athletes and basketball players. A 2015 follow-up covering 2003–2013 reported an SCD rate of 1 in 5,200 athlete-years in Division I men's basketball. It found autopsy-negative sudden unexplained death more often than hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. She was a co-author of a 2024 Circulation study covering 20 years of data, which found that SCD incidence in college athletes had declined. She has co-authored multiple other studies analyzing death rates in athletes. Sickle cell trait

title: Findings (journal)
text: Findings is a peer-reviewed, open-access academic journal published by Findings Press in Australia. It publishes short research articles on transportation, cities, energy, resilience, and safety. The general editor is David Levinson of the University of Sydney. History The journal was founded by David Levinson. It began publication in 2019 as Transport Findings. It was renamed Findings in 2020. The new title reflected an expansion beyond transportation research to include urban studies. Its subject sections include Transport Findings, Urban Findings, Energy Findings, Resilience Findings, and Safety Findings. Publication model Articles are limited to 1,000 words, excluding references, and have three main sections: Questions, Methods, and Findings. Separate introductions, literature reviews, and conclusions are omitted. In a 2020 interview, Levinson said that the short format was intended to reduce the time needed to write and review research papers. Ann Forsyth describes Findings as a micro-publication journal in urban planning. Abstracting and indexing The journal is listed in the Directory of Open Access Journals and indexed in Scopus.

title: Symplocos hylandii
text: Symplocos hylandii is a species of plant in the family Symplocaceae, native to northeast Queensland, Australia. It is a rainforest tree, first described in 1982, and has a conservation status of least concern. Description Symplocos hylandii is a shrub or small tree up to 6 m (20 ft) tall. The young twigs and shoots are sparsely hairy, the leaves are simple and may be toothed. They measure up to 15 cm (5.9 in) long and 4.5 cm (1.8 in) wide, and young leaves may be hairy on the underside. The inflorescence is a spike up to 2 cm (0.8 in) long, carrying small flowers about 3 mm (0.12 in) long, which have five cream or white petals. The fruit is a purple or blue drupe about 12 mm (0.5 in) long and 9 mm (0.4 in) wide, containing a single brown seed. Distribution and habitat This species grows in mature rainforest from Mount Bellenden Ker to the area near Millaa Millaa, where it occurs as an understory shrub or tree. The altitudinal range is from 500 to 1,075 m (1,640 to 3,527 ft). Taxonomy It was first described by Dutch botanist Hans Peter Nooteboom in 1982, based on material collected by Bernard Hyland. Conservation status This species is listed as least concern in the Queensland Government's WildNet database. As of November 2026, it has not been assessed by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

title: Attack on Mohamed Yusuf
text: On November 14, 2026, Mohamed Yusuf, a 51-year-old Somali American Uber driver, was critically injured during a ride in Hopkins, Minnesota, a suburb of Minneapolis. Prosecutors allege that his passenger, 25-year-old Samit Apurva Patel, strangled Yusuf with a seat belt and ran him over with Yusuf's own vehicle, shortly after telling him he did not like the name Mohamed. Patel was charged with attempted second-degree murder and first-degree carjacking. Yusuf's family and the Minnesota chapter of the Council on American–Islamic Relations (CAIR-MN) described the attack as a hate crime and called for it to be investigated as one. Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said her office did not have sufficient evidence to prove that the attack was motivated by bias. The attack drew national and international news coverage and prompted vigils and rallies in Minneapolis–Saint Paul. Background News coverage placed the attack in the context of hostile rhetoric toward Minnesota's Somali community, including repeated disparaging remarks about Somali immigrants by President Donald Trump. In October 2026, Trump wrote on Truth Social that Minnesota was being taken over by Somali immigrants, and several candidates in that year's midterm elections ran advertisements depicting Somali Minnesotans as fraudsters. The president of the Minnesota Uber/Lyft Drivers Association said that a growing number of drivers of Somali or Muslim background had reported harassment before the attack. Attack The following account is drawn from the criminal complaint filed by Hennepin County prosecutors, as described in news reports. According to Uber records, Yusuf picked up Patel near a bar in northeast Minneapolis at 12:47 a.m. on Saturday, November 14, 2026. Yusuf was on a phone call with his brother, who also drives for Uber; the two often talked during their shifts. The brother told police he heard the passenger ask Yusuf his name and, on hearing the answer, reply, "I don't like that name." The brother said that Yusuf brushed the remark off and told him the passenger was drunk. About two blocks from Patel's home, the passenger told Yusuf to turn, and the two argued about the destination. The brother then heard Yusuf screaming in Somali that he was being choked with a belt and, afterward, that he was being run over. GPS data showed that Yusuf's Toyota RAV4 stopped for several minutes on Hopkins Crossroad at about 1:05 a.m., then crossed the northbound lanes and entered a ditch at 1:07 a.m., leaving it about 20 seconds later. The vehicle then passed the spot where Yusuf lay, stopped at a gas station for about two minutes, passed the spot again, and was driven to the home of Patel's parents. At about 1:20 a.m., Patel's parents called Hopkins police to request a welfare check, saying their son had come home intoxicated, confused, and distressed, and was afraid of an unfamiliar vehicle parked outside. Officers found the RAV4 running and unoccupied, with damage to its front and rear, and found a phone inside still connected to the call with Yusuf's brother. Police traced the last known location of Yusuf's smartwatch to the area of Hopkins Crossroad and Minnetonka Boulevard, where a police drone detected a heat signature. Yusuf was found in a ditch about fifteen feet (4.6 m) from the road, with tire tracks leading into and out of it. Before charges were filed, Yusuf's relatives had given a similar account to The Somali Brief, saying the passenger objected to Yusuf's name, choked him with a seat belt, and ran him over several times. Victim Mohamed Yusuf, 51, of Blaine, Minnesota, is a Somali American father of five who had driven taxis and rideshare vehicles for years. According to the criminal complaint, Yusuf sustained broken ribs, a broken leg, spinal injuries, collapsed lungs, and internal bleeding that required the removal of organs; the complaint described his prognosis as poor. title: Jetzen López
text: Jetzen Riley López (born 14 January 2007) is a professional footballer who plays as an midfielder for Braga. Born in Australia, he has represented Australia internationally at youth level and has been called up to represent Chile internationally. Early life López was born on 14 January 2007 to a Chilean father and an Australian mother. Born in Australia, he grew up in Perth, Australia. Club career As a youth player, López joined the youth academy of Australian sideMJ Soccer Academy. Following his stint there, he joined the youth academy of Vitória de Setúbal in Portugal. Ahead of the 2024–25 season, he joined the youth academy of Portuguese outfit Braga. International career López is an Australia youth international and has been called up to represent Chile internationally. During the summer of 2025, he played for the Australia men's national under-18 soccer team at the 2025 UEFA Friendship Cup. Style of play López plays as a midfielder. Chilean news website wrote in 2026 that "López is a versatile midfielder, left-footed but also using his right. His greatest strengths are his technique, vision, and ability to link up with his teammates".

title: Wayne Hollowell
text: Wayne Hollowell is an American painter based in Northern Virginia who makes colorful acrylic portraits of classic Hollywood actresses, television stars and camp figures. In 2025 his paintings were used for the covers of six reissued volumes of filmmaker John Waters's early screenplays from Picador. He has exhibited in New York City, Baltimore, Washington, D.C., and Provincetown, Massachusetts. Early life Hollowell grew up in Rocky Mount, North Carolina. He has said that his mother, a teacher, found out about the North Carolina School of the Arts' high school art program, which he entered at age 15. He told Baltimore Fishbowl that a teacher there gave him Waters's book Shock Value, and that he later saw Female Trouble at a midnight screening while at art school in Atlanta. In interviews he has also said that he attended film school at New York University, lived in New York City in the 1990s, and made early films that starred the future drag performer RuPaul. Career New York In June 2013 Hollowell held a solo show, Drama Queen, at Michael Mut Gallery on Avenue C in the East Village. Bedford + Bowery called him a "Southern pop artist" and described his saturated portraits of figures such as Liberace and Elizabeth Taylor in Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?. Provincetown In 2023 the Post Office Cafe and Cabaret in Provincetown, Massachusetts, hung 18 of his paintings for sale. His portraits of Liza Minnelli, Patti LuPone and Barbra Streisand hang there, with more due in 2026. On May 15, 2026, he was one of six artists in the opening exhibition of ShowQueen Gallery in Provincetown, which announced a solo show of his work, The Wicked Womb, for August 7, 2026. Baltimore and Washington Hollowell showed Waters-themed paintings at The Club Car, a Baltimore bar, during Artscape 2023, and nine such works appeared that year at the Bmore Queer-Scape Gallery. His work was also displayed at Everyman Theatre in Baltimore during its 2025 production of The Mystery of Irma Vep. During WorldPride 2025 in Washington, D.C., his portraits of Dorothy Zbornak and Sophia Petrillo from The Golden Girls hung in a Pride suite at the Kimpton Hotel Monaco, and portraits of Minnelli, Alyssa Edwards, RuPaul and Judy Garland were offered for sale at the hotel's restaurant, Dirty Habit. The Washington Blade called him a "local LGBTQ artist." John Waters screenplay covers Waters has said he usually picks fan art for his book covers and found Hollowell's work online. GO Magazine reported that Waters noticed Hollowell's paintings of Divine at the Club Car and asked the owner who made them, then wrote to Hollowell through the contact form on his website in 2024. Hollowell thought it was a prank. With Waters and Picador art director Alex Merto, Hollowell produced covers for six screenplay volumes, each published on its own for the first time after earlier collected editions. Four of the covers use paintings he had already made; two, for Multiple Maniacs and Flamingos Forever, were painted for the project. Pink Flamingos, Desperate Living and Flamingos Forever were published May 27, 2025, and Multiple Maniacs, Female Trouble and Hairspray followed on October 21. It was the first time Hollowell had made book covers. Style and subjects Hollowell works mainly in acrylic on canvas, often in square formats such as 36 by 36 inches. His subjects are mostly women of film and television, among them Joan Crawford, Cher, Judy Garland, Liza Minnelli, Elizabeth Taylor and Diana, Princess of Wales, and characters from shows such as The Golden Girls, Designing Women and Dynasty. Characters from Waters's films recur. He has also painted a series of deceased adult film performers, each labeled with its subject's cause of death. He has named Andy Warhol, Waters, the duo McDermott & McGough, Patrick Angus and Tabboo! as influences. title: 2028 United States House of Representatives elections in South Carolina
text: The 2028 United States House of Representatives elections in South Carolina will be held on November 7, 2028, to elect the 7 U.S. representatives from the state of South Carolina, one from each of the state's congressional districts. The elections will coincide with other elections to the House of Representatives, the presidential election, elections to the United States Senate, and various state and local elections. The primary elections are to be determined. District 1 The 1st district straddles the Atlantic coast of the state, and includes most of Charleston. The incumbent is Democrat Nancy Lacore, who flipped the seat and was elected with 49.7% of the vote in 2026. title: Leonardo Mosso
text: Leonardo Mosso (1926 – 14 December 2020) was an Italian architect and artist. Biography The son of the architect Nicola Mosso, Leonardo was born in Turin in 1926 into a family originally from the Biella area. He graduated in architecture in Turin in 1951 and began his professional career alongside his father. Inspired by reading Space, Time and Architecture by Sigfried Giedion, Mosso moved to Finland with the aim of working with Alvar Aalto. He spent some time as an international student at the Helsinki University of Technology before joining Aalto's architectural practice as an intern, helped by a letter of introduction from Ernesto Nathan Rogers. He worked there until 1959 and, from 1964, collaborated with Aalto as an equal partner on the Finnish architect's projects in Italy. Their collaboration continued until Aalto's death in 1976. While working with Aalto, Mosso continued his involvement in his father's architectural practice. In 1957, together with his father and the engineer Livio Norzi, he designed the church of Gesù Redentore in Turin. In the late 1950s, he collaborated with the engineer Gustavo Colonnetti, who had also commissioned the project, on the design of the Benedetto Croce Library in Pollone. In 1962, he designed the Cappella per la Messa dell'artista (Chapel for the Artists' Mass), a work based on a repetitive and transformable structure. It was one of the early results of his research into structural design, which he continued to develop in subsequent years. Alongside his architectural practice, Mosso taught at the Polytechnic University of Turin, initially in ornamental sculpture and later in social architecture and architectural composition. He held these teaching positions until the 1986–1987 academic year, when he resigned from the university. He subsequently continued teaching, mainly abroad, in Berlin, Rotterdam and Karlsruhe. His teaching went hand in hand with his research into design theory. Mosso focused on the relationship between structural elements and their joints, experimenting with structures composed of rigid or flexible elements connected by mechanical, elastic or movable joints. His research involved a continuous interplay between theoretical work and practical experimentation. It also extended to automated design and spatial planning. The models developed by Mosso gradually became independent works and were eventually exhibited as art installations and works of art in their own right. In 1969, Mosso was selected by Umbro Apollonio to represent Italy alongside Getulio Alviani and Gianni Colombo at the first Biennial of Constructive Art in Nuremberg. In addition to his architectural, research and artistic activities, Mosso was involved in the cultural life of Turin. In 1953, he was among the founders of the association behind the National Museum of Cinema in Turin, and in 1979 he founded the Alvar Aalto Institute in Pino Torinese. The institute later developed, in conjunction with the MAAAD, into the Museum of Architecture, Applied Arts and Design. Mosso was also involved in designing the Museum of the Resistance within the National Museum of the Italian Risorgimento at Palazzo Carignano. The exhibition used a modular system that he had patented under the name Mosstrut. His Nuvola Rossa (Red Cloud), a suspended structure covering approximately 400 square metres and consisting of red-painted wooden strips connected by elastic neoprene joints, was installed in the chamber of the former Subalpine Parliament. From the late 1970s onwards, his experimental works were presented at several exhibitions in Italy and abroad. A selection of his works also entered the collections of the Centre Pompidou in Paris, where they were exhibited in a dedicated space. In 2017, Mosso was appointed an honorary member of the Society of Engineers and Architects in Turin. He was also an honorary member of the Associazione per il Disegno Industriale (Association for Industrial Design). Mosso died on 14 December 2020

title: Lophoproctus
text: Lophoproctus is a genus of millipedes that belongs to the family Lophoproctidae. Members of the family can be found in Eurasia ranging from Portugal to Central Asia and Northern Africa. They have a pale-yellow coloration. They have lengths that are almost equal to the widths of their heads being several millimeters long. They have very long antennae and do not possess eyes. This genus has a possible fossil record with a female and three other possible representatives being found described in Dominican amber. Taxonomy The genus was described in 1895 by British zoologist Reginald Innes Pocock where it was described as the type genus of the family Lophoproctidae. The specimens he used to describe the genus were collected from soil at Nervi in Liguria, Italy. The genus are millipedes that belong to the order Polyxenida, commonly known as bristly millipedes. Species The genus currently contains six described species which are listed below: Lophoproctus coecus Pocock, 1895 Lophoproctus israelensis Short, 2020 Lophoproctus jeanneli (Brölemann, 1910) Lophoproctus lucidus (Chalande, 1888) Lophoproctus pagesi Condé, 1981 Lophoproctus viator Rodríguez-Flores & Giribet, 2024 References

title: 2021 WPT Córdoba Open
text: The 2021 Córdoba Open (officially 2021 World Padel Tour Cervezas Victoria Córdoba Open) was the fifteenth tournament of the ninth season organized by World Padel Tour, the most prestigious padel circuit at the time. In the women's category, the top two ranked pairs reached the final, facing each other for the fourth time in a title match. The first finalists were the world number ones, Alejandra Salazar and Gemma Triay, who defeated Aranzazu Osoro and Victoria Iglesias in the semi-finals. Their opponents were the second-ranked pair, Ariana Sánchez and Paula Josemaria, who reached the final by eliminating the third-ranked pair, Lucia Sainz and Marta Marrero. In the decisive match, Gemma and Salazar defeated Ariana and Paula in three sets, securing their eighth title of the season. With this victory, besides claiming their first title in Córdoba, Gemma and Salazar mathematically guaranteed that they would finish the year as the world number ones. In the men's category, the second and fifth-ranked pairs reached the final, setting up a rematch of the Sardinia final. The first finalists were Alejandro Ruiz and Franco Stupaczuk, who eliminated the world number ones, Alejandro Galán and Juan Lebrón, in the semi-finals. Their opponents were the second-ranked pair, Martín Di Nenno and Paquito Navarro, who had defeated Arturo Coello and Fernando Belasteguín to reach their fifth consecutive final. In the decisive match, Di Nenno and Paquito defeated Ruiz and Stupaczuk in straight sets, securing their second title of the season and their first-ever victory in Córdoba. title: YUNG DSA
text: Yung DSA (born Harsh Vijay Machare) is an Indian rapper and songwriter from Yerawada, Pune, Maharashtra. He gained recognition through his single "Yeda Yung", released in 2024 through Gully Gang Records. In 2026, he participated in the twentieth season of the Indian reality television show Bigg Boss, where he became the first captain of the season. Early life Yung DSA was born as Harsh Vijay Machare and grew up in Yerawada, Pune, Maharashtra. He developed an interest in rap music at an early age and began rapping at approximately 12 years old. Before pursuing music professionally, he worked at a business process outsourcing (BPO) company while continuing to develop his musical career. Career Musical career 2021–2023: Early releases Yung DSA began releasing music independently in 2021. His early releases included "Yung Sitar", followed by tracks such as "Sangeet" and "Straight Outta Yerwada". These releases helped establish his presence in Pune's independent hip-hop scene. 2024: Breakthrough with "Yeda Yung" In 2024, Yung DSA released "Yeda Yung" through Gully Gang Records. The song brought him wider recognition and marked a turning point in his career. Following its success, he left his BPO job to pursue music full-time. 2025–present: Subsequent releases In May 2025, he released "Maaf Kar", produced by Cosmo Drop and distributed through Sony Music India. Other releases associated with his career include "Chala Kalti", "Rade Rapate" and "Fachadi". Musical style Yung DSA's music is associated with Indian hip-hop and Marathi rap. His work combines contemporary hip-hop influences with elements of Indian music. His lyrics and artistic identity draw on Marathi language, Pune's local culture and his experiences growing up in Yerawada. Television career 2026: Bigg Boss 20 In September 2026, Yung DSA entered the twentieth season of the Indian reality television show Bigg Boss, hosted by Salman Khan. He was among the contestants introduced during the season's premiere on 6 September 2026. During the premiere, he spoke about his background in Yerawada and his experiences as a rapper. His interaction with Salman Khan attracted media attention. First captaincy On 10 September 2026, Yung DSA became the first captain of Bigg Boss 20 after winning the season's first captaincy task. He competed against Aasif Khan and Kushal Tanwar, also known as Gullu. Following his victory, he received the responsibility of captaincy inside the house. Discography Selected singles References

title: Rob Monaco
text: Robin Gabriel Monaco (September 5, 1961 – January 25, 2016) was an American professional football player who was a center for the St. Louis Cardinals of the National Football League (NFL). He played college football for the Vanderbilt Commodores. Early life Monaco was born on September 5, 1961, in New Haven, Connecticut. He attended Hamden High School in Hamden, Connecticut. College career Monaco played college football for the Vanderbilt Commodores from 1981 to 1984 and was a four-year letterman. In 1982, he recovered a fumble in the end zone for touchdown against Florida. As a senior, Monaco earned first-team All-SEC honors. Professional career Monaco was selected in the eighth round, with the 212th overall selection, by the St. Louis Cardinals in the 1985 NFL draft. On July 22, he signed his rookie contract with the team. Monaco played in six games as a reserve center and on special teams. On October 13, against the Philadelphia Eagles, he was suffered a torn quadriceps muscle on a kickoff and was placed on the injured reserve. On June 26, 1986, Monaco underwent surgery to relive blood clots along his abdominal wall. On July 19, he was placed on the Reserve/Physically Unable to Perform list. On September 16, Monaco was waived by the Cardinals. Personal life In a 1991 Los Angeles Times article, Monaco revealed that at 30-years old, he had chronic pain and weakness in his legs and that he was unable to hold a job due to his injury with the Cardinals. His orthopedist said the pain is caused by traumatic arthritis but because his agent never recommended it, he had no disability insurance. Monaco died on January 25, 2016 in Branford, Connecticut, after a short illness. References

title: Italy and the Russo-Ukrainian war
text: Italy has supported Ukraine during the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine, during both Independent and Conservative governments. After it began on 24 February 2022, then Independent Prime Minister Mario Draghi condemned the invasion, provided military and humanitarian aid to Ukraine, and sanctioned Russia and Belarus, the two countries most involved in invading Ukraine. Support to Ukraine has continued under incumbent Conservative Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni. History On 24 February 2022, Russia invaded Ukraine; Draghi harshly condemned Russia's attack, calling for an immediate ceasefire and promising "whatever it takes to restore Ukrainian sovereignty". He added that it was "impossible to have meaningful dialogue with Moscow", demanding Russia to unconditionally pull its forces back to the internationally established borders. Despite initial reluctance, on 26 February, during a phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Draghi agreed to support the exclusion of Russia from the SWIFT network, the international financial transactions system. On 22 March, Draghi broke with other European leaders when he publicly supported the application of Ukraine to join the European Union. Draghi was also among the main proponents of the freezing of a large part of Russian Central Bank's 643 billion dollars of foreign currency reserves. The Russo-Ukrainian War, with the deployment of Russian troops along the entire border with Ukraine and the subsequent Russian invasion of Ukraine, led Italy to open a diplomatic channel to resolve the crisis. Italy has severely condemned the Russian aggression and expressed full support to Ukraine. The Russian aggression against Ukraine surprised and disconcerted Italy and European countries. Former Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi also expressed shock at Vladimir Putin's decision to attack Ukraine but later on in October 2022 he began to defend the invasion by blaming Zelensky for the war. Initially, Italy was opposed to applying harsh economic sanctions against Russia, also because they were much more penalizing economically for Italy itself than for Russia, however it had to adhere to the European plan of harsh but gradual economic sanctions against Russia. Italian public opinion has been strongly shocked and worried by the attack on Ukraine, also because it considered this war as unjustified and unjustifiable, fratricidal between populations of Rus' origin and with the same Orthodox Christian religion. The significant presence of Ukrainian immigrants in Italy demonstrated in the Italian squares and churches for peace and to ask for support from Italy. After the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine started, Italy, as one of the EU countries, imposed sanctions on Russia, and Russia added all EU countries to the list of "unfriendly nations". Italy joined other countries in spring 2022 in declaring a number of Russian diplomats persona non grata. Bilateral relations between Italy and Ukraine have changed. The Italian government, through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, declared its “strong condemnation of Russia’s unjustified and unprovoked aggression against Ukraine”. Italy has also underlined the violation of international law perpetrated by Russian authorities and has expressed its full support for the territorial integrity of Ukraine. Like other European nations and the European Commission itself, Italy supports the EU's action to isolate and exert economic pressure on Russia. Initially, the government of Italy was not manifestly determined to impose economic sanctions on Russia as a form of countermeasure after the breakout of the war. The Ukrainian president Volodymir Zelenskyy, through his official Twitter account, then criticised Italian Prime Minister Mario Draghi for his reluctance to apply more severe sanctions against Russia. Subsequently, Italian support to the Ukrainian resistance became stronger: for example the Italian Ministry of Culture has offered to rebuild the Donetsk Academic

title: Lego v. Twomey
text: Lego v. Twomey, 404 U.S. 477 (1972), was a United States Supreme Court case in which the Court held that the prosecution may establish the voluntariness of a confession by a preponderance of the evidence, rather than beyond a reasonable doubt. Background Lego was convicted of armed robbery in 1961 and sentenced to 25–50 years. The evidence included a confession he made to police after his arrest. Before trial he moved to suppress the confession, claiming police had beaten him. At a hearing he introduced a photograph showing facial injuries taken the day after his arrest and testified about the alleged beating. The police officers involved also testified. At trial, the judge resolved conflicting testimony in favor of the police and admitted Lego's confession under Illinois law, which required only a preponderance of the evidence to establish voluntariness. The judge did not instruct the jury to independently determine whether the confession was voluntary before considering it. After the Illinois Supreme Court affirmed the conviction on direct appeal, Lego sought a federal writ of habeas corpus, arguing that voluntariness must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt or, alternatively, submitted to the jury. Both the U.S. District Court and the Seventh Circuit denied relief on the merits. Since Jackson v. Denno (1964), state and federal courts had reached conflicting conclusions on the standard of proof for determining whether a confession was voluntary. To resolve this question, the Court granted review. Supreme Court The Court decided Lego v. Twomey by a close 4–3 vote, with William J. Brennan Jr., William O. Douglas, and Thurgood Marshall dissenting. The case was argued before Lewis F. Powell Jr. and William Rehnquist joined the Court, and neither took part in the decision. The defendant argued that the prosecution should have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his confession was voluntary, to help ensure a reliable verdict. In an opinion written by Byron White, the Court held that determining voluntariness by a preponderance of the evidence did not undermine the requirement that guilt be proved beyond a reasonable doubt. The stricter "beyond a reasonable doubt" standard from In re Winship (1970) applies only to proving the actual elements of the crime at trial, not to preliminary suppression rulings. Subsequent developments Chief Justice William Rehnquist wrote in Colorado v. Connelly (1986) that prosecutors must prove a Miranda waiver by a preponderance of the evidence—the same burden Lego established for proving that a confession was voluntary.

title: Oceanit
text: Oceanit Laboratories, Inc. is an American research and development company and engineering firm headquartered in Honolulu, Hawaii. History Oceanit was founded in 1985 by Patrick K. Sullivan to conduct research, development, and instrument design for ocean engineering. Operating from an office on Fort Street Mall, its first contract was to design a marine dock for the Ala Wai Canal. Later, Oceanit expanded into general research and product development. During the 1990s and 2000s, Oceanit became a contractor for federal agencies, including the U.S. Department of Defense, Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), and U.S. Department of Energy, and participated extensively in the Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) program. Between 2008 and 2015, Oceanit received approximately $23.7 million in SBIR grants. Oceanit has spun out several private equity financed companies. These include Hoana Medical in 2001, Nanopoint in 2002, and Ibis Networks in 2013. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Oceanit developed a new rapid antigen test under the brand ASSURE, starting with a saliva-based test evaluated with The Queen's Medical Center in downtown Honolulu. An additional nasal-swab rapid antigen test, ASSURE-100, received FDA Emergency Use Authorization for point-of-care use in February 2022 and for over-the-counter home use in December 2022. In 2022, Oceanit launched EDGE, an internal energy incubator, and began to work with Hawaii Gas and the U.S. Department of Energy to test an internal pipeline treatment for hydrogen blending. In 2023, Oceanit opened H2XCEL, a Houston laboratory for testing hydrogen and methane mixtures in pipelines. In 2026, Oceanit received an Engineering Excellence Award from the American Council of Engineering Companies of Hawaii for erosion control work on 'Aliomanu Road at Anahola Bay, Kaua'i. Operations Oceanit is based in Hawai'i with research facilities in Houston, Texas. It uses laboratory research to develop commercial products for industries such as energy, aerospace, defense, and life sciences. Its products include Blast Ninja, an abrasive blasting nozzle for industrial sand blasting; HydroPel, a pipeline coating designed to reduce hydrogen embrittlement inside pipelines; Nanite, a smart cement with real-time load monitoring; AeroPel APW100, an anti-corrosion nanocomposite surface treatment for aerospace platforms, and HeatX, an anti-fouling surface treatment for heat exchangers used in oil and gas. title: Fomo (app)
text: fomo is a mobile and web application for social trading of cryptocurrencies and perpetual futures, operated by a company headquartered in New York City. It allows users to trade crypto assets across several blockchain networks and to follow the trades of other users. History fomo was founded in 2025 by Paul Erlanger, Se Yong Park and Prashan Dharmasena, who had previously worked at the cryptocurrency trading platform dYdX. The company launched its app in May 2025 and added support for Apple Pay about one month later. In November 2025, fomo announced a $17 million Series A round led by Benchmark, bringing its total funding to $19 million. On 11 June 2026, fomo added perpetual futures contracts powered by Hyperliquid for users outside the United States. On 22 June 2026, fomo announced a $75 million Series B round led by Index Ventures at a valuation of $550 million. Union Square Ventures and Benchmark also participated, bringing the company's total disclosed funding to about $94 million. In August 2026, fomo acquired the data-indexing software and team of Mobula for $17 million. Operations fomo is a non-custodial application, meaning the company does not hold customer funds, and it lets users trade across multiple blockchains without managing bridges or gas fees. Its social features include a feed of other users' trades and leaderboards of top traders. As of November 2025, the app charged 0.5% per trade, with a $0.10 minimum on Solana and no minimum on Base or BNB Chain. References

title: Edmond Jouve
text: Edmond Jouve (French: [ɛdmˈɔ̃ ʒˈuv]; 14 September 1937 – 13 November 2026) was a French political scientist and academic. A graduate of the University of Paris, he spent his career promoting third-worldist views, demonstrated by his work at the Institut libre d'étude des relations internationales and the Arab University of Sciences. He also assisted in the drafting of the 1991 Constitution of Burkina Faso, serving as an advisor to President Blaise Compaoré on term limits. He also maintained close ties with North Korea, though his pro-Pyongyang stance led others to label him a "propagandist". Jouve died in Paris on 13 November 2026, at the age of 89.
