title: Ruth Swift
text: Ruth Swift (née Livingston; September 18, 1827 – August 31, 1881) was an American woman who served as the First Lady of Minnesota from 1863 until 1864 during the administration of her husband, Governor Henry Adoniram Swift. Early life and education Swift was born Ruth Livingston on September 18, 1827, in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. Ruth studied at the ladies seminary in Gettysburg before her family moved to Pittsburgh. Marriage to Henry Adoniram Swift Ruth met her future husband, Henry Adoniram Swift, while he was serving as the chief clerk of the Ohio House of Representatives. Ruth was married to Henry Swift in 1851 in Ravenna, Ohio, together they had a total of five children. In 1853 Ruth and Henry moved to Minnesota Territory, originally living in Saint Paul, Minnesota but ultimately settling in St. Peter, Minnesota by 1856. First Lady of Minnesota When Alexander Ramsey resigned from the office of governor of Minnesota on July 10, 1863, Henry Swift was serving as the Lieutenant Governor of Minnesota, Henry thus assumed the office of the governor of Minnesota for Ramsey's remaining term. Ruth served as the third overall First Lady of Minnesota from July 10, 1864, until January 11, 1864, during her husband's term as the third governor of Minnesota. Henry did not seek reelection as governor, choosing instead to live with his family in St. Peter and working for the St. Peter land office. Later life Following her term as first lady, Ruth and her husband moved back to St. Peter. Henry died on February 25, 1869, from typhoid fever. Following the death of her husband Ruth lived with her daughter and son-in-law in St. Peter. Death Ruth died on August 31, 1881, in St. Peter from a stroke brought on by paralysis. References

title: Manor Grove
text: Manor Grove is a street in the North Sheen area of Richmond in London. Its houses form the "Richmond Experiment", an early example of council built housing sometimes described as the first council estate in the Greater London area. History The Municipal Borough of Richmond was established in 1890, the same year as the Housing of the Working Classes Act 1890 (53 & 54 Vict. c. 70) which extended the powers of local authorities to build housing beyond the Housing of the Working Classes Act 1885 (48 & 49 Vict. c. 72) which had established the power exclusively in relation to slum clearances. The Metropolitan Boroughs of London at the time were not granted the same rights until a further Housing of the Working Classes Act 1900 (63 & 64 Vict. c. 59), which allowed Richmond, then in Surrey, to provide possibly the first example of its kind. The new Borough of Richmond was one of the first to make use of this power, largely backed by William Thompson a councillor and future mayor of the borough. A site was found on land next to the railway tracks of the London & South Western Railway, next to where North Sheen station now stands. It was originally acquired with the intention of building a dust destructor, but the housing scheme was proposed in 1892, with a loan secured by 1893. The first phase comprised Nos 1-62. Manor Grove, built between 1894 and 1895 at three "classes", and taking architectural cues from the model dwelling companies which had been the main source of housing aimed at the working classes in the preceding decades. Their designs are likely the work of the borough's surveyor E. J. Lovegrove. The houses were all occupied by 1896 and construction began on the second phase, consisting of 70 new dwellings opposite.

title: Mary Ann Alexander
text: Mary Ann Alexander (born 25 October 2000), is an Indian singer and songwriter known for her work in R&B, and pop music. She gained wider recognition from her release of "Sthuthi" from the Malayalam film Bougainvillea in 2024, and for her collaborations with international artists, including Craig David and Tiwa Savage. She has appeared at festivals including Magnetic Fields, Lollapalooza India, Echoes of Earth, Rolling Loud and NH7 Weekender. Early life Alexander was born on 25 October 2000 in Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala]]. Her father, Alex, is a playback singer associated with the Malayalam film industry. She was introduced to recording studios at an early age, accompanying her father to recording sessions from the age of five. She began recording vocals as a child, contributing to studio recordings that required children's voices. During her childhood, Alexander developed an interest in music, participating in school cultural programmes and singing competitions. She moved to Bengaluru to pursue a bachelor's degree in visual communication at St Joseph's College. During her college years, she became involved in the city's independent music community and began developing her career as a singer-songwriter. Career 2021–2023: Early recordings and independent releases Alexander's debut release was with the guitarist and producer Sanjeev T. She contributed vocals to "Take My Life With You", featuring singer Sid Sriram. She also recorded "Over the Ocean" for the Malayalam film Kolaambi. The composition originated from a song she had written as a teenager, which came to the attention of filmmaker T. K. Rajeev Kumar during the film's development. The song was later included in the film's soundtrack. In December 2022, she released her first solo single, "In My Zone", which combines R&B, pop and hip-hop genres and addresses introversion and extroversion. 2024–2025: Film music and wider recognition In 2024, Alexander gained widespread recognition through her release of "Sthuthi" from the Malayalam psychological thriller Bougainvillea, composed by Sushin Shyam. Her original compositions and short performance videos attracted attention on social media platforms, particularly Instagram, where she shared excerpts of unreleased songs and acoustic performances. The same year, she made her Hindi film debut with CTRL, releasing the track "Ulfat" with Sneha Khanwalkar and Anvitaa Dutt. In 2025, Alexander was mentored by American musician Anderson .Paak. She participated in the global remix of British singer Craig David's song "Commitment", alongside Nigerian singer Tiwa Savage, the collaboration involving recording session with Craig David in the United Kingdom. She also became the first Indian singer-songwriter to appear on DJ AG's live session in London in 2025. 2026–present: EP, Vevo In March 2026, Alexander released the extended play Love or a Lesson, produced with Linden Jay. Her other releases by 2026 include "Bling Bling", "Good Girl", "The Lovey Dovey Song" and "Round 2". Alexander appeared in the "Future of Music" programme at India Film Project (I F P) Season 15, alongside other Indian artists, in a session presented with Rolling Stone India. The same year, she was featured in Vevo DSCVR. References

title: Lincoln Minor
text: Lincoln B. Minor (born January 22, 1950) is an American former professional football running back who played for the New Orleans Saints of the National Football League (NFL). He played college football for the New Mexico State Aggies. Early life Lincoln B. Minor was born on January 22, 1950, in New Orleans, Louisiana. He played high school football at Ravenswood in East Palo Alto, California. He led his league in receptions in 1966 with 21 for 326 yards and one touchdown. As a senior in 1967, Minor led the league in rushing yards with 960 and scoring with 103 points (16 touchdowns, seven extra points). College career Minor enrolled at New Mexico State University to play college football for the Aggies. He was on the freshman team in 1968 and had a "sensational" year but then dropped out of school. Professional career On January 8, 1989, it was reported that the 18-year-old Minor had signed with the Montreal Alouettes of the Canadian Football League (CFL). He was not eligible for the NFL draft until 1972. On Jun 23, 1969, during training camp, it was reported that Minor had quit the team. Minor signed with the CFL's Edmonton Eskimos in 1972 but was released during training camp. Minor was signed by the Washington Redskins on February 24, 1973. He had an impressive performance during the Redskins' rookie scrimmage on July 14, 1973. However, he was waived on August 1, 1973, before the first preseason game. Minor was claimed off waivers by the Kansas City Chiefs on August 6, 1973. On September 5, 1973, he was traded to the New Orleans Saints for a sixth-round draft pick. He played in nine regular season games for the Saints in 1973 as a reserve running back, rushing three times for ten yards while also catching one pass for five yards. Minor was released on September 8, 1974, before the start of the 1974 regular season. Minor signed with the Birmingham Vulcans of the World Football League (WFL) in 1975. He was released in late July 1975, before the start of the regular season. Minor was signed by the Houston Oilers on March 8, 1977. However, he was later released. References

title: Steve Jackson (defensive back, born 1955)
text: Stephen Loran Jackson (born April 6, 1955) is an American former professional football player who was a safety for the Oakland Raiders of the National Football League (NFL). He played college football for the LSU Tigers. Early life Jackson was born on April 6, 1955, in Chatom, Alabama. He attended Washington County High School in Chatom. College career Jackson played college football for the LSU Tigers from 1973 to 1976 and was a three-year letterman from 1974 to 1976. He played at defensive back and at punter, recording five interceptions and averaged 35 yards per punt as a senior. Professional career Oakland Raiders (first stint) After going unselected in the 1977 NFL draft, Jackson signed with the Oakland Raiders as an undrafted free agent. San Francisco 49ers On August 30, 1977, Jackson was traded to the San Francisco 49ers with Rod Martin in exchange for draft picks. On September 6, he was waived by the team. Oakland Raiders (second stint) On November 7, 1977 Jackson was re-signed by the Raiders. He played in six regular season and two postseason games, logging one interception and one fumble recovery. On July 17, 1978, Jackson was waived by the Raiders. New York Jets On July 17, 1978, Jackson was claimed off waivers by the New York Jets. On August 9, he was released by the team. Montreal Alouettes On March 26, 1980, Jackson signed with the Montreal Alouettes of the Canadian Football League (CFL). On June 20, he was released.

title: Melocactus stramineus
text: Melocactus stramineus is a species of succulent flowering plant in the genus Melocactus, within the family Cactaceae. It is endemic to Aruba. It is characterized by its cephalium, an apical structure covered in wool and spines from which develop the flowers and fruits. Description Melocactus stramineus is a species of solitarily-growing cactus with a depressed, globose to short-cylindrical stem. It measures 15 to 18 cm in height and 9.5 to 25 cm in diameter. Its epidermis is medium to dark green (or glaucous gray-green) in color. The stem has 10 to 18 ribs with more or less sharp, straight, or tuberculate margins; on these are situated the areoles. It is difficult to distinguish between the central and radial spines of this species; all of the spines gray or red-brown to brown, and occasionally become black with age. There are 1 to 4 central spines, which measure 3 to 4 cm in length, and 5 to 12 radial spines which may be shorter or longer, measuring 3 to 4.5 cm in length. When the vegetative growth of the juvenile stage has been completed, a cephalium develops at the apex of the plant. This woolly structure is made up of many tightly spaced areoles, which are covered in white wool and bright red to red-brown bristles. The cephalium can reach 12.7 cm in height and 8 cm in diameter, and its minimum width is half that of the vegetative stem. Even with age, the cephalium's diameter does not increase; it grows taller at a constant rate for many years. The flowers develop from the areoles of the cephalium. They are rose pink in color, 1 to 1.4 cm in diameter, and open approximately between 2:00 and 4:00 pm. The fruits are magenta in color, and measure 3 to 3.4 cm in length. Distribution and habitat Melocactus stramineus is native to Aruba. It primarily inhabits seasonally-dry tropical regions at altitudes of 0 to 100 meters above sea level. It grows on rocky outcrops in scrubland, sympatrically with Melocactus macracanthos and Melocactus curvispinus. Ecology This species' flowers are pollinated primarily by hummingbirds. The seeds are primarily dispersed by lizards. Taxonomy Melocactus stramineus was described by the Dutch botanist Willem Frederik Reinier Suringar and published for the first time in the scientific journal Verslagen en Mededeelingen van de Afdeeling Natuurkunde ser. 3, 2: 185 in 1886. Etymology Melocactus: the genus name is derived from the Greek words mēlon (meaning "apple" or "tree fruit") and kaktos (meaning "thistle" or "spiny plant"). This name references the size and shape of the plant, and how they resemble those of a fruit. stramineus: the specific epithet is derived from the Latin word strāmĭnĕus (meaning "straw-colored"), in reference to the color of this species' spines. Synonyms Conservation status It has been proposed that Melocactus stramineus should be classified as being Endangered (EN) under the criteria of the IUCN Red List, a category corresponding to a very high risk of extinction in the wild. This is mainly due to its highly restricted distribution, which has an area of approximately only 52 km2, as well as the reduction of the number of localities in which this species is present, currently between 2 and 5. Furthermore, its habitat has been declining in area and quality due to urban development. Although this species is found within a protected area, tourism development in the area also constitutes a significant threat. Cultivation This species is primarily cultivated as an ornamental. It is propagated only via seed. It is not recommended for beginners. References

title: Robust (film)
text: Robust (French: Robuste) is a 2021 French comedy drama film, written and directed by Constance Meyer and starring Gérard Depardieu and Déborah Lukumuena. The story recounts the relationship between a famous, weary actor and his young female bodyguard, who is also a wrestler. The film premiered at the 2021 Cannes Film Festival, where it was the opening film for the Critics' Week; it received a general theatrical release in March 2022. Plot Georges, an aging, disenchanted, and grumpy movie star, is being annoyed by a female stalker. With his usual chauffeur-bodyguard unavailable, Georges is assigned a replacement "minder", who turns out to be a young woman, Aïssa. Tall and powerfully built, Aïssa makes a living as a security agent while training in freestyle wrestling, a sport in which she aims to become a professional, and even a champion. The story chronicles Aïssa's interactions with Georges, alongside her training and her relationship with her boyfriend, Eddy. An unlikely friendship develops between the cantankerous, wealthy, old actor and the independent-minded, working-class, young woman, though Georges starts to become intrusive. Cast Gérard Depardieu as Georges Déborah Lukumuena as Aïssa Lucas Mortier as Eddy Megan Northam as Cosmina Florence Janas as Adeline Steve Tientcheu as Lalou Théodore Le Blanc as Gabriel Lola Dueñas as Magali François Loriquet as Régis Florence Muller as Elvire Georgia Scalliet as Emma Sébastien Pouderoux as Nicolas Canteret Production Robust was the directorial debut of Constance Meyer, who had met Gérard Depardieu while working as his prompter on the stage play The Beast in the Jungle. She later worked with him as an assistant director on several films, including Bellamy (2009). Principal photography began in October 2020. The scenes at Georges's house were shot in the 16th arrondissement of Paris. Reception Critical reception in France was generally positive. Première wrote that it was Depardieu's "best role in years". Le Figaro found the film "inspired" and praised the performances of the two leads. Télérama gave the film a more mixed review, calling the dialogue "overly explanatory" but mentioning Lukumuena's performance as its saving grace. The Guardian reviewed it positively, appreciating the "odd-couple" dynamic and commenting that it was "Maybe not a real stretch for Depardieu, but good work all around, especially from Lukumuena." French-Canadian newspaper Le Devoir, on the other hand, gave the film a negative review, finding the script underwhelming and the dialogue mediocre, and commenting that the film also suffered from technical flaws — even though Depardieu delivered a good performance, and the wrestling scenes were filmed in an interesting way. The film was a box-office failure in France, where it sold only 32,226 admissions. Home media Robust was released on DVD, Blu-ray and several VOD streaming services.

title: Andi Jackson
text: Andi Jackson (born June 15, 2005) is an American college volleyball player for the Nebraska Cornhuskers. She was the overall #4 draft pick for Major League Volleyball Omaha Supernovas. Early life Jackson was born in Soldotna, Alaska, to parents Heidi and Dennis. Since her father worked in the energy sector, Jackson's family moved around frequently at a young age; she spent time living in California and Dubai, United Arab Emirates until 2012. Her family eventually settled in Brighton, Colorado, though Jackson recalled continuing to split time between Colorado and Alaska during the years. She is also accomplished in track & field, qualifying for USATF National Championships in the long jump at age 10. College career Jackson has recalled that her initial top two college choices were the University of Texas at Austin and Baylor University, but selected Nebraska after speaking with the coaches and seeing the fan support for the program. During her freshman season in 2023, Jackson partook in the Cornhuskers world record-setting for attendance at a women's sports event when more than 92,000 people attended Nebraska's match against University of Nebraska-Omaha at Memorial Stadium. Jackson was named the AVCA Middle Blocker of the Year in the 2025, a recognition awarded to the top middle blocker in the country. International career Jackson was part of the United States under-19 team that won the 2022 Girls' U19 NORCECA Pan American Cup. She was also part of the women's U21 team that won a gold medal at the 2024 Women's U21 NORCECA Continental Championship in Toronto, Canada. Professional career Jackson was the number 4 overall selection in the Major League Volleyball Draft held on November 23, 2026. She was selected by the Omaha Supernovas. References

title: Third System Movement
text: The Third System Movement (Movimiento Tercer Sistema; MTS) is a Bolivian political party on the center-left.The party was founded in 2010 by Félix Patzi, originally as a citizen grouping called Integration for Change (Integración Para el Cambio; IPC) and later transformed into a political party and renamed the Third System Movement. Patzi served as governor of La Paz department from 2015 to 2021, elected as the candidate of the Sovereignty and Freedom for Bolivia party. History Between December 20 and 22, 2017, the conversion of Movimiento Tercer Sistema from a citizens’ group to a national political party was formalized before the Supreme Electoral Tribunal. The process was completed on October 30, 2018, when the acronym MTS was officially recognized, based on a total of 131,132 signatures and pursuant to Resolution TSE-RSP-ADM No. 0513/2018. Regional elections of 2021 The MTS participated in the 2021 subnational elections, winning two gubernatorial races—in the departments of Pando and Beni—but losing in the rest. Its candidate in Pando, Regis Germán Richter, won a runoff and served as governor from 2021 to 2026. MTS candidate Alejandro Unzueta won as governor of Beni, though he maintained relative independence from the party.. In the 2021 subnational elections, it won 10 mayoral seats across the country, mainly in the departments of Pando and Beni. References

title: The Chain (short story)
text: "The Chain" is a work of short fiction by Tobias Wolff originally appearing in Esquire, July 1996 and first collected in The Night in Question: Stories (1996). Plot “The Chain” is written in the third-person. Brian Gold is the focal character. His wife Mary and he have a child, Anna, a toddler. Gold runs a video rental store. Gold takes Anna, whom he adores, to go snow sledding in a public park. Without warning a huge dog, tethered on a 40-foot chain in an adjoining property, charges and attacks the child, seizing her by the shoulder. Gold, frantic with fear and rage, manages to tear the animal’s jaws from the stunned girl. Though Anna sustains only bruises, doctors are astonished that the little girl escaped major nerve damage or disfigurement from the assault. Mary is content that her daughter will fully recover, but Gold remains traumatized by the event. The police inform Gold that the owners had lawfully contrained their pet. Gold’s attorney sympathizes, but counsels him to drop the matter. After a week, Gold shares his discontents with a cousin, Tom Rourke. Rourke instantly registers outrage at the injustice: “What is it with Nazis and dogs? They’ve got a real thing going, ever notice that?” Rourke offers to dispatch the dog himself by an undisclosed method and coaches Gold on how to establish an alibi the day of the killing. Gold reflects on the incident in light of Rourke’s remark about Nazis. Gold’s paternal side of the family is Jewish, and he recalls some anti-semitic remarks directed towards him from members of the community. He associates the failure of the authorities to provide justice with the failure to rescue Jews from the the Shoah. Gold contacts Rourke and sanctions the killing. The night of the operation Gold takes Mary to a fancy restaurant for several hours to provide an alibi; she is ignorant of his purpose. That evening Rourke calls and reports success; he has taken the dog’s collar as a trophy gift for Gold. The following spring, Rourke tells Gold about a minor vehicular accident he suffered involving a hit and run driver, identified as a popular deejay named Victor Barnes. Rourke’s insurance covers the $800 body shop repair but not the $300 deductible. He repeatedly calls Barnes to recover the money and is rebuffed. Exasperated, Rourke discovers the nightclub where Barnes works and tells Gold of his intention to vandalize Barnes’ BMW. Gold feels obligated to act on his cousin’s behalf, and hatches a scheme to pour corrosive wood stain on Barnes’ car and slash the tires. Rourke likewise arranges for his own alibi. Arriving in a dark parking lot, Gold determines he will simply dent the expensive car with a crowbar. He delivers a blow “knowing just as the act passed beyond recall how absolutely he had betrayed himself.” He drops the crowbar and flees. Barnes discovers the vandalism hours later and suspects—not Rourke—but a drug dealer named Devereaux to whom he owes money. He picks up the crowbar and drives to the dealer’s home and breaks in the front door, crowbar in hand. He is confronted by a teenage family member, Marcel Foley. They struggle, and Barnes crushes the boy's skull with the crowbar and flees. The murder is reported the next morning in the local news as an unprovoked and senseless homicide. Foley had been active in community youth events and is mourned by his peers. School is cancelled in his honor. Two of Marcel Foley’s classmates, Garvey and Tiffany are young lovers. They go to Gold’s video store to rent Breakfast at Tiffany’s because of its title. Gold inquires as to why the kids are not in school, and they inform of Marcel’s murder. Garvey extols the virtues of the young man who was affectionately known as “Peacemaker.” Gold is clearly troubled by this news. Garvey reassures him that the murderer will suffer at the hands of the law: “That man’ll get his. He’ll get what’s coming to him. Count on it.” Critical appraisal Kirkus Reviews offers fulsome praise of this “terrifyingly vivid” st

title: I Could Go On Singing (soundtrack)
text: I Could Go On Singing is a soundtrack album by American singer and actress Judy Garland of the 1963 film of the same name, released by Capitol Records in the same year. The album received favorable reviews, which praised Garland's performances and the musical arrangements. It appeared on the music charts of Cash Box and Billboard, peaking at No. 27 on the former's Stereo chart and No. 45 on the Billboard 200. Promotion and single release The single "I Could Go On Singing", backed with "Hello Bluebird", was released ahead of the soundtrack album. Billboard selected "I Could Go On Singing" as a "Four Star" release, indicating strong commercial potential. Cash Box described it as a "fine nostalgic, vaudeville-like number" and wrote that Garland might "adopt it as one of her many theme songs". The magazine rated the single "B" and described "Hello Bluebird" as an "old-time item". An extensive promotional campaign for the soundtrack album was planned in connection with the film's Canadian debut, involving Haines, Archie Laurie of United Artists, and Charlie Mason of Odeon. Critical reception Billboard described the album as part of Garland's continuing "career revival", noting that it featured "several good Garland music showcases" and praising her performances as delivered "in telling style", accompanied by "great Mort Lindsey backings". AllMusic noted that the album introduced only two new songs to Garland's repertoire, "I Could Go on Singin' (Till the Cows Come Home)" and "Hello, Bluebird", describing both title-track renditions as "show stoppers for Garland". The review also called the album "a nice souvenir" of what became her final film appearance. Commercial performance The album debuted on Cash Box's Stereo and Monaural charts on April 20, 1963, peaking at No. 27 and No. 42, respectively, and spending a total of 10 weeks on the charts. On the Billboard 200, the album debuted on May 11, 1963, peaked at No. 45, and spent a total of six weeks on the chart. Track listing Charts Personnel Credits adapted from I Could Go On Singing CD. Notes by John Sowerwine Album produced by Bill Miller References

title: Lindy Lauro
text: Lindoro L. Lauro (June 3, 1921 – January 12, 2012) was an American football player and coach. He played college football for the Pittsburgh Panthers and professionally for the Chicago Cardinals of the National Football League (NFL). He was the head football coach at New Castle High School from 1961 to 1992. Early life Lindoro L. Lauro was born on June 3, 1921, in New Castle, Pennsylvania. He attended New Castle High School. Lauro served in the United States Army Air Forces during World War II. He played on the 1944 Third Air Force Gremlins football team. College career Lauro enrolled at the University of Pittsburgh to play college football for the Panthers. He was a four-year letterman from 1946 to 1949. Professional career After going undrafted in the 1950 NFL draft, Lauro signed with the Chicago Cardinals on April 4, 1950. He was released on September 11 before the start of the 1950 regular season. Lauro played in six games, starting five, for the Jersey City Giants of the American Football League during the 1950 season. Lauro signed with the Cardinals again on October 24, 1951. He played in one game for the team in a reserve role. Post-playing career Lauro was a football, baseball, and basketball coach at Dickinson College for several years during the 1950s. He was the head football coach at his alma mater, New Castle High School, from 1961 to 1992. The field at New Castle is named jointly in honor of Lauro and Philip Henry Bridenbaugh. In 2012, the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette said Lauro was "one of the greatest coaches in Western Pennsylvania Interscholastic Athletic League history." He died on January 12, 2012, in New Castle. References

title: Dean Barnett (American football)
text: Donald Dean Barnett (born June 6, 1957) is an American former professional football player who was a tight end for the Denver Broncos of the National Football League (NFL). He played college football for the Fullerton Hornets and UNLV Rebels. Early life Barnett was born on June 6, 1957, in Long Beach, California. He attended Lowell High School in San Francisco, California. College career Barnett played college football for the Fullerton Hornets from 1976 to 1977 and UNLV Rebels from 1978 to 1979. In 23 games at UNLV, he had 38 receptions for 592 yards and a touchdown. Professional career New York Giants After going unselected in the 1980 NFL draft, Barnett signed with the New York Giants as an undrafted free agent. On August 25, he was released. Detroit Lions On June 8, 1981, Barnett was signed by the Detroit Lions. On July 27, he was waived. Denver Broncos On June 6, 1983, Barnett signed with the Denver Broncos. On August 30, he was released by the team. On September 13, Barnett was signed to the active roster. On October 14, he was placed on the injured reserve with a knee injury. On November 9, Barnett was released and re-signed to the active roster on November 11. On December 22, he was again placed on the injured reserve after his injury was still bothering him. Barnett played in eight games as a reserve tight end. On July 24, 1984, he was waived by the Broncos. References

title: Aemia
text: Aemia (stylized in all caps) is a Persian-Canadian alternative rock duo based in Vancouver, British Columbia. Formed in 2024, the band consists of vocalist Kimia "Mia" Ravangar and guitarist Kourosh Zarandooz, a married couple who met in Tehran, Iran. After releasing four independent singles, Aemia signed with the label Artist House in 2026 and released the single "Nowhere to Hide", produced by JT Daly. History Background Zarandooz was born in Toronto and lived in Vancouver as a child before moving with his family to Iran. He began playing guitar at age 12, and has said that he met Ravangar in Tehran at a rehearsal where he was playing with her brother. Public singing by women was restricted in Iran. Ravangar has said that she sneaked into other bands' rehearsals, singing backing vocals and playing keyboard, and that rehearsal studios were regularly raided by police. She later set performing aside and studied industrial design at the University of Tehran. In Iran, Zarandooz was the guitarist of the Persian-language alternative rock band Az Shanbe (از شنبه), which formed in 2018 and released its first single, "Har Ghadam", in 2019. Ravangar helped write lyrics and melodies for the band but could not perform with it publicly. After a band the couple played in was raided by police and their instruments were confiscated, they relocated to Canada, arriving a few months before the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. Before forming Aemia, the couple were established Persian-language content creators. Ravangar started the gaming channel Mia Plays on YouTube in 2017 while still in Iran, and Zarandooz co-hosts the food and challenge channel Kouman with Iman Dastpak. The three run their channels and podcasts through the company Kouman Entertainment, based in a studio in North Vancouver. The couple also shared songs on their YouTube and Twitch channels before forming the band. Formation and independent releases (2024–2026) Aemia was formed in Vancouver in 2024 and performs in English. The music video for its song "Stars" was released in December 2024. The duo chose to build an audience on social media by releasing individual singles rather than an album, beginning with "Stars", "From" and "Kleptomaniac". They worked with producers JT Daly and George Lever to develop their sound. In February 2026, Loudwire included Aemia in its list of new rock and metal bands to know in 2026. The band's fourth single, "Zendebad" (lit. 'Long live'), was described by The Line of Best Fit as a tribute to Iranian resilience. In March 2026, Aemia performed "Kleptomaniac", released in September 2025, for the Recording Academy's Global Spin performance series, and the music site Ones To Watch ranked them first among its best new hard rock bands of the year. Artist House (2026–present) In August 2026, Aemia signed with Artist House and released "Nowhere to Hide", their first single for the label. Written by Ravangar and Zarandooz, produced by Daly and mixed by Joseph McQueen, the song examines psychological abuse and is written from the perspective of the abusive voice. Ravangar directed its music video. The band played its first concert on October 4, 2026, at The Pearl in Vancouver, supported by FKA Rayne and In Pieces, followed by a show at Lee's Palace in Toronto on October 8. Both shows sold out. Reviewing the Vancouver concert for Quockerwodger, Wren Laurenn McNab wrote that the band moved between "angelic vocals and ruthless metal instrumentals", and described the show as feeling like a homecoming given the members' history in Iran. As of October 2026, the band was working on its debut EP. Musical style and influences Loudwire described Aemia's music as pairing dense, lush and sometimes ethereal atmospheres with heavy low-end rhythms, and compared the band to Poppy, Evanescence and Deftones. Ones To Watch categorized the band as hard rock. Their lyrics draw on the members' experience of leaving Iran, as on "Zendebad", as well as on personal themes such as psych

title: Powder (short story)
text: “The Powder” is a work of short fiction by Tobias Wolff originally appearing in Fish Stories, 1996 and first in The Night in Question: Stories (1996) by Alfred A. Knopf. The story was included in The Best American Short Stories of 1997. Plot The story is told in the first-person by an unnamed adolescent boy. The setting is a ski resort on Mt. Baker in Washington state on the afternoon of Christmas Eve. The boy’s father and mother are separated with little chance of reconciliation. The father has visitation arrangements and takes his son on challenging field trips. He is determined to introduce his son to a range of experiences: together they once visited a nightclub to see Thelonious Monk, for which his wife reprimanded him. Under the influence of his mother the boy adopts a skeptical attitude towards his impulsive father. The mother expects her spouse to return the boy home by that evening for holiday celebrations. The father delays, insisting on making a final run on the slopes even as a severe snow storm is rolling into the region. The temperature turns bitterly cold. As they finally prepare to depart the resort the father mounts chains on his sports car. Entering the roadway they are confronted with an emergency roadblock and informed by a state trooper that the highway is closed due to snow. Despite the father’s assurance that his car can handle “five, six inches” of snow, the officer orders him to turn back. The father anticipates his ex-spouse’s reaction and tells his son: “She won’t forgive me. Do you understand? Never.” The boy silently recognizes this truth. They return to the lodge and from a phone booth the father contacts the mother. He returns without comment, now determined to risk making the drive through the mountain pass. When the trooper unexpectedly departs on an emergency call, the father speeds to the roadblock and orders his son to drag aside the barricade. The two proceed onto the highway which is covered with virgin snow; there is no trace of any other vehicular traffic. The roadway can only be discerned by the orange delineator rods. The father cautions his son never to attempt this feat of driving, as he considers that he, and not his son, possesses anthe innate talent. The boy demurs and demands to know what might be his own strong points. The father acknowledges his son has many, one which is that he always thinks ahead. Indeed, the boy’s interior monologue confesses to his own obsession with anticipating every conceivable future event: “And maybe for that reason I stopped moping and began to enjoy myself.” With this epiphany the boy realizes that for all his father’s eccentric behavior “he was a great driver…I actually trusted him.” As such, the son discovers he can take pleasure in the unfolding adventure. Theme Los Angeles Times critic Richard Eder reports that this “vignette” is a dramatization of a similar father-son adventure from Wolff’s autobiographical This Boy's Life: A Memoir (1989). In the midst of the ordeal, the 12-year-old boy discovers the joys of risk-taking, “thrillingly abducted, for a moment, into his father’s world of exuberant peril.” Kirkus reviews dismisses the story as “too nakedly personal” and suggests readers concentrate other selections in The Night in Question. Footnotes Sources Eder, Richard. 1996. The Child Is the Father of the Man : THE NIGHT IN QUESTION: Stories. Los Angeles Times, October 13, 1996.https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1996-10-13-bk-53233-story.html Accessed November 15, 2026 Wolff, Tobias. 1996. “The Night in Question.” The New Yorker, April 15, 1996.https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/1996/04/22/the-night-in-question Accessed October 24, 2026. Wolff, Tobias. 1996. The Night in Question: Stories. Alfred A. Knopf, New York. ISBN 978-0679781554 (hardback).

title: Embassy of Iran, Paris
text: The embassy of Iran in France is the diplomatic mission of Iran to France. It is located on 4, Iéna Avenue, in the 16th arrondissement of Paris, the capital of the country. Building The legation, and later the embassy, was initally housed at 5 Fortuny Street, in the 17th arrondissement, in a private mansion that has belonged to the Iranian state for nearly 150 years. It was the residence of the kings of the Qajar dynasty before it became the resdience off the ambassador. In the 20th century, the Iranian legation was located on 64 Malakoff Avenue, while its chancery was located on 9 Sontay Street (16th arrondissement) and the consulate general at 14 Londres Street (9th arrondissement) The current embassy building is the Hotel Sanchez of Laragotti, a hotel designed by Xavier Schoellkopf at the end of the 19th century and constructed in 1899 (in just one year), and was commisioned by a Portuguese princess. This building was occupied by the American Embassy and later the World Bank, until the 1960s, when the shah of Iran instructed the then-ambassador Hassan Pakravan to purchase the building and establish it as the Iranian Embassy. The inside of the building was fully renovated in 2003–2004 (under ambassador Kharazi) Ambassadors of Iran in France Notable events in the history of Iranian ambassadors in France: Ali Ahani was ambassador to Paris 3 separate times (in 1988 under François Mitterrand, in 2006 under Jacques Chirac and Nicolas Sarkozy, and in 2012 under François Hollande) He was known in Paris as the "firefighter of bilateral relations" because he became ambassador to Paris whenever there were significant tensions arose in political bilateral relations. In 2017, Abolghassem Delfi had a very short time as ambassador (only 6 months between the issuance of his letter of credence at the end of his diplomatic mission). Consulate The embassy also has a consulate with an entrance at the back of the building, on 16, Fresnel Street. History On 4 July 1980, the embassy was occupied by a group of Iranian students, who held ambassador Amiralai and several other staff members hostage. On 23 November 1981, a young Iranian man was wounded by a gunshot fired by an employee of the Iranian consulate. In 1987, the Gordji Affair involved an employee of the Iranian embassy. Since 2012, the ambassador of Iran in Paris is also an accredited ambassador to Monaco. The Iranian cultural centre is found on Jean-Bart Street (6th arrondissement of Paris).

title: Joel Kaye
text: Joel Kaye is an American historian who studies the intellectual history of the later Middle Ages, including the history of science and of economic and political thought. He is a professor emeritus of history at Barnard College, Columbia University. His book Economy and Nature in the Fourteenth Century (1998) won the Medieval Academy of America's John Nicholas Brown Prize. A History of Balance, 1250–1375 (2014) received the American Philosophical Society's Jacques Barzun Prize in Cultural History in 2015. and the Medieval Academy's Haskins Medal in 2017 Education Kaye received a B.A. from the University of Wisconsin–Madison in 1968, an M.A. from the University of Massachusetts in 1984, and a Ph.D. from the University of Pennsylvania in 1991. His doctoral dissertation was titled “Quantification of Quality: The Impact of Money and Monetization on the Development of Scientific Thought in the Fourteenth Century.” Career Kaye was a lecturer at the University of Pennsylvania (1990), and a visiting assistant professor of history at the United States Naval Academy (1991–1992). He joined the faculty of Barnard College, Columbia University, in 1992 as an assistant professor of history, became an associate professor in 2000 and a professor in 2005, and was named Ann Whitney Olin Professor of History in 2016. He chaired the Barnard history department from 2010 to 2013. Columbia University lists him as a Barnard Professor among its emeriti faculty. Research Kaye’s research concerns the intellectual history of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. He has examined how university scholars’ direct experience of a rapidly changing economy was connected to changes in how they conceived of nature, the medical body, the body politic, and the cosmos. Economy and Nature in the Fourteenth Century: Money, Market Exchange, and the Emergence of Scientific Thought (Cambridge University Press, 1998) argues that a major change in the conceptual model of the natural world in scholastic philosophy, centered on the universities of Oxford and Paris between about 1250 and 1375, was tied to a significant degree to the monetization of European society and the growth of markets over the same period. A History of Balance, 1250–1375: The Emergence of a New Model of Equilibrium and Its Impact on Thought (Cambridge University Press, 2014) examines the emergence of a new model of balance, which Kaye describes as a new sense of what balance is and can be, and its effect on four areas of university thought: economics, medicine, political theory and natural philosophy.The book first identifies more than a dozen elements of this model. It then traces how each of those elements appears in scholastic analyses of contemporary economic conditions and practices, including the recognition that a systematic equilibrium, a newly imagined form of balance, governed activity in the urban marketplace. Finally, it argues that major elements of balance understood as equilibrium lie at the core of scholastic advances in natural philosophy. A French translation of A History of Balance was published by Les Belles Lettres in 2017, and an Italian edition of Economy and Nature was published by Le Due Rose in 2022. He co-edited Law and the Illicit in Medieval Europe (2008) with Ruth Mazo Karras and E. Ann Matter, and served as an associate editor of the Dictionary of the Middle Ages supplementary volume (2004). Reception Economy and Nature in the Fourteenth Century was reviewed in several history journals. John W. Baldwin, writing in the American Historical Review, called it a "persuasive circumstantial case" and said that it rested on a sophisticated history of ideas, not on crude economic determinism. He added that the final chapters could be developed further. Diana Wood, in the Economic History Review, described the book as "original, thought-provoking, and full of insight" and said it was written clearly enough for non-specialists. title: Saligramam metro station
text: Saligramam metro station is an upcoming metro station on the Yellow Line of Chennai Metro. It is one of the 18 stations that form the elevated section of the Yellow Line, the section that runs from Kodambakkam Powerhouse to Poonamallee Bypass. With the other stations on the Yellow, Red, and Purple lines of Chennai Metro, it forms Phase II of the network, with the Yellow Line specifically labelled as Corridor 4 of Phase II. It is expected to be opened in mid-2027. The metro station serves and provides access to the neighbourhoods of Saligramam, Ottagapalayam, and the western sections of Vadapalani. Landmarks and facilities accessible from the station include Nexus Vijaya Mall, AVM Productions, Kamala Cinemas, and the Passport Seva Kendra (Passport Service Centre), Saligramam. Kauvery Hospital and Vijaya Hospital are also located close to the station. History A 2021 tender worth ₹1173 crore to construct elevated stations starting from Kodambakkam Powerhouse and proceeding westward to Porur Junction, including Saligramam, was awarded to Larsen & Toubro. For the supply, installation, and commissioning of standard-gauge tracks for the entirety of the Yellow Line, a ₹337-crore tender announced in 2021 was awarded to IRCON International Limited in 2022. In July 2022, a ₹396-crore tender for the design, manufacturing, supply, and installation of the RSS (receiving substation), ASS (auxiliary substation), SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition) system, OHE (overhead equipment), and switching stations for the Yellow Line was awarded to Siemens India Limited. In February 2023, a ₹151-crore tender for the fire protection and VAC (vehicle-actuated control) systems was awarded to Universal MEP Projects & Engineering Services Limited. The line was labelled the Orange Line until 2025; when it was changed to the Yellow Line in the latter half of the year, the station was reclassified accordingly. In October 2026, the section of the Yellow Line between Vadapalani and Poonamallee Bypass was inaugurated by the Prime Minister of India, Narendra Modi, along with Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu, C. Joseph Vijay. This was also an inauguration of the Phase II network of Chennai Metro as a whole. However, the stretch between Saligramam and Alapakkam remained under construction and closed to the public, with trains leaving from Vadapalani making their first stop only at Porur Junction, skipping all intermediary stations. title: Biblioteca Italiana
text: The Biblioteca Italiana was an Italian literary magazine published in Milan from 1816 to 1840 during the Habsburg period. Originally titled Biblioteca Italiana, ossia Giornale di letteratura scienze ed arti, it played a significant role in the cultural debate of the early Italian Risorgimento, and served as the initial forum for the controversy between Classicists and Romantics. The Romantics eventually broke away from the Biblioteca Italiana – which they perceived as too closely aligned with the Austrian occupiers – and founded a new journal, Il Conciliatore, in 1818. Background During the Napoleonic period, when it served as the capital of the Kingdom of Italy (1805–1814), Milan became an important cultural and literary centre. Virtually all of the era's prominent literary figures, including Foscolo, Grossi, Monti, Giordani, Porta, and Romagnosi, were based in Milan, alongside a new generation of writers, which included Manzoni, Pellico and Berchet. On 10 August 1814, the French writer Stendhal settled in the city, where he remained until 1821, "... only leaving after these, the happiest, years of his life, through fear of being implicated in the Carbonari troubles.". The Napoleonic era came to an end in 1814 with the return of the Austrians to Milan. The Habsburg government was initially represented by Field Marshal Heinrich von Bellegarde, who was succeeded in 1816 by Count Franz Joseph Saurau. Intellectuals did not submit to the new regime. It was during Bellegarde’s governorship that Manzoni wrote the anti-Austrian poem Il proclama di Rimini (1815), which was circulated alongside the patriotic poem Marzo 1821 during the revolt of 1848. The poem celebrated Joachim Murat's Rimini Proclamation, which urged the Italians to fight against Austrian rule. On 20 April 1816, Tommaso Grossi circulated the satirical poem La Prineide, which denounced the violent death of Giuseppe Prina, the Minister of Finance for the Kingdom of Italy, who had been murdered amid the unrest following Napoleon’s abdication in 1814. Grossi was identified as the author by the Austrian authorities, who sentenced him to two days in prison (24–26 January 1817). In an attempt to win over, or at least secure the support of, the Italian intellectual elite, Bellegarde and Saurau decided to fund a literary journal. A government-sponsored literary magazine In 1815, Bellegarde approached Ugo Foscolo, one of Italy’s most prominent intellectuals, with the idea of founding and directing a new periodical to promote pro-Austrian sentiment among the educated classes. At first, Foscolo agreed to draft a prospectus for the journal, which was subsequently approved by Saurau. However, upon learning that he would be required to swear an oath of allegiance to the Emperor of Austria, he fled Milan for Switzerland on the night of 30 March 1815. This was a significant setback, but Bellegarde did not give up. Following Foscolo's departure, he approached Vincenzo Monti, who agreed to serve only as assistant director. Eventually, the directorship of the magazine was entrusted to the naturalist and explorer Giuseppe Acerbi, who named it Biblioteca Italiana, taking inspiration from the Swiss monthly Bibliothèque Britannique. Acerbi's aim was to make the Biblioteca Italiana a scholarly journal and avoid political controversies that might compromise its standing with the authorities. Several intellectuals opposed the creation of the magazine and openly boycotted it. Manzoni, for example, declined Acerbi's invitation to contribute to the publication. The magazine, however, managed to attract prestigious figures of contemporary Italian culture, including Pietro Giordani, Gian Domenico Romagnosi, Angelo Mai, Scipione Breislak and Melchiorre Gioia. Bellegarde and Saurau took an additional precaution by ensuring that the periodical’s survival depended on state subsidies. title: Hans Stuber
text: Hans Stuber (died 3 March 1956) was a Swiss racing driver, active in the years before the Second World War. Career Stuber was born in Bern in 1895 and was trained as a mechanic. He opened his own garage in Bern, and had his first race in 1924, at Zugerberg, driving a Buick. He enjoyed some successes in Swiss hillclimbing events in the Buick in 1925, and bought an Ansaldo in 1926. In 1929, he took a more serious step towards a higher standard of racing, buying a Bugatti Type 35C, which helped propel him to the four Swiss hillclimbing titles in the 1930s, and 6th in the 1930 European Mountain Championship; in 1934 he took the Sportscar title in an Alfa Romeo Tipo B with maximum points from the four rounds. It also enabled him to make his Grand Prix debut, at the 1930 Monaco Grand Prix. Stuber ran 4th at one-third distance, but mechanical problems dropped him back, and he soldiered on to a 6th-place result; it would turn out to be his only national Grand Prix finish. He eventually sold the 35C to Armand Hug. In 1931, he bought a Bugatti Type 51, which enabled him not only to dominate the domestic hillclimbing series, winning events such as the Klausenrennen, Schauinslandrennen, Rheineck-Walzenhausen, Gurnigel, Semmeringrennen, Gaisbergrennen, Königsaal-Jilovište, and Lückendorfer Bergrennen, and recorded his best Grande Epreuve finish in it with 3rd at the 1932 Avusrennen, beaten only by Rudolf Caracciola and Manfred von Brauchitsch. However, his later race appearances were few and far between. His last Grand Prix entry was in the Scuderia Maremmana Maserati 8CM at the 1936 Swiss Grand Prix, at which, having been comfortably last in qualifying, he was replaced for the race by Jacques de Rham, but the reason for his slow pace in qualifying was shown up by engine problems ending de Rham's race on the first lap at Kielsgrube, after the first corner. Stuber's consolation was winning his class in the sportscar support race (the Preis von Bremgarten) in his Alfa Romeo. The 1937 event, in which he retired, seems to have been his last. Personal life Stuber was also a captain in the Swiss Army. He was married twice, first to Ida Niederhauser, with whom he had one son, and later to Marianne Schoenemann. He died of a heart attack on 3 March 1956, at the funeral of a friend. Results Single-seaters European Mountain Championship References

title: Li Junpeng
text: Li Junpeng (simplified Chinese: 李钧鹏; traditional Chinese: 李鈞鵬; pinyin: Lǐ Jūnpéng; born 19 February 2009) is a Chinese professional footballer. He plays as a centre-back for China League Two club Shandong Taishan B. Early life and youth career Li was born on 19 February 2009. He is 1.88 m tall. He was listed as a player of the Shandong Luneng Taishan Football School. In 2022, he led Shandong Taishan U13 to the China Youth Football League U13 title. Club career In January 2026, Shandong Taishan promoted Li and Zhang Xuyao to the club's B team. The B team was expected to compete in the 2026 China League Two season. On 5 April 2026, Li made his China League Two debut as a substitute in a 4–1 win over Beijing Institute of Technology. In the 2026 China League Two season, he made eight appearances and scored one goal. International career In May 2024, he was called up to the China U16 national team for its fourth training camp, held in Shanghai. In October 2024, he was included in China U16's 23-man squad for the AFC U17 Asian Cup qualifiers. In April 2025, he scored in China U16's 2–1 Montaigu Cup win over France Vendée U17. In November 2025, Li said he was proud to represent the national team at the AFC U17 Asian Cup qualifiers. In April 2026, he was named in China U17's squad for the AFC U17 Asian Cup. Li served as captain of China U17. In November 2026, he was named in China U17's 21-man squad for the FIFA U17 World Cup in Qatar. He started in China's U17 World Cup match against Morocco on 23 November 2026. title: Chapal Khasnabis
text: Chapal Khasnabis is an Indian prosthetist and orthotist who worked for two decades at the World Health Organization (WHO) in Geneva on disability, rehabilitation and assistive technology. He founded the Bengaluru-based non-governmental organisation Mobility India in 1994, coordinated WHO's Global Cooperation on Assistive Technology (GATE) initiative, and was executive editor of the WHO Standards for Prosthetics and Orthotics (2017) and of the first WHO–UNICEF Global Report on Assistive Technology (2022). Career India Khasnabis began his career as a prosthetist/orthotist in the Indian Ministry of Health before moving to the Ministry of Social Welfare. He headed the department of prosthetics and orthotics at the National Institute for the Orthopaedically Handicapped (NIOH) in Kolkata, since renamed the National Institute for Locomotor Disabilities (Divyangjan) (NILD). On 2 August 1994 he co-established Mobility India in Bangalore with Albina Shankar and became its first executive director. The organisation, which provides rehabilitation and assistive technology services with a focus on rural and low-income communities, became an ISPO-accredited training centre. In 1996 he was awarded the fellowship of the Orthotics and Prosthetics Society of India (OPSI), a society he led for close to two decades. World Health Organization Khasnabis joined WHO in Geneva in 2003 to promote prosthetics and orthotics and community-based rehabilitation (CBR) services. He co-edited WHO's Guidelines on the provision of manual wheelchairs in less-resourced settings (2008) with Johan Borg, was an editor of the subsequent WHO wheelchair service training packages, and was chief editor, with Karen Heinicke-Motsch, of the WHO/ILO/UNESCO/IDDC Community-Based Rehabilitation: CBR Guidelines published in 2010. From the mid-2010s he was programme manager of WHO's Global Cooperation on Assistive Technology (GATE) initiative, which sought to improve access to affordable, high-quality assistive products worldwide and produced the WHO Priority Assistive Products List in 2016. In 2015 he delivered the Knud Jansen Lecture, the traditional opening lecture of the ISPO World Congress, on the GATE concept. He was executive editor of the WHO Standards for Prosthetics and Orthotics (2017), developed with ISPO and USAID. As acting head of WHO's Access to Assistive Technology and Medical Devices unit, he supervised the development of the WHO–UNICEF Global Report on Assistive Technology (2022), of which he was one of three executive editors with Johan Borg and Wei Zhang, and oversaw the 2023 WHO Wheelchair provision guidelines and the assessment package for the prosthetics and orthotics standards. He left WHO in 2023. Later work After leaving WHO, Khasnabis served as senior advisor on assistive technology to the Asian Development Bank. On 17 June 2025 he delivered a keynote lecture, "Prosthetic and orthotic science is the key to sustainable rehabilitation and beyond", at the 20th ISPO World Congress in Stockholm. Honours Fellow of the Orthotics and Prosthetics Society of India (1996) Fellow of the International Society for Prosthetics and Orthotics Honorary Fellow of the Rehabilitation Engineering and Assistive Technology Society of North America (RESNA), 2019 Honorary Member of the Association for the Advancement of Assistive Technology in Europe (AAATE), 2022, "for his tireless work towards including AT in a Global perspective" and his role in the Global Report on Assistive Technology Selected publications Khasnabis, C; Mirza, Z; MacLachlan, M (2015). "Opening the GATE to inclusion for people with disabilities". The Lancet. 386 (10010): 2229–2230. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(15)01093-4. PMID 26681277. The Gerontologist. 56 (Suppl 2): S293–S302. doi:10.1093/geront/gnw005. PMID 26994268. Tebbut

title: Lothar Birckenbach
text: Lothar Georg Birckenbach (21 April 1876 – 22 September 1962) was a German chemist and university professor. Life and education The son of a senior district judge, Lothar Birckenbach studied chemistry at the Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and was admitted to the Corps Makaria Munich in 1899. He received his Ph.D. in 1905. In 1933, Birckenbach signed the Vow of allegiance of the Professors of the German Universities and High-Schools to Adolf Hitler and the National Socialistic State. After his retirement, Lothar Birckenbach lived in Hamburg, where he died at the age of 86. He was buried in the Clausthal cemetery. Research, work, and service In 1907, Lothar Birckenback joined the Baden Aniline & Soda Factory (BASF) in Ludwigshafen am Rhein as head of the analytical laboratory, and he undertook the re-determination of the atomic weights of thallium, bismuth, and beryllium with Alexander Gutbier. He served in the First World War as a reserve officer, ultimately reaching the rank of captain in the reserves, and he became an associate of Otto Hönigschmid at the Chemical Institute of the University of Munich after the war. In 1922, he became the Professor of Mining and Metallurgy Chemistry at the Clausthal University of Technology, and he served as rector in 1924/25. In 1925, he and Karl Kellermann introduced the term pseudohalogen, a class of polyatomic analogues of halogens. Writings The methods for examining hydrogen peroxide, 1909 Practical guide to weight analysis, 1907 Revision of the atomic weight of thallium, analysis of thallol chloride, 1923 Practical guide to dimensional analysis, 4th revised edition, 1924 Revision of the atomic weight of bismuth, analysis of bismuth chloride, 1921 Revision of the atomic weight of beryllium, 1922 References

title: Manop Sriphueng
text: Manop Sriphueng (Thai: มานพ ศรีผึ้ง; 7 July 1959 – 23 November 2026) was a Thai politician who served as the member of the House of Representatives for Nakhon Sawan province from 2019 to 2025, representing the Bhumjaithai Party. He also served as the Chief Executive of the Nakhon Sawan Provincial Administrative Organization from 2010 to 2014. Early life and career Manop Sriphueng was born on 7 July 1959, in Nakhon Sawan, Thailand. He graduated with a Bachelor of Business Administration in Human Resource Development Management from Valaya Alongkorn Rajabhat University. On 5 September 2010, he began his political career when he ran in the election for the Chief Executive of the Nakhon Sawan Provincial Administrative Organization. He won with 207,850 votes, over the other four candidates. His term later ended on 1 September 2014. In 2019, Sriphueng joined the Bhumjaithai Party and ran in the 2019 Thai general election for the Nakhon Sawan's 4th Constituency. He won with 33,642 votes, over the other 32 candidates. In the 2023 Thai general election, Manop ran for re-election for the same constituency. He got re-elected to his seat with 32,934 votes, over the other ten candidates. He remained in office until the dissolution of the House of Representatives in 2025. His son, Marut Sriphueng, replaced him for his seat in the 2026 Thai general election. Personal life and death Sriphueng was married to Phannee Thayida; they had one son named Marut Sriphueng, Thai politician and the representative of the 2026 Thai House of Representatives. Sriphueng died on 23 November 2026, at the age of 67. His death was announced by his son, Marut Sriphueng. References

title: Timeline of the ADF insurgency (2026)
text: This timeline of the Allied Democratic Forces insurgency covers the ADF's militant activity in central and east Africa 2026. Background Following the radicalization of its founding leader, Jamil Mukulu, the ADF was formed as a merger of several rebel groups (initially called ADF/NALU) in 1995. The ADF initially operated in western Uganda but has since, and currently continues to operate solely in the eastern DRC; this includes the North Kivu and Ituri Provinces.The ADF's leadership shifted after the imprisonment of Mukulu on 30 April 2015. Musa Seka Baluku, Mukulu's second-in-command since the group's formation, stepped forward in his place shortly after. Under Baluku's leadership, the group made contact with the Islamic State (IS) as early as 2017, were formally recognized as a chapter of IS–Central Africa Province (IS-CAP) in 2018, and formally pledged their allegiance to the IS in 2019. By that year, the ADF had split, with one part remaining loyal to Mukulu and the other to Baluku; the latter renewed their allegiance to the IS in April 2022. Since joining IS-CAP, the ADF increasingly targeted civilians into their attacks. In response to growing causalities at the hands of the ADF, the Congolese and Ugandan armed forces created a joint military force called Operation Shujaa in November 2021. The Operation's already mixed perception, due to views of Uganda's role in the Second Congo War, was further put into question regarding its effectiveness in actually preventing ADF attacks. According to BBC Monitoring, 90% of the IS' operations were carried out in Africa by September 2025, of which the ADF committed the second-highest number of civilian killings by a non-state actors globally in 2025, according to Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED). Timeline January February March April May On 29 May, a human rights group reported that over 100 people were killed and several were abducted by the ADF during May in the Babila Babombi chiefdom, Masisi Territory, Ituri. The group called for more humanitarian aid to displaced persons, and stronger joint operations against the ADF by the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) and the Ugandan People's Defense Force (UPDF). Two days later, on 31 May, an ADF attack in the Ruwenzori commune of North Kivu killed at least 19 civilians. June July August September October November On 2 November, the ADF released a statement claiming attacks on the villages of Mangwandam, Bokoka and a third unnamed place in Ituri Province which occurred October 31st, self-reporting to have killed 11 Christian civilians, scorching multiple homes and looting possessions. On the night of November 5–6, ADF militants raided a rural health clinic in the Christian village of Cantine-Aloya, North Kivu Province, killing 44 civilians and causing the release of six clinic patients suspected to have Ebola, with one being a confirmed case. The ADF later affirmed its responsibility for the attack via its Amaq News Agency, claiming 60 civilian deaths and 200 homes scorched in combination with other smaller-scale attacks to nearby villages. On November 11, the ADF claimed an attack that allegedly occurred on November 8 on a Congolese army barracks in the town of Mabanga, North Kivu province. No casualties were mentioned. In response to the growing number of attacks by ADF militants and civilian doubt in security forces, the FARDC counted as few as 30 civilians killed in "recent violence." Lubero's military administrator, Colonel Alain Kiwewa Mitela, offered "very sincere condolences to this population of the Bapere sector and to part of the Baswagha chiefdom" before appealing to the population to "have trust, total trust" in Operation Shujaa forces. Underscoring that they "had no army other than [theirs]," Kiwewa requested residents to work with security forces to fight against ADF threats throughout the Territory. title: Anastasiya Rahatko
text: Anastasiya Rahatko (Belarusian: Наста Рагатко; also transliterated as Anastasia Rogatko), is a Belarusian journalist, editor and writer. She is a former editor-in-chief of KYKY.org, former head of communications at the Office of Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, and co-founder of the strategic communications agency StratComLab. She published her debut short story collection Nosi s soboy in 2025. Early life and education Rahatko was born in Novorossiysk, Russia. She spent part of her childhood in Zolotonosha, Ukraine, before moving to Belarus, where she grew up. She graduated from Belarusian State University in 2016 with a degree in journalism. As of December 2025, Rahatko lived in Warsaw. Career Journalism Rahatko joined the Minsk-based online publication KYKY.org in 2014, working as a journalist and picture editor. In May 2017, she succeeded Alexandra Romanova as editor-in-chief. She held the position until December 2022. In August 2020, following the presidential election and the ensuing political crisis in Belarus, Rahatko and some of the KYKY.org editorial team left Minsk. Communications In September 2020, after moving to Vilnius, Rahatko joined Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya's team, initially combining her communications work with her role at KYKY.org. She became head of communications at Tsikhanouskaya's office. Together with Nastassia Kastsiuhova, she contributed to Tsikhanouskaya's New Year addresses in 2022 and 2023. Rahatko left the office in March 2023. In April, she co-founded StratComLab with Kastsiuhova and Aliaksandra Lohvinava. The agency was established to provide strategic communications support to political initiatives, non-governmental organisations and media outlets. Writing In November 2025, Rahatko self-published her debut book, Nosi s soboy (Носи с собой; Carry It With You), in Warsaw. The Russian-language collection comprises twelve and a half stories in the genre of autofiction. The collection explores emigration, identity, relationships, war, and the author's experiences in journalism and political communications. In September 2026, Lohvinau published a Belarusian translation by Ivan Stasevich under the title Nasi z saboy (Насі з сабой). Rahatko wrote a new preface for this edition. Reception The Belarusian Council for Culture reviewed the book as an example of independent Belarusian publishing. It welcomed Rahatko's literary debut but questioned aspects of her publishing and marketing strategy. In a review reproduced by Nasha Niva in January 2026, historian Tamara Eidelman praised the combination of autobiographical material, fiction and irony, highlighting the treatment of relationships, war and the search for meaning. Yevgeny Kogan, co-founder of the Babel bookshop in Tel Aviv, described the collection as an intimate account of emigration and memory, noting its use of humour. Bibliography Nosi s soboy (Носи с собой). Warsaw: self-published, 2025. 172 pp. ISBN 978-83-946356-4-0. Nasi z saboy (Насі з сабой). Translated into Belarusian by Ivan Stasevich. Lohvinau, 2026. title: Makkatang Daeng Sibali
text: Makkatang Daeng Sibali (9 February 1925 - ?) was an Indonesian politician and armed officer who served as a member of the House of Representatives (1977-1982) and Regent of Takalar (1965-1967). Biography Sibali was born in Takalar on 9 February 1925. He was the brother of Ranggong Daeng Romo. In 1945, he participated in the Indonesian National Revolution and was appointed as the commandant of Lipang Badjeng in Polongbangkeng. He became the group's delegate to be sent to Java in January 1946. On his way to Java, the ship was broken, forcing him to return to Polongbangkeng. After the formation of Lipang Badjeng's structural organization, he served in various positions within the group, including as a member of the strategic command section of the defense and security division, a member of the General Governance and Information section of the General Governance division, and Head of Coordinator of People's Representatives division. In 1947, Sibali served as the deputy commandant of Lipang Badjeng after the death of his older brother. From January 1948 to December 1949, he was imprisoned. After his release, his position as deputy commandant of Lipang Badjeng was restored. He was then promoted to commandant of Lipang Badjeng. In early 1950, the TNI rejected Lipang Badjeng to be included in its units, causing him to hide in the forest. On 28 April 1952, Sibali became an army officer with the rank of captain after Lipang Badjeng joined the TNI. The group was included in the TNI 721st Battalion. He was deployed to Southeast Sulawesi in 1956 and served there for one year. From September 1957 to October 1958, he studied in Indonesian Army Command and General Staff College (SESKOAD). Upon finishing his studies at SESKOAD, he served as the commandant of the 315th Battalion of Siliwangi Division in 1958. He also got involved in negotiations with DI/TII groups in Takalar and Polobangkeng led by Bahar Mattalioe. Subsequently, he became the assistant V responsible for territory and community affairs at the Interregional Command of Eastern Indonesia (KOANDIT) and Mandala Command from 1959 to 1965. In 1965, Sibali was appointed as the Regent of Takalar, serving in that position for two years. He opposed an attempt of After stepping down as regent, he served as Deputy Chief of Staff of (XIV Military Regional Command/Hasanuddin from 1967 to 1971. In the 1977 election, he was elected as a member of the House of Representatives for the 1977-1982 term, representing South Sulawesi from the Golongan Karya party. He died in unknown year and date. His name was immortalized as the name of a stadium in Takalar. Work Sejarah Perjuangan Kelaskaran Lipan Bajeng (1988).

title: Amor de Encava
text: Amor de Encava is the debut studio album by the Venezuelan music collective Weed420. The album was released on 14 February 2025 through the label Deprerreo. Background Weed420 is a Venezuelan online music collective formed in 2021 in Valencia, Venezuela, with its founding members being Álvaro Gutiérrez (djALVARO), Glitch (gL1tChhhvkVmv), Gabriel, and Swan (swan duhr). They all use social media groups to organize their creative process, such as WhatsApp, Discord, and Facebook. Initially, its early releases consisted primarily of bitcrushed remixes of Venezuelan trap songs. These recordings were later combined to create the Rare Venezuelan Real Trampa mixtape trilogy, which culminated in RVRT 3 (2023). During the production of RVRT 3, Juan Diego Bustillos (DJ Juan) and Samuel (samuelpochi) joined the collective. Around this time, its members also began considering the possibility of forming a more cohesive group, inspired in part by Brockhampton. This direction developed further with Malandreo Conceptual (2024), a mixtape that blended reggaeton and experimental Latin electronica while addressing Venezuelan street culture and the social figure of the malandro. The members later described the release as a turning point in defining Weed420's sound and their commitment to working together. Production on Amor de Encava took place amid the political and economic crisis in Venezuela, particularly following the reelection of Nicolás Maduro in the country's contested presidential election in July 2024. Álvaro recalled that the period between July and September of that year was marked by a sense of despair among the members and people around them, describing the experience as one in which "everything was disappearing before our eyes". Early plans included bringing on various guest collaborators, but these guest spots fell through because they did not fit the emerging narrative core of the project. Weed420 reportedly considered abandoning the record on several occasions due to the member's deep sadness and doubt during this period. However, producer DJ Sueldominimo encouraged the members to complete the project and maintain a consistent direction. Initially conceived by Álvaro in early 2024 as a lighthearted "silly EP", Amor de Encava developed into a more serious and melancholic project during its production. In late 2024, Gato (frowningato) joined the group. Due to economic instability and mass migration from Venezuela, the collective did not meet in person until 2025. Musical style and production Amor de Encava has been described by critics as plunderphonics and epic collage. The album combines elements of Venezuelan and other Latin American popular music with experimental electronic production, drawing on styles such as reggaeton and salsa baúl. Critics grouped the album under the emerging "Latincore" internet scene. Its production incorporates sampling and sound collage, with the group manipulating existing recordings through distortion and reharmonization. The album's concept is structured around the culture surrounding Venezuela's encavas, a line of public transit minibuses produced by Ensamblaje de Carrocerías Valencia since 1962 that serves as a primary mode of transportation in Venezuela. The collective's choice of concept was when Álvaro watched the 13-second short film Heart-Beat by Argentine director Diego Noir depicting a failed romance on a public bus. Encavas operate dynamically without set schedules or calling cards; the driver's assistant shouts out route destinations to pedestrians along the way. Their drivers, known as encaveros, often customize their vehicles with elaborate decorations, including personalized names, family photographs, religious imagery, and references to musicians. They also play music through onboard sound systems, with selections including slowed-down reggaeton, Venezuelan salsa (salsa baúl), merengue, and vallenato.
