title: He Sifan
text: He Sifan (Chinese: 何思凡; pinyin: Hé Sīfán; born 14 January 2009) is a Chinese professional footballer who plays as a forward or left winger for China League Two club Wuhan Three Towns B, on loan from Shandong Taishan Youth. Early life and youth career He Sifan was born on 14 January 2009 in Hefei, Anhui. He attended Hefei Zhuxi Primary School, where he was selected for the school team during his primary school years. In 2018, he entered the Weifang Sports School men's football team. In 2019, he passed the selection for the Luneng Football School and joined its youth system. In 2022, he scored the winning goal in the final of the inaugural China Youth Football League U13 tournament for Shandong Taishan U13. Club career On 22 July 2026, Wuhan Three Towns B completed the loan signing of He Sifan from Shandong Taishan Youth. On 26 July 2026, he made his professional debut and scored his first professional goal in a 1–1 away draw against Hubei Istar in the China League Two. In the 2026 China League Two season, he made 7 appearances and scored 2 goals for Wuhan Three Towns B. International career In March 2025, He Sifan was called up to the China U16 national team. In May 2025, he scored in a 2–1 win over Saudi Arabia U16 at the Hohhot International Football Tournament. In May 2026, he represented China U17 at the 2026 AFC U-17 Asian Cup. He scored in a 2–0 group stage win over Qatar U17, a result that secured China's qualification for the 2026 FIFA U-17 World Cup. In the quarter-final against Saudi Arabia U17, he provided an assist and scored a stoppage-time goal in a 3–1 win. In late 2026, he was named in the China U17 squad for the 2026 FIFA U-17 World Cup. Career statistics Club As of 24 November 2026 Honours Shandong Taishan U13 China Youth Football League U13: 2022 China U17 AFC U-17 Asian Cup runner-up: 2026

title: Sack of Tana
text: The Sack of Tana occurred in September 1343 when the local Tatar population and forces of the Golden Horde, under Khan Jani Beg, attacked, killed, looted, and expelled Venetian, Genoese, and other Italian merchants from the Black Sea trading port of Tana (present-day Azov, Russia). The conflict was precipitated by the murder of a local Mongol (Tatar) official by a Venetian nobleman and the subsequent refusal of the Venetians to hand over the perpetrator for trial under Golden Horde jurisdiction. The resulting uprising led to the flight of the Venetians and Genoese from Tana, the slaughter of those who were unable to reach their ships, the capture of dozens of prisoners, and massive commercial losses. The expulsion severed a gateway of the Silk Road, causing immediate commodity shortages in Europe and the ensuing Siege of Caffa (1343-1347). Background Located near the mouth of the Don River on the Sea of Azov, Tana (known to the Golden Horde as Azak) was one of the most important European gateways of Eurasian trade during the 13th and 14th centuries. Under concessions granted by the Khans of the Golden Horde, Venice and Genoa maintained prosperous merchant quarters in the city, using it as a hub to import Eastern silks, spices, furs, and grain into Mediterranean and Western European markets. Under the terms of these treaties, disputes and capital crimes involving subjects of the Golden Horde fell under the judicial authority of the Khan's local officials. Indeed, the treaty stiupulated between Jani Beg and the Venetians, continuing the 1332 agreement between the latter and Jani Beg's predecessor Ozbek, clearly stipulated that the area inhabitated by the Italians, namely the inner city of Azak, was under the authority of the Mongol governor of Crimea, whose seat was Solgat, and who in 1343 was probably a Mongol named Ramadan, and that that authoriry superseded any other. Further, the treaty even expressedly contemplated the event of an altercation between a Venetian and a non-Venetian of any nationality residing in Azak, stipulating that in such a case the consul and governor of Crimea would have examined and judged the matter. Relations between the Italian colonists and Golden Horde authorities deteriorated after Khan Jani Beg took power in 1342. His policies were indeed less lenient towards Italian merchants than those of his predecessor Öz Beg Khan. In September 1343, a Venetian nobleman, Andreolo Civran, became involved in a dispute with a local Mongol official, Khoja Omar. Following the altercation, Civran lay in wait for Khoja Omar and murdered him (or, alternatively, after a brawl in which Khoja hit Civran, perhaps with a punch or a slap, the latter followed the Mongol with a group of Venetians to his house and murderd him there in the night, alongside his whole family). When Golden Horde authorities demanded that Civran be handed over to face justice under Mongol law, the Venetians refused to surrender him, triggering a violent breakdown of order in the city. Sack Following the murder and the Venetian refusal to surrender Civran, the local Tatar population rose up in fury against the Italian merchants in Tana. Supported by Golden Horde authorities, local forces attacked and looted both the Venetian and Genoese quarters. Caught off guard, Italian merchants, sailors, and residents scrambled to evacuate aboard galleys and merchant vessels anchored in the Don River. Those who managed to reach their ships fled across the Black Sea to the fortified Genoese colony of Caffa in Crimea, while those trapped ashore were killed and their warehouses looted. The captain of the Venetian muda Nicolò Belegno found on board of his ship one of the looters and decided to execute him on the spot, an action for which he later would've to provide explanations to the Venetian government. title: Meinrado Paredes
text: Meinrado P. Paredes (21 January 1947 - 11 July 2026) sometimes referred to using his nickname, as "Judge Menmen," was a Filipino human rights lawyer, and former political detainee who later became a Cebu City trial court judge and law educator. He is best known for his leading work in the resistance to the Marcos dictatorship, establishing the Cebu Chapter of the Free Legal Assistance Group which defended the Marcos regime's political detainees in court, and also helping establish similar chapters throughout the Visayas. Among the prominent cases he handled at the time were those of University of the Philippines Cebu student activist Ruben Carranza and Redemptorist priest Rudy Romano. After the People Power Revolution, Paredes eventually became presiding judge of Cebu City Regional Trial Court Branch 13, and later presiding judge of Branch 14. And then he was eventually designated as executive judge of Cebu City's trial courts. After retiring, he focused his attention in teaching law subjects, becoming known for his extensive knowledge of remedial law and constitutional principles. In his student days, Paredes had been a political detainee himself. Having joined the Samahang Demokratiko ng Kabataan, he was arrested by Marcos' forces on 23 September 1972, and was kept for a held at Camp Sergio Osmeña and Camp Lapu-Lapu. He was admitted to the bar a few years later, in 1975. A member of the nationalist coalition Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) in 1986, Paredes was one of only six members at its national convention who cast a dissenting vote when the decision to boycott the 1986 Philippine presidential election was made, but he said that he respected the convention's internal democratic process. After the election, Paredes was present at Fuente Osmeña Circle in Cebu to witness his city participate in the People Power Revolution which would eventually lead to the ouster of Ferdinand Marcos from power. Paredes died of natural causes on 11 July 2026.

title: 2027 Northern Super League season
text: The 2027 Northern Super League season will be the third season of the Northern Super League, the top level of women's Canadian soccer. The regular season will run from April to October, followed by play-offs ending in November. Teams The league expanded to seven clubs this season, with the addition of Winnipeg Ember FC. Stadiums and locations Personnel and sponsorship Regular season Format Each club will play 24 matches during the season, playing each other club twice at home and twice away. The regular season winner will be awarded the Supporters' Shield. Standings Results Positions by week Play-offs The format of the play-offs have not yet been announced. Attendance Foreign players Rosters consist of 20–25 players, of which a maximum of eight can be international players. The following international players are signed for the 2027 season. Note that players may be considered domestic for NSL purposes (Canadian citizens, permanent residents, or refugees) while still representing other countries in international competitions. Broadcasting All 84 regular season matches will be available nationally across multiple platforms, through TSN and CBC. title: Nour Hooshmand
text: Nourijune "Nour" Hooshmand is a Filipino actress. She began as a theater actress, appearing as the Stepdaughter in a local production of Six Characters in Search of an Author staged by Tony Mabesa. She made her film debut in Blue Room (2022), for which she received a Best Supporting Actress nomination at the 2023 FAMAS Awards. She garnered critical acclaim for her lead role as Shirin in the supernatural horror film Cinemartyrs and was subsequently nominated for Best Actress at the 49th Gawad Urian Awards. In 2026, she played the title character, a folk punk musician, in Ria and Janine, friend to the protagonist Isabel (Jorrybell Agoto), in Filipiñana, among numerous other roles. Early life Nourijune Hooshmand is of Filipino and Iranian descent. According to Hooshmand, she was bullied as a child due to her "boyish" demeanor. In high school, she directed a local production of Les Miserables. She graduated cum laude from the Bachelor of Arts Theater program at the University of the Philippines Diliman (UP Diliman). Her Iranian father died in 2026. Career 2018–2022: Beginnings According to Hooshmand, other people often told her that she would likely fail to land acting roles due to her facial features. She developed self-image issues as a result, and decided to focus on backstage work as a theater student at UP Diliman. She took up apprenticeships with stage directors and dabbled in set design. In 2018, stage director Tony Mabesa cast her as the Stepdaughter the school's adaptation of Six Characters in Search of an Author "seemingly out of nowhere". Hooshmand credits Mabesa for being "the first person to believe that I could be onstage". During the COVID-19 pandemic, she auditioned for a Globe Telecom commercial directed by Antoinette Jadaone, of whom she was a fan. This led to Hooshmand being cast as Amber Morado, an intern for Kara Teo (Angelica Panganiban), in The Kangks Show (2021). After several more years of theater performances, Hooshmand made her film debut in the Cinemalaya's Blue Room (2022), portraying Rocky Montinola, the bassist of a fictional indie rock band called Rebel Rebel. She was also cast as Lorie, the love interest of Lili (Yani Villarosa), in the queer coming-of-age series The Marahuyo Project. 2023–present: Awards and growing recognition In 2023, Hooshmand earned a Best Supporting Actress nomination at the 2023 FAMAS Awards for her performance as Rocky in Blue Room. In the same year, she portrayed Alma in the black comedy film A Very Good Girl. The Marahuyo Project was released in 2024. Writing for the Filipino magazine Village Pipol, Chud David Dulay commended the show for "mak[ing] a clear statement that queerness is beyond just being a funny side character but heroes of their own true stories". In August 2024, she starred as Filipino singer Stell's love interest in the music video for his song "Di Ko Masabi". A year later, she played the lead role Mira in Agapito, an official entry in the Short Film Palme d'Or competition of the 2025 Cannes Film Festival. Later in 2025, she starred as Shirin, a young director who shoots a film at a location haunted by the angry souls of slaughtered people, in the supernatural horror film Cinemartyrs. She received critical acclaim for her performance. For her performance in Cinemartyrs, she received a Best Actress nomination at the 49th Gawad Urian Awards. In 2026, Hooshmand won Pangalawang Aktres (lit. 'Secondary Actress') at the Puregold Cinepanalo Film Festival for her performance as Pia, the lead character Boyet's younger sister, in the short film Starfish. She played Janine, a friend of the lead character Isabel (Jorrybell Agoto) in Filipiñana. The film received widespread critical acclaim. In September, Hooshmand played Filipino activist Edgar Jopson's sister Sucel in the biopic Edjop. Sometime before landing the title role in Ria (2026), Hooshmand was struggling to book new roles, as she refused to sign with a talent management agency. In the film, she portrays Ria

title: The Family Idiot
text: The Family Idiot (French: L'Idiot de la famille) is an unfinished work in three volumes in French by Jean-Paul Sartre. The Family Idiot is a sequel to the Search for a Method (in the preface of Critique of Dialectical Reason). It is through his study of Flaubert, that Sartre seeks to demonstrate how the progressive-regressive method, as outlined in Search for a Method, operates in a concrete case. “What can we understand about a man today?” is the question Sartre asks himself. An interest that dates back to his youth Sartre's interest for Flaubert dates back to his youth. —Flaubert's novel of provincial life, published a century earlier—dozens of times, without ever understanding why Charles Bovary let his beard grow, why he died, or why an autopsy was performed on him (see The Words). In Being and Nothingness (1943), Sartre annonces a study on Flaubert in the chapter on existential psychoanalysis. But it was not until 1960—after his study on Baudelaire (1946) and his more than 500-page study on Jean Genet, i.e. Saint Genet (1952), that Sartre finally begins work on his magnum opus on Flaubert. Sartre's study of Flaubert, which runs to thousands of pages, is the result of ten years of tireless research. While the studies on Baudelaire and Genet were essays in existential psychoanalysis, The Family Idiot takes this approach a step further by no longer disregarding objective history. The Two types of neurosis The subjective neurosis The first two volumes cover Flaubert’s early life, from his earliest childhood through his breakdown in Pont-l’Évêque, Calvados in 1844 (the famous crisis) and the illness (epilepsy, hysteria?) that followed. Sartre draws on the future writer’s early writings to reconstruct Flaubert’s youth, his relationships with family members—such as his strict father (chief surgeon in Rouen) and his older brother Achille (the future head of the family)—and his difficult relationship with his mother, who loved Gu’s younger sister above all else. The objective neurosis The third volume focuses on objective neurosis. Sartre asserts that all the authors of Flaubert’s era were neurotic. Society prior to 1870 would allow them only the path of “art for art’s sake,” not a commitment such as that of Zola after 1870, and later that of Sartre, during the period in which he wrote this work on Flaubert. Reception and critique of the work Pierre Bourdieu, the french sociologist, criticizes this work by Jean-Paul Sartre in his book The Rules of Art. He rejects Sartre’s existential psychoanalysis and replaces it with a “socio-analysis” that situates Flaubert’s creative work within the French literary landscape, which was then in the process of taking shape in the 19th century. Pierre-Marc de Biasi, an academic, also criticizes Sartre’s approach, particularly in his essay Gustave Flaubert : une manière spéciale de vivre (Grasset, 2009), in which he asserts that “it is not possible to follow Sartre in all the conclusions he draws from Gustave’s illness regarding his nihilism and the meaning of his work”. Publications Jean-Paul Sartre. L'idiot de la famille : Gustave Flaubert de 1821 à 1857. Paris : Gallimard, 1971-1972, 3 tomes. Jean-Paul Sartre. Sur «L’Idiot de la famille». Situations X, p. 91-115. Paris: Gallimard, 1976.

title: She and Her Girls
text: She and Her Girls (Chinese: 山花烂漫时; pinyin: Shānhuā Lànmàn Shí) is a 2024 Chinese biographical television drama series directed by Fei Zhenxiang and written by Yuan Zidan and others. Inspired by the life of Zhang Guimei, the founder of a free girls' high school in Huaping County, Yunnan, it stars Song Jia as Zhang. The 23-episode series premiered on CCTV-1 and Tencent Video on 10 September 2024. Song Jia's performance won the Best Actress awards at the Magnolia Awards in 2025 and at the Golden Eagle and Feitian Awards in 2026. Premise The series is inspired by the work of Zhang Guimei, a teacher who founded the Huaping High School for Girls in Huaping County, Lijiang, Yunnan, in 2008, offering free education to girls from poor rural families. It follows Zhang's efforts to set up the school and keep its students in education, including her attempt to stop a 14-year-old girl from leaving school after the girl's alcoholic father presses her to marry a stranger for a dowry of 30,000 yuan. Gu Yu, the school's first student, later returns to teach there. Other characters include Ali, a local woman who helps Zhang, and the deputy county head Ma Yongqiang and the head of the county education bureau Zhou Shanqun, who are used as comic supporting figures. Cast Main Song Jia as Zhang Guimei, the founder and principal of the girls' school Lan Xiya as Gu Yu, the school's first student Du Lan He Shiyu Yang Yanjia Special appearance Nie Yuan Production Development In 2022, the National Radio and Television Administration approved a 20-episode drama based on Zhang's life under the working title A School for Girls in the Mountains. Preparations had begun in June 2020, and the scriptwriting, filming and post-production took about three years. The screenwriter Yuan Zidan, known for the Ode to Joy series, was approached in early 2021, and she wrote the script with Ding Han, Huang Shiyang and Li Xiwei. Yuan described the script as original, with characters drawn as composites of several real people, and she chose a light and humorous tone for the story, which she called an "entrepreneurship drama" about building a school. The creative team spent about three years researching in Huaping, retracing the routes of Zhang's visits to her students' homes and interviewing students, villagers and her colleagues. Casting and filming The producers chose 100 girls for three months of training before filming, believing that non-professional performers would portray rural students more convincingly. Lan Xiya auditioned in 2022, and many of the cast were local people from Yunnan, whose dialect and habits shaped their performances. The series was filmed in Huaping, near the real school, and students from the school appeared in some scenes. Song Jia met Zhang while preparing for the role. The producer-in-chief was Yang Yuming, the chairman of Yunnan Radio and Television Media Group, and the producer was Li Xing. Release She and Her Girls premiered in the prime-time slot of CCTV-1 on 10 September 2024, the eve of Teachers' Day, and streamed exclusively on Tencent Video. From 18 September 2024, it also aired on Dragon Television and Beijing Satellite TV. Its first run on CCTV-1 ended in late September, shortly before the National Day holiday. Reception Viewership The series ranked first among dramas airing in the same period for average audience rating, reach and audience loyalty, according to the critics Dai Qing and Shi Tianyue of the Communication University of China. An official of the National Radio and Television Administration's planning institute said that it led several television viewing measures and performed particularly well in the region where its story is set. China Daily reported in October 2024 that it held a score of 9.4 out of 10 on the review site Douban, the highest of any Chinese drama released that year. title: John Vadakel
text: John Vadakel CMI (born 17 August 1943) is an Indian Syro-Malabar Catholic bishop who served as the second bishop of the Eparchy of Bijnor from 2009 to 2019. He is a member of the Carmelites of Mary Immaculate (CMI) and is the bishop emeritus of Bijnor. Early life and education Vadakel was born on 17 August 1943 in Bethlehem parish, now part of the Eparchy of Kothamangalam in Kerala. He joined the Carmelites of Mary Immaculate and made his first religious profession in 1964. He studied philosophy and theology at Dharmaram College in Bangalore. He obtained a bachelor's degree in physics from the University of Kerala, a master's degree in sociology from Hemwati Nandan Bahuguna Garhwal University, and a licentiate from Dharmaram Vidya Kshetram. Priesthood Vadakel was ordained a priest on 19 December 1975 by Bishop Sebastian Mankuzhikary at Sacred Heart Monastery in Thevara, Kerala. He spent much of his priestly ministry working in mission stations within the Eparchy of Bijnor in northern India. He also served on the staff of Dharmaram Vidya Kshetram in Bangalore and as a member of the provincial council of the Bijnor province of the Carmelites of Mary Immaculate. Prior to his appointment as bishop, he served as vicar general of the Eparchy of Bijnor. Episcopal ministry On 14 August 2009, Pope Benedict XVI appointed Vadakel as the second bishop of the Eparchy of Bijnor, succeeding Gratian Mundadan. He received episcopal ordination on 22 October 2009. He served as bishop of Bijnor for approximately ten years, until 2019. During his episcopate, St Joseph's Cathedral in Kotdwar was consecrated on 31 October 2011. Retirement On 30 August 2019, the Holy See announced that Pope Francis had assented to the election of Vincent Nellaiparambil as bishop of Bijnor by the Synod of Bishops of the Syro-Malabar Catholic Church. Nellaiparambil received episcopal ordination and was installed as the third bishop of Bijnor on 1 November 2019. Vadakel became bishop emeritus of the eparchy.

title: Soviet Union–Vietnam relations
text: Relations between the Soviet Union and the Democratic Republic of Vietnam (North Vietnam) date to January 1950, when the Soviet Union became the second country to recognize the Democratic Republic of Vietnam. The Soviet Union provided aid to North Vietnam during the Vietnam War. After the Sino-Soviet split, Vietnam attempted to balance its relations with the USSR on one hand and China on the other. Vietnamese leadership was divided over which of the two countries to support. As a result, Vietnam's relations with both had cooled by 1975. Ultimately, the pro-Soviet group led by Lê Duẩn developed momentum, especially as China sought to improve its own relations with the United States, which many in Vietnamese leadership viewed as a betrayal. From its perspective, the USSR sought to improve relations with Vietnam in order to develop an ally in southeast Asia. The USSR and Vietnam formed a military alliance in November 1978 and the USSR supported Vietnam's invasion of Cambodia a month later. Vietnam's increasing relations with the USSR in turn alarmed Chinese leadership, which feared encirclement by the USSR. That contributed to China's decision to invade Vietnam in the 1979 Sino-Vietnamese War. The USSR provided some intelligence and equipment support to Vietnam during that war. Vietnam joined the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance on June 28, 1978. History The Soviet Union was the second country, after the newly established People's Republic of China, to diplomatically recognize the Democratic Republic of Vietnam during the First Indochina War in January 1950. The Soviet Union pressured the Viet Minh delegation to accept partition as a compromise solution to the conflict at the 1954 Geneva Conference. Later, in 1964, Soviet Premier Alexei Kosygin visited Hanoi to try to dissuade Lê Duẩn against escalating the Vietnam War against South Vietnam and the United States. Nevertheless, the USSR was traditionally one of Vietnam's strongest allies and offered crucial military aid to North Vietnam during the war. Aid included air-defense equipment such as radar and surface-to-air missiles. It also included pilot training and aircraft, such as "some all-weather MIG fighters" and several IL-28 light bombers. A group of Soviet Armed Forces military specialists in Vietnam came at the invitation of Ho Chi Minh personally to render military and engineering assistance to the Vietnamese People's Army. From July 1965 to December 1974, more than 6000 generals and officers and more than 4,500 soldiers were sent to Vietnam as specialists. Small contingents of auxiliary forces from other states like Bulgaria and Cuba accompanied the Soviets. From 1975-2002, forty-four Soviet servicemen were killed in Vietnam, mainly in aviation accidents. During the Sino-Soviet split, Vietnam initially sought to balance relations with China on one hand and the USSR on the other. Vietnamese leadership was divided over which of the countries to support. By 1975, Vietnam's relations with both China and the USSR were cooling as a result of Vietnam's attempt not to take sides in their dispute. The pro-Soviet group led by Lê Duẩn eventually developed momentum, especially as China sought to improve its relations with the United States, which Vietnamese leadership viewed as a betrayal of the China-Vietnam relationship.On its side, the USSR sought to improve relations with Vietnam in order to develop an ally in Southeast Asia. Vietnam's increasing closeness with the USSR in turn alarmed Chinese leadership, which feared encirclement by the USSR. This contributed to China's decision to invade Vietnam, beginning the 1979 Sino-Vietnamese War. Vietnam joined the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance on June 28, 1978. Soviet military aid to Vietnam increased from $75-$125 million in 1977 to $600-$800 million in 1978. On November 3, 1978, Vietnam and the Soviet Union signed a formal military alliance via the Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation. The Soviet Union supported Vietnam

title: District of Columbia Office of Planning
text: The Office of Planning is the department of the government of the District of Columbia. responsible for setting the framework of city's physical and socioeconomic planning. History The Office of Planning was established in January 3, 1983. Work Comprehensive Plan The organization is responsible for maintaining the Comprehensive Plan. The first version of the plan was published by the Office of Planning in 1984. Zoning Regulations The Office of Planning writes proposals for changes to the Zoning Regulations for the District of Columbia. They are approved by the Zoning Commission. Height of Buildings Act 1910 In 2013, the Office of Planning worked with the National Capital Planning Commission to make recommendations on reforms to the Height of Buildings Act of 1910. Small area plans The organization publishes small area plans which set out government planning policy for specific neighborhoods. New Stadium at RFK Campus The Robert F. Kennedy Campus Revitalization Act, an act of Congress, transferred control of the campus from the National Park Service to the Government of the District of Columbia. In 2026, the Office of Planning published a masterplan for the area.

title: Villa Achterwerk
text: Villa Achterwerk was a children's programming block produced by the VPRO. Originally stemming from a half-hour children's block it had on Nederland 2, it received its name in 1992. Essentially, it was an anthology of animated and live-action programming, mostly produced for the VPRO, as well as international acquisitions. History On 13 December 1983, the government gave the VPRO B-status, since, as of latest count at the time of the decision, it had over 313,000 members; 300,000 was the minimum requirement to upgrade. This upgrade was first put to place on 1 October 1984, when it expanded its airtime on television from 2,5 hours a week to six. Until then, the VPRO barely produced children's programs of its own, and saw the upgrade as the right chance to do so. From 7 October, the first VPRO children's block aired on Nederland 2, Het huishouden van Jan Steen, for one hour on Sunday evenings. Over time, the format changed, before becoming its most recognized form, Villa Achterwerk, in 1992. The name was derived from Achterwerk, a column at the back of the children's section of its magazine, VPRO Gids. Its twentieth anniversary was marked with three parties held throughout the Netherlands, as well as repeats of old productions, such as Theo & Thea. Burny Bos, however, noted that the success of commercial children's channels, such as Fox Kids and Nickelodeon, had cast the future of Villa Achterwerk in uncertainty. In 2014, the VPRO announced the end of Villa Achterwerk, and that all children's programs it produced were now under the VPRO Jeugd umbrella. Content Young filmmakers were given the chance to produce animated or live-action content. Most content was subversive and dealt with controversial topics. Notable shows included Zaai, Achterwerk in de kast, Loenatik, Familie van der Ploeg, Rembo & Rembo, De 3 dikke dames, Theo en Thea, Max Laadvermogen, Ffukkie Slim and Purno de Purno. References

title: Richard D. De Veaux
text: Richard D. De Veaux is an American statistician and statistics educator. He is the C. Carlisle and Margaret Tippit Professor of Statistics and chair of the Department of Statistics at Williams College. His research focuses on applied statistics, data mining and statistical learning, including the use of neural networks for prediction, and the application of statistical methods to problems in science and industry. He is a Fellow of the American Statistical Association (ASA) and received the association's Founders Award in 2024 and the Waller Distinguished Career Education Award in 2026. Early life and education De Veaux graduated from Princeton University in 1973 with a Bachelor of Science in Engineering in civil engineering and a Bachelor of Arts in mathematics. He began doctoral studies in statistics at Stanford University, but left at age 23 to pursue modern dance, working professionally as a dancer for four years. He toured the western United States with Tandy Beal & Company, performed with Tanzprojekt in Munich, and co-founded Wimmer, Wimmer and Dancers in Salt Lake City in 1979. The company relocated to Philadelphia in 1980. He received a master's degree in dance education from Stanford University in 1980 and retired from professional dance in 1981. While working at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, he returned to Stanford during the summers to complete his dissertation, Mixtures of Linear Regressions, under Persi Diaconis. He earned his PhD in statistics in 1986. Career De Veaux joined Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania as a research associate in 1980, became a lecturer in January 1984 and an assistant professor later that year. In 1986, he became an assistant professor of civil engineering and operations research at Princeton University. He became a senior lecturer in statistics in 1992 and chaired the university's Committee for Statistical Studies from 1992 to 1994. In 1994, De Veaux joined Williams College as an assistant professor of mathematics; he became associate professor in 1997, professor of statistics in 2001, and in 2013 was appointed the C. Carlisle and Margaret Tippit Professor of Statistics. He chaired the Department of Mathematics and Statistics from 2019 to 2023, served as its associate chair for statistics from 2023 to 2025, and became chair of the Department of Statistics in July 2025. He has held visiting appointments at the Institut national de la recherche agronomique in Montpellier, Université Paul Sabatier in Toulouse and Université René Descartes in Paris, and was William R. Kenan Jr. Visiting Professor for Distinguished Teaching at Princeton in 2006–2007. De Veaux has consulted for companies including American Express, Hewlett-Packard and Alcoa, and has worked with Mickey Hart of the Grateful Dead. De Veaux served as an elected vice president of the American Statistical Association from 2019 to 2021 and earlier on its board of directors as a Council of Sections representative (2012–2016). He was a co-founder of the ASA Section on Statistical Learning and Data Mining and chaired it from 2015 to 2018, and served as program chair of the Joint Statistical Meetings. He was an associate editor of Technometrics from 1992 to 2004 and of Environmetrics from 1997 to 2012.[8] In 2021, he was a member of the ASA President's Task Force on Statistical Significance and Replicability. Research and scholarly works DeVeaux's research has focused on applied statistics, industrial statistics, data mining and predictive modeling. His paper with J. Michael Steele on transformations for estimating soil-water diffusivity received the 1989 Frank Wilcoxon Prize for best practical-application paper in Technometrics. His subsequent work examined prediction intervals for neural networks, comparisons of nonparametric regression methods, including MARS and neural networks, and data quality in an essay co-authored with David Hand. title: Aurore Selormey
text: Aurore Selormey (born 1931) is the first female chartered accountant in Ghana and the first female president of the Institute of Chartered Accountants in Ghana. Early life and education Selormey was born in 1931 and was raised in Tudu and Osu, two neighborhoods of Accra. ) As a pupil, she won awards from the Accra Municipal Authority (AMA), which helped her get a scholarship to Achimota School, which she entered in 1946. Her secondary education was almost cut short when a friend of her father argued that paying for a girl's schooling was a waste. A woman who was a friend of the family changed his mind, which enabled her to continue her education. Career Her first job was in the accounts department of the Post Office. She then went to the United Kingdom for three years of accountancy training. There, she earned the ACCA, AIA and ACIS qualifications and became Ghana's first female accountant.Back in Ghana, she took a job at a major accountancy firm but subsequently left after learning that the men there earned more than she did. At her next employer, she was promoted to assistant manager.When the country secretary was due to leave, she was put forward to replace him, and the company's New York headquarters confirmed her appointment.She was among the founders of the National Investment Bank where she trained several staff who later qualified as accountants. Professional bodies Selormey was the first woman to lead the Institute of Chartered Accountants in Ghana. She also headed the Association of Accountancy Bodies in West Africa (ABWA). As the first president of the Association of Women in Accountancy Ghana (AWAG) she mentored women joining the profession. Award and recognition She was awarded the Order of the Star of the Volta for her work. References

title: Sorcha McCartan
text: Sorcha McCartan is a camogie player originally from Castlewellan in Down. She moved to Cork in 2021 and since 2022 plays as a forward for St Finbarr's and the Cork county team. She has won 3 All-Ireland Senior Camogie Championships and was named player of the year in 2026. Career Sorcha McCartan is from Castlewellan in Down, daughter of the two time All-Ireland Football champion and 1994 Gaelic Football All Star Gregory McCartan. Her first major success was winning the All-Ireland Intermediate Camogie Championship in 2020. She contributed 0-10 from play in the final to overcome Antrim at a scoreline of 4-16 to 2-10 and was awarded a Soaring Stars award at the end of the season. In 2021 Down also won Division 2 of the National Camogie League. Since moving to Cork in 2021 she plays for St Finbarr's and the Cork county team. Since then she's reached five All-Ireland Senior Camogie finals and won three of them in 2023, 2024 and 2026. She also won the National Camogie League in 2025. In 2026 she received her first Camogie All Stars Award and was named Player of the Year. With her club St Finbarr's she won three Cork Senior Championships and two Munster Senior Championships in a row. She reached the All-Ireland Senior Club Championship in 2025 where they fell short to Athenry in a replay. title: The 4thWrite short story prize winner – a tale of teenage girlhood
text: Content warning: This story includes a description of a sexual assault Nadia and I lay on the asphalt road, playing our favourite game for the last time. My older brother Abdullah had taught it to me when I was nine: lie down on a speed bump, legs long and both arms outstretched by your ears, making your body a long pencil. I was in the wrong position that day – it was so hot that the backs of my shins seared when they touched the road, so I had to bend my knees. Nadia wasn’t allowed to have her legs exposed anymore, so her linen trousers protected her. The game was intuitive – when you hear a car coming, roll down the slope and run away as fast you can. If you turned around only to find that the car was a decent way away, you were a baby. Abdullah never explained the underlying objective to me, but I think he enjoyed how much it agitated and scared adults at the same time. Simple and stupid, like most things he taught me at that age, but I liked that it gave me an opportunity to see just how fast I could run; the 100-metre track at school never drew out of me what running for my life did. Nadia didn’t care about any of that, but she humoured me anyway. She and I locked our clammy hands together and raised opposite arms up. Sharp barbs of hair peeked out from the bottom of my T-shirt sleeve, and I wiggled my shoulder to coax the fabric down my arm. I had shaved for the first time a couple of weeks prior, just after my 13th birthday. Nadia told me to lather Radox shower gel on the hair first to prevent cuts, but I had still nicked my skin. ‘If someone tells on us for this again Zara, I swear –’ Nadia said without looking at me. She shaded her eyes from the sun with her arm, eyelashes crumpled against her skin. ‘They won’t. Plus my parents aren’t even home, I told you. There’s no one to tell on us to.’ She sighed and I sighed back mockingly. She reminded me of myself the previous week, when I’d agreed to sleep in my 8-year-old brother’s bed after we’d watched The Ring, but only after I’d doled out a few eyerolls. We heard a low growl emerging from several feet away. Through the open windows of the car came the sound of LMFAO’s Party Rock Anthem. I wasn’t going to any parties at which I could enjoy that anthem, but nonetheless, it had been inescapable all summer. ‘It sounds close – on the count of three this time,’ Nadia said, instead of our usual five. I counted down, scrunching my eyes shut so I could focus on the rumbles of the car. On one, I heard it come to a halt, expelling a gravely noise. I trundled down the speed bump, dragging Nadia with me at first and then letting go of her hand because she was running slower than me, like always. I heard her footsteps behind me as I bounded down the road. It was a few seconds before I noticed I couldn’t hear Nadia anymore and spun around on my heels, gasping for air. She was going in the wrong direction, walking back to the speed bump. Looking at her from behind, I could still tell she was smiling. Her waist-length hair swished in the air as she bobbed her head, but I noticed her shoulders had wilted inwards like they always did when she was shy. And she was shy because the person who had been driving the car, the person I’d expected to be mid-tirade because of our silliness, was Sami. Sami was a 17-year-old boy we had always known. Our mothers were friends in the way that justified mutual invites to big daawats but little contact outside of them. Nadia and I had been at the same girls’ school since we were 4, so Sami was one of the only boys we knew that wasn’t a relative. He got his driving licence that summer and drove a cobalt blue Ford Fiesta that made the sky look pale. No car had ever been cooler. Neither Nadia nor I knew him very well, seeing progressively less of him as we got older. But he saved me once when I was 7 years old. A group of us had been playing darkroom at his house – hide and seek in the dark – and I was doing my best to hide my panic. I was still used to my m

title: Secrets by Bob Woodward review – the world’s most famous reporter reveals all
text: ‘I have always disliked the term ‘investigative reporter’.” So writes Bob Woodward , one of the most celebrated reporters of our time – the man whose Watergate reporting with Carl Bernstein undoubtedly changed the US presidency and journalism itself for ever. His longtime boss, the Washington Post editor Ben Bradlee, disliked the term too: “All reporting is investigative,” Bradlee would say. The term conjures a certain sophistication, perhaps, but part of the beauty of a reporter’s work is how deceptively unsophisticated it can be. Secrets is a far-ranging, revealing memoir of an extraordinary career, but more than that, it is an ode to grinding it out – knocking on doors, asking and asking again, listening, taking notes, making notes on the notes, patiently following every lead to exhaustion. In a media ecosystem saturated with fast and flimsy takes, this feels like a tonic. The real star of his story, Woodward seems to insist, is the shoe leather. Secrets was written with his assistant, Claire McMullen, who is credited at length in a preface for making possible “a project in self-discovery for me at age 83”, by playing the role of shrink and interrogator. It turns out Woodward’s drive to uncover the truth began at the age of 11, when he discovered his parents were on the brink of divorce and his mother was having an affair. “You have to snoop, I concluded,” he writes. “You must look everywhere things could be hidden because they are being hidden.” He kept up the habit as a teenager, working as janitor at his father’s law firm, where he had unfettered access to an attic-full of files on the residents of Wheaton, Illinois: documents detailing the never-spoken-of arrests, sexual assaults and disputes of his neighbours. So much was hidden under the surface. Mark Felt – the FBI source who would later be known as “Deep Throat” – arrives not even 50 pages into this 500-plus-page account, in a chance meeting when Woodward was still in the navy. Woodward began instinctively cultivating Felt well before he even knew he wanted to be a reporter. Was it destiny or simply good intuition and a healthy imagination? The early years of Woodward’s career unfurl in similarly fateful fashion. His first attempt to get hired at the Washington Post – a two-week tryout, granted thanks to a recommendation from a navy admiral – was a spectacular but exhilarating failure: “I had finally found something that I seemed to really like, even love, doing.” Rejected by the Post , he went to work at the Montgomery Sentinel , where he learned the basics of reporting, then renewed his campaign to join the Post, leaving an “obnoxious” number of phone messages for the metropolitan editor, Harry Rosenfeld. Finally, Rosenfeld’s wife asked: “Isn’t this just the kind of reporter you always say you want to hire?” As the Post’s lowest-rung journalist , Woodward was assigned a night shift at the DC police headquarters. Then, 10 months into the job, the Democratic party headquarters was burgled. It was off to the races; soon, Robert Redford was calling. After Watergate, Woodward switched focus to other kinds of secrets: in-fighting on the supreme court, the shadowy workings of the CIA, and one White House administration after another. With the publication of each new book – nearly two dozen in total – yet another stronghold of power found itself unpleasantly exposed. “That Woodward’s an evil guy,” was how Bill Clinton put it after the publication of The Agenda: Inside the Clinton White House. Over time, Woodward became something of a Washington institution himself. To receive a call from him, Clinton aide George Stephanopoulos would later note, was to be struck with two simultaneous thoughts: “ Oh no! and I have arrived! ” A key tenet of Woodward’s was to take seriously the work of everyone he interviewed. Ordinarily tight-lipped political operatives found it hard to turn down the opportunity to unburden themselves to someone who was really listening, who believed their w

title: Vaim Hotel by Jon Fosse review – not your typical ghost story
text: V ery strange things happen in Jon Fosse’s 2025 novel Vaim . A man meets a woman he secretly loved in his youth while running an errand in a nearby town. She asks him to take her away with him, to the place where they both grew up, on the boat he named after her. She wants to live with him, she tells him, even though she is married, and he has never admitted his feelings. This same man, in another section, has now died. The woman returns to her husband, and tells him he must get back with her, but he has to answer to the name she gave him when they lived together. He must also move into the home of the man she had left him for. “All was strange,” the husband admits, and decides those words should be on his tombstone. Indeed, all is – and remains – very strange to the reader: the powerlessness of these men before this woman they hardly seem to know; the randomness of the events in their lives; their spooky, dream-like surreality. But most of all: Fosse’s narrative choices that thwart easy rationalisation. Vaim Hotel is the second volume in the Nobel laureate’s loosely connected trilogy-in-progress set in the fictional Norwegian town of Vaim. Told in Fosse’s hypnotically recursive style, in a nimble translation by Damion Searls, it is ostensibly a tale of captivity that is only a touch less disorienting than its predecessor, thanks in part to the thematic correspondences it establishes. Beckettian in its relish for the absurd and the tediously mundane, this single-sentence novel opens with a man in his 50s who, for reasons he cannot quite explain, drives to Vaim, and decides to lodge at the empty Vaim Hotel, as yet unaware that he might never leave. Here, too, we have a mysterious female figure before whom male agency fails: Brita, owner of the hotel. The man, throughout referred to as the Guest, seems to be on the run, although from what or whom we are never told. Indeed, we are given very few facts about him: thrown crumbs that we snatch in the course of his ruminations as well as his reticent interactions with the novel’s slender cast of characters. Besides Brita, these include a shopkeeper and a sailor who is something of a carry-over character from the previous instalment. There is mention of “a woman I used to be married to”. We also know that the man possesses some kind of notoriety, having appeared in the newspapers many years back, and as a result is vaguely familiar to the people he encounters. He is also a believer in God, and either a consummate dissembler, or a true amnesiac. With him are two heavy suitcases, which may or may not mean he intended a long stay. Why Vaim? Has he been before? Does he have family there? He has “no way of knowing for sure”.

title: ‘It was a cover-up’: HarperCollins accused of using lawyers to shut down concerns about David Walliams
text: The publisher HarperCollins used a leading legal firm and a non-disclosure agreement to “cover up” David Walliams’ inappropriate behaviour towards women two years before the children’s author was unexpectedly dropped, according to former staff. Women had complained to the company’s management for years about the author’s alleged misconduct and harassment. The concerns raised included that Walliams had an “inappropriate” sexual relationship with a woman who was an intern when he first met her, had inappropriate interactions with at least three other women connected to the company including asking two for dates, and approached a girl who appeared to be in her teens at a book signing event. The concerns were ignored for nearly a decade, according to multiple sources, who said employees would instead warn each other to avoid him. It was not until 2023 when managers took action and brought in the City law firm Allen & Overy to investigate the allegations. At least five women spoke to the inquiry, some with first-hand experience of the alleged misconduct. Walliams was never interviewed. His lawyers subsequently said he denied all allegations of harassment or inappropriate behaviour in the workplace. The inquiry quietly wrapped up in early 2024 with no consequences at the time for the author. Walliams, whose bestselling children’s books have been compared to those of Roald Dahl, went on to publish a further five books before HarperCollins severed ties with him in December 2025 . Several former employees said they believed the inquiry was a means to shut down complaints. One, who would only speak anonymously, said: “It was not an inquiry, it was a cover-up.” For one woman who spoke to the inquiry, it led to the end of her career at the publishing company. She was reportedly given a five-figure payout. She told the Guardian and ITV News she wanted to speak out but could not. It is understood she is prevented from doing so because she was gagged by a strict non-disclosure agreement (NDA) as part of her settlement. The women questioned were told they could not discuss anything related to the inquiry or their concerns about Walliams, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the process, and they still feel unable to speak openly. The development comes after a joint investigation by the Guardian and ITV News revealed accusations that Walliams used his celebrity status to prey on young women and teenagers for sex. Two were aged 15 when he first contacted them. Walliams’ lawyers said he denied being a sexual predator or abusing his power. Walliams is now the focus of an investigation by the Metropolitan police into separate “serious sexual misconduct” allegations. Walliams earlier told the Guardian and ITV News he had not broken the law. The new claims about HarperCollins’ handling of complaints raise significant questions for the Rupert Murdoch-owned company, one of the biggest publishers in the world. Leading figures said the law should not be used to silence concerns about inappropriate behaviour in the workplace. Zelda Perkins, who broke an NDA to reveal the sexual misconduct of the Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein and is currently speaking to the UK government about further changing the law to prevent their misuse, said: “Nobody can ever understand what having your voice taken away means.” Victoria Barnsley, who was the chief executive of HarperCollins in the UK until 2013, said it was “absolutely outrageous” how the company allegedly dealt with its bestselling author. She said it was not right that the women “have to move to other companies or be forced out or paid off. That really shouldn’t be happening.” A spokesperson for the publisher said: “We are shocked by the allegations contained in the ITV and Guardian reporting relating to teenage girls. “HarperCollins UK previously terminated its publishing relationship with David Walliams. We take the safety of our people incredibly seriously.” When the Guardian and ITV News publ

title: First Children’s Booker prize reveals ‘Great Eight’ shortlist
text: Books by the Oscar-winning artist Shaun Tan, Artemis Fowl author Eoin Colfer and Nero award-winner Liz Hyder are among the eight titles shortlisted for the first Children’s Booker prize . The award, the Booker prize foundation’s first for children’s fiction, launched last year amid concern that children’s enjoyment of reading had fallen to its lowest level in 20 years . Frank Cottrell-Boyce, the writer and former children’s laureate who chairs this year’s judges, believes the prize can help get more children reading. “I do believe firmly that there’s a book for every child,” he says. “The best thing a competition like this can do is to bring books into the limelight that might not have found their way into the limelight normally, and to start a conversation about the importance of reading.” The winner will receive £50,000, the same as the Booker prize for adult fiction. “That parity is partly why I got involved in the prize,” says Cottrell-Boyce. “There’s very little cultural conversation around children’s books and very little prestige. Why shouldn’t a great children’s book have the same status as a great adult book?” He argues that children’s books are squeezed out in the wider culture as well as on the shop floor. “Even if you walk into a big bookshop, there’s a crime section, there’s romance, and then there’s children’s,” he says. “That means every aspect of children’s is on these few shelves, and half of that is going to be Roald Dahl.” The prize is open to fiction for eight- to 12-year-olds, written in or translated into English and published in the UK or Ireland. The shortlist, billed as the “Great Eight” as opposed to the adult prize’s “Booker dozen” longlist of 12 or 13 books, was chosen from 89 submissions by Cottrell-Boyce, the Ghosts and Horrible Histories actor and comedian Lolly Adefope and the bookseller Sanchita Basu De Sarkar. The list includes Tan’s Hometown, in which a girl raised on an alien planet is told her real home lies elsewhere, and Colfer and Andrew Donkin’s graphic novel War, illustrated by Giovanni Rigano. Iqbal Hussain’s The Night I Borrowed Time is a time-travel adventure, while Hyder and Tom de Freston’s The Teller of Tall Tales follows a teenager drawn into fairytales. Mikey Please is on the list for The Rambler’s Curse, his latest comedy featuring a goblin waiter, as well as Jessica Scott-Whyte and Becka Moor for Séamus Almost Famous, which the adult judges called “a dewy-eyed puppy of a book”. Guy Bass and David Roberts’s The Worst Thing That Could Possibly Happen, a collection of eerie short stories, is “the most beautiful book you could possibly hold in your hand”, according to the judges. Completing the list is Catherine Bruton’s Tadpole Summer, in which a girl pitches a tent in her garden and ends up living there all summer. Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker prize foundation, called it “an energising and varied list, one that respects a wide range of tastes in children”. She added that “for adults, these books are a reminder of the humour, empathy and resilience of young people, and offer a window on to the complexities of their worlds”. “Any of these books stands comparison with any adult book, whatever the category, on its own terms,” says Cottrell-Boyce. Four child judges, picked from more than 4,000 entries, will now join the panel to choose the winner, which will be announced at the Young V&A in London on 2 February. They are Ibrahim, 12, Lainey, 12, Luna, eight, and Myla, 11. “They had to be enthusiastic about books, and about speaking their mind,” says Cottrell-Boyce. “I can’t wait to hear what they think.” Several of the books deal with grief, illness and war. War follows 14-year-old Kat through a city under siege, and Tadpole Summer centres on a girl whose younger brother is seriously ill. title: The Song of Stork and Dromedary by Anjet Daanje review – don’t miss this glorious epic inspired by Emily Brontë
text: I had a plan. I was going to nibble away at this great wedge of a book, a morsel a night, like a little reading mouse. But then the story swallowed me whole. I read Dutch author Anjet Daanje’s The Song of Stork and Dromedary over three feverish nights, and spent the days in between longing for the dark. This 720-page novel should come with a warning label: may cause severe infatuation. We begin in the fictional Yorkshire village of Bridge Fowling with Susan Knowles-Chester, a woman who attends to the dead. The year is 1847, and Susan knows the old ways, the threshold rituals: how to arrange a corpse so it doesn’t gape and gawp at the living. “The villagers have a horror of her work, for wherever she goes, she leaves grief like driftwood in her wake, yet when the time comes, many ask for her help, it is an open secret.” Susan knows the local parson, Robinson Drayden, far too well. She has helped him bury every woman in his household: first his wife, claimed by a breech birth, then each of his five daughters. These doomed sisters are already becoming mythic to Susan (imagine a tubercular version of The Virgin Suicides). But one of them will have a long literary afterlife: Eliza-May Drayden’s raw-toothed novel Haeger Mass – published under an androgynous pen name – will scandalise readers for generations before becoming a classroom classic. Eliza will shapeshift with it, from village girl to gothic icon. It is Susan who will provide one of the earliest tales of Eliza lore – a ghost story. She has seen things she can’t explain. Eliza is an invocation of Emily Brontë, that windswept daughter of the moors, now obscured by 177 years of cult embroidery. The harder we look for the woman, the more elaborate the legend becomes. And so Daanje invents Eliza and puts us in the room with her (though never quite in the inner room of her mind). We read letters, witness statements, journal fragments, poems – watch as Eliza’s body is buried in the dark Yorkshire soil. But she is as elusive as her inspiration. And Eliza refuses to stay buried – perhaps literally. Her coffin is empty, except for some decoy rocks. Did she fake her death, or somehow defy it? The Song of Stork and Dromedary traces the mystery through 11 lives and three centuries: from the first stirrings of the Industrial Revolution to the near future. We meet book collectors, bone hunters and disgraced biographers; spiritualists, physicists and many pairs of sisters; a man who wonders if he might have unknowingly married the cult author (it would explain why his late wife was so secretive). A cryptic notebook keeps appearing and disappearing; a cryptic rash too (literary stigmata?). Meanwhile, the enterprising citizens of Bridge Fowling turn the landmarks of Eliza’s novel into real-world attractions: photo ops for the book buffs. We join these characters at very different points in their lives: some at birth, others as they fall in love. But we follow all of them to the very end, and this novel refuses to hurry death along. Daanje takes her cues from Susan Knowles-Chester, and honours the old ways. To linger over death is to linger over life. The Song of Stork and Dromedary belongs to a lush and playful tradition of literary imposture, alongside AS Byatt’s Possession, Peter Carey’s My Life As a Fake and Anthony Burgess’s Earthly Powers: novels that make a parlour game of literary history. A favourite of mine is Ryan O’Neill’s 2016 Their Brilliant Careers, which offers a potted history of Australian letters told through 16 fake biographies: a glorious piss-take of a book. The more you know about the Brontës, the more you’ll find in Daanje’s novel (is that Elizabeth Gaskell, waving from chapter three?). But we all know more than we think. Summon Emily and a world comes down with her. Not just Wuthering Heights, but the whole wild, gothic Brontë mythos: the lonely sisters, the inky savagery. It’s all spliced into our pop-cultural DNA. title: Green Kingdom by Ben Dark review – a luscious natural history of plant life
text: J ohn Ruskin, the Victorian writer and critic, hated the way science insisted on turning his beloved natural world into something smutty. Botanists, he complained, used “microscopic malice” to reduce the spurs, petals and stamens of his favourite flowers to “obscene processes and prurient apparitions”. Others were less squeamish. In 1908, Marie Stopes, the scientist who later became a champion of birth control, spent three days in Japan’s Matsushima Bay in a state of “grand excitement” hunting ginkgo sperms. Oliver Sacks, the neurologist, passed his adolescence at Kew gawping at the cycads’ sexual organs. Reading Ben Dark’s excellent account, it is hard not to conclude that even the most modest plants are living in a state of permanent arousal. Each of Dark’s chapters tells the story of one plant dynasty, from rootless, seedless pond scum to alpine meadows. Some 97% of all the species that have ever existed are already extinct, but traces of them live on in their descendants, and it is these ancient threads that Dark pursues in this absorbing book. He is a professional gardener, yet his tastes run to the surprisingly sludgy. Orchids and roses have their place in the Green Kingdom, but nothing thrills him more than an evil-looking pond, rich in microscopic nutrients. Sometimes Dark follows plants out of the botany books and into folklore. Overlay a map of Britain’s dragon legends with its coal seams, he explains, and the two match perfectly, from the Scottish Borders to south Wales. Take the Lambton Worm, the eel-like creature hooked in a County Durham brook by young John Lambton, a medieval boy who flung the creature down a well in disgust. There it grew monstrous enough to coil “in glistening black seams” around a hill, until Lambton, now a knight home from crusade, hacked it to pieces in the River Wear. In 1820 the antiquarian Robert Surtees remembered being shown a lump of the worm’s skin “rough and patterned like bull hide”. It was almost certainly a fossilised lycophyte, one of the giant clubmoss trees whose remains became the region’s coal. Elsewhere, history needs no such embellishment. In Hiroshima, Dark visits Shukkeien, a centuries-old garden laid waste in August 1945 by the atomic bomb. The only survivors were a single pine and a ginkgo. Stripped bare by the blast, the ginkgo had nonetheless leafed out again by the end of that terrible summer. This means that buried in its trunk will be a double ring, “the record of a year in which life stopped and restarted”. No matter how many centuries the tree endures, it will always carry the record of that skipped heartbeat. Some of this material has been covered many times before, but what lifts the book is Dark’s writing, which would have gladdened Ruskin’s crabby heart. Mosses sit on the earth “as toupées for the world’s scalp”; Colocasia esculenta has “leaves like Norman shields”; “civilisations disappear, ice shrinks away and the campanula abides”. Dark has a sharp eye for the startling detail too: giant bamboo can grow a metre a day and the stalks weigh the same as an Asian elephant. Beneath the pleasures of Green Kingdom runs a serious argument about how we come to know the natural world. The book opens with the wartime destruction of the Berlin-Dahlem Botanical Museum’s collections, in which 3.5 million specimens were burned in a single night. These were the life’s work of the “miners of science”, the patient classifiers who catalogued the plant world one dried sprig at a time. By the time of its destruction, such painstaking work had come to seem “flabby and washed-out”. Since then DNA sequencing has begun to cast “a bright torch” through the tree of life. All the same, argues Dark, it cannot convey the beauty of an orchid’s “white petals above a burnt-caramel lip”. This is a tad ironic. Having spent much of the book rebutting Ruskin’s nostalgia, Dark ends by remaking the Victorian critic’s case against a new and powerful way of understanding the natural world. His pl

title: The Man Who Broke Reality by Philip Ball review – the inspirational genius of Niels Bohr
text: N iels Bohr shares with Albert Einstein pride of place in the pantheon of 20th-century science. The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications of their work. But Bohr differed from Einstein in one crucial respect: his extraordinary personality. In his gripping biography Philip Ball ensures we feel the intense pull of Bohr’s genius. Today he would probably be considered neurodivergent; he possessed a passion for physics that cast a spell on all who knew him. Solving problems is the raison d’etre of any scientist, but Bohr went far beyond that: having inaugurated quantum mechanics with his model of the atom in 1913, he simply would not give up until the rest of it was understood. This relentless passion attracted to him a large group of young researchers who later became famous in their own right: Wolfgang Pauli, Paul Dirac, Lev Landau, John Wheeler, Max Delbrück, Felix Bloch and many others. Bohr was helped in this by an unusual circumstance that would be worth imitating. His Copenhagen institute, funded by the Carlsberg foundation (the beer people) had labs on the ground floor, and floors of accommodation above it which hosted a cast of collaborators, some staying for days, others years. They all revered Bohr, whose Socratic manner, kindly disposition and seeming lack of ego created a true Republic of Numbers. Carl von Weizsäcker best described the atmosphere as one of “love without limits” for the man. Bohr’s life story in essence parallels the first half-century of quantum mechanics. Biographies of physicists frequently either stumble on the physics itself, or veer unnecessarily technical. Ball, one of the few people alive today who is equally at home in biology, chemistry and physics, brings decades of explanatory expertise to the task. The amazing discoveries are explained so effortlessly that the reader hardly realises what just happened. Bohr emerges as someone who greets even half-formed discoveries with enthusiasm, makes sure that credit is given where due, and keeps the momentum going, often exhausting his collaborators with discussions lasting long into the night. His famous intellectual tournament with Einstein at the Solvay Congresses of 1927 and 1930 – probably the greatest in the history of physics – is grippingly recounted (Bohr won in five sets). Ball doesn’t shrink from the contentious aspects of Bohr’s career, and in fact illuminates them convincingly. The Copenhagen School he headed has sometimes been described as dogmatic and cult-like. Ball argues that this, insofar as it is true, is not to be laid at Bohr’s door. When the physics remained stubbornly opaque, Bohr tried to steer a prudent course between conflicting interpretations. His followers lapsed into dogma only after his death. Even when he worked at Los Alamos in the 1940s, Bohr did not materially contribute to development of the atom bomb, though his model of the nucleus had started it all. He was in fact very concerned about the consequences of fission weapons, and the book describes his disastrous encounter with Winston Churchill, during which he suggested sharing atomic secrets with the Russians to avert nuclear war. Churchill angrily took this to be nonsense, and treasonous. Ball also recounts Werner Heisenberg’s famous trip to see Bohr after the Nazi invasion of Denmark in September 1941. Heisenberg, scheduled to give lectures at the German Institute in Copenhagen, was, obtusely, surprised and upset to see that no Danish scientists turned up, despite his long association with and almost filial devotion to Bohr. They subsequently had a guarded conversation about nuclear weapons, each wary of revealing secrets. Ball convincingly argues that Heisenberg’s self-serving rewriting of history after the war, according to which he and other German scientists had done all they could to avoid giving Hitler the bomb, wa

title: Belonging by Sonia Gandhi review – India’s elder stateswoman breaks her silence
text: B y any measure, it is one of the most extraordinary political stories of our age: a shy Italian girl locks eyes with the scion of an Indian political family, falls instantly and steadfastly in love, “transplanting herself” as a result, suffers soul-shattering tragedies, then takes the reins of power in the world’s largest democracy. It is a life that spans the extremes of privilege and distress, and half a century of seismic national history. No wonder publishers have been keen to secure the memoirs of the famously guarded Sonia Gandhi , soon to turn 80. Yet when the chance came, the deal with the country’s biggest publisher, Penguin Random House India, fell through at the last minute over what it termed “an impasse over a particular issue” in the text, with HarperCollins stepping into the breach. For those unfamiliar with the sensitive political context, the Nehru-Gandhi family has been in charge of India for about half the eight decades since independence – and the principal opposition to Narendra Modi’s prickly BJP regime for the past 12 years. As it turns out, Belonging does not read as incendiary. It errs, rather, towards discretion and legacy-building. It is also, at its best, a heartbreaking story of love and loss. Gandhi’s voice is measured and generally frill-free. Flourishes do accompany the meet-cute at a Greek restaurant in Cambridge in the mid-1960s that sets off the story. “That January Sunday, which was to change my life,” she writes, “the sky [was] a beautiful azure dotted with puffy white clouds as in a Tiepolo fresco.” The introduction to fellow student Rajiv Gandhi was “a bolt of lightning”. And, as in a film, there is parental resistance. Sonia’s father, a businessman who worked in construction in a small Italian town, is a second world war veteran, nicknamed Maino the Lion. A 1998 New Yorker profile by Patrick French, briefly a collaborator on Belonging, had him down as “an unrepentant fascist” until his death. Well, was he? We don’t get to find out. Wherever expedient, Gandhi maintains her strategic silence. Stefano Maino, at any rate, is “ padre padrone ” – literally, “father master”. When he hears about his middle daughter’s love interest, he brings “his fist down on his writing table” with a shout of “ Basta! ” And yet, he buys her a ticket to India the moment she turns 21. On the boy’s side is the person who would come to be described as the world’s most powerful woman, Indira Gandhi, the daughter of India’s first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru. Barely has Sonia landed in Delhi than Indira decides the pair must wed (the news reaches the Mainos via radio; Signor Maino stays away). Indira then manages Sonia’s first pregnancy, directs the name-giving ceremony – you get the picture. Gandhi refers to her, factually, as “my mother-in-law”, but, subverting the stereotype, she becomes a devoted daughter. Walking us through her induction into elite Indian family life, she draws an affectionate portrait of this formidable 20th-century figure. But family and party allegiance are a distorting lens through which to view history. Charged events, such as Indira’s crushing of a huge railway strike, acquire a benign gloss. The 21 tumultuous months of the 1975 Emergency – which saw members of the opposition arrested, civil liberties curtailed, the press censored, while a despotic nepo-baby (Sanjay, Indira’s younger son) ran amok – are rendered with a brisk calm. Tenderness is reserved for the repercussions on the family in its subsequent period out of power. Sanjay’s death at 33, just after Indira’s return to power in 1980, leaves the matriarch broken. “In her eyes [Rajiv] was the only one who could come to her rescue.” Gandhi does not interrogate the hereditary approach to democratic politics, but she does recount, affectingly, the fight to protect herself and Rajiv – a commercial pilot with no greater ambitions – and their two children from the inferno. In the book’s strongest scene, she waits disoriented in a cro

title: The Sensualist by Gary Shteyngart review – a delectable romp through life’s pleasures
text: I n 2024, the novelist Gary Shteyngart flew from New York to Milan in search of the perfect midnight-blue suit. There he chose fabric, before flying to Hong Kong to be fitted for four shirts, and on to Tokyo, where he was measured by master tailor Yuhei Yamamoto and master shoe­maker Yohei Fukuda. A short king (“five foot five and a half, with that ‘half’ doing a lot of work”), Shteyngart dreamed of a fit to disappear his 52-year-old moobs (“my tatas”, “my chimichangas”) and melt the heart of the toughest maitre d’ at the most in-demand restaurants. And guess what? The world’s finest craftsmen will give you all that – though Shteyngart, who emigrated from Leningrad to the US in 1979, argues that a great suit serves a deeper need than vanity. Trying it on two days after Trump’s second election, “it was the final certificate of naturalization … I couldn’t make my adopted country fall out of love with fascism, but at least I could enjoy my new shoes.” Clothes become an advanced form of self-care. In this first collection of essays, Shteyngart makes the case for pleasure in a world of joyless productivity. Screw Mark Zuckerberg in his monk’s hoodie. Screw the oligarchs and the mindful drinkers. Here’s a better life hack: choose two best friends “and form a martini trio for life”. Shteyngart adores chilled vodka, old watches and giant rodent TikTok. Again, this is self-care: “‘They regulate you down,’ my shrink told me … as we watched a video that featured superimposed capybaras sashaying down a fashion runway.” When Shteyngart loves a thing, he is all in. His capybara odyssey takes him from Tokyo to Florida and on to South America, where he shadows a Brazilian capybara influencer and witnesses a standoff between marauding rodents and a swanky new development in Buenos Aires. Yes, they are weird and cute, with their “coconut-shaped” bodies and buck-teeth that never stop growing – but Shteyngart also feels they are the animal for the zeitgeist: “a desperately friendly creature always afraid of being attacked … Do we all feel trapped in a world that encourages us to be hyper-social yet rewards us with nothing but endless existential anxiety?” He got into martinis for health reasons (less sugar than beer or wine) though this is easy to forget when Shteyngart is 10 drinks down on a New York bar crawl, trying to engage a wall mural in conversation. A martini is “the elixir of quietude”, he tells us, quoting EB White, though he prefers “friendship juice”. Friends are another revolt against the individualist new world order, and in an introduction Shteyngart mentions he has lost three close ones in the past five years. He doesn’t dwell on this; instead he takes Gerri from Succession (Shteyngart was a consultant on the TV show) to her favourite martini joint in the Village. Fine suits, cuddly capys, cool celebrities: the world unfurls smoothly before Shteyngart, except in Brooklyn, where he is ignored by waiters while millennials down their fruits de mer. As befits a sensualist, his style is deeply pleasurable, great lolloping sentences meeting the punchline of a short one, the jokes generous and surprising. The tone is confiding, charming, often unreservedly silly. I have no idea why Shteyngart decides that wearing a T-shirt with the slogan DADDY’S LITTLE MEATBALL will be the perfect icebreaker on a cruise ship but he brilliantly milks it: “the very sight of me (small, ethnic, without a cap bearing the name of a football team) elicits no reaction from other passengers”. Shteyngart teaches writing at Columbia and mentions that pleasure has been notably missing from his students’ work. Could it be that they can’t afford it? His sensualism is very expensive, a long way from touching grass, and the moral case for it retrofitted to a series of articles that tell us more about American magazine budgets than the national mood. title: Bill Wyman’s Rock & Roll Lists review – greatest hits and biggest misses
text: A s veteran US music journalist Bill Wyman (no relation to the Stones bassist) would be the first to point out, the listicle is not a revered form of internet journalism. It labours under a ghastly portmanteau name that simply jams together “list” and “article” but somehow carries a hint of the diminutive about it, which the listicle’s detractors would say is absolutely right: a chart – a Top 20 or 50 or 100 – with each entry warranting a brief paragraph of explication, they are reviled as a cheap, largely effortless way to fill space online. They are also astoundingly popular, particularly when the subject is music, perhaps because people were compiling rock and pop’s history into listicles decades before the internet came along. The NME got there first, in 1974, with what it called a “Writers’ All-Time Top 100 Albums” list – a bold early attempt to define a canon of classic rock, with Sgt Pepper at No 1 and black and female artists sorely under­represented. But it wasn’t until the 90s that the idea really grew legs. Suddenly the music press was awash with retrospective charts, evidence that an increasingly rosy view of rock history was abroad: the 90s also saw the rise of the heritage rock magazine, the expensively packaged retrospective box set and, indeed, of Britpop, an entire genre more or less predicated on evoking vague memories of the past, as if something of its magic might rub off through imitation. In Britain, Q magazine seemed to publish one every other issue: not just the 100 Best Albums of All Time (three times in the space of nine years), but the 100 Greatest British Albums, the 100 Greatest Songs of All Time, the 1001 Songs You Must Own, the 100 Greatest Singers, the 100 Greatest Guitar Tracks Ever, the 100 Best Albumsof the 90s, the 100 Greatest Stars of the 20th Century. In a very American bit of supersizing, Rolling Stone magazine – which had first printed an 100 best albums list in 1987 – dramatically upped the ante by expanding their best-ever lists from a mere 100 entries to 500. You might have thought the public’s appetite for all this had been satiated to the point of nausea, but clearly not. The listicle remains an almost foolproof way of attracting attention (full disclosure: I compile the Guardian’s fortnightly Ranked lists of the best tracks by a given artist, and they’re almost invariably among the most-read music features on the paper’s website). Presumably imbued with a certain if-you-can’t-beat-them spirit, Wyman – whose CV includes the New Yorker, the New York Times, Rolling Stone and a stint at NPR: no fly-by-night hack he – has taken it upon himself to apply a certain rigour to the enterprise. His lists, initially published by New York Magazine and Vulture, involve ranking the entirety of a given artist’s catalogue, weaving context and biography among the judgments to provide a neat career overview. That this is obviously a fairly mammoth undertaking is underlined by the sheer length of the print version: rating every song from the oeuvres of seven artists – the Beatles, Michael Jackson, Led Zeppelin, Pink Floyd, the Eagles, the Clash and Nirvana – it weighs in at around 500 pages. Wyman is a good writer. You can take issue with his opinions, which are expressed in time-honoured loudmouth US rock-crit style (indeed, taking issue with his opinions is part of the point, to which end I’ll just note his belief that the Beatles’ I’ll Cry Instead is a better song than Yesterday, Come Together, I Feel Fine, Taxman and We Can Work It Out is frankly insane and leave it at that). But you’d have a harder time finding fault with his turn of phrase, which is pithy and incisive in equal measure. The steroidal thunder of Good Times Bad Times, the opening track on Led Zeppelin’s debut album, is evidence “the terms of the debate had been changed” – an impressively succinct description of the band’s impact amid the more measured practitioners of the late 60s-blues revival.
