title: Adder Stone by Clare Clark review – the story of a drowned Welsh village
text: I n the author’s note accompanying her eighth novel, Adder Stone, Clare Clark recalls first learning how a lake in the Welsh valleys shrank during the drought of 1976 only to reveal an abandoned village underneath. As a child, Clark became obsessed with the idea, envisaging a sort of Welsh Pompeii – houses and lives frozen in time, buried beneath the water and the mud. Fifty years since that uncanny occurrence, Clark’s richly researched novel seeks to tell the story of that forgotten Welsh village: not abandoned by choice, but forcibly evicted in order to make way for a new reservoir needed to service Liverpool’s growing population. Clark charts how this event had a profound impact on individual lives, but also how it served as a flashpoint in the broader conversation around Welsh independence. Adder Stone opens with a group of men emptying the Jones family home, boxes of treasured possessions roughly carried out, items of furniture unceremoniously dumped in the middle of the driveway and left “huddled together like mourners at the wrong funeral”. The digger then moves in and, with just a few violent sweeps of its yellow claw, razes the house to rubble and dust. This act of destruction is a source of profound grief for the family’s patriarch Dai, as well as for his sensitive teenage son, Emyr. But for Olwen, wife and mother, it presents a chance for a “fresh start, away from the bad memories, all the bitterness and rage”. In short, she declares: “I was free.” What seems to follow, then, is a story of female emancipation. We learn of Olwen’s impoverished upbringing; of the illegitimate pregnancy that only added further shame to her outcast status. After they married, we learn how Olwen struggled to navigate Dai’s erratic temper and her mother-in-law’s open hostility; five years after the old woman’s death, we are told she still “hung about the place like washing on a wet day”. But now, thanks to The Worshipful Corporation of Liverpool, Olwen has a new place, a new house to call her own. For the first time she also takes up work outside the home – a cleaning gig that comes with a pay cheque and the use of a Jeep (she quickly enlists Emyr to teach her how to drive). The cottage she cleans is rented by two Englishmen, a famous painter and his photographer friend, and here Olwen encounters a different kind of life: a life of art and music and poetry. It is, she thinks, “like someone had opened a door”.

title: The best recent crime and thrillers – review roundup
text: The Taper Man by Nick Harkaway (Viking, £22) The second George Smiley continuation novel from John le Carré’s son Nick Harkaway is set in 1965 and features early iterations of several characters who appear in Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy and Smiley’s People. The cold war is at its height, and British intelligence is keen to protect one of its most important sources, Red Army general Vladimir Vasilev. When a colleague is shot in Helsinki, Smiley discovers a connection to a group of Soviet agents who, through their links to a now defunct spying operation in the US, may jeopardise this key asset. Smiley travels to California to find the “Taper Man”, a sleeper agent whose job is to remain behind when the rest of the network is burned. Meanwhile, leftwing academic Roy Bland goes undercover in Moscow, but things do not go according to plan. Intricately plotted and densely written, The Taper Man takes time to get going, with a fair bit of cold war history and analysis to be digested, but it is a worthy and welcome addition to the le Carré canon. Watch the Quiet Snow by Mick Herron (Baskerville, £22) This beautifully presented collection of previously published novellas is the perfect Christmas present for fans of Slow Horses. Two of the stories shed further light on Slough House supremo Jackson Lamb – “a grubby Santa, putting the grot into grotto” – and his shared past with MI5 archivist Molly Doran, while the other three take us into the farther reaches of Herron’s espionage world, where washed-up boozehound John Bachelor works as a “milkman”, looking after retired assets who have “come in from other nations’ colds”. Bachelor’s needs may be simple – shelter, and enough money to pickle himself in peace – but his drunken stumbles into the murky world of double and even triple agents invariably lead to complications and the unwelcome attention of fearsome Service chief Diana Taverner. With Herron’s trademark blend of cynical humour, sinister undercurrents, suspense, irony and pathos, this is a splendid read for a dark night. Revenge Plot by Stephanie Wrobel (Michael Joseph, £1 8.99) It’s Christmas, and literary agent Claudia Conley has rented a remote Catskills treehouse for solo festivities. Not only does she have family problems, she also has money worries, the sales of books by her star author Jo Stone, whose true identity is a closely guarded secret, having declined dramatically. Heavy snowfall means that when aspiring writer Arnie Tenderton deliberately crashes his car on Christmas morning, Claudia, unaware of the subterfuge, feels obliged to invite him and his young passenger to share her dinner. It gradually becomes clear that Arnie, who is determined to get Claudia to read his manuscript, isn’t just a fanatical wannabe author. He knows Jo Stone’s secret, and, as the revelations start to pile up, Claudia realises that she’s about to lose everything she’s worked so hard to build. Tense and pacey, this is a well-executed, bittersweet tale of ambition, artistic integrity, trauma appropriation and collusion, with plenty of entertaining side-eye directed at the publishing industry. The Voices of the Dead by Nicola Upson (Faber, £16.99) The latest instalment in Upson’s impressive Josephine Tey series takes the real-life mystery writer, here turned detective, from the horrors of the May 1941 London blitz to Portmeirion in north Wales. Detective chief inspector Archie Penrose is there on honeymoon, and Noël Coward is finishing his latest comedy, Blithe Spirit, but the relative peace doesn’t last: the National Gallery’s precious paintings are being hidden in a nearby slate mine, a woman’s skeleton is discovered, and Tey and Penrose find themselves investigating a 40-year-old mystery in the midst of a tight-knit community. Psychics have become popular during the trauma of wartime, and the eponymous voices help to cast light on proceedings. In plot terms, it’s a slow start, with the body not discovered until a third of the way through, but Up

title: The Hill by Harriet Clark review – distinctive debut of growing up with a mother in prison
text: A merican author Harriet Clark’s first novel, partly inspired by her own life, is narrated by a girl whose mother is in prison. Suzanna is being raised by grandparents while her mother serves a life sentence for driving the getaway car for a botched bank robbery intended to fund revolutionary political activism. Although Suzanna refuses the narrative, in some ways this is a coming-of-age story, but with a protagonist whose overwhelming need is to go nowhere and change nothing. The Hill is shaped by the tension between the novel’s need for a plot and Suzanna’s rejection of her own role in the Bildungsroman. Prison visits structure Suzanna’s life, their rituals and repetitions at once marking and resisting the passage of time. At first, her grandfather drives her from their shabby urban apartment to the hilltop prison and escorts her to the entrance to the children’s centre, where on a good day the prisoners are allowed to play with their children under close surveillance. Later, the grandfather dies, activities in the centre are restricted and Suzanna’s visits take increasingly constrained forms. Abjuring ordinary teenage activities, she takes the train towards the hill every Saturday, submits to searches, and follows rules about how to move and what and whom she may not touch. Time passes most visibly in Suzanna’s grandmother’s body, the passage towards death harder to deny than the passage towards adulthood. The grandmother, herself a sometime communist with vivid memories of a trip to Russia as a young mother, lives surrounded by friends who are similarly jaded – war-weary Jewish radical thinkers in old age, looking back together on children mostly estranged, dead or far away; husbands who in various ways did not stay the course; wars and regimes more or less survived. Whatever care they receive comes from each other and rarely with good grace. The liveliest conversations – often darkly funny – are about what, if anything, daughters owe to not-good-enough mothers. Perhaps surprisingly, this isn’t a question that preoccupies Suzanna, who has difficulty acknowledging her own agency. Practically competent as her situation requires her to be, she does not want to ascend the ladder of secondary education or break free from a mother who has no freedom. In some ways, the novel’s tight spatial and temporal circles reminded me of Solvej Balle’s On the Calculation of Volume, in which the same day replays itself for the same people in the same place. Suzanna, whose origin story is abandonment, whose estrangement from her mother runs wide and deep, is in many ways arrested, willing immobility in a small world whose narrowness is no protection from time. This is, broadly, realist fiction. The material of low-budget, low-energy domesticity is vivid: smelly bedding, mucky floors, stale food. Avoiding sensationalism, Clark writes more about the low-key, cumulative humiliations and discomforts of incarceration than the horror, which is more effective for its shadowiness. A woman newly released from months of strip-lit solitary confinement keeps asking “what time is this”: the worst punishment seems to be the physical manifestation of the timelessness Suzanna craves. Almost all the physical journeys in The Hill are between the apartment and the prison, mostly by train. The train is another enclosed, shared space, the time on it both liminal and definitive. This feels like a closed-room novel, but it isn’t, or not much more than most novels are. We move from one confinement to another, and back. It took me a few chapters to trust that the novel was teaching me how to read it. There is much conversation, or at least many interweaving monologues from hard-bitten old women, many of whom speak elliptically, leaving Suzanna and the reader to work out the relevance or significance of half-anecdotes from decades gone by. No one goes anywhere or does anything new, and a lot of the talk is rambling. But it coalesces round incidents and themes, and mome

title: ‘We are dream-walking into a desperate situation’: the Booker prize winner on his sci-fi alien invasion wakeup call
text: W ith his twinkling eyes and silver ponytail, M John Harrison doesn’t seem anything like his 81 years. The M stands for Michael, Mike to his friends. And last night he became the oldest author to win the Booker prize for fiction, for his 13th novel, The End of Everything. Our interview is delayed because of wifi issues, which is fitting given that the novel is about – among many things – what happens when non-human intelligence takes over. The End of Everything is the first sci-fi novel to have won the prize in its 58-year history, which is almost as long as Harrison has been writing. “It’s interesting,” he replies, when asked if he feels vindicated, “that something that has an SF-adjacent feel can be regarded as a serious book and given the Booker prize . My problem has always been that I don’t believe in genre. I don’t believe in it in any way.” He gently wags his finger at me. It is a bit like having coffee with a cheerier, more neatly bearded Gandalf – it will surprise no one that, in his youth, Harrison read The Lord of the Rings every year for a decade. Whether he likes it or not, Harrison is hailed as a titan of literary science fiction. His fans have included giants such as the late Ursula K Le Guin and Iain Banks, as well as China Miéville today, and more surprisingly the Sex and the City star, and last year’s Booker judge, Sarah Jessica Parker . But he is not, as he would be the first to say, a household name. Although that has been changing. In 2020 he won the Goldsmiths prize for The Sunken Land Begins to Rise Again , and in 2022 he was himself a Booker judge. The End of Everything took around 15 years to write, with real-world events overtaking him. AI, late capitalism, environmental collapse, the refugee crisis, Brexit – nearly all the manifestations of today’s omni-crisis can be found in the pages of this slim, elusive novel. As its title suggests, this is the work for our end times. “I suddenly thought, ‘Well, you’re 80, you might as well have a go at pushing it over the cliff one more time.’ My rule has always been push it as far as it will go, then move back slightly from the edge. But this time I thought, ‘Let’s push it over and see what happens.’” And what happens is anyone’s guess. As critics have pointed out, The End of Everything deliberately resists definition. It is a triumph of obfuscation. “I could explain some of it to you,” the author says tantalisingly. “But no, I don’t want to.” For Harrison, the world ends not with a bang, but with endless confusion. “It was a book designed to present the explanatory collapse and epistemological collapse that you see in societies that have suddenly lost their grounding.” He describes it as a mix of gothic horror, road movie, science fiction and fantasy – even “a seaside novel”. I would add satire to the list. One thing it is not, Harrison is clear, is a dystopia, but rather a post-disaster novel in the tradition of early JG Ballard or John Wyndham. But he wanted to play with the conventions; he didn’t want the reader to know more than the characters. “It would be ordinary sci-fi,” he says, “if you were told it was the triffids.” Set in an unnamed coastal town somewhere in Kent (“If this is hell, it looks a lot like Margate,” as Peaky Blinders famously had it ) in the nearish future, The End of Everything depicts a disintegrating Britain, after an invasion by an alien species called the iGhettis, which appear as “tall writhing bursts of light”. The iGhettis are a play on “I get it” (explanation), “I get stuff” (capitalism), Getty (extreme wealth), Apple (tech), I (Freud). “I wrote it down and I thought, ‘This is cheap.’ And then I looked at it again and thought, ‘Oh my God, there are so many ambiguities packed into that one word,’” he says with glee. The germ of the novel was the financial crisis of 2007-8. “I had the rage, but I couldn’t make it work.” So he put what he had written away in a drawer and in 2015 “cannibalised” it for a short story called The Crisi

title: ‘No tech, no texts, just childhood’: author Liz Pichon on the secrets behind her multi-million selling Tom Gates series
text: I f you ever find yourself in an airport newsagent, it might be worth peering inside one of Liz Pichon’s books. “I do guerrilla signings,” she tells me conspiratorially. “They let me go in and I sign all the books, just in case. I love the idea of kids buying a book, going on holiday and seeing that I’ve signed it. Sometimes I write ‘surprise!’” It’s a wonder that she hasn’t got sore hands. Pichon is one of the UK’s foremost children’s authors, and this is a big year for her. Not only has she just published the 25th book in her Tom Gates series, Tom Gates Is Not Famous (Yet), but this is the 15th anniversary of the first instalment. She has, at last count, sold 16.5m books in 47 languages, and her work has been adapted for both stage and screen. “I can’t believe it’s 15 years since the first one came out,” she says on a video call from her home. “Now I get 19- and 20-year-olds that grew up with my books. They’ll turn up at an event with a big stack of them and go ‘these were my favourites’, which makes me feel very old.” Although by no means Pichon’s only project – her comic book series The Mubbles is going from strength to strength – Tom Gates seems more and more like her life’s work. A decade and a half is a long time to maintain any series, let alone one in which the main character has been at the same school all along. But the magic of Tom Gates is that the books never feel as if they’re covering old ground. The stories (usually about Tom’s scrapes with his best friend, Derek, older sister Delia and irritating classmate Marcus Meldrew) remain fresh, while the presentation – scrappy, handmade, packed with bonus content and extra features – is just as endearing as ever. “There’s always that moment of slight panic when you first start, where you think: ‘What am I going to write about this time? What haven’t I covered?’” she says. “But I write about small details of family life, things that might happen at home and school, with friends and pets. There’s always something that comes up.” The newest book is based on something that once happened to her husband, songwriter and producer Mark Flannery, who spent his early career as a studio runner for U2. “He told me a story about how he was trying to go to a Simple Minds concert with a friend and they couldn’t get in,” she says. “All of a sudden this big limo pulls up, and U2 get out. The drummer goes, ‘Mark come with us, we’ll get you in.’ I always thought that would be a fun plot for a book.” Pichon enjoys a weird kind of success. Unlike those who write for adults, whose readers might stay with them for a lifetime, children’s authors only have their followers for a short stretch before they grow up and move on. As such, Tom Gates has managed to entertain a rolling caravan of new fans, which is astoundingly hard to maintain. Pichon puts this down to her refusal to cater to modern tastes. “There’s not much technology,” she explains. “You won’t get much text messaging or anything like that. There are some things in childhood that just don’t change. Sibling rivalries, stuff like that. Children in different territories enjoy reading these books, and I think maybe one reason is because I’m not very specific, so they can really put themselves into the setting.” Now 63, Pichon grew up in London and lives in Brighton. She didn’t start writing until she was in her mid-40s, having previously worked designing album covers for Jive Records and a range of greetings cards, and then illustrating picture books for other writers. The late start is something she puts down to insecurity over her dyslexia as a child. “I came from a generation where people just thought I wasn’t academic,” she says. “Of all the things I was good at, none of them were considered to be things you could actually make a living from. So you grow up with that in the background, a lack of expectation. I didn’t have a clue what I wanted to do.” Tom Gates came from what she describes as a desire to start making things she was ge

title: Jodi Picoult: ‘Reading Ta-Nehisi Coates made me rethink racism’
text: My favourite book growing up I loved Maurice Sendak’s Where the Wild Things Are. Max’s visit to the land of monsters is escapist, of course, but there’s darkness and poetry in it, too. “The walls became the world all around” has always stuck with me. The book that changed me as a teenager A Tree Grows in Brooklyn by Betty Smith. My mom gave it to me at around 12 or 13, and I remember thinking it was such an adult book at the time. It gave me a protagonist to admire who thrived in spite of the setbacks in her life, and also helped put into perspective the charmed life I’d been living. The writer who changed my mind Ta-Nehisi Coates. When I read Between the World and Me in 2015, I was working on a book about white privilege (and its flip side, racism), Small Great Things . I had truly believed myself to not be a racist in my everyday life, and reading Coates inspired me to attend social justice workshops. I came to understand there is a difference between being “not a racist” and being antiracist. One is passive, the other is active. The book that made me want to be a writer Gone With the Wind by Margaret Mitchell. I read it at 13 and memorised huge swaths of the book (which also explains why I didn’t have a boyfriend until I was 15). I distinctly remember looking up from the text when she described Atlanta burning, because the image she had crafted of the war and the smoke and the injured soldiers was so real I could smell and see and taste it. I thought: “She created a world out of words. I could do that, too.” The author I came back to Dostoevsky. I tried in high school, and then again in college. It’s just a lot of very long names and philosophical rants that seemingly go nowhere, punctuated by the occasional murder or suicide. I admit that when my eldest son took a high school course on Russian lit, I tried for a third time and … nope. The book I reread When I was in high school, I read Almost Paradise by Susan Isaacs every other year or so. It’s the only book I’ve repeated multiple times. It’s a comfort read about a midwestern part-Jewish girl who marries the Wasp of her dreams, and the life that follows afterward. I think at that time I was trying to imagine a love that encompassing, one that transcended backgrounds. I was going to Princeton, I was surrounded by trust fund babies, children of politicians, people who used “summer” as a verb. I was very much the outsider, and like Jane in this book, I wanted to believe that didn’t matter in the long run. (I wound up happily marrying a Wasp from Princeton. So maybe this book was not just a comfort read, but a how-to primer.) The book I could never read again I have to choose Gone With the Wind again, with a special side mention to Ta-Nehisi Coates and all the others who made me realise that the stereotypical portrait of Black people in this book is something I should have noticed the first time around. The book I discovered later in life The Book Thief by Markus Zusak. Using Death as a narrator is such a bold move, and making Death compassionate rather than terrifying is an even bolder one. Ironically, I now know this book as well as I know any of my own. For the past eight years I’ve been adapting it as a musical, which has been even more rewarding. The book I am currently reading I’ve just finished Everything Was Beautiful and Nothing Hurt by Ben Reeves. It, too, personifies death, but in a very different way. It’s a beautiful exploration of loss, grief and what it means to be human.

title: How can we explain psychosomatic illnesses?
text: W hen Diego started seeing bright flashing lights in his field of vision and felt his legs go weak, he thought he knew immediately what was happening. His mother had a stroke in her 60s, and although Diego was active and (unlike his mother) didn’t smoke, he had always expected that the same would happen to him. So it was a huge relief to be told – after seeing a stroke specialist and having a brain scan – that he had not had a stroke at all. Unfortunately the relief was short-lived. The visual disturbances and the weakness were real and debilitating. If this wasn’t a stroke, what was it? Some illnesses aren’t caused by disease or damage, but arise when the coordinated functioning of the body goes awry. In a percentage of these cases a person’s psychological health is an important element in their symptoms. Intuitively this seems mysterious. We are accustomed to thinking about physical symptoms as being caused by physical events; viruses, inflammation, bleeding. How can something as intangible as a thought have any impact on something as physical as a leg? How can the mind make us ill? The work of Freud still dominates the public and medical imagination here, even though there are important ways in which he was wrong. Freud proposed that quite dramatic physical symptoms can arise as a result of repression, where the memory of an upsetting experience is pushed into the unconscious, leaving a sort of free-floating emotional energy. He saw the mind as being like a pneumatic device: emotions represented energy and that energy had to go somewhere, often leading to the development of a physical symptom. These days, psychologists are more sceptical about this, but the influence of Freudian psychology lives on in the way we talk about psychosomatic illness – a condition where there’s no damage or disease, but clear impairment nonetheless. The terms “conversion” and “somatisation” are derived directly from Freud and still pop up frequently in the literature. Their use is a stark reminder of the fact that, when it comes to explanations, our language can lead us astray. Importantly, the words conversion and somatisation strongly imply an active, even deliberate, process; that the patient with a psychosomatic illness is doing something that brings their symptoms about. They are converting their distress into paralysis, or somati sing their sadness into pain. Is that how things really are? There is still much to be explained about how, in the absence of damage or disease, a body can produce a symptom as dramatic as paralysis or a seizure-like episode. But we are beginning to understand what seems to be important in getting these experiences going. First, remember that our bodies often respond to acute distress in dramatic ways. Strong emotion can entail so called tonic immobility, in which motor areas in the brain are inhibited, and voluntary movement prevented. More familiarly, it can induce trembling, speechlessness and confusion, all of which resemble neurological symptoms. Our perception of these experiences is important. Recognising strong emotion for what it is makes it more manageable. If I tremble while understanding that I am afraid, I might give myself time for the fear to pass and my nervous system to settle down. But when these feelings are taken as a potential sign of disease, we tend to become anxious, with consequences for how we experience and attend to our bodies. Fear increases pain, so any feeling that there is bodily damage (a frightening idea) can be enough to turn up the perceptual volume on physical discomfort or unusual sensations. Paying attention to and trying to control a shaking limb will tend to increase the trembling; attending to a difficulty with movement is likely to increase how severe we think the problem is. What might have started small becomes amplified. People vary in terms of how easy they find it to identify emotions. The term “alexithymia” (translatable as something like “no words for emotions”) ref

title: Abandoning a Cat by Haruki Murakami review – the Norwegian Wood author uncovers the story of his estranged father
text: W hen Haruki Murakami was a child living in Nishinomiya, Japan, his father announced they were getting rid of their cat. He put his son and the cat on his bike and cycled along the Shukugawa river to a beach 2km from their house. There, they put the box with the cat in it on the ground among some trees and cycled away “without a backward glance”. When they got home, they opened their door to find the cat they’d just left “greeting us with a friendly meow, its tail standing tall. It had beaten us home.” Murakami always wondered how the cat got home so quickly, and why his father had wanted to banish her. These are just some of the unanswered questions that surface in Abandoning a Cat, an essay that first appeared in the New Yorker in 2019, and which is now being published as a book and audiobook. Translated by Philip Gabriel and read with gentle warmth by Kotaro Watanabe, it finds the author telling the story of Murakami Sr, from whom he was estranged for 20 years and who remained a mystery to him in his lifetime. He learns how his father had been sent away as a boy to be adopted by a priest and his family, but their plans changed and he was returned to his parents. In adulthood, his plans to become a priest were thwarted when he was drafted to fight in the second world war, during which he witnessed untold horror. In tracing the story of his father, and the multiple ways he was abandoned, Murakami unearths deeper truths about family, memory and human vulnerability. Available from Vintage digital, 1hr 17min Look What You Made Me Do John Lanchester, WF Howes, 9hr 4min This black comedy by the Capital author revolves around a married couple who share a private language. When they find their life and language replicated on a TV show; suspicion lands on a young screen­writer. Read by Louise Brealey and Genevieve Gaunt. Lifeboat at the End of the World Dominic Gregory, William Collins, 8hr 29min Gregory, part of a crew of lifeboat volunteers in Dungeness, Kent, narrates his lyrical memoir about how it feels to set out on the English Channel and save lives, often in the face of anger from anti-migrant protesters.

title: Where to start with: John Berger
text: J ohn Berger was born a hundred years ago today. He was an artist, critic, novelist, poet, polemicist and playwright who made impassioned, idiosyncratic, fiercely attentive and deeply humane contributions to a swathe of artistic and intellectual disciplines across six decades. In fact, the diversity of his output can make it “difficult to grasp,” as Geoff Dyer observes, in his introduction to the Selected Essays. “Even admirers tend to know him in only one or two of his many incarnations.” I hope the recommendations below provide a somewhat representative handle on Berger’s range. I have limited myself to books he assembled himself, which means I haven’t allowed myself to include anthologies, such as the excellent Understanding a Photograph, edited by Dyer, or Tom Overton’s collections Landscapes and Portraits, or the recent selection Across a Frontier, chosen by the similarly interdisciplinary critic, photographer and novelist Teju Cole. There are many ways to approach Berger, but wherever you choose to start, you will be encountering, as Susan Sontag said of him, “a wonderful artist and thinker”. Berger is best remembered for Ways of Seeing, his 1972 BBC television series and accompanying Penguin paperback. Radically, he combined art and social criticism, discussing artworks in relation to advertising, mass reproduction, the female nude, the male gaze and social status. The book’s format is equally revolutionary: the text appears to begin on the front cover, and three of the seven chapters are made up of images only. Ways of Seeing is a sui generis design classic and a swift introduction to Berger’s enduring preoccupations with art, sex and politics. The same year that Ways of Seeing was published, Berger won the fourth Booker prize with G. (1972) . The novel itself has been somewhat overshadowed by Berger’s acceptance speech, in which he pilloried the sponsor Booker McConnell Ltd for their “extensive trading interests” in the Caribbean, announcing that he would be donating half his prize money to the British Black Panther movement. This experimental novel follows a young man (G) and his vigorous sex life as he travels across Europe on the eve of the first world war. G is mostly oblivious – but inextricably connected to – the world-historical events taking place around him. Another excellent place to start would be A Fortunate Man (1967), the first collaboration between Berger and the Swiss photographer Jean Mohr. It is a deceptively simple portrait of a country GP in the Forest of Dean, told through stark photography and haunting prose. Word and image interweave to powerful effect: the minutiae of one man’s vocation reflect compellingly on the whole of society. Berger and Mohr became close friends working on this project and collaborated several times over the following 50 years. One of Berger’s lesser-known titles is Photocopies (1996), which presents a series of exquisite prose vignettes, titled as if they were photographs. Berger captures real moments, reproducing them – photocopying them – with pinpoint attention to detail. The book has an air of delicate stillness: it is a masterclass in clarity and an inspiration for prose stylists. Ways of Seeing may have made his name, but much of Berger’s best art criticism is collected in About Looking (1980), which includes essays on Turner, Giacometti, Magritte, Francis Bacon and Walt Disney. It also includes his famous essay Why Look at Animals?, which considers the fact that we rarely interact with animals today, despite living in a world full of animal imagery. Berger’s third collaboration with Mohr was Another Way of Telling (1982), a revelatory investigation into the art of photography. Despite its diffident subtitle – “A Possible Theory of Photography” – this landmark work stands alongside those of Walter Benjamin, Roland Barthes and Susan Sontag. A photograph is “a meeting place,” writes Berger, “where the interests of the photographer, the photographed, the viewer and th

title: Reeling in the years: how Hollywood fell for its own vanishing glories
text: I f Los Angeles was a person, it might just be a laid-back fiftysomething trouper with cool sunglasses and an even better haircut. Some dodgy episodes in his past, but still handles himself with style. In other words, Los Angeles personified is Cliff Booth – the over-the-hill stuntman played by Brad Pitt in Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood , now turned studio fixer in the sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. Set eight years later in 1977, Further Mis-Adventures is more plot-driven, more Elmore Leonard-esque than the pure expansive “memory piece” of Once Upon a Time. But both films are steeped in the ambience and lore of old LA, drawn in part from Quentin Tarantino’s memories of cruising around the streets aged six in his stepdad’s Karmann Ghia (the car Booth also drives). They’re part of the recent intensely nostalgic LA revivalist mini-boom of work that also includes Paul Thomas Anderson’s Licorice Pizza (2021), Damien Chazelle’s Babylon (2022) and Ti West’s MaXXXine (2024). It’s no accident that this retrospective crew is in high gear just as Los Angeles , and Hollywood, hit the skids in real life. Runaway production to other states and overseas has been sapping the heartland of the California film industry for decades: from its peak in 1996, feature film activity in the city had dropped by 50% by 2013 – and has further declined since. The cardiac arrest suffered by theatrical box office during Covid and the post-2022 streaming slowdown pushed it deeper into the red zone: 42,000 jobs have been lost over the last two years. With half-empty studio lots, landmark talking shops like Patrick’s Roadhouse dying out and swathes of iconic neighbourhoods ravaged by wildfires, the current fear is that job-stealing AI will further hollow out the city, inducing an irreversible state of digital dereliction. No wonder returning to the 60s and 70s to soak up the agent chat at the bar at Musso & Frank, or bask in Sharon Tate basking in her own image at the Bruin theater, is comforting. The late middle-aged LA revivalists like Tarantino, David Fincher (who’s taken over directing from Tarantino on Further Mis-Adventures) and Anderson (who also made the similarly LA-besotted Inherent Vice in 2014) were too young to have experienced that era directly. But hitting working age in the 1990s, the final generation to experience Hollywood’s pre-digital imperial phase, they are the ones now memorialising its heyday as a creative powerhouse. Like today’s AI inflection point, many of the LA revivalist films deal with a moment of transition. Once Upon a Time is caught between the tail end of the stodgy studio system represented by Leonardo DiCaprio’s floundering star Rick Dalton and the New Hollywood noisy neighbours of Roman Polanski and his ilk. And like today’s furore over AI slop supplanting human-led film-making, a strain of panic runs through the new films about the survival of true cinema. “You know what we gotta do? We gotta redefine the form,” says Pitt, playing a silent-film veteran staring down the barrel of the talkies in Babylon. “The man who puts gasoline in your tank goes to the movies – why? Because he feels less alone there. Don’t we owe him more than the same old shit?” Mia Goth’s porn star Maxine Minx, hoping to cross over to “real” movies in 1985 LA, is on the receiving end of a similar pep talk from her director in MaXXXine. So staring into the abyss of the San Andreas fault and fearing for its soul is nothing new for Hollywood. Often for the current revivalist crew, it’s an elusive woman who crystallises this search for a halcyon authenticity: “This is the girl” , as David Lynch intuited a long time back in Mulholland Drive. In Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood, Sharon Tate is the golden-tressed spirit of aspiring LA – and actor Margot Robbie repeated a similar job with her wild-child ingenue in Babylon (with a near-identical scene of watching herself in the cinema). Inherent Vice isn’t specifically about the film industry

title: The Slightest Touch review – running marathons in Colin Farrell and Emma Fogarty’s odd-couple friendship
text: T he personal scenes in this film from Rachel Fleit have been carefully controlled and curated, the privacy of both parties being important, for different and understandable reasons. But it is an unexpectedly intimate, emotional piece of work, a big-hearted odd-couple story, which is perhaps slightly more complex than at first appears. Emma Fogarty is a smart, garrulous woman from Abbeyleix in County Laois in the Republic of Ireland who has EB: epidermolysis bullosa, a rare condition which means that her skin is permanently, agonisingly painful and requires a daily calvary of bandaging and re-bandaging. While getting an award at the People of the year event in 2010 for her campaigning work educating the public about this illness, Emma met and struck up a friendship with Colin Farrell, a supporter and patron of the EB charity Debra Ireland . Their relationship continued for 15 years and in 2025 Farrell agreed to run the Dublin marathon for EB, with the final two miles pushing Emma in her modified wheelchair; a serious physical challenge for any runner. The film shows Emma and Colin in their different worlds preparing in their various ways for the marathon. (They are in fact only shown physically in the same space in the film’s final section.) But the film also shows a candidly emotional Farrell talking about his father, Eamon, who was on his deathbed in Ireland at the time, and talking also about his eldest son James, who was born with Angelman syndrome , similar to cerebral palsy. Clearly, the ebullient Farrell in his middle years is going through something; coming to terms with his recovery from alcohol and substance abuse, with his dad’s final weeks and days, with their difficult relationship in his childhood, and with what his own fatherhood means to him. Emma is helping him get through it. (There is a funny, if somewhat alarming sequence in which Colin lays out the huge store of crisps and chocolates he intends to devour after the marathon and grins: “I can’t get sugar from alcohol any more!”) Perhaps it might have been interesting to put more personal questions to Farrell directly, but Fleit might well have felt that this was too obvious. At all events, this is a very touching and worthwhile double portrait. The Slightest Touch is on HBO Max from 26 November

title: 14th review – Ava DuVernay takes on a bully president and his viper’s-nest court of Maga sycophants
text: A va DuVernay’s previous documentary 13th , energised by the Black Lives Matter movement, was a brilliant polemic about the Thirteenth Amendment to the US constitution , which she argued perpetuated a link between slavery and prison for African American men. Ten years later, and after an almost continuous decade of Trumpism, DuVernay has made a follow-up film about the Fourteenth Amendment , and she has evidently arrived at a rather different attitude to the constitution and its authors’ intentions and good faith. Now she sees the enemy as Maga and the constitution as something that must be defended against a tinpot bully president and his viper’s-nest court of sycophants. The shift in view is not acknowledged, but the overall effect is similar. Utilising a gallery of very smart talking-head interviewees, including conservative Republicans, DuVernay has mounted a vehement and exhilarating defence of what might be called the second American Enlightenment, created by the 13th, 14th and 15th “reconstruction” amendments, drawn up between 1865 and 1870 after the American civil war. The 14th specifically established birthright citizenship, due process and equal rights for all races under the law, and furthermore barred insurrectionists from holding public office, all of which Trump appears casually intent on vandalising, airily amnesiac about his oath to uphold the constitution. As before, DuVernay does a really good job of schooling the audience in how all this stems from the historical trauma of the civil war, at the end of which the south was defeated – less like Germany in 1945, more like Germany in 1918. She shows that in the decades that followed, the secessionists had to be appeased and placated in the interests of calm coexistence: the statues of Robert E Lee and other standard-bearers of the “Lost Cause” which proliferated, some as late as the 1940s and 50s, were tolerated as a kind of cultural identity expression, and the Confederate flag transformed from an icon of slavery into a quaint, picturesque style accessory for T-shirts, hubcaps and electric guitars. This all came out of a backlash that followed the war and DuVernay elegantly shows that Maga is an analogous, microcosmic backlash to the unthinkable disgrace of having had a Black president from 2009 to 2017. Only this time, the United States is actually coming very close to smashing up constitutional rights that somehow stayed in place, at least theoretically, throughout the Jim Crow era. At all events, for a British audience, the idea of a written constitution seems like a utopian luxury. 14th is in UK and US cinemas from 27 November, and on Netflix from 4 December.

title: ‘I said no thanks to the casting couch. But other actresses had problems’: Jane Alexander on 50 years of stardom
text: J ane Alexander will never forget the play that won her a Tony award, a husband and her first film role. The Great White Hope, which ran on Broadway from 1968 to 1970, was based on the life of Black boxer Jack Johnson, who in 1908 became world heavyweight champion in segregated America. Alexander played Eleanor, a white woman married to an African American boxer also called Jack, at a time when interracial marriages were still illegal in many states. Decades later, when the play opened, the US supreme court had only recently struck down all remaining bans – and Alexander received hate mail and death threats for the role. The play also attracted a famous fan: the boxer Muhammad Ali . He came to watch it several times, says Alexander. “He said, ‘This is my story, all except that white chick,’ Alexander remembers. “And in many respects it was.” The previous year, after refusing to be drafted to fight in the Vietnam war, Ali had been stripped of his world heavyweight boxing title and banned from boxing. The few times Alexander saw him, Ali seemed “hurt and angry – rightly so”. She remembers watching him once, unseen by Ali, after the show. Everyone else had left, except the stage doorman, and Ali wandered out on to the stage. He reprised the end of the second act, in which Johnson thunders “in a Hungarian train station thousands of miles from home, ‘You want me? You come and get me. Here I is. Here I is. Here I is.’ And that’s what Muhammad Ali did. ‘Here I is, here I is, here I is!’ to an empty house.” He walked off the stage but Alexander hadn’t “moved an inch. I was left stunned how much it meant to him. Beautiful.” In 1970 a film adaptation of the play was released. The following year Alexander’s performance earned her an Oscar nomination and, although she lost to Glenda Jackson, her career was set. The next 60-odd years saw a wealth of film roles: All the President’s Men, Kramer vs Kramer, Testament. Interesting modern TV roles: last year, she had a guest role in Apple TV’s dystopian thriller Severance. And a lot of theatre, still her passion. “I love being in a room with musicians or actors, the collective experience,” she says. Now 87, Alexander is speaking via video from her home in Canada, where she has lived for nearly 30 years. She also spends half her time in an experimental retirement complex on a college campus in New York, where the residents can take courses and mentor students. “I’m the only actress, but there’s plenty of lawyers, doctors,” she says. It’s working so well, with “so many cognitive and physical experiences going on”. “Hardly anybody’s died in three years,” she adds. “We have people going into their late 90s and 100s. We’ve filled up all the places, and nobody new’s coming in.” When she’s in Canada, she is mostly outdoors. She walks her dog, sees friends. Birdwatching is her great love. “I’m out every single day birding,” she says. One of her current projects is working to prevent bird collisions , most of which are from striking windows and glass buildings. Such strikes may kill more than 1 billion birds in the US alone each year. But, she says, “it’s pretty exciting because it’s all human-made, and so we can fix this problem”. Alexander has many good stories and is writing a memoir. But some of the best ones predate her. Her grandfather, Daniel Quigley, was a doctor whose patients included William Cody, the wild west showman known as Buffalo Bill. Quigley was interested in the use of radium to treat cancer, and established one of the first radium hospitals in the US. He obtained two chunks of the element from Marie Curie in Paris. “My grandmother had half of her brain removed in her late 40s – I think because they kept the radium in the icebox in the kitchen.” Quigley lost a finger to it. When he died, Alexander inherited his unused radium. What did she do with it? “I buried it. I didn’t know what to do with it. I probably should have given it to the Soviet … Smithsonian,” she says, course-correctin

title: Blade Runner 2099 review – every scene of this TV version is packed with terrifying visual beauty
text: M emory: the mother of the muses, and the heart of the Blade Runner franchise. Science fiction is forever asking what it means to be human and, in the future dystopia first painted by Ridley Scott’s 1982 movie, the answer is that we are what we remember: we are the experiences we preserve as a collection of short films inside our heads. In the original Blade Runner, Rachael (Sean Young) is devastated to learn that her childhood memories aren’t real, and she is therefore a robot “replicant”; in Denis Villeneuve’s sequel, Blade Runner 2049, K (Ryan Gosling) knows he’s a replicant but hopes his memories are a sign that he is something close to human. Blade Runner has always been relevant to the age of AI, in that its starting point is that enslaved robots have rebelled. But the new version, the story’s first expansion into television, is acutely topical in an era where we’re increasingly anxious about whether what we’re seeing – or reading – is the work of machines. Fifty years on from the events of the last movie, the replicants have won: “Blade runners” are now replicants hunting down disobedient humans rather than the other way around, and the capture and storage of human memories is illegal. As humanity dies, what it remembers has become valuable contraband. Since it is ultimately about the video fragments in our minds, Blade Runner has, from the start, presented its conception of the future as more of a mood than a story. One of the many things Blade Runner 2099 creator/writer Silka Luisa gets right is keeping that allusive wooziness, prioritising images over details and vibes over the desire to build a complete, logically functioning world. It’s important to, uh, remember that before diving in. But what images, and what vibes! Switch off all the lights and get drunk on Blade Runner 2099’s rich neons and fathomless, paranoid shadows, its abandoned spaces and urban centres that teem like an unfamiliar capital city too packed for you to find your bearings. Retro cathode-ray screens flicker; dangling wires and botched concrete hang haphazardly from ceilings; to a soundtrack that mixes shimmering synths with insistently soulful saxophone. Anyone unlucky enough to be alive in 2099, human or not, determinedly copes as well as they can with everything being broken, while dreaming of something better. Our protagonists are Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a veteran blade runner nearing the end of her lifespan, and Cora (Hunter Schafer), a human posing as a replicant who infiltrates the blade-running operation and becomes Olwen’s sidekick. For different reasons that may not need to make perfect sense, both of them have the same quest: to track down Olwen’s former colleague/lover Marek (Johnny Harris) – who, along with a group of replicants, appears to have gone rogue. Blade Runner 2099 is a fear-of-discovery thriller, with Cora constantly required to react to situations in an authentically replicant way on pain of death, and an Andor -style political allegory, as a fragile network of rebellious humans plot their resistance, swapping intel in rainy alleyways and backstreet bars. Like Andor, it likes to throw in a British actor when it needs a bit of extra irony or intrigue: as well as Harris there’s Tom Burke, Daniel Rigby and, as an inscrutable administrator who enjoys being unhelpful from within a scratched glass booth, Tim Key. The striking visuals are indelibly vivid, from the backstreet pleasure parlour where replicants cosplay as humans, hiring skin suits with puckered flesh and distended pregnancy bellies, to the way humans placed under arrest have their heads smothered by sacks with built-in intubation tubes. Death scenes include a forced hanging after a crunching hand-to-hand fight, and an eerily pretty immolation. Every scene has something gorgeously unsettling. As Olwen and Cora’s shared mission progresses, it becomes clear – not very clear, but as near to it as Blade Runner has ever felt the need to be – that their quest is an emotio

title: Steal a chopper listening to Liszt! I love how Grand Theft Auto VI went crazy for classical
text: I blame Yuja Wang for crashing my car. You know how it is, you’re cruising as fast you can on the freeway, listening to Symphony FM. And then DJ Yuja says: “It’s afternoon here in Vice City: for the worst of you, the day is just starting. Maybe the next piece will inspire you to turn your life around.” And then she played Tchaikovsky – the finale of the Fifth Symphony – and I just lost it to the music. The energy and tempest of the finale turned me into a driving maniac, and I ended up crashing into a G-Wagen down a one-way street as the minor-key maelstrom took over. Thanks Yuja. I’ll send you the repair bill. Such are the hazards of discovering that among the 24 stations you can listen to in Grand Theft Auto VI – and not only in your car – is Symphony FM, hosted by the in-game Yuja, who really is the real-life piano superstar Yuja Wang . And in choosing her “favourite pieces and curating a playlist for players to discover”, she’s put together a set of 16 pieces that only she could have come up with. She’s included herself on the list – and why not, in showstopping performances of Ravel’s La Valse and the finale of Prokofiev’s Second Piano Concerto – but gamers can also romance Jason and Lucia, GTA VI’s central couple, to the final movement of Janáček’s Sinfonietta; they can fly stolen helicopters with Liszt’s Les Préludes, rob banks to the elemental soundtrack of the last movement of Sibelius’s fifth symphony, or cruise the clubs with the first movement of Lutosławski’s Concerto for Orchestra, music that in-game Yuja says “would be the national anthem in a perfect world”. Most impressively, in one of the longest music cues in any video game ever, the whole of the first movement of Mahler’s Sixth Symphony – 24 minutes of it in the recording they’ve chosen, from Antoni Wit and the Polish National Radio Symphony – can be your choice of accompaniment to scenes in which you blow up your rivals, mow down some blameless alligators, or indulge in the many legal – and illegal – activities that GTA inspires . Yuja’s hosting for Symphony FM is both very funny and scurrilously insightful. “Classical music has a reputation for being complicated and therefore better than pop music … It really depends on how drunk you are,” or “some people find classical music boring. Personally every time I press a piano key, my heart rate doubles. Doctors say this is not ideal.” And there’s this: “If you stumbled on this station, but want some heavy metal: classical music can be hardcore. You can head-bang to Stravinsky. I mean everyone head-bangs to Stravinsky.” That’s before she plays Handel’s “I know that my Redeemer liveth” from Messiah – and admittedly there’s no Stravinsky on the playlist – but it’s a good point. This is the longest classical station that GTA has had in its history. (The operatic Double Clef was in GTA III, and there was Sinowav FM in some versions of Chinatown Wars.) We all might have different choices – couldn’t The Rite of Spring have been there; or Lili Boulanger’s Du fond de l’abîme , to hear the emotional consequences of all the mindless violence in the game? – but really that’s just me being persnickety (Apart from the fact that Yuja announces the Nuages movement from Debussy’s Nocturnes and then we hear Fêtes. We’ve all been there, Yuja …) Symphony FM is giving a massive potential listenership, in the biggest single entertainment phenomenon there is right now, the chance to immerse themselves in musical worlds that are as multi-dimensional as GTA VI’s seemingly infinite sandbox of immoral opportunity. It’s a brilliant use of Yuja Wang’s reach, and it opens up whole new worlds of meaning for classical music and gaming. And those worlds are just beginning to be discovered: the comments underneath this YouTube video on how you might use Yuja’s classical playlist to accompany GTA VI’s story of guns’n’romance story are fabulous: “... a video targeting the most terrifying demographic of all: classical gamers” – guilty as charged

title: Post your questions for Carl Cox
text: Beatifically smiling as he sends another packed dancefloor into raptures, Carl Cox is one of the most enduring and reliably euphoria-inducing figures in UK club culture history. As he prepares to close out the current season at Drumsheds, the UK’s biggest nightclub, and looks towards a return of his residency at Ibiza nightclub Unvrs, he will join us to answer your questions. Known for playing a banging yet nuanced blend of house and techno, Cox’s career stretches back to the age of 10, learning his craft growing up in London and later Brighton, funding nights out by trimming his neighbours’ hedges. As Chicago house, Detroit techno and other new styles hit the UK, Cox was primed to receive them: fluidly mixing across three decks at once, he immersed himself in both the illegal rave scene and the new wave of nightclubs cropping up to showcase this music. As Ibiza went from bohemian enclave to the global centre of dance culture, Cox was one of those helping to make that shift happen, including in a long and fruitful partnership with the nightclub Space. Elsewhere, he managed to DJ at midnight on millennium eve twice, by flying across the date line, and his Carl Cox & Friends banner helped to introduce generations of new electronic talent to festival crowds around the world. Cox published his memoir a few years back and earned an OBE, but at the age of 64, this august DJ still maintains an impressive diary of bookings. At Drumsheds on 20 December, he closes the club’s season alongside techno legends and cosmopolitan young pretenders, and next summer, he’ll return to Unvrs in Ibiza – named the best club in the world by DJ Mag this year – for the third year of his weekly residency there. Ahead of those dates he’ll answer your questions on his globetrotting, hugely impactful career. Post them in the comments below before 2pm GMT on Monday 30 November, and we’ll publish his answers in the 11 December edition of the Film & Music section, as well as online.

title: Tidal bans 100% AI-generated music with plans to delete more than 27m tracks
text: The music streaming service Tidal has announced it will ban entirely AI-generated music from its platform and remove millions of songs, saying AI music “diverts streams and royalties away from the artists, and confuses fans”. “To ensure Tidal remains the best place for artists to share their work, and for listeners to enjoy it, we’re removing all tracks that we determine are 100% AI generated,” the company announced on Tuesday. Tracks that were made with assistance from AI will still be allowed but tracks will be rejected if their metadata reveals they were generated solely using AI tools. Tidal’s ban will go into effect on 9 December. The Norwegian-US streaming service, which promises higher quality audio fidelity as a point of difference from streamers like Apple Music and Spotify, revealed it has seen a huge increase in the number of AI-generated tracks on its platform over the past several months. In the past 90 days, 43% of tracks distributed on the platform were identified as 100% AI-generated, Tidal said, with 27m songs on the platform – 6.3% – tagged as entirely AI. On a single day – 6 November – 60% of songs uploaded on a single day were 100% AI. “Yet Tidal subscribers are not listening to these tracks: 96% of them have received zero streams in the last three months,” the company said, adding that it had taken down 65,000 tracks that were flagged as suspected impersonations of real artists. “Wholly AI-generated music intended to mislead listeners and impersonate artists is another serious problem that has only increased in scale,” Tidal said. “It’s true that not all songs catch on immediately, and artists should have time to build their fanbases. But this situation is different – at this scale, the authentic music and artists that Tidal subscribers are looking to listen to and discover get buried.” The company said it would “always fight for artists to get paid more”. “Everything in this update comes back to that,” the statement said. “If you make music, you should be able to put it on Tidal knowing it won’t be buried under tracks no one asked for, or copied by someone pretending to be you.” Tidal’s policy is the most stridently against AI among all the music streaming services. Bandcamp announced its ban on music “generated wholly or in substantial part by AI” in January. Spotify and Apple Music, the two biggest music streamers, label AI tracks and artists as such but still allow fully generated songs to be distributed on their platforms. Spotify has promised users a tool to make AI-generated remixes and cover songs but in October it also revealed that it had removed about 50m “slop” tracks from its recommendations to users and outright deleted 75m “spammy” tracks.

title: Meher Iqbal wins 2026 4thWrite prize with ‘evocative’ coming-of-age story
text: Meher Iqbal has won this year’s 4thWrite prize for short fiction with her story Darkroom, after being longlisted twice in the past. The writer wins £1,000, publication of her story on the Guardian website, and a one-day workshop at the publisher 4th Estate. Darkroom traces the friendship between two teenage girls, Zara and Nadia, as they navigate the excitements and challenges of adolescence. The 4thWrite prize, run in association with the Guardian, is each year open to unpublished short stories by writers of colour based in the UK and Ireland. This year’s judges were literary agent Emma Paterson, writers Kamila Shamsie, Gurnaik Johal, Chanté Joseph and Sanam Mahloudji, 4th Estate publishing director Kishani Widyaratna, and myself. Johal was shortlisted for the prize in 2018 and has since published two books, We Move and Saraswati. Johal was struck by Iqbal’s “ability to build such a complex friendship so efficiently”, while Widyaratna said Darkroom stood out as a “highly compelling and evocative story that vividly conjures the heightened emotions of our early teen years and the intensity of female friendships as we come of age”. Mahloudji described the story as “a sensitive and sensorially rich coming-of-age story about a young teenage friendship, the first jealousies that heighten awareness, as well as the betrayals from the outside that give such friendship new meaning. Written in the heady emotional key of first crushes and disappointments, the story captures the isolation and regret of jealousy with beauty and depth.” Iqbal is a British Pakistani writer born in London. She was longlisted for the prize in 2024 and 2025. Last year, she received a London Writers award, through which she developed her first short story collection, titled Stinging Nettles. Darren Chan was given a special commendation for Love Bite, which Shamsie described as a “really impressive and affecting” story. “The voice is alive immediately – sharp and funny and shot through with darkness. And it’s technically adept too, displaying wonderful control in intercutting backstory with forward momentum.” Also on the shortlist was I Only Mug Girls by Clementine Wolodarsky, Omugwo by Ope Adedeji, Minty Fresh by Diya Nair and London 2060 by Svetlana Chigozie Onye. Iqbal’s story will be published on the Guardian website on Wednesday.

title: Alia Syed wins £10,000 Jarman award for ‘depth and maturity’ of her experimental films
text: Alia Syed has won this year’s Film London Jarman award , the prestigious UK prize for groundbreaking artist film-makers in the UK. The Welsh-Indian film-maker’s work, which incorporates themes of memory, migration and hidden histories, was praised by judges for its “restless will to play, experiment and change”. Syed will receive £10,000 in prize money. Born in Swansea, but working between London and Glasgow, Syed has been making cutting-edge work since the 1980s when she was part of the London Film-Makers’ Co-operative. Her films often revolve around stories handed down from her parents and grandparents. 2019’s Snow is a video diary using hi-8 footage originally shot by her father on a snowy day during the winter of 1995/6. At the time it was filmed, the artist and her father were not on speaking terms, and Syed recounts her experience of viewing the footage, reflecting on elements of the past that cannot be uncovered. Other works have looked at the diaspora experience. Last year’s The Dhaba was a poetic work that used the testimonies of two men who had migrated to Glasgow to examine racism, colonialism and the ever-changing laws around UK immigration. Ka Ba Ddi: A Breath, A Move, A Game, also from 2025, explores the popular south Asian team sport and draws parallels with the way territory is contested in other areas of life. Three other artists made up this year’s shortlist: Sadia Pineda Hameed, Ilona Sagar and Rhea Storr. Commenting on what helped Syed clinch the prize, the jury said they were “struck by the depth and maturity of Alia’s work, which continues to surprise audiences and defy predictability. The beauty and compelling nature of her work is combined with a deep understanding of and inventiveness with the craft of film-making.” Now in its 19th year, the Jarman has built a reputation for spotlighting artists who then go on to gain international acclaim. Previous shortlisted artists have included future Turner prize nominees Lawrence Abu Hamdan, Monster Chetwynd, Heather Phillipson, Sin Wai Kin and Project Art Works. Syed joins a recent winner’s list that includes Grace Ndiritu (2022), Rehana Zaman (2023), Maryam Tafakory (2024), and Onyeka Igwe and Morgan Quaintance (2025). This year’s award was announced during a ceremony at the Soho Hotel, London. Work by the four shortlisted artists is being screened at Whitechapel Gallery, London, until 13 December . A conversation with Syed, alongside viewings of four of her works, will take place at the Barbican on 8 December .

title: Chicken Shop Date host says she ended YouTube show … to find a real date
text: Amelia Dimoldenberg, the host of Chicken Shop Date, has said she decided to end the popular YouTube series which had increasingly left her feeling “isolated” and made her search for real relationships more challenging. The comedian, 32, also revealed she had questioned the future of the interview series after suffering two panic attacks, saying she wanted to end it “before I start resenting it”. Dimoldenberg announced in September that Chicken Shop Date was concluding, with the final episode due to be released on YouTube on Friday. The presenter began the series aged 17 as a magazine column before transitioning to YouTube in 2014, interviewing celebrities in local chicken shops with her unconventional questions and deadpan silences. Dimoldenberg wrote in The Cut magazine : “When you are a child who desires fame, you are really a child who yearns for connection. “I thought the more famous I became, the more likely it was [that] someone would fall in love with me. “If anything, playing a decade-long role of the serial dater has made my real dating life challenging. “People often meet you with a preconceived idea of who you are, their curiosity misplaced. I am so proud of my success, but it has isolated me in some ways.” Dimoldenberg said when she first started the show in 2014, initially interviewing figures from the UK rap and grime scene, part of her believed she could fall in love with someone on-camera, which she believes “grew into a delusion”. She wrote: “Why wouldn’t a hot celebrity want to be with me? I wondered. I started this show when I was a teenager, so of course I’ve had crushes on guests. “I have gone through every emotion a twentysomething woman might experience: fear that they might not like me back, overthinking if and how I should reach out to them again, wondering if they will be at the same glamorous awards show.” She added: “To actually date a guest would have been transgressive and implausible in this constructed reality. “Nevertheless, this belief has been what kept me going and I think kept the audience believing too. Now that the prophecy has gone unfulfilled, a new one must take shape.” The presenter’s interviewees have included Ed Sheeran and Jennifer Lawrence. Paul McCartney turned up for a date in a vegan chicken shop, declining Dimoldenberg’s suggestion that he adopt a pet otter. The comedian also spoke of the panic attacks she has experienced. She wrote: “I knew my perspective on Chicken Shop Date was changing around 18 months ago, when I had my first and then second panic attack ever in the space of a week.” Dimoldenberg continued: “I had stopped drinking at the time because I was trying to pinpoint exactly why I felt so unlike myself. “All of my emotions felt so much more visceral; I figured that’s what happens when you cut out a sedative.” Dimoldenberg told the Edinburgh TV festival earlier this year she is writing a Hollywood romcom, in which she will star as a journalist who finds romance with a celebrity after interviewing them.

title: Proposed Beatles attraction on Savile Row faces rooftop gigs ban
text: The Beatles stunned onlookers when they pitched up on the rooftop of 3 Savile Row in London in 1969 for their final public performance, but now Westminster city council is seeking to ban live music being played there ahead of plans to convert the site into a tourist attraction. On Tuesday, councillors will vote on proposals to turn the Grade-II listed building in Mayfair into a seven-storey “cultural experience and exhibition” commemorating the history and legacy of the Fab Four. Apple Corps, the intellectual property company established by the Beatles in 1968, re-acquired the building – which was the band’s headquarters between 1968 and 1972 – in May, announcing plans to open it to the public as a visitor attraction in 2027. Westminster council set out a number of conditions for its approval as a visitor attraction, including terms ensuring any amplified audio would have to be controlled through noise limiters, and imposing a restriction on live music on the rooftop to avoid “unacceptable noise levels”. The installation of a 2-metre-high acoustic barrier has also been proposed. But the plans have faced opposition from businesses on the street, renowned as the heart of British tailoring. The Savile Row Bespoke Association, an organisation representing the area’s tailors, said the street’s narrow pavements “would lead to dangerous congestion and have a significant negative impact on those who visit and work” there. Planning officers said the proposed changes clashed with local land use policies, but that the building’s unique connection to the Beatles warranted an exception. Apple Corps said the attraction, which would include a cafe-bar and an exhibition shop, could attract up to 900 visitors on weekdays and 1,140 visitors at weekends, but the Mayfair Neighbourhood Forum said the number of tourists would “need to be greatly reduced” and requested that the planned attraction be monitored for 12 months before an expansion. The proposed attraction would feature a re-creation of the studio where the band recorded the album Let it Be, as well as giving fans access to the rooftop where the famous concert took place. Items from the Apple Corps archives would also be on show alongside temporary exhibitions. Paul McCartney called the plans “terrific”. “Tourists come to England and … go to Abbey Road, but they can’t go inside [the studios] – it snares up the traffic and the drivers get really annoyed,” he said. Tom Greene, the chief executive of Apple Corps, said: “Every single day, fans are taking pictures of the outside of 3 Savile Row – but next year they can go in. “Even the railings remain the same from that famous day in 1969.” On 30 January 1969, the Beatles played their last public concert on 3 Savile Row’s rooftop to an audience on the street, before the Metropolitan police arrived and ordered them to reduce the volume. Over a 42-minute set, the band played songs from their final studio album, Let It Be, including Get Back, Don’t Let Me Down, I’ve Got a Feeling and Dig a Pony, as well as an impromptu jam of the national anthem. The performance was documented in The Beatles: Get Back (2021), an eight-hour documentary series released by Disney which reworked footage from Michael Lindsay-Hogg’s 1970 film, Let it Be. This article was amended on 24 November 2026. An earlier version described Let It Be as “the final album [the Beatles] recorded together”. Abbey Road would best fit this description, though Let It Be was released later.

title: ‘I was physically beating myself up before a take’: Rory Culkin on anxiety, fatherhood and his famous brothers
text: R ory Culkin is enjoying the autumn afternoon in a Manhattan park. The trees are a dazzling blur of yellows, greens, oranges and reds; the background silence is so pure you can hear it. “I’m here with my baby daughter, Havoc,” he says. “Havoc Moon.” I tell him that is the spookiest name ever. “Thank you,” he says. Culkin chuckles like a revving moped, his huge blue eyes lighting up. “Yes, it’s a weird one. I think she’ll probably be the opposite. A sweet, quiet girl. She’ll play a harp or something.” He explains its origin. “I just threw out names to my partner one night when we went to dinner. She wasn’t taking to anything. I then suggested Havoc, and she really liked it. She came up with the Moon part. When we got home there was fresh graffiti on the wall across the street saying ‘Havoc’, and I was like: ‘That is a sign from the gods – we’ve got to do it.’” No one familiar with Culkin’s work will be surprised by the name or the story behind it. The 37-year-old actor, the youngest of the seven Culkin siblings, has been drawn to the dark from day one. In his movie debut, The Good Son, he exists only as a photograph and a memory – the murdered baby brother of Henry Evans (played by his real brother Macaulay Culkin). Then there is the magnificent Mean Creek, in which he is bullied by a boy with learning disabilities, after which his older brother’s gang decides to exact revenge. In the early days, Culkin specialised in victims: of bullies, killers and creeps galore. These days he is better known for playing bullying, creepy killers. He says it has been a pleasing evolution. “Now I get to victimise people. So there’s another layer to me I’m finding out about. Ooh, I can be a creep, too! That’s exciting.” Over the years Culkin has accumulated an impressive gallery of weirdos. In the brutal biopic Lords of Chaos, he played Øystein “Euronymous” Aarseth , leader of Norwegian black metal band Mayhem, notorious for burning down churches and murder. Then there’s Scream 4, where his soft-spoken film nerd Charlie Walker turns out to be not so nice; cult leader Kappa in Black Mirror, who kills the family of an astronaut; psychotic stalker Gabriel in the film of the same name; and on it goes. Culkin has a talent for bringing a stillness to these characters, for making the terrifying low-key and the monstrous comprehensible. In Nocturne , Apple’s new crime drama, he plays an empathetic psychiatric nurse seduced by Stephen Graham’s sing-song serial killer. What is it with Culkin and evil? Another moped-revving chuckle. Was he trying to distinguish himself from his older actor brothers? “No, it wasn’t a conscious thing to try to separate myself. I was just drawn to darker stuff. I was into scary Todd McFarlane toys ever since I was five or six.” Actually, he says, it goes back way beyond that. “As soon as I could talk, I wanted to be the devil for Halloween, so for the first 10 years of my life I was a different version of Satan every year. That unsettled my mum. The first time I wasn’t Satan I was the Ghostface killer from Scream. I was 11, and then 10 years later I was him on set.” Did his mother think he needed exorcising – or therapy at least? “I think deep down she was pretty charmed by it. ‘Ah, this guy is a little weirdo.’ Maybe that’s why I named my daughter Havoc because I want her to be into the devil as well.” And was he a little devil as a child? God no, he says. “I was a pretty shy kid. Polite and quiet. I think I liked the devil because he was the ultimate bad guy.” He’s wearing a huge gold ring, with writing on it that I can’t make out. What does it say? “Goblin.” He tells me that Havoc’s mother, Kate Arizmendi, a cinematographer, also wears one. Why? “I don’t know. It’s sort of …” He coughs bashfully. “She’s my goblin, I’m her goblin, and now that we have a little goblin we’re a tribe of goblins.” Culkin is almost nine years younger than his brother Macaulay and seven younger than Kieran.
