title: Prue and Sandi’s South African Adventure review – you’ll feel lucky to have this joyful show in your life
text: S andi Toksvig is one of TV’s great pootlers. There are few sights as cheering as that of the tiny Dane, bundled up in a scarf, bimbling along a coastal path, or scurrying down a continental alleyway, like a Womble that’s just been chased out of a boulangerie after a misunderstanding over a bun. Said perambulations are generally accompanied by an accessory of some sort, an unofficial mascot for each of her pootle-based travelogues. In Sandi’s Great Riviera Rail Trip, for instance, it was a small suitcase. In Extraordinary Escapes With Sandi Toksvig it was Britain’s orangest cagoule. Now, in Prue and Sandi’s South African Adventure, it’s Prue Leith. “Prue?” booms a panicked Sandi as she hurtles down a slope in the foothills of Table Mountain. “PRUE?!” Having wandered off in search of South Africa’s national flower, the king protea (pink and spiky, like a toddler’s medieval flail), Sandi has misplaced her former Bake Off colleague. Could she have nodded off in the afternoon sun? Or, having mistaken a rocky outcrop for Paul Hollywood, become lost among the mountain’s many sandstone caves? But no, phew, here she is, emerging from behind a nearby tree, a vision of meteorological calm in cloud-print jumper and rainbow scarf. The relief! “Oh Prue,” pants Sandi, “there you are! I’ve seen owls! I am having the BEST time.” As is Prue. As, indeed, are we. If you’re looking for a scene that encapsulates the mood of this six-part trundle across South Africa, here, splendidly, it is. To wit: Toksvig (68) hopping excitedly from trainer to trainer while Leith (86) grins serenely down at her, like an Anglepoise lamp directing its beam at a favourite armchair. This, then, is the gist of Prue and Sandi’s South African Adventure, a gentle travelogue that finds the “dear friends” meandering around Prue’s beloved home country while basking in the warmth of one another’s company. Although this is, ostensibly, Prue’s series – the retired restaurateur in gracious host mode as she “shows off the spots that I love” – it is very much a two-hander; with Prue’s childhood reminiscences (she left South Africa for England at the age of 20) punctuated by Sandi’s puppyish bursts of enthusiasm. First stop? Cape Town. “It pulls in over three million visitors a year,” barks Sandi, nose squashed into her guidebook, but Prue has already wandered off to the 1950s. Here is the beach where she ate grilled cheese sandwiches with her uncle. And over there was the district – long since bulldozed – where she once taught adult education classes. Memories of apartheid are, inevitably, everywhere. There is a profoundly moving chat with a black woman whose family was forcibly moved to a township in the late 60s. Prue was raised in a “very liberal” family and was “taught from birth that apartheid was wrong”. Yet she remains, she says, “ashamed” of not being more conscious as a teenager of the daily injustices. Sandi offers mitigation. There’s not a country in the world that can look at its past, she says, and be “entirely pleased with itself”. She is right, of course, but later, while watching the clouds roll over Table Mountain, like steam off a Sunday roast, there are sniffles. “It just gives me such pleasure,” says Prue, to see present-day Cape Town thriving. Her home city has finally “become right”. Six thousand miles away from the UK, two friends in linen trousers are pootling thoughtfully towards the sunset. “I’m running out of time,” says Prue in voiceover, as the camera swooshes over the duo’s silvery bonces. “I’m 86!” she chuckles. “If we don’t do this (series) now, we won’t be strong enough to do … anything. It’s got to be now.” A toast, then; to friendship, South Africa, memories, owls and now. “We’re so lucky,” smiles Sandi, huge gin cocktail in tiny, grateful hand. As are we, to have them. Chin-chin. Prue and Sandi’s South African Adventure is on Channel 4

title: Mariella Frostrup calls AJ Odudu ‘aggressive’ – and here we go again. We tire of this angry black woman trope | Natalie Morris
text: W hen I heard Mariella Frostrup call AJ Odudu “aggressive” over the weekend on I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!, my heart sank with sick recognition. For her part, AJ’s mother has since said that watching her daughter experience this all-too-familiar dynamic was a “living hell”. I know many Black women tuning in will have felt a collective shudder of disgust and solidarity. Of course, there is pushback. “Our addiction to offence is tearing us apart,” wrote a Telegraph pundit on Monday . But, this language is not neutral. There is a long history of Black women having their conduct and tone disproportionately scrutinised by white people. And what happened between Odudu and Frostrup is a tale as old as time. A Black woman stands up for herself and, no matter how reasonably she presents her argument, she is accused of aggression. It is an efficient tactic to flip the focus on to the behaviour of the Black woman, and it is rooted in racist stereotypes. I have witnessed and felt this dynamic play out in my personal and professional life. I frequently self-censor and push down a whole host of emotions for fear of how I will be perceived. Of course, people-pleasing tendencies are not specific to Black women, but I am considerably more conscious of how I present myself when interacting with white people. And, as a mixed-race woman with white heritage, I am conscious that I experience a watered-down version of this phenomenon. In an old job, I comforted a dark-skinned Black woman after her manager said her quietness in meetings came across as “hostile”. What happened with Odudu and Frostrup was similarly overt. Odudu’s conduct was clearly not aggressive. Watching, it felt like a baffling characterisation of her behaviour, which had the effect of derailing the argument and painting Odudu in a negative light, while casting Frostrup as the victim. It came across as a textbook example of the “angry Black woman” trope. Throughout history, Black women have been repeatedly and unfairly painted as combative and antagonistic. It stems, in part, from the slavery era in the US , where Black women were dehumanised through racist caricatures – often depicting them as irrationally irate – to help justify their exploitation. You only have to look at recent depictions of women such as Serena Williams and Michelle Obama to understand how enduring this perception is. What might look like a mild disagreement on a reality TV show is something more complicated. This is about an insidious societal double standard that judges Black women more harshly than white women, holding them to higher standards of behaviour while simultaneously denying them the same understanding and latitude. It also creates a trap in which Black women can’t stand up for themselves without having their argument – no matter how valid – undermined, diminished and wilfully misconstrued. It’s something that is instantly recognisable to those who have felt it, just as women will often innately feel when they are experiencing sexism, even if it is hard to pinpoint. It’s about antennae and, of course, its calibration. And there are real-life consequences: Black women are often cast as bullies , and being perceived as irrational can stifle careers and limit progression. In schools, Black Caribbean girls and mixed white and Black Caribbean girls are permanently excluded at more than double the rate of white girls. It wasn’t long before Nigel Farage waded into the debate. Frostrup’s “sharp comment” should not be conflated with racism , said the man whose party seems a magnet for racists. Frostrup’s comment is not the most egregious offence, but, for all of us, the microaggressions pile up. The visceral response many women of colour will have felt – such as Frostrup’s Loose Women colleague Judi Love, who said she was triggered , comes from many small things accumulating over time. What could have been a learning moment for Frostrup and the viewers became more damaging because of her failure

title: TV tonight: a gripping psychological thriller that keeps you guessing
text: 9pm, Channel 4 The more unsavoury secrets that emerge about each member of the Not Alice Bell group, the harder it is for each of them to avoid suspicion. When Graham Hunter (Ralf Little) escalates his campaign against them, cracks start to appear. Ahead of Thursday’s finale, this mystery is doing a credible job of keeping us guessing. Phil Harrison 7.30pm, BBC Two Researchers estimate that the next five years will see 1 billion extra people online – but how will they gain access to the internet? Prof Fry concludes her series by visiting a Google research lab, where they’re tinkering with transmitting information using light beams, and the streets of Nairobi, where cheap smartphones and some ingenious data-sharing are enabling more and more kids to get connected. Jack Seale 8pm, BBC One There’s nowhere to go but up, as the celebrities celebrate reaching their fourth checkpoint with a helicopter ride over the Great Barrier Reef. Then it’s time to get to their next destination: Toowoomba, Queensland. Sam and Kaz are in the lead with Junior and Princess – but which pair will be split when one half manages to miss the boat south? Hollie Richardson 8pm, Sky Arts Nine more hopeful artists have a brush with fame as they strive to capture the essence of three celebrity sitters. Arbiter of taste Grace Dent, peppy prankster Munya Chawawa and candid comic Grace Campbell are the models – but which one is “elegance personified” and who takes time out for a pilates break? Graeme Virtue 9pm, BBC Two In the concluding episode, Cameron’s girlfriend, Bex, wakes up from her medically induced coma to hear the devastating news about her boyfriend. After the police change the status of the Hogmanay house fire from “domestic fire” to “deliberate arson attack”, will the identity of the masked figure seen near the house finally be revealed? Priya Elan 10pm, Channel 4 You’d think that psychic Barbara would have seen a plumber coming into her life. But Jon is totally unexpected when he walks into the First Dates restaurant tonight. Is that because he isn’t the one? On another table, sparks fly between expat Zac and drag queen Sab. HR Way of the Warrior Kid (McG, 2026 ), Apple TV There are distinct echoes of The Karate Kid in McG’s light moral drama, based on a children’s book by a former Navy Seal. Marc (Jude Hill) is being bullied at school in San Diego and has zero confidence, despite the best efforts of widowed mom Sarah (Linda Cardellini). Luckily, his uncle Jake (Chris Pratt) is coming to stay … and he’s in the special forces. Jake sets up a training programme for his nephew to boost his self-worth – and teach him a few moves – but the officer has his own demons to face. title: ‘Two million people tuned in to see me mash potatoes!’ Gregor Fisher on his remarkable rebirth after Rab C Nesbitt
text: G regor Fisher’s kitchen is so tidy – it looks as if he has just finished cleaning it – that I begin to worry he has forgotten (or was possibly never apprised of) our arrangement. After he makes me a coffee and we sit at the square table, I feel obliged to raise the subject: aren’t we gonna cook something? “I thought we’d do some brunch,” he says. He steps into his larder and returns a moment later with the makings of kedgeree, prepared and covered in clingfilm: chopped onions, minced shallots, hard-boiled eggs, halibut from a fishmonger in Largs. He lifts the lid of his big range – familiar from the hugely popular cooking tutorials he’s been posting on Instagram for over a year – and puts a pan on it. The star of Rab C Nesbitt and The Baldy Man, and films including Love Actually – says he now only gets recognised in the supermarket for his cooking. This makes sense: at 72, hale and trim, he bears very little resemblance to his most famous character, and he hasn’t worn Rab’s string vest for 12 years. “We want to get a good dollop of butter in there,” he says, pointing to the pan. “And when I say a good dollop, I mean a good dollop.” I try to do as he instructs, following my first undersized dollop with another. Evidently, it is still not enough. The cooking thing came about, he tells me as I fry the onions, because he was trying to sell tickets to his stage show, An Evening With Gregor Fisher, with no social media profile to speak of. He had an Instagram account, but he didn’t want to face the camera and “wank on” about himself. His daughter Cissie suggested he whip up some potato scones instead. “I said, ‘Cissie, catch a grip of yourself,’” he tells me. “‘Who the hell is going to tune in to see me make potato scones?’ Well, fuck me, 2.5 million people tuned in to see me mash some potatoes and flip some scones. I couldn’t believe it.” The videos were short and unpolished – with Fisher cooking and Cissie filming – but they had an easygoing charm, and it was evident that Fisher knew his way round a kitchen. Almost immediately, he found an audience. “But something even nicer happened, actually, in doing it with my daughter,” he says. “It was quite a good laugh. There was nothing to gain, there was nothing to lose. There was no paymaster. There was nobody saying you can’t say this, you can’t say that – can we do that again?” Recently the project has migrated to Fisher’s new YouTube channel, where the videos can be a bit more meditative – “and not the three minutes you get on Instagram,” he says, “where you’ve got to be runnin’ about like a blue-arsed fly.” On his instruction, I add the fish fillets to the pan, whole. “The only thing that’s going to happen now,” he says, reaching across me, “is we’re going to push it all together – don’t use the metal spoon on the nonstick pan – and we’re just going to gently break that up, but not too vigorously, because we want slightly chunky bits.” To the best of my ability, I do as he says. “And now just leave it be,” he says. “We could actually put a lid on it, couldn’t we? I’ll get a lid.” Apart from occasionally helping his mother in the kitchen, Fisher reached adulthood knowing nothing about cooking, and not much more about eating. “I didn’t know what pasta was until I went to drama school,” he says. During his time working in rep in Dundee, where he met his wife, Victoria Burton, he was plagued by stomach pain, and was diagnosed with an ulcer. “I went to the doctor, and he said, ‘What are you eating?’” The answer was rubbish, mostly: pies, chips and pints. “He said, ‘I want you to buy yourself a cookery book. Don’t buy a fancy one. Just get a basic one and start making yourself some proper meals.’ So I took him at his word.” The ulcer, however, persisted until many years later, when a course of antibiotics finally cured it. He learned to cook, I suggest, for nothing. “Waste of time,” he says. “I could have got a maid in or something. Hired a fucking housekeeper.” Even now the recipes he f

title: ‘The brains of a pea and the mouth of diarrhoea!’ It’s the wildest I’m a Celebrity spats
text: T he unique selling point of I’m a Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here! is that it is currently the only show on television where you get to watch animal abuse and reputation-destroying arguments at the same time. The former is an ongoing affair, with petitions and boycotts rumbling on as always. But the latter has just exploded, thanks to Mariella Frostrup and all her microaggressions. If you haven’t been watching, and in this day and age why would you, here’s a brief precis. Last Thursday, latecomer AJ Odudu offered to help Frostrup cook a meal, which Frostrup took as unwelcome criticism of her skills. But when they cooked together the following night, things went badly, Frostrup snapped and Odudu cried. But last night, during an attempt to clear the air, Frostrup said she had actually been glad to have had help. Odudu’s’s reply was essentially that she had a funny way of showing it, to which Frostrup replied: “You see, that’s just aggressive and that’s what keeps happening.” Odudu’s response was to sigh: “Please don’t use those words towards me.” Nevertheless, the altercation was enough for Frostrup to be called to the Bush Telegraph so producers could “discuss why what was said might make someone uncomfortable, how to address it, and how to move forward.” The spat has caused something of a backlash against Frostrup. Fellow campmate Leomie Anderson has said that, “Black women are always painted to be aggressive when we’re just expressing ourselves,” while Judi Love posted on social media: “For most of us black women who have been through this in all scenarios, workplace, the shop, schools, wherever, we know what AJ’s feeling in that moment.” Good Morning Britain host Narinder Kaur wrote on X that, “Reality TV has never been a safe space for any person of colour,” while Alesha Dixon wrote: “Mariella in the bin.” On the other hand, Nigel Farage has defended Frostrup, so there’s that. But if you’ve watched I’m a Celebrity for any length of time, you’ll know that flare-ups – when they happen – tend to be slightly more pathetic than this. Here are some of the more notable instances. Quite honestly, you could make a whole list from this series. The biggest, and easily the most entertaining, blow-up came when Lady Colin Campbell picked a live beetle and threw it on to a campfire. Tony Hadley from Spandau Ballet reacted badly to this, informing Campbell of her cruelty. It is not an exaggeration to say that Campbell took this particularly badly. In the ensuing melee, she called Hadley a “bully”, a “liar”, a “gutless creep”, a “total zilch”, a “greedyguts”, a “dumbo”, a “hypocrite”, a “pretentious arsehole”, “the lowest of the low” and a “chippy oik”, while adding that he had “the brains of a pea and the mouth of diarrhoea”. Oh fine, let’s have another. This time, despite her best efforts, Lady Colin Campbell ended up being outheckled. The context is that her team had just won a banquet, while the opposing side were left to go hungry. Campbell had previously purchased a can of soup from a jungle vending machine, and proposed that the best way to end the suffering of the other team would be to give them a quarter of her can of soup between them. Duncan Bannatyne objected, saying it might be fairer if they had the whole can. Campbell took this particularly badly, calling Bannatyne a “mouse” and a “little pussy”. But Bannatyne fought back, calling Campbell a “nasty woman” and “the most selfish person I have ever met”. After winning the camp a reward of strawberries and cream, Iain Lee and Amir Khan decided to eat the whole thing themselves then tell the other campmates there had been no reward. A long and tense stalemate followed before Lee eventually relented. This enraged Dennis Wise, who informed them both that they were banned from eating any other future treats. It is also worth pointing out that Amir Khan was dressed as a cat when he apologised. The wildest blow-up to ever happen during I’m a Celebrity happened relatively early on in it

title: Lucy Worsley’s Keys to the Castle review – heavenly TV that instantly brightens up your day
text: W hen I think of Lucy Worsley, I am immediately cheered up. Partly it’s the coats. (So neat! So bright! So wonder where she gets them and if I could carry one off!) Partly it’s the hairclips. (How big has she gone this time? Is it going to stay in?) But mostly it is her; her energy, her indefatigability, her determination to impart what she knows in the most accessible way and, above all, her abundant confidence without ego. It’s the latter that allows for that rare thing – other historians to be interviewed and share their knowledge with the lay person at home without the presenter champing at the bit to show that he or she knows this already and that they are just letting them simplify things for the good of the show. This is my personal bugbear, so thank you for letting me exorcise it here, and thank you to Worsley for not adding to my burdens. To feel cheerful as you approach a history lesson is a great boon. To have it be also about one of your favourite subjects is another, and so Lucy Worsley’s Keys to the Castle has me practically insensible with delight before we so much as shift the first tumblers on the lock to the Doge’s Palace in Venice , where the four-part series begins. It then moves on to Versailles and Blenheim before finishing up with – joy of deepest joys, though not perhaps for its poor, lonely conceiver and inhabitant Ludwig II – Neuschwanstein Castle in Bavaria. The Doge’s Palace is really, Worsley notes, a government building. More untraditionally palatial than that, even, it was the nerve centre of an imperial spy network back in the days when Venice was a rich and ruthless beneficiary of its geographic position on the Adriatic as the gateway to maritime trade between east and west, rather than a honeymoon hotspot. Floorplans and cutaways (oh, I am in heaven) show us where in this enormous gothic fortress, disguised as a home for a figurehead, disguised as a ruler (the doge was an elected noble but fell in line with whatever his Council of Ten dictated) we are. We move up golden staircases, fly drones around the ceiling friezes of the great hall, then descend into the depths of the piombi prison to see cells beneath the water level (quite as unpleasant as that suggests, even before we see the explicit graffiti left behind by prisoners – “Disappointing,” says Worsley). Next, we follow the route of the bold escape taken by its most famous detainee, Casanova, before looking inside the special post boxes set up by the increasingly totalitarian government for citizens to tip their denunciations of others into, and at a possibly ill-advised demonstration of the council’s preferred method of torture. By the end of the set pieces, interspersed with chats with other historians and experts, you find – as always with Worsley – that you have absorbed an awful lot with remarkable ease. We have moved through the history of the castle, of Venice, its politics and economy, its influential adoption of quarantine (hence the word’s derivation from the Italian for 40 days) to deal with the plague that landed on its 15th-century shores and its eventual decline in powers (thanks to the emergence of competing trade routes and the fact that all days in the sun come to an end), Napoleonic takeover and its evolution into tourist destination and Cornetto-shifter. But now we can all go and see beyond the beauty to the darkness below. Happy honeymooning, y’all! The same trick is effected at Blenheim (early adopter of the corridor, dontcha know!, as well as the childhood home of Winston Churchill who largely grew up there with his grandparents while Randolph and Jenny, his parents, found more fun things to do elsewhere), and then at Versailles, with an emphasis on Marie-Antoinette’s misery there. From the libertine Sun King’s glittering abode we move to the lonely, nocturnal Ludwig II of Bavaria’s alpine retreat from the world. title: From Sovereigns to Servants by Alexandra Prokopenko review – Putin and his yes men
text: W hen Vladimir Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine four and a half years ago, it was a shock, but it wasn’t a surprise. The US and the UK had been publicly warning their allies for weeks about what Russia was planning, as well as threatening the Russians with a wave of sanctions unprecedented against a major power. Putin’s foreign policy had long relied on confusion and untruth. By saying that they knew exactly what he was up to, Britain and America were hoping first to deny him his usual ambiguity, and second to pressure the men around him into making him stop, since war would deprive them of the stolen assets they’d stashed in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods. Alexandra Prokopenko’s excellent new book takes us inside the Russian elite before and after the outbreak of Putin’s “Special Military Operation” and reveals why the UK-US strategy failed. Western decision-makers thought the men around Putin were greedy, brutal, self-interested kleptocrats who would stop his war to save their offshore fortunes. But that calculation overestimated the virtue of this parade of sycophants. When the crunch came, they lacked the courage even to speak up for themselves. From Sovereigns to Servants is the latest in a line of valuable analyses of the regime Putin has built in his image. A decade ago, Peter Pomerantsev dissected the puckish, postmodern propaganda that hid the Kremlin’s intentions. Five years ago, Catherine Belton looked at the money that bankrolled the Kremlin’s power. Now Prokopenko takes their work forwards, showing there are no longer any limits, logical, financial or moral, constraining the regime. Putin gets what he wants, whatever it is. Prokopenko knows Russia’s inner sanctum, having served in the Kremlin press corps, which is a quasi-official position, before advising the Russian central bank until she left the country in 2022. She now works at a thinktank in Berlin, and her book is based on dozens of conversations with anonymised members of the Moscow elite. The people who run Russia exist now for a single purpose: to tell Putin what he wants to hear, to do what he wants to do, and to ignore the consequences for their country, for the Ukrainians, and for the world. Shocked by the occasional arrest or defenestration of a fellow insider, worried about losing their place in the hierarchy, they are too cowardly to do anything else. The irony is that many of the most effective enablers of Putin’s disastrous fancies are the supposed westernisers of the first half of his reign. As journalists, we knew these men (and, occasionally, women) as intelligent, thoughtful, hard-working professionals trying to turn rickety ex-Soviet ministries into efficient machines that could ultimately improve the lives of their millions of fellow citizens. That instinct has completely vanished, replaced by craven conformity. “They had lost not only the habit of political action but the habit of political thought itself – the capacity to picture what a better world, or a clear victory, would actually look like. The notion that personal participation might bring the conflict’s end closer seemed absurd,” Prokopenko writes. It is a deeply disturbing book, but well written, well reported and vital to anyone who wants to understand the catastrophe that has befallen Ukraine. History will condemn the Russian ruling class utterly: obviously for the death and misery they have heaped on to the blameless Ukrainians; but also for the ruin they have piled on to their own country – a maimed generation, a blackened reputation and a future pawned to the Chinese government – all in the service of a man who doesn’t even look as if he’s enjoying his job any more.

title: More sex, different endings: how fan fiction makes our dreams come true
text: S hortly after this year’s London book fair , rumours began to circulate of a seven-figure book deal for the author of the wildly popular work of Harry Potter fan fiction All the Young Dudes. First published between 2017 and 2018 by user MsKingBean89 on the online platform Archive of Our Own, All the Young Dudes is arguably the most-read work of fan fiction of all time. Now its author will write a trilogy under the pen name BN King, with the first novel, Wolfboy, due to be published in autumn 2027. This is by no means the first example of fan fiction crossing over into mainstream publishing: the bestselling debut of 2025, Alchemised, also started off as fan fiction based on the Harry Potter series, with some inspiration from The Handmaid’s Tale too. And nearly 15 years earlier, EL James published Fifty Shades of Grey, which began life as Twilight fan fiction before proceeding, in its new guise, to sell millions of copies worldwide. The appeal for publishers seems obvious enough. The best loved works of fan fiction (or “fics”, as they are known), many of which are multi-chapter epics running to hundreds of thousands of words, are published online, chapter by chapter, to a passionate and hyper-connected audience of readers. Not only do these works inevitably retain echoes of the much-loved creations on which they are based, they also bring with them a ready-made audience, bound by their love of the urtext and buoyed up by the pleasures of collective obsession. Some fics become so popular they beget fandoms of their own, generating fan fiction, fan art and even translations into other languages. The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend. If you have never read a word of fan fiction, if you have never stayed up into the early hours searching for Buffy the Vampire Slayer fics (Buffy/Faith for ever and always), you might be wondering: what could possibly possess thousands of people with jobs, friends and families to spend hours of their time writing stories based on other stories, and hundreds of thousands more to read them? What is drawing a whole new generation of fans to fan fiction through the gateway drug of gay ice-hockey romance Heated Rivalry , with tens of thousands of fics published on Archive of Our Own, and thousands more for the Game Changers book series on which the TV show is based? The answer is simple enough: fan fiction is the cheapest and most easily customisable medium of cultural wish fulfilment. As a quick glance at any fan fiction platform will tell you, it seems that when you love a particular cultural product, you tend to wish there was more sex in it. Maybe the product itself is sexy in its own right, the chemistry (on screen or on paper) overt and undeniable. Maybe there’s just a hint of sexual tension, or none at all, but a wealth of deeply drawn characters upon which your fandom can project its own most fervent desires. What do you do when you cannot personally strong-arm the author to write a sequel in which your two favourite characters finally give in to the feelings you have long suspected them of harbouring? What do you do when you have neither the time nor the resources to single-handedly script, cast, shoot, produce and professionally edit another season in which the warrior princess and her plucky sidekick finally get together? You turn to fan fiction. There are other, more obvious, wishes that fan fiction is uniquely equipped to fulfil. You might love a story so much you wish you could be in it. Well, you can be if you’ve got the time and inclination to write fan fiction; all you have to do is include a “self-insert” (or a “Mary Sue”, as they are sometimes less charitably known). title: ‘I needed to purge it out of me’: the shocking true story behind harrowing drama Josephine
text: T he film-maker Beth de Araújo likens the personal experience that inspired Josephine, her disquieting second feature, to a slow-acting poison. Early one Saturday morning when she was eight years old, Araújo and her father were playing soccer in Golden Gate Park, near their home in San Francisco, when they heard a woman scream. Her father, a former Olympic runner for Brazil, told her to stay and bolted to help; Araújo, scared and alone, ran after him, and instead found the woman in a clearing, naked from the waist down. Araújo was too young to understand what had happened, but she knew something was wrong. So, too, does an eight-year-old Josephine, played by the remarkable newcomer Mason Reeves, in the one scene crafted exactly to Araújo’s memory: Josephine, confused and restless, observes as the woman tucks her hands under her legs to keep them from shaking. She is further confused when her father, Damien, played by the aspirationally everyman actor Channing Tatum , seems extra keen to return to their soccer game afterwards, one of many echoes of Araújo’s memory in this taut drama. In real life, Araújo’s father “put on a face, put on energy and made it seem fun,” she recalled. “And I was like: ‘This is so weird. Why is my dad being so extra fun right now?’” The two never discussed the incident. In the meantime, Araújo developed a sense of hyperawareness for potentially fragile safety, often double-checking the locks of her family’s home. Occasionally, she overheard her parents talk about the morning in the park, or the subsequent rape trial, or the fact that the perpetrator was released from prison when Araújo was 15. She often struggled to sleep. Then, in 2014, another incident – a stranger groped her in a theater – tipped her “functional hypervigilance” into a dark spiral. After 20 years, she finally asked her father about what they had both witnessed; she learned, for the first time, that the perpetrator had pulled a knife on her father, who tracked him at a distance until police arrived. “I asked him why he didn’t explain it to me on the day, when I asked what was going on, and he said he didn’t want to scare me,” she recalled. “But with his best intentions, of exactly how he wanted to protect me and love me, the exact opposite occurred. I became much more scared.” In the days after that phone call, Araújo wrote a “vomit draft” in a near-literal sense, a regurgitation of that long-ago poison. “I needed to purge it out of me,” she said. The result was Josephine, which arrives, more than a decade and many revisions later, in theaters this month after a heralded festival fun; the film won both the grand jury prize and audience award at Sundance, where it left me stunned – by its refusal to blur what Josephine sees, by its bravura performances and by its precise evocation of a child’s mind ruptured by darkness she can’t yet comprehend. Like Araújo, Josephine learns the word “rape” from the incident (and then sneaking her mom’s phone to search “raip”). Writing from Josephine’s perspective became a question of: “Can I transport the audience back to being de-assimilated, to a time before they knew what sexual violence was?” Araújo said. “I learned about it in a very specific and very harsh way, but everyone learned it at some point. And so how did it then inform how we moved our bodies through the world, how we thought about our own safety?” The film is “fictionalized, but factual”, tracing a different arc of aftermath to Araújo’s, one contained to Josephine’s immediate fear and confusion – in the days after the incident, Josephine begins to view all boys or displays of adult intimacy with hostility – and her parents’ fumbling attempts to help her. Both Gemma Chan , as her mother, Claire, and especially Tatum are superb as parents whose own coping mechanisms for male violence – calm dissociation on the one hand, fighting back on the other – cloud their well-meaning but inadequate responses to their daughter. title: Way of the Warrior Kid review - Chris Pratt’s family film is as subtle as a military recruitment video
text: I t’s hard to avoid the reports that boys and young men are in trouble . Across the US and UK, they’re outpaced by girls on reading tests, are more likely to have behavioral difficulties and exposed to impossible body image standards by the manosphere. You might think that all of this would make you think extra carefully about a film that centers on a 13-year-old boy. Not in the case of Way of the Warrior Kid, a cliche-ridden celebration of machismo and the military that greets the current climate with a shrug. At times, I had to remind myself that I wasn’t watching a Maga-funded after-school special. The young actor Jude Hill ( Belfast ) plays Marc, an eighth-grade kid who is a walking target for bullies and doesn’t seem to be able to walk to the school bus without tripping over his shoelaces. He is the victim of cruel bullying in class and online, where he’s branded the #Gloat (“greatest loser of all time”) by his tormentors. He downplays his struggles to his widowed single mom Sarah (Linda Cardellini in a thankless role), who has enough to worry about with her busy job managing an ice cream parlor. Without a father figure to teach him how to swim or play sports, he is adrift. Luckily, Uncle Jake (Chris Pratt) is on injury leave from the Navy Seals and on hand to teach him how to beat the bullies. So far, so Karate Kid – the film even nods to the 1984 classic in a sequence where Marc and Jake practice jiu-jitsu in silhouette against an orange sunset. Pratt’s character puts the boy on a strict physical training regimen, aiming to turn him from wimp to warrior by the summer’s end. As well as training to do pull-ups and run a seven-minute mile, the plan also involves him getting a summer job and staying on top of household chores. Bizarrely, it also involves the kid learning to cage-fight, which feels less like a proportionate response to getting picked on in class and more like, say, the kind of training that Trump ally Pete Hegseth has in mind for his “high-T Department of War” . Way of The Warrior Kid is based on a popular middle-grade fiction series of the same name by Jocko Willink, who is also a co-writer on the film and cameos as an MMA instructor. Violence is rarely the answer, says Uncle Jake, but that doesn’t prevent him from making tone-deaf jokes about it. While driving Marc to a date with a classmate, he gives the boy a pep talk where we assume he is about to give him a condom (the gift turns out to be Tic Tacs). “It’s like a concealed weapon,” Pratt’s character says. “It’s better to not need it and have it than to need it and not have it.” At one point there was a certain doofy and at times even rakish charm to Pratt’s performances, even if he was best used in ensemble IP such as Guardians of the Galaxy than as a leading man. Here, he has the emotional depth of a dumbbell, his limited abilities not flattered by an unimaginative script by Willink and Will Staples. At times the film hints that his character is disillusioned and perhaps even traumatised by his experiences in active combat, particularly given that he sleeps hugging a picture of a colleague that was killed to his chest. But any hint that the film is going to make a nuanced point about the moral complexity of war is soon glossed over, and as Jake prepares to return to duty Way of the Warrior Kid increasingly feels like military propaganda. (Willink has praised Hegseth for prioritizing “warriors over ballerinas” in the military, which feels like a deceptively folksy way to frame what many see as the US defense secretary’s racist , sexist and anti-trans agenda .) Frustratingly, Way of the Warrior Kid can be a good time when Pratt disappears, with an exciting third act that sees Marc putting his newfound skills to the test on a school trip gone awry. But I couldn’t ever quite get past the film’s finger-wagging at his mom’s parenting skills, in an ugly bit of moralising that demonises Sarah for … having the gall to raise her kid alone after her husband dies

title: Hexed review – Disney’s witchy caper is a wicked disappointment
text: A s bleak as Disney’s overreliance on sequels might have become, it’s not quite as bleak as the crumbling state of its original output. Obviously because of the former, the latter category has become that much less populated but even when the studio has recently bothered to release something without a number in the title, it’s been hard to really see the point. With or without Pixar, films like Elio, Strange World, Raya and the Last Dragon, Luca, Elemental, Onward and Wish have all felt as uninspired as something a rival might try to desperately cobble together in an attempt to lure kids away from Disney. Three Thanksgivings ago, Wish was a particularly poor yet extremely smug example of how rubbishy things have got, a personality-free princess tale that doubled up as a 100th anniversary victory lap. It was Disney’s worst-reviewed animated film in almost two decades and its deserved box office failure cost about $131m. Unperturbed, its co-director Fawn Veerasunthorn (along with Moana 2 director Jason Hand) is back this holiday with another rote rip-off adventure that doesn’t deserve its place in the kingdom. In an attempt to conjure up that long-gone magic, Hexed is a film absolutely stuffed with it, a tale of witches, spells, cauldrons and curses that is at the very least neatly timed. Interest in all things Harry Potter remains sky-high (next month’s HBO adaptation is set to be the year’s most-watched TV show) as streaming hits like Carrie and The Body and a growing YA fantasy audience have shown that witchcraft, and all similarly categorised high school powers, have started to overtake the flagging superhero genre. But then why does something like Hexed still feel so dusty? Like Wish, it’s a film clearly crafted by people who have deep affection for the Disney back catalogue but who can’t quite turn reverence for what came before into any real idea of where to take things going forward. Again, there’s something too calculated and businesslike, with nods to previous films and regurgitated life lessons, and while Disney adventures have always emerged from a Goliath-sized mega-corporation, the best ones can make you briefly forget that. Sure Disney might have, shamefully, tried to trademark Day of the Dead before the release of Coco (!) but the film itself was charming, sweet and genuinely moving. While the company might have turned Ratatouille into everything from a theme park ride to a branded set of cheese knives, thoughts of merchandise were not in one’s head while watching a rat’s thrilling journey from gourmand to head chef. But Hexed is too soulless and synthetically corporate to distract us from its ultimate Q4 marketing aims. It takes place in a universe where witches have been Salem trialled away to another magic-filled realm (hello new Disney World section), where they live under the tyrannical control of Queen Celeste (voiced by Jodie Foster). A powerful young witch called Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) doesn’t yet know she’s a powerful young witch after her mother (Rashida Jones) decided to keep her talents hidden via a magic-suppressing bracelet (perfect merch op) forced on her wrist at a young age, a way to keep her safe in a world that does not take kindly to people like her. But as a rebellious teen, Billie discovers her true self and after a portal opens, she travels to the world of witches to team up with a three-eyed cat called Beef Roger Crummchuk (Walton Goggins, also a stuffed toy to be) to try to save her fellow witches from their evil queen. It’s a story of mothers and daughters and how both can try to foster empathy for the other but even a lower-tier Disney film like Brave managed to teach this same lesson with far more skill and infinitely more heart. There’s no real joy or fizz in Billie’s discovery of her powers or ingenuity to how she then uses them and the film quickly starts to resemble not just a by-the-numbers, save-the-kingdom Disney tale but also a Marvel-like superhero adventure, especially in

title: You Can See Everything’s chaotic battle for the narrative about Elizabeth Holmes
text: T hank you for signing up to the Close Up newsletter. This is our first-ever edition! And, just like on the show , I’ll be zooming in on the big culture questions and recommending things I’m obsessed with. I’ll also give you a sneak peek of what’s coming up on the show and what the team have been talking about behind the scenes. OK, I’ll admit it: I wanted to hate You Can See Everything, the A24 documentary about Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes, which finally arrived in UK cinemas last week. The marketing was slick, the hype was unparalleled. I didn’t believe a three-hour documentary about a disgraced tech CEO could be that good. But, like our colleague Adrian and basically every film critic who’s seen it, I left the cinema thinking: that was amazing and what on earth did I just watch? In my 20s, I worked in corporate PR. Big companies employed our agency to promote their chief executives, tell the company’s story to the media and politicians, and protect everyone’s reputations. Our job, my job, was to create and control the narrative – to tell stories that made our clients the good guys. If you find the right angle, anyone can become the hero of a story. A betting company becomes one of the biggest employers on the UK high street, with bricks-and-mortar shops that provide much-needed jobs. An arms company is “one of the world’s leading manufacturers” – a national asset to be proud of. My colleagues were bright, young and talented. Most of them now work for big tech companies. You Can See Everything is a chaotic and confusing battle for the narrative about Elizabeth Holmes. Her husband Billy Evans’s version of the story is that a smart but overly trusting young woman who was manipulated by others (and is madly in love with her brilliant spouse). Directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim encourage you to question Billy and Elizabeth’s relationship, presenting him as potentially controlling, narcissistic and money-hungry. Holmes, meanwhile, paints herself as misunderstood, innocent and unassuming, afraid of the limelight and at times Madonna-like. The appearance of Amanda Seyfried (who played Holmes in The Dropout, a 2022 TV drama about the CEO) is a much-needed pressure valve, in that she voices what most of the audience has been thinking for the first half of the film: what the hell is going on?. But even she attempts to shape the narrative around her portrayal of Holmes and the duty actors have to tell the truth about real-life subjects. At times, different versions of all these stories win out. If I were advising Elizabeth Holmes on her image, I would have recommended she make a documentary. From Beyoncé to the Beckhams, biographical documentaries that let high-profile people construct a plausible-but-rose-tinted version of their lives have become part of the PR playbook. And a famous director is increasingly part of that package. Oscar-winning film-maker Fisher Stevens directed the David Beckham documentary, largely sidestepping the more uncomfortable aspects of Beckham’s public life, including allegations surrounding Rebecca Loos, along with any other controversies that might have harmed the family brand. Rick Rubin made an eight-part (!) docu-series about Jay-Z. Jon M Chu, who was behind Crazy Rich Asians and Wicked, directed two Justin Bieber documentaries. I’m not sure I would have suggested Holmes invite Nathan Fielder to move into her home. That level of round the clock access makes it harder to control the image you present. But while You Can See Everything may not have been the film Holmes and Evans wanted, it has already changed the conversation around the former Theranos CEO. A pe ek into what we’re obsessing about in our team Whats App group In the Close Up group chat, we’re already planning our spring around two very specific things: hockey and yearning. 🏒💕 Season two of Heated Rivalry – the queer Canadian ice hockey romance that became one of this year’s biggest breakout shows – is dropping in April. title: Robert Pattinson is not enough: who should become the new Bond girl?
text: A fter years of speculation, Robert Pattinson has been officially cast as James Bond for a new Amazon-produced film directed by Denis Villeneuve. There’s no release date for the project yet, though fall 2028 seems a likely target, given the release dates of all of the Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig installments. This leaves plenty of time left on the clock for more speculation – namely, about who will be cast as the so-called Bond Girls for this rebooted installment. Past Bonds have usually been recognizable from earlier work, but none of them had yet reached Pattinson’s level of fame before actually playing Bond. Given that, in addition to sterling indie work for directors like David Cronenberg, Claire Denis and Lance Oppenheim, Pattinson has also been in Twilight, Batman and Christopher Nolan movies, he’s arguably already as famous as Brosnan and Craig were at their 007 peak. It must be this shift in the casting status quo that has inspired some predictions or hopes for a quantity as known as, say, Sydney Sweeney to play a Bond girl. It’s possible to draw a line between Sweeney’s bombshell status and the most recent wholly American Bond girls; Teri Hatcher in Tomorrow Never Dies and Denise Richards in The World Is Not Enough were both well-known actors with substantial pin-up appeal when they were cast. But Sweeney is a bigger deal than those actors – neither of them ever had a non-Bond hit as substantial as The Housemaid or Anyone But You – while also seeming like a profound mismatch with whatever form Pattinson might take for this role. In terms of performance styles, Pattinson’s slightly alien affect, even at its most charming, feels too eccentric to sync up with Sweeney, who has specialized in 1990s throwbacks. Smirky suggestions of Pattinson’s The Drama co-star Zendaya feel off for a similar-yet-opposite reason: She’s both too big a star on her own to be Bond’s second banana, and almost too much of a temperamental match with her partner in an off-kilter black comedy. Yet Pattinson’s presence does allow for a bit more leeway in fantasy-casting Bond girls, going beyond the Craig era’s mix of continental prestige hotties (Léa Seydoux, Eva Green, Monica Bellucci) and more genre-friendly variations on that theme (Gemma Arterton, Olga Kurylenko, Ana de Armas). Those Craig entries largely eschewed the traditional dichotomy between good-girl sidekick and femme fatale betrayer – Paloma (de Armas), for example, neither sticks by Bond’s side for the entire film nor sells him out to the bad guys in No Time to Die – and hopefully the Villeneuve film will similarly allow for less rigorously defined gender roles while still having some fun with the archetypes. All that said, wouldn’t it be fun to see Lily James play a femme fatale? She has a sunny countenance that made her excellent casting as a Disney princess as a younger woman, and an adorably underwritten love interest in Danny Boyle’s disappointing Beatles sorta-musical Yesterday. She might look like a damsel in distress as Bond’s main love interest. But as a character with more noirish ambiguities, she could make an oft-thankless role feel like a personal challenge. The Craig period also seemed to pause (or at least de-emphasize) the Brosnan-era lip service to the idea of an allied female agent who is supposed to be Bond’s equal, a part with a surprisingly strong Oscar track record; Michelle Yeoh was in Tomorrow Never Dies decades before her Everything Everywhere All at Once Oscar, while Halle Berry shot her role as Jinx (once earmarked for a spin-off!) shortly before winning hers for Monster’s Ball. Let’s not presume, though, that only seeming Oscar inevitabilities like Carey Mulligan or Amanda Seyfried may apply to a newer version of this type. Callina Liang is still early in her career, but she buffed up for the recent Street Fighter and could be equally believable fighting at Bond’s side or beating the holy hell out of him. Amber Midthunder is another genre actor with a ton

title: Olivia Colman as a fox and Sam Neill as a sweary magpie: The Fox is one of the best Australian movies in years
text: W hen Emily Browning first read the synopsis for The Fox, her response was one of confusion. “I was like, what?” the actor says, scrunching up her face. “A guy talks to a fox and throws his wife in a hole? Huh?” Explaining this Australian comedy is not an easy task, even for its writer and director, Dario Russo. “It’s a movie about a guy who gets tricked by a talking fox into pushing his fiancee in a magic hole,” he says. “That’s it. That’s what happens.” That is what happens but don’t let that description deter you. Despite its oddball premise, The Fox is one of the best Australian movies in years – and looks poised to win over viewers when it hits cinemas on Thursday, having already picked up the award for best Australian feature at Sydney film festival in June. Beyond that absurd log line about a fox and a magic hole, it’s a dark comedy about relationships, expectations, men, women and small towns; where animals can speak to humans, magpies are the town gossips, and the going rate for dirt on your cheating spouse is a freshly cooked rotisserie chook. To say much more would be to spoil what’s to come. You just have to go with it. But if all that doesn’t sell you, perhaps the cast will. Browning – who was won over by page 10 of the script – stars as Kori, the woman who is pushed into the magic hole. Joining her is an all-star list of Australian actors, including Jai Courtney as Kori’s fiance, Nick, alongside Damon Herriman, Heather Mitchell, Miranda Otto and Claudia Doumit (the latter a clear standout amid stiff competition). Sign up for the fun stuff with our rundown of must-reads, pop culture and tips for the weekend, every Sunday morning But the biggest names of all don’t appear on screen, instead lending their vocals to a pair of janky animatronic puppets designed to “look like taxidermy come to life”. Voicing the titular fox is an utterly perfect Olivia Colman , while that gossipy, chicken-mad magpie is played by the late, great Sam Neill, for one of his final film credits. Russo – the co-creator of the Australian cult favourite Danger 5 – and the team at the production company Causeway Films assembled the live-action cast first then approached Colman, who was at the top of his list for “dream gets” for the fox. She said yes, so then the question was: who could possibly be a worthy enough companion for the other loquacious animal? As a longtime Jurassic Park fan, Russo swung big and went for Sam Neill. He, too, signed on. Before long, Russo was on a Zoom call with Neill, figuring out the exact cadence his character’s voice should have. Neill felt that magpies were “too wobbly” for a character who delivers vicious barbs and bribes, and instead based his performance on “a specific crow he knew in [the Sydney suburb of] Surry Hills”. “He called it the ‘disappointing orgasm crow’, because Australian crows have this weird sound they make –” Russo says, before imitating the croaky, gradually deflating call a crow makes, which does, indeed, sound a lot like a bird having a disappointing orgasm. “So he based the performance on that particular crow. But I also think it’s a sly Bryan Brown impersonation.” Those two quintessentially Australian references worked. Neill’s voice role is, as Browning says, “the best bit of the movie” – scene-stealing at every turn. Neill die d just a couple of weeks after coming out for the premiere of The Fox at the Sydney film festival in June. It feels “incredibly sad and bittersweet” to have worked with Neill on one of his last projects, Russo says. “The outpouring of love for the man after he passed away is completely warranted because he was humble and collaborative, and more than anything, it was clear how much he loved his work,” Russo says. “He was dedicated to doing the best version of a magpie possible, and then when we were in breaks between sessions, he regaled us with tales of his other movies. “He was a big storyteller and an unforgettable spirit. I’m so glad that now every time I look a

title: The Royal Court’s new mission? To boldly go back to the 60s space race with The Afronauts
text: R yan Calais Cameron has proved himself a playwright of stratospheric talent. His previous plays For Black Boys Who Have Considered Suicide When the Hue Gets Too Heavy and Retrograde both streaked their way into the West End. This new one is filled with mighty ambition but does not lift off in the same way. It is based on what he calls a “true(ish)” story. The figure of Edward Mukuka Nkoloso (Lucian Msamati) is taken from Zambian history. A freedom fighter for the nation’s independence in the 1960s, he set up a national academy for science and trained a group of “afronauts” in the hope of beating the US and the Soviet Union in the race to reach the moon. Nkoloso, a kind of Dead Poets Society inspiration figure here, picks 17-year-old Martha (Ama Qamata) for the mission. Co-directed by Cameron and Monique Touko, the play introduces us to the characters and sets the scene in a largely comic first half, which is too soft and slow, dissipating tension or intrigue. Soutra Gilmour’s set is beautiful though, with its old-school Star Trek aesthetics: a circular ascending stone ramp with a giant Spaceship Enterprise-like portal, looking out to planetary matter. Nkoloso is trying to “teach the young to look at the sky”. This is a lovely phrase and idea, which ties his space programme to the story of rebuilding Zambian selfhood, post-independence, especially in the face of derision at this apparently tin-pot project. But if the play wants to use the metaphor of finding freedom on Earth by taking flight, it does not go far enough in filling in the political detail and the combined concepts of liberation remain vague. The telling of the story takes precedence over its drama, while character building is also subsumed by it. Grace (Pamela Nomvete) represents elder wisdom and acts as a foil to Simon (Ivanno Jeremiah), who has been shaped by western science (he was sacked from Nasa). The centre of the drama is unfocused: is it ultimately about Martha who has a romance with fellow afronaut David (Prince Kundai)? Those elements do not develop beyond the generic. Or is it about Nkoloso, who might be a visionary but is also an immoral figure and fantasist? The play can’t, or won’t, resolve the colliding versions of him. Msamati is brilliant as ever, full of charm and conviction, but his complex character is not given enough material in the script to come alive. It’s an interesting story that heads in many directions but ends up lost and atmosphere-less. At Royal Court theatre, London , until 19 December

title: Simon Brodkin: ‘Which of my pranks went badly wrong? Well, Boris Johnson became PM after the Theresa May one’
text: How did you get into comedy? I was booted out of every class for making jokes and then I discovered, at medical school, there is such a thing as a career in comedy. I was encouraged by being able to entertain the patients and went straight from that into comedy. Who did you admire when you were starting out? It was always the character comedians: Sacha Baron Cohen , Ricky Gervais, Steve Coogan. On the circuit Al Murray was doing the Pub Landlord. I admired anyone doing characters who could be dropped into multiple situations. As I started doing character comedy myself, I was inspired by people who might not have known how funny they were, such as a big batch of Premier League footballers from Beckham to Gerrard to Rooney. Can you recall a gig that’s so bad it’s now funny? Every comedian’s got a few tales. If they say they haven’t, they’re lying. I remember getting booed off at the Hackney Empire early on in my career as [the character] Lee Nelson . I think someone threatened to bottle me, which was alarming, but also quite inspiring that he really was taken in by the character. Nothing’s going to faze you after that one. You’ve done character comedy, high-profile pranks on world leaders and now straight standup. What keeps you switching things up? Stay in your lane, Brodkin! When I was doing characters, that was absolutely what I wanted to do with all my heart. When I was chucking golf balls at Donald Trump , that was absolutely what I wanted to do with all my heart. And now the standup is what is floating my boat. Keep changing the menu … It keeps me stimulated. Easily bored is probably the answer. Which prank came closest to going badly wrong? After the Theresa May one [when Brodkin handed her a P45 on stage during her speech ], Boris Johnson became prime minister – so things went pretty badly wrong then. Are the pranks finished ? They’re chilling. What inspired your latest show, Unleashed? The energy that I’ve brought to the stunts and the characters, I’m bringing on stage as me now. It’s straight standup and I’m feeling unleashed in where I can go and what I can say. Do you have any preshow rituals? Reminding myself of what the show is – my memory is pretty bad. You’ve been billed as the most-viewed British comedian ever on TikTok. Has it changed how you write jokes? I think that the jokes I write neatly package up in TikTok form anyway. So that’s probably why things exploded so much on there. Plus, I’m a pretty good dancer. Best advice you’ve ever been given? Many a mickle makes a muckle. What’s the worst advice you’ve ever been given? You definitely won’t break the law if you join the Manchester City squad in warming up on the pitch before a Premier League football match. Do you have any regrets, big or small? If I read the tattoo on my index finger that says “no regrets”, then I shouldn’t have any. But in all honesty, I regret getting that tattoo. What’s one of the strangest fan encounters you’ve had? You get autograph hunters who go to shows and wait outside but haven’t actually seen the show. I remember coming out and I said to the guy: “Did you enjoy the show?” He said: “Yeah, I loved it.” I thought that there was some BS going on. So I said: “Do you want Simon’s autograph?” He’s like: “Yeah.” I go, “Simon, come here,” and I beckoned over my tour manager, who had left the building with me. I go: “Simon, he’d love your autograph. He absolutely loved the show. Thank you, Simon,” as my tour manager signed his paper. They sell the stuff on eBay, so I felt the guy had it coming. Any bugbears from the world of comedy? People could wash the microphone a little more frequently. It’s pretty whiffy. What is next for you? Probably a shower in Colchester Charter Hall theatre. Simon Brodkin: Unleashed is at the Apollo, London , on 13 December and 11 March and on tour in the UK until 26 May

title: Nine Night is back and proves itself a modern classic full of secrets, squabbles and laughs
text: T he death of a parent has a way of blowing up the lives of family members it leaves behind. The combustions of grief, greed and secrets revealed around a barely buried coffin litter the tragicomic works of playwrights such as Tracy Letts (August: Osage County) and Branden Jacobs-Jenkins (Appropriate). You might want to add Natasha Gordon’s debut play to that canon, although it comes wrapped in its own distinct cultural tradition. Its structure revolves around the Caribbean funeral ritual that commemorates the death of a loved one over nine nights. A debut play written by a young Black British woman, featuring an almost entirely Black British cast, it got a huge reaction at the National Theatre in 2018 . Set in the past (the 1970s orange print wallpaper on Libby Watson’s set design gives it away), it takes place in the home where matriarch Gloria has died. The action remains in the kitchen next to the room in which mourners convene to eat, drink and share memories. You hear the noise of that unseen party, like that in Abigail’s Party. This space is filled with the ordinary squabbles of family life, much of them spoken in Jamaican Patois. There is tension between siblings Lorraine (Dani Moseley), the main carer to their mother, and Robert (Javone Prince), who already has an eye on selling her house. His mixed-race marriage to Sophie (Sonya Cassidy) brings its own fractiousness but there is laughter, too. Several characters are comical without becoming stock. Lorraine’s right-on daughter Anita (Ava Hinds-Jones) is one of them; Auntie Maggie (Llewella Gideon) is another, full of eyebrow-raised judgment. But she also carries an unspoken secret that expresses itself in digs at her husband, Uncle Vincent (Gary McDonald). Blasts of music, including infectious calypso, serve as interludes that lighten or change the atmosphere. The passing of nine days is marked in this way and, under the direction of Amit Sharma, the play has both a light touch and a depth of feeling that builds in a controlled way. The arrival of the third sibling, Trudy (Estella Daniels), who has travelled over from Jamaica, brings more comedy but also hurt, and cracks open the emotions of the play. It is moving but without an ounce of mawkishness, all exquisitely acted. So Gordon’s play holds it power and proves itself to be a modern classic in its tragicomic portrayal of family grief. At Kiln theatre, London , 23 November to 9 January

title: Pink Rabbit: the provocative bedroom drama about a Muslim OnlyFans star interrupted by her mum
text: A t home, Amna is the modest and dutiful Muslim daughter of her parents’ dreams. Online, armed with a webcam and an OnlyFans account, she is PersianBaby – an exoticised version of herself complete with fake accent, designed to entice men willing to part with their cash. Pink Rabbit, writer-performer Farah Ashraf’s provocative and darkly funny solo play, is a nuanced account of being caught between the private life of desire and the cultural expectations that shape how she is perceived. “I loved this idea of push and pull, and two different worlds,” says Ashraf who began work on the play during her final year at the Oxford School of Drama, before which she had trained with the National Youth Theatre . “At the time, I was really struggling and had an inner frustration with how I thought I was going to be perceived when I entered the industry and the roles that I might be limited to playing.” Since graduating, however, Ashraf has appeared in roles across film, TV and stage, including in Netflix’s The Witcher, Riz Ahmed’s series Bait and in a lead role in the coming-of-age play Santi & Naz. Her initial idea for Pink Rabbit centred on a young woman who appeared comfortable with herself but there was something clearly missing. A breakthrough came when she imagined that character in her bedroom, engaged in a scandalous online encounter, only for her mum to arrive unexpectedly at the door. Ashraf takes on the challenge of portraying both Amna and her ammi (Urdu for mother). Although the play is not autobiographical, Ashraf acknowledges some deeply personal elements. “A lot of Amna’s soul is very much a mirror of me and my life,” she says. As Ashraf herself has grown, so too has the production. At its core, Pink Rabbit works to challenge the limited representations of south Asian and Muslim women that have historically dominated cultural narratives. Rather than presenting a single, uncomplicated experience of identity, however, Ashraf allows Amna to be contradictory, vulnerable and largely unpredictable. She is particularly conscious of the importance of sharing this perspective with audiences who may not have encountered it before. Reflecting on performing at the Edinburgh fringe this summer, where she was aware that she would be met with a predominantly white audience, Ashraf says: “There’s some people sitting in there, and this might be their first experience of hearing this kind of perspective from a brown woman.” Ashraf also recalls feeling nervous about how older south Asian audience members might respond, particularly to the scenes involving Amna’s online alter ego and her explicit interactions with her customers, as well as the prominence of her bright pink sex toy. “But overall, they were so open to the experience and the story,” she says. By playing both Amna and Ammi, she brings the tensions between generations into sharp focus, resisting the temptation to position either as entirely right or wrong. The show’s distinctive theatrical language further enriches the complexity of dual identity. Directed by Alessandro Babalola, Pink Rabbit draws on Ashraf’s longstanding relationship with poetry, as well as her experiences growing up between London and Pakistan. Urdu and Punjabi feature alongside English, creating a rich linguistic landscape. Gradually introducing prose allowed her to discover new ways of expressing Amna’s emotional journey, retaining the rhythm and lyricism of poetry while giving other moments room to breathe. “There’s something beautiful about theatre and how it allows for that.” During the play’s Edinburgh run, Ashraf performed in a small, tightly packed space. It created a real intensity as she switched seamlessly from Amna to Ammi to PersianBaby’s subscribers, Ashraf’s physicality bringing to life the story both online and in the bedroom without the use of props, complex lighting or rigorous sound design. As Pink Rabbit prepares for its forthcoming Soho theatre run, Ashraf and her team are keen to experiment

title: Northern Ballet’s Cinderella spices the fairytale with festive fun and a sweet twist
text: I t wouldn’t be the first time an ugly sister has stolen the show. Andrew Tomlinson is a hoot in Northern Ballet’s new Cinderella as a klutzy, vainglorious stepsister with a great line in lovably grotesque facial expressions. He certainly provides some panto-like festivity in the midst of an otherwise very nice ballet. Getting its UK premiere, this pretty Cinderella is choreographed by Michael Pink, who was associate artistic director at Northern Ballet in the 1990s, and it feels very much like the Northern Ballet of old: accessible and enjoyable mainstream dance with clear storytelling. (It was originally made for Milwaukee Ballet, where Pink has been artistic director since 2002.) The Northern Ballet of now, under director Federico Bonelli, is successfully striking a balance between interesting new commissions (the choreography of New York ballerina Tiler Peck; their ballet version of Gentleman Jack ) and box-office bankers that can tour the country with broad appeal. The latter may be less exciting for crotchety critics, but at a matinee in Norwich it was going down a treat. Saeka Shirai dances Cinderella with sheer grace; lightness and sweetness infusing Pink’s neat choreography. Her boyish father (Harry Skoupas) is wet and useless in the face of sharp-edged stepmother (Alessia Petrosino) wielding pointed toes like a weapon. Instead of the standard fairy godmother, Pink’s version has Cinderella’s own mother (Heather Lehan) beatifically looking down on her and sprinkling a little magic, which is a nice twist, although the transformation scene isn’t quite as wondrous as you might wish. Cinderella’s other saviour is houseboy Jack (the excellent Harris Beattie), a new character who is kind and bright and full of life. They have a laugh together and he flirts with her in a silly way between zipping around the stage in whizzy jumps. I was secretly hoping Cinders would ditch the somewhat self-regarding prince (Jonathan Hanks) and run away with Jack instead. But it’s not that sort of remake. Prokofiev’s spirited and dramatic score, full of characterful motifs, is played live by the Northern Ballet Sinfonia, which is always great to hear. And the company as a whole look polished. It isn’t groundbreaking but it all makes for a lovely afternoon. At Norwich Theatre Royal until 21 November. Then at Leeds Grand , 15 December to 2 January

title: Can depression really become dazzling dance? The biggest ever BalletBoyz show is a huge feat
text: ‘I f I write what I feel, will you feel it, too?” That was the question behind singer-songwriter turned composer Keaton Henson’s Six Lethargies. Perhaps that is every artist’s mission, but for Henson it was specifically his experiences with anxiety and depression that he wanted to translate into music. Now it has been turned into dance by the BalletBoyz . If they dance it, will we feel it? Six Lethargies is the largest production in the 25-year history of the BalletBoyz. Once just two ex-Royal Ballet dancers, Michael Nunn and William Trevitt, this iteration is a company of 44 dancers (male and female), a 37-piece string orchestra, and not one but two choreographers working together: former Dance Theatre Heidelberg artistic director Iván Pérez and talented newcomer Seirian Griffiths . It’s a piece made with a limited sepia-toned palette, the mud-coloured costumes lit with misty glow, and musically it is all very minor chord (often the same one). The mood is achingly sad, mournful, ethereal and sweet; the sound of beautiful distress. Henson (incidentally, the son of ballerina Marguerite Porter) doesn’t read or write music and devised the work first as a graphic score, then collaborated with orchestrator Ben Foskett. It’s a kind of slow-moving minimalism, sometimes stuck, sometimes hollow – yes, that’s what depression can be like. Then a sudden, unnerving scurry of dissonant notes racing up the neck of the violin. Movement-wise, you can’t see the seams between the work of the two choreographers, who created together in the studio, and the long phrases are seamless too, like circular breathing, delving back into repeated motifs, surge and flow, swaying and walking. To its credit, nothing is overwrought. And it’s all very easy to get lost in. There are eight lead dancers, joined by students from the Rambert school. We’ve seen a lot of this massed dance, multiple bodies morphing together, in work by Crystal Pite and her imitators, but this group manage to find subtly different approaches. There’s dancer Kai Tomioka lost in a fast-moving crowd that churns around him (very cinematic); or leading the throng of bodies behind him who echo his movement in waves. It’s like watching a visible reverb, or iron filings chasing a magnet. The solos are the most arresting, Tomioka’s light, lyrical touch, swept up by forces larger than himself; Dan Baines spinning and swirling on his feet, hands, back, using his B-boy talents plus Griffiths’ influence, a choreographer who draws from martial arts and breaking. There’s a lot of strength, played in understated ways. When they started out, Nunn and Trevitt were notable for partnering each other, playing with the balance of energy between two men. Back then it could feel a bit effortful, now these young dancers are so deft it’s almost unnoticeable who’s lifting who. When a woman lifts a man, pulling his weight off the ground, circling his body around hers, it’s all part of the flow. To answer Henson’s question: No, you don’t feel exactly what he feels. The effect is more distant, unspecific, more beautiful, although those notions of overwhelm, rumination and melancholia are all there. The artist’s need to pour their soul and neuroses into their work is one thing, the audience’s reception of that something else. But in this case, it’s a good something else. At Sadler’s Wells, London , until 21 November

title: ‘Most of the video budget went on Steve Strange’s makeup’: Midge Ure on how Visage made Fade to Grey
text: Visage were an amalgamation of three bands: Rich Kids, Magazine and Ultravox. Since all three were touring, getting everybody in the studio at the same time was nigh on impossible. Still, we were making our debut album and were a track short, when along came this gift from God. We had no money so I’d been moonlighting with Thin Lizzy, and keyboardist Billy Currie had been playing with Gary Numan. Fade to Grey started life as an instrumental that Billy had been jamming with Chris Payne from the Numan band in soundchecks. They’d tried to release it but nobody was interested. I thought it was wonderful and suggested writing lyrics so we could use it on the Visage album. The instrumental created this brilliant atmosphere – mysterious, melancholy, dark, dystopian, film noir – which put pictures in my head. I imagined a guy sitting on a train station with a suitcase, trying to escape his life, hence: “One man on a lonely platform, one case sitting by his side …” There’s a term in video-making, “fade to black”, but I changed it for the song because it gave the impression of a transition to something else. I imagined the man getting on a train not knowing where he’d end up. The music was already recorded so we didn’t do a huge amount to it. I think Rusty Egan played some electronic drums. Steve Strange was the frontman but wasn’t a natural singer. So I put down a vocal, then he sang while listening to my vocal in headphones – what came out of his mouth was the same melody, but in his voice. You can hear me on the “aahs”, the “fade to greys” and some of the harmony parts. Rusty had a Belgian girlfriend, Brigitte Arendt, so someone – probably Rusty – suggested she read the title in French along with a translation of the lyrics. It was the icing on the cake. Godley and Creme wanted to showcase themselves as video-makers so they made one for us for just £1,500: most of that went on makeup artists for Steve. The song and the video just seemed to capture a moment: the Blitz club , New Romantics, synthesisers. Then suddenly it was in the charts all over Europe. Fade to Grey started off in 1976 or 77 when I was a music student at Chichester and we had to compose something. I was really into pre-Raphaelite paintings – Millais’ Ophelia and the like – so I wrote a romantic study with the chords that eventually became Fade to Grey, but played on piano in a different manner. After I joined the Gary Numan band, I used to mess around playing the chords on a Polymoog synth and a bassline on a Minimoog. One day Billy and drummer Cedric Sharpley joined in. As the tour progressed, we developed it in soundchecks. After the tour, Billy was due to go back to Ultravox, so we wanted to record it as a keepsake. We used producer Martin Rushent’s studio in London, but when we set up the gear the Minimoog wasn’t there, just the Polymoog. However, the brass setting gave the bassline the distinctive attack on Fade to Grey. Cedric started the song with a CR-78 drum machine and put the drums down. Billy sprinkled synth over it and that was it. The arrangement was created on the fly. Then Billy called asking: “Do you mind if it goes on the Visage album?” And the rest is history. The next thing I knew my publisher called me to say it was at No 45. Then my neighbour came in going: “It’s on Top of the Pops! And there’s this most amazing video.” Then it was in the Top 10 – and No 1 in some countries. I’m really happy with its success. On YouTube, there are loads of people doing different takes. I’ve just done a version for Midge’s new album, and my wife sang the French bit. It’s come full circle. Midge Ure’s Chapters: The Best Of is out now on CD, 2LP and a 3CD deluxe version including Chris Payne’s remix. A new version of Fade to Grey is available digitally and on 7” vinyl from midgeure.tmstor.es . Midge Ure is on tour this month

title: ‘My name was poison’: Donny Osmond on fame, failure – and his friend Michael Jackson
text: F or a brief period in the early 1970s, Donny Osmond ruled the world. He was the global teenage heart-throb. Even Michael Jackson trailed behind him. He was 14 when his most famous song, Puppy Love, spent five weeks at No 1 in the UK. My sister had a huge poster of him on her bedroom wall. Then again, everybody’s sister had a poster of him on their bedroom wall. Between 1972 and 1973 he had six Top 5 hits in the UK, three of them No 1s (including The Twelfth of Never and Young Love). He was equally successful back home in the US. Osmond was clean-cut, religious and respectful, with a mighty ability to punch out cover versions of saccharine standards. From his purple velvet cap to his doleful eyes and dazzling all-American smile, he was a marketing dream. We’d only just finished with Beatlemania. And now there was Donnymania. Did Osmond realise how big he was back then? “You better believe it,” he says today. What was it like? “Incredible. Incredible .” In October 1973, a viewing balcony at Heathrow collapsed after fans went wild when Osmond and his brothers arrived in the country.
