Just after that, David Dimbleby hosted a debate on the BBC on teenage “hysteria”, asking whether the Osmonds were bad for the nation’s girls and if they should be deported. “My brother Alan said: ‘Donny, don’t forget this moment because nobody ever gets this!’” How did it make him feel? “I was enjoying every second of it. I was thinking this is so cool.” Osmond was not deported. But in 1974, his solo career lurched to a sudden end. He continued having hits with his brothers for another year, then that all came crashing down, too. At 18, he was a pop has-been on two fronts. Osmond and his sister Marie reinvented themselves with a TV show, but ratings dropped after Osmond got married. The show was cancelled in 1979. By the age of 21, his career had gone kaput for a third time – and there appeared to be no coming back. It wasn’t simply that Osmond was no longer popular, but that somehow he had become an embarrassment. Even to himself. And yet almost half a century on, Osmond has a Vegas residency six months a year, he released his 65th album a few years ago, and is about to embark on a tour of the UK. At 68, he is the father of five boys and a grandfather 16 times over. We meet in a London studio where he is having his photo taken. Today, he looks both distinctively Donny and, unsurprisingly, different. He’s got the slight body of a teenager and the monumental face of a Mount Rushmore president, giving him the air of a marionette. The hair is still bluey-black, the teeth pearly white. How does he manage it? “Well, as far as my hair is concerned, I have a lady who takes care of it. Her name is Clairol.” He pauses. “It’s a joke!” he says, patting my knee playfully. Osmond is one of life’s knee-patters. “I’d have grey sides if I didn’t take care of it. I’m not going to do that. But I’m really careful with what I eat. And I guess I was lucky in the DNA department. My mom had perfect skin.” Has he had any plastic surgery? “No!” But, he says, there was a period when he tried Botox. “I hate it.” Why? He freezes his face into a rictus grin. “Nothing works. I tried it 15, 20 years ago. It took away my crow’s feet and I worked really hard for these crow’s feet.” He laughs. Osmond, who is from Ogden, Utah, was five years old when he entered showbiz. There’s footage of him on the Andy Williams Show singing You Are My Sunshine. He was the youngest Osmond brother in the band at the time and clearly the standout, just as Michael was in the Jackson 5. It was an extraordinary period in music. The Beatles and the Rolling Stones, arguably the two greatest bands of all time, had spent the 60s fighting for supremacy. Now there were the Osmonds and the Jackson 5, the greatest boybands, battling it out. There was a perfect symmetry between them – five brothers, similar ages, with Donny and Michael both solo stars in their own right. The Jackson 5 were black, soulful and funky

title: Interpol and Bloc Party review – two of 00s indie’s most revered acts go toe-to-toe
text: T ry as one might to resist comparison, the balance of this particular yin and yang has been shifting for some time. Twelve months ago, when Interpol and Bloc Party announced a UK and European co-headline tour, the pairing looked like an even contest: two of 00s indie’s most revered acts, whose landmark debuts remain touchstones of the era. Since then, their fortunes have diverged. As an opening bass drone strafes the room, Bloc Party arrive in Cardiff in superficially fine, if puzzling, form. Their seventh album, Anatomy of a Brief Romance, has been met with diminishing returns, its Snapchat-caption triteness – “Every day is such a vibe”, runs one refrain – and creative inertia doing little to win over listeners. That leaves the London four-piece with the more challenging task tonight, their arena-readiness arguably in limbo. Kitted out in the band’s own merch, Kele Okereke, ever the compelling frontman, stomps across a loop pedal during Love Bombs, layering vocals until they blare, before Traps arrives like a desert storm. But as they turn to earlier material, the set begins to lose its way, rattling along like a runaway train. Helicopter, played twice following a minor crowd issue, feels rushed, its euphoria undermined by a half-hearted chorus; signature track Flux follows with dutiful familiarity. That early blaze of energy has been reduced to embers. Okereke’s all-or-nothing conviction in the newer material is admirable, if misplaced; tonight’s crowd, a sea of pint-swigging thirtysomethings in wax jackets and plaid shirts, seem less convinced, their attention fixed on nostalgia – a mode Interpol appear better suited to, simply turning the lights down and letting it glow. As four mirrorballs begin to turn, so does the mood. Daniel Kessler and Paul Banks’s twin guitars drag-race through C’mere and Obstacle 1, while See Out Loud, from August’s This Mirror Weighs a Ton, is hooky yet glowering. Described by this paper as a “masterpiece” , the New Yorkers’ eighth LP signalled a metamorphosis, embracing trip-hop’s darker reaches; live, the effect is hypnotic, Banks’s vocals shifting from spittle-flecked to soulful with exquisite control. Behind them, video screens flicker in grainy, soft-focus fragments, images bleeding into washes of red as Iron City unfurls. The band sound resurgent and at ease, the equilibrium of this double bill now decisively in their favour. Get music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every week At Aviva Studios, Manchester , 23-24 November, then touring until 2 December

title: ‘I do a really good version of AC/DC’s Highway to Hell, which throws people’: Sharleen Spiteri’s honest playlist
text: The first song I fell in love with My mum gave me an old Dansette record player and a pile of albums. I must have been eight or 10, with my younger sister Corinne, getting butterflies to These Boots Are Made for Walkin’ by Nancy Sinatra. Years later, I read that she was told to sing it with a much more provocative attitude. You can hear the sass and the strength. Maybe that’s where my whole “don’t fuck with me” thing came from. The song I do at karaoke Give me any Marvin Gaye song, like You’re All I Need to Get By, and I’m all over it, but I’d normally pull someone up to duet with me. The song I inexplicably know every lyric to Tired of Being Alone by Al Green is ingrained in my DNA. I know every lyric, every nuance. Years later, Texas did a cover of it, and we still occasionally play it live. The best song to play at a party I love everything Daft Punk do. Get Lucky is one of those songs everybody knows and it just makes everybody smile. The song I can no longer listen to My grandparents used to play Ave Maria when I was growing up. My mum absolutely loved it and had asked for it to be played at her funeral, just before lockdown. She also loved Queen. She used to say: “They’re doctors of music.” Last year I was awarded a doctorate of music from the University of Glasgow, so I phoned my sister and she just started laughing: “Oh my God. If Mum was here, she’d have a freakout. You’re now a doctor of music – just like Queen.” I’m just waiting for somebody to shout: “Is there a doctor in the house?” I can say: “Yes!” I can’t save your life, but I can sing you a song. The song I secretly like but tell everybody I hate I don’t have guilty pleasures, but I can rattle out a really good version of Highway to Hell by AC/DC, which normally throws people. The first single I bought Oliver’s Army by Elvis Costello & the Attractions, from a little record shop inside an old cinema. We’d moved from Glasgow to Balloch, and used to go “down the Vale”. There was an arcade with Centipede, Defender, Pac-Man and a pool table, then this record shop tucked away in the corner. I was intrigued because he was called Elvis. I thought: “Who is this fucker calling himself Elvis?” The song that changed my life I Don’t Want a Lover by Texas. I went from being a hairdresser in Glasgow to this. It was the first song Johnny [McElhone] and I ever wrote, one week before my 18th birthday. He asked: “Do you write?” and I said: “Yeah,” because I was a cheeky little bitch. I thought: “How hard can it be?” The best song to have sex to If you ever want to put anybody off a record, tell them which song you have sex to. I don’t want to put people through that shit. Get our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every Friday The song that makes me cry Thin Line Between Love and Hate by the Persuaders. The whole idea of there being this thin line between loving someone and hating them is so true. If you truly love somebody, you’re incredibly close to that love being turned if something goes wrong. The line about the sweetest woman in the world becoming the meanest – it’s one of the greatest lines ever. The song I want played at my funeral Blackbird by the Beatles. White on Blonde 30th anniversary reissue is out 5 February .

title: ‘We’re the most arrogant of all apes!’ A delightfully mind-expanding encounter with Peter Gabriel
text: P eter Gabriel asks me to fetch my laptop: he wants to show me a video of himself playing a keyboard duet with a bonobo called Kanzi. In fairness, said footage is, as Gabriel suggests, “extraordinary”. Working with primatologist Sue Savage-Rumbaugh, who developed a means of communicating with bonobos involving sign language and a speech-synthesis keyboard, Gabriel plays droning chords on a synthesiser while Kanzi picks out complementary notes on a piano. “Look, she likes that note, which is a ninth, and then she finds the octave,” he enthuses as the video plays. “There’s a real musicality there.” It is all deeply unlikely, but it seems the perfect illustration of how easily a conversation with Gabriel can go wildly – if fascinatingly – off-piste. I’ve only been in his company for 10 minutes, long enough to ask a solitary question about his epic new album o\i: its 13 tracks last nearly 90 minutes, the result, he suggests, of a longstanding interest in African music “which made me realise that a song could last as long as a song could last”, and of “being old enough to think ‘fuck it’, really”. For anyone who feels that an hour and a half of exquisitely arranged, beautifully produced, occasionally deeply strange art rock – its sound shapeshifting from the folk-flecked A Hard Lesson to the glowing pop hues of Till Your Mind Is Shining – is too meagre an offering, it arrives in two versions: a “dark” mix by US producer Tchad Blake and a “bright” version that’s the handiwork of Mark “Spike” Stent, famed for working with everyone from U2 and Madonna to Frank Ocean and Harry Styles. I had mentioned the two versions, a routine enough inquiry, but it quickly turns into a discussion about the potential replacement of car stereos with immersive sound systems, which then unexpectedly shifts into an explanation of the work of Michael Levin, an American professor of bioengineering who specialises in morphogenesis. “He’s found some bio-electric instructions that can make an eye grow on the leg of a frog, for example,” says Gabriel, and has apparently “created life forms that never existed before, which really challenges evolution.” Gabriel is interested in “sonifying” some of his data and using it in a subsequent mix of the album. From there, we move on to software engineer Blaise Agüera y Arcas, whose experiments with an esoteric 90s programming language called Brainfuck have led him to “the radical idea that some constants in maths might actually have some form of life”. This leads us, via the “re-evaluation of what consciousness is and what intelligence is”, to the belief of internet pioneer Vint Cerf that attempting to communicate with other intelligent species might prepare us for the possibility of encountering aliens, and thus to Savage-Rumbaugh and Kanzi the bonobo. “She used to allow the bonobos to watch videos, and to choose the videos they watched,” Gabriel says, laughing, “and their favourite, perhaps obviously, was Planet of the Apes, then Harry and the Hendersons, which is a film about a sasquatch who came to live with a family. The whole thing blew me away. I think we’re the most arrogant of all apes, and there’s just so much intelligence we’ve chosen to ignore and instead see the world as something that’s entirely available for our exploitation, and I think that’s cost us, as we are now learning.” M orphogenisis, inter-species communication, the re-evaluation of consciousness: it should go without saying that you don’t usually end up discussing these things when you ask an august rock legend about his latest album. But, as it turns out, that’s what inevitably happens when you ask Gabriel a question. We meet in a pub not far from his home in Notting Hill. He says he’s here “to sell the new album”, but almost every query about it seems to lead him somewhere completely different: science, activism, the nature of consciousness, how language is “a fairly crude tool” for communication, the controversial 1970s self-improvement cours

title: Fontaines DC review – thrilling gothic grandeur from a band vaulting into greatness
text: A mere seven years since their debut, Dogrel, Fontaines DC have enjoyed a virtually seamless passage from Dublin dive bars to arenas, with stadiums to follow next year. Each step has been taken seemingly effortlessly in their stride and this latest outing is no exception. Bathed in shimmering blue light, the band are well into hymnal opener Six Shot Morning before we even see sight of singer Grian Chatten. He wanders on while singing, an entrance worthy of Frank Sinatra. Chatten has previously seemed to distrust showbiz, but if anything the singer seems far more comfortable on the bigger stage than he ever did on smaller ones. With his Korn T-shirt, unfeasibly baggy trousers and tiny tattoo reading “deadly” in capitals, he leaps around, raises his arms to whip up the crowd and points the microphone towards them to sing key lines. Similarly, music this intense, dark, elegiac and even bleak – which speaks to the void at the heart of much modern life – is hardly typical arena fare but works brilliantly by taking on a more anthemic, celebratory aspect. It’s certainly weirdly thrilling hearing Chatten’s lines such as “We’re all depressed, running on a wheel” or “I don’t feel anything in the modern world” – or a song as plainly dark as Jackie Down the Line – become enormous, arena-uniting sing-songs. The band’s racing progress is demonstrated by the setlist: just one song remains from each of their first two albums (Boys from the Better Land and A Hero’s Death respectively) and there are a whopping nine from Dopamine Chamber , their rave-reviewed latest. Driven by the band’s powerhouse rhythm section and walls of guitars and electronics, the new songs are already crowd favourites. Marianne is haunting and Mimesis is epic, gothic, European-sounding rock. A sea of phones illuminates Japan, a spectral near-ballad, and the crowd’s massed voices fill in for Rosalía (who duets with Chatten on the record) for Where Is Gone? It’s another unabashed triumph from a band who are yet to put a foot wrong. Fontaines DC play AO Arena, Manchester, 21 November; then touring UK until 27 November

title: RPO/Hisaishi review – Studio Ghibli’s genius brings his concerto to a rapt London
text: I f anyone tells you that classical music is dead you need just two words to refute them: Joe Hisaishi. The 75-year-old Japanese conductor, composer and pianist may be best known for his soundtracks, particularly his long association with Hayao Miyazaki’s Studio Ghibli films, but has parlayed his popular success into serious concert-hall credentials. You can debate style and genre, but there’s no arguing with the impact of a man who can sell out the Royal Albert Hall on a Monday night in November with an evening of music by Steve Reich, David Lang and Hisaishi himself – and not a film score in sight. The centrepiece of his latest collaboration with London’s Royal Philharmonic Orchestra was the UK premiere of Hisaishi’s Concerto for Orchestra. Co-commissioned by an astonishing 11 ensembles spread across six different countries, its musical DNA is no less international. Hisaishi’s programming emphasised its lineage in American minimalism, but there’s Vivaldi in there, a nod to Stravinsky’s Shrovetide Fair, to Bernard Herrmann and even Caribbean colours in the kaleidoscopic mix. Five movements are identified only by number – no performance direction or speed marking to frame our expectations. We start where Reich and Lang left off, in fiercely patterned, meticulously layered processes. As the beat is divided smaller and smaller the surface starts to gleam with sequinned texture: a mathematical exercise dressed up in black-tie. It’s off to carnival in the genial second movement, which together with the queasy cross-rhythms of the central panel features a series of jazz-style breaks for sections or solo instruments (a trio of bassoons supply gusty comedy, and there are some arresting histrionics from double basses). A Ravellian pastoral leads into a meaty, contrapuntal finale. This is a well-established partnership, and the RPO were glued to Hisaishi’s precise beat: riding the bucking rhythms of this intricate score, moving seamlessly between solo and ensemble spirit. This shapeshifting was also uppermost in Steve Reich’s 2018 Music for Ensemble and Orchestra: at once monumental and playful in the RPO’s polished account. But Lang’s Mountain (2014) swapped musical metamorphosis for a monolith. A single idea – a big thump for brass and timps that ricochets through the strings, followed by silence – isn’t enough to sustain its span. A note by the composer himself describes the holiday view that inspired it. “Unchanging” may be a virtue when it comes to a mountain; it’s not for music.

title: Saariaho’s Adriana Mater transcends horror for hope. Female composers are rejecting opera’s legacy of violence | Annilese Miskimmon
text: I n 1992, the Finnish composer Kaija Saariaho saw a Salzburg festival production of Messiaen’s Saint François d’Assise. A series of meditative theological tableaux in which naturalism and plot is secondary to the revelation of deeper spiritual truths, it is now hailed as a masterpiece although it divided critics on its Paris premiere in 1983. Saariaho, one of the painfully few female composers in opera’s 400-year history, recalled thinking: “If that is an opera, then I can write one”. And she did, to notable international acclaim. Her first opera L’Amour de loin (Love from Afar), a tale of medieval courtly love with a libretto by war correspondent and writer Amin Maalouf was premiered, appropriately, at 2000’s Salzburg festival and came to the UK when English National Opera staged it in 2009 . Her second opera with Maalouf was Adriana Mater . The work charts a clear path towards hope and reconciliation. Amid the backdrop of a civil war, Adriana is raped and becomes pregnant by Tsargo, a man from her own community. She chooses to give birth to the son she conceives, raising him with hope for the future, while shielding him from the truth about his father. Many years later her son discovers the truth of his origin and becomes consumed by the desire to kill Tsargo. But faced with the reality of his now old and blind father, Yonas cannot bring himself to avenge Adriana and returns to his mother feeling a failure as a man and a son. This is her moment of triumph – “This man deserved to die, my son, but you did not deserve to kill … We are not avenged, Yonas, but we are saved.” Saariaho’s opera illuminates the decades long, often unrewarded work of peace-making after civil conflict that many women across the world quietly commit to – my native Northern Ireland included. As Peter Sellars, the director of the 2006 world premiere, said of the piece, “In the 21st century we have a responsibility to do more than sit around and tell sad stories. Here we see there will be a future. And that future has been guaranteed all over the world by women, women who, in impossible situations, nourish and cultivate human dignity.” The uncompromising themes and sound world of this second opera so contrasted with the mystical romanticism of her first that Saariaho disconcerted many. “After L’Amour de loin, I felt the need to write an opera reflecting the world around me. My rela­tionship to music as an intimate and protected universe had broken down after the events of 11 September 2001,” she said. Her creative courage cost her critical appreciation at the time – a price that perhaps a male composer would not have paid. It is only now after the immediate acclaim that met her final opera Innocence about a school shooting (seen at the RBO in 2023 , shortly before she died aged only 70 ) that Adriana Mater is being reassessed – the recent Esa-Pekka Salonen recording won both the Gramophone and Grammy opera recording of the year . For centuries, men have been using the death and pain of female characters as a bedrock of the art form. It is notable that Saariaho and the female composers of today are not reacting to this legacy by rejecting the subject of violence in their own work – just the opposite. They are championing the relevance and impact of opera by using it to confront modern life’s most difficult issues and, as Cesar Cruz’s aphorism declares – proving that art should “comfort the disturbed and disturb the comfortable”. Du Yun’s Angel’s Bone , which opened ENO’s London season after an immersive run in Aviva Studios in Manchester, is a harrowing parable about the human trafficking that underpins the dark reality of modern capitalist societies. Our upcoming production of Breaking the Waves by Missy Mazzoli is an adaptation of the devastating film by Lars von Trier about love, faith and marital martyrdom. And for one night only we have a guest performance of To Die For – a darkly comedic exploration of the search to find meaning in a meaningless world

title: Flottiana album review – 10-cd collection celebrates a very, very great Dame
text: W hen Dame Felicity Lott died in May this year, the world lost a truly singular talent. An effortlessly elegant soprano, Flott, as she was known, was as at home in German, and especially French, as she was in her native English. This 10-CD boxset from Hyperion brings together some of her finest recordings from a career that spanned half a century. It’s curated by Graham Johnson, who in 1976 recruited Lott for The Songmakers’ Almanac, the pioneering vocal ensemble whose mission was to explore neglected corners of the repertoire. First, the voice; an instrument that appears incapable of anything indecorous. It never spreads or strays from the note, maintaining a purity and brilliance even when hovering in the musical stratosphere. Then there’s the diction, crisp and clear, wedded to an intelligence that lays bare the inner meaning of a song without mannerisms or affectation. With Lott it was straight and to the point, every emotion subtly and honestly conveyed. The set opens with a 1981 Brahms and Schumann disc that finds the singers of The Songmakers’ Almanac at their most imaginative; listen to Lott’s seamless technique in Brahms’ Nachtwandler, or the frisky allure of Schumann’s Singet nicht in Trauertönen. It’s followed by a composer-by-composer stroll through the uplands of German lieder. A consummate Schubertian, Lott offers absorbing accounts of Der Liebliche Stern, Suleika II and a surprisingly fervent Auf dem Wasser zu Singen. The latter draws supple support from the ever-resourceful Johnson, whose tensile piano line ripples and swells. Her Schumann includes sparkling duets with Ann Murray, while Wolf features excerpts from the Italienisches Liederbuch with the late Peter Schreier. Richard Strauss was one of Lott’s happiest places. His operatic miniatures show off her breath control, phrasing and dramatic characterisation, culminating in affecting interpretations of Ruhe, meine Seele! and Morgen. Comedic skills are on display too, in the sparky humour of Schubert’s Der Hochzeitsbraten, for example, where she and Anthony Rolfe Johnson’s plucky poacher turn the tables on Richard Jackson’s susceptible gamekeeper. Cabaret songs such as Noël Coward’s A Bar on the Piccola Marina are delivered with charm and charisma alongside more serious English songs by Quilter, Walton, Warlock and Britten. Fallen Women and Virtuous Wives, a live 2005 Wigmore Hall recital, rounds off the set. It’s the three discs of French mélodies , however, that reveal Lott at her most insightful, from the melancholy introspection of Chausson to the lightly perfumed utterances of Gounod and Fauré. There’s a tart wit and wisdom to her Poulenc (La Dame de Monte-Carlo is a masterclass in understated despair), while her ease with the lyrical line is complemented by an idiomatic instinct for all things Gallic. Johnson ties it all together with erudite sleeve notes full of insight and fond memories.

title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
text: I n GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it. For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. Jason is muscular, handsome, ex-military, steady and unflappable, sincere but spare with words. Lucia has been boosting cars since the age of 14, has a wicked sense of humour and takes zero bullshit. (Lucia is the scarier one; I found myself turning much more quickly to violence when playing as her.) At the start, Lucia is incarcerated and Jason is making a go of things in the sunbeaten Keys, working for a dodgy guy down on the marina and renting a run-down house on stilts with a jetty round the back and a pet snake. When Lucia gets out of prison, the two of them try to make some kind of life for themselves – but before long they get caught up with the wrong people and have to flee the cosy life they’ve just started building. For a long time you really are two-bit criminals on the run, getting in with every dirtbag petty thief and drug-runner you come across in order to scrape some cash together and stay under the radar. You meet hillbilly pill-heads and biker gangs, friendly conspiracy theorists, a shady doctor, Lucia’s former prison friends and their lowlife boyfriends. By the time I actually got to Vice City – a glitzy den of sin, the centre of all Leonida’s pleasures and all its most extravagant criminality, where the gangbangers hustle on social media and even the narcos are obsessed with their Instagram clout – I had been playing for 30 hours. It took me 70 hours to finish the game and I could have taken longer. Leonida is so lifelike that at times it beggars belief, so vast that it feels overwhelming, and outside the story missions you can do whatever you please. There are nightclubs, gyms, flea markets, malls, restaurants, clothes shops, basketball courts, shooting ranges, aircraft hangars, projects and mansions, places to hunt and fish or go kayaking, gas stations and thousands of individuals engaged in conversation as you pass by. Interesting things are always happening in your peripheral vision. You might witness the cops chasing someone down to plant drugs on them, or overhear an interesting confrontation, or see a car speeding away and wonder where it’s going – though interesting things always seemed to happen when I was driving a stolen car at high speed towards a discerning buyer, or otherwise unable to stop and follow my nose. Thankfully, another opportunity would always present itself. I often felt that the only thing messing up Rockstar’s perfect simulation was me. All this detail and realism comes with some disadvantages, namely complex controls and a tendency for the game’s systems to collide with my intentions in unexpected and sometimes annoying ways. Here I am, driving at high speed through the city before clipping the kerb and flipping my car, causing a massive pile-up. Here I am pressing the wrong button and accidentally punching a random passerby rather than greeting them as in

title: Man Theft Auto – why did so few women review GTA VI, the biggest video game of the decade?
text: G rand Theft Auto VI is now the biggest video game launch of all time, and is likely to become the biggest video game of all time. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime event, a phenomenon that will shape games as a medium and pop culture at large for years to come, set against the backdrop of its developers fighting for their rights at studio Rockstar Games . It has snatched sales and streaming records and become the best-reviewed game ever (pulling ahead of 1998’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time). It’s also the first GTA game with a female protagonist, who also happens to be a woman of colour. Yet very few women (and seemingly no women of colour) played and reviewed it before release. When GTA VI’s review embargo lifted on 18 November, the gender imbalance was immediately obvious. Out of 156 reviewers, only six appeared to be women. As journalist Lex Luddy noted in a BlueSky post , that is 3.8%. The lack of diversity of voice is depressing. The unfortunate reality is that there aren’t that many women writing about video games in 2026, thanks to a mix of media consolidation, firings, hostile takeovers and burnout. Public ire – something, sadly, that all public-facing critics and journalists have to deal with – is also especially intense for female, queer and non-white writers. Though an Entertainment Software Association report this year suggests that women make up 46% of the gamer population in the US, they do not make up half of the people writing about video games. A glance at the editorial teams for some of the top video game sites in the US and UK – GamesRadar, PC Gamer, Polygon, Kotaku, Eurogamer and Game Informer – reveals 100 writers, of whom 27 are women. That’s just over a quarter. The only GTA VI reviews on those sites were from men. As it was such a big launch, many outlets will have assigned GTA VI reviews to the most “senior” games writers. But that is precisely the problem: there aren’t more women at this senior level, more female household names, because the games industry chews them up and spits them out. Given that this is the first GTA game in 30 years with a female protagonist – apart from the mute characters Candy and Gretchen in the Game Boy Color versions of GTA 2 – the lack of female perspectives on the game is even more glaring. GTA VI stars Lucia Caminos, the Bonnie to Jason Duval’s Clyde. She is a Latina woman played by a Latina woman, struggling to thrive in a dark-mirror version of modern America, where the crooks are in charge and the only way to get by is to break the rules. We’ve known about Lucia since the first trailer debuted in 2023, and with three different delays, you would think the enterprising leaders at the biggest video game websites or verticals would have allocated a review or two to one of the dozens of talented women working this beat. Wouldn’t female game journalists, who have lived through years of male-centric GTA discourse, have a take on the series’ shifting perspective? Wouldn’t it be interesting to hear from American women about what it’s like to try to make ends meet or simply exist in a country that has overturned abortion access and locked up and brutalised brown people en masse, and how those real-world experiences intersect with the experience of the game? But alas, here we are. Six women have reviewed GTA VI in 2026. Maybe there’s hope. Manni L Perez, who plays Lucia, was nominated for best performance at the forthcoming Game Awards 2026, while Jason was not. Reviews, livestreams and reactions thus far suggest this is a GTA game that, while still steeped in satire, biting critiques of modern American society, and absurdist violence, is a love story. And Lucia is at its centre. Perhaps her character and her journey, coupled with a gameplay loop that models a functioning and considerate relationship, could mean the GTA player base shifts to reflect the gamer population at large. More women may buy and play this game than any other Rockstar game ever. Maybe 13 years from now,

title: Twenty years ago, the Wii and PS3 predicted the future of gaming – did they get it right?
text: T he main focus of the games industry this week is, of course, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI – a game that could define the next decade for the industry. For this week’s newsletter though, I wanted to direct your attention two decades into the past. In November 2006, two console manufacturers launched their competing – and wildly different – visions of what the future of video games would look like. Twenty years later, it’s clear that somehow they were both right. And yet, in some ways, they were both wrong. For Nintendo , the Wii was the natural extension of its famous maxim, Kareta Gijutsu no Suihei Shikō – roughly translated as lateral thinking with withered technology. Coined by the company’s legendary engineer Gunpei Yokoi, father of the Game Boy, the phrase described a philosophy in which old tech could be combined with smart ideas to provide amazing new gaming possibilities. The Game Boy itself used a slow, old Sharp LR35902 processor and a sickly green monochrome screen, but it also came with Tetris and worked for ages on four AA batteries. With sales of 65m, it was vastly more successful than hi-tech rivals such as the Atari Lynx and Sega Game Gear. Before its release, the Wii was famously described as “two GameCubes duct-taped together” by game developer Chris Hecker, and its limited hardware specs drew almost as much derisive laughter as its weird name. But … it came with a motion controller that everyone could use and understand, and in Wii Sports, it had a game so perfectly compulsive it became a must at family gatherings for a decade. In fact, Wii Sports bowling leagues are still operating to this day. So in 2006, Nintendo told us the future would be about accessible games on accessible hardware – a point it made again with the Wii U (less successfully) and the Switch (more successfully). This philosophy has also driven the vast mobile games market, where the communications device that almost everyone has in their pocket happens to be perfect for playing technologically simple but compulsive puzzle games such as Candy Crush Saga and Subway Surfers. However, the PlayStation 3 also launched in November 2006. At the time, it was so technologically advanced that Sony had to delay its release by a year. The machine’s proprietary Cell processor featured eight specialised Synergistic Processing Elements (SPEs), which could be simultaneously applied to different computing tasks. It was a radically new approach, and research labs around the world began buying and interconnecting dozens of them to use as comparatively cheap supercomputing clusters. In 2010, the US Air Force built a computing project known as Condor Cluster, which used 1760 PS3s to perform 500 trillion mathematical calculations per second. So you know who to blame if you couldn’t get one for Christmas that year. The PS3 also came with an ethernet port and native support that improved its online connectivity. Slightly behind Microsoft, Sony had understood that, with the rollout of affordable broadband, multiplayer gaming was going to be a big thing – and its key first-party title at the time, the slick sci-fi shooter Killzone, really leaned into this. Unlike with the Xbox 360, though, online gaming was free on PlayStation Network – and that was another thing the Sony of 2006 realised: in the digital age, people really weren’t into paying for things. Other than online play, what the PS3 really became famous for was its epic single-player action adventures, such as The Last of Us , Demon’s Souls, Metal Gear Solid , God of War, Heavy Rain and, yes, Grand Theft Auto V. While Nintendo was telling the world “everyone can play now!”, the PlayStation 3 was saying “Actually, no, you need to be really good at games and be prepared to play for hundreds of hours”. That’s not entirely fair. As well as epic action adventures, the machine did also support and encourage an emerging community of indie developers; hence, brilliant titles such as Journey and Hotline Miami

title: ‘I had to reject a lot of shame’: Michaela Yearwood-Dan on queerness, Catholicism and her extravagant artist dinner parties
text: T he artist Michaela Yearwood-Dan is on the hunt for her missing cat. Pinto disappeared from her home in east London a couple of weeks ago and has so far defied the forecasts of tarot readings and the “witchy ladies” predicting his return. A lost pet is not the only thing she’s searching for. “I’m at a stage of life where I’m looking for answers” she says on the eve of her exhibition The Practice of Liberation, at Towner Eastbourne. Her other, more existential questions are those of many women in their early 30s: “Do I want to have children? How do I want to have children? What does my future look like?” She is “big into astrology”, but recently her thoughts have turned to her Catholic upbringing in south London, which serves as a large theme of her exhibition, which debuted at the Whitworth Gallery in Manchester earlier this year. Religious ritual has always appealed to her, and her show uses paintings, ceramics and a musical composition by her friend and longstanding collaborator Alex Gruz to evoke the ritual space of a church. “I was thinking a lot about the place of religion in my past and where that intersects with my femininity, with my queerness, with my blackness, and where that then intersects with history and colonialism and all of the things that have built me as a person”, she explains. “Part of that is the rejection of a lot of those things – Catholic guilt and shame about queerness, feeling held down by the patriarchy.” The tensions she feels are complicated by the appropriation of Christian values by the far right, but she is also thankful for her time in a girls’ convent school: “We all came out as little feminists – we never had to compete for a voice.” Her exuberantly gestural, lusciously colourful paintings are large, loud and joyful, but stay with them and they reveal a quieter, more diaristic character. Often embellished with ceramics and glass beads they typically include scraps of text that read as affirmations or lines of poetry, confidences and notes to self that seem private and yet declamatory. Intuitive as they seem, it took a leap of faith and the financial security of a residency with the Sarabande Foundation in 2018 for Yearwood-Dan to abandon the figurative style that had seen her through university, but never felt right. Still working as a nanny, “I’d been given this free studio for a year”, she explains: “The work quickly became more abstract, and it had these elements of diary writings in them, like old text messages, and things that I couldn’t say or didn’t want to send – it was this realisation that if I just made work that was really honest, it would also be very relatable to other people.” “Can you let go of your idea of heaven?”, asks her painting Radical Dreams; “ Once the hate is gone, where will my pain live?”, reads a note, stuck like a memo to the canvas of I’m Nowhere But Here. They read like snippets of conversations, ongoing and multi-voiced, the paintings less like a glimpse inside the artist’s soul, and more as if we have tuned in to some vast, shared archive. In a sense this is literally true: for the past couple of years, Yearwood-Dan has held dinners in her studio, to which she invites 20 to 30 artists, journalists, curators and friends, to eat and make a painting together as an antidote to the isolation and hyper connection of our time. “The most hesitant people to get up there and do something are artists,” she says. In contrast, her friend Ian, who works in HR, had no inhibitions: “He was gagging for that brush. He was bouncing, he knew exactly what he was going to do.” The dinners are a social experiment that have yielded some interesting findings, she reveals: “There’s always a smiley face. There’s always a star, and there’s always an animal.” But once completed, “It’s like I’ve been given a map – there are movements and motions that I can interact with, lovely little dots and splats that I can embellish with beads and bring forward, colours I can flesh out with oil bar

title: ‘The Terence Conran of his day’: the visionary Victorian futurist adored by design superstars today
text: V ictorian industrial designer Christopher Dresser was always a visionary. As a child, he was so artistically gifted he went to design school in 1847 when he was just 13. He became a professor at 21, dreaming up theories based on plant structure that changed the way designers worked. But it was after he quit academia that he really started to break boundaries. As a self-declared “design doctor”, he experimented with production techniques that brought beautiful, futuristic homeware into everyday houses. He was one of the first western designers to travel to Japan, helping introduce Japonisme to British life, which has had a transformative effect on furniture and decoration ever since. Using his ideas on botanical form, he created designs strikingly at odds with the aesthetic of the times. He took the everyday – teapots, toast racks and pitchers – and made them unfamiliar and futuristic. But his achievements are now not widely known. “Everyone knows about William Morris and the Arts and Craft movement,” says Ian Robinson, a collector of Dresser’s work. “Morris’s politics kept him in with the era’s movers and shakers, and subsequently on the radars of curators and historians. But Dresser was focused on technological developments and using mass production to bring design to every home, which didn’t sound as sexy. It’s interesting how history plays out in these stories. Dresser was embracing new methods; Morris was looking backwards.” A new exhibition, Christopher Dresser: The Pursuit of Beauty at the Hub, a centre for craft and design in Sleaford, hopes to reinstate the designer’s legacy with a survey of his modernist ceramics, fluid glassware and sharply angular metalwork. “Ask your friends if they’ve heard of Christopher Dresser, and nine times out of 10 they’ll say no,” says Joshua Lockwood, exhibitions manager and curator at the Hub. Robinson, who has lent work to the exhibition, is such a Dresser fan that he’s got one eye on an online auction for a piece while we talk on a video call. “If I show people his designs, they recognise some pieces, such as the sugar bowl that Italian design brand Alessi brought back into production in the 1990s, but they don’t know who made them,” Robinson says. “He was the Terence Conran of his day, but he’s not remembered.” Dresser was born in Glasgow and studied structure and science at the Government School of Design (later renamed the Royal College of Art) under influential academics architect Owen Jones and art critic Gottfried Semper. He became professor of artistic botany there himself, but after missing out on the chair of botany at London University in 1860, Dresser ditched academia and worked instead as a consultant for businesses such as Wedgwood pottery, Minton’s porcelain, Liberty of London and Tiffany & Co. He created an experimental body of work, remarkable in terms of technology and influence. In his metalwork, Dresser experimented with unusual metal alloys and then cutting-edge processes such as electroplating to make exceptionally sleek household objects. He was co-founder and art director at Linthorpe Art Pottery, a revolutionary workshop set up in 1879 that was the first in the country to use gas-powered kilns. This innovation let Dresser develop his signature mottled glazes, and he designed over 1,000 vessels in the three years he worked there. He travelled to Japan in 1876 on behalf of the South Kensington Museum (now the V&A), and helped start the Victorian craze for Japonisme. “That was his thing, to bring beautiful things to the home,” says Robinson. “He wanted to bring good design to as many people as possible. To buy Morris’s furniture you had to be very wealthy. Dresser mainly worked in silverplate or even painted tin. It was beautiful design but it was also affordable.” Dresser’s family tried to continue his design studio after his death in 1904, but when that proved unsuccessful they disposed of all his account books and drawings, effectively destroying his archive. “

title: What happened when the man who took a million photographs embraced colour?
text: D espite his wide renown, there have been hardly any major exhibitions of Sanlé Sory’s work. His last UK show was in 2019, concentrating on the black-and-white images the Burkinabé photographer made in the first two decades after opening his own studio, Volta Photo, in Bobo-Dioulasso in 1960 – a period that coincided with the first two decades of independence in Burkina Faso . This new Photographer’s Gallery show shifts the focus to the 1980s and 1990s, when Sory began working in colour. It’s easy to see why, even with few exhibitions, Sory has made such an impression on audiences. There are the familiar west African studio photography tropes westerners love, where sound, image, fashion and pose collide. The props are popping, the style is irrepressible, the energy is irresistible. I wonder if Sory’s speed and instinct came from the time he spent early in his career racing on his motorbike to photograph car accidents for newspapers and the police. These portraits are the opposite of a car crash, they’re remedially joyful, wilfully alive – but they share that feeling of being inside the moment, at the edge of something. The works here also bring out the insouciance and humour in Sory’s portraits. In a wall of selected studio photographs, reprinted from negatives in his archive, the poses are sometimes gloriously over the top: fingers pointing skywards, a fake phone held to the ear, an imitation of Grandmaster Flash. It’s all about the mash-ups: a girl in a traditional pagne paired with Nike Air Slants. Sory seems to encourage his subjects to take their fantasy roles as far as they can – the bolder, the better. Driving a motorbike into the studio? No problem. One man is almost transformed into a sculpture, draped in ceremonial, traditional and western fabrics, a religious portrait held tightly to his chest and one clenched fist raised. But Sory can be understated, too: a young man in a leather-shoe shop in the market, one leg kicked out to the side as he holds up one of the shop’s models. It’s thought that Sory has taken more than one million portraits; at Volta Studio’s peak, 250 people would come to be photographed every day. In the 1970s, Sory had his subjects stand against specially commissioned painted backdrops – an Ivory Coast beach setting, an aircraft boarding bridge, a generic north American city – familiar but fantastical, for his clients to project themselves into. A few of those examples are included here, in black and white, too. In the colour studio portraits here, the backdrops are replaced with a simple brown curtain, and prismatic patterned rugs, shifting the focus back to the people in front of the camera, to the here and now. If they wanted, Sory loaned his clients clothes or props; but what he couldn’t give them is the attitude. In a vitrine in the back room, there’s a small collection of original prints given to clients who came to the studio – their album-size scale totally changes the picture, and reminds you of the purpose of these keepsakes: private souvenirs for personal histories, loved ones. Enlarged and displayed on the gallery walls, they become something else – something that reaches beyond the individual. At night, the buzz of the studio blurred seamlessly into long nights on the dancefloor. As well as creating record sleeves for groups such as Dafra Star, Orchestre Volta Jazz, and Echo Del Africa, Sory was also an organiser of DIY raves around Bobo-Dioulasso, known as bals poussières (dust balls). As he recounts in his 2017 book, Sanlé Sory: Volta Photo 1965-85 : “I would drive down to some remote village in the bush and set up a player, a few records, some loudspeakers and a few lights and get the party going. We started around 8pm and people would tell me, ‘Sory, you need to set the place on fire!’ It would go on until 5am.” Of course, the party became a Sory photoshoot, too. title: ‘The lack of fun is as noticeable as the lack of content’: the reborn Museum of London is all piazza, no punch
text: T he Museum of London at the Barbican was the capital’s local museum, a crowded and quirky presentation of its history from the Dagenham idol to Vauxhall Pleasure Gardens . But apparently the location deterred casual visitors, and maybe it just wasn’t grand enough to reflect London’s self-conscious significance. For not since ancient Rome has a capital dominated its nation’s history and culture like London. So now we get the rebranded and reimagined London Museum Smithfield. History surrounds you in this neighbourhood: Black Death burials by the Charterhouse, the Knights of St John, the Smithfield martyrs, William Wallace’s execution site. So goodbye scruffy brutalist Slough House location, hello deep history. Except when you enter the new museum, all that history, all those layers going back to the Romans and earlier, have been brushed away. If you want an illustration that bigger is not better, this is it. When Sharon Ament, the director, asked me if I liked it, I couldn’t find the words. I was heartbroken, speechless, unlike the museum’s management who have their own way with language. Displays have nonsensical themes: “London as Ritual”, “London as Stage”, “London as Sunrise”. One wall text begins: “London is a city of people.” Read that twice. What is this? Cunk on London ? Two vast ground floor spaces are called Real Time and Our Time. Neither has much to see in the way of exhibits – a bell, a stuffed giraffe, the Lord Mayor’s coach in an absurd vitrine. But that’s not the point, for really they are all about the cafes and restaurants, chill-out spaces and vibing. I was proudly told the 24-hour Temperance cafe will serve people coming out of nearby Fabric. This place wants to be up there with the club, to be more than a stuffy old museum. It ends up being so much less. It strains to be part of the city and definitely is a good indoor piazza to hang out, have coffee, read your texts. But so is nearby St Pancras station and it has more respect for its Victorian heritage. Where is the heart of this museum, its vast and fascinating collection of artefacts from London’s long history and even prehistory? That has been shoved downstairs into a third space called Past Time. The assumption seems to be the past is dead in contrast to the living present, though surely history is the process of change in which we all live. Past Time doesn’t have galleries of different periods: just one long open space telling the entire story of London in a potted, bullet-point version addressed to someone who in the curators’ imaginations can’t cope with the least hint of complexity. I say entire, but it cuts out the prehistory of the Thames landscape, which got its own gallery in the old museum. Ament told me that the gallery was not “popular”, so it’s sayonara to the stone age handaxes. Yet the lack of fun is as noticeable as the lack of content. I may have made the old Museum of London sound serious, but it found space for a son et Lumiere 18th-century pleasure garden, Victorian shops, a Roman house. There’s nothing like that here. Instead everything is presented with chic conceptualism, like a taster menu. There is a Roman shop and tavern, yet this is done in such a minimalist, cool way it has no atmosphere. Kids will shrug. The whirl through time continues as medieval London is jumbled into the Tudors and Stuarts. In next to no time, you reach a single case covering both world wars. Well, I don’t suppose they made much impact on London … but wasn’t there a blitz or something? The lack of space or time to explore the collections in depth destroys any chance to connect with objects emotionally: as you proceed from chronological displays to themed ones, the randomisation is numbing. London is a venerable place yet also a city of amnesias. Accidental destruction by the Great Fire and attempted obliteration by Nazi bombs are not the only enemies of its past. title: Cat’s whiskers: Nan Goldin proves that she’s the greatest US artist since Warhol – review
text: I t’s the dirty realism of Nan Goldin ’s images, her unfazed photography of the rough seams of spontaneous, dangerous lives, that enables her to create a film of such unlikely ambition as Stendhal Syndrome. This ecstatic condition is named after the French novelist who in 1817 fell ill in Florence, after gorging on the beauty of the Renaissance city’s treasures until “I had palpitations of the heart … I walked with the fear of falling”. Goldin, too, has suffered a bout of this aesthetic delirium, not in Italy but Paris – “the first time I was alone in the Louvre”, she explains on screen. She infects you with it in a ravishing work housed in what looks like a bronze yurt entered via a vaulted corridor. If this seems ostentatious, the film justifies the ceremony. A montage of sensual images teems with Goldin’s uniquely raw, immediate feel for the human presence as she photographs her friends, mostly in the nude, legs wrapped round each other, or lying in a swoon, or touching themselves, or bathing together. Here is the unfeigned, honest impact her work has had since she first put her world viscerally on camera in her early photo series The Ballad of Sexual Dependency . But there’s a difference. A Caravaggesque young man looks with bedroom eyes at the camera. Then we cut to an actual Caravaggio painting for comparison. The resemblance is magical. And the 17th-century queer outlaw and murderer is not the only great artist whose images are collaged with Goldin’s photos. As Goldin relates on the film’s soundtrack, she saw, wandering the Louvre in a trance, her friends’ faces in sensual masterpieces including works by Correggio and Canova. These timeless portrayals of beauty and love, in glowing paint and smooth marble, are intercut with Goldin’s erotic snaps to a rousing score. And here’s the thing. Intentionally or not, her live subjects pose their bodies in ways that mirror the old masters: lovers fondle like Cupid and Psyche, their warm living flesh as sculpted and perfect as Canova’s marble. Meanwhile, Goldin tells tales of desire from Ovid’s Metamorphoses. It turns out that this Roman poet’s kinky versions of Greek myth uncannily anticipate 21st-century boho life. She photographs a Pygmalion and Galatea she happens to know, a Narcissus in love with his own reflection. You expect mythological references from your Twomblys and Kentridges but when an artist seen as an unvarnished recorder of opioid America mixes her world with high art and ancient mythology, it poses acute questions. What is beauty? What is art? Are they both just ways to freeze, for a moment, the passing glory of life? In another film, Memory Lost, Goldin looks back on her and her friends’ experiences of addiction. A photo of a mattress with a huge dark hole, burnt into it by an addict’s cigarette (you guess), is juxtaposed with enraptured romantic images of red skies and wintry woodlands. There is beauty in us and all around us. But do drugs, from heroin to prescription opioids, make you see it sharper or lose sight of it in the cravings and wastings? Art is a healthier high, suggests Stendhal Syndrome, but even that can make you swoon. Goldin campaigns against opioids, but the lure of the addictive sublime pulses through her work in the Romantic spirit of American creativity from Edgar Allan Poe to Lou Reed. Even when it’s at its sweetest. And what could be sweeter than a pussycat (unless you’re a bird)? Cat’s eyes stare at you in the film You Never Did Anything Wrong, parts one and two, that gives this show its title. They keep staring. And not just cats – owls and alligators, too. It’s a disturbing montage of glaring animal faces that makes you ponder the nature of other-species consciousness. “You never did anything wrong”, it transpires, is an inscription from a gravestone in a pet cemetery. Another says: “We are sorry.” You may laugh. You may wonder why the pets’ owners are apologising. Then you get it. We all should be sorry. Goldin is showing us the inno

title: ‘A fight to demand that humans are worth investing in’: Theaster Gates on taking over America’s last porcelain factory
text: “T he worth of hand-painted china depends mainly upon the hand ,” reads an advertisement dating from 1910 and displayed just inside the entrance of the Pickard China factory, a sprawling, 60,000 sq ft brick building just outside Chicago . “Most of the large staff of artists at the Pickard studios have been trained in the great art centers of Europe, and each piece of Pickard is painted from start to finish by the same master craftsman.” Those statements are a distant echo from another age. These days, Pickard – the last operational porcelain fine china factory in the US – is in a shocking state of disrepair, its 12 remaining employees struggling to fulfill longstanding orders for the White House (Pickard began producing official White House china in 2008 when the company was commissioned by Laura Bush), Williams Sonoma, US embassies, private golf clubs and anxious brides-to-be. Inside the building, decommissioned machines the size of school buses remain frozen in their final moments of functionality, collecting dust, cobwebs and slip splatter. The roof is patched by a checkerboard of blue and green tarps strung from rafters and draped into makeshift troughs, water trickling into large commercial garbage cans. The doors to some rooms have remained locked for decades in an attempt to contain the toxic mold spreading inside. Thousands of pieces of porcelain plates, cups, pitchers and bowls sit stacked on ancient wood shelves, languishing in various stages of incompletion. Some lights are functional, most are not, casting the whole eerie scene into semi-darkness. The lights are about to be flipped back on. In September, Theaster Gates , the celebrated artist and radical urban interventionist, became the new owner of Pickard China – its client roster, its design archive, and this massive, crumbling factory surrounded by cornfields in Antioch, Illinois, 50 miles north of Chicago. I visited the factory on a damp, early fall morning, a few days after the staff had learned of the ownership change. Just five employees were on site, stamping, trimming and lining individual pieces among the battered machinery and crumbling walls. I was instantly struck by the magnitude of what the new owner was up against. “It feels like I was slowly building the muscle and aptitude to be ready for a project like Pickard,” says Gates, a ceramicist, sculptor and art world heavyweight who is best known for transforming sections of his South Side Chicago neighborhood by buying up abandoned buildings and deftly turning them into inspired spaces of community, art and learning. “It’s like I’ve been preparing for a decathlon for 20 years.” Gates was formerly professor at the University of Chicago and an urban planner, but when his star began to rise in the art world he used his earnings to become something of a real estate Robin Hood, scooping up old buildings, businesses and archives on the brink of extinction. In 2013, he purchased the Stony Island Bank for $1 from the city of Chicago, transforming the derelict 113-year-old neoclassical behemoth into a thriving cultural center that includes a cinema screening Black films, the personal vinyl collection of the pioneering DJ Frankie Knuckles, the full archive of Ebony and Jet magazines and a Korean-inspired tea salon. Just last year, Gates opened the doors to The Land School , a 40,000 sq ft former parochial elementary school that, following his $14m reimagining, now serves as a center for experimentation in art, music and community engagement. But Gates admits that this latest acquisition is on a completely different scale. While his other projects have been bought, renovated and run by his arts non-profit, the Rebuild Foundation, his purchase of Pickard marks the first time Gates is taking over a floundering business and hoping to make it profitable.
