title: Weird lifestyle advice from Gwyneth Paltrow: best podcasts of the week
text: The second podcast from her wellness empire is ostensibly centred on Paltrow’s incredibly niche lifestyle advice: where to eat the “best cacio e pepe in Rome”, for example, or “whether it’s weird to use an obsidian gua sha tool on a plane”. In reality, the show is a weekly cosy chat with a showbiz pal (first up, Zoe Saldaña) peppered with a few practical tips – such as how to eat enough protein if you can’t face any more eggs. Rachel Aroesti Widely available, episodes weekly Boys and their (literal) toys: this new series sees SNL alumni Bobby Moynihan, Aristotle Athari and Taran Killam get together to geek out over their favourite collectible items. From the action figures they loved as kids to the memorabilia they splurge on today, they banter about nostalgia, celebrity etiquette and the psychology of their mutual hobby along the way. RA Widely available, episodes weekly Kwajo Tweneboa is an excellent housing campaigner and he is equally passionate and thoughtful as host of his first podcast . He has weekly guests from Bridgerton’s Adjoa Andoh to housing secretary Angela Rayner, and gets straight into chats about their backgrounds and overcoming adversity. Hollie Richardson Widely available, episodes weekly This new look at the issues shaping children today starts with a modern classic: how to protect kids from social media without cutting them off from their friends. It’s hosted by Dr Oscar Duke – the resident GP on BBC One’s Morning Live – who leads experts in an interesting, personable roundtable talk. Alexi Duggins Widely available, episodes weekly Get our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every Friday “I couldn’t even remember what she was like, because the darkness envelops you as well.” So opens this highly personal take on dementia , in which former PM David Cameron reflects on the loss of his mother, as well as delving into the science and looking at the future of its treatment. Given the host, it’s a surprisingly affecting, absorbing look at a looming “quiet crisis”. AD Widely available, episodes weekly What have you been listening to this week? Share your top tips below …

title: ‘The numbers are very stark’: This primary school is the heart of a Welsh village. Can it be saved?
text: T he kitchen in the Alman family farmhouse is large, airy and decorated with hundreds of rosettes awarded over the decades for prize-winning dogs, sheep and cows. I grew up just up the hill, so I know this kitchen well. Apart from the video feed in the corner, showing what the cattle are up to in the barn, it hasn’t changed much since the 1980s when we’d pile in here after helping our fathers with the baling. From the kitchen, Gladestry’s small, slate-roofed primary school, set against the steep green slope of Hergest Ridge, is clearly visible, and – it being playtime when I visited – clearly audible too. That hasn’t changed much either since the days when Joseph Alman and I were pupils at that tiny school, and our own parents looked out of that same window and heard us calling to each other as we played football. “It’s so lovely to hear them,” said Alman, whose son is in year 5. “I used to hear them before Charlie was in there, and now I go out there and I know he’s one of them, and it’s really nice to see him playing. I’ll drive by there, and there’ll be a couple of footballs that have gone over the fence and rolled to the verge. They try to flag someone down to throw back the ball so the game’s back on. It’s the heartbeat of the village, you know.” Gladestry is home to 400 people and sits (just) on the Welsh side of the border with England. Indeed, if you’ve ever walked the Offa’s Dyke footpath that runs, more or less, along that border, you’ll have passed right through the small cluster of buildings that mark its centre. The school has been educating Almans since Joseph’s grandfather and great-uncle arrived in 1917, but Charlie could be the last. In June, just before the start of the summer holidays, Powys county council announced that it wanted to close the school. “It all seemed to come as a bit of a bolt out of blue,” said Alman. “We didn’t know nothing about it.” It was, however, just the latest episode in a slow-motion erosion of the foundations of life in mid-Wales, which is caused by generations of politicians failing to engage with an important question: how do you provide adequate services to a sparsely populated place if you’re not willing to spend more money? In other words, how do you solve a problem like Powys? P owys was once a kingdom, from which Britain’s native population resisted the remorseless westwards expansion of the Anglo-Saxons for half a millennium or more. The kingdom disappeared in the 13th century, when the English conquered the last independent Britons, but seven centuries later – in 1974 to be precise – its name was dredged out of obscurity. (The word itself derives from pagus , the Latin word for countryside.) At the time, the government in London was trying to rationalise local administration by combining smaller units into larger ones that were better able to meet the needs of their populations. The result was new inventions such as Greater Manchester, Avon, Humberside and Mid Glamorgan. A basic principle of the reform was that local authority areas needed at least 250,000 people to be viable. And this is where mid-Wales ran into trouble. The existing counties of Breconshire, Radnorshire and Montgomeryshire were clearly too tiny to justify their continued administrative existence. Even combined into a single entity called Powys, however, the population was less than half the supposed minimum. “There are more sheepdog exemption licences than there are members of the population,” one peer said when the House of Lords debated the reform in 1972. “Powys, as we all recognise, is a county with too few people and too few resources,” said another. There was no easy answer. The new county already covered 5,200 sq km (2,000 sq miles), and combining it with yet more parts of Wales risked creating something too unwieldy to be manageable. Merging it with anywhere in England was clearly unacceptable, so Powys was left as a vast underpopulated exception – its population density lower than any part of Bri

title: Nothing but highlights: is Power Slap the sport we deserve?
text: I n the days before Power Slap 22, in Belgrade, Serbia, in late July, the organisers of the world’s newest combat sport were taking no chances. At the Crowne Plaza hotel, where competitors were booked to stay, those facing off had been separated by floor, lest any unauthorised violence took place. It turned out there was little need. The night before the main event, contestants mingled amiably in the lobby and bar. The atmosphere was more specialist sales conference than brewing barroom brawl. In the lobby, I joined Louis “Razor” Robinson, and Ryan “the Punisher” Kenny. “We’re all friends in slap,” Robinson said, earnestly, by way of a greeting. Robinson, a Brit from Stalybridge, Greater Manchester, is 30, stout, intense. Kenny, a Canadian, is 34, lofty, laid back. The two had become fast friends since they met at Power Slap 17, which took place last October in Saudi Arabia. They host a podcast together, called The Slappy Hour (sample chat: “I had questions for his chin … but the chin question’s gone”). “As the sport’s so new, it’s great to have someone to bounce ideas off,” said Robinson. It’s not uncommon for competitors to destroy each other on stage, then later compare notes. When I spoke to Damien “the Bell” Dibbell, an affable 24-year-old American heavyweight whom many consider the greatest slap-fighter alive, he mentioned that he met his best friend, Duane “the Iron Giant” Crespo, after knocking him unconscious in the second round. In the Crowne Plaza, conversation veered from recent rule changes – beards were now limited to a few millimetres, much glorious facial hair had been lost – to a controversial incident in Power Slap 21 when Anthony “Kiing” DeFrank had refused to alter his stance after being accused of “turtling”, breaking the rules by tucking his chin flush into his neck to receive the slap. Despite his protests, he was disqualified. Word was he’d never slap again. Seen from a certain perspective, Power Slap is less a sport in its own right than one whittled down from other sports: think football reduced to penalties or rugby with just conversions. Like boxing, it is a combat sport, separated by gender and weight divisions (from flyweight to super-heavyweight). Unlike boxing, competitors are forbidden from dodging or blocking the blows. Like darts, Power Slap is turn-based. Unlike darts, contestants effectively take turns at being the board. The rules are straightforward. Competitors stand either side of a central podium. In each round, they are permitted to strike their opponent – open-handed, ungloved, cheek only – a single time. After one minute of recovery time, they must allow themselves to be struck back. Bouts range between three and five rounds. Victory can be earned on points – the three judges look for clean technique and the impact a strike makes – but about half are won via knockout. The podium is padded, as the competitors sometimes collide with it on the way down. Behind each competitor stand two catchers to grab them as they fall. When Power Slap introduced a super-heavyweight division, where contestants can weigh the same as an upright piano, they hired professional strongmen for the job. This is a sport precision-made for our moment. It is designed to be viewed on TikTok and YouTube Shorts and Instagram Reels, one thumb-swipe at a time. Power Slap’s CEO, Frank Lamicella, a former corporate lawyer from New York, will happily admit it was created with short attention spans in mind. The only real buildup comes in the contestants’ walk to the stage and the brief seconds they spend rehearsing their slap before striking, like snooker players feathering a cue. A round lasts a couple of minutes; titles can be decided in seconds. As every action is a potential knockout, the highlights come pre-packaged. It is nothing but highlights. Since its launch in November 2022, Power Slap has gained 4 million YouTube subscribers. On TikTok it has more than 9 million. Perhaps even more importantly – though admitte

title: ‘Nothing they said made sense’: down the rabbit hole with Britain’s sovereign citizens
text: I n the early morning of 20 June 2023, 13 police officers raided a five-bed barn conversion in rural Hampshire. The occupant, a 57-year-old man named Iain Clifford Stamp, was rudely awoken. The police informed him that they were executing a warrant on behalf of the Financial Conduct Authority, the body that regulates financial services in the UK. FCA raids are rare. They are only permitted when the regulator can persuade a judge that there are reasonable grounds for believing the person or firm that they are investigating will not cooperate . In this case, it seems, there was good reason to believe that Iain Clifford Stamp might cause trouble. Stamp’s frosty relationship with financial authorities dated back to 2008, when his first company, a financial product provider called Integrity, imploded and was left facing claims from clients of up to an estimated £80m . Back then, Integrity had been publicly censured by the Financial Services Authority for not fairly communicating to customers the risks in the products it was selling. This time was more serious. Stamp was arrested for suspected breaches of the Financial Services and Markets Act: the FCA believed it had evidence he was offering financial services, such as debt and investment advice, without a licence. The day he was arrested, police also raided an industrial estate in Chessington, south-west London, where Stamp’s company had its offices, and seized dozens of computers and files. The company, Matrix Freedom, offered its “members” a simple and attractive prospect: freedom from debt. For fees of up to £8,000, it would sell them a set of instructions that would supposedly allow them to reclaim mortgage payments, write off tax bills and cancel fines. Customers were taught how to file legal claims in arcane language that referenced ancient law. One email from Matrix claimed their process for getting mortgages “discharged” had a “100% track record”. As strange as this may sound, what Matrix Freedom was doing overlaps with a worldview that is growing in influence, from the US and Canada to Australia, New Zealand and the UK. Adherents to this worldview call themselves sovereign citizens. Sovereign citizens – who, in Britain, often call themselves “freemen on the land” – have a variety of beliefs, but their central idea is that the state’s claim to authority over its citizens – its capacity to fine us, to force us to pay debts, to jail us – is much more limited than people realise. For those armed with specialist knowledge, the thinking goes, the power of the state and large corporations can be overcome. “The strange thing about sovereign citizens is that they don’t reject the idea of law,” says Harry Hobbs, the co-author of Outlawed, a new book on the global spread of sovereign ideology. “They believe in it too much. They think the law contains hidden powers. And, if properly understood, those powers can make governments and corporations answer to them.” Behind this philosophy lie even more bizarre precepts. Sovereign citizens believe that every person is, in fact, two distinct entities. There is the real, flesh-and-blood person and then there is a legal fiction, a “strawman” that is created by the state. When the state issues an arrest warrant or a fine, it is targeting the strawman, meaning there is legal room for the real person to slip away. Sovereign citizens are obsessed with the idea of consent. The basis of state power, they believe, is a series of unspoken contracts between the individual and state in which silence means consent. By explicitly refusing that consent, sovereign citizens believe they can free themselves from its authority. Stamp does not describe himself as a sovereign citizen, but that is not unusual for figures in this world. Listen to what he says and the affinities with the ideology become clear. As he was being arrested in 2023, he was offered the services of a lawyer. He immediately declined that offer because, he claimed, it would “give away” his

title: Alien menace or victim of xenophobia? The battle over Britain’s parakeets
text: B efore we saw a single parakeet, we heard them: a disembodied static that grew louder as we approached Hither Green cemetery in south-east London . It was an early evening in late June, and we had come to witness an invasion. By the time my friend and I reached the cemetery’s western edge, the clamour was all-encompassing. We hopped the fence and picked our way through the gravestones. Above us now were the birds themselves, their kryptonite-green plumage, scab-red beaks, pearly black collars and trailing tail feathers unmistakable: Psittacula krameri , the ring-necked parakeet. Hither Green cemetery hosts one of the city’s largest roosts. Every day at dusk, a sizeable chunk of London’s feral parakeet population returns here, to a specific line of poplars. They like to spend the night in the company of their own kind. We watched them come first in ones and twos, and then in larger chirrupping squadrons. Hundreds of them, and then thousands. At maximum capacity, the trees fizzed. Here was a pandemonium, a parakeet concourse. It gave the impression of community, greeting and conversation. “This,” my friend said, “would make a great cheap first date.” These birds are not from around here. For the past half century or so, the ring-necked parakeet, an arrival from Asia, has been making itself at home in Britain. In that time the population has become genetically distinct from its forebears, an admixture of two subspecies: P k borealis , whose native range spans Pakistan, northern India and Nepal, and east into Bangladesh and Myanmar; and P k manillensis , from southern India and Sri Lanka. Of the two, the boreal is the dominant stock, which might help explain why the birds have taken so well to Britain’s cooler, wetter climate. They are not, as their colour suggests, a tropical species, but creatures of the Himalayan foothills. Most immediately, they are noisy and they are green. Even after seeing these parakeets all my life, the sheer scale of this gathering in an old, oaky English field still felt like encountering a glitch. Thousands upon thousands of bright-green parrots hanging out in drowsy suburban London, a phenomenon every bit as awesome as a salmon run or a migrating swarm of monarch butterflies. For a metropolitan experience of nonhuman life, it is difficult to think of a more impressive display. As dusk accelerated, the roost began to quiet, and then, in a single moment decided upon only by the parakeets, it fell silent. The day was flown. Time for bed. My friend and I looked at each other, as if released from a vision. We saw for the first time how the ground had been befouled by their presence. The gravestones, trees and lawn speckled white with uric paste and cottony down. For all their splendour, the parakeets are a bit of a scandal. Politicians, conservation bodies, land management and the public have all begun to ask: do we want tens of thousands of Himalayan parrots squabbling all over our cities? Across their native range, they are known as a pest. European studies suggest the parakeets have negative impacts on various native bird and bat populations. We know they are a vector for Newcastle disease, a viral ailment that primarily affects poultry, and for Cryptosporidium , a parasite with more general tastes whose characteristic symptom in humans is violent diarrhoea. Though plans for a government cull were allegedly considered in 2021, they were abandoned due to potential expense and general impracticality. So parakeet numbers keep climbing and their range keeps expanding. An Oxford researcher estimated in 2003 that the Greater London population was growing so rapidly that it would need to be cut by 30% each year just to keep it stable. A 2014 headline in the Northern Echo – “Who’s a chilly boy, then?” – announced their arrival in Scotland. Glasgow is now home to the world’s most northerly wild parrots . Maybe officialdom doesn’t have the stomach for mandated eradication. Maybe its administrative talents are be

title: What’s the most sustainable way to eat fish? Forget it. There isn’t one | George Monbiot
text: D rumroll please. I am about to unveil the species of fish that’s best to eat if you want to protect the living seas. Ta-dah! It’s … I hope that clears things up. Unfortunately, over the past few years, a noisy industry has developed to tell you otherwise. You’re doing the planet a favour if you eat mackerel , sorry, cod, I mean haddock, no coley, make that pollack – oh, whoops! These choices might make you feel better about yourself. But they do nothing but harm to marine wildlife. The fish you should choose is none of the above. Cause, could I introduce you to effect? In April, the Marine Conservation Society, through its Good Fish Guide, suggested you stop eating cod and eat hake instead . Six months later, it lamented that hake is now overexploited thanks to “increased fishing pressure” , and downgraded its sustainability ratings. How on earth did that happen? Beats me. The society now gives bluefin tuna caught in the UK a green rating , which means the “most sustainable seafood option”: let the killing continue. Yet, as the government told me last year , “there are no estimates of the number of bluefin tuna in UK waters”. As a leading marine conservation charity notes , “it’s not yet clear if populations have reached sustainable levels that can withstand increases in commercial fishing pressure”. Which charity? Ah yes, the Marine Conservation Society. We also know that very large animals are especially vulnerable to population collapse and extinction . How did a “conservation” charity end up advising us to eat marine megafauna? What next? Eco-friendly whale meat? Another group, the Marine Stewardship Council, slaps its happy fish logo on your packet of fish fingers, and you feel like a good person, which doubtless you’re trying to be. A little while later, you discover that your fish-friendly fish turns out, astonishingly, to be unfriendly to fish . Who knew? Earlier this month, the council recertified Antarctic krill as sustainable, despite the fact that, once again, we know far too little about the likely impact of the industry, while the major fishers refuse to make fundamental concessions to lessen that impact. Krill underpin the entire Southern Ocean ecosystem, feeding the great whales whose numbers had at last begun to recover, as well as seals, penguins and other seabirds. The giant fishing ships operate among the major whale pods, and compete directly with them for prey. A fishery that could take down everything gets the blue tick of approval. Macmillan Cancer Support doesn’t certify lung-friendly cigarette smoking. Age UK doesn’t advocate slaughtering elderly people. Why do our conservation and animal welfare groups (the RSPCA with its “assured” labels on slaughtered livestock is another astonishing example ) so often side with the killers against the creatures they were founded to defend? In the 19th century, the fishing industry claimed that ploughing the seabed made it more productive. Now we know that the seabed in many places was once as rich and complex and multi-storied as a rainforest, and that dragging trawl nets or scallop dredges across it, as has happened almost everywhere, smashes this delicate system, which can take centuries to recover. But it’s as if the old myth persists. Perhaps this is why bottom trawlers are still allowed into marine protected areas, and why Greenpeace is left to do the job of the government, by dropping boulders on the seabed to try to stop them. But guess what? Fish caught in these “protected” places get the same sustainability rankings as fish caught outside them. There are plenty of organisations trying to reconcile marine protection with the demands of the fishing industry. But where are the major groups campaigning for an end to commercial fishing? It’s never going to be good for the ecosystem, however it’s done, just as tobacco is never going to be good for your health. And surely, whatever we’re seeking to achieve, we should bargain high? title: Still racist, misogynistic and homophobic. I’m putting Britain’s biggest police force on notice – we won’t tolerate this | Sadiq Khan
text: I n March 2023, Baroness Louise Casey published her damning review into the Metropolitan police. The review – which I commissioned after a series of appalling scandals – called for systemic reform to a failing organisation unable to tackle the profound problems it faced. But yesterday’s independent follow-up report by Dr Gillian Fairfield shows that, while the Met has made some important improvements, nowhere near enough has been done. I agree. Fairfield’s report concludes that the Met remains institutionally racist, sexist and homophobic. This will be acutely concerning for communities across the capital. So, too, will evidence of the Met’s failure to treat many victims of crime with care and compassion at the very moments they need it most. Londoners expect change – and so do many of the hardworking officers and staff who, faced with organisational failures, find themselves unable to do the job they joined the force to do. There must be no cherrypicking or spin with this report – and the commissioner and his team must respond with humility and reflection, not hubris. The fact is, it is simply not possible to change the culture of the Met if the existence of institutional racism, sexism and homophobia continues to be denied, underplayed or tiptoed around. The commissioner and his team must move much further and faster to proactively embed a positive new culture that recognises and promotes the highest standards, prevents misconduct and prioritises inclusivity and wellbeing, enabling them to attract and retain the very best officers and staff. The drive for reform must also reach the sealed-off spaces where change has been resisted and prejudice has too often been left to fester in the past – from toxic group chats to specialist teams working away from the public eye. There can be nowhere to hide for officers who fail to meet the standards expected of them – and top-to-bottom cultural change must include every custody suite and corner of the organisation. The Met must also change its attitude towards scrutiny. We have already taken some significant steps to improve accountability, including the creation of the London policing board and the appointment of the capital’s first independent victims commissioner. But too often we have been met with defensiveness where there should have been openness. The Met must recognise that operational independence is not the same as independence from constructive challenge, and I am looking at how public oversight can be strengthened further. Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more I now expect thecommissioner and his team to reset their relationship with those of us tasked with holding the Met to account. Recommendations made by successive independent victims commissioners, which have too often been ignored by the Met, must also be urgently looked at again and actioned. The history of law enforcement in Britain is long and complex, but there is one idea which threads through it all: “policing by consent”. The authority of our police officers does not derive from sheer force. Instead, it stems from their ability to gain and retain the trust of the public. When it comes to cutting crime, we have made impressive progress. In 2025, London’s per capita homicide rate fell to its lowest level on record. Neighbourhood crime is falling across the capital and mobile phone theft is down significantly year-on-year. The Met’s V100 programme has seen the conviction of more than 200 of London’s worst perpetrators of violence against women and girls, and in the two years to October, the force reports that it has doubled its positive outcomes – including arrests and charges – for rape. But the fact remains that successful policing depends on public confidence. The Met must prove to all the capital’s communities, particularly those who it has failed in the past, and is still failing, that it has their best interests at heart. And it must prove it will tre

title: Men have used wealth and fame to get away with abuse. No longer | Andy Burnham
text: P owerful men using their fame and money to silence anyone who calls out their behaviour. Victims treated as though they’re the ones who’ve done something wrong. And a culture where abuse can hide in plain sight because people in positions of power think they can get away with it. That’s what we’ve seen in the past few weeks. This must be a watershed moment. Not just for the culture of the entertainment industry but for us as a nation. Things have improved in the past decade or so, but we are still far from being where we need to be for women and girls to feel safe and be safe. Sadly, many women and girls will find the recent stories all too close to home, whether it’s casual disrespect in the workplace, undermining “jokes”, or being told they are somehow at fault for something that has happened to them. Too often, the powerful have been protected and the vulnerable exploited. When women report assault, too often they are treated as though they are the ones on trial. And our culture has too often put men’s interests ahead of women’s welfare. This needs to stop. We need to get to a place where women and girls feel confident that if they report a crime, they will be treated with dignity and compassion and action will be taken. In his sentencing remarks, the judge in Russell Brand’s case said: “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts.” I was struck that that still needs to be said, but clearly it does. People still ask what someone was wearing, whether they fought back or if they reported what happened immediately. Let’s be clear. No one “asks for it” or deserves to be assaulted – ever. We know people react differently to traumatic events. And we know people are often reluctant to come forward because these accusations and stereotypes put the shame on women rather than on the perpetrator where it belongs. That culture of silence extends to the misuse of NDAs. NDAs should protect sensitive business information or commercial interests. They should not protect powerful men who have abused, harassed or discriminated against women. So, we’re changing how they work. From January, NDAs will no longer gag employees who have suffered harassment or discrimination. And victims of crime will be able to tell their story to whoever they choose – whether that’s the police, family, friends, victim services or the media. No exceptions. No loopholes for lawyers to exploit. But I will keep working to make sure NDAs can’t be used to silence others, including freelance employees and fans who experience abuse, while still keeping victims’ identities protected if that is what they want. On International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women and Girls, and the start of 16 Days of Activism , this is about rebalancing the scales of power away from perpetrators and towards victims. We are also considering what more we can do to protect victims. This includes actively looking at whether or not we should change the law to stagger the age of consent. This is a complex issue with different views, so we are inviting parents, young people, victim support services and the wider public to come forward to share their experiences and inform the process. We’ll only stop the violence when we end the silence. It’s time for us all to speak up.

title: AI's shock-and-awe raid on maths looks like pride before a fall | Rafael Behr
text: I n most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven. That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week . Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof. I don’t pretend to understand much of what Bernhard Riemann proposed in 1859. I know it relates to primes – whole integers greater than 1 that are divisible only by 1 and themselves – and the pattern of their distribution along the infinite number line. But you don’t need to know what a zeta function is to recognise that the solution to a near-170-year-old problem is a big deal in maths, or that the role of AI in completing the quest is a big deal for humanity. Around two years ago, large language models that mesmerised users with their verbal dexterity sucked at maths. They made basic arithmetic errors. Now they resolve unfathomably hard problems with ease. In Alpöge’s breathless account of the process, Claude “flew, and danced, and sparkled” towards its conclusion. It left him “in awe”. Other mathematicians whose discipline is being eaten by machines report more complex feelings . In October, OpenAI published hundreds of AI-generated papers containing proofs to unsolved problems, stunning faculties that had been toiling over the relevant questions for years. Some called it the “mathocalypse”. There is still a long process of verification to run. Humans have to check that the machines haven’t taken rogue shortcuts, but early indications back the AI. Researchers are witnessing intricate edifices of abstract cognition, their life’s work, crushed under silicon bulldozers. Many are upset, angry. Some are excited by the future possibilities, some more sceptical or feeling a combination of emotions that an LLM can describe and imitate but not, as far as we know, experience. Mathematicians are not the first people to worry that a rising technological tide will wash away their livelihood. But their position is unusual in ways that go beyond the conventional fear of obsolescence. Maths describes fundamental laws of the universe. Nothing is truer than a mathematically proven truth. The limit of what advanced mathematicians know delineates the frontier of human knowledge – or it has done until now. The soaring rate of computational capability raises the prospect of machines exploring dimensions that humans cannot comprehend, generating proofs that have to be taken on trust. What kind of knowledge even is it if no organic mind knows how it came to be known? In the past, when great mysteries have been solved, the method has been as thrilling as the result. Andrew Wiles cracked Fermat’s Last Theorem by building bridges between previously disconnected realms of maths, opening new vistas of theoretical space for further exploration. It was an arduous ascent to higher truth. AI-generated proofs are windowless lifts that hoist you to the summit with little sense of how you got there. They are also weird, according to people who can decrypt them. Hannah Fry, Cambridge maths professor, broadcaster, author and one of the world’s best communicators of hard concepts to a lay audience, called one of the recent OpenAI proofs “almost hilariously ugly”. That might sound like a marginal quibble if the underlying logic is sound, but the aesthetic of an answer is not a minor consideration in maths. The human mind is gratified by the elegance of a solution. It is hard to celebrate an insight extracted by tens of thousands of AI agents torturing equations day and night, burning tens of millions of dollars of computing power, just so a tech company with an eye on its prospective stock market valuation can say it got to the answer

title: What do Brexit and an Australian cricket scandal have in common? Sometimes it’s right to reopen old wounds | Jonathan Liew
text: Just move on. You lost, get on with it. Why rake up the past? And why, for the love of all that is holy, is Theresa May back on my television? Of all the many regrettable political figures to have surfaced over recent days, perhaps May has been most triggering of all: a bleak reminder of unhappier times. But of course she has been far from the only former prime minister lured from obscurity by the irresistible siren call of Brexit Revisited. David Cameron has been portending a “very long and painful argument”. “Divisive” and “all-consuming”, argued Rishi Sunak. Boris Johnson warned Andy Burnham – with no apparent sense of irony – that reopening the Brexit negotiations would be “wasting his premiership”. Here they come, the cast of the Tory remake of Avengers: Doomsday, presaging of rancour and paralysis from the people who brought us years of rancour and paralysis. Of course, Brexit fatigue is real. And so for years the idea that Brexit was a stone tablet, fixed and immutable, something that needed to be moved on from rather than renegotiated, felt like a kind of unchallengeable dogma, perhaps even an act of self-care after the years of endless traumas and defeats. But the original sin never died, however deep it was interred, however many fresh governments and catchy three-word slogans (“Brexit means Brexit”; “get Brexit done”; “make Brexit work”, “Brexit me harder”) were layered upon it. Instead it lay dormant and undead. In this respect it was not unlike another scandal currently taking on a second life, albeit many thousands of miles away and on a much smaller scale. Perhaps you vaguely remember the Australian cricket ball-tampering scandal of 2018. Perhaps you’re wondering why it’s back, given that punishments were handed out and blame neatly apportioned at the time. But there is, of course, a universal lesson here: if a status quo is built on a foundation of lies and unfairness, it is not really a status quo at all. Sooner or later, the debt must be repaid. And when the time comes, “don’t reopen old wounds” is no kind of defence. Eight years ago, the Australian men’s cricket team were caught on camera blatantly cheating during a Test match in South Africa by rubbing sandpaper on the ball. Fury was focused on three players: the captain, Steve Smith, who allowed the plot to unfold; the vice-captain, David Warner, who devised it; and the junior batter, Cameron Bancroft, who actually administered the sandpaper, all of whom were banned for between nine months and a year. Everyone else got away with the consequences, even though anyone with even the most rudimentary knowledge of cricket will be aware that such conspiracies are generally enacted by teams, not individuals. No matter. Australian cricket moved on. Australian cricket got on with it. The fast bowlers who benefited from the tampered ball are now some of the greats of the game, and one of them – Pat Cummins – is now the captain. And so when the former batter Usman Khawaja published a book this month testifying that everyone in the team was aware of the sandpaper plot – a revelation since backed up by multiple witnesses – an array of players and ex-players instantly mobilised to not just deny the charges, but condemn Khawaja for bringing it up again. Cummins called an extraordinary 68-minute press conference to flatly deny any knowledge of any plot, and instead accusing Khawaja of being “casual” with his reputation. It was toxic, they said. It was divisive. It was raking over the past. Above all, it was a gross inconvenience to the people who appear to really matter: namely Cummins and the governing body, Cricket Australia, which seems to have botched the original investigation in its haste to draw a line under the entire sorry episode. And yet, as a result of Khawaja’s book, through an adversarial and often messy process, Australian cricket is a little closer to correcting the record, addressing the deceit of the past. Cricket Australia has stopped short of reopening

title: You Can See Everything in Elizabeth Holmes’s unblinking eyes. Or can you? | Jason Okundaye
text: E lizabeth Holmes doesn’t believe that she’s ever told a lie. She “knows” that she hasn’t committed any crime. And she has no reason to deceive you. While speaking, she is gazing at her interviewer, Nathan Fielder, with those enormous, blue, vacant, unsettling, unblinking eyes. She doesn’t break eye contact. This is You Can See Everything, Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary, which, at her invitation, follows Holmes and her husband, Billy Evans, at their home in San Diego in the weeks up to her surrender to custody at federal prison. Holmes is the disgraced tech ex-billionaire whose startup Theranos claimed the ability to run hundreds of comprehensive blood tests from a single pinprick of blood. This false claim posed “immediate jeopardy” to the health of thousands of patients and defrauded investors of more than $700m. What the film promises is what it says: that you can see everything, because the couple have nothing to hide. Unprecedented access is given to their lives: the cameras come in, and they don’t leave. You can see them discussing plans for a Theranos 2.0, you can see Billy’s penis in the shower, Elizabeth, or “Liz”, breastfeeding. You can see that Liz doesn’t whisk eggs vigorously enough for Billy’s liking. You can, following their logic, see that Holmes is innocent. You Can See Everything has become a phenomenon, surpassing $100m globally since its release in the US last month, and breaking the record for the biggest opening weekend for a non-music documentary in the UK since opening here last Friday. But why does Holmes’s story remain such a draw, 11 years on from Wall Street Journal reporter John Carreyro’s exposé? Fraudsters fascinate, of course. Anna Delvey posing as a wealthy German heiress; “the Monster of Wall Street” Bernie Madoff’s decades-long Ponzi scheme; the Tinder Swindler . Yet beyond the thrill and dreadful amazement, there is another pull: the question: “Could you detect a fraudster?” And if reality is broken down and blurred right in front of you, would you have the mental fortitude to withstand such an orchestrated illusion in real time? While watching the film, you ask whether Holmes is manipulating us, or being manipulated herself? Or does the answer lie somewhere in between? Did she genuinely believe in Theranos or did she know all along that it was bunk? Is she really just that good at deceiving people? You Can See Everything asks whether you can ever know where someone’s performance begins and ends. That is what the cameras go in to find, but thanks to the limits on what can be recorded, a documentary premised on observation and seeking truth is forced to rely on the techniques of fiction: performance, reenactment and selective disclosures. After Holmes is shown being sent to prison, the actor Amanda Seyfried, whose portrayal of Holmes in the 2022 series The Dropout earned her an Emmy, enters the frame – literally walking into Holmes’s home and making porridge on her stove in a reenactment. There’s an unsettled dispute around a New York Times interview in which Holmes, in reference to The Dropout, is quoted as saying: “They’re not playing me. They’re playing a character I created.” Holmes claims she said “a character they created”. But in the documentary she seems to have dropped certain memorable elements of her previous public persona: the baritone voice, the Steve Jobs-apeing turtlenecks, the private headbanging to hip-hop music. The home Holmes invites the film-makers into is so devoid of character or lived-inness that it may as well be a film set. So if Elizabeth Holmes is a performance then who, or what, are we watching in You Can See Everything? That is why we are so fascinated by Holmes’s eyes. The film-makers know this; a single eye is the centrepiece of the film’s poster. Even while overwhelmed by the scale of Holmes’s deception, it’s her piercing eyes that Seyfried is most invested in imitating. But what can we ever really learn from looking into a person’s eyes? Pop-psych

title: Why the genocide verdict against Myanmar has big implications for Israel | Geoffrey Robertson
text: F or the first time ever, a state has been found guilty of genocide – that “crime of crimes” – and has been ordered to compensate victims and to prosecute and punish the perpetrators. This judgment came from the international court of justice (ICJ), which has convicted Myanmar of killing and expelling many thousands of Rohingyas in Rakhine state in 2017 . The court did not change the definition of the crime, settled by the genocide convention in 1948 as requiring proof of an intention to destroy, in whole or part, a racial or religious group as such. But it made the prospect of proving this against a nation a good deal easier than against an individual. It set a precedent for its next case concerning state liability, namely the case brought by South Africa against Israel . Genocide is notoriously difficult to prove: If Benjamin Netanyahu were prosecuted, it would be hard for the prosecution to show that he had the necessary specific intent to kill Palestinians “as such” (the term used in international law) given his frequently proclaimed intention to liquidate Hamas as a political organisation. This distinction may be legalistic, but it stems from the definition of the crime. Hence Pol Pot’s henchpeople could not be prosecuted for genocide for killing about 1.7 million Cambodian citizens, because of their crazed political intention to return the country to “year zero”. This might be termed “politicide” but that is not a crime under international law. The distinction was the basis of Myanmar’s defence that its intention was to conduct counterinsurgency operations to clear out terrorists. But the court examined the history of the conflict and conducted its own investigation, which established the racial and religious roots of the massacres. The intention of an individual defendant may be difficult to fathom, but to discern the “mind” of a state the court must draw inferences from a much wider set of facts, including the historical context of the atrocities and the previous behaviour of the government – for example, whether it has introduced apartheid-type laws oppressing or discriminating against the targeted group and whether its ministers have used hate speech against the group. Israel is vulnerable on these grounds. Although the court insisted that the burden of proof required the evidence against the state to be “fully conclusive” (ie beyond reasonable doubt), the means of establishing liability will be inferential rather than direct. As one influential judge, Prof Hilary Charlesworth, put it, the true test of state liability is whether genocide is the only reasonable inference to be drawn from the evidence as a whole. The evidence against Israel includes the destruction of 90% of Gaza’s infrastructure and about 75,000 deaths so far (compared with an estimated 10,000 deaths in Rakhine state and about 43,000 in the blitz). This disproportionality alone means that Israel will have a case to answer. Israel may also be discomforted by the way the ICJ examined and interpreted the actual atrocities in Myanmar. In order to assist the inference of genocide, it focused on the killing of children – usually an indication of an intention to stop the propagation of part of a race. It drew attention to sexual violence for the same reason and to the shooting of soldiers as they were running away or after their capture. This showed that they were not simply engaged in a “clearance operation”. Importantly, the court made the point that state actions may have a number of purposes – if racial or religious hatred is among them, it may be arraigned for genocide. The further advantage of indicting a state is that it may be ordered, as Myanmar was, to provide compensation, to pay for rebuilding and to allow the return of those of the targeted group who have fled. The government can be ordered to prosecute those of its politicians or army commanders who personally directed the genocidal attacks. This is important because individual defendants, by t

title: The Ukraine-Russia war is escalating – and it will go global unless Europe speaks with one voice | Simon Tisdall
text: U kraine’s spectacularly successful weekend drone attack on a spanking new Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi, more than 1,300 miles (2,200km) from Kyiv, is further proof, if it were needed, that the catastrophic full-scale war Vladimir Putin launched in 2022 is escalating and spreading uncontrollably. The sinking follows a similar incident in the Baltic last week, which crippled a Russian cargo ship, and previous Ukrainian attacks on oil tankers and Russian navy ships and bases in the Black Sea region. Last week, Russia was blamed for a missile and drone strike on Nato member Poland , which Donald Tusk, the Polish prime minister, claimed was intentional, and for deliberately targeting western diplomatic compounds in Kyiv. While Moscow’s murderous winter bombing of Ukrainian civilians and energy infrastructure continues apace, provocative and disruptive Russian hybrid warfare operations across all of Europe, including sabotage, arson and cyber-attacks, are becoming daily occurrences. After almost five years of continual fighting, the Ukraine war has become deadeningly familiar to those looking on from the outside who, unlike tens of thousands of Ukrainian citizens and more than 400,000 hapless Russian soldiers , are not already dead. The lamentable failure of numerous, mostly half-hearted, half-baked US efforts to negotiate a peaceful way out of the morass is no longer news. Partly because it’s so difficult and so protracted, ending the war somehow appears to many Europeans and Americans to have become less urgent, even less of a priority. That’s a dangerous mistake. The huge human, economic and geopolitical damage it has already done is nothing as to what could follow if the conflict goes truly global . This latest, alarming string of attacks from the Mediterranean to eastern Europe to the high north must finally vanquish an enervating, collective western complacency that simultaneously condemns Russian aggression, and pledges increased financial and materiel support for Kyiv, while in effect tolerating the continuation, intensification and widening of what could become an existential conflict for all concerned. European leaders say they are fully awake to the hazards. Meeting in Berlin last week, the western, pro-Ukraine “coalition of the willing” declared it was ready for direct talks with the Kremlin and was even prepared to discuss Europe’s wider post-Soviet security architecture – Putin’s longstanding, contentious demand. “Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position,” Andy Burnham said. But that’s not the whole story. Agreement the war should end immediately is hardly the same as taking concrete steps to make it happen. The EU – principally represented in this instance by France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, plus the leaders of Italy and Poland – has even struggled to agree with the European Commission who should be lead negotiator. Logically, it should by Kaja Kallas, the EU’s hawkish foreign policy chief. Russia claims her appointment would collapse any future talks . As ever, Europe, acting in close coordination with Kyiv, needs to speak with one voice on Ukraine; and the Kremlin cannot be allowed a veto on who does the talking if, as is proposed, a European delegation, including a UK representative, travels to Moscow in the coming days. Just as vital if there is to be any chance of lasting diplomatic success is a clear, prior understanding between Europe and the Trump administration over red lines, what’s wanted, and what can and cannot be conceded. On this as on so many other international issues, Donald Trump is a liability who speaks without thinking, lacks strategic grasp, and shows no loyalty either to his allies or to the values of liberty, democracy, law and justice for which the US once stood. Speaking during and after last week’s trilateral Shenzhen summit with China’s president, Xi Jinping, and Putin, Trump floated some vagu

title: The Guardian view on disability benefits: Timms’s radical review is rooted in experience | Editorial
text: F our million people with disabilities or long‑term health conditions in the UK claim personal independence payment (Pip). A review by Sir Stephen Timms, the social security minister, offers a blueprint for how to overhaul it . Its recommendations pose a difficult question for ministers: are they prepared to meet the needs that a more accurate assessment of the costs of disability might reveal? Sir Stephen worked as one of three co-chairs with a steering group of 12 people with a range of professional and lived experience. There is broad agreement that Pip needs to be reformed. The announcement on Tuesday that the government would accept the recommendation of a new fast track for claimants whose conditions are lifelong or unlikely to improve, and abolish unnecessary benefit reviews, signalled that ministers are ready for change. The decision, affecting one in 10 claimants in England and Wales, is welcome but long overdue. Ministers should work with the devolved administrations to ensure similar progress elsewhere in the UK. For the other 90% of claimants, the prospects are less certain . There is no repeat here of the Starmer government’s crass attempt to slash £5bn from the overall bill by raising thresholds across the board. Sir Stephen and his colleagues have accepted the message sent by Labour MPs last year, that they were not elected to strip benefits away from vulnerable people in the middle of a cost of living crisis. But while the recommendation is for the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) to run its new impact assessments in a flexible, responsive and personalised way, the outcome, at least for some claimants, is likely to be reduced entitlements. Ministers should establish disabled people’s requirements before deciding what to spend. Sharing out too little money more fairly cannot be described as progress. The proposal that disabled people should be involved in reform in an ongoing way sets a challenge for ministers. But the practical difficulties of participatory methods must not be allowed to obscure their advantages. This review gives an unusually vivid account of the DWP’s failings. Ministers should accept the principle of a “person‑centred” system despite its significant resource and workforce implications. They must find alternatives to processes that are frequently experienced as dehumanising. This review is distinct from the recent Fonagy and Milburn reports, and should be treated as such. The Timms report’s focus on the costs of disability sits uneasily with the Milburn report’s emphasis on getting young people into work. Pip is not an unemployment benefit. For some, it is what makes working possible. Until ministers set out what new job support and training opportunities will look like, especially in the deprived areas where they are most needed, it is difficult to judge whether such measures are likely to succeed. But the Timms review makes clear that a cash benefit such as Pip cannot simply be abolished. Labour should resist the scapegoating of disabled people: the working-age benefit bill is stable as a share of GDP. What has changed is its composition. How much of rising disability spending reflects worsening public health, failing public services and an inflexible labour market? Rising ill health among claimants is concerning, but cutting Pip would deepen generational inequality and hardship without addressing its causes.

title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham and Wales: a devolution blindspot at No 10 | Editorial
text: A s he headed for Downing Street this summer, Andy Burnham said that he aimed to be “as collaborative and pragmatic as possible” in his dealings with the governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. His predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, had notoriously warned ministers against being “overly deferential” in discussions with the devolved administrations. But Mr Burnham’s signature commitment to distributing more power and responsibility out of Westminster, and his consensual style, appeared to augur well for a positive reset in relations. In Wales, this early optimism has just been brutally quashed by an uncharacteristically peremptory letter from Mr Burnham to the first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth. In it, the prime minister flatly rejected Welsh calls for the devolving of powers in relation to policing and justice, the crown estate and rail infrastructure. In the case of policing, Mr Burnham is in the curious position of denying to Mr ap Iorwerth the type of power that he enjoyed as the mayor of Greater Manchester. At the level of political optics, which this prime minister usually handles adeptly, it seems a strangely insensitive and high-handed approach. At last May’s Senedd elections, Welsh Labour suffered a historic political meltdown that saw voters defect in large numbers to the progressive nationalists of Mr ap Iorwerth’s Plaid Cymru. Responding this week to Mr Burnham’s letter, the first minister professed himself “gobsmacked” and said that Wales was not being viewed as “an equal nation” by Downing Street. An apparent refusal to engage at all with Plaid’s devolution agenda – which is also largely backed by Welsh Labour – risks becoming a gift for the nationalist cause. Substantively, the government’s determination to maintain the status quo means persisting with anomalies that it is hard to justify, and which have fuelled an understandable sense of resentment towards Westminster. The unfairness (and stark inaccuracy) of defining HS2 as an “England and Wales project” rankles still. Scotland and Northern Ireland, where rail services and infrastructure are devolved, benefited from related Barnett formula money amounting to billions of pounds. Wales missed out, and its rail services and infrastructure have been historically underfunded from London. Commissions such as that led by the former lord chief justice, Lord Thomas, have strongly recommended that justice be devolved in Wales as it is in England, Scotland and Northern Ireland. The case in favour, based on a recognition that priorities are best determined at close hand rather than remotely, resembles that made many times by Mr Burnham in his own advocacy for place-based politics. And if the crown estate and its revenues can be devolved in Scotland, it is hard to see why the same cannot apply to Wales. Mr Burnham’s letter points to a potential loss of the benefits of cross-border cooperation in policing, and the intended role of Great British Railways in determining future investment in rail. But for a prime minister who understands how deeply political loyalties are rooted in place and belonging, the reluctance to engage with Wales’s sense of nationhood is striking. It also seems surprisingly shortsighted. At the very least, a lengthier and more collaborative examination of the issues involved is in order. Mr ap Iorwerth has requested urgent talks with Downing Street. That wish should be swiftly granted, allowing a better, more constructive conversation to begin. title: The Guardian view on Cop31: a just transition needs more than fine words | Editorial
text: I n a negotiation the maxim is usually that no deal is better than a bad deal. But the failure of Cop31 in Turkey to get a climate pact – the first time this has happened in 17 years – should not be an excuse for leaving the planet with the damaging status quo. A hard bargain needs a credible route to agreement: by making commitments, seeking concessions and getting others to reciprocate. This did not happen at the weekend. Responsibility for the breakdown lay principally with petrostates resisting a transition away from fossil fuels and wealthy nations that are unwilling to finance it properly. With the US absent, the EU was foremost among the latter. European governments’ objection to fossil-fuel backsliding by a Saudi-Russian coalition was right, but they were wrong to rule out fresh EU funding for developing countries’ climate action. Despite their reservations, others – notably China and the African group – were prepared to accept a flawed package to keep multilateralism alive. While the failure to agree Cop31’s “cover decision” dominated the summit’s headlines, other decisions did pass. The work on a just transition will continue for three years, but the mechanism to make it operational is missing. There was progress on how to assess adaptation needs for developing nations, but not on how to pay for it. Such gaps highlight the unresolved political conflicts at the heart of the UN talks. An agreement to transition away from fossil fuels was made in 2023. A tripling of adaptation finance was promised in 2025. Yet the Australian-Turkish joint presidency diverted attention away from delivering these commitments towards a cover decision promoting controversial technologies and electrification without tying this to renewable energy . The latter has an energy-security rationale: disruption from the US-Israel war on Iran strengthens the case for replacing imported fossil fuels with homegrown electricity. But how that electricity is generated matters – and poorer countries need support to fund the switch. Wealthy nations don’t have much of a moral pedestal upon which to lecture them. The UK government is spending less on climate finance per year over the next three years than it did over the last five and is expected to give a nod to Rosebank – the biggest undeveloped oilfield in UK waters – by the end of 2026. More egregiously, Sweden’s environment minister, Romina Pourmokhtari , who led the EU’s finance group at Cop31 , publicly backed a weakening of the country’s emissions rules that lay behind its 7% greenhouse gas increase in 2024. The UN process remains the only forum where every country has a voice and an opportunity to shape outcomes. Before the next Cop, in Ethiopia, trust between parties must be repaired through a transparent negotiating process. Strenuous efforts must also be made to avoid last-minute wrangling over a text that displaces the original agreed agenda by making progress on turning finance pledges into action. This year brought glacier collapses, record European heat and wildfires across Asia. The world must do much more to confront a human-made catastrophe. It is unarguable that fossil fuels are the primary cause of global heating. What is required is a fair and equitable transition on a global scale to cleaner energy. “The climate crisis will not wait for governments to find common ground. Neither can we,” said UN secretary general António Guterres. It is impossible to disagree.

title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s EU intentions: undogmatic consensus building is a sensible strategy | Editorial
text: D uring the 1980s and 90s, the French president of the European Commission, Jacques Delors, consciously pursued deeper EU integration via a gradualist approach that sought to minimise confrontation. Rather than focusing on ambitious end-goals, risking a showdown with some member states, Delors calculated that taking steps such as the creation of the internal market, in 1993, would eventually generate the momentum to go further. One thing would lead to another, in a logic of deeper union. Mindful of the unique capacity of the Brexit debate to divide and polarise, Andy Burnham appears, for the time being, to be adopting a version of this strategy. On Friday, the prime minister rightly hailed the signing of a reset deal with the EU on food exports, emissions trading and youth mobility as a “good day” for the UK. He then reiterated that further discussion was needed on finding the right long-term relationship with Brussels. Over the weekend, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, made the case for closer ties and a bigger British voice in Europe’s affairs. The country needed , Mr Miliband told the BBC, to move beyond a status quo in which Britain is a passive rule-taker in relation to its largest trading partner, rather than exerting a direct influence inside the decision-making room. As the EU continues to move to protect its industries against Chinese and US competition, to the possible detriment of British interests, that is an argument that will only grow in force. There is frustration in some Labour quarters that having unexpectedly opened up the possibility of the UK rejoining the EU in the autumn, Mr Burnham shows no sign of moving towards explicitly advocating for it. But the prime minister’s cautious and undogmatic strategy is sensible politics on deeply treacherous terrain. Without committing himself in a way that would worry some “red wall” members of his own cabinet, Mr Burnham’s unequivocally pro‑European stance has positioned Labour at the head of a progressive electoral bloc at a time when the right is bitterly divided. The national verdict that Brexit has been a disappointment gives space to argue for building on Friday’s direction of travel. Implementing the reset deal will take up the remainder of the current parliament, as the prime minister indicated on Monday in his statement to the House of Commons. But that leaves the way open for the prime minister to make a broader pro-EU case at the next election – whenever that comes. An open‑ended approach also allows necessary room for manoeuvre during what is set to be a febrile and destabilising period in European politics, with the possibility of a far-right French president entering the Élysée in the spring. In his Commons statement, Mr Burnham made reference to that continental volatility, while at the same time underlining that Friday’s agreement could be followed by further major changes following an election. The contemplation of options and “ informal brainstorming ” sessions with Brussels cannot go on for ever, particularly as the nascent “stay out” movement revives the kind of false arguments that blighted the 2016 referendum. Eventually, the government will have to nail its colours to the mast and choose a case to make. But it is right to undertake that process of discernment with a sense of caution and an emphasis on building consensus.

title: There’s probably a cult hiding in plain sight on your high street. At last, Britain is confronting the problem | Rachael Reign
text: Britain is confronting its cult problem. Better late than never. They don’t advertise themselves as cults. They don’t register as cults. And they certainly don’t have the word above the door. But make no mistake: cults operate in communities across Britain. Chances are, there’s one on your local high street. Today, I support survivors through Surviving Universal UK, the country’s only Black-led specialist organisation dedicated to spiritual and cultic abuse. After years of campaigning, 2026 is shaping up to be a historic year for survivors in Britain. The silence is finally beginning to break. On Monday, MPs debated support for people leaving what are officially called “high-control religious groups”. Led by Labour MP Sam Carling, the debate brought a neglected issue into mainstream British politics. Carling explicitly described the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (UCKG) as a cult. Other groups were also named in the debate. MPs raised concerns about constituents harmed by high-control groups and inadequate protections. For survivors watching, the significance was immense. Many had waited years for this moment of public acknowledgment and political attention. The UCKG is no obscure underground movement. It is a registered charity with branches across Britain, investigated by the BBC’s Panorama and by national newspapers. But what made the debate even more significant was the discussion of change. MPs pressed for stronger protections and a serious examination of whether existing legislation is fit for purpose. The government was urged to act. Survivors were finally being heard openly in parliament itself. I welcome that political attention. I also know that recognition alone cannot protect anyone. There have been other encouraging developments. In February, the Crown Prosecution Service included spiritual abuse in its updated guidance on honour-based abuse, including harmful practices associated with supposed demonic possession. Plans for an all-party parliamentary group examining spiritual, ritual and cultic abuse are taking shape. Meanwhile, Surviving Universal UK has demanded a national call for evidence. Britain has hardly been short of warnings. From the Jesus Army to SPAC Nation , alleged and documented cases of abuse involving high-control groups have made headlines for years. Yet each scandal is treated as isolated. Such abuse is not exclusively religious. High-control groups can emerge in political movements, therapeutic settings or around charismatic individuals. What matters is not what members believe, but how power is exercised over them. We already recognise coercive control within domestic abuse. We understand how manipulation erodes independence. Yet when similar behaviour occurs within a group, our legal and safeguarding responses become far less assured. I know how frightening that control can be. When questioning authority supposedly endangers your relationships or salvation, leaving is rarely as simple as walking through a door. In February, the Home Office said it did not intend to extend the coercive control offence under the Serious Crime Act 2015 beyond personally connected relationships. Asked specifically about cults, extremist groups and gangs, it argued that expansion could create uncertainty for police and prosecutors. That response troubled me deeply. Since when did the complexity of protecting survivors become a justification for leaving them without adequate safety? Existing laws can address rape, assault and fraud. But sustained psychological coercion does not always fit neatly into those offences. Survivors should not have to wait for another crime to occur before the harm they are experiencing is recognised. Elsewhere, governments are beginning to approach this differently. France has a dedicated public body, Miviludes, monitoring harmful sectarian practices.
