title: Council tax and stamp duty: both are a disaster zone. Scrap them and start from scratch | Polly Toynbee
text: W hen voters were asked in 2020 which tax they would cut first , council tax came out on top, and rightly so. Still, it’s taken six years for an array of Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs to call for reforms to this most grotesquely unjust tax. Prompted by a public petition organised by the campaign Fairer Share, a Westminster Hall debate heard calls for a review into property taxes, which would lay out options for replacing council tax and stamp duty land tax. Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan . Among flotillas of economists and thinktanks who signed the letter is Lord O’Neill, a Burnham adviser and former Goldman Sachs economist, who calls UK property taxation “utterly nonsensical”. Burnham has frequently backed reform of the “highly regressive” council tax and stamp duty, labelling them as “a tax on the aspiration of young people”. Back in the day, when poll tax riots brought down Margaret Thatcher, the issue was that a duke paid the same flat poll tax as the dustman. But nowadays King Charles pays less council tax for Buckingham Palace than nearly half of his subjects . The palace “sits in band H and is charged £1,828 [per year] by Westminster city council, less than an average three-bedroom semi in Blackpool,” notes economist Paul Johnson. The groundswell for reform may explain the king’s hasty announcement last week that he would now volunteer to pay more council tax. He may foresee the upcoming row about Rachel Reeves’s radical mansion tax , the “high-value council tax surcharge” arriving in April 2028, which will charge homes worth £2m or more £2,500 per year, and those worth £5m or more £7,500 per year. (But why have that cap when the purchaser of a £265m Chelsea property this year would hardly notice the extra pennies?) It’s easy to see why Jonathan Brash, chair of the all-party group for council tax reform, leads the campaign: he is Labour MP for Hartlepool. If property taxes became proportional to property values, the north and north-east would gain hugely, while the rich in the south would lose. A huge study from the Institute for Fiscal Studies suggested a reform of the system whereby 10.1m households would gain more than £200 a year, while only 4.2m would lose more than £200 a year. The case against council tax is one of straightforward injustice. The case against stamp duty land tax is one of gross distortion , creating business-sapping stasis, deterring older people from downsizing, homeowners from moving away for better jobs and pricing young people out altogether by adding about £4,750 to the cost of buying a typical home. An anomalous hangover from the transition from the poll tax to council tax gives a damaging 25% council tax discount to single people, with no good reason to disadvantage larger households. With so many more winners than losers, what’s prevented every recent government from council tax reform when all politicians privately agree it’s needed? We may be about to find out whether their cowardice was justified, as complaints about the forthcoming mansion tax grow from households living in properties worth more than £2m. My local paper, the ace Camden New Journal , frequently publishes letters such as one from this week: “We’re not cash rich so why do our MPs back this unfair tax?” Jill Henry protests that in many districts in the north London borough, “a property valued at £2m is in no way a mansion”. Well, by definition, £2m is a mansion, even if it doesn’t have turrets. Prime location can make it so. There are only about 156,000 of these mansions in England, so block your ears to their noise and their rightwing media foghorns. The trope is the little old lady with a fixed pension sitting inside the goldmine that is her lifelong home. The answer is it’s time for her to move: she’d do better somewhere cheaper to heat. If not, then she can take out an equity-release loan.

title: How many more ‘landmark’ reforms of benefits for disabled people are we expected to take? | Frances Ryan
text: W hen Stephen Timms announces his long-awaited recommendations regarding personal independence payments (Pip) on Tuesday , it will be the third time in 16 months that the government has trailed “landmark” reforms to the key disability benefit. First seen last year when Keir Starmer’s proposed Pip cuts were stifled by a Labour backbench rebellion, it was only last week that the Milburn review pitched pulling the benefit entirely from under-25s . Or perhaps I’ll put it another way: it was only a few days ago that disabled people on social media were last sharing their fear they will lose the money they need to live on. What exactly Timms – a New Labour stalwart who is now minister for social security – will propose is still unknown , but leaks suggest his will be a “ much softer ” approach than Milburn’s £3.6bn a year of proposed cuts , in part because it has been co-produced with disabled people’s organisations. It is likely that Timms will recommend the assessment process for Pip should be made simpler and easier to complete, particularly for people with fluctuating conditions – something that will be welcomed by the many people who have become accustomed to being wrongly rejected for the support they need. The review is also expected to say that all ages should keep the benefit – putting Timms at direct odds with Milburn’s call last week for many young people with health conditions to lose their monthly cash and instead apply for one-off payments for specific goods, such as therapy or a mobility aid. No matter where you fall on the political spectrum, that will sound like a colossally inefficient way to reform a system. Why did we spend last week discussing Milburn’s proposals if Timms was going to make different ones, days later? Will disabled people aged 25 and over have a separate assessment and entitlement from that for younger people or not? Why did Milburn even have Pip – a benefit that pays for the extra costs of disability and is for those in work too – as part of his brief on unemployment? That a source has told the Times that the two reports will “converge” and form part of yet another government policy paper early next year does suggest that Labour might be doing all this as some sort of an elaborate bit. As the political class wrestles with how to tackle the benefits bill and a sicker population, it feels as if the nation is doomed to ride a perpetual cycle of ideas. The government presents a plan for reforming the benefits system. Rightwing parties cry it doesn’t go far enough. Charities and disabled people’s organisations express concern. Then we go again. “Welfare reform” in 2026 is effectively stuck in Groundhog Day, except in the film Bill Murray at least learns something . The irony, of course, is that Pip is in desperate need of overhaul. Since 2013, when the coalition government brought in the benefit as part of its wider austerity agenda, Pip has, by any measure, been a disastrous piece of public policy: pushing disabled people to food banks , physical and mental decline , and, in extreme cases, death . Meanwhile, public resentment grows at the mounting cost, while private companies are given multimillion-pound contracts for running inaccurate assessments (currently, nearly two-thirds of appeals over Pip decisions are successful at tribunal). We will soon see whether Timms’s recommendations finally buck the trend and offer some genuinely useful solutions for what is a deeply complex issue. And yet there comes a point where we have to ask whether another government review into disability benefits is actually about doing something to help those who rely on those benefits – or about being seen to be doing something by those who don’t. Few things demonstrate this more than the way snippets of the two benefit reviews have been leaked to the press in the days before publication. That this is standard practice doesn’t mean feeding frenzied media speculation doesn’t have a very real impact on what are often vulne

title: Connecting with Britain’s unsung carers has allowed me to feel a deep compassion for my younger self | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
text: A s the years have passed, I have often observed that caring for another person is a responsibility that few human beings completely escape. “Hardly anyone gets off scot-free in this life,” I recently said to a friend, as we discussed our various loved ones and their care needs, the worry and the responsibilities. Whether it’s our children, siblings, friends or parents, some sort of care work is usually required of us on our life’s journey. Illness, disability, mental health issues, ageing, accidents and other vulnerabilities inevitably touch our lives. There are 5.8 million unpaid carers in the UK, but I suspect there are far more who don’t identify as such, yet regularly care for loved ones or neighbours by helping with bills, shopping, appointments or more personal tasks. If you stood in a busy street in any town or city and stopped a passerby to ask them about the care they’ve given, or indeed the care they have received, many people would have a story to tell. As someone who was a child carer for my profoundly autistic brother , this thought – that caring is something that unites us as human beings – is one I find comforting. This unspoken, hidden and often unwritten club is one that took me a long time to realise existed, simply because when you are little, most of your peers aren’t doing care work yet (and the ones who are might not talk about it). You also don’t necessarily see it as care because to you the tasks just feel normal: making their tea or helping them go to the toilet is simply a part of loving that person. Yet, having that level of responsibility as a child can feel very lonely, because you are a child with adult responsibilities who has had to grow up far too quickly. At the time you don’t realise that getting older means the size of this “club” keeps expanding. Now I am in my 30s and, having seen what life has thrown at the people I know and love, and their families, I understand that caring is less exceptional than it used to feel. I recently contributed to an anthology for supporters of the Carers Trust called Lives Less Seen: Untold Stories from Those Who Care. Among the contributions are several from young carers. Oliver writes about looking after his mum, who had a stroke four years ago, and how being put in touch with the trust’s young carers network and campaigning politically for the rights of children like him has made him feel not only less alone but proud to be a young carer. Like the all-party parliamentary group that Oliver has attended, I’d like to see improved attempts to identify young carers, whose education, wellbeing and future prospects are all impacted by their roles, and better, earlier support for them, including when they transition to adulthood. Caring is so often thankless, and its role in keeping society afloat is so often underestimated, that learning to feel pride in it is crucial. The anthology also contains moving drawings from the Honeypot Children’s Charity, which supports young carers and children aged five to 12. Being put in touch with other child carers and being encouraged to creatively process their feelings must make such a difference. I rejected groups like these when I was young, I think from a mixture of pride and fear. In retrospect I think such initiatives would have really helped me make sense of what my home life involved. For a long time, I was so allergic to the idea that people may feel sorry for me that I had emotionally blocked off the possibility of ever feeling compassion for myself. I think a lot of carers do this, especially when they are in survival mode. It’s very easy to view being sad about it as something self-indulgent and unproductive, especially when you feel you’re not suffering anywhere near as much as the person you’re caring for, and so it’s easier to put your feelings in a box. My own contribution to the anthology is a letter to my younger self, but really it is for all child carers. I wanted someone in my position to know how much I re

title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
text: E veryday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be. All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict . But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of sexism. But one of the tragedies of Labour’s 18 long years of exile from power and the climactic defeat of organised labour in the miners’ strike was the fact that they opened the way for the wholesale reinvention of work and watershed developments that we seem to be only just waking up to. The Welsh writer Richard King’s oral history of his home country , Brittle With Relics, contains a fascinating quotation from Nicky Wire of those sons of the South Wales coalfield the Manic Street Preachers . Wire’s father was a miner before he joined the army and then came home to work as a carpenter and builder in a local economy that was thriving. Back then, to be working class did not axiomatically mean you were short of money; workers’ collective clout, moreover, delivered exactly what the 21st-century labour market so lacks. “The pay levels in the 60s and the 70s were brilliant for working-class people,” says Wire. “Everyone in our valley was wearing suits and going to Tunisia on package holidays … My dad just worked his bollocks off; he was one of the great workers. When he passed away, we had ‘Father, son, brother, worker’ on his memorial stone, because that’s what he did.” Far too many lives, in wildly diverse parts of the economy, are now a long way from that kind of everyday pride and contentment, something proved by no end of research. Only a few weeks ago, for instance, the Resolution Foundation published analysis of new information from the British Social Attitudes survey. The headline findings were that job satisfaction in the UK has dropped to the lowest level ever recorded and that “the proportion [of workers] willing to work harder than required to help their employer succeed has fallen to its lowest ever level over the past decade” (it stands at a pretty miserable 55%). The proportion saying they had an interesting job fell from 74% to 63%. The share reporting opportunities for advancement went from 35% to 26%. In its soul Labour still thinks its basic mission is to right such wrongs. But from the Tony Blair years onwards, the party’s thinking has also been regularly warped by inclinations that it ought to find objectionable: to shove people into work irrespective of what that entails, and to emphasise the need to redesign human beings to somehow fit with the mercurial, often cruel ways of modern capitalism rather than making perfectly justified demands for the latter to change. Which brings us to the report about young people and employment – and more specifically Neets, or those not in education, employment or training – put together by the former New Labour high-up Alan Milburn and published this week. On a long train journey I read all 1,005 of its numbered paragraphs and was struck by a few things: the thoroughness of its research and the urgency of its tone – but on

title: After Russell Brand, and now another horrific rape verdict, shame really does have to change sides | Jonathan Freedland
text: T he only thing they have in common is that they are men. Those convicted of the rape and sexual assault of Joanne Young – who was drugged by her husband, so that he could offer her unconscious body to strangers – do not come from one class or ethnic group or age cohort. Like the 50 men convicted alongside Dominique Pelicot for the serial rape of his wife, Gisèle, which this case resembles, they run the full range. Young’s oldest abuser is now 62, her youngest was 22. The four convicted on Thursday included two who were white, two who were not. Among them was a former music producer, a taxi driver and a one-time contractor for the Ministry of Defence. The only thing they have in common is that they are men. That closes off a delusion that many reach for when confronted with heinous crimes committed against women: the claim that such appalling acts are peculiar to a specific category of man. Last week, the focus was on famous men, prompted by the rape conviction of Russell Brand and the allegations of underage grooming and predatory behaviour by David Walliams , accusations Walliams denies. There was earnest discussion of the enabling power of celebrity, how stardust blinds people from seeing what’s in front of them. Some suggested the problem was narrower still, with abuse cast as a function of the way British comedy operates, lacking a recognisable HR structure or protection for junior workers from big names with clout. In parallel, a debate began about staggering the age of consent , addressing the particular dynamics of older men who target younger women, including those who would be regarded as children by any definition except the letter of the law. All of those are valid questions, by the way. But if, underlying them, is the consoling hope that we are facing a limited problem, one confined to, say, high-status men or those whose victims are very young, then Thursday’s verdicts should dispel it. The grimmer truth is that this problem is wider and deeper: the guilty were ordinary men, carpenters and cabbies, ready to violate a middle-aged woman who was audibly and visibly unconscious. Even this especially shocking crime – in which a man recruits other men online to rape his sedated wife – may not be as rare as we imagine. A similar case is now being tried in Manchester and, according to Wiltshire police: “This may be a significantly under-reported crime type.” Of course, there are specific elements and contexts that make rape and sexual abuse more possible. Just as the entertainment industry provided a hospitable environment for Brand, so Philip Young could advertise for fellow rapists thanks to online forums such as Craigslist and Reddit. The internet made it easier for him to secure sedative drugs. But these things facilitate rather than drive the impulse. They are not the heart of the matter. Which is, to state it plainly, male hatred of women. Of course, such hatred is not universal; not every man is infected by it. But it is embedded in our world and sits deep in our culture. (After Pelicot and Young, you look again at Sleeping Beauty: what exactly did we think was going on in a story that, in its 17th-century telling , had the king discover the unmoving, unconscious body of a woman, rape and impregnate that woman, and then flee?) In Afghanistan, the Taliban have imposed gender apartheid, prohibiting girls and women from learning, singing, taking a bus without a man or walking to the park. According to Human Rights Watch, one directive ordered the removal of windows, lest Afghan women, “imprisoned in their homes, might see the outside world”. Closer to hand, you look at the manosphere, whose leading lights delight in the degradation and humiliation of women, treating their girlfriends as, at best, unpaid domestic servants or, at worst, property and chattel. You contemplate the rates of femicide, which include three women killed every fortnight in England and Wales by a current or former partner. You look at the rape s

title: The UK government ridicules villages such as Piddington – but it’s these ‘Nimbys’ who show us the way | Simon Jenkins
text: P oor Piddington. The Oxfordshire village of just 350 people was told last week by the communities secretary, Angela Rayner, that it must almost quadruple in size. That wasn’t all. The newcomers would be 1,250 young asylum seekers, mainly from Afghanistan and Eritrea, victims of Britain’s chaotic asylum appeal system. They will be housed in former military cabins on the village’s outskirts. Rayner said that this was an “urgent crown development”, which allowed her to ignore local objections. And there had certainly been objections. In September, Piddington villagers declared they were fed up with Britain. Led by their parish council and on a 92% turnout, they voted overwhelmingly to leave the UK and become a “principality”. They are joined in their protest by Barnham in Suffolk, where locals have been told this week that they are to host nearly 1,000 asylum seekers. They have set their own date on a referendum to leave the UK. These gestures may be ridiculed as “passports to Pimlico”, but they reflect a deadly and earnest predicament. An emergency Commons debate last month heard the immigration minister, Anna Turley, proclaim Piddington’s fate as “in the national interest” . It would help stop the need for asylum hotels in the middle of towns and cities at a cost rising to billions. But shouldn’t these villagers have a say? In the planning policy framework introduced by David Cameron’s government in 2012, communities were invited to prepare “neighbourhood development plans”. But from day one, central government treated these as mere wishlists. Delivery targets were progressively introduced that overruled local planning control, none more radical than Labour’s “growth targets” in 2024. Prime ministers of both parties have drawn up housebuilding targets for every English locality. Councils, it was suggested, should disregard labels such as green belts or areas of outstanding natural beauty when planning where to build. This was despite independent surveys constantly protesting that the national target of 1.5m new homes could already be met within existing built-up areas, with two thirds of sites already with planning permissions. The reality is that private developers make more money building in the country – and the government is in thrall to them. The name of the game is profit. Hence the imposition from government now witnessed in small towns and villages across England’s south and midlands. Last year, Moreton-in-Marsh in Gloucestershire was ordered to double in size . In a poll, 96% of local people protested, but to no avail. The town is now a gallery of housing horror, encased on all sides by bland private estates. No attempt has been made to build in a village style, let alone fuse estates with the rural landscape. All that matters is the number of houses. Southern England is seeing a repeat of the suburban sprawl over London’s home counties between the wars. What is stark is the total impotence of local people to play any part in combating this assault. Soon after taking office, Keir Starmer was insulting villagers as “blockers and Nimbys” , as if defending one’s environment was a crime. Andy Burnham then upped the ante by removing powers to block rural development from local planning committees. This disempowerment is inconceivable in other European countries. In France, Germany, Switzerland or Scandinavia, local communities enjoy sovereignty over their future. They call it democracy. France’s 35,000 communes build plenty of houses, but they grow organically, not by an invasion of “volume builders” whipped on by central government. The status of small communities is not a quaint archaism. The English village is a valued social construct. Its institutions are the school, the church, the pub and the youth club. Its lifeblood is the high street. Such an informal cohesion of the neighbourhood came to life during the Covid-19 pandemic. It supplied mutual help in time of trouble. It was a salve to loneliness. title: It’s unfashionable to say it, but class still matters – and young people know that | Polly Toynbee
text: T his should come as no great surprise: young people are more keenly aware of the significance of social class than those who came before them. The yawning gap in life chances at birth is something they know better than complacent older generations. Class may be unfashionable in the language of politics – long damned by the right as the politics of envy, avoided by many on the left for fear of sounding chip-on-the-shoulder – yet it’s part of the daily experience for young people. Nearly half of 16- to 34-year-olds in the UK now say class is important to their identity – and not in a good way – according to a new Ipsos poll . That’s nearly twice as many as among the over-55s. Maybe that’s because more young people are better educated at each level, so they know more, with a grounding in reasoned thinking. More likely this new class consciousness springs from their sharpened experience of life chances among their own generation. They are more likely to think class has become increasingly significant over the past two decades and they’re right: within their own generation, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) has found inequality in the UK is growing more than within other cohorts. The class antennae of young people have been honed by the obstacles they face that older generations felt less, when class was better disguised by generally rising living standards. What they see around them is the growing inheritocracy – the widening chasm between those who get substantial help from parents at crucial points in their lives and those with no backup. The IFS has been sending warnings for years: choosing your parents well matters more than your own talents and hard work. Rewards for merit and effort are declining – and young people see it everywhere. Political platitudes about working hard and playing by the rules ignore the evidence they see with their own eyes. For those receiving inheritances in the UK, the gap between expectations at the top and bottom is greatly widening: the bottom fifth are projected to get 5% of their lifetime income from inheritance, while the top fifth, already better paid, could get 29%. The better off are likely to receive it earlier, making it easier to buy a house, take time to choose their job carefully, save less and retire earlier. As so many young people – many more than the million Neets – struggle to make their way into a career they are qualified for, they can see how class matters far more than money and inheritance. Getting a leg-up from your family background and connections, or just worldly advice from those in the know, is worth everything. The under-35s consider nepotism a serious issue: nearly twice as many are concerned about it as among the apparently socially contented over-55s. This week’s LSE research on cross-class friendships in the US and UK was heartening: they make jokes to get over the awkwardness of revelations of privilege, described by Sam Friedman and Rose Butler as the “omnipresent threat” between them. How well I recognise that. Admitting to being middle class can be embarrassing. That’s why I have tried in my memoir, An Uneasy Inheritance: My Family and Other Radicals , to be honest about how powerfully privilege is passed down the generations, bequeathing self-confidence and security with second and third chances if you mess up. My family of successful leftwing professionals were all confounded by how to square their advantages with their beliefs – sometimes comically, never denying that privilege, just blushing. How strange is the social obtuseness or denial of the over-55s, of whom only 14% believe they would have done better if they came from another class. They may be victims of the classlessness myth spread with skill by the right to hide how their wealth

title: The moral panic over Neets needs to stop. The problem is bad jobs, not young people | Aditya Chakrabortty
text: O ne big number has been repeated over and over this week: 1 million. As ministers and journalists keep telling us, about 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds are not in education, employment or training (Neet). They’re the subject of Alan Milburn’s review, which, although not commissioned by Andy Burnham, has become the first big policy of his new government. Rather than launch into my conclusions, let me give you three more numbers by which to judge Milburn for yourself. These figures have not appeared in any of this week’s coverage, but to understand the review’s context and its chances of success they are vital. Let’s start with 1,500%. That is how much more the press talks about “economic inactivity” now, compared with 2017. Back then, a newspaper reader would barely see the phrase; by 2024, it was appearing literally thousands of times, often on front pages. There was a similar huge rise in the use of the term “sicknote”. From near-silence a few years ago, these phrases have become a daily drumbeat, sounded across print and broadcast. And their major motif is young people. Yet it is not news, not even close. As Milburn says, the Neet rate has been roughly the same for a quarter of a century. This is a serious and long-lasting problem, rooted in economic and social failure, rather than a shock event. But Britain’s rightwing media is unrivalled at manufacturing an urgent crisis. A decade ago, they helped turn Brexit from a fringe obsession of men with red faces and pink trousers into a national referendum and then a racist reality. In the 2020s, they have done a number both on people seeking asylum here and youngsters out of work. The 1,500% figure comes from James Morrison , who in his new book The Workless : Stigma, Unpaid Labour and the Myth of Economic Inactivity, charts a “moral panic”. Take the first lady of Reform UK, Isabel Oakeshott, laying into the “parasites” who “prefer to just sit on the sofa and order their Deliveroo and drive their Motability free vehicle and take everything that the state can offer”. Oakeshott delivered this reportage on a TV channel owned by the Australia-born American billionaire Rupert Murdoch, before herself leaving the UK tax system to live in Dubai . Parasites come in many shapes and sizes. This rightwing moral panic over kids off work and playing Grand Theft Auto forms the backdrop against which Keir Starmer last year turned to Milburn. As Westminster reporters often remind us, Milburn is a grandee from the Blair years. As they are too discreet to mention, he also left his post as health secretary and went on to make millions from private equity healthcare . His review is that familiar Blairite tug of war between two opposing forces: an acceptance that poverty and inequality are “at the core” of the problem, and policies that strip many young disabled people of benefits and make them still poorer. Our next number is 0, which stands for zero employees. Because the overwhelming majority of companies in this country have no staff . Think: Uber drivers, gas fitters, pilates instructors. These are sole traders. And here lies the problem for Milburn, who plans to pay employers to hire Neets. Of the £3.6bn of benefits taken off young people, £1.1bn will be handed to businesses that recruit them. But hardly any of those ideal companies exist. Politicians still imagine the UK as a land of toolmakers and assembly lines. Burnham promises to “reindustrialise Britain”, while George Osborne pledged a “march of the makers”. In reality, our largest private employers include Tesco and Asda, and Amazon warehouses . There is a land dominated by Volkswagen and Siemens – it’s called Germany. You can’t push people into jobs that aren’t there, offered by employers that don’t exist, in an economy that you’ve dreamed up. One of Milburn’s own surveys shows that only 17% of businesses think a Whitehall bung will prompt them to hire more young people than they otherwise would. Far more likely is that companies pocket

title: Neets and needs: a loss of focus on harmful life experiences | Letters
text: Mark Mon-Williams praises Peter Fonagy’s emphasis on needs-led mental health care, while mourning the loss of Sure Start and cuts in health visitors ( Childhood neglect, unmet needs, mental health struggles: this is the making of a Neet, 18 November ). Mon-Williams’ article also chronicles intergenerational neglect by disconnection: a mother can’t afford to travel to an antenatal class, then information following her premature baby daughter’s NHS care is not shared with social and educational services; she is effectively excluded from a school with an outstanding Ofsted rating and joins the ranks of those not in employment, education or training (Neet). The strength of Prof Fonagy’s report on mental health conditions, ADHD and autism is his recommendation to respond to needs, rather than wait months or years for a diagnosis. Yet health visitors and Sure Start were doing just that. These were universal services dedicated to development, while health and learning problems could be picked up on the way. The outstanding long-term impact of the original Sure Start programme (1999-2003) was only fully revealed by the Institute for Fiscal Studies last year, having followed the children up to their mid-teens. The billions spent on it were all recovered in better education and health and fewer convictions, with the poorest children making the greatest gains. These were open multidisciplinary neighbourhood centres that parents helped to run, creating social capital. But that was before the diagnostic revolution now dominating mental health practice, which Fonagy and Mon-Williams do not challenge. This paradigm shift is now structured into health, social services and education, focusing professional minds on developmental disorders rather than on the child’s life experiences. Without a secure community base in which to work, it is inevitably safer to share categorical “information” than the unique personal stories on which human connectedness depends. Dr Sebastian Kraemer NHS consultant child and adolescent psychiatrist 1980-2015 Lola Okolosie’s article resonated deeply with me ( Teachers want to prepare pupils for post-16 life. This is why it’s so difficult, 19 November ) . My husband and I adopted three siblings from care, now aged 23, 24 and 26. All three are employed and doing well, but their experiences highlight major gaps in Alan Milburn’s proposals for young people at risk of becoming Neet. Two of our children had education, health and care plans, and all struggled at school. Two were discouraged from taking practical subjects such as food technology due to written coursework requirements, yet both now work successfully in catering. This raises a fundamental question about how our education system measures ability. While Mr Milburn acknowledges the link between low qualifications and becoming Neet, increasing participation is meaningless unless opportunities are genuinely accessible. We urgently need practical vocational routes that do not rely solely on GCSE English and maths passes or inaccessible functional-skills tests. For instance, our son was offered an apprenticeship after work experience, but no training provider would accept him without a grade 3 in English. Care-experienced young people often carry vulnerabilities into adulthood. While our children benefited from Sure Start while in foster care, we had to source all support to get them into work ourselves – there was no coordinated pathway into employment. Is Mr Milburn directing sufficient resources toward accessible training and sustained, in-work support, rather than simply boosting enrolment figures? Our children have proven their capabilities; the system must stop defining them by what they cannot do. title: Backward steps for police on participation in Pride marches and anti-racism | Letters
text: The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, says police in uniform should not participate in LGBTQ+ pride events, saying that “at those marches, you will often have campaigners, on gender identity … and those issues are now contested … the marching alongside looks like a political act” ( Shabana Mahmood backs ban on police marching in pride events in uniform, 18 November ). She also said that it is wrong for the police not to be colour-blind in policing, as in the previous anti-racism commitment – a commitment that reflected the recognition of the history of systemic racism, and of the perceptions of the police by communities who are policed – and that the police should not engage with “activist groups and campaigners”. Instead, they should adhere to “a new impartiality standard”. In effect, Mahmood is saying that the police should not adhere to anti-racism and anti-homophobia in its policies, practices and culture. This “new” standard is not non-political. In reality, it represents a return to a past policy of treating those who oppose bigotry and violence against racialised and marginalised communities as being the problem. It panders to the far right’s attempt to portray racists as victims. It equates anti-racists with racists and is reminiscent of Donald Trump’s notorious remarks about neo-Nazis and those opposing them that “there were very fine people on both sides”. Official neutrality between racism and anti-racism is institutionally racist. Chris Sinha Cringleford, Norfolk I am one of those gay men whose early years of campaigning for our equality were at a time when the police were ruthlessly persecuting, and the law prosecuting, our community. After decades of struggle, we achieved, in the 2010 Equality Act, recognition of LGBTQ+ people as equal citizens, and police officers – like other services from which we had previously been banned – were able to take part in our Pride parades, celebrating our community’s history and diversity. Now Shabana Mahmood’s decision to end this sends the signal that our equality is not recognised by a (Labour) home secretary. Your editorial ( The Guardian view on ‘two-tier policing’: tackle the myth, don’t pander to it, 18 November ) is spot-on: you don’t defeat bigoted mythology by appeasing it. Dr Peter Purton Southall, London Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Gordon Brown’s ideas on zero-sum beliefs don’t add up | Letters
text: The broad thrust of Gordon Brown’s argument is correct ( The far right is menacing Europe – but it is fragile. What the extremists and voters want isn’t the same, 22 November ). However, he is wrong to suggest that zero-sum beliefs are erroneous. Many things in life are zero-sum. If I own a house, you can’t also own it; if I burn some gas to heat it, you can’t use the same gas. If the UK makes all the cars for the European market, other countries’ carmakers won’t be making them. Yes, growth can come from collaboration and trade, but the proceeds are not infinite and take time to achieve. Brown rightly doesn’t want people to blame others – migrants, other countries, those richer than them – for the fact they can’t afford the essentials. The best way to do this is to ensure that the products of our economy include enough of the essentials, and these are shared in such a way that we all have them. The “knowledge economy” of New Labour is the epitome of non-zero-sum activity, but houses, heating and food are always going to require finite physical inputs. A good economy is not one where we have a glut of online services and low-quality consumer goods, and winners buy multiple homes and losers can afford none. Gavin Bailey Keele, Staffordshire Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Why white-tailed sea eagles are a danger to Britain’s seabirds | Letters
text: Your article on white-tailed sea eagle reintroduction ( Reintroduction of white-tailed eagles puts seabird colonies at risk of wipeout, say experts, 8 November ) highlighted the risk that white-tailed sea eagles are likely to pose to Britain’s seabirds. To argue, as Prof Ian Convery and Rebecca Wrigley did in their responses ( Letters, 15 November ), that the re-establishment of white-tailed sea eagles will somehow restore a lost paradise is fallacious. Where is the evidence that sea eagles will restore that balance? There is no evidence. Also, suggesting that because in the distant past sea eagles and seabirds coexisted, their reintroduction will pose no problems is naive. By failing to acknowledge that past marine ecosystems were much more robust, and seabird prey more abundant, than they are today, these two authors miss the point that it is precisely because our seabirds are currently short of food that they are so vulnerable to disturbance and predation from white-tailed sea eagles. The evidence from Norway is unequivocal: sea eagle predation and disturbance especially, has caused many thousands of seabirds to abandon their colonies. White-tailed sea eagles in the UK will damage our fragile, food-deprived seabird colonies, and adding more sea eagles than there are already, therefore seems ecologically irresponsible. Tim Birkhead Emeritus professor of ecology and evolution, University of Sheffield Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
