title: The World of Love review – beautifully directed and compellingly elusive family mystery
text: K orean film-maker Yoon Ga-eun creates a strange world of bewilderment, sadness and pain – but not much of love – in this involving and mysterious family drama. It seems always to be gesturing at an indefinable sense of loss, a poignant keynote struck by the recurring soundtrack piano arrangement of Bach’s Sheep May Safely Graze. Seo Su-bin gives an excellent performance as Joo-in, a high schooler possessed of a cheeky, madcap sense of fun, like her wacky, magic-obsessed kid brother Hae-in (Lee Jae-hee). She is keen on taekwondo and often shown (in borderline-uncomfortable closeup) kissing boyfriends that she will later dump. But when classmate Su-ho (Kim Jeong-sik) asks her to sign a petition objecting to the release and local rehousing of a convicted child rapist, Joo-in refuses, on the ostensible grounds that the petition talks about the permanent damage done to rape victims. Joo-in astonishes and upsets the class by announcing at the top of her voice that she herself is a rape victim, and she has not been permanently damaged – and then says it was just a joke. Meanwhile, Su-ho is concerned at the way his own kid sister seems to be picking up injuries at the preschool day care centre run by Joo-in’s mum Tae-sun (Jang Hye-jin), who has become an alcoholic since Joo-in’s dad ran out on them. It is an eerie, ecosystemic confluence of rumour and abuse, made more unnerving by the spiteful, anonymous notes that Joo-in now starts to receive, demanding to know why she is behaving in this way. Is this going to be an insoluble enigma, in the time-honoured arthouse tradition of Antonioni, Haneke and Farhadi? Not exactly. We find out the truth about the abuse and – in a kind of supernatural way – the truth about the ubiquity of abuse and cruelty that young people must learn to cover up. Opinions may divide about a final reveal about collective trauma, but this is a very absorbing, tremendously directed drama. The World of Love is in UK cinemas from 27 November

title: To Hold a Mountain review – a spectacular setting for tough savvy woman’s fight against the government
text: A n award-winner in Sundance, where it premiered earlier this year, this slow-burn documentary follows a middle-aged Montenegrin livestock farmer called Gara and her 13-year-old daughter Nada. The two of them eke out a hardscrabble living on Sinjajevina, a breathtaking mountain plateau on which Montenegro’s government would like to conduct training exercises for its own army as well as Nato’s. This goes down about as well as a wolf in the sheep pen with flinty Gara, who rallies her neighbours as well as the local media to fight the proposal. She displays a savviness that’s somewhat surprising, even if her fortitude and strength of conviction seem completely in character. However, that fight against the state is just one element of a film that, through long, languid takes, reveals the women’s stately pastoral existence, one taken up above all with care for their menagerie of animals (cows, sheep, goats, cats and dogs) and each other. Co-directors Petar Glomazić and Biljana Tutorov gradually reveal the family setup isn’t exactly what it appears at first. Although Gara calls Nada her daughter, the young girl is actually her niece; Gara adopted her after her sister, Nada’s mum, was killed by a violent husband. Gara’s profound grief and loss haunt her every day, felt most painfully, perhaps, when an animal dies on the heath, reminding them of the fragility of life. Thankfully, that anguish is balanced out with some spectacular landscape photography as the camera drinks in Sinjajevina’s nearly treeless grasslands, sinuous peaks and troughs, and milky summer light. To Hold a Mountain is in UK and Irish cinemas from 27 November

title: Everything Else Is Noise review – a musician attempts to raise her art above the cacophony of city noise
text: T his latest docufiction from Mexican-Canadian film-maker Nicolás Pereda finds rhythm amid chaos. The film opens with an amusing visual game of Tetris; at a busy intersection in Mexico City, the concept of designated lanes and traffic signals appears to be symbolic only. Here, driving is all about carving your own path, as crisscrossing cars squeeze their way past each other. Reminiscent of Jacques Tati’s ending to Playtime (1967), this entrancing dance of machines encapsulates Pereda’s central dilemma: the question of seizing one’s personal and artistic space amid a world of distractions. The cacophony of honks and revving engines is accompanied by an expressionistic cello piece, played by a composer called Teresa (played by Teresita Sánchez). To some of her neighbours, however, her music is no different from the traffic noise. On this particular day, Teresa has opened her home to fellow musician Rosa (Rosa Estela Juárez Vargas), who wants to use the space for her interview with a two-man television crew. From a nearby dog’s loud barking to intermittent power cuts, the shoot is beset with continual interruptions; but the film also foregrounds the subtle frictions that grow between the characters. Panning shots swing from the banal questions posed by the male interviewers to the women’s unimpressed faces. We can sense that this is not the first time they have been faced with mediocrity. Pereda also uses camera pans to filter new characters and pieces of intrigue into the film; one such concerns Teresa’s grownup daughter Luisa (Luisa Pardo) and her complicated lineage; she is the clandestine offspring of her mother’s affair with a well-known composer. Far from a mere backdrop for an interview, Teresa’s home gradually becomes filled with revelations of discontent, doubt and resentment. Pereda’s expert blocking, however, beautifully accentuates kinship alongside fractures. These artists might still struggle to find their footing, but all is not lost. Everything Else Is Noise is at the ICA, London, from 27 November

title: Focker In-Law review – triangle of sadness as Ariana Grande joins Stiller and De Niro in the circle of trust
text: S o to the fourth film in the most consistently moderate but undeniably lucrative comedy franchise in modern Hollywood history, often featuring heavyweight actors (Dustin Hoffman, Barbra Streisand, Harvey Keitel) who don’t appear to be completely sure about what they’re supposed to be doing. Even now, even after all this time, I’m still not convinced that the great Robert De Niro is 100% on top of it. He sometimes gives the impression – the same impression he’s given in the previous three movies – that he’s thinking about something else. This started more than a quarter of a century ago, when gags about beta-males employed as nurses and called Gaylord Focker were cooler than they are today and this film is possibly the last surviving example of old-school grossout cringe comedy from the 90s era of There’s Something About Mary. Ben Stiller was Focker himself, the nervy, prickly guy engaged to Pam (Teri Polo); he had to meet his future father-in-law, former CIA agent Jack Byrnes (De Niro) who put Gaylord through an excruciating process of assessment over a mortifying weekend, in the course of which Focker met Teri’s impossibly charismatic ex, Kevin (Owen Wilson). Now, in a movie written and directed by John Hamburg, who has script credits on this franchise and Zoolander, we’re a generation further on. This latest iteration features the formidable comedy talent Ariana Grande who does, in fact, show every sign of having mastered the material. But she’s given so little material to work with. Focker is now the age that Jack was when they first met – and Stiller plays him as a lean, drawn, glassy-eyed figure. He is very close to his son Henry (Skyler Gisondo) and wary and suspicious of meeting Henry’s serious new girlfriend Olivia, played by Grande, with whom he has an embarrassing meet-uncute on a plane. A family gathering for Jack’s 80th looms: also present will be Gaylord’s daughter Samantha, gamely played by Beanie Feldstein, and her goofy boyfriend Eduardo (Eduardo Franco). Does Focker now get to be the glowering, disapproving patriarch alpha … just as Jack was (and still is)? Not really. Olivia is a supercool former FBI agent who instantly gains Jack’s respect. For her, membership of the “circle of trust” is a mere formality and poor, maladroit Focker is humiliated by his father-in-law and future daughter-in-law. The movie rattles along with one or two gags here and there – there’s some funny stuff about Jack’s aggressive new dog, a German shepherd to whom Jack speaks in rasping German. There is a wince-making scene in which Focker sings John Legend’s All of Me in a horribly inappropriate context. But the film always has a weird ingredient of bland to counteract the vinegar of comedy and the Fockers and their eternally recurring crises have become overfamiliar.

title: Who Is Still Alive review – grief-stricken stories of the places and people lost in Gaza
text: A sombre documentary from the Swiss musician and film-maker Nicolas Wadimoff, who returns to his longstanding interest in Gaza . In this film, a group of survivor-refugees who made it out of Gaza and into Egypt during the bombing gather in an enclosed studio and are invited to draw out a kind of floor plan of what they remember of their neighbourhood. First, this is on paper and then on the studio floor itself; they use that as a basis for their memories of what and who they have lost. (The people who have died are described as having been “martyred”.) The result is almost unbearably painful. The raw and agonising grief, which perhaps stays just at the waterline of consciousness most of the time, is here brought above the surface. They are people suffering from trauma, carrying videos on their phones of their lost loved ones. One interviewee talks of attending the Edward Said conservatory , now rubble; another talks of her work in film-making and animation. Another man plays poignantly beautiful music on his qanun, a type of zither, and then specifies the point in the music at which he was showered with glass from an explosion while he was playing it in Gaza. Perhaps the most tragic story comes from the Gaza writer and journalist Mahmoud Jouda, who recounts his experience as an eight-year-old of having his face brutally slapped by a soldier for throwing a stone at a military Jeep – a slap that he says radicalised him. This is a story about lived experiences and the immediacy of pain; it does not specifically cover politically retributive anger. The film gives a platform to fierce and heartbreaking stories. Who Is Still Alive is in UK cinemas from 27 November

title: Clashing Through the Snow review – Amazon’s Christmas romcom is a bust
text: C redit where credit is due: it takes some nerve for Amazon to open its latest holiday romcom, Clashing Through the Snow, with characters bemoaning the enervated state of the book industry. Publishing isn’t the cultural epicenter it once was, reports boutique press head Jeremy (PJ Byrne) before announcing some impending new year’s layoffs. Alas, things have changed – “if Faulkner were alive today, he’d be making ASMR videos with Mr Beast” (or, perhaps, competing on Prime Video’s Beast Games?) Self-awareness can be key to the ludicrous joys of a Christmas romcom confection, though Clashing Through the Snow, starring 1923’s Michelle Randolph and homegrown Amazon star Christopher Briney (The Summer I Turned Pretty), tests one’s patience for beating you to the branded punchline. Briney’s Ryan, a numbers-driven, macro-counting kind of book editor, pitches a “financial trends with benefits” romance that could be “Rebecca Yarros big”. Soulmates, says Randolph’s rival workhorse editor Hannah, are as mythical as “ethical billionaires and pain-free bikini waxes”. Due to said budget cuts, both have a week to land “a book so big it makes Harry Potter look like a Buzzfeed listicle” for only one to keep their job. What are two LA workaholics going to do on Christmas but take meetings in New York? A Christmas romcom must necessarily strain credulity; still, what do you mean Randolph’s Hannah, toned and styled like a Sun-belt sorority queen in her matching Alo-branded set, has never done yoga in her life? (A physical gag played for laughs alongside Tan France’s book agent/guru). “This job is my LIFE!” Hannah pleads, entirely unconvincingly, to her IT co-worker sidekick (Zarna Garg). Randolph may not be able to sell lone-wolf book nerd (Briney, on the other hand, can believably shapeshift into corporate shark), but I was willing to buy that these sniping rivals, trading barbs like bargain insult comics, would and should somehow end up in a rental car together due to cataclysmic circumstances (Clashing Through the Snow benefits from the full-body chill I got when I heard “full ground stop” on the LAX intercom). Less easy to take, in their hijinks-filled road trip spiced with several haunted hotels, one very pallid Lukas Gage (perhaps stricken by inanity he’s signed on for) and Paris Hilton as herself, is a veritable corporate who’s who. Whereas Netflix’s holiday fare tends to exist in a fantasy world of placeless gazebos and Canada-as-New York, Clashing Through the Snow, written by Daniel Mackey and Rebecca Ewing, aims squarely for your shopping algorithm. There are more brand name-drops (or spoofs, in the case of the beaver-branded rest stop “Luc-ees”) than a Target display (also mentioned), from planes to candy to one use of ChatGPT as therapist – enough that I considered it noble of an Amazon movie to name-check the Google-owned GPS service Waze (which does, naturally, lead our couple astray). That couple, at least, offer moments of levity in an otherwise dull and gratingly contrived road trip across an America so indistinct I almost wish the film had just stayed on that Delta flight (as evidenced by Upgraded , director Carlson Young knows how to do romcom banter on a plane). Randolph may be a poor fit for a character whose one personality trait is defending her intellectual taste in books, but she is a warm screen presence when allowed to melt a little. But it’s Briney, who near single-handedly elevated The Summer I Turned Pretty from a run-of-the-mill streaming adaptation to lustful summer smash, who does the bulk of the work here; he is uncommonly good at spinning self-tortured angst into charm. If only that were enough to recommend Clashing Through the Snow above the rest of the season’s self-knowingly mid offerings – though perhaps it needs no advertising help from me. Clashing Through the Snow is out now on Amazon Prime Video

title: The Boy and the Suit of Lights review – a sensitive portrait of an aspiring toreador in a changing Spain
text: W here last year’s bullfighting documentary Afternoons of Solitude by Albert Serra was a tightly trussed formalistic affair concerned by the question of style in the arena and in art, this Scottish-produced film is a looser, more social-realist approach to la corrida . Swerving a portrayal of the butchery itself, it focuses on the wider community significance of this tradition in the eastern Spanish city of Castellón, via the figure of aspiring teen toreador Borja. Supported by his harried, cigarillo-smoking single mother, Raquel, Borja hopes that wearing the sequined “suit of lights” will help lift his family out of poverty. Everything in his vicinity seems to point in the direction of the bullring: the Playmobil corrida he stages with his little brother, Erik, the mechanical rodeo bulls they ride at the fairground, the lessons in handling the muleta – the red cloth – he gets from grandfather, Matias, whose own bullfighting ambitions were scotched at an early age. But, as the protesters piling into the arena one day highlight, the bell may already be tolling for the kid’s chosen profession. The wistful Borja, even at his tender age, has a certain melancholic-heroic bearing and a trenchant set of Sergio Leone eyebrows. Director Inma de Reyes’s patient documentary places notable emphasis on the simple act of observation, as if everyone in Castellón is envisaging and rehearsing the noble stance they believe life should conform to. Matias scrutinises Borja’s form, Raquel watches her son from the stands, Borja watching the older toreadors perform. This traditionalist theatre is buttressed by other rituals from daily life: the close-knit family culture in which Erik washes his exasperated grandmother’s hair and the boy’s first communion. As De Reyes tips a hat to this conservative Spanish culture, sitting in with street kids as they plead with an elder to strum some flamenco, she seems to have a noncommittal ambivalence about it too. Bullfighting itself is not judged; rather, she focuses on the growing controversy swirling around it, including the incensed protesters and fired-up apprentices fretting about whether anti-corrida parties will win the elections. This last-days framing does, however, cast a certain fatalistic shadow, on top of Borja’s only semi-explained decision to give up his toreador dreams. If the film doesn’t spend the necessary time with bullfighting’s opponents to fully understand where ending the tradition would lead, it’s nonetheless a sensitive, family-level portrait of a changing Spain . The Boy and the Suit of Lights is in UK cinemas from 27 November

title: You Can See Everything review – unblinking, unhinged and unmissable
text: Thrillingly reckless, deliciously irresponsible and as gripping as any thriller, this situationist docu-hybrid masterpiece from co-directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim gets up close and personal with convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes . It was Holmes’s US biotech firm Theranos, run jointly with her then partner Sunny Balwani, which in 2003 notoriously claimed to have invented a little box that could diagnose all manner of illnesses from a single drop of blood, its corporate prestige pumped by credulous board members including George Schultz and Henry Kissinger. Yet Holmes has now met her match, perhaps even her predatory-platonic love match, in the film’s presenter Nathan Fielder , who is basically the Aleister Crowley of modern documentary satire, the hilarious dark master of turning truth into fiction and back again. His film delivers an extraordinary twist at around the halfway mark, and readers wanting to preserve the shock had better bail out here. Fielder was invited by Holmes to spend intimate time with her in 2023 in the weeks before prison, in the rented San Diego beachfront home she shared with her protective new partner Billy Evans , an alpha-dog blowhard, wannabe tech entrepreneur and Charlie Kirk enthusiast, with whom she has two small children. Holmes still claims to be innocent, a position she maintains here with the wide-eyed gaze and vacuous smile of a beauty pageant victor. (When she switches from contact lenses to glasses for the final car ride to prison it is a poignant moment of vulnerability.) It is Fielder’s mission to find out if she knows she is lying and to make her admit the truth, a job that will need considerable indirection and sympathetic subtlety, rather like Gitta Sereny’s conversations with Albert Speer . At any rate, he might discover how and why she has bought into her own delusional mythology. What we get is an Olympic stare-out contest between two gladiators of the polite straight face. Fielder’s conversations with the equally pop-eyed Evans have the same tension. Who is going to lose their cool first? Holmes repeatedly insists that the technology works, by which she appears to mean that the technology has caused her to be certain in the present that it could and will work in the future; the theory is impeccable and all that remains is the small matter of getting whatever tech stuff they need to go in the little box. You could call this approach fake-it-till-you-make-it, but Holmes clearly believes that faking it and making it are the same thing. Fielder is fascinated and suspicious at her evasive, ersatz-childlike failure to grasp what he is asking her, yet she appears also genuinely to lack a sense of truth and falsehood. She also seems to lack a sense of humour, revealed when Fielder shows her a clip of Abbott and Costello performing the legendary “Who’s on first” bit – a gloriously funny, insightful sequence. But Holmes flinches and sobs when Fielder shows her clips of Amanda Seyfried playing her in the dramatised miniseries The Dropout . Is Holmes exactly the villain of this film? What sort of a dysfunctional, co-dependent relationship did she once have with Balwani? Is her gift for disingenuous idealism, ersatz innocence and a demure need to be insulated from the consequences of her actions something that always attracts a Rasputin, an abusive puppetmaster? Why did Evans and Holmes agree to Fielder as their interrogator anyway? It was supposedly because they liked the way he “thought outside the box”. But perhaps they appreciated the humour behind Fielder’s superb HBO TV show The Rehearsal , which recreates with elaborate sets real situations in ordinary people’s lives, a show that famously involved him getting a pilot’s licence to fly a 737. Maybe Holmes and Evans liked the way reality and fiction were merged or superimposed, and that this relativist approach to the facts would be congenial. But what can Fielder and Oppenheim do, what should they do, once Holmes has been p

title: Josephine review – Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan ballast knotty drama about a child witness to a rape
text: B eth de Araújo’s new movie takes a very big swing, and it has won prizes and acclaim since its premiere at Sundance. I was unsure about some of the film’s high-concept ideas but the lead performance from its eight-year-old newcomer Mason Reeves is outstanding. Those concerned about spoilers had better look away. Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan play Damien and Claire, a smart professional couple in San Francisco with a bright young daughter called Josephine, marvellously played by Reeves. Damien takes Josephine to Golden Gate Park one morning to play football (they turn out to enjoy watching the English Premier League on TV). She mischievously runs on ahead of her dad to a secluded spot in the park where Damien can’t immediately find her and it is there that Josephine witnesses a rape – not less horrifying for being filmed in long shot. Damien catches up with Josephine, and gives chase to the rapist; Josephine and the rape victim find themselves in the back of a police car while the cops and Damien deal with matters, almost as if they are culprits and prisoners. Deeply affected by something she cannot understand or process in her mind, Josephine starts acting out in school, not helped by Damien bizarrely insisting she take self-defence classes. Her disorientation borders on psychosis, and all the time the court date nears when Josephine has to give evidence in front of a jury. There are some strong moments here, but also moments when Damien and Claire’s furious rows look like an acting improv class. And the big motif of the whole film is that the rapist himself keeps appearing silently in scenes, like a ghost that only Josephine can see. Of course, this arguably approximates what many people in this situation can experience, but after a while it feels contrived. The victim herself is supposedly going to be absent from court, not being subject to a subpoena, but the procedural chill of this plot point is cancelled when she arrives at the end to give courageous Josephine an emotional thank you for her evidence. And the verdict? It is not actually shown. The defence tries to undermine Josephine’s testimony and suggest something more complex was going on, some consensual role-play, but the film itself does not create any complexity or ambiguity arising from what Josephine saw and from what we see from her point of view. Perhaps the point is that the verdict is not relevant, as Josephine and her parents will still have to get on with their lives and deal with the after-effects of this trauma. That’s fair enough, although in the real world the verdict would surely be very important. So some misjudgments here – but Reeves is impressive. Josephine is out on 20 November in the UK and US, and 18 February in Australia

title: Steven Spielberg to make a western written by Paul Thomas Anderson
text: Steven Spielberg has announced his next project: a western scripted by Paul Thomas Anderson . According to Deadline , the two Oscar-winning film-makers will collaborate for an adaptation of Kevin Barry’s 2024 novel The Heart in Winter. The film is set to bring together the Oscar-winning actors Jessie Buckley, Cillian Murphy and Mark Rylance. It tells the story of two fugitives on the run in the 1890s. “It’s really the excitement for me to get to work together with my dear friend and colleague Paul Thomas Anderson on a genre, but more particularly, the genre notwithstanding, a story that quite quickly became close to both our hearts and we felt that we could do as a team,” Spielberg told Deadline. Earlier this year, Spielberg also spoke about the film while at SXSW. “Can’t reveal anything right now, but I have a western in development,” he said, before adding that “it kicks ass” and “there will be no tropes”. It will be the first time Anderson will have written a complete script for a different director, although he was involved in uncredited rewrites of Martin Scorsese’s Killers of the Flower Moon and Ridley Scott’s Napoleon. He recently won three Oscars for One Battle After Another. The Guardian’s Sandra Newman called The Heart in Winter one of the best books of 2024, writing that it “effortlessly walks the line between goofy and gothic”. “This story is about the people who refused to settle for a life that is less than they deserve but maybe more than they can handle,” Spielberg also added. “Jessie and Cillian were the first people to ever come to mind for this and they also have never made a film together.” Earlier this year, Buckley won the best actress Oscar for her performance in Hamnet, produced by Spielberg, and will next be seen in The Three Incestuous Sisters alongside Saoirse Ronan, Dakota Johnson and Josh O’Connor. Murphy, who won the best actor Oscar for Oppenheimer, was last seen reprising his role of Jim in 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple and in Peaky Blinders: The Immortal Man. Next summer will also see him return to the Quiet Place franchise. The film will follow Spielberg’s sci-fi thriller Disclosure Day which made $247m worldwide upon release this past summer. A release date is yet to be officially confirmed yet but the film is believed to be scheduled for 2028.

title: You Can See Everything passes $100m at global box office as UK release starts strong
text: Elizabeth Holmes film You Can See Everything has crossed the $100m mark at the global box office as it recorded the highest ever opening weekend figure for a non-music documentary in the UK. Directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, You Can See Everything earned an estimated $2.5m over the weekend on its sixth week of release in North America, according to Box Office Mojo , bringing its total there to $93.5m. This has been augmented by successful releases in a number of international territories, which has added an estimated $9m for a total of $102.5m. This means the film is already the seventh highest grossing documentary of all time, in a list currently headed by the 2009 film Michael Jackson’s This Is It on $267.9m. In North America alone, it is now the third highest grossing documentary, behind Fahrenheit 9/11 and Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour. Despite releasing a month and a half later, the UK has seen stellar figures on the film’s first weekend in cinemas. Variety reports it took an estimated $3.2m (£2.4m) from more than 590 venues, itself a record for a non-music documentary. You Can See Everything has proved to be a significant commercial success for its backers, which include distribution outfit A24, with the film reportedly costing $7m to make.

title: Home Alone sequel reportedly in development with Macaulay Culkin returning
text: A Home Alone sequel is reportedly in development with original star Macaulay Culkin set to return. According to Puck’s Matthew Belloni , Culkin met with Disney executives earlier this year with a pitch for a follow-up and now the project has been met with a green light. The new Home Alone film will bring the 46-year-old back to the franchise as Kevin McCallister for a comedy that, according to Deadline , will be from the father’s point of view. The film will also recruit Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg as writers and producers and they will work with Culkin to craft the script. Rogen and Goldberg recently worked with Disney on a Muppets TV special. Home Alone was a major box office hit upon release in 1990, grossing $476m worldwide and becoming the year’s second-biggest movie. Culkin returned for the sequel Home Alone 2: Lost in New York, which made $359m two years later. The franchise continued without the actor for three further movies and then in 2021, after Fox had been bought by Disney, there was a straight-to-streaming reboot . Culkin later reprised the role in a 2018 commercial for Google and this year has once again returned as Kevin for a new McDonald’s advert . Last year, he was asked about a sequel at an anniversary event. “I kind of had this idea,” he said. “I’m either a widower or a divorcee. I’m raising a kid and all that stuff. I’m working really hard and I’m not really paying enough attention and the kid is kind of getting miffed at me and then I get locked out.” In his pitch, the character’s son won’t let him in and would be the one setting the traps with the house as “some sort of metaphor for our relationship”. The original film’s director, Chris Columbus, who later went on to direct the first two Harry Potter adventures, has spoken out about a possible sequel. “I think it’s a mistake to try to go back and recapture something we did 35 years ago,” he said. “I think it should be left alone.”

title: Gérard Depardieu and Michel Houellebecq investigated over on-set rape and assault allegations
text: French police are investigating allegations that the actor Gérard Depardieu and the author Michel Houellebecq gang-raped and assaulted a woman during a 2018 film shoot. The alleged attack took place in December 2018 during the shooting of Thalasso, a film starring the two men as versions of themselves who meet at a health spa and have long philosophical conversations while in white bath-robes. Two sources following the case confirmed to Agence France-Presse on Friday that a police investigation was under way. The investigative website Mediapart reported this week that an actor, given the pseudonym Alexandra, had made a complaint to police in 2025. Alexandra, an eastern European actor and dancer who was 32 at the time and working in France, told Mediapart that she was attacked by Depardieu and Houellebecq as they pinned her down during one scene and while cameras filmed. Mediapart reported that Alexandra described being “in a state of stupefaction and disconnect”. In her police complaint she had spoken of “deep humiliation” and “indescribable shame”. The film’s director, Guillaume Nicloux, had been accused of complicity in the sexual abuse, AFP reported. Nicloux told Mediapart that at the moment of filming he had not “noticed any constraint”, but he had “apologised” to Alexandra. Alexandra’s lawyers did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian. Depardieu’s lawyers did not respond to a request for comment. The Guardian contacted Houellebecq’s publishers, who did not respond. This week Depardieu, 77, dropped his appeal against a 2025 conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a different film set in 2021, and apologised to them. At his trial last year, Depardieu was found guilty of sexually assaulting a 55-year-old set dresser and a 35-year-old assistant director during the shooting of the feature film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters) in Paris in September 2021. His suspended sentence will now stand and his name has been added to France’s sex offender register. A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day After Depardieu’s apology this week, the assistant director whom he sexually assaulted said: “The monster of cinema has fallen.” Depardieu’s conviction last year was a turning point for the #MeToo movement in France . He became the biggest figure in the French film industry to be convicted of sexual assault after years of criticism of the country’s reluctance to take women’s claims of abuse seriously. He has appealed against a separate decision requiring him to face trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting the actor Charlotte Arnould at his Paris home in 2018. Appeal judges will rule this month on whether to uphold his appeal or allow the trial to go ahead next year. In an open letter to Le Figaro in October 2023, Depardieu denied all allegations and said any encounter with Arnould had been consensual. “Never, ever, have I abused a woman,” he wrote. Houellebecq, 70, who is among France’s most translated authors, is also under investigation for alleged incitement to discrimination in France over comments he made in 2022 about Muslims. Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland , or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland . In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

title: ‘I’m opening the cage of a monster’: Taxi Driver scriptwriter Paul Schrader on unleashing AI at 80
text: Paul Schrader was sipping white wine in a Greenwich Village trattoria when he said how he felt about using AI to make films: “I am opening the cage of a monster and I don’t have a leash.” The 80-year-old film-maker behind Taxi Driver , Raging Bull and American Gigolo, is embracing the technology as he enters the final act of a prolific career in which he has collaborated with Martin Scorsese, Robert De Niro, Sigourney Weaver and Richard Gere. Defying orthodox resistance among the Hollywood guilds to using AI to create synthetic actors, special effects and even scripts, Schrader is doing all of those things. It is part of what he sees as AI’s inevitable takeover, not just of cinema, the art he has pursued for half a century, writing and directing dozens of films to international acclaim, but of humankind more broadly. “I don’t see, quite frankly, a place for Homo sapiens in the larger scheme of things,” he told the Guardian. “I don’t think there’s a story where we come out on top. In order to create a story where … man defeats the threat of AI – it’s just a bogus story.” Yet, while directors ranging from his 1970s collaborator Steven Spielberg to the Odyssey’s Christopher Nolan , express deep scepticism about AI, Schrader is running towards, not away from, what he describes as a monster that he fears may soon imprison him. Schrader appears comfortable with the situation. He is after all, a film-maker who has done more than most to explore the anatomy of human alienation, most famously through Travis Bickle, played by De Niro in 1976’s Taxi Driver, who was partly drawn from Schrader’s early life as a drifter in seedy Los Angeles. Plus, he said: “I’m 80 years old, so … I’m going to be able to ride this broken horse to the sunset.” His solution appears to be: embrace AI both in work and in life. After this interview, Schrader had a date to dine with strangers matched up by the technology. He has had relationships with AI, intentionally and inadvertently. He is announcing details of a new horror-thriller, The Doors of Perception, which is being built around a series of AI-generated psychedelic hallucinations. Schrader experimented with the psychedelic drug ayahuasca shortly after the death of his wife of 43 years, the actor Mary Beth Hurt, in March. He took it eight times during a two-week retreat in Costa Rica, and was disappointed not to experience visual hallucinations himself. “I got to sit there for five hours looking at a wall,” he said. “I loved the music. It was kind of cool to be in a room of 40-50 people who are all puking at the same time.” Schrader will rely on a collaboration with the San Francisco-based AI film studio Fable to imagine the hallucinations in his new film. These will be an integral part of the story of two brothers’ hunt for their mother’s killer, who they believe can be tracked by getting inside the trip. The script calls for an AI version of an ayahuasca ceremony in the Peruvian jungle and Schrader has been impressed by the technology’s ability to make judgments about how such things are shot. “They vomit, they puke and they start to have visions and the AI said to me: ‘How graphic do you want [this] to be? I suggest you do it more discreetly.’ I said I think it’s a good idea. It’s making a conscious artistic choice.” On other projects, he has also been screen-testing AI actors, concluding “you could certainly do a whole film” and remarking that at least AI actors are always available, free and on time. In September, Schrader sparked a storm of controversy when he said he was turning to AI characters to realise his script Three Guns at Dawn – a story about three Black, criminal brothers – after leading Black actors declined parts. “We sent it out to actors, and no Black actors wanted to play in a movie where there are no good Black people,” he said . “And it sort of died. But then AI came along, and I didn’t need Black actors.” Schrader has also been weighing up an AI version of a western, which he has

title: ‘My body started consuming itself. I was a millimetre from death’: Andrey Zvyagintsev on Covid, Putin and life in exile
text: A ndrey Zvyagintsev tells the tale of a knight who is riding through a dark forest and sees a stone sign at a fork in the road. The sign says that if he turns left he will lose his horse and if he turns right he will lose his head. So the knight has a dilemma; there are only bad options here. Zvyagintsev smiles and says: “It is a very Russian fairytale.” Terrible things tend to happen, that’s the way the world works, and a person is defined by how they respond to each challenge. That goes for the knight in the forest and the characters in a film. It probably goes for Zvyagintsev, too, who has lost not his horse but his home and very nearly his life. The Russian director almost died during the Covid-19 pandemic and spent 40 days in an induced coma . He now lives in exile as an enemy of the state. “I’m with the birds,” he says by way of explaining his situation. “Birds have no borders. They’re not thinking about tomorrow.” Zvyagintsev’s new film, Minotaur, is a mighty, mesmerising drama of personal and political corruption that has Ukraine as its touchstone, or perhaps its dark fork in the road. He makes no bones about his opposition to the war. Taking the stage at this year’s Cannes film festival, where Minotaur won the grand jury prize, he called on Vladimir Putin to “stop this butchery”, adding that “the whole world is waiting”. In September Russia named him as a “foreign agent” spreading disinformation. He now risks arrest and imprisonment if he dares to go home. Today he is living out of a suitcase in a central London hotel; sipping bottled water and buffing the lenses of his specs. At 62, Zvyagintsev has the air of a college professor hosting a one-on-one tutorial. He’s erudite and charismatic, peppering his answers with quotes from Borges, Nietzsche and Savonarola. Who’s Savonarola? “A medieval friar,” he says. “A Catholic preacher. Very fierce.” Zvyagintsev looks well but explains that his health is precarious. “My illness in 2021, 2022 has been following me ever since. It caused irreversible damage and presents serious challenges to the peripheral nervous system. So I’m not confident in my steps. I spend a lot of energy just to keep my balance. In Cannes, if you remember, I stumbled going up the steps to collect the award.” He shrugs. “Maybe you didn’t notice. My friends all noticed. Zoe Saldaña noticed. She had to reach out and catch me.” There are no stumbles in Minotaur: it barely puts a foot wrong. Zvyagintsev’s film tells the tale of Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov), a businessman caught between the proverbial rock and hard place. Gleb suspects that his wife may be having an affair, but he has also been asked to sacrifice 14 employees to fight on the frontline. Ukraine, one comes to realise, is the film’s peripheral horror and malign guiding spirit. The war is at once a faint, distant rumble and a monster so present that it might be breathing down Gleb’s neck. Minotaur, Zvyagintsev’s first film since 2017’s acclaimed Loveless , is a loose remake of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 thriller La Femme Infidèle. The director explains that he initially tried to make it back in 2018 but wasn’t able to obtain the rights. “Looking back now, this was a good resolution. It would have been a completely different film, without any historical context.” Ukraine provided the project with the spark that it needed. Tangentially perhaps, his illness did too. In the summer of 2021, he was given the Sputnik V Covid vaccine and came down with a fever. He was transferred from Moscow to a hospital in Germany where his condition became critical. Insofar as he knew what was happening, Zvyagintsev feared the worst. “August 2021. I associate it with death. Because the reality is that I should have died. Every day, that’s what my wife heard from the doctors. ‘Be ready, be prepared. It could be today.’ They were signing me off to the afterlife.” Was the vaccine to blame? He shrugs. “No one knows. title: Alex Cox: ‘John Lydon said Sid and Nancy was a nightmarish piece of garbage’
text: Looking back, how do you regard your experience with Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas? And did you watch Terry Gilliam ’s version? AwapBamBoogers No, I didn’t watch it. I felt very sad about the whole thing because my wife and I were co-screenwriters. We went out to meet Hunter S Thompson and the poor guy was in a terrible state. He was hoovering up cocaine the whole time we were there. He had a great big TV screen, with a Post-it note saying: “Don’t watch too much TV.” We said we felt like his caseworkers, because all these guys in Hollywood like Johnny Depp were winding him up: “Dr Thompson, do something crazy, go out in the back garden and shoot a can of propane.” That’s all very well, but they were treating him like the freak in the county fairground. How many years was it after Fear and Loathing that the poor guy killed himself? He really needed an intervention. Instead, he was being encouraged by these Hollywood bastards. The giant boar in Razorback gave me nightmares when I saw it on Moviedrome . Did it give you nightmares too? Sootsayer I don’t remember. The films in Moviedrome were picked by [producer and director] Nick Freand Jones, who had access to all the films the BBC had under licence and didn’t know what to do with. Some of them I remember really well, but as I’m not so into horror films, I don’t remember Razorback. What does Liverpool mean to you and how has it influenced your career? AmongstTheWaves I was born just outside [in Bebington], so I’m not really a scouser. When Liverpool was awarded European capital of culture in 2008, it wasn’t because of the Three Graces on the Pier Head . It was because of the incredible creativity of the people. Liverpool doesn’t really look towards London, it looks across the Atlantic, because of the shipping, so it’s always been very independent. It’s a very interesting city, but, of course, I’m prejudiced. How did Michael Nesmith from the Monkees help get Repo Man made? Melquiades We were looking for somebody to executive produce the film and find the money, so I was introduced to him by another producer called Harry Gittes. He liked the script, partially because it had a four-page cartoon at the beginning, and he was very into comic books. Nesmith said to me: “Cox, I don’t think you’re going to have punk rock music all the way through. I want to see a variety of music.” But one song at a time, we put in all these punk songs, and Nesmith went with it. He was a very cool guy. Do you still agree with the line from Repo Man: “The more you drive, the less intelligent you are? ” rewilder That’s something my wife said when we were still students at UCLA and, at the time, I did believe it. Now I think that if you’re not relying on driver-assist technology, driving is an interesting occupation. It enables you to focus on something in the distance rather than staring at a screen in front of you. Right now I’m crowdfunding Repo Man 2, set in a world of driverless cars. Instead of sneaking down people’s drives, hotwiring cars and running away, the repo man just sits at a computer, takes control and drives the car to the sheriff’s substation or repo yard. It’s a different world, but the same kind of malevolence. Has crowdfunding become the best way to remain genuinely independent? NorthPixel27 For independent film-makers, yes, because the studios and the big streamers are really only interested in franchises and massive IPs. They want to spend a lot of money, but they don’t really care what the film is. Often they don’t read the script. In the case of Repo Man, it was obvious Universal hadn’t read the script. It got greenlit because of some people Nesmith met in a bar. The people who will back a Kickstarter actually want to see the film.
