title: Chemicals, Covid and cabbage: why 2026 has been an amazing year for documentaries
text: T here comes a time in the life of every film enthusiast when they must set aside foolish fictions and face up to some hard truths. Specifically, that time arrives each November in the form of the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam (IDFA for short), with its tales of crisis and strife, angry resistance and everyday human kindness. The world’s largest documentary festival plays out in the city’s twinkling downtown district, quite near the torture museum, and provides a sharp corrective to the confected dramas and A-list pageantry of Cannes, Toronto and Venice. The forecast is bracing, stormy, and occasionally chilling. Hours of darkness; no stars. We might not wish to live in the world IDFA shows us, but unfortunately we do, and so it pays to stay informed, be engaged. This year’s lineup of 250-plus documentaries steers us around the geopolitical hot spots, from tales of forced displacement in the West Bank to the rolling hell of Gaza; from a jungle-based guerrilla army in Myanmar (in White Tiger Column, the event’s opening night film) through to the traumatised children of the Vietnamese boat people (Carol Nguyen’s superb Still Night, Burning House). Some of these films could have been torn from the headlines. Others, like Raluca Lupascu’s gripping kitchen-sink tragedy A Modern Roma Fairytale, contain stories previously tucked away out of sight, just waiting to be told. Blame the planet, says Isabel Arrate Fernandez, IDFA’s artistic director. The film-makers are responding to the world they have witnessed. “I know there’s the idea that the films will all be too depressing,” she says. “Yes, sometimes documentaries can take you to places of suffering and pain. But that’s all around us. If we turn away from that we’re only staying in our privileged bubble. And documentary cinema is so much more than just depressing and gruelling. Sometimes a film can enter your heart. And sometimes, yes, it can hit you in the stomach.” Documentary is traditionally seen as the industry’s poor cousin, although that wealth gap may now be closing. IDFA’s 39th edition lands at the end of a breakout season for the genre, spearheaded by the success of Alex Gibney’s four-hour-long Musk , the Guardian-produced NAZA and Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything , which has just passed $100m at the global box office. All three films are on the bill at IDFA. A panel discussion with the makers of NAZA lands as a last-minute addition to the programme. “It’s been tough for documentaries since the pandemic,” says Fionnuala Jamison, the managing director of NAZA’s sales agent, mk2. “This is the first year you’ve seen documentaries outside the music sphere that have broken through. So it absolutely gives us hope that things might be changing.” Arrate Fernandez agrees it’s been a vintage year. All the same, she is keen to inject a note of caution. “It’s the buzz around a few titles that is generating this wider idea about [the success of] documentaries,” she explains. “Everyone is saying the same thing, but does that mean it is real? It’s difficult to say. At IDFA we have films from all over the world. If you fix on a few specific films – I’m thinking mainly of You Can See Everything and Musk, not so much NAZA – then there is a danger of leaving out other parts of the world.” On balance, it is good. It means renewed interest; bums on seats. “What’s interesting for me about films like Musk or You Can See Everything is not so much that they’re breaking the rules of documentary cinema as that they are breaking the expectations and assumptions of what a documentary can achieve and the people it can reach. That’s how they’re breaking the mould and that’s what’s valuable to me. These films show that the gatekeepers have been underestimating the audience.” I’m not sure there’s a direct line from Fielder and Oppenheim’s showstopper to the other, more obscure films on the schedule. But if it cracks open a door, that may just be enough. Beyon

title: You can see everything on this list: the 20 most jaw-dropping documentaries – ranked!
text: A 50-second dispatch from daily life blew the whistle on the approaching juggernaut of cinema and its unbeatable horsepower of verisimilitude. But if we must be strictly factual about the iconic Lumière brothers’ short, the anecdote about audience members fleeing their seats in fear of being crushed by the oncoming locomotive probably never happened . The dramatic re-enactment is the car chase of the documentary industry: a crude way of keeping our attention. But by using rotoscoped animation, Keith Maitland’s riveting account of the 1966 mass shooting at the University of Texas completely revitalises the re-enactment as part of the documentary toolkit. It leaves us prone under the killer’s crosshairs with the emotional immediacy of a thriller and an oddly elegiac comedown. Amid the 21st century true-crime deluge, it’s a relief to stumble on a less violent mystery that foregrounds women’s lives rather than their deaths. But the Chilean director Maite Alberdi’s docudrama still skirts the boundaries of credibility: it focuses on Ale, a desperate Mexican mother who, after three miscarriages, duped her husband into believing she was pregnant. With Alberdi also trying to verify whether Ale was a child-snatcher, the story of this bizarre long con doubles up as a metaphysical inquiry into the ultimate knowability of people. Documentaries often introduce us to indelible personalities, but it’s vanishingly rare when they initiate us, Narnia-style, into entire new realms. Marc Singer unearthed one in the homeless community of “mole men” living in abandoned subway tunnels extending out of Penn Station in New York City. With DJ Shadow’s mindscape compositions lighting the way into the gloom, this is a grimly transfixing voyage to the centre of urban deprivation. This early Alex Gibney cut was shocking in the mid-00s – surely boardroom cynicism and corporate fraud couldn’t occur on this scale? Now, its revelations about the collapse of the US energy company – and the underlying profit-falsifying – feel like a taster for You Can See Everything ’s tech-company chicanery and the post-truth air we all breathe. A prime cut of Werner Herzogian insanity, yet somehow the great master never laid claim to this high-seas tragedy . The amateur sailor Donald Crowhurst bit off more than he could chew when he entered a 1968 solo circumnavigation race. Floundering in the Atlantic, he faked his own positions for seven months. The quixotic madness seems to infect everyone: a French competitor, Bernard Moitessier, having rounded the globe once, opts to keep going. From Frank Capra’s recruitment drive to Ken Burns’ Vietnam panorama , war documentaries employ all manner of tactics. But for sheer concussive immersiveness, it’s hard to beat Sebastian Junger’s and Tim Hetherington’s stint embedded with the US’s lost boys in the Korangal valley in Afghanistan. Although it ducks political commentary, the ever-present sense of threat from the Taliban is indictment enough of the forever war. The city-symphony documentary is as old as cinema – and Godfrey Reggio’s Gesamtkunstwerk is the most monumental. Pulling a Kubrick, it starts by juxtaposing neolithic drawings and a rocket launch, then blasts us through ever-accelerating stages of human civilisation in between, soundtracked by Philip Glass’s incantatory score. How about an update for capitalism’s endgame phase of AI chaos? Stowed aboard a Massachusetts trawler, this experimental marvel is like swilling around in the chowder of Captain Ahab’s dreams. It’s a narration-free montage of hurtling anchors, churning spume, loitering seagulls and asphyxiated fish sliding into the maw of the boat – presumably the leviathan of the title. Attended to by tattooed, cigarette-toting seadogs, you feel as if you’re merging with the vessel’s consciousness. Any footage of someone climbing the 900-metre Yosemite landmark El Capitan would have captured our attention. But doing it unroped for the first time , as the daredevil Alex Hon

title: You Can See Everything’s vibes-check approach is an insult to objective truth
text: S ometimes, people who have lied lie about whether or not they’ve lied. They even, on occasion, fail to tell the truth despite having sworn to do so – in court, for instance, or staring deeply into the eyes of someone who is sitting right there . Is that a shock? Probably not. We all engage in versions of such behaviour every day. We understand that the current climate of mutually clueless echo chambers helps claptrap gain traction. But we can still recognise the difference between little white lies and big red flags. We know that the moment anyone starts using the phrase “my truth” it’s time to cancel the wedding. You Can See Everything acts as if this isn’t the case. It operates in a realm of smart and artful naivety. In order to interrogate whether or not Elizabeth Holmes, founder of magical medical tech company Theranos, is – as she claims – the tragic victim of a miscarriage of justice, Nathan Fielder moves into the annexe of her home for a few weeks before she starts her 11-year prison term for fraud. “You can see everything,” she promises him brightly, juggling babies and her godawful boyfriend. Fab access! A gift to the documentarian! So Fielder duly blinkers up and blinds himself to anything concrete. He does not discuss the court case. He does not examine the reams of actual evidence that resulted in her conviction. Beyond a long chat about the semantics of the word “can”, he does not ask Holmes what the hell she was playing at. Instead, his technique is an extended vibes check. He looks into Holmes’s eyes, noses nearly rubbing. He asks her if she was lying. He does this a couple more times, just in case. This is undoubtedly compelling (for a while, at least). The fine line between profundity and banality means a lot of the movie, with its pore-boring closeups, is pretty gripping. But it’s also perverse and dangerous. You Can See Everything rejects the idea of a generally agreed consensus over what has happened – even as an aim, and even at a time when that concept is under considerable threat. In its clever, meta way, Fielder’s film therefore presents the most pernicious attack on objective truth I’ve seen – precisely because it’s so liberal and slippery. Rather, the film represents a massive slap in the face for the judicial system, as well as for Tyler Shultz and Erika Cheung, the primary Theranos whistleblowers. Plus all the journalists who meticulously investigated the case over many years, including John Carreyrou and Amy Chozick, whose New York Times reporting is not covered by the film, except to dispute one barely-relevant element of it. It is also an insult to the victims of the Theranos scandal. Not just the millionaires who lost money but the many, many people who suffered because they were fed false medical results by Holmes’s dodgy box. That background means the film’s soapiness can stick in the throat. The more we’re encouraged to wonder whether Fielder might fancy Holmes a bit, and maybe it might actually be mutual, the more the real-world consequences of her actions seem to hover unhelpfully over footage of them flirting. A fascinating and bleak fraud case is digested into a thin vehicle for dopey ponderings. Things like: are you for real? Am I for real? Can you ever really tell if anyone’s for real? And that, I think, is one of the reasons the film has been so successful. Just like the rest of us, Fielder seems uninterested in facts – he’s all about the feels. We all appear to believe that the really essential truth now is an emotional one. You Can See Everything taps the zeitgeist like few movies before it. For me, that’s what makes it so frightening.

title: Delays mean Robert Pattinson doesn’t have to do a third Batman movie. DC Studios had better persuade him – and fast
text: C an one actor play both Batman and James Bond? This is the question many have been asking since Robert Pattinson was announced as the new 007 . The obvious answer is yes: the 40-year-old Englishman has the poise, charisma and steel to join His Majesty’s Secret Service, and saving Gotham could soon become something he fits in between assignments. Among all the furore over Pattinson’s appointment, it would have been easy to miss some rather less cheering news for the citizens of Gotham. According to the Wrap , delays to The Batman: Part II have freed the actor from his contractual obligation to make a third film. The sequel is now due in February 2028, almost six years after the first instalment. He could still sign a new deal, of course, but Warner Bros will have to persuade its caped crusader to stick around. Four years ago, when The Batman hit cinemas to a chorus of critical acclaim for its brooding blend of detective noir and superhero spectacle, there would have been little question that the studio was all in. The film took more than $770m worldwide and seemed to promise a trilogy that might one day give Christopher Nolan’s Dark Knight triptych a run for its money. But much has changed since then. For one thing, Matt Reeves is no longer directing the remainder of the sequel’s principal photography, having stepped away from the production in October to focus on a family matter. Steven Soderbergh has been drafted in to finish filming, though Reeves says he remains committed to the project. Nevertheless, the unexpected change of director adds another layer of uncertainty to the franchise. Meanwhile, the takeover of Warner Bros by David Ellison’s Skydance has brought a changing of the guard at DC Studios , with James Gunn and Peter Safran departing and former Marvel executive Jeremy Latcham taking charge. The new regime wants to get DC’s superhero universe moving rather faster, which may not bode well for maintaining two separate versions of Batman. Gunn and Safran had envisaged a new, non-Pattinson caped crusader appearing in a project titled The Brave and the Bold, alongside Reeves’s standalone films. Whether Latcham maintains that enthusiasm remains to be seen. You can see why the new management might want to cut the number of Batmen in half. Gotham’s defender of the night has been something of a law unto himself for decades, with successive directors allowed to reinvent him, while Warner Bros struggled to establish a coherent universe featuring Superman, Wonder Woman and the rest of the Justice League. For a studio desperate to emulate Marvel’s success at interconnected storytelling, maintaining a separate, apparently incompatible Batman might seem like an unnecessary complication. But would anyone really want Reeves’s Batman sharing a universe with Superman? His dark knight inhabits a grimy, rain-soaked city of corrupt politicians, mobsters and serial killers, where he is unlikely to encounter a rampaging alien warlord. The introduction of Superman would risk puncturing the film’s carefully constructed atmosphere. Reeves has managed to make Batman feel like a detective again, rather than a billionaire who occasionally takes time off to investigate local crime. None of this necessarily means Pattinson cannot play both roles. Bond is likely to occupy a substantial chunk of his working life for the foreseeable future, but it is hardly as though Reeves’s films have been arriving at a furious rate. And Harrison Ford managed to play both Han Solo and Indiana Jones, after all. The bigger question is whether the actor really wants to spend his time leading two of the most demanding franchises in cinema, particularly when he is no longer contractually obliged to complete the Batman trilogy. It would be ironic if Warner Bros ended up sacrificing one of its few genuinely distinctive superhero franchises just as the wider DC universe was beginning to find its feet. Pattinson may yet be persuaded to return – and the studio and Skydanc

title: Robert Pattinson’s gift for cool, sensual menace makes him an exquisite choice as James Bond | Peter Bradshaw
text: I f it wasn’t Bond … maybe it would have been Dr No in some hi-tech reboot. But Robert Pattinson – with his movie-star chops and track record in hip A24-type character turns, and his gift for cool, inscrutable appraisal and sensual menace – is an exquisite choice as 007, playing on the darker and more sophisticated notes of Pattinson’s performing personality. And let’s hope, incidentally, that the actor now isn’t forced into a five-hour daily gym regimen to bulk up. I like the taller and more willowy Bond that Pattinson represents, the Bond from whose frame the tux hangs gracefully, the Bond with elegant abandon who’s a former British Naval officer, not a former US Navy Seal, the Bond who with a crinkly-eyed reptilian grin can style out waking up with a hangover after too many whisky-and-sodas at the baccarat table. But I like to think also that Pattinson could convert the diversionary cuff-shooting gesture of consulting his Rolex, to delivering a single lethal punch to the enemy’s unguarded solar plexus. (Although fisticuffs will be for the lower order of henchpersons; the Pattinson 007’s final confrontation with the primo villain will probably involve more hi-tech weaponry.) Pattinson could be a Bond to combine Roger Moore’s insouciance with the chill of Michael Lonsdale’s portrayal of plutocrat-villain Hugo Drax. At 40 years old, Pattinson’s Bond will be a more worldly and mature agent, and his entire career has arguably been leading to this moment – establishment schooling at Hogwarts (rather than Fettes) as the doomed Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire all the way through to the darkly conflicted caped crusader Batman in Matt Reeves’s 2022 film, lurking athletically in the shadows – like Bond, used to working in secret. He didn’t play Batman for Christopher Nolan, but for Nolan he interestingly played the slightly seedy British intelligence insider Neil in Nolan’s 2020 sci-fi Tenet and the unscrupulous Antinous this year in The Odyssey – both not good guys, character roles, both showing Pattinson’s class as well as his presence. Yet perhaps his most intriguing pre-Bond or proto-Bond outing might have been the alienated super-rich guy cruising the New York streets in his stretch limo in David Cronenberg’s Cosmopolis. Like Bond (or a future Bond) that was someone developing a tough, invulnerable carapace. Yet for all the saturnine, even serpentine presence, Pattinson’s 007 could well be the one to find something other than the traditional cliched machismo and sexism in Bond in his relationship with female characters and indeed female colleagues – perhaps we might even see Bond’s feminine side. It’s an exciting bit of (long-delayed) casting.

title: The DCU’s James Gunn and Peter Safran are out – this is the biggest disaster to hit superhero movies in years
text: W hat was Warner Bros’ plan in 2022 , when the studio decided to reboot its superhero output, jettison the increasingly muddled DC Extended Universe (DCEU) and replace it with a sparkling new DC Universe (DCU)? In part it was to wipe the slate clean after years of false starts, abandoned storylines and tonal lurches. There was a little bit of Marvel envy to proceedings, and quite possibly a desire to avoid having to ever again discuss Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice’s numerous failings . But mostly it was to take advantage of hiring of a man whom nobody could accuse of being short of ideas on how to make comic book movies. To a greater or lesser extent, the plan was James Gunn. Fast forward four years, and that plan lies in tatters. Gunn and his fellow DC Studios CEO Peter Safran have this week been fired (though they will reportedly stay on as film-makers), and Jeremy Latcham, another former Marvel man, is the new boss. What is the plan now? Nobody seems to know, and there is not much point asking David Ellison, the man whose Skydance empire has now gobbled up two of the former big five Hollywood studios (Paramount last year and Warner last month). That would be like asking for directions from a man who has just set fire to the map. We were told that Gunn was going to finally make sense of DC – which had always been Marvel’s poor relation on the big screen – and deliver a shared universe that would take advantage of the comic book publisher’s rich cavalcade of heroes, villains and assorted caped lunatics. Warner Bros Discovery CEO David Zaslav spoke of a “bold 10-year plan” for the superhero studio after the Gunn-directed Superman delivered a strong start for the franchise last summer, with $618m at the global box office and decent reviews. Since then, results have been mixed. The lukewarm Supergirl drastically underperformed earlier this year, but last month’s horror spin-off Clayface has quietly done respectable business, taking around $111m worldwide on a reported $40m budget. On the small screen, shows such as Peacemaker and Lanterns wove connections into the studio’s movies that Marvel would have killed to generate, even if the latter series has – inexplicably – not yet been renewed. The output may not have been perfect, but fans were encouraged by the sense that a film-maker who actually understood comic books was holding the reins. That optimism has now been rudely punctured. The concern is that Gunn was fired precisely because he was making bold choices, and that Latcham is the unwelcome antidote. The incoming CEO has spoken openly about his desire to make films that feel “redemptive” and “hopeful”, and about the informal “grandmother test” he used at Marvel: if his grandparents in Oklahoma might not understand or enjoy something, perhaps it was not sufficiently universal. None of this necessarily means DC is about to become the comic book equivalent of the Lifetime channel, and Latcham’s credits do include Guardians of the Galaxy and Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves. But fans who have enjoyed Gunn’s foul-mouthed antiheroes, exploding torsos and creatures that look as though they have crawled out of a cheese dream may be wondering whether the next phase of the DCU will come with considerably more approved family seating. The Hollywood trades suggest that Ellison had grown impatient with the DCU’s slow-burn approach, and rapidly wanted to bring back the big guns – Superman, Batman and Wonder Woman, the nucleus of the Justice League. It is at this point that we have to question whether anyone in the corridors of power has been paying attention. The most recent DC universe to fail, the DCEU, began its long descent into chaos and diminishing returns precisely because Warner Bros encouraged film-makers into crossover events and ensemble movies such as Batman v Superman and Justice League, before it had properly established most of its core heroes in their own right. A rush to get to the good stuff feels like exac

title: Concertgoers criticise ‘atrocious’ lack of security at Manchester Co-op Live gig
text: Concertgoers in Manchester have criticised an “atrocious” lack of security at the Co-op Live arena after suspected teargas left fans “screaming for help” and caused thousands to be evacuated. A second person was taken to hospital on Monday with burns to their nose and throat following the incident during a show by the American rapper Don Toliver on Sunday night. Greater Manchester police (GMP), which declared a major incident, initially said it believed teargas had been released into the 12,000-strong crowd, but investigations into the nature of the substance were continuing. One person was taken to hospital on the night and 88 were assessed by clinicians at Britain’s biggest indoor arena, which opened in 2024. A 16-year-old boy, who did not want to be named, was taken to hospital on Monday with burns to his nose and throat after standing next to the concertgoer believed to have released the gas. His mother told the Guardian: “He saw it go off and then he said literally within three breaths he could feel it in his chest burning. He said it was the worst pain he’s ever experienced in his life, like someone was stood on his chest. He tried to get out of the building then he fell to the floor.” The teenager was one of dozens taken to a makeshift quarantine centre at the tennis courts opposite Co-op Live where they had to take off their clothing and shoes before changing into white boiler suits, she said. After about two hours outside in near-zero temperatures, the young patients were taken to a VIP area inside Co-op Live but parents were not allowed to take them home until they had been medically assessed. The boy’s mother said other fans, many wearing balaclavas, were setting off flares and smoke canisters despite them being banned. She said venues appeared to have “learned nothing” from the Manchester Arena terror attack, in which 22 people were killed at the end of an Ariana Grande concert in 2017: “This time it was just teargas but if they can carry that in what else can they carry in? It doesn’t bear thinking about.” Toliver, who was performing on his Nitrous tour, was forced to postpone Monday’s planned show at the O2 in London due to production delays as a result of the abandoned Manchester concert. Co-op Live, which is owned by the US entertainment giant Oak View Group, was accused of having an “atrocious” lack of security at Sunday’s concert, where witnesses saw fans being allowed in without having their bags checked and some without tickets were allegedly let in after “hopping the barriers”. Jobe O’Connor, 18, said the checks were “really shocking” and that he and his friends felt “quite traumatised” by the ordeal, describing how fans were “throwing up, some were blinded and were getting carried out by their friends”. O’Connor said he saw several people walk through “lacklustre” security without being checked: “After the Ariana Grande concert nearly 10 years ago, you would’ve thought Manchester, of all places, would be really, really tight, but to see it quite relaxed was really shocking, really poor.” Toliver was about 40 minutes into the show when he suddenly ran offstage and the main lights came on. It was nearly another hour before fans were told the concert was cancelled, and in that time there was “zero communication”, some said. Witnesses described seeing fans “coughing up blood” and others “crying and screaming for help”. Dozens of armed police and emergency response vehicles raced to the venue, which is next to Manchester City’s Etihad stadium, after GMP declared a major incident at about 10pm. Another concertgoer, who gave his name as Harper, told BBC Radio Manchester he was in “disbelief” at seeing fans allowed in after “hopping over the ticket barrier”, adding: “There was one measly metal detector that people could easily walk around – which people did – and no bag searches. “There was a few security on that just didn’t care, which is even worse than having none. They still put wristbands on people they saw

title: They’re one of the UK’s greatest cult bands – who swore they’d never reunite. What brought Life Without Buildings back together?
text: ‘I’m excited, I’m scared, I’m anxious – that bubbling feeling, like when you’re on a rollercoaster, at the very top, just before the big drop.” On a drizzly afternoon in July, huddled with her three bandmates in the cramped cupboard that’s the dressing room of Glasgow venue Mono, Sue Tompkins is managing her feelings ahead of her first proper gig with Life Without Buildings in almost a quarter of a century. “Everybody coming is invited, it’s secret, nobody paid much to get in, the profits are going to charity,” adds guitarist Robert Dallas Gray, sat beside her, as much to steady his own nerves as to explain the circumstances of tonight’s show. “I hope people aren’t looking at it like we’re fucking entertainers .” Sat inches across from them, drummer Will Bradley breaks into a dry chuckle. “We are certainly not going to entertain.” Life Without Buildings ended too soon, just before a post-punk revival in the early 00s that would have embraced their taut, innovative music, and years before the recent sprechgesang (spoken singing) movement – Dry Cleaning, Yard Act et al – that seemed to draw inspiration from Tompkins’ unique vocals, though her inspired flood of babble and rhythmic poetry has a disruptive, joyful magic that sets her far apart. In three years, they released one sublime studio album and a handful of singles, and played numerous shows, sometimes to packed rooms, often to just five to 10 people, before splitting in 2002 having achieved “only minor cult/niche success”, says Bradley. Long after their trail went cold, however, this buried treasure of turn-of-the-millennium indie was rediscovered. In 2018, Frank Ocean played The Leanover, their signature track, on his Apple Music show. Then, one morning during lockdown, Beatrice Laus (AKA Beabadoobee) mimed along to the evocative first 11 seconds of The Leanover to entertain her followers on TikTok, who then shared themselves miming to those same 11 seconds (Beabadoobee’s initial TikTok has now been streamed almost half a million times). Two decades on, Life Without Buildings found their audience, who will finally get to see the group play this week, as they briefly reunite for four gigs marking Rough Trade’s 50th birthday celebrations. “Robert, Will and I started playing music,” says bassist Chris Evans, of the group’s origins in late-90s Glasgow. “But that didn’t work out.” The trio were under the spell of experimental German electronic music, listening to lots of Underground Resistance, techno and post-rockers Disco Inferno. “We’d combine electronics with live guitar and drums,” says Gray. “And it always sounded bollocks.” They reformatted as a guitar, bass and drums unit, though the music they played was far from traditional, often chasing the same riff for hours at a time. “But everything changed when Sue joined,” says Gray. Tompkins was a member of Elizabeth Go, a local art collective whose number included Cathy Wilkes, Victoria Morton, Sarah Tripp and Tompkins’ sister Hayley, at whose events she would perform from sheets of handwritten and typewritten paper. “She was brilliant ,” says Bradley. “We all said, ‘This is it’. There was no doubt.” They invited her to their practice space, playing song ideas at length, Tompkins selecting pieces she could work with as they pared their riffs back to the melodic bone. The music was “rock’n’roll, but like Television and the Modern Lovers were rock’n’roll, not Status Quo,” says Gray. “It was about doing the unexpected. We were conscious to not be boring.” Some songs took a direction they dubbed “Krautrock Keith Richards”, while others were “tumbling around, falling over themselves”. The Leanover was of this second category and was “the breakthrough. We recorded the demo in my bedroom, Sue with a cheap microphone, the rest of us squashed up on my bed watching her.” During rehearsals, Tompkins would write on sheets of A4 that she’d later edit at her electric typewriter, which she operated like a musical instrument, creating rhyt

title: ‘I have to sell my bum on OnlyFans to go on tour’: Kate Nash on fame, feminism and fighting the music business
text: K ate Nash was standing on a fire truck in a showgirl outfit complete with white tights and pink G-string, shouting through a loudhailer about the music industry’s failure to pay artists fairly, when she wondered if she’d gone too far. It was 2024 and the truck, which made pit stops outside the London offices of Spotify and Live Nation, had a large black-and-white picture of Nash’s bum on the back along with the words “Butts for Tour Buses” – a reference to her newly launched OnlyFans account, which she was using to fund her tour. That afternoon, she called her manager Kat. “I told her: ‘I’ve thrown a brick through the window at Spotify.’ She went: ‘What, literally?’ and I said: ‘No, but I’ve been standing outside their offices with a megaphone, so that relationship is over. I don’t think we’ll be making their New Music Friday feature.’” (She did.) Nash, the Brit award-winning singer and actor who rose to fame 20 years ago in the Myspace era, is not one to run away from a fight. Frustration and fury burned early in her career when she spoke up about the trolling from the tabloid press, which ran derogatory pieces about her appearance, and from strangers on the internet. She recalls receiving a message shortly before her chart-topping debut album Made of Bricks came out in 2007. “The title of the message was, ‘You are …’ and I opened it wondering: ‘Ooh, what am I?’ I thought it was fanmail. And this person said: ‘You are everything that’s wrong with music distilled into one slag.’ So it’s been a journey. It takes a long time to get to a place of ‘I don’t give a fuck’.” It’s a crisp October day when Nash and I meet in a cafe near her home in north London. She is nursing a cold, though that hasn’t diluted her fervour when talking about the plight of working musicians. In the last 12 months, she has appeared before a parliamentary select committee to talk about the financial impact of Brexit on touring artists. “I’m in a position of privilege because I am making money from my catalogue,” she tells me. “But I still need to sell my bum on OnlyFans to go on tour. I’ve got friends who are selling all their instruments and furniture to tour, or they’re not going on tour and they’re depressed.” Nash bangs the table. “It makes me so mad!” she continues. “Where will we be in 20 years when we only have stadium acts? I’m not dissing those who do it, but I don’t want everything to be mainstream. I also want to see mid-level and small gigs. Without that, there’s no culture and no fanbase. It’s a broken system and I don’t think it’s fair.” She stops, and laughs. “Sorry, I get a bit passionate.” To understand the roots of Nash’s fighting spirit, her forthcoming album offers some clues. Recorded in Spiddal on the west coast of Ireland, Cailín – it means “girl” in Irish – sees her exploring her Irish heritage through music that blends uilleann pipes, flutes and the tin whistle (Nash has played it since childhood) with punk and hip-hop. “I came in wanting to mess with trad Irish music and do something with it that hadn’t been done before,” she says. Nash, whose mother is Irish, grew up in an Irish-Catholic community in north-west London, though she came to realise that “being half-English, I didn’t know about my own history, and I wanted to learn. It’s all quite emotional for me.” It wasn’t until she began recording, for instance, that she learned her grandfather was part of a group of men who tried to travel to Spain to fight Franco, though were intercepted en route and imprisoned at Curragh Camp in County Kildare. “We have a family motto: ‘I’m not looking for a fight, but if you’ve got one, I’m your man,’” Nash says. Among the most arresting tracks on Cailín is her cover of Famine, Sinéad O’Connor’s song about the Great Hunger in Ireland that left a million dead. The lyrics tell how it was not a natural disaster, but a human-made catastrophe created by British rulers who shipped vital food supplies out of the country while the potato crop failed

title: Is Lorenzo Senni’s All Ages the year’s wildest electronic album?
text: T he opening line of the biography on Lorenzo Senni’s Bandcamp page is striking. “Lorenzo Senni was never a raver,” it reads, something of a blunt admission from a dance producer, or at least a producer who works in an area of electronica influenced by dance music: one might reasonably assume you need some first-hand experience of the dancefloor’s ineffable freedom in order to make music for it. But the Milan-based Senni has made a USP out of his arm’s length distance from what that Bandcamp bio calls a “neon-hued chemical world”. A straight-edge punk fan in the late 90s, he accompanied friends to Rimini’s hardcore and gabber clubs as a kind of anthropological exercise, a self-styled “rave voyeur” who “just liked to observe and analyse my surroundings”. Accordingly, his albums to date have dealt in what approving critics like to call deconstructions or interrogations of dance music rather than dance music itself: 2012’s Quantum Jelly and 2014’s Superimpositions featured what Senni called “pointillistic trance”, spinning the icy, staccato notes and arpeggiated synth lines of the genre’s epic breakdowns into lengthy, beatless tracks that never reached the climax implied. Released at the height of the 2020 Covid lockdown – when everyone was, by default, some distance from the dancefloor – his last album, Scacco Matto , expanded his palette to include lush ambient electronics, quasi-classical chord structures and something of the teeming chaos of Rustie’s digital maximalism. Six years on, All Ages approaches the tension of his initial encounters with dance music – the sober punk kid looking on intrigued – from a different angle. From its titular reference to booze-free punk gigs, to the straight-edge-symbolising Xs that litter the track names – Self eXamined Endurance, XGood Clean FunX – to the sound of skateboarder Jamie Thomas explaining how quitting drinking and weed “changed my life” on opener Art Life and Skateboarding, it makes Senni’s own background more explicitly part of the action. Likewise the music, a bold, idiosyncratic attempt to meld what you might call Senni’s trademark sound – a trebly, kick drum-free clutter of rave-y synth stabs, chattering trance-influenced electronics and more off-beam, occasionally atonal noises – with the hardcore punk that informed his teenage years. There are moments when the level of distortion applied to the electronics makes them vaguely resemble overdriven electric guitars. While there are tempo changes – the moment when Jealous of Michelangelo slows down momentarily gives the synth arpeggios a curiously proggy feel – there’s a noticeable lack of dynamic shifts. It just blares at you, as indeed an old-fashioned loud-fast-rules hardcore band might. Elsewhere, tracks are topped with vocal samples from Refused’s Dennis Lyxzén, the late Tim Taylor of post-hardcore experimentalists Brainiac, and, in an impressive bit of crate-digging, Sam Loose, frontman of an obscure East Anglian metal band called Smokescreen. These are the most straightforward of Senni’s attempts to square the circle between hard rock and avant-electronica, and the most successful. Raw throated and guttural, their voices are clearly the last thing you would expect to hear on top of music like this, but the effect isn’t as jarring as you might think: on Self eXamined Endurance or Your Favourite DJ, they take on a propulsive, percussive quality, driving the tracks along in lieu of a beat. The results are exciting enough to counter any accusation that Senni is indulging in an arid, academic exercise. Likewise a collaboration with Xiu Xiu’s Jamie Stewart, whose anguished voice pushes the warm, glitchy ambience of La Persuasione e la Rettorica into a new, more troubled emotional space. Not everything here works as well as that. It’s a big task that Senni has set himself, and it occasionally leads him to some curious places. You struggle to see what the lambent piano and strings of Purely Coincidental have to do with either pun

title: Take That: Dreamers review – 50-something boyband fail to relight the fire on nostalgia-drenched return
text: L istening to Wonderkids, the string-laden opener of Take That’s new album, it seems the three remaining fiftysomething boybanders are feeling reflective. “Forgiving you, forgiving me / This vicious circle is now complete,” sings Gary Barlow. In the years since their last record, the band – and former member Robbie Williams – have indeed laid out the trials and tribulations of 35 years of Take That in several documentaries, some more candid than others. Earlier this year, they even embarked on a revival of their blockbuster 2009 Circus tour. Unfortunately, all this reminiscing has left their 10th album feeling so steeped in nostalgia that any moments of greatness struggle for attention. There’s pallid disco revivalism on Best Heartbreak and Higher, the latter more S Club 7 than Dua Lipa, while guitar-bothering folk stomper Feel My Love is so tired you wonder if they still think Mumford & Sons are hip young gunslingers. Then there are the ballads: Who Do You Think You Are is lovely, with its finger-clicking, wounded lounge singer lilt, but Mark Owens’ raspy My Love Is Yours is the band’s weakest song in years. When it’s good it’s really good: Wonderkids is genuinely stirring, Sweet July is like Shine’s sleazy little sibling and the galloping Change of Season is so delightfully strange it proves Take That could push themselves should they want to. But given they’re rolling out a vintage tour to pay the bills, Dreamers suggests they don’t.

title: The month’s best experimental album: Stella Z’s ambient adventures into lucid dreaming
text: L ucid dreaming is one of the influences behind Thunder Is the Sky Dreaming, the new record from Fujian-born, London-based producer Stella Z. “Every night is an adventure,” she writes in the liner notes, “I can even smell things in certain dreams.” The eight tracks here are suitably sensory, scattered with effervescent sounds, ephemeral whispers and polyrhythmic percussion. Many of the sounds and textures were recorded during trips back to China – the ambient noises of a pharmacy or the Fujian mountains late at night – a curious, collage-like approach that underpins the record. On The Somnium Is Awaiting My Cue, we hear what appear to be insects buzzing around a plodding bassline and sporadic woodwind motifs, while electronics softly spiral. Similarly hypnotic is Mira Miruna, on which the echoes of words gradually reveal themselves among the fizzing, softly discordant arrangement: a warped, increasingly urgent call to “wake up”, reminiscent of the foggy state as you rise from sleep. Z amplifies this heady feeling later on in Exit, Elsewhere, where her overlapping narration and rattling bells cause total disorientation. While all the tracks embrace the spacious and amorphous forms of ambient and new age, there are also traces of 90s downtempo, acid and dub. The title track is a swampy stepper, tipped off kilter by glitching effects and Z’s low, whirling repetitions. Saudade Moss has a Balearic sensibility while other tracks embrace a darker atmosphere. My Pillow Grows a Forest combines stormy samples, squelches and ghostly arpeggios. The remix of Exit, Elsewhere by experimental drummer Valentina Magaletti upends the wistful tone of the original with swathes of echo and loud, whining loops: eerie, but a little grating. Even at clumsier moments like these, the record conjures invigorating visions of woozy wilderness excursions. In the four decades since its release, Anna Domino ’s 1984 record East and West has become a cult classic, beloved for its sultry sophistipop sound. This month, the original mini album is reissued with a handful of previously unheard demos (Domino). Here, we hear the bones of the US musician’s langourous, candle-lit songs, plus some wonkier four-track experiments. Another exciting archival release is Popol Vuh ’s quietly epic score to Werner Herzog’s 1974 documentary The Great Ecstasy of Woodcarver Steiner (Latency). Alongside the group’s original compositions, which were never officially released, the new record offers a trio of atmospheric and futuristic variations from avant-pop all-stars including James K and ML Buch. Similarly expansive is the debut collaborative album from Takeshi Nishimoto and Hiroshi Watanabe (Lo Recordings). Recorded together over 12 years and two countries, the instrumentals on Curving Time are warm, stripped back and slow to unfurl. It’s an ideal soundtrack for steady winter mornings.

title: Blackhaine: Saints in the Wethouse review | Alexis Petridis's album of the week
text: O n the second track on his debut album, Tom Heyes accuses lesser artists of copying him. “What the fuck you even take me for?” he barks on Northside Needs Me , over a grinding, distorted bassline that comes punctuated with stammering, rave-y vocal samples. “Too much noise shit, replicating what I played before.” Of course, charging that others are merely imitating what you did previously is a venerable rap tradition: the track that gave said practice its longstanding name, Bite’n My Stylee by Original Concept, is now 40 years old. Perhaps it’s true that others have been copying the approach that Heyes has minted under the alias of Blackhaine, but if so, it seems faintly remarkable, because his approach is so determinedly unique. Whatever you thought the early 2020s were going to throw up musically, it’s highly unlikely you would have predicted the arrival of an artist who expresses northern working-class despondency through dance – involving choreography Heyes suggested was inspired in equal part by Japanese butoh theatre and the staggering gait of synthetic cannabis users – and a sound that that splits the difference between UK drill and extreme electronics. The comparison that kept suggesting itself during Blackhaine’s more scourging moments – 2021’s And Salford Falls Apart, or Cold Summer , his 2023 collaboration with French producer Aho Ssan – was Whitehouse, notorious pioneers of post-industrial power electronics, whose early pitch involved making “the most violently repulsive records ever conceived”. Heyes’s creativity seemed destined to exist entirely on the far left-field margins, but no. He ended up working with a pre-cancellation Kanye West and appearing on stage as a choreographer/dancer/hype man with Playboi Carti (“bald British guy the GOAT” offered one impressed Carti fan online). At the other extreme, his work has been presented at the Venice Biennale, Tate Modern and Centre Pompidou. This album arrives on XL Recordings, which makes him a labelmate of Radiohead, the xx and Fontaines DC, and it’s executive produced by Wraith9, known for working with EsDeeKid and Drake. Nevertheless, his music remains far from the mainstream. There are moments Saints in the Wethouse at least vaguely resembles a straightforward UK rap album, albeit one of a spectacularly bleak, noir-ish hue (as on Pyrex) but they’re outnumbered by tracks that seem to have slipped the moorings of that genre entirely. The influence of Whitehouse is still much in evidence here, particularly on 5 Days, which dispenses with a rhythm entirely, and sets Heyes’s vocal against a mass of punishing electronics and squeals of feedback, and on Born from Wound [Floodlights], with its screamed vocal and ominous tones that give way to a wall of noise that, depending on your mood, could feel either deeply distressing and claustrophobic or oddly cathartic. Elsewhere, Heyes leans into standard rap tropes only to subvert them entirely. There’s his voice, which is certainly aggressive, but usually presents itself as a desperate, garbled bark, filled with panicky gulps for breath. He sounds like a cornered man, frantically yelling at gunpoint, which serves to utterly undercut the sprinkling of boasts and threats in the lyrics: “Do you even know you’re fucking with a real one?”; “The north side needs me, I’m the drug they abuse”; “You used to fucking stand for summat.” Rap has been awash in Auto-Tuned vocals for 20 years, but it’s hard to think of an example of their use that sounds more despairing than at the end of Consumer , already a discomfiting listen with its siren-like synths and raw samples of dancehall MC Mad Cobra and its funereal thud in lieu of a beat. The aforementioned stammering rave-y vocal sample on Northside Needs Me keeps repeating the phrase “jump, baby”, an invitation to dance that, coupled with the increasingly worrying lyric – “stare out the tower, girl, it’s easy to fall” – takes on a profoundly disturbing resonance. title: Ocean Colour Scene review – no other band of their era can do it like this
text: ‘I t’s only 30 years ago,” Simon Fowler says of Moseley Shoals. He would seem to mean it, but 30 years makes Ocean Colour Scene’s breakthrough album as old now as Revolver was when they were making it. The band once derided for raiding the 60s are now heritage themselves. They open the album’s anniversary tour on the stage where Led Zeppelin first played Stairway to Heaven, and you can’t help but appreciate the lineage. They walk on to Green Onions, fresh from the Crown Bar, and open with You’ve Got It Bad, all supreme Motown stomp. Fowler sings with a hand in his pocket and looks taken aback by the welcome. The casualness is a conduit: his voice has aged into something close to peak Joe Cocker, grained at the edges, honey underneath. Lining Your Pockets is more resounding than ever. All 12 album tracks are played, shuffled in among later hits such as Hundred Mile High City and Profit in Peace. The six-piece have become a family firm: Steve Cradock’s son Cass switches between guitar and keys; drummer Oscar Harrison’s son Leon works congas and tambourine and sings backing vocals. On The Circle, the first big singalong, father and son drum as one. Fleeting Mind is pure refraction, Cradock’s lead all glacial pull-offs and slow runs, as if he’s still finding colours in a palette he mixed when MiniDiscs were the future. Get Away still welds, then transcends, Dear Prudence and When the Levee Breaks. Wistful craft and maximum R&B are their two modes, and nobody in their class moves between them so easily, or soulfully. One for the Road’s closing refrain, “I’ll sing my sorrow”, is longing worn without embarrassment. That’s the gift: songs about fragile feelings, sung back by people seldom licensed to have them. The ballads cluster early on, trading a little momentum for some of the night’s finest singing. Alone on stage for the encore, Fowler introduces Robin Hood as “the night I came face to face with Christ, all for £2.50”, and Belfast takes it from him. The Day We Caught the Train closes, as it must: a Beatles-schooled heirloom few have bettered in the 30 years since, and seismic with it. Consensus has lazily filed them under dad-rock. With two dads and two sons on stage, the term has never sounded less like an insult. Their flowers are overdue. There are 20 more nights to send them. Ocean Colour Scene play Ulster Hall, Belfast, on 15 November; then tour Ireland and the UK until 12 December

title: Paris Paloma review – arena-scale alt-pop drama from a singer on her way to bigger things
text: P eople are dancing to a song they don’t know, with flower garlands in their hair and their arms around their friends. This reaction to Fairy Dance, an unreleased track written about the community that has sprung up around her music, says a lot about the moment Paris Paloma finds herself in, and tonight’s show feels for all the world like a stepping stone to bigger things. Throughout, Paloma leans in to the built-in drama of songs from her second album, The Fatal Flaw, which pairs ornate folk arrangements with the sort of arena-sized alt-pop production favoured by Florence + the Machine. With a sculpture inspired by surrealist Ithell Colquhoun ’s Tree of Veins dominating the stage, she falls to her knees to deliver high notes and seeks out wind machines at the prow of the stage, her flowing crimson dress buffeted as if on a wintry moor. Building upon the ground staked out by her breakout single Labour, her set melds timely feminist fury with open-ended questions about culture and identity. Particular disdain is reserved for tech bros, manosphere influencers and their lickspittles, with Good Girl’s “I will break your nose” payoff shouted out from the stalls with venom. When it ends, Paloma is in a heap on the floor, spent from pogoing. While less pugilistic, Rothko is equally effective. Paloma wraps a teenage encounter with one of the artist’s paintings in a patient melody, her failure to cry at the sight of it seemingly confirming her belief that she is broken. There is a little of Patti Smith in her desire to be awestruck by art, even if the punk pioneer’s abrasive sonic approach is nowhere to be heard. But there is plenty to be said for airing these sentiments in an accessible fashion. It would be easy to knock Paloma’s earnestness, particularly in the face of day-to-day awfulness, but she has a point about celebrating the stuff that brings us together. “I won’t let you take it from me,” she belts during Miyazaki, framing creativity as a base need in the face of AI evangelists. That her voice is drowned out by the crowd is something. At O2 Apollo, Manchester, on 15 November, and touring the UK and Europe until 13 December

title: The week’s best new tracks and the act you need to know: the rangy folk-prog songwriting of Threshold
text: From New York via Montana Recommended if you like Cameron Winter, Tobias Jesso Jr, Alex G Up next Supporting Caroline on tour in Canada and the US until 19 November Isaac Eiger is something of a scene legend in the world of American indie-rock. Raised in Bozeman, Montana, he was the founder and lead singer of the cult shoegaze-adjacent six-piece Strange Ranger, who left heartbroken a small, fervent fanbase when they announced their breakup in 2023. Taking a discernibly British approach to their sound, Strange Ranger traversed C86-y jangle-pop before landing on Madchester rave-up for their final album, 2023’s Pure Music. But Eiger is nothing if not musically worldly: he has written and produced with both underground heroes (Cassandra Jenkins, Chanel Beads) and nascent pop stars (Adéla, Frost Children). Ever-prolific, Eiger also has a solo project under the name Threshold, with which he released a gauzy, 19-minute EP in 2024 called Thief. Earlier this year, he released Stillwater, the first single from the debut Threshold album, due for release in 2027 on the London-based label Untitled. Although Stillwater has some clear influences – it owes some phrasings and intonations to Alex G, but what indie-rock song doesn’t these days? – it’s still a remarkable song: expansive and pathos-drenched, loping forward like an aimless but essential winter morning walk. While Stillwater captures the spirit of 70s singer-songwriter piano ballads, the rest of Eiger’s forthcoming record is rangier and harder to pin down, touching on traditional folk and loose, minimalist prog. It is undoubtedly the best of his projects to date, and is sure to be one of the year’s breakouts, if recent successes by sharp-tongued songwriters such as Cameron Winter and This Is Lorelei are anything to go by. Shaad D’Souza Heavensouls – Today I Learned to Fly Again The year’s breakthrough experimentalist finds yet another mode with a 10-minute epic that sounds like a star being born, detritus and screams giving way to cosmic guitar that expands as if acquiring life force. [ Listen on Bandcamp ] LS BexBlu and Paul Stephan – They Know (ft Unknown T) One of the best UK rap albums of the year drops today, with dizzyingly diverse beats from BexBlu and dextrous, forceful flows from Stephan: They Know is throbbing and noirish, leaving burn marks on the tarmac. BBT Erika de Casier – Whispers In which Casier accepts that all memories will fade, a bleak conclusion tempered by the sweetness of her Cafe del Mar-worthy mix of spectral acoustic guitar and William Orbit-era electronic detailing. LS Rema – Velvet Tony Allen might have nodded appreciatively at the monumentally funky shuffling beat here: his Nigerian countryman Rema harks back to classic Afrobeat but with an earnestly crooned R&B-style vocal on top. BBT Studio20 – Wish I Still Knew Suffused with midwestern emo energy but actually hailing from Kent, this quartet alternate contemplative post-rock verses with a cathartic, chest-clutching chorus that makes a virtue of their doubled-up male-female lead vox. BBT Kacey Musgraves – The Vacation Song Holiday romance has Musgraves learning Spanish and contemplating life in Mexico: the norteño sound of Middle of Nowhere returns, but the middle eight’s knowing telenovela-worthy melodrama suggests any move might be a bit hasty. LS Joã o Bosco & Guto Wir tti – Escadas da Penha Taken from a superb compilation of spirited live jazz sessions hosted by east London’s Church of Sound, this is a highlight: the Brazilian duo play with such lightness, even through rhythmic right hand turns. title: ‘My dad said Great Balls of Fire was pagan music – and threw it out of the window’: Leo Sayer’s honest playlist
text: The first song I fell in love with I first heard Bob Dylan through my cousin David when I was about 16. I fell in love with his voice. Don’t Think Twice, It’s All Right is still one of the best songs ever written. We were young rebels then, looking for a moral compass, while everybody older seemed to be wearing bowler hats and pinstripe suits. Dylan made us think differently. The song I inexplicably know every lyric to Astral Weeks by Van Morrison. I’m going to record it myself some time because it’s just an amazing song. The first single I bought Great Balls of Fire by Jerry Lee Lewis from Fine Records in the Lanes in Brighton. When my dad heard it, he said: “I won’t have any of that pagan music in here,” then threw it out of the window. I thought: If he did that, it must be good. I retrieved it from the bushes, took it to a friend’s house and we played it all day. My karaoke go-to I hate karaoke, but I once sang Bohemian Rhapsody by Queen with a group of supermodels after the 2006 Australian Grand Prix in Melbourne. I was only singing because they were all beautiful. The song I can no longer listen to Imagine by John Lennon – not because I’m bored with it, but because the world clearly isn’t listening. Everything is about dividing people into races, classes, haves and have-nots, when Imagine is about joining people together. The best song to play at a party I Love Your Smile by Shanice, because it grooves like nothing else. The song I secretly like, but tell everyone I hate I don’t really have guilty pleasures. But people probably wouldn’t expect me to love Pennies from Heaven by Arthur Tracy. The best song to have sex to Sexual Healing by Marvin Gaye is just the sexiest song in the world. Marvin is a monster with that voice. He’s who every man would like to think he is and who every woman would probably like to go to bed with. The song that changed my life I sang Oh, Boy! by Buddy Holly at school when I was about 14 in a band called the Buddies. Our drummer didn’t even own drums – he hit schoolbooks with his sticks. Buddy Holly made me think: I could actually do this. The song that gets me up in the morning Lovely Day by Bill Withers is exactly what you want first thing in the morning. The song that makes me cry I was at the Lyceum, standing at the side of the stage for the concert in 1975 where Bob Marley and the Wailers famously recorded the live version of No Woman, No Cry. Everybody was in tears. Later I toured with Bob – I’d designed one of his record sleeves [for Catch a Fire] when I was a graphic designer for Island Records. He was a lovely man. The song I want played at my funeral Keith Jarrett’s recording of Over the Rainbow. It’s just beautiful. Leo Sayer’s 18-CD box set Leothology: The Studio Albums 1973 – Now is out now. He is touring to 15 November .

title: The week’s best new tracks and the act you need to know: crowd-pleasing anticapitalist rockers Sans Froid
text: From Bristol, UK Recommended if you like Puscifer, Julie Christmas, the Mars Volta Up next Supporting Every Hell at Bristol’s Exchange, 4 December; playing UK festivals Strangeforms, Noizzefest and Arctangent in 2027 Even a cursory scroll through Sans Froid’s influences will make you expect chaos. In interviews, members of the west country rockers have acknowledged Radiohead, the Mars Volta, the immersive folk of Linda Perhacs and even the haywire opera/metal/breakbeat of French button-pusher Igorrr. Combine that array with the four-piece’s sole collective inspiration – San Franciscan indie experimentalists Deerhoof – and it’s amazing there’s any coherence at all. Yet the band have emerged as eclectic yet catchy conceptual upstarts. Released in June, their second album, Back Into the Womb, is stylistically all over the place: opener Go On stabs with noise-rock discordance, while the bouncy Bags Packed could enjoy pride of place on any indie playlist. But each song is united in anthemic intent, built around urgent hooks and some hypnotic performances from singer Aisling Rhiannon Trafford. Her wails as Of the Mother builds towards heavy, chord-based riffing would wow any vocal coach. The lyrics are all centred on life under late-stage capitalism’s patriarchal overlords: “Parasitic industrial movement leaking consistent flaws / Thirty thousand hours so far spent on this losing draw / But I push push push …” goes the single The Exploiter of Art. That overarching theme wasn’t intentional, but it’s even more evidence that Sans Froid have found consistency amid disparate sounds. In the process, they have become one of the British avant-rock underground’s most exciting, and potentially crowd-pleasing, new names. Matt Mills Dawuna – Love Is ... Pitched somewhere between D’Angelo, the Weeknd and Jai Paul, Dawuna blew our minds with his lo-fi debut, Glass Lit Dream, and his songcraft just keeps evolving. This track, at the heart of his new LP, Love’s Arp, is all softly pattering sensuality. Slayyyter – Hey Boyyy Catherine Grace Garner’s upcoming companion album to smash hit Wor$t Girl in America is shaping up to be even better than the original: sweetness leaches in and out of this new-wave stomper in such an expert manner. Sam Girling – Primrose Mountain Released on powerhouse UK electronic label Hessle Audio, both sides of Girling’s new speed garage 12in are fire, but this has an extra dash of thermic energy from the whomping bass and lurching effects. D(Juno) – Carré With her breathy, feathery yet robust voice, this Parisian pop-R&B singer brings bags of character to her new EP, (D), where symphonic funk numbers rub up against slinky Afropop tracks such as the chatty Carré. Star’s Revenge – Don’t Worry Dynamite Fronted by Geese’s Emily Green and Sunflower Bean’s Olive Faber, Star’s Revenge will soon be releasing their second album. This lead single is powered by a loopy, punch-drunk riff sent from the indie-pop heavens. Toumani Diabaté, Sidiki Diabaté, Balla Diabaté & Ahmed Diabaté – Mande The final album from late kora master Toumani Diabeté is out in January, made in a quartet with his sons. Mande has his signature melodic pirouettes, set to the subtlest of steady rhythms. Spiral – Fruits of the Earth UK experimentalists Teresa Winter and Tom James Scott combine for this ambient stunner leading off their new self-titled cassette; Winter locking into a dream-state vocal pattern as watery tones ebb around her. ( Available on Bandcamp. ) Subscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it to Apple , Tidal or other services

title: Clem Cattini obituary
text: The drummer Clem Cattini, who has died aged 89, had the distinction of playing on more than 40 No 1 singles. Largely unknown outside the music business, he was revered inside it as one of the best session musicians of his generation. Over a 45-year period from 1960 to 2005, Cattini provided the backbeat for dozens of British No 1s, including The Sun Ain’t Gonna Shine (Anymore) , by the Walker Brothers, You Don’t Have to Say You Love Me , by Dusty Springfield (both 1966), and Everlasting Love , by Love Affair (1968), as well as many other top 20 hits. He also played with the Kinks, the Yardbirds, the Bee Gees, Roy Orbison, Paul McCartney, the Hollies and Lou Reed . Not everything Cattini touched turned to gold, and not all of his No 1s were necessarily of lasting value – he also appeared on Chirpy Chirpy Cheep Cheep , by Middle of the Road (1971), Grandad , by Clive Dunn (1970) and Ernie , by Benny Hill (1971) – but he had no time for snobbery, and as a self-proclaimed “musical navvy” was as happy to receive his fixed fee for a turkey as a prize bird. “I’m not ashamed or embarrassed to admit that I played on anything,” he said. “In the end it was all just work.” Cattini began his career as a rock’n’roller, and two of his early chart-topping singles were as a real-life band member – first as the drummer for Johnny Kidd and the Pirates, with whom he released the quivering Shakin’ All Over in 1960, and then the Tornados, whose other-worldly 1962 instrumental, Telstar , not only reached No 1 in the UK but made them the first British group to top the US singles chart. Eventually, however, he tired of life on the road and settled into the more structured existence of studio work, where his economical and utterly reliable style made him the go-to drummer for hard-pressed producers. Doggedly down to earth, wryly humorous and unfussy, Cattini possessed a chameleon-like ability to fit in with whoever, or whatever, was thrown at him. At the peak of his involvement in the British pop scene, from 1966 to 1971, he was averaging about four No 1s a year, from Green, Green Grass of Home , by Tom Jones (1966), and Something in the Air , by Thunderclap Newman (1969), to Love Grows (Where My Rosemary Goes) , by Edison Lighthouse, in 1970, and I’d Like to Teach the World to Sing , by the New Seekers, in 1971. The run continued well into the mid-1970s as he played on When Will I See You Again , by the Three Degrees (1974), and So You Win Again , by Hot Chocolate (1977), before he gave up session work to tour with the Kids from Fame show and a re-formed version of the Tornados. His last No 1 came in 2005, when he featured on the Comic Relief single (Is This the Way to) Amarillo , by Tony Christie and Peter Kay. Born in Stoke Newington, north London, Clem was the son of Lena and her husband, Clemente Sr, who ran a cafe, having emigrated from Italy. He left St Ignatius grammar school in Tottenham at 15 to work with his father, serving cups of tea and working the till. The move into music came when he and a friend, Terry Kennedy, saw Bill Haley playing Rock Around the Clock in the film Blackboard Jungle (1955). They immediately formed a skiffle band, Terry Kennedy’s Rock and Rollers, with the self-taught Cattini on washboard and drums. Initially playing in pubs around London, they eventually upgraded to a residency at the 2i’s coffee bar in Soho, where Cattini also picked up work as the house drummer. After a late stint there one night, he overslept for work at his father’s cafe and was sacked, prompting a move into music full-time. In 1957 the Rock and Rollers were signed for a six-month tour supporting the comedian Max Wall , after which they became the touring band for the singer Terry Dene. In 1959 Cattini married Anna, who was also of Italian stock. Shortly afterwards he joined the Beat Boys, a backing band for, among others, Billy Fury. Johnny Kidd and the Pirates followed in 1960, and he quickly found himself in the studio recording Shakin’ All O

title: Juan Atkins built a cybernetic future for music – but invested it with humanity
text: Juan Atkins, the originator of techno who died on 31 October, spent his lifetime translating a fascination with the future into sound. He was the oldest of the founding fathers of techno known as the “Belleville Three”, along with his junior high school friends Kevin Saunderson and Derrick May. He was the first of the trio to buy a Korg MS-10 synthesiser, and also taught the others how to DJ on turntables. His work in the duo Cybotron alongside Rik Davis was the sonic blueprint that sketched out what later became known as techno – indeed, he is the one who gave the genre its name. Without Atkins, and the way he empowered those around him, electronic music certainly would not exist in its current form today. After moving from his birthplace of Detroit to nearby Belleville, Michigan, Atkins holed himself up in his bedroom, toiling away for hours creating drum kicks. “I more or less knew I was doing stuff that was not the normal thing to do,” he said in a Red Bull Music Academy interview in 2017 . As a teenager in the 1970s he wouldd listen to The Midnight Funk Association, a five-hour late-night radio programme by DJ Charles “The Electrifying Mojo” Johnson, which opened with the space-age introduction of The Landing of the Mothership before braiding together selections from Prince, Michael Jackson, Parliament-Funkadelic, the B-52s, the Human League and Atkins’s biggest influences, Yellow Magic Orchestra and Kraftwerk. Atkins was a conduit for a particular moment in musical and technological history: able to draw from this increasingly accessible globalised pool of music, and put those influences to bear on musical hardware that just a few years earlier would have been the wildly expensive preserve of universities or computing companies. Atkins also loved anything about space, time travel, UFOs, religiously consuming TV shows such as Star Trek and Lost in Space, and the books of HP Lovecraft and Isaac Asimov. Three texts in particular defined the extraterrestrial reach of his sound: Childhood’s End by Arthur C Clarke, and Future Shock and The Third Wave by Alvin Toffler . The latter two were how he initially developed a bond with Davis at Washtenaw Community College in Ann Arbor, Michigan, as they discussed Toffler’s idea of the third wave, a way of living that would come after agrarian and industrial societies. Inspired by Toffler, Atkins deployed words such as Metroplex, the name of his record label which evokes a sprawling future city, and Cybotron, the name of his duo with Davis which calls to mind a brutally efficient robot who may or may not be benign. He also applied Toffler’s idea of “techno rebels” to music – those people who wield technology for their own creative empowerment; a third option between destructive luddites and uncritical techno-optimists. Atkins reportedly rejected Derrick May’s suggestion to label their music “hi-tech soul” on the Virgin Records compilation that introduced the propulsive Detroit sound to the UK. Instead, the compilation was titled after one of Atkins’ tracks on it, Techno Music, and that became the name of a whole global movement. Crucially, and like his hero Toffler, Atkins wasn’t naive or needlessly optimistic about the impact technology would have on the future, even if it was giving him the means to make a totally new style of music. Living in and near Detroit, where the city’s car manufacturing industries had badly decayed by the 1980s, Atkins had a front row seat to see how an industrial society could become obsolete and end up far from a techno-utopia. In the 1996 Arté documentary Universal Techno, he is filmed against the backdrop of post-industrial Detroit, explaining: “The general attitude here with the powers that be is that industry must die to make way for technology … I think that we probably wouldn’t have developed this sound in any other city in America … There is a certain atmosphere here that you can’t find in any other city that lends to the technological movement.” Det

title: Keep your wig on! Hairy paintings and sex worker photographs are the free art shows to see this week
text: It’s usually the eyes that follow you around the room in paintings, but in Louise Giovanelli’s new work, it’s the hair. She’s one of the leading young painters in the country, with a knack for washed out, nostalgic theatrical imagery, but these new works have some hirsute twists. There are three distinct bodies of work here. Tightly cropped photorealistic paintings of people snogging, super lavish images of faces seen through glittering stage curtains, and psychedelic, nearly abstract paintings of wigs. The first two don’t do a huge amount for me, mainly because there’s a lot of cropped melancholy painting based on found imagery around these days, it’s one of the big aesthetic trends in post-2020s art. They’re all nice enough paintings, I’m just not totally wowed by them. But the wig paintings will absolutely floor you. She paints swooping webs of fake hair hanging and swaying. They’re ultra-lush, textural, fetishistic images, blonds and browns fading into parma violet purples and toxic greens. Their surfaces look reflective and plasticky, like nylon and polyester stretched into impossible, undulating forms. Wigs are tools of artifice and adornment, they hide and conceal, they decorate and exaggerate. They imply that the wearer has the power to construct their image, to shape their identity, but usually in a knowingly, obviously fake way. I could take a whole show of just the wigs and their delicate, weird experiments in light and distortion, femininity and falseness. They feel like an artist genuinely finding their voice, and totally wigging out. White Cube Mason’s Yard, London, until 16 January Absence, loss, grief – French conceptualist Sophie Calle makes work about things that are unseen, unfinished and hidden away. It starts with Picasso’s paintings, photographed during lockdown when the Musée Picasso covered the works for protection, leaving behind nothing but ghostly rectangles and titles, making you paint the images in your head. You see a reclining figure reading, a minotaur attacking a woman, a bather reclining, all being triggered in your mind. Damn, Calle is good, conjuring the violence and brilliance of Picasso, of art itself, through its absence. She takes humorous photos of graves and street signs, makes art out of lonely hearts ads filled with unrequited desire and the need to be seen and wanted. But the best work here is her collection of unfinished projects, a whole room of unrealised ideas, catalogued, preserved and analysed, each one given context and a reason for why it was abandoned: ‘No time’, ‘unnecessary’, ‘impossible to convey’, ‘what’s the point’, ‘Max died’. It’s dozens of moments of creative passion and intuition left to rot, abandoned and almost forgotten. It made me think of everything I’ve left unfinished, everything I’m too tired, too stressed, too sad to do. It feels desperate, final, and brutally affecting. A lot of the work involves speaking to people about absence and loss. She asks museum security guards to describe Turner paintings that have been stolen. She meets people who have never seen the sea, and films them seeing it for the first time. In one work, she asks people who were born blind to explain what their image of beauty is. It veers wildly between funny (the “erotic breasts and a terrific ass” of a Rodin), poignant (“I saw my son in a dream … he was very beautiful”) and heartbreaking (“since I cannot appreciate beauty I have always run away from it”). And that’s Sophie Calle, digging through loss and absence to talk about the things that really matter in life. Turner Contemporary, Margate, until 24 January Things are pretty filthy down in Quench’s basement, literally and figuratively. There’s dust and debris on the floor, and porn on the wall in the two side-by-side exhibitions in this experimental Margate art space. The nudity and erotica is all by MJ Mac, documenting 15 years in the sex industry. The people in these relaxed, funny, personal photos are Mac’s friends: sex workers

title: Roll up, roll up! Marc Chagall’s Circus is the most mesmerising big top you’ve ever seen – review
text: A t the opening of The Circus, a self-portrait of Marc Chagall is placed next to a lithograph of a clown. The portrait is small and sketched simply in a blue crayon, as if Chagall had quickly dashed it out to pacify an inquisitive fan. In contrast, the clown is rich in colour and texture, with a heavily detailed backdrop of musicians, spectators and performers. But there is something uncanny about this pairing, created more than 40 years apart. They both wear small, brimmed hats with hair springing out from underneath, and their facial expressions are somewhat inscrutable. It is the perfect introduction to an exhibition that explores Chagall’s lifelong fascination with the circus, both as a subject and as a symbolic motif. In placing Chagall and the clown side by side, we understand this immediately – the clown is both a clown and a metaphor for the artist. In his 1967 art book Cirque, Chagall writes: “This clown – he is he and I.” Featuring more than 50 works, The Circus is a dazzling exploration of one of the 20th century’s most distinctive artists, delving into the way this magical arena and its cast of intriguing characters captured Chagall’s imagination, dancing across his canvases for more than 60 years. For Chagall, the circus is a mesmerising space beyond reality where it is possible to find childhood memories, artistic inspiration, spiritual enlightenment and both radiant light and deepest darkness. The show includes his theatrical collaborations, paintings he produced in a box at the Cirque d’Hiver, pieces he made after his return to Paris after the second world war, and autobiographical works relating to Vitebsk, then in Russia but now in Belarus, where he grew up. But shimmering at the heart of this exhibition is Cirque, an art book, large suite of lithographs and essay (newly translated into English for The Circus). An entire, windowless space in a deep red is the setting for Cirque, which is presented here in its entirety. With the colourful lithographs popping off the walls, it feels as though I have disappeared into a big top. This is enhanced further by the decision to record Chagall’s Cirque essay, which is read by a French actor to give the language the artist’s accent. I pop on the headphones and for 24 minutes I am no longer in misty Wakefield but in the rafters of a tent watching hoops spin – or centre stage beside a ferocious lion. The language in Cirque is as important as the visuals; as with Chagall’s art, where bodies float and animals shapeshift, so the text moves from a memory of street performers in Vitebsk, to the tail of a circus horse, to the story of Noah, to the greed of humanity. While I listen, I observe the vivid, swirling colours of a red leotard, a clown’s painted face and a bouquet of flowers. In many of the lithographs reality melts away – a moon bursts through the big top, a fish plays a drum, a Janus-faced figure plays music and weeps at the same time. For all their sparkling joy, each work features a looming audience, their round faces in rows, indistinguishable but heavily present, judging and reminding us of the outside world. Chagall’s words play through the headphones: “Alas, in life I have seen a ridiculous circus: someone thundered to terrify the world, and a thunder of applause answered him.” The circus is not all fun and games, on either side of the canvas. The clever thing about placing Cirque at the start of the show is that it is then possible to follow these motifs through the rest of Chagall’s work, both before and after Cirque’s creation. The Four Heads – one of 19 paintings Chagall created from a box at the Cirque d’Hiver – was made in 1927 and, featuring a clown atop a many-headed creature, captures an early interest in the momentary spectacle of circus. Much later pieces from 1980 of his home in Vitebsk also include acrobats, lovers dancing and instrumentalists, indicating that these performing artists had inhabited his mind since childhood.
