title: Take me to the fatberg! The £437m new Museum of London is an astonishing sight
text: ‘A ll the grit and glitter,” trumpets a big illuminated sign on the roof of the old Smithfield general market, beaming out as if advertising a raunchy burlesque show. It is the jazzy tagline of the new-look London Museum, which has gone from being marooned on a roundabout in an armpit of the City to taking over this prime Victorian market complex, following an arduous decade-long transformation. The slogan is fitting for a museum that displays everything from priceless Tudor jewels to a lump of congealed fat and rags dredged from a Whitechapel sewer. Just as the colossal fatberg was scraped from the murky depths, so has the former market hall (and its extensive warren of basement vaults) been meticulously scoured and scrubbed up. London’s centre of butchery for 800 years, which Charles Dickens found “all asmear with filth and fat and blood and foam”, has been lavished with a £437m glow-up, reborn to tell the story of the capital in all its gritty, glittery glory. And the finished result is an astonishing sight. It may be hard to remember now just how off-putting the museum’s previous home was. Since 1976, it had been imprisoned in a windowless brick bastion , throttled by traffic and accessed by a couple of elevated bridges, like a fortified keep. “We still got 700,000 visitors a year,” says Alec Shaw, director of transformation. “But they wouldn’t come back.” It was a dingy ordeal, somewhere you went because your school dragged you there, not for the active pleasure of spending time. Now it is hoped people will drift in off the street, possibly without even knowing they’re entering a museum. “We’re essentially wrapped with 250 metres of high street,” says Asif Khan, one of the architects involved, alongside Stanton Williams and conservation specialists, Julian Harrap Architects. The 44 shop units that used to ring the market, where grocers and butchers hawked their wares to the street, have been converted into 12 outward-facing “houses” for the museum and its partner organisations, “making it more like a coral reef than a singular organism”, says Khan. Encrusted with these retail barnacles, which will range from cafes and pubs to galleries and shops, the museum hopes to lure in passersby who might never have thought of going. Inside, they will find a place that is light years from the city museum stereotype of a dusty, fusty repository. Opened in 1883, the general market was the last of Smithfield’s three market halls designed by City architect Horace Jones, also the author of Tower Bridge. Jones concocted a dazzling cathedral of commerce: a majestic dome rises above the vast former market hall, where decorative iron “phoenix columns” support a lattice of trusses that hold up a roof of vaulted skylights. Around the edges, dilapidated shops have been stripped away to reveal the building’s raw brick shell, with iron fireplaces left hanging surreally halfway up the walls. The former shop of James Burden Ltd, purveyors of premium meat, now houses a stepped theatre for educational programmes. Another unit has become the museum store, where the wares of London artisans will be on sale. In every nook, historic architectural details have been lovingly preserved, making the building itself, and its accrued layers of history, a prime exhibit. Bucketloads of fragments in the museum’s collection – known as “bulk archaeology” – have even been cast into the polished concrete floor, forming a sort of archaeological terrazzo from bits of old pots, pipes and tiles. “It’s a gesture to our primordial reflex to dig, to find,” says Paul Williams, co-founder of Stanton Williams. Kids will love searching for curious fragments. Thirteen displays are scattered around the perimeter of the main hall, loosely themed around “Our Time”. Topics range from greyhound racing – there’s a rotating “totalisator” contraption used to calculate betting odds at Harringay Stadium – to an altar of shop signs, where the likes of Morley’s fried chicken and Topshop glow

title: Grade I interiors, gold bars, cost fears: Bank of England faces headache over £160m revamp
text: A ndrew Bailey may spend his days closely watching developments in the strait of Hormuz or US stock markets for signs of shocks to the global economy – but the Bank of England’s governor has a £160m problem brewing much closer to home. A secretive major revamp of the Bank’s historic headquarters in the heart of London’s Square Mile presents a huge test of Bailey’s project management skills. The central bank, with its reputation staked on carefully counting the nation’s pennies, will be keen to avoid delays, budget-busting or any echoes of the expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that left his former peer Jerome Powell awkwardly clashing with Donald Trump on camera . Bailey and his senior managers believe they can modernise the Bank’s Grade I-listed structure and interiors while 3,500 staff are still busy at work on site. By the summer of 2028, 1,400 Bank staff who work in a nearby office at 20 Moorgate will be relocated to Threadneedle Street, have taken voluntary redundancy or have been offered an alternative job in a new outpost in Leeds, also being refurbished. It appears a unique project for Britain’s struggling building trade: overhaul a site with a globally recognised exterior; preserve its Roman mosaic floors, stone columns and vaulted, ornate ceilings while keeping exact floorplans under wraps, for fear of terror attacks. The Bank itself began in rented premises in 1694, moving to Threadneedle Street in 1734. Nicknamed the Old Lady of Threadneedle Street after a satirical cartoon of William Pitt the Younger , it has been refashioned and remodelled – first by Sir John Soane between 1788 and 1833 and then again in the 1920s when the interior was largely demolished and rebuilt. The building is owned by the Bank, which was given independence to set interest rates by Gordon Brown in 1997 , and, after the 2008 financial crash, it was later handed responsibility for regulating the banking sector by George Osborne. Cash to fund the scheme will come from an estimated £100m of savings each year for three years that the Bank says will accrue from 450 redundancies and other cost savings. As one member of Bank staff told the Guardian: “It’s like there is a leaving party every week.” What the Bank wants to avoid is a repeat of the delays and cost overruns that dogged the Federal Reserve in Washington, which led to Trump threatening the US central bank with court action. Over the life of the Fed’s renovation project, construction costs have soared. The initial budget of $921m (£696m) in February 2020 was revised several times before December 2024, when it hit $2bn. Construction was supposed to be completed in mid-2024 but is now expected to run until December 2027. The final cost is likely to be nearer $2.5bn. The Bank’s scheme is on a much smaller scale, and pales against the possible £60bn it will cost to renovate the Palace of Westminster . It is more akin to the £80m Elizabeth Tower restoration. What Bailey will want to avoid is joining the Elizabeth Tower, which houses Big Ben, as the subject of parliamentary scrutiny after its budget doubled and then rose by a further 20% , giving ammunition to critics who have long accused the Bank of mishandling its core purpose of helping to manage the economy by setting interest rates at the appropriate level. The Bank project was first announced in July 2025 and work was due to start this month, but it was only in October, with a month to spare, that the construction company Sir Robert McAlpine was awarded the building contract. Described as an “incredibly complex project” , it aims to transform the neoclassical building, which sits opposite the Royal Exchange and adjacent to the Mansion House, into what some staff hope is a Google-like workplace of friendly office spaces, breakout rooms and in-house cafes. title: ‘It’s an architect’s dream’: five beautiful eco buildings around the world
text: W ith construction accounting for more than a third of global emissions, sustainable architecture is central to the world meeting its climate targets. The following five creations from around the world exemplify how “green” buildings can also be beautiful. In Tocantins, central Brazil, the Canuanã school is a boarding school whose pupils come from remote farming communities across the region. In 2017, architects gave the school’s 540 boarders two new “villages” of dormitories, one for girls and one for boys. The buildings are made from locally sourced timber and earth bricks. A vast canopy shades the complex, and perforated brick walls let air pass through, so the bedrooms stay comfortable without air conditioning even when temperatures reach 45C. Under the roof, rooms open on to shady, landscaped courtyards and airy verandas. David Mikhail, the co-founder of Mikhail Riches, a UK practice specialising in sustainable design, says: “It is absolutely fantastic. So beautiful. It does a lot with little resource, which is the essence of a sustainable approach.” He adds: “I love the economy of it, and the huge sense of place they managed to evoke through such elegant and limited means.” The architects have said their biggest challenge was convincing pupils and teachers that earth, brick and timber could feel modern rather than old-fashioned. They managed to do so by listening to students through 10 days of workshops to understand what they wanted from the design. The Green school in Bali is surrounded by jungle and promotes sustainability through learning in a natural environment. Since it opened in 2008, it has been built almost entirely in bamboo. Its gymnasium, the Arc, was completed in 2021. Inspired by a mammal’s ribcage, the Arc’s bamboo arches span a 760 sq metre sports court without a single column interrupting the floor space. The arches support an undulating canopy, and natural ventilation comes from breezes that flow in at the base, while warm air escapes through vents at the top. Bamboo is a highly sustainable building material because of how quickly it can regrow; large varieties reach building strength in just three to six years. “It is so fast-growing and sequesters a lot of carbon dioxide very quickly, so using it for building is a bit of a no-brainer if you can make it work,” says Mikhail. “And not only have they made it work, they’ve done it absolutely beautifully.” Skellefteå, a small city just south of the Arctic Circle, is surrounded by 480,000 hectares (1.2m acres) of forest, and features wooden schools, a wooden road bridge, even a wooden multistorey car park. In 2021 it added Sara Kulturhus , a 20-storey cultural centre and hotel that is one of the tallest timber buildings in the world. It houses two theatres, a museum, an art gallery, the city library and a hotel. The building is made of glulam – layers of timber glued together – and cross-laminated timber, a kind of super-sized plywood. The hotel rooms arrived as prefabricated wooden pods and were stacked into place. Building in wood saved a year in construction time compared with steel and concrete, while the timber came from trees harvested within 40 miles of the site, and replacement trees have since been planted. “It promotes a love affair with wood and timber, and the localism of that in an area like Sweden is fabulous,” Mikhail says. “The lovely thing about cross-laminated timber is that the trees you use to make the panels don’t have to be elderly specimen trees. They can be relatively fast-grown and sustainably farmed.” When the University of Tasmania was planning the redevelopment of its main campus in central Hobart, the architects chose to adapt what was already there rather than demolish it and start again. Two early 20th-century brick warehouses and a heritage-listed glass dome were stitched together into a single campus of classrooms and study spaces, which opened in February 2026. title: Art psychotherapists are already regulated | Letters
text: We welcome the discussion about public protection, professional accountability and the importance of appropriate regulation within counselling and psychotherapy ( Letters, 5 November ). However, we feel it is important to highlight a distinction that may be helpful to readers. Art psychotherapists are already a statutorily regulated profession in the UK, regulated by the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC). The HCPC regulates 15 health and care professions, including arts therapists (art psychotherapists, art therapists, drama therapists, music therapists) and the titles art therapist and art psychotherapist are legally protected. Practitioners must meet HCPC registration requirements, standards of proficiency, conduct and ethics, and continuing professional development requirements. This means that art therapists occupy a different regulatory position from counsellors and psychotherapists, whose professional registration is currently voluntary. We do recognise the importance of extending statutory protection across professions where it is currently absent, but would appreciate recognition that we, along with drama therapists and music therapists, are a statutory regulated profession. Elizabeth Donnelly Chief executive officer, British Association of Art Therapists Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Participating in art and culture has measurable benefits on our wellbeing | Letter
text: Reading Emma Brockes’ response to a recent Art Fund study, I felt the significance of the research may have been lost in its packaging ( Art is good for your health? Allow me a quick eyeroll, 5 November ). The language of “prescribing” art has its roots in social prescribing. I understand why this might make people uncomfortable, particularly if it suggests that culture is being instrumentalised rather than enjoyed for its own sake. Yet these findings matter for two reasons. First, they provide evidence for what many of us know intuitively: that participating in and experiencing art and culture are not only enriching, but also have measurable benefits for our health and wellbeing. Second, with budgets for culture under pressure, this evidence strengthens our case for public investment. Surely that’s another argument for keeping our national museums free and ensuring everyone can access their wellbeing benefits. Rather than viewing this study cynically, we should recognise the opportunities it presents. As Daisy Fancourt, who is quoted in Brockes’ article, explores in her excellent and insightful book Art Cure, the evidence extends far beyond visiting galleries and museums. In the London borough of Ealing, we’re piloting a free creative health programme bringing residents and council staff together through activities ranging from clay workshops to Islamic geometric drawing. Almost all participants have reported improved wellbeing following these sessions. But beyond the evaluation, conversations have shown me how even an hour spent being creative can positively change the course of someone’s day, while regular participation can have a lasting impact on their lives. Art shouldn’t have to justify its existence through its health benefits. But understanding those benefits strengthens the case for everyone to experience, participate in and benefit from art and culture. And if the thought of visiting a museum makes Brockes’ eyes roll, I’d happily invite her to one of our workshops. She might leave having learned a new skill, but I suspect she’d take away rather more than that. William Rees Culture officer, Ealing council Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Lend them your ears! Julius Caesar is staged with just four actors – and a great big gong
text: A ny modern reformulation of Julius Caesar may inevitably be compared with Phyllida Lloyd’s innovative, all-female 2012 production, now revived by the Royal Shakespeare Company , which reimagined the tragedy as a play-within-a-play in a women’s prison. This reworked version, adapted and directed by Joe Hill-Gibbins, does not match its depth and originality but certainly does something different. It is performed at 90 minutes straight-through with just four actors who take on the central roles of conspirators Cassius (Natey Jones) and Brutus (Caoilfhionn Dunne) alongside Mark Antony (Adam Gillen) and Caesar (Kate Duchêne, who also plays the soothsayer and Octavius). It is not as gimmicky as you may think. Sound is key to the effects, with a fantastically expressive and almost constant drumming throughout, the atmosphere thrumming with rising discontent and the percussionists (married duo Louise Anna Duggan and Zands Duggan, collectively known as Minihi) are as important as the actors. Sometimes, this sound is a substitute for the lines themselves. The stage is kept in prevailing darkness with elongated shadows, firelight and handheld candles, which – just about – illuminate the performers’ faces. As the backdrop to Rosanna Vize’s set design there is a great Rank-style gong that is bashed. It is immensely effective as a motif for battle propaganda and saber-rattling as well as meteorological disturbance in Rome: it sounds like thunder at times or a ferocious wind sent from angry gods. Rome here floats dislocated from a specific time and place, bringing a kind of universality in its presentation of power, rebellion and the place of rhetoric in it. Characters crawl or kneel before each other, in supplication or disassembling demonstrations to power. They are all barefoot and almost like bare-knuckle fighters. The darkness and candlelight exude conspiracy well, but you lose out on clearly seeing actors’ expressions, and the pace is slow, despite the circling movements on stage and the thriller tropes. The weight of Shakespeare’s verse is almost lost in the midst of it all. Gillen gives a standout performance as Mark Antony but you wish Dunne’s Brutus was not quite so featureless, and that Duchêne’s Caesar bore either more braggadocio or gravitas. Caesar’s death comes with immense wallops of sound, and the performers themselves are loud, but the volume feels a little too one-note. There is potential confusion, too, for those who are not familiar with the play when Caesar begins doubling up as the soothsayer (“beware the ides of March”), and you miss the presence of Brutus and Caesar’s wives as two of Shakespeare’s commanding women. What you get is an elemental sense of the play, almost its essence, but not the beauty of its verse and the subtleties of language, which is a great shame for a play based on the power of oration and its ability to harness (or manipulate) the masses. At Sam Wanamaker Playhouse, London , until 14 February

title: Sir Stanley Wells obituary
text: In 1978 Oxford University Press made Stanley Wells, who has died aged 96, director of a Shakespeare department specially created so that he could produce a new edition of the complete works. Starting from scratch, he went back to the early printed copies, the quartos and folios, and thought through every editorial and textual decision – how to modernise the spelling and punctuation, and edit stage directions and speakers’ names, while giving the rationales for emendations. The single volume Complete Shakespeare appeared in 1986, edited by Stanley, with Gary Taylor, John Jowett and William Montgomery. It proved to be groundbreaking, startling and controversial. Shakespeare was presented as a man of the theatre, one who revised his work in the light of performances. Unconsidered collaborative elements of his works were identified, attributions to him of little-known works were reconsidered, and some new attributions were made. From 1982 Stanley was also general editor of OUP’s individual play series, starting with Henry V, and completed in 2011 with Richard II. He thus became the first person solely to shape, supervise and complete an entire Shakespeare series. From 1988 to 1997 he was the University of Birmingham’s professor of Shakespeare studies and director of the Shakespeare Institute , based in Stratford-upon-Avon. There he presided over the International Shakespeare Conference, the International Shakespeare Association and the Royal Shakespeare theatre’s summer school; he also served as vice-chair of the theatre’s governors (1991-2003). His many projects ranged from editing 19 volumes of Cambridge University Press’s annual Shakespeare Survey, and Shakespeare in the Theatre: An Anthology of Criticism (1997), to being a special adviser on Shakespeare: The Animated Tales (1992-94) for BBC Two and S4C. Deeply committed to Shakespeare on the stage, he brought together the worlds of academia and the theatre through discussion, teaching and publication. Nonetheless, he was a keen critic, approaching directorial conceits with humour, and sometimes bewilderment. Actors admired and consulted him. His vast knowledge of the plays and theatre history is evident in Shakespeare: A Dramatic Life (1994) and Great Shakespeare Actors: From Burbage to Branagh (2015). Shakespeare for All Time (2002) is a comprehensive overview of the playwright’s wide influences on culture; Shakespeare & Co (2007) considers him alongside his fellow dramatists; and Shakespeare: Sex and Love (2010) discusses his personal life, and his use of sex and romance in the plays. Born in Hull , Stanley was the eldest of four children of Doris and Stanley Sr. His father ran a bus company, and one day brought home a complete set of Dickens from the editor of the Hull Daily Mail. Stanley, aged 12, hid behind the sofa and was heard laughing out loud at The Pickwick Papers. Later he saw touring productions of Shakespeare to Hull featuring the actor-manager Donald Wolfit. At Kingston high school, the English teacher who encouraged his interest in Shakespeare was a Mr Large. He introduced his class to Sonnet 29, “ When in disgrace with fortune and men’s eyes ”, which spoke to Stanley’s teenage angst. In 1948 he went to University College London , and gained a degree in English. Then he was, as John Aubrey described Shakespeare , “a schoolmaster in the country” – at Hilsea college, near Basingstoke, Hampshire. In 1957 he wrote to Allardyce Nicoll, the then director of the Shakespeare Institute, asking for a summer job in Stratford-upon-Avon. This led to Nicoll offering him a PhD scholarship, with which he produced an edition of Robert Greene’s novel Pandosto, or The Triumph of Time, Shakespeare’s main source material for The Winter’s Tale. As a fellow of the institute from 1962, Stanley developed popular short residential courses for international undergraduates, and got to know the actors and personnel of the RSC. title: Dylan Moran goes looking for trouble and disappears off the beaten track in this baffling comedy show
text: I s Dylan Moran joking when he opens his show by telling Northampton’s audience “I didn’t write anything, or prepare”? By the end, you wouldn’t bet on it. Bleary directionlessness may be par for the course for the Irish comic, whose work has always combined poetic-philosophical dazzle with a certain wooziness. But after a promising start tonight, his new touring show, Looking for Trouble, conspicuously loses its way, as Moran frets about forgetting a significant chunk of material, before abandoning his encore and leaving a bewildered audience in his wake. That’s a shame, because there are shards of trademark brilliance in the opening 20 minutes, which see the 55-year-old address himself, albeit obliquely, to the mysteries of being human in 2026, AKA “the burning ball of what you don’t understand” From Trump to AI, Moran surveys it all in wide angle not closeup, as symptoms of our confusion, atavism and fear of expulsion from the tribe. The quality of his thinking in this section, while cheerfully offering himself up as Exhibit A in this prosecution of humanity’s perplexity, is arresting. And there are zingers, too, including a word-picture of the genitals that, once heard, may never be forgotten. But Moran turns his back on this material part-way into the hour-long set, asking instead: “What can we discuss that won’t depress us?” From which point the show becomes increasingly noodly, with our host drifting between artist’s easel – on which he paints portraits of favourite foodstuffs and audience members – and a bank of musical instruments, none of which he can play. That doesn’t stop him twanging strings and plonking keys along to an assortment of half-baked ditties that are seldom apropos of anything. “That song doesn’t go anywhere, or end,” he admits at one point. You don’t say. Throughout this grab-bag of a show, Moran’s company remains enjoyable enough and, amid the pottering, there are droll routines on Irish accents, office life and the British Isles reimagined as travellers in a shared car. But – like Britain, you could say – the show hangs together awkwardly at best. At Corran Halls, Oban , on 25 November, then touring until 30 May

title: Ben Whishaw and Kathryn Hunter are a dynamite duo on the road to nowhere in Eurotrash
text: Y ou would be hard-pushed to find a more charismatic double act than Kathryn Hunter and Ben Whishaw. She dazzles as a dowager, bringing flamboyant physical flourishes as she knocks back the cooking wine; he is her lugubrious son, Christian, a novelist with writer’s block. Their story trades on kookiness but the chemistry would keep you captivated even if they watched paint dry for the duration of this interval-free drama. Based on Swiss author Christian Kracht’s bestselling novel, adapted by Colin Teevan, it is charmingly directed by Walter Meierjohann. The third big star is Lizzie Clachan’s set, so full of mischief that it is like a magician pulling out imaginative visual jokes and clever thrills and spills. Glyn Pritchard heroically plays ancillary roles (from taxi driver to waiter) with lightning-quick wardrobe changes while the sound effects are visibly, wittily created in a glass studio. All of it almost papers over the cracks in the story but something is still amiss. Mother and son embark on a road trip across Switzerland with a plastic bag full of euros to give to a worthy cause. There is an early mention of the mother’s German heritage and a father who was in the SS as they drive around with their “dirty money”. A review of Kracht’s book by Der Spiegel called it a work about “the destructive power of silence – over decades, over generations”. The silence relates to how Christian and his mother have contended with, and put away, their family history of nazism – and, by extension, Germany’s relationship to the second world war. The puncturing of silence around guilt and culpability comes wrapped in their irascibly lovable mother-son escapades, which take them from a vegetarian commune where they find a comic fascist in plain sight, à la The Producers, to a failed high-altitude search for edelweiss. The show, like the book, is full of heartwarming comedy and moments of fractiousness, and on that level works beautifully. But Kracht’s book is unforgiving and full of interrogations of the mother, as well as disgust at Germany’s past, which is absent here. Christian, as delightfully as he is played by Whishaw, does not quite feel believable in his passivity. His diffidence seems so British that you are left wondering where he is from (a Canadian boarding school is mentioned). There seems to be a subtle attempt at universalising the story by distancing it from the specific context of its central trauma. The mother wants to go to Africa to distribute her money but later suggests they give it to Syrian refugees. The themes inhabit similar ground to the film Fatherland , about novelist Thomas Mann’s reckoning with Germany’s shame, but the silence between Christian and his mother is tied to historical forces that are not fully interrogated. We come to the source of the big, howling silence between them towards the end of the play, not at the beginning as in the book: what was done to her, what was done to him, a mirror trauma she failed to prevent. It is a searing moment, but there is not nearly enough follow-through. What you get instead is the strange accomplishment of brilliant streaks of drama in a story with holes. The silence, sadly, remains.

title: James McAvoy’s random encounter triggers a delusional fantasy in Parasocial Activity
text: K nowing what to believe is getting harder. Technology has blurred the line between truth and lies. Certain facts, though, we can demonstrate. We know, for example, that James McAvoy appeared in Cyrano de Bergerac at the Theatre Royal in Glasgow in the mask-wearing spring of 2022. We can also take playwright Briony Martha at her word when she says she bumped into the actor in a nearby coffee shop. It is even true that McAvoy was in the audience of Martha’s Parasocial Activity towards the end of this summer’s run on the Edinburgh fringe: a performance that can only have had a heightened air of unreality. Because Martha’s play, which she performs with wide-eyed energy, imagines what might have happened after that chance encounter. In a pink jumpsuit and Hello Kitty T-shirt, she plays Jenny, physically a woman, emotionally a child, who meets the celebrity in the Sauchiehall Street branch of Costa Coffee and convinces herself there is romantic significance in his gift of two tickets to see him on stage. In another era, Jenny’s fantasy would have remained just that: an innocuous dream. But in the age of generative AI, she has the digital tools to sustain that fantasy. In Megan Brewer’s high-precision production, the delusion is as convincing to the audience as it is to her. Sure, if McAvoy has gone to the trouble of following her on Instagram and posing for a picture at the stage door, why would he not also text her an affirming message, sweetly reflecting back her desires? The more she engages, the more he tells her what she wants to hear. We all love a rags-to-riches love story, so we want to hear it too. Except when the interaction goes beyond innocent flirting and into AI psychosis , we find ourselves, like Jenny, adrift on the wrong side of the truth/lies divide. At Òran Mór, Glasgow , until 21 November. At Southwark Playhouse, London , 13-30 January.

title: Is Donald Trump beyond caricature? Not at all – here’s his hilarious origin story
text: H is manner and actions often seeming like improbable caricature, the current US president sets a challenge for satire, any comic exaggeration likely to be trumped by reality. Mike Bartlett’s play The 47th (2022), staged between Trump’s administrations, pursued wild fantasies about the politician’s future career that were soon superseded by odder events. Ali Abbasi’s movie The Apprentice (2024) more sensibly focused on the period from 1973 to 1986 in which the New York realtor developed the behavioural and verbal tics that make him probably the most ridiculed figure in modern history, though such mockery, until the recent midterms, largely consoled detractors while being ignored by supporters. Closer to Abbasi’s approach, Donald by the Italian dramatist Stefano Massini resembles his play The Lehman Trilogy – an international hit about the banking dynasty – in being a psychological analysis played by three actors with lightning switches of character and costume. In this case, the cut-up structure reflects Massini’s seeding conceit that only about 10 minutes of any life really matter, a total of the brief sequences in which someone makes formative or destructive choices. Hence we jump between such moulding moments as Trump learning biographical reinvention from his father, scamming primary school mates for cash, clocking the crowd-building power of television, and being tutored by lawyer Roy Cohn. Previous Trump fictions and documentaries covered these pivots, but Massini also more freshly suggests Trump sensing destiny after surviving near fatal car and plane accidents and his ingestion of lessons from Muhammad Ali (lose the top title but win it back) and PT Barnum , a circus showman who became a politician. Elliot Cowan’s scarily convincing Trump captures the mouth pouts, chin juts, sculpting hands and sudden stretched or staccato intonations. At first sight, he looks too slight until it becomes clear that, like Sebastian Stan in The Apprentice, he is just the younger man, the play leaving him in Trump Tower decades before the White House residencies. Lehman-style, the other actors perform multitudes, Oscar Batterham most striking as an influentially repulsive Cohn, a baseball coach and Trump’s father, while Jo Herbert excels as his mum, as well as a military instructor and various of Trump’s blond quarries. Farce (even of this serious sort) must be played fast, but adapter-director Sean Foley is the Usain Bolt of comedy, changes of clothes and locale so rapid that the actors require athletic breath control. Matching the hectic metronome, Akhila Krishnan’s three-walled video design exhilaratingly places the actors amid speeding traffic or soaring and falling skyscraper elevators and the sky above and sewers below. Massimo and Foley sidestep easy satire to give a funny but profound account of how Trump happened. At Ustinov Studio, Bath , until 5 December

title: ‘We can rage’: Michael Sheen fires up the gripping medieval epic Owain & Henry
text: N o one does rousing like Michael Sheen. Whether urging on the Welsh World Cup squad or vowing “apocalypse” on The Traitors, he surges forward on waves of rhetoric. As Owain Glyndŵr, beacon of Welsh resistance, he doesn’t disappoint. “We can die gently and be forgotten,” he exhorts his followers. “Or we can rage .” Rage and resignation, the sword and the song, resonate through Gary Owen’s absorbing medieval epic for Wales Millennium Centre and Sheen’s new Welsh National Theatre . Glyndŵr is a marginal figure in Shakespeare’s Henry IV plays, a thorn in the unstable king’s side. Here he stands central, a fitting protagonist for a moment of both surging populist politics and a disillusionment with power play. Who is Glyndŵr? In Shakespeare, he’s “a great magician” or a blowhard spouting “skimble-skamble stuff”. In Owen’s play, he’s variously described as God’s anointed, a faithful guard dog or “a chippy little shit”. Under the newly crowned Henry IV, his lands are stolen, his people abused. Sheen’s voice is a wonder: he growls and soars and flecks with wit, especially when swivelling aside to address us. Glyndŵr resists a lurking saviour complex: he’s haunted by vulnerability, even (especially) in triumph, and his doubts rumble through an improvised coronation. “England was an experiment,” declares Glyndŵr, “and it has failed.” You take his point as the English swagger and mispronounce placenames. Nigel Barrett, inheriting the role of Henry from an indisposed Linus Roache, makes him a narky middle manager, clinging to power. But the Henry looming larger here is Prince Hal, the future Henry V. Ned Costello portrays a slavering manchild, entitlement coursing through his veins: “the whole world will be England’s oyster – and we will swallow it down”. Even Owen’s small-cast plays ( Iphigenia in Splott , Violence and Son ) inhabit a landscape of pain and dispossession. Here, writing on an epic scale, he summons the hue and cry of Shakespeare’s history plays: ghosts that haunt a showdown, victory that tastes like loss. A strong cast includes Rakie Ayola as Glyndŵr’s wife, a sardonic strategist (“a hope-starved people will follow the man who feeds them”), and Sophie Melville , ferocious as a widow turned warrior. It’s still a top-down history of fractious aristocrats, but Owen notes its cost: the defeated faces, the guts slipping from severed bellies. A fluid production (Sheen co-directs with Steffan Donnelly) deals briskly with battle and riot, despite a throwback design of cloaks and scaffolding – though clouds flare on Jack Phelan’s video backdrop, the drama heightened by Aideen Malone ’s chiaroscuro lighting. Characters don’t enjoy their Shakespearean ends, whether Falstaff, David Judge’s impressively contained Hotspur or Henry himself. As with Shakespeare, it’s not a night for fact-checking, but one which wonders how to build a myth, and whether you can step out of the cycle of rebellion and grubby realpolitik. A vast theatre is packed for Owen’s stirring epic: “our verse in the song of humanity”. At Wales Millennium Centre, Cardiff , until 28 November. Streaming on National Theatre at Home from 1 March

title: Kelly Gough is simply astounding as Desire Under the Elms reaches the heights of Greek tragedy
text: Y ou would not know that Eugene O’Neill’s play was originally set on a mid 19th-century farm. This version by director Ebenezer Bamgboye brings modernity with its sleek storytelling, but also nods to the ancient Greek drama O’Neill was emulating in his 1924 play about illicit desire and the father-son fight for land. It makes for a strange mix at first, beguiling and bewildering in equal measure. Bamgboye employs some of the striking theatricality that he brought to his magnetic adaptation of The Lonely Londoners two years ago. It is an original refashioning, the script sharper with less of the exposition that might date it, but the directorial flourishes come so thick and fast that it is stylised to the bone. Bamgboye has previously worked with Rebecca Frecknall (who staged the leaden O’Neill drama A Moon for the Misbegotten last year) and the first half seems to pay too big a debt to her style of work. Ephraim (Antony Byrne) is an irredeemably tyrannical father and Eben (Zackary Momoh) his calculating son. Eben sees off his two half-brothers in hope to claim this farm, passed down from his late mother, as his own, when Ephraim brings home a young new bride, Abbie (Kelly Gough). “I can’t believe all this is mine,” she says, crowingly, when she sees the farm. So begins the fractious relationship between Abbie and Eben. There is an attempt to tell O’Neill’s story on another level, with a racial element added. Set in the deep south rather than its original north-east, the dynamic is that of a white father and Black son through its casting. Eben speaks of his father’s slave-driving and his wrongful ownership of stolen land; Ephraim’s iron-rod rule begins to look like that of a plantation owner. As in Frecknall’s production of A Streetcar Named Desire, music interprets emotion, from screams to sexual overtures and angry clashes. A live, roving trumpet and guitar interject in these moments, the musicians stalking the auditorium like musical ghosts, along with the spectre of Eben’s dead mother, singing languorously. Movement is key, with sex or violence also transposed to dance, or jagged, jittery twitches. The effect is sometimes arresting but also overwrought. The sexual chemistry between Eben and Abbie is so choreographed that it does not give off enough heat. The ghostliness and gothicism seems over-egged with smoke rising from the blank canvas of darkness on Basia Bińkowska’s non-realist stage design. But it rights itself and the overload of manufactured expressiveness gives way to something far more elemental in the second half when this production allows its actors simply to act. Momoh is good but Gough (whose sister Denise played the same role in a production 14 years ago ) is off the scale. Part-Phaedra, part-Medea, she is a woman who has a purity of desire alongside her steeling ambitions and strength: she is the one to activate the attraction she feels towards Eben. Her unravelling is painful to watch, and her performance really does rise to the heights of Greek drama, intense and unstoppably tragic. The tension takes on a vice-like grip as the music, movement and gothicism come together. This is artistic director Rupert Goold’s final production before his departure and is not perfect yet it rises to become incredibly powerful. At Almeida theatre, London , until 23 December

title: Tamsin Greig is sensational in a Cranford where comedy and pain are in perfect balance
text: T here’s more than one worry for any new dramatisation of Elizabeth Gaskell’s novel to contend with. There is the risk of this story, set among the unmarried women and widows of a fictional English town, being considered Middlemarch lite – and overshadowed by the Royal Shakespeare Company’s luminous adaptation of the George Eliot novel, currently running in Stratford-Upon-Avon . Then there is the 2007 BBC adaptation of Cranford, which threw every national treasure at it, trowelling on the lovable humour and sentiment as it did so. This production, however, co-created by Lin Coghlan, Shaun McKenna and Josh Roche, bypasses all those dangers by leaning into theatricality – and sheer good acting. The script is by Coghlan and McKenna, who previously adapted The Forsyte Saga, staged last year by the RSC. They confidently fillet the original and also add their own little inventions. Directed by Roche, it feels neither truncated during its shortcuts nor contrived in its new bits. The production gets to the heart of these women, who face death, heartbreak and the loss of men around them, but come to gain from the strength of female friendship. It is lovely to see a play led by such strong women – characters and performers. Tamsin Greig seems made for the role of Matty Jenkyns, the more obedient and awkward sister to Deborah (Abigail Cruttenden). She is sensational, balancing gawky comedy with a yearning for a life unlived through duty and misfortune. Eliza Cleghorn (Phoebe Pryce) is their visitor from Manchester in place of Gaskell’s Mary Smith and her name plays on Gaskell’s own, as does her storyline of secret loss. Pryce makes an upright Eliza with a passing resemblance to Eliot’s young Dorothea in her uncompromising morality, while Sara Crowe serves up naively comic one-liners as Mrs Forrester, and Alexandra Gilbreath brings a gossip’s winking ways as Miss Pole. The storyline of housemaid Martha (Saffron Dey) and her relationship with Jem (Robert Merriam) acquires additional elements, while the reason for the disappearance of Peter Jenkyns (Jonny Glynn) is graphically spelled out. There is a beautiful light touch to Natalie Johnson’s set design: curtains swish down for the women’s trip to the magic show; a circle of chairs are brought on for the women to become card-playing gossips, and fast friends. The theatre’s auditorium, in the round, and Jamie Platt’s emotional lighting, burnish it all with intimacy. The play between sentiment, humour and private pain is perfect: the last two elements stop the effect from becoming too mawkish. A delightful surprise and a must-see for the festive season. At Orange Tree theatre, London , until 16 January

title: ‘Loaded with potential’: stage version of TV smash It’s a Sin has the dancefloor at its heart
text: Russell T Davies’s award-winning series It’s a Sin, about young gay friends living through the Aids crisis in 1980s London, is getting a new life as a dance piece , with a trailer released on Monday ahead of an opening at Aviva Studios in Manchester in February. “We had a few approaches, but a lot of people wanted to make it a musical, which made my heart sink slightly,” said Davies. “I always imagined an aria between those two women on the seafront at the end and I thought: ‘Oh, that could be so terrible!’” Dance was different, he said. “It felt so original and so pure. The story distils down to these emotional moments that are going to be done so beautifully on stage.” The idea came from Benoit Swan Pouffer, artistic director of Rambert, which celebrated its centenary this year with a commitment to bringing in new audiences, in part by reinventing familiar titles, as in its dance version of Peaky Blinders . “Dance needs to be democratised and this is the way to do it,” said Pouffer, who is choreographing It’s a Sin. Davies has a cameo in the trailer, although his own dance career peaked with a performance for Princess Diana with West Glamorgan youth theatre (she told him he should continue to “Dance, dance, dance!”). The dancefloor, however, has always been an inspiration. “They’re such potent places, so loaded with potential.” Davies spent many nights in the clubs of Manchester’s Canal Street, watching lives play out to music. “Those dancefloors were places of such extraordinary freedom,” he said. “Especially in the 80s, with that layer of secrecy. That’s where you’d be out – you might not be out at home – becoming the person you aspired to be.” The dance world was notably affected by the Aids epidemic. “I had friends and colleagues who left us too early,” said Pouffer. He was dancing in the US in the mid-90s, and saw as much stigma about HIV and Aids in the dance world as anywhere else. “There was shame, it was hidden. Even Alvin Ailey, that’s not what we said [that he died of an Aids-related illness] when he passed. Even now there is still a stigma,” said Pouffer. “The trauma, you put it in a little capsule and you don’t talk about it. Now we have this young PrEP generation who don’t know how traumatic it was. The closest they can think of is Covid,” he suggested. “Remember in the beginning when we didn’t know anything about the virus?” Pouffer also wants to convey the excitement and creative spark of the era. “The fashion, the music, the dance of the 80s, it was one of the peaks of history,” he said. There will be video and narration to help tell the story, with scripts by Kaite O’Reilly. Davies is an executive producer, as are Pet Shop Boys, whose title song will feature alongside an original soundtrack by Roman GianArthur. When Davies originally pitched the TV series he was turned down by all the major UK networks, even Channel 4, which eventually commissioned it. “It was simply an assumption that it would be miserable, even when they had the first script to read,” he said. The series went on to be a huge hit. “Not a week goes past without someone stopping me in the street,” said Davies. Yet it was hard to celebrate, “because no matter how proud we were, it’s a story that’s founded on a lot of deaths”. There is “a great heaviness at the heart of it, a great sadness and loss,” he continued. “But we told it with joy and vigour and life. The most important thing is to remember the life that those people had, not the death … I think the show worked because it turned around and said: ‘Hey, we loved those boys. Remember the love.’” It’s a Sin is on tour from 16 February to 13 November 2027

title: ‘Turner prize for dance’ winner Christos Papadopoulos: failure, friction and my forgotten youthquake
text: C hristos Papadopoulos is talking about how to spend £40,000. Specifically the winnings he scooped from the first ever Rose international prize for choreography in 2025 – the dance world’s equivalent of the Turner and the Booker. The Greek choreographer came out top of four finalists, picked by a judging panel including Arlene Phillips and PJ Harvey, for his piece Larsen C, a shadowy, trance-like and glacially paced crescendo of a dance named after an Antarctic ice shelf. Forty grand is not a bad bounty. Did he blow it on designer gear and exotic holidays? He did not. A big chunk went to his dancers, “because they are very hardworking and not so well paid – that’s the Greek reality”. The rest he invested in his new production: “I had some holes to fill, you know, in the budget.” The win may not have made Papadopoulos a household name (this is contemporary dance we’re talking about), but his work is touring worldwide . We speak over video call from Shanghai, where he is performing My Fierce Ignorant Step before its UK premiere. The title, he admits, is a bit weird. It came to him before he’d started making the dance and refers to Papadopoulos’s younger self, full of naive optimism, youthful hope and revolutionary zeal to change the world. Growing up in a small town in the Peloponnese, Papadopoulos spent much of his time in nature. In the summer, he would be out all day “just wandering the mountains and playing”. When everyone else was sheltering from the sun, Papadopoulos would roam the forest on his own: “these quiet moments stimulated my awareness”. Young life was full of freedom and possibility. Today, in middle age, he is “frustrated by the future” and the daily bombardment of doom about world events. “I felt that I was losing hope, and I was getting drier and drier inside,” he says. “I started thinking about my teenage years, when I had this fierce, almost arrogant certainty that we would create a great world ahead. We were naive and we were very romantic. Now that I’m more mature and I can think of the political situation in a more three-dimensional way, I can easily be discouraged.” That can lead to inaction so My Fierce Ignorant Step isn’t a nostalgic look back to a lost time, but an attempt to “restimulate our lives to really do something about it”. Papadopoulos’s first attempt at making the show was disastrous. “The first month it was a complete failure,” he says. “A dead end.” He was trying to recreate that energy and positive force he remembered, and have the dancers express it, but “you cannot create a ‘happy’ piece, or an ‘optimistic’ piece”. Instead, he had to create the conditions to generate that feeling for real among the dancers. That meant causing friction, in the shape of long, technically and rhythmically difficult phrases that the dancers struggled with. They had to help each other, “their antennae of awareness would go out”, they’d be signalling to each other, supporting each other. You attempt something “so epically difficult that we need each other in order to do it”, Papadopoulos says, then when you actually achieve it together, a sense of joy floods in – and with it the sense that anything is possible. Further inspiration came from the Axion Esti , a poem by Greek Nobel laureate Odysseus Elytis from 1959. It speaks of the best and worst of humankind, and has vivid descriptions of the natural world, which connected with Papadopoulos when he read it as a teenager. “It was also the period when my political consciousness was forged,” he says. “Elytis was proposing a world, a political world, but also a world where through morals and through love you can achieve beauty. He was suggesting that beauty is not an aesthetic choice; it is a consequence of a way of being.” A version of the poem set to music by composer Mikis Theodorakis became a symbol of Greek resistance to military dictatorship in the 60s and 70s. title: Adam and Joe on spoofing ‘Christopher No-Laughs’ with a toys’ Odyssey – and Patrick Stewart’s haunted house
text: ‘W arning: The Adam and Joe Show is a high-density programme.” In the late 90s, that was your Friday-night cue to press record on the video player for Adam Buxton and Joe Cornish’s pop-culture potpourri of sketches, pranks and lovingly crafted, lo-fi movie parodies featuring figurines and cuddly toys. Thirty years after its debut, the duo – now both 57 – recreated their old den in the improbable environs of the Royal Albert Hall for a three-hour anniversary show as packed as the rapid-fire series. Here’s a select few things we learned from an evening of clips, chat and ridiculously catchy songs … The pair’s first TV episode featured Trainspotting recreated with knitted animals addicted to sherbert and their later spoofs included Toytanic. On Wednesday night, Buxton presented a first look at his new epic pastiching The Odyssey by Christopher Nolan – or “Christopher No-Laughs” as Cornish had it. A toy of Zendaya’s Athena holds a poster from the high-street chain of that name, there’s a longship with a crew of toys and the Sirens are played by Party Rings and other tempting snacks. Cornish had a hit movie with Attack the Block in 2011 and was a writer that year on Steven Spielberg’s Tintin film. Encouraged to show the Hollywood heavyweight one of the toy parodies, he feared insulting him with the bad-taste riff on Saving Private Ryan. He plumped instead for the sweary “Shakesbeare” in Love, with its subplot about Romeo and Juliet Bravo, gags about British theatrical royalty and copious soft-toy sex. “He found it funny for a minute,” said Cornish. “Then he stopped laughing. And there were two minutes left …” A&J’s rise meant they ended up meeting many other celebrities whom they’d spoofed. Their Star Trek Next Generation sketch, set aboard the Kinder Surprise on the fluffy frontier, had a tennis-playing Borg with Björn-style headbands and a porcine version of Patrick Stewart’s Jean-Luc Picard. Cornish recounted meeting Stewart and expecting him to be a master of rational thinking. However: “The first thing he said to me was how heavily his house was haunted.” Buxton and Cornish met as teenagers at Westminster School alongside Nick Clegg and, somewhat more influentially for them, Louis Theroux . In the duo’s early film Twitch of the Death Nerve, named after a Mario Bava horror movie, Theroux can be seen chewing the scenery in his best hard-boiled manner. When Theroux found work on Michael Moore’s TV Nation, he introduced the pair to the cult US public access show Squirt TV which would influence them along with American zine culture. It was Theroux’s idea for Adam and Joe to go into their local Brixton minimarket and devour the “10% free” bit of various snacks until slurping the 15% free bit of a Ribena carton proved the last straw for the staff. The sketch could have been longer but nervous Buxton’s hand was shaking so much when he filmed that they couldn’t use all the material. The duo’s Channel 4 boss was Peter Grimsdale, head of history, religion (much to their amusement) and features. His vision for the show was “layers of minutiae” and it was at one point going to be called Stüffe. (Other rejected titles, listed in the first episode: Vidiosynchracy, Slackervision, Nocturnal Emission.) The show was essentially an analogue pick’n’mix of the kind of short, sharable content that would soon explode online. And with the weekly pop culture critiques by Adam’s father, ex-Sunday Telegraph journalist Nigel Buxton – aka BaaadDad who I’d forgotten even starred in a Frank Black video – they were ahead of the trend for comedians roping in their parents. BaaadDad would have approved of the Albert Hall setting, the duo agreed – and for any 90s teenagers like me who’d hit record on Friday night to see what they’d cooked up that week, it was certainly surreal to join a Bobby De Niro calypso singalong at the home of the Proms.

title: ‘Thicky thicky dumb dumb’ satirist Cody Dahler on his viral videos: ‘my material is presented to me on a silver platter!’
text: Why did you get into comedy? My mum was a professional dancer and always encouraged me to perform. Given that I have zero rhythm, comedy was my other option. She wrote me a poem called Mrs Brown’s Moggy, about a cat that was often very soggy, for my school’s talent show. Because you can’t tell the difference between real and polite laughter at the age of six, I assumed I’d killed my first gig and convinced myself I was born to do nothing else. Where do you find your material? In a world where Robert Jenrick claims Nigel Farage has “ probably done more than almost anybody to stand against racism ”, the answer is that my material is presented to me on a silver platter each morning. When did it click that you might be on to something with your “ thicky thicky dumb dumb ” videos? When Donald Trump captured the Venezuelan president, Nicolás Maduro. Up until that point I was covering four or five stories in each video. But obviously Trumpty Dumpty’s top-class diplomacy meant that people only really wanted one story breaking down for them. That was the video that really exploded online. If you look closely at the picture of the blindfolded Maduro in that US military helicopter, you can see my career taking off with him. What can readers expect from your new book? An attempt to help them understand why everything is so crap, written in a way that won’t make them feel like a thicky thicky dumb dumb in front of all their mates. Partly because the book answers questions that my followers sent in to me. While researching it, I was pretty shocked by how inaccessible books about British politics were. Everything seemed to be Margaret Thatcher 1973-74: The Pre Policy Years and Governed! – A Battle for the Soul of Britain’s Fiscal Policy Within the Bank of England. No disrespect to the fiscal policy nerds but I’m pretty sure even they don’t want to read that. I know from doing political videos online how interested and engaged people are about politics – it’s just that nobody is talking about it using language they actually understand. What’s a topic you’ve found particularly difficult to explain? I genuinely believe that things are made to sound more complicated than they are to exclude people from engaging with politics. And often to get politicians off the hook for not knowing what the hell they’re doing. So basically, my big-headed answer is once I’d waded through the academic guff that’s used to make people feel cleverer than you, most things were actually very simple to explain. You’ve got more than two million followers online. What’s one of the strangest fan encounters you’ve had? At the live recording of my podcast, The Truth (In My Opinion), at the Bedford pub in Balham, an audience member called Bethany came up to me to say she’d travelled from Chicago that day specifically to see the show. Given that many of my north London friends thought south London was too far for them, I thought that was pretty amazing. Any bugbears from the world of comedy? Oh God, absolutely – but I’d like to keep my career for now, thank you very much! Best advice you’ve ever been given? Make your own stuff. Worst advice you’ve ever been given? Say yes to everything. What’s next for you? Frostbite. I’ve made the mistake of basing my entire brand around wearing shorts in all weathers. Now winter and El Niño are on the way … The State of This! is published by Blink (£16.99). To

title: My fiancee, my foreskin and me: the comic who turned adult circumcision into a jaw-dropping show
text: W hen Max met Eliana at the Edinburgh fringe, the romcom vibes were strong. Shots, songs, falling headlong in love. Less vibey was the conversion Max Olesker had to navigate to marry his Orthodox Jewish beloved. The comedian had always thought of himself as Jewish – when his parents married, his mum converted to a less rigorous branch of Judaism . But to the Beth Din, the rabbinical court, that didn’t count. To be with the woman he loved, Max would have to go all in – including undergoing an unwelcome adult circumcision. We’re chatting at a kosher restaurant in central London. Olesker, 38, pulls out a camera, snapping his hefty salt beef on rye from several angles (“I’m trying to learn a skill”). As on stage, he’s an engaging presence: bright eyes, smart, ribbed knitwear, unwaveringly polite. He would surely be a credit to any religion. Yet, as the book and show that chart the agonising process attest, it’s not that simple. His tale sent me into scalding fury at the Beth Din, this all-male panel wielding inscrutable power over their supplicants. They delay, they demand, they withhold approval and bark: “Is comedy a job for a Jew?” (How did they respond to Olesker’s comedy wrestling? Don’t ask.) The sluggish pace feels especially cruel as Max’s dad endures dementia and Eliana’s grandmother advances into her 90s. How did Olesker remain sane through what feels so capricious a process? “There’s little evidence that I successfully kept myself sane,” he smiles. “It was extraordinarily challenging.” He’s not gunning for the rabbis, he insists, but “I wanted to communicate the way it caused me a great deal of pain and anguish, and put extraordinary stress on my relationship. It pushed us incredibly close to the line.” Keeping a journal helped corral the sheer oddity of the journey – especially when lodging with an Orthodox family, feeling like their thirtysomething foster child. “It was so dislocating,” he says, “sat at the edge of a single bed, using an ironing board as a desk. I began writing so that I wasn’t just staring at the ceiling with anxiety dancing through my brain.” During those sleepless nights, did Olesker think: this material is golden? “Definitely not,” he says. His daffy shows with comedy partner Ivan Gonzalez (as Max & Ivan ) increasingly tapped an autobiographical impulse, mayhem amplified by emotion. But with the conversion, “it was only when things began to go disastrously rough that it began to feel that some sort of emotional reflection was the way to process it. None of us could have predicted the juddering crawl towards the finish line – I felt it was sitting on the top of my psyche and had to be engaged with.” His captivating memoir is now distilled into a 60-minute show. The title, Making the Cut, refers to circumcision – but we’re eating, so we don’t go there as Olesker tucks into his meaty tower. More broadly, his path is “a zigzag thing – a journey that was funny, stressful, frustrating and heartbreaking at various points, and none of it in a straight line”. Scribbling is one thing – performing your rawest moments to a roomful of strangers must be another? “It was both draining and energising,” Olesker confirms. “Catharsis is perhaps the word. At times I choked up and struggled to get through the show.” It must also hit differently to perform this show at what is, as Olesker acknowledges, “an incredibly strange time to be Jewish. Jews of all stripes have found themselves contemplating their identities and their relationship to Judaism. I’m aware of so many fraught conversations. For me, part of the importance of the show was creating a story that [followed] the complexities of the human Jewish experience, through all manner of Jewish communities, and to write something reflective of that lived experience.” Wrestling Max and comedy Max are now making space for theatre Max. title: The play that changed my life: ‘John Berger’s Pig Earth became something magical – they licked milk off bodies’
text: T here are many things you see that are impactful, but few you can genuinely say change your life. I saw Complicité’s The Three Lives of Lucie Cabrol aged 16 on a school trip to Riverside Studios in London and it really reached me. I’d been educated in a very language, words-based way. Here the story was told – with such intensity! – through people’s bodies. The world they were conjuring, from a story by John Berger in his book Pig Earth, was about this remote French village – a world of labour. And the strife and struggles of these characters was expressed through the physical work of the company. It travels in time from the turn of the 20th century. There were Lucy’s three lives, the first being her real work life with Lilo Baur playing Lucy. Then her husband abandons her and she’s expelled from her community. And she then goes on a quest, which eventually leads her to love in the afterlife. Physically they were unlike anyone I’d ever seen – Baur, Simon McBurney and Tim McMullan were not conventional-looking actors. It felt like somewhere between meeting a group of aliens and a kind of arthouse circus coming to town. You were completely lifted out of the norm and transported – it opened up very intense, deprived, raw experience into something magical. I remember images more than story. There was an incredible sequence where the company told a love story within a cowshed. They played the cows, they played the lover, there was milk licked off bodies. It felt like something I’d never seen before. The actors were properly sweating doing it, reaching a sort of mystical level. It was amazing and made me realise just what theatre could do. You didn’t judge these people. You weren’t ever allowed to, you had to go with them, whatever difficult turns their lives took. I don’t make theatre like that. I don’t have the kind of physical storytelling language; I always look at it dreamily wishing I had that kind of training. My play Giant uses much more conventional, one-set, closed-time storytelling devices. But I hope that the audience experience something similar in terms of feeling compelled by something and made uncomfortable by it at the same time. Giant can be seen in cinemas from 19 November

title: ‘How can we make it riskier?’: the trans theatre troupe turning Virginia Woolf’s Orlando into a ‘porno-biography’
text: A s Orlando’s on a comedown after a ket-heavy night out in Berlin, surrounded by a group of sharp-tongued trans sex workers, Charli Cowgill and Laurie Ward pause the read-through. The scene is new and “it’s feeling a little safe,” Ward says, drumming the table. “How can we make it riskier?” Cowgill and Ward are piss/CARNATION, a theatre-making duo creating fearless, messy and intellectually rigorous work. Audience spit was collected and thrown in their first production, 52 Monologues for Young Transsexuals , a show that collated trans women’s experiences of men and sex work. Ugly Sisters, the pair’s riotous follow-up, relived a brief encounter between a trans woman and Germaine Greer who wrote a caustic article about it. “As a company,” Ward says, “we tend more towards brutal than twee.” Now they’re tackling Virginia Woolf’s twisting, erotic, time-leaping Orlando. Woolf’s novel may be “campy and frothy and fun,” Ward says as we sit in the park during the company’s lunch break, but “there is a real edge of violence in it”. Created and performed by five transfemme performers, Orlando: A Porno-Biography is an “anti-adaptation”. This means, Cowgill says, “we get to be in dialogue with people’s expectations, and dance over and desecrate them”. For Woolf, the sex transformation of the title character is a platform to “discuss the position of women as subjects of history”, Cowgill says. They are more interested in how the text serves discussions around transfemininity. “Orlando is a text that many trans people are enamoured of,” Cowgill says. But having seen several staged adaptations across Europe, the duo have been disappointed. “The stylings of a lot of the way people do Orlando is this frothy campy costume drama,” Ward says. Casting tends towards androgyny where sex can be seen as staging a “restoration rather than a transformation” by the audience. “One of the whole points of transition as a lived experience is that there is no magical sex transformation,” Ward says. “It’s a lot of labour. It’s kind of like throwing yourself against an idea and hoping you like where you land.” With the 17th-century’s frozen River Thames serving as a metaphor for English masculine repression as the modern world butts in, this is not a nudging of text-to-stage in the way of most modern adaptations. In Woolf’s book, Orlando has 10 years of solitude, while in their version, the courtier is stuck in a goon cave – in their room masturbating obsessively. “There is a smuttiness that’s very alive in the book,” says Ward, “that Virginia Woolf was Trojan horse-ing in because of all the obscenity laws.” In their version, Orlando is engaging in “sissy” pornography in an attempt to access a transfeminine world. “A lot of trans women discover this desire for themselves to transition through the body of another trans person,” considers Cowgill. “It’s in the wanting that other person where you actually realise what you want for yourself.” This is the company’s first commission and their first time getting Arts Council England funding, after six attempts. “We came up through the Edinburgh fringe circuit, where it feels like you’re knocking on doors until you get a convert, and that is totally gruelling,” says Cowgill. “For the previous two shows, we’ve only known by the last performance whether or not we’ve made enough money to pay us back,” adds Ward. “Now we know we have the money to pay everyone for the run.” “Everyone” includes their cast of five, with the writing duo joined on stage by Sharon Le Grand, Mary Malone and Macy Seelochan, who begin the show by playing men. “We’re making a big ask of our transfemme ensemble by asking them to play men in a really earnest way,” says Cowgill. “We’re interested in doing things with trans actors that are a bit button-pushing.” If trans women get cast, they say, their roles tend to be unchallenging. “Dolls deserve complex roles,” says Ward. “And when dolls are cast, there’s an attitude of: handle with care,” says Cowgil

title: Souped-up and now on screen, Starlight Express is moving in all sorts of ways
text: I hardly ever cry at the theatre but can think of three recent cases. 1. The beautifully jittery balcony scene in Liverpool Everyman’s Romeo and Juliet . 2. Dear Theodosia as co-sung by Leslie Odom Jr (actual OG Aaron Burr!) in Hamilton . 3. An embarrassingly large amount of Starlight Express . Why on earth does this ridiculous fantasy of rollerskating trains, with their high-speed scrapes, leave me feeling like an emotional wreck? That’s what happened when I first saw director Luke Sheppard’s souped-up London revival – and again this month, watching a new film of that production. The film arrives just in time for Christmas. In its introduction, Andrew Lloyd Webber calls Starlight a Cinderella story: steam engine Rusty is our Cinders, the ugly sisters are diesel and electric engines, and there are panto-grade puns and innuendo as well as flamboyantly inventive costumes. Panto is generally considered most kids’ introduction to theatre and Starlight was expressly designed to do the same, but a lot of the original 1984 cast recording sounds positively middle-aged, with as much of a whiff of Brut aftershave as exhaust fumes. There’s a sluggish, chugging quality to some numbers, not just in the comedy of how “freight is great”. Newly orchestrated by Lloyd Webber and Matthew Brind, the score has gained greater dynamism but Sheppard’s vibrant revival also benefited from youthful casting with professional debuts from Jeevan Braich as Rusty, Kayna Montecillo as Pearl, Al Knott as Greaseball, Eve Humphrey as Dinah and Tom Pigram as Electra. Part of what makes it so moving is seeing a new generation of scorching talent emerge. Braich, who had a show-stopping number in a Cinderella panto last year, is now a magnetic Angel among the phenomenal cast of Sheppard’s West End Rent revival . There is a laser-like focus to Sheppard’s Starlight, from the precision moves of all the whizzing singers (who had to attend skating school) to the clarion call of the lyrics in I Am Me (“and that’s all I need!”) which matches the pride and defiance of The Greatest Showman ’s This Is Me. A spirit of inclusivity is key to the overhaul. Pearl’s 1984 song He Whistled at Me, which suggested there was a heart-filling joy in being catcalled, is transformed into Whistle at Me, her sweetly caring duet with Rusty about finding mutual understanding. The original Greaseball was a rockabilly diesel engine played as a 50s throwback – Skatin’ Stevens, if you like – whose solo Pumping Iron becomes a grind despite the honkytonk flourishes. Knott sends it soaring as a bodybuilding anthem of ecstatic force. The Starlight reboot’s Greaseball is female, which fuels a queer attraction with dining car Dinah. Knott has praised the “ joyous rebellion ” of Pumping Iron and it’s a high point on screen, too, with Greaseball now played by Olivia Ringrose, who lends the character a growl and scowl. The film could have made more of Greaseball’s iconic spark gun, and also misses an opportunity to really show off Electra’s self-inflating costume, but designer Gabriella Slade’s other eye-popping outfits benefit from being seen up close. The Troubadour Wembley Park, where Starlight was revived, is within the former Fountain TV Studios and is a huge, flexible space which allowed set designer Tim Hatley to let his imagination run riot with the skating tracks that weave around the audience. As well as using fixed, floor-level cameras, the film captures the vertiginous view from the top of the ramp that the scooter-riding referees use for tricks. The height of the venue allows for swooping shots and a sense of perspective that reveals the set as one big fairground attraction. Lloyd Webber was inspired by Thomas the Tank Engine but another great thing about Starlight is that it is not explicitly based on existing IP like so many kids’ shows, such as the Paddington musical ( another Sheppard hit ).
