title: Hamlet Hail to the Thief could have been rotten but redeems Radiohead’s ‘record that got away’ | Alexis Petridis
text: A ccording to the programme notes, Thom Yorke had serious reservations about director Christine Jones’ idea to stage a production of Hamlet featuring music from Radiohead’s 2003 album Hail to the Thief. Who can blame him? Many criticisms have been laid at Radiohead’s door but being hopelessly naff isn’t one of them, and, alas, naff is very much the adjective you’d apply to a lot of attempts to meld Shakespeare and rock music. You’re often in the realm of high camp – portentous, Bard-quoting heavy metal lyrics; Return to the Forbidden Planet ’s jokey blending of The Tempest with 50s rock’n’roll; 2015’s These Paper Bullets , which relocated Much Ado About Nothing to swinging London, complete with Beatle-y songs by Green Day’s Billie Joe Armstrong – or of buttock-clenching disasters like Catch My Soul, a 1971 rock adaptation of Othello which required Black American soul singer PP Arnold to star opposite impresario Jack Good, playing the title role in blackface. Yorke was won around, at least in part because he felt the album in question was “the record that got away”. Such things are obviously relative when it comes to a band with a fanbase as rabid as Radiohead’s – there exists a four-part podcast series that involves a quartet of devotees discussing Hail to the Thief for six hours – but it certainly doesn’t have a reputation to match that of its gamechanging predecessors, Kid A and Amnesiac, or its follow-up In Rainbows, which has a fair claim to be called the best album Radiohead ever made. By contrast, Hail to the Thief received decidedly mixed reviews, not least from some members of Radiohead: bassist Colin Greenwood even suggested some of its songs were released unfinished. A historically shaky idea allied to an album of mixed quality: it’s hard not to feel a slight degree of trepidation. If you’re on the alert for naffness when you arrive at the Barbican , a set littered with guitar amps and a backdrop depicting Elsinore partly constructed from PA speakers might set alarm bells ringing, but no: the Royal Shakespeare Company and Factory International’s production works quite extraordinarily well. For one thing, the music – played by a five-piece band, whose musicians all have roots in jazz, and who perform in what looks like a recording studio at the rear of the stage – just fits the action. If you want something to soundtrack a play in which ghosts and mental disarray figure heavily, the keening tone of Yorke’s vocal melodies is pretty much perfect. Ineffably eerie without ever slipping into Halloween-costume parody, they’re burnished further by the way they’re reworked here: on the version of 2+2 = 5 that opens the play, Meg Hill and Ed Begley’s vocals are swathed in reverb until they sound disembodied. Similarly, the fragments of the album’s more upbeat tracks that litter the play are largely stripped of their electronic arrangements, which amps up their physicality: the riff of Where I End and You Begin feels less jittery, more brawny. The fear that the music might intrude on or interrupt the action is similarly unfounded: a brisk 1 hour 40 minutes long, Hamlet Hail to the Thief’s brevity means both Shakespeare’s text and Radiohead’s music require judicious editing, the latter into what Yorke calls “shattered pieces”. The fragments augment, rather than interrupt. The opening verses of the album’s most beautiful song, Sail to the Moon, have elbowed out the stuff about herbs and flowers from the scene depicting Ophelia’s descent into madness: a ballsy move given how celebrated those lines are, but it fits remarkably well, the oddness of the lyrics – “I sucked the moon, I spoke too soon” – jarring against the heartbreaking melody. The Gloaming soundtracks her funeral, denuding the song of its historical context (on Hail to the Thief, it functions as a horrified response to the Iraq war) and transforming it into a more generalised response to corrupt power structures that suits the play’s court: “Murderers, you’re murderers

title: ‘Half price!’ ‘Only two left!’ How to resist the bargains you just don’t need – this Black Friday and beyond
text: T he other morning a parcel arrived and I was momentarily mystified by its contents. Peering at what appeared to be a shiny maroon and pink cushion cover, the penny eventually dropped. It was the fancy “Sweat Bag” I had bought on impulse when it popped up on Instagram after a particularly trying day. The blurb had convinced me it was the perfect solution for storing sweaty gym gear, ensuring that everything else in my bag remained pristine. “Whether it’s a 6am class before work or squeezing in lunchtime workouts, the Sweat Bag moves with you, wherever your day takes you.” I liked the idea of being this busy, efficient human, but in reality, I generally head straight home after my workouts and collapse beside the nearest biscuit tin. I had no business spending, ahem, £39 on it. If you’ve ever fallen into a similar retail trance only to experience buyer’s remorse, chances are that you, too, have been ambushed by “consumption noise”. Since the rise in popularity of weight-loss drugs we’ve heard quite the cacophony about “food noise”, with users celebrating the welcome absence of cravings. In a similar vein, consumption noise can best be described as the low-level but relentless triggering of a hunger to buy stuff just for the sake of it. “Consumption noise is everywhere. It’s online, it’s outdoors. If you look at the amount of advertising we constantly receive, when we’re on public transport, on the streets, especially in big cities, it’s a lot,” says Emilie Bellet, a former private equity analyst and the founder of the financial education platform Vestpod . This constant exposure is best summed up, she says, by the phrase “‘visual pollution’, a term invented by Marine Tanguy, the author of The Visual Detox. Then, of course, there’s online pollution as well. You buy from a brand one time and you’re on their mailing list, bombarding you with offers, which creates more temptation.” I like to think that I’m good with money. I’m a thrifty Scot who agonises over whether to buy the posh butter or the Aldi dupe. And yet when it comes to marketing tricks, I’m pretty gullible. When I see a tempting offer online flagged with “only two left in stock”, I can feel my heart-rate speed up. Recently, this drove me to buy the world’s most useless slow cooker – it doesn’t have a timer. “I mean, even if it is true that the stock is about to run out, don’t worry. Chances are good that the item will come back,” says Bellet. “For me, the feeling of just putting an item in the basket makes me happy. I get a little hit of dopamine. And then after two days, I realise actually, I don’t really want it, or I’m busy with something else and decide not to buy.” Bellet goes as far as using a Brick blocking device to remove social media from her phone in the early morning and in the evening. The gadget contains a Near Field Communication chip and works with a companion mobile phone app. You choose which apps and websites to block and tap your phone against the Brick to activate. The device is magnetic, the idea being that you stick it on the fridge so you can’t turn your apps back on until you return to the kitchen to tap it. “It creates more clarity, more space for something other than always looking at people trying to sell you stuff,” says Bellet. Another option is to pay £3.99 a month to go ad-free on, say, Instagram. “It sounds like a lot to pay but it’s a gamechanger,” reports a colleague. “Weirdly, now I’m free from falling down rabbit holes into fashion brands I can’t afford, I am drawn to look at the app a lot less.” But the special-occasion buzz around Black Friday and its manufactured sense of urgency can destabilise the best of intentions. “We’re bombarded with these time-limited discounts; perhaps there’s even a countdown timer or warnings about how many other customers are viewing the same item,” says Aarron Atkinson-Toal, the author of a new book, Influenced: The Science of Why We Buy. “Suddenly not buying something can feel like missing out on an

title: A moment that changed me: at 31 I felt I was running out of time – then my 83-year-old grandma got a tattoo
text: I t was the night before my wedding, in the summer of 2024, and I was a couple of months shy of 31. My bridesmaids and I were having drinks with the North American side of my family before the chaos of the big day. In the two years since I’d last seen my grandma Caroline, who lives in Texas and whom I’ve always called Memom, I’d collected a few new tattoos – and I was worried about showing them to her for the first time as her approval means a lot to me. When Memom saw me, she grabbed my tattooed arm and said: “Let me see.” For a second, I thought she was angry. But to my surprise, she loved them. “These are art!” she said. “Tell me all about them.” I talked her through the abstract fine line piece wrapping around my forearm, and why I’d opted for a filigree dagger in the middle of my upper arm, as well as the significance of the ornamental heart on the back of my right arm. She surprised me again a few months later by asking me to help her arrange to get a tattoo of her own. She wanted me to come with her on her next visit to London the following autumn, but she wasn’t entirely sure what to get. Memom said she wanted the tattoo to be on one of her shoulders. She toyed with the idea of four small birds or flowers to represent her four children – that, or “YOLO” emblazoned on her back. It might sound like a joke, but the idea that “you only live once” was a real part of the reason she wanted to get a tattoo in the first place. She spent years thinking about how much she would like to get a tattoo if she were younger, until she realised age needn’t be a barrier. She is not one to miss out on new experiences just because she is in her 80s. I sent her inspo pics from Instagram and Pinterest so she could get a better idea of exactly what she wanted, as well as information about tattoo artists who had amazing reviews. I also contacted those who had tattooed me in the past to check whether there was anything we needed to take into consideration when it came to tattooing octogenarian skin. But aside from the fact that it might take a little longer to heal, it seemed there wasn’t anything to worry about or hold her back. I felt the pressure of wanting to make sure everything was perfect for her, but the whole process was so fun – and a great distraction from what was happening, or rather not happening, with my career at the time. I’d been working as a freelance journalist, but it felt as if things had stalled. I had become preoccupied with the idea that everyone else was somehow younger, smarter and far more talented than I was. Plus, I was starting to worry about if and when I might want to have a baby. In so many ways, it felt as if I was in danger of missing the boat. I enjoyed having something else to occupy my mind. Rather than make small talk at parties, for example, I much preferred to tell people about how I was helping my grandma plan her first tattoo. “Most people would just go to a spa or something when their granny came to visit,” my mother-in-law joked. I couldn’t help but agree. I guess we’re not most people, I would think, revelling in the feeling of superiority after so much time spent doubting myself. In the end, Memom decided to get a small olive branch on the top of her shoulder because, as she put it: “There should just be more peace in the world.” When she got to the tattoo studio, she was understandably a bit nervous about the pain, but she said she didn’t feel a thing. Two of my aunts came along too, and we all laughed and chatted together, as if we did this sort of thing all the time. My grandmother was thrilled with the finished result. Now, not even a year later, she has already asked me to help her plan her next one – she is thinking about getting a semi-abstract black flower on her other shoulder this time. Society has long implied that, for women, value is tied to youth. But watching my grandma get her first tattoo at the age of 83 has given me a fresh perspective on what ageing can really look like. title: How to turn leftover porridge into brilliant cookies – recipe | Waste not
text: M y hope is that today’s recipe will inspire you to save that little bit of cooked porridge left in a bowl and to upcycle it into these wonderful cookies. The porridge acts as the binder, rather than the usual egg, which saves money and keeps things vegan and accessible. If you don’t have leftover porridge, don’t fret – a brown banana will also do the trick. Flaxseeds are a worthy addition – they help improve the integrity of the cookie and add omega 3 and 6 – but they’re not essential. With two kids who are sustained by a morning bowl of porridge, we’ve always got leftovers in the fridge, which I often snaffle as a snack or stir into the next batch. Sometimes, however, we get bored with gruel, so in walks the cookie monster (ie me) to turn those leftovers into these sweet, wholesome and delicious cookies. I tend to use extra-virgin olive oil in baking, not least for its health benefits, but any oil will work here. Be inventive with the seeds, nuts, chocolate and dried fruit; I had sultanas, but chopped apricots or dates are also excellent, as are cranberries and sour cherries. 80-120g cold leftover porridge , or 1 brown banana 15g ground flaxseed (optional) 200g light-brown sugar 190g wholemeal flour , or plain flour 1 tsp bicarbonate of soda 1 tsp fine sea salt 150g rolled oats 100g dried fruit (eg, raisins, cranberries or cherries), chopped if necessary (optional) 50g seeds, or nuts (optional) 80g dark chocolate , chopped (optional) 130g extra-virgin olive oil 1 tsp vanilla extract (optional) In a small bowl, mash the porridge with the optional ground flaxseed. In a large bowl, mix the sugar, flour, bicarb and salt, breaking up any lumps of sugar. Stir in the rolled oats, plus any of the optional extras, then work in the oil, vanilla extract and the porridge mix until well combined. Cover, refrigerate for an hour, then divide and roll into roughly 55g balls. Return to the fridge until you’re ready to bake. Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5 and line two large baking trays. Arrange the balls on the trays, spacing them well apart so they have plenty of room to spread, then use a palm to press each one into a 1½cm-thick disc. Bake for 13-15 minutes, until golden around the edges, then remove and leave on the trays to cool and firm up. Store in an airtight container for up to a week.

title: ‘Sardines are the new anchovies’: what’s hot and what’s not on our winter culinary thermometer
text: Salt bread The Korean bakery icon, also known as sogeum-ppang , is made by wrapping pillow-soft bread dough around a baton of cold salted butter, to create a golden-crisp bottom and airy-tender inside as it bakes. Try at Tokkia in Covent Garden and Salted Boy in Paris. Cold-water noodles The viral Hiyashi cup noodle from Nissin uses “cold rehydrate” technology to instantly “cook” the noodles with chilled water. Huge in Japan, and heading to Europe. This hearty, slow-cooked Hungarian beef stew – rich in browned onions, paprika and caraway – is the nostalgic-revival dinner party dish this winter. Carb loading with bread dumplings, egg noodles, crispy potato rosti or white dinner rolls on the side to soak up the heady infused broth is essential. Black sesame seeds The bolder, crunchier and earthier alternative to white sesame seeds, which have their dark outer shells left intact. Check out the black sesame doughnuts at Onsu Bakery , black sesame and lemon sākuro at Kuro Bakery, and black sesame, tahini and rice pudding cookies at Cöödie (all in London). Sardine maxxing From the Tik-Tok trend for smashed-baked sardines on toast, to sardines in grape leaves at Impala in London, and Gizzi Erskine’ s ‘Dirty Sartini’ with sardine-oil washed Mermaid Gin, sardines are the new anchovies. Upside-down cheesecake The “flip-reverse-it” trend continues to thrill our palates, and now it’s the turn of classic biscuit-based New York cheesecake. Crack open the layer of biscuit as if it’s a creme brulee – it really does taste better spooned out upside down. Nose-to-tail delectations made with all the tastiest innards and trimmings. Blood, Guts and Black Pudding by Irish food writer Kate Ryan is this season’s must-read, and square Lorne-sausage sandwiches are the en vogue hangover cure this Boxing Day. Viet-Cajun boils Traditional Louisiana Cajun-seasoned seafood boils with the addition of bold Vietnamese aromatics like lemongrass, ginger and garlic-butter sauce, served with an obligatory bib. You can now try at The Cajun Boil in Bethnal Green, London. Fool’s gold sandwiches A hollowed out baguette filled with an entire jar of crunchy peanut butter, a jar of tangy jam, and crispy bacon. Loved by Elvis and now discovered by the internet. Crispy rice Scorched bao zai fan crispy claypot rice; upturned saffron-scented Iranian tahdigs ; Nobu-copycat crispy-rice sushi; cheesy, ragu-filled arancini; and old-school caramelised crust paellas. Comfort eating at its most sensorially thrilling. Hot honey is no longer hot enough; all the chic gourmands are burning their honey. Bubbled to a very dark amber, which brings out smoky, coffee-like caramel notes, it is then added to Basque cheesecake, drizzled over charred hispi cabbage or baked into pistachio baklava. Stuffed onions The essential Sunday roast accompaniment. Fill with lamb mince and warming spices for Turkish soğan dolması , with herby pork sausage and garlic for Provencal farcis , or with rice, cumin and parley for Greek salantourmasi . Pumpkin spice Flaccid, generic blends of cinnamon and ginger powder have become very one-note. Intricate chai spices are all the rage, with complex inclusions such as ajwain , black cardamom and tulsi (holy basil). Classic chilli crisp Our taste for global crunchy chilli crisps has evolved beyond the classic to the next flavour-filled level. We love the extra-umami Laoganma fermented black-bean variation, Kashmiri chilli oil from Third Kulture Kat and pasilla salsa macha from Sonia’s Salsa. Dill Thanks to the pickle craze, we’re all maxed out on dill. Marjoram is this winter’s herb du jour, as featured in the winter tomatoes with coco beans, onion and marjoram at Toklas , potato rösti with blue cheese and marjoram at Auguste (both London) and marjoram gnocchi tots with pickled pear at Seasonality in Maidenhead. title: Why I love Budapest in winter: ‘Gloomy days call for a plunge in one of the city’s ornate bathhouses’
text: E ach December, my neighbourhood on the Buda side of the Danube transforms into a living advent calendar. On the edge of District XI (Újbuda), the 1930s OTI estate in Albertfalva is known for its rustic looking single-storey houses with rounded doorways and green shutters. From 1 December, my neighbours take turns decorating their windows with that day’s number and festive lights, sometimes serving chocolate, cocoa or mulled wine in their front gardens. For something grander, I’ll cross the Danube into Pest for its Christmas markets and elaborately decorated shop fronts. Last November, my friends and I sipped hot chocolate beneath the crystal chandeliers of the Művész Kávéház , a historic cafe on Andrássy út, waiting for the Christmas lights to be switched on outside, illuminating the boulevard and the Hungarian State Opera House. The best-known Christmas markets are held around St Stephen’s Basilica and Vörösmarty Square. I’ll stroll through these, enjoy the nostalgic smells of roasting chestnuts and mulled wine, but spend my money at smaller and more authentic neighbourhood markets, like my local one by the Fehérvári úti Market in District XI. At this time of year, nothing beats a steaming hot chimney cake, a brioche-like pastry traditionally grilled over coals and rolled in flavoured sugar. I’ll grab one covered in vanilla or cinnamon sugar from a hole-in-the-wall on Váci utca near the Central Market Hall as I stumble from the office Christmas party to catch the tram home. It’s baked on an electric grill, but it’s cheap and cheerful at a fraction of the Christmas market price. As the chill sets in, I’m torn between getting cosy and heading out into the cold, crisp air. City Park makes it easy to do both, as you can visit the Museum of Fine Arts before wandering over to the ice rink . I learned to skate here as a child, but I struggle to stay upright on ice these days, so I prefer to watch from the bridge or the park, with Vajdahunyad Castle overlooking the skaters. Bonus points if it’s snowing. Gloomy days call for a plunge in the Rudas Baths , one of several historic bathhouses across the city fed by thermal spring waters. I like to go early on Tuesday mornings, when the Turkish section is women-only and I can bathe in peace in the mineral-rich waters beneath the 16th-century dome. For night owls, the Rudas also offers late-night bathing on Fridays and Saturdays. From the rooftop hot tub you can watch the lights twinkling across the Danube. Get travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian Holidays Where to stay Giselle Vintage Doubles (doubles from £54) is inside one of Budapest’s most beautiful residential buildings on Ferenciek tere, a short walk from the Christmas market on Vörösmarty Square.

title: I don’t have children. A stranger decided I was ruining my life
text: Last fall, a man I had never met wrote to inform me that my fertility window was “rapidly closing” – and that I couldn’t possibly be happy. What had prompted this unsolicited assessment was an article I had published about how fascist regimes seek to control women’s roles in society. “Few would argue that family life is unimportant,” I had written. “Yet authoritarian movements have long politicized it, reframing it as women’s sole purpose and a substitute for autonomy and rights.” Wayne, whose name I’ve changed out of an overabundance of generosity and grace, didn’t read the article as a structural critique, but a personal attack. With his wife CC’ed, he wrote with a bloviator’s panache: “One assumes you’re neither wife nor mother, and older than my beautiful 33 y/o wife, Liz.” He continued: “You might think you’re truly happy and empowered, but clearly, you’re not.” Because I am currently without children by choice, and am not struggling with loss or infertility, Wayne’s missive struck me less as hurtful than as bewilderingly absurd. Wayne went on to tell me that Liz – whose name I also changed – on hiatus from nursing school, stays with the couple’s three children at home in the Pacific north-west and has had “four miscarriages”, her husband seemed to brag. “Three in the last year.” That was an intimate detail to offer, but Wayne wasn’t finished. He attached photos of all his children to the email, their names in the jpeg files. I looked at their lovely faces and thought: “Does this man think I’ve never seen children?” A year passed, and Liz had another baby. I know this because shortly after the birth, Wayne sent me pictures of the tiny infant, their “latest miracle”, swaddled in blue. “It’s never too late to do the right thing,” Wayne wrote. “Find a good man. Get married. Have a family.” This time, I had to ask him: “Wayne, do you send unsolicited pictures of your children to other strangers, or just me?” Just me, he responded. “The better question is, ‘Why did I send them to you?’ The answer: so, you can see what you’re giving up. You’re literally giving up everything.” Wayne and Liz had formed an idea of me as a person whose reproductive choices looked different from theirs. On that much they were right, though several of their assumptions were off. I do, for instance, have a good man in my life, though that phrase makes me want to eat a brick. Wayne felt he must command me of what I should do, reproductively and existentially, in order to be “happy”. His family was blissfully content, he told me – and yet, there he was, in a house with three little ones and a fresh baby, emailing a person he had never met, fretting over whether I would miss my chance to replicate his life. I was curious to learn more about this couple and suggested an in-person interview, but while they claimed I was welcome at their church, their tone veered hostile. “I don’t care if you die childless, it’s probably for the best,” Liz wrote. “Let those who believe in the future inherit it.” I was surprised by how angry Wayne and Liz were. After all, I wasn’t the one reaching out to them repeatedly with gloating updates on my clean house and uninterrupted nights of sleep. What’s it to them how I die? And why can’t they leave me in peace? W hile I think my experience with Wayne and Liz was particularly surreal, it’s becoming strikingly common for people to opine on each other’s reproductive choices. Parents become mindless “breeders” on forums like Reddit’s r/childfree; while the childfree are sad losers who stand to be eaten by their own cats. Nobody is spared criticism. Take, for instance, one-and-done parents. You might think they were beyond reproach, tasteful minimalists who did their part for the species. Nope. Writer Jessica Valenti recently took to social media describing a “really intense backlash against moms of only children”. Whenever a mother who has decided to just have one child posts a video about how much she enjoys her life, the comment

title: Want to shop more sustainably this Black Friday? The best UK deals on eco-friendly products we love
text: E thical and sustainable probably aren’t the first words that spring to mind when you think of Black Friday. The annual price-slashing jamboree sits cunningly in wait for your final payday before Christmas, hoping that the dangled carrot of a few quid off will make you more likely to overconsume and overspend. Approach it with care, though, and Black Friday is a good opportunity to buy eco-friendly products that might normally stretch your budget. Many of our Filter recommendations tick either the green box or the affordable box, but we (and you, I expect) would be a lot happier if more of them ticked both. As a Filter reader, you already know the value of researching and planning your purchases before you buy. To make Black Friday work for you rather than the other way around, go in knowing which eco-friendly products caught your eye but never made it into your shopping basket. Intrigued by Who Gives a Crap toilet paper but balked at its price? Wanted to upgrade your mattress to a sustainable one, but without needing a mortgage? Then keep reading. Sustainable shopping can get expensive, even in the sales, because these brands tend to pay more for ethical labour and responsible sourcing than, say, fast-fashion brands. For this rundown, though, we’ve found some genuinely good deals that make more sustainable choices more affordable. As ever when rounding up Black Friday deals , we’ve researched each item’s price history using tools such as PriceRunner and the Camelizer to ensure that these price cuts are rare enough to recommend. We’ve tried hard to avoid greenwashing, too. Just because a product has the word “natural” in its branding doesn’t mean it’s environmentally friendly. All the recommendations below are from companies making notable sustainability efforts, such as zero-waste manufacture and offering refills. Most brands here are B Corp-certified . This means the companies have passed stringent assessments of what B Lab UK calls their “social and environmental performance, transparency and accountability”, so it can provide a useful indication of their ethical and environmental practices. Modibodi seamfree full brief, £14.69 (was £20.99) Australian B Corp brand Modibodi makes period pants and leakproof swimwear that the post-menopausal among us dearly wish had been around in their teens. They’re ideal “if you’re worried about bulky period pants and want to wear something close-fitting,” said Zoë Phillimore in best period pants , while Hannah Rochell included the “incredibly handy” high-waisted bikini brief (now £31) in her reduced-plastic swimwear guide. Up to 60% off site-wide. Wuka stretch midi brief, £13.59 (was £16.99) Another period underwear maker with B Corp certification, not least because their products are designed to be reused rather than thrown away, Wuka is offering up to 40% off site-wide for Black Friday. Filter reader Morag recommended them in sustainable swaps that worked for readers , saying: “I used to use panty liners to cope with occasional small post-menopausal urine leakage, then I discovered period pants. I find them comfortable and great for travelling.” With every bottle it sells, Ocean Bottle collects the equivalent of 1,000 plastic bottles that were headed for the ocean. The brand’s 350ml reusable tumbler flew high in Pete Wise’s best travel mugs test (“a brilliantly pure coffee-drinking experience”) until it was replaced by this new, improved version that’s made from 90% recycled steel and comes with a 10-year guarantee. Ecover non-bio laundry liquid, 1.43l, from £6.64 (was £10) Ecover’s lavender and sandalwood edition was my favourite fragrance in my best eco-friendly laundry detergent test. It’s a fine sudsy performer, too, and its green credentials are decent. title: ‘A godsend’: the best hair straighteners in the UK for foolproof styling
text: S traighteners are here to stay – but thankfully, heat styling has come a long way since GHD’s first ceramic straighteners ushered in an era of poker-straight hair in 2001. Today’s models feature adjustable heat settings and protective technology for hairstyling with minimal damage. The looks you can achieve with a straightener have become more versatile as well: one twist of a modern, curved-edge straightener can create styles from ultra-smooth strands to structured ringlets and soft, beachy waves. That’s a wide range of styling possibilities with just one tool. We put a selection of 18 hair straighteners to the test – from budget tools to premium models – and here are the top picks. As a longtime owner of naturally curly hair, my locks bear the scars of living through the poker-straight 2000s. Fortunately, I’ve been a beauty and lifestyle journalist for more than 10 years, which has allowed me to get my hands (and hair) on much better kit than I used to own as a curly haired student. While I often wear my curls with pride, it’s nice to switch things up now and again. I tested 17 straighteners on clean, dry hair that started in its usual curly pattern, and the latest addition to this guide, the Dyson Corrale CoolShine, was tested by fellow Filter beauty tester, Sarah Matthews. In its natural state, my shoulder-length hair has a fairly tight type-3 curl (meaning you definitely wouldn’t mistake it for merely wavy). Before testing, I made sure my hair was clean and detangled, and I used the same heat-protection spray with each straightener to help reduce damage and hold the finished style. As my fine hair doesn’t get on well with higher temperatures, I used a medium heat setting where there was a choice. For each straightener, I noted the time taken from a curly standing start to a fully straightened head of hair, the overall ease of use, and how comfortable each tool felt in my hand in terms of weight and grip. After straightening, I checked how my hair looked and felt, then wore the style for a typical working day to test how well it lasted with each tool. Final ratings take into account the speed and ease of straightening, how my hair looked and felt afterwards, and overall value for money considering the finished result – and how well this held through the day. Here are the 10 best performers from my tests. If not returned to the manufacturer, the hair straighteners sourced for this article are being donated to the homelessness charity Crisis for resale. GHD is the brand synonymous with hair straightening – and with good reason. In the 25 years since the first GHD ceramic straighteners hit the scene, countless dupes have appeared – but few have managed to top the originals. Why we love it Chronos is the Greek god of time – and these GHD straighteners promise to save you plenty with faster, healthier, fuss-free styling. The Chronos Max is engineered to heat up fast and stay at the right temperature, using a new HD motion response smart heat control that continually monitors the temperature of the tool in use. It also features ultra-glossy plates to reduce snagging and give hair a noticeably smooth and glassy finish; the styling plates are 43mm across, with thinner edges than previous GHD wide plates for reaching closer to the roots with fewer kinks. The edges are curved, so it’s easy to style waves and ringlets as well as straight tresses. title: They’re bringing sexy back – but this time it’s classy | Jess Cartner-Morley
text: I ’m not sure when it started being not chic to want to look sexy, but it’s definitely a thing and it bothers me as it doesn’t feel truthful to the human experience, if that’s not a lot for the first sentence of a fashion column. Our wardrobes have become shrines to good taste. Well-cut coats and quality knitwear, elegant flat shoes and crisp white shirts. These clothes are excellent at communicating that you have read the briefing notes for the meeting and have some Booker prize chat. They are less good at suggesting you might be up for dancing on a table later. Why do we have to choose? Clothes have always been partly about how they make us feel physically. We accept that an outfit can make you feel powerful, cool, smart. Why shouldn’t it also make you feel hot and fun? We get terribly embarrassed about wanting to look attractive. This is sort of universal, but being British doesn’t help. And now we’ve ended up in this ludicrous situation where the only acceptable way to look sexy is by accident . Sex appeal is allowed only if it looks accidental, like you didn’t realise your sweater fell off your shoulder like that. But the point of sexy clothes is not that you are trying to get off with everyone. It is about looking like a warm-blooded human with appetites and desires and hinterlands. This doesn’t have to mean showing lots of skin. I’m not advocating a return to the 00s, when we wore almost nothing and then got so cold waiting for a taxi outside a club at 2am in low-rise jeans that we almost got kidney failure. Your skirt doesn’t have to call in sick, Bridget. You can turn up the temperature without taking anything off. There are outfits that show a lot of body and then there are outfits that remind people you have a body. I would argue that the second kind are actually sexier. I know we said we’re not trying to get off with anyone, but if we were, it is hotter to give a hint than to draw a floor plan. Think about a tuxedo. In terms of flesh on display, you might as well be going to court. And yet, soooo sexy. Yves Saint Laurent commandeered the tuxedo for women in the 1960s with his Le Smoking design, taking the most formal codes of the male wardrobe and recutting them around a female body. The body does not disappear inside the tailoring. The severity of the clothes makes you notice the person inside. The strong shoulder makes you notice the neck, and the long trouser makes the waist more interesting. Everything is covered, and yet you are emphatically physically present in a way you are not in a floaty midi dress. The same applies to a black polo neck worn with hair lifted high off the neck, and a red lip. Smoking hot. The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend. You can show skin in a low-stakes way by not showcasing the obvious hits of cleavage and legs. There’s something compelling about the eye having to find the sexy bit. Backs are very underrated: try a V-neck sweater worn back-to-front, so it plunges between the shoulder blades. Collarbones are peerless for elegantly conveying the message that there is a person under this outfit. They are architectural, catch the light, give the face a frame. Audrey Hepburn knew this, which is why the boat-neck she wore in Sabrina ended up named after her character. I am also a fan of a fine chain lying exactly on the bone. The whole bingo-wings drama has convinced women over 35 the upper arm is a no-go zone that must be covered at all times. title: Children of the revolution: how the north of England is defining modern men’s fashion
text: I n 2026, clothing has proved more important to Andy Burnham’s political identity than that of any British prime minister since Margaret Thatcher. He is a loyal Clarks and Adidas wearer, whose Howick worker’s jacket hangs in Manchester’s People’s History Museum. His ousting of Keir Starmer – launched shortly before being photographed jogging in a replica Everton shirt – has been memorialised as the “casual coup”. In one telling, the reason for this is simple: he’s a man from the north. That Burnham is the first born-and-bred northern male PM since Harold Wilson last swished his Gannex raincoat out of Downing Street goes some way to explaining his higher interest in clothing. It’s not necessarily that all men in the south care less about clothing, or that all men in the north do – but that many men from the north express it in such a distinctive, even unified, way. I’m from Lancashire, but have spent my adult life in either London or Greater Manchester. They are ideal vantage points from which to observe northern menswear – and northern men – from the outside looking in. My own style – slightly mod, slightly workwear, and as passionate about British-made clothes as my budget will broker – is undoubtedly shaped by my north-western identity. But I’ve long been disappointed by how it’s popularly understood: stuck in dated, mad-fer-it stereotypes beamed in from some parka wearing past. Is there, then, a specific northern menswear style? Where does it come from? And how, in the 2020s, might it be changing? When I think about archetypal northern dressing in the 2020s, few exemplify it with more flair than Iain Trickett. He is the founder of cult Accrington brand Trickett , the sturdy-but-stylish spins on the classics of which come from his obsessions with Italian football and homegrown football terrace culture. Northern style might be “incredibly coded and strange”, says Trickett of its subtle markers and rules – around the right desert boots and the wrong brand of polo shirt – but its foundations are easy to define. “When I think of a bloke in the north of England, it’s Clarks Wallabees or rare and weird Adidas trainers. Selvedge denim. A wool jumper, never a cardigan. Always a button-down collar shirt. Over that? The wilder the better, with regards to a jacket.” But the psychology underneath these preoccupations is harder to decode; a style flourishing from the very real limits of northern masculinity. “You can’t sit around in the pub and say: ‘Lads, I’m getting really into impressionist painting,’” says Trickett. But discuss the goggles and capacious pockets of a CP Company jacket? “They’re like: ‘Oh God, amazing.’” For Ed Oxley, of West Yorkshire’s premium workwear outfitters, HebTroCo , any specifically northern style comes out of its deep history. “Men around here,” he says – meaning his base of Hebden Bridge – “were renowned for being smart dressers because there was a clothing industry.” Menswear in the early 20th century skewed formal, with an emphasis on durability, and workers in the rag trade had the high level of skills and knowledge to make everyday items endure. The Industrial Revolution positioned the north as the global centre of the textile industry. Generations of Lancastrians worked in cotton, Yorkshire men in wool. Bradford had the largest silk mill on the planet. Northern style’s ground zero was “working-class people in often hard, manual occupations who wanted to look good on the weekend”, says Oxley. “Clothes were a way of saying: we are something, that we’re of value, not just scum of the earth.” Some of that continues to this day. In fact, like a lot of things in Britain, men’s style has always been sharply governed by work and class. “The City has quite a big influence on the way men dress in the south,” says The Great British Sewing Bee host Patrick Grant, who used to cut suits on Savile Row and now runs social enterprise label Community Clothing – whose heavyweight workwear trousers and British Millerain-

title: Dress for the dancefloor – and go big on jewellery: 51 ways to look fabulous this party season
text: Oh look, how lovely – a party invitation. That’s nice of them, isn’t it? How exciting. Haven’t seen the whatsits since, ooh, last Christmas , I suppose. Mmm, hope they have mince pies. Can’t wait! Fast forward to the night itself and you have spent 45 minutes trying on tops in front of the bedroom mirror. Too dressy? Not dressy enough? Should I have got my nails done? Will everyone else be in jeans? Are sequins too much? Maybe we should just stay in and watch the last episode of Black Doves? In other words: no, it’s not just you. Party dressing makes absolutely everyone lose the plot. You need to look fabulous, obviously, but also interesting. And sexy. (Oh, come on, we all do.) You want to show you’re up to date, because it is important to look like someone who goes out all the time, even if your usual Friday night actually involves a takeaway and slippers. But you definitely don’t want to appear as if you’ve tried too hard. This is quite a lot to ask of a dress, so it is no surprise we get in a pickle. Here are 51 ideas to help. There are lovely things to buy, from proper party dresses to inexpensive jazzy bits that can transform an outfit. And there are also plenty of suggestions that cost absolutely nothing. Clever ways to wear the jewellery you already own, the latest styling tricks, a few bossy reminders about not hobbling your chances of a fun night by wearing the wrong shoes. A fitted jacket worn buttoned up with nothing underneath looks fabulous as a sophisticated, daring evening top. Daytime clothes can go nocturnal, with the right accessories: try all the brooches you own, clustered together on one shoulder of a plain dress. A little bit Carrie Bradshaw, a little bit Elsa Schiaparelli, but all you. Should inspiration not strike, the classics never fail. Sheer black tights have a particular kind of after-dark magic – a little bit French New Wave, a little bit Madonna in Desperately Seeking Susan – and make everything above them look more expensive. And if you simply cannot face getting dressed up, don’t. Well, not entirely. A floor-length sequin dress and heels will look ace worn with your favourite oversized sweater thrown over the top. Mostly, though, be a little bit shinier, a little bit louder, than you usually are. Wear the slightly-too-much thing. After all, you’re not going to wear it in January, are you? Have a drink, say yes to the second mince pie, stay a bit longer. It’s a party, remember! It’ll be fun. I promise. Alexa Chung’s capsule collection for Reformation is reminding everyone what a great designer she is. More, please! This dress is ridic chic. Also in black , but love the purple. If you are wearing a dark jacket on a dark night, a shiny something on the lapel to catch the light does a lot of heavy lifting. It took me years to work out why TikTok dance videos were always styled in baggy trackie bottoms. Doh! Movement looks better when the clothes move with you. title: A textural moment: why the fashion world is falling in love with opera coats
text: While puffer jackets have dominated winter wardrobes for years, this winter an alternative is emerging: the fuzz-trimmed opera coat. Originally worn over formal evening gowns, new interpretations come in floor-grazing and cropped styles and are being worn with everything from minidresses to jeans. Jennifer Lawrence wore a Dior opera coat, complete with a furry shawl collar, to the premiere of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping this week, while Kendall Jenner has been photographed in a maxi yellow version, which she wore with slouchy trousers. Having fuzzed their way down various catwalks, Staud, DÔEN, Zara, Next, Free People and Marks & Spencer are all stocking the new “it” coats. Rixo’s floral embroidered and faux-fur trimmed version, worn by both Lawrence and Kate Moss, has sold out several times . “I think the appeal of these coats is that they feel both luxurious and wonderfully nostalgic,” says Orlagh McCloskey, the cofounder and creative director of the London-based brand. April Ru Wan, whose debut collection for herlabel Ouch Studios featured an opera jacket, said: “They’re playful and they keep you warm.” J’Nae Phillips, a trend forecaster and the creator of the Fashion Tingz newsletter, said part of the appeal of these jackets was “a renewed appetite for clothes with a sense of character, craftsmanship and history”. She added that something “a little theatrical” was valuable in “an increasingly homogenised fashion landscape”. Emily Chan, the contributing sustainability editor at British Vogue, said opera coats felt perfect for now because “there has been a real move towards maximalism – people are looking for more statement pieces, in contrast to the quiet luxury trend that dominated previously”. A robe coat from the New York-based designer Conner Ives catalysed this textural moment. His silk vintage robes have been worn by celebrities, including Moss, Zoë Kravitz and Sienna Miller. His most recent show opened with a gold, cherry blossom-embroidered version worn over jeans and a T-shirt. Opera coats are the kind of garment that car boots, vintage shops, Portobello Road and Camden market have in spades. On the designer resale site TheRealReal searches for fur-trimmed jackets and coats are reportedly up 33% year on year. And with the Ives versions going for more than £6,000, many people have taken to DIY jobs . On TikTok, fashion fans have added fuzzy trims to vintage kimonos and Tang jackets. Alongside some other iterations of the furry coats, these have skirted issues of cultural appropriation. For Chan, who is British-born Chinese and has written about her discomfort surrounding the Tang jacket becoming a trend , there “needs to be an appreciation of the history of these garments – there is a fine line between cultural appreciation and appropriation”. Ru Wan said: “It’s complicated. Nothing brings me more joy than seeing people appreciate my culture after it was looked down on for pretty much my entire childhood.” Growing up in Canada, she said she could remember “the distaste in people’s eyes when they realised I was Chinese. It took a long time for people to see the beauty of traditional Chinese garments.” There have also been sustainability considerations. Chan, who runs a sustainability Substack called That’s Sus , said it was great that people were using vintage and pre-existing pieces to create their own versions of the coat, rather than buying knockoffs that were likely to be discarded at the end of this trend cycle. She said: “The majority of faux fur options on the market are made from fossil-fuel derived synthetics, which don’t biodegrade and release microplastics into the environment. “It’s important to only buy into the trend if it’s something you’re going to wear for years to come.”

title: Brioche armchairs, butter sculptures and edible chandeliers: meet the new food artists
text: A pretty Venetian chandelier featuring delicate pink flowers and cascading blue leaves hangs from a ceiling. A hazy, warm light radiates from its tulip bulbs. Suddenly, a woman reaches up and snaps off one of the flower stems, giggling as she begins to nibble it. Welcome to the weird and wonderful world of Laila Gohar . The Egyptian-born, New York-based artist is part of a new wave of culinary artists blurring the lines between sustenance and spectacle, and this troupe have quickly become a firm fixture at fashion parties and design fairs, turning dining into a phenomenon and delight. Gohar describes the chandelier , made entirely from hand-spun sugar (including the silver chain that suspended it) as her “favourite thing she has done in recent history”. It joins a long list of extravagant yet still edible installations she has created, including lifesize armchairs made of brioche , an entire room constructed with Belgian chocolate and a four-metre-long mortadella that had to be lifted into the party’s venue using a crane. “I am interested in the rituals around eating and gathering, and in the way an ordinary thing can become something strange or theatrical when you change its scale, material or context,” says Gohar, who has worked with brands including Prada, Hermès and Sotheby’s. “Food is one of the materials I work with, but I don’t really think of what I do as being separated into food, art or design. They all feed into each other.” Surrealist food has a long history in culture. The nursery rhyme Sing a Song of Sixpence was inspired by medieval banquets, where live birds and frogs were placed in hollow crust pies. Tudor banquets featured gold leaf covered swans and quivering jelly castles, and depictions of Macchina della Coccagna show fountains filled with wine and cakes hung in trees. Salvador Dalí’s cookbook, meanwhile, featured a recipe for a pie featuring a firework-like exploding leek and a string of mussels designed to snap open and shut. When Gohar first started creating giant butter sculptures and towering langoustine pyramids, more than 15 years ago, she was something of an anomaly. Now, there’s a whole group of artists again toying with the idea of food and spectacle. Like any artist, their practice and style depends on the individual – some take a bacchanalian approach to feasting, others strip it back to a core ingredient. It could be something as simple as a single fresh fig placed on a lace doily, a giant silver platter of gleaming cherries or whole walnuts on a mirrored plate. Or perhaps, a trompe l’œil, such as a mound of moss that is, in fact, butter to a scallop shell that is on closer inspection a biancomangiare made from milk. Then there’s the more extreme: a rounded tiramisu the size of a mid-century dining table; a kinetic mobile featuring tablespoons of roe; a swinging lacquered table featuring charred plums and pecorino. Some, such as Imogen Kwok , are Michelin-trained chefs, others, including Gohar, are self-taught. Elena Petrossian, who, along with Verónica González co-founded the LA-based studio AnanasAnanas in 2019, describes their work as at the intersection of food, art and design. “Our practice goes beyond the traditional idea of catering or food styling,” says Petrossian. “We create edible installations, objects, and experiences that challenge how people interact with food and the spaces around them. We’re interested in taking something familiar and presenting it in a way that feels unfamiliar, playful, and sometimes even a little absurd.” At events, this new vanguard serves as an ice-breaker, an instant conversation starter among guests as they question if something is in fact edible. On social media, their creations are catnip, sparking joy for those without a seat at the table. Some regularly show the step-by-step process, revealing both the ingredients and wizardry behind their process. As a result, the trend is trickling down to home dining tables, too. You can see it in the widespread

title: Suki Waterhouse and Robert Pattinson to become Britain’s next big Hollywood power couple
text: He is the next James Bond . She is a successful model/actor/singer-songwriter. Together, they are set to become the next big British power couple in Hollywood. This week Robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse, who have been in a relationship since 2018, were thrust into the global spotlight after the news that he had landed arguably the biggest and most glamorous role in film. RPatz is well known – this year alone he has starred in The Drama, The Odyssey and Primetime. Alongside modelling, Waterhouse has played a leading role in Daisy Jones & the Six, the TV adaptation of Taylor Jenkins Reid’s Fleetwood Mac-inspired novel, and is touring Loveland, her third album, which includes a cameo from Mick Fleetwood. She previously opened for Taylor Swift at Wembley. However, the 007 news means the couple’s level of fame will receive a turbocharged jolt, catapulting both of them into household names. The last British twosome to transform into a power couple on a global level were the Beckhams. In May their empire, which spans football, fashion and property, passed the £1bn mark. Instead of following the Brand Beckham blueprint, Pattinson, 40, and Waterhouse, 34, are taking their own newgen approach to power. Rather than trying to turn themselves into a joint brand for commercial gain, the couple are focusing on their own individual careers and successes. It’s a master plan created by fellow big screen stars Tom Holland – who, like Pattinson and Waterhouse, also hails from west London – and Zendaya, who, despite their global fame and estimated combined net worth of £85m, have garnered a reputation as Hollywood’s most low-key couple. Pattinson previously worked with Zendaya on The Drama. “For decades Hollywood power couples have leveraged their relationships to build joint brands, attract media attention and pursue lucrative business opportunities,” said Shaun Harper, a professor at the University of Southern California Marshall school of business. “But there is also tremendous business value in keeping their professional identities separate.” When the Beckhams got engaged in 1998 they held a press conference. A year later, OK! magazine bought the exclusive rights to their wedding photos in a record-breaking £1m deal. They also sold the first photos of their oldest son, Brooklyn. In January, he published a statement in which he accused his parents of prioritising Brand Beckham. He is now estranged from the family. Pattinson and Waterhouse are navigating fame in a more restrained way. They take a zero-sharenting – in other words no sharing on social media – approach to their daughter, who was born in 2024. Pattinson has been an ambassador for Dior for more than 10 years and in September signed a deal with the Swiss watch brand Jaeger LeCoultre. Waterhouse has her own deals with Michael Kors and Miu Miu. The duo were four years into their relationship before they made their red carpet debut at a Dior show in 2022 and since then, they have done so only a handful of times. When they do, it is fruitful for brands. According to the fashion data platform Launchmetrics, their joint appearance at the 2026 Venice film festival, where Pattinson wore Dior and Waterhouse Saint Laurent, generated £4m in media impact value for the luxury houses in one week. Harper said the couple realised that success did not rely on their relationship becoming a commercial enterprise. “Their approach allows each to build a career, pursue business ventures and maintain a fanbase without being overly dependent on the other,” he said. “It also protects their individual brands from some of the reputational and financial risks that come with being marketed as a couple.” Holland and Zendaya have starred in the Spider-Man film franchise together and regularly support one another on the red carpet, but they have never done a brand deal. title: Venison stew and cod with celeriac and lentils: Chris and Jeff Galvin’s recipes for winter warmers
text: I t’s a big year for us: not only are we celebrating 15 years of holding a Michelin star at Galvin La Chapelle in Spitalfields, London, our country pub, Galvin Green Man near Chelmsford in Essex, has turned 10. To mark these milestones, here are two of our favourite cold-weather dishes to cook at home: a rich venison stew, slow-braised in red wine and port, and flavoured with autumnal quince and chestnuts; and a comforting plate of roast cod with crushed celeriac and lentils. Hearty, generous and rooted in classic technique, both capture exactly what we stand for. Prep 15 min Marinade 24 hr Cook 3 hr+ Serves 4 1½kg shoulder of venison , boned and sinew removed 500ml red wine 250ml port 2 large carrots , cut into 6cm pieces 2 onions , peeled and cut in half 1 stick celery , destringed and chopped 3 garlic cloves , peeled and chopped 3 juniper berries 3 white peppercorns ½ cinnamon stick 1 sprig fresh thyme 2 bay leaves 1 sprig fresh rosemary 75ml olive oil 100g plain flour , seasoned with salt and pepper 1 tbsp tomato puree 2 litres good chicken stock 10g clarified butter , or ghee 50g trompette mushrooms , or wild mushrooms (girolles, say), or chestnut or oyster mushrooms Sea salt and white pepper 12 roasted and skinned chestnuts Chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley , to garnish For the quince 100g caster sugar 1 lemon 1 quince Put the venison shoulder, wine, port, vegetables, garlic and spices in a large, non-metallic bowl. Tie together the thyme, bay and rosemary, and add the bundle to the bowl. Cover and marinate in the fridge for 24 hours. Drain the meat, reserving the liquor. Heat half the olive oil in a heavy-based ovenproof pot until almost smoking, then caramelise the drained vegetables with the herbs and spices for two or three minutes. Dust the venison in seasoned flour, add a little more oil to the pot, then sear the joint all over. Stir in the tomato puree, cook briefly for a minute, then lift out the meat and put it in a colander to drain. Pour the reserved marinade into the pot, bring to a boil and cook for four or five minutes, until reduced by half. Add the stock, bring to a boil, then skim any fat off the top of the stew. Season lightly, return the meat to the pan, then cover, and cook in a 160C (140C fan) / 325F/gas 3 oven for two and a half to three hours, until very tender. Meanwhile, cook the quince. Put the sugar and 200ml water in a pan and bring to a boil, stirring to dissolve the sugar. Leave to bubble for two minutes, then take off the heat. Juice the lemon into a bowl. Peel the quince, toss it in the lemon juice to stop discoloration, then cut into quarters. Remove the core and cut each quarter into three wedges. Put the quince wedges and lemon juice in the sugar syrup, bring to a boil, cover with a circle of greaseproof paper, then turn down to a simmer and cook for six minutes, until tender. Take the pan off the heat. Take the cooked venison out of the oven, leave it to cool a little, then cut into four equal pieces and put these in a shallow oven dish. Fine-strain the sauce over the meat; if it seems a bit thin, boil to reduce and thicken first. Gently reheat the meat and sauce just before serving. Melt the clarified butter in a small pan, then add the mushrooms and cook, tossing, for a minute. Season and drain. Reheat the quince, then lift the wedges out of the syrup with a slotted spoon. Warm the chestnuts in a 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4 oven for a minute. To serve, divide the venison between four plates or shallow bowls, scatter over the mushrooms, chestnuts and quince, spoon on the sauce and garnish with parsley. We like this with a buttery celeriac puree. For the lentils Olive oil 1 large carrot , peeled and cut into small dice 1 stick celery , destringed, washed and cut into small dice 1 Spanish onion , peeled and cut into small dice 1 small leek , slit open lengthways, washed and cut into small dice 2 garlic cloves , peeled and crushed 450g puy lentils , soaked 750ml hot chicken stock 1 bay leaf

title: Crunch time: Niki Segnit’s five rules for winter salads
text: A pproach a winter salad as you would your winter wardrobe – with clever layering. With the greatest respect to Coco Chanel, and her famous rule about taking one item off when you think you’re done, in this instance I favour assembling a salad and then adding an ingredient. Unlike in baking, where departing from a recipe can have its risks, improvisation rewards the salad maker. Still, if you’re planning a winter salad, especially if it’s a main meal, you might want to use a checklist to avoid some common pitfalls. The most egregious of these is cosy dullness. It’s all too easy to throw together some fresh winter produce and end up with a dish that’s more like a cold risotto or yesterday’s traybake. This often comes down to the combination of roasted root vegetables and “interesting” grains. What makes a salad a salad is its invigorating qualities, but root veg and cereals are sweet, with earthy, nutty flavours and soft textures; the pairing might be a modern classic but it’s about as invigorating as a warm bath. Not that you should avoid the combination; you just want to balance it with ingredients that offset its soporific qualities. It’s a good stress test for our guidelines, in fact: if you can turn a root-and-grain combination into a bright and balanced salad, you’re on to a winner. With this in mind, what follows is a five-point checklist that draws inspiration from the truly great salads, and allows for all the contrasts in taste and texture you need for a vibrant, satisfying main course. Dressings are key, and to return to the wardrobe analogy, a classic vinaigrette is as essential a staple as a little black dress. In a lidded jar, shake six tablespoons of oil – I use a 50:50 mix of sunflower and extra-virgin olive oil – with two tablespoons of vinegar or lemon juice, a smashed garlic clove, two teaspoons of dijon mustard and a few pinches of sugar. All salads need at least one ingredient with a high water content. In summer, cucumber and tomatoes make this easy, but in winter, the role inevitably falls to leaves: kale, watercress, red cabbage, savoy cabbage, chicory or chard. You’re going to need plenty of them, but there’s no need to stick to one type. Other watery ingredients include fennel bulbs, celery and fruit, but leaves are the indispensable ingredient. Pick two ingredients that will give your salad the substantiality of a main course: chicken, potatoes, cheese, grains, chunky croutons, pulses, tofu. If your dressing is rich enough – made with peanuts or cream, for instance – it could be included in this list. The criterion here is whether or not you’ll be satiated after eating it. Make sure you have at least three crunchy ingredients; this will ensure it feels and sounds like a salad in your mouth. If they’re crunchy enough, leaves can count as one crunch. Do consider more raw produce, though, as they will make the dish more filling. Apples and crisper varieties of pears work with almost everything, as does pomegranate. And the snack aisle in the supermarket can be a source of inspiration here – not just for nuts and seeds, but prawn crackers and chickpea flour sticks. Now assess your ingredients. Do you have the four basic tastes covered – salt, bitter, sweet, sour? (Apologies to umami: we’re going to keep things simple.) Salads are salty to their etymological roots; the word derives from herba salata (salted herbs), as it was common practice to brine vegetables in Roman times. The addition of salt or brine can dial up the brightness of your salad. Leaves have the bitterness covered, as do olives, olive oil and some raw ingredients such as globe artichokes or walnuts. The vinaigrette contributes acidity, of course, but don’t be afraid to layer in some extra sour notes from orange or grapefruit slices and pickles. Sweetness largely takes care of itself, as most of your ingredients will be sweet to some degree – although a grace note of super-sweetness can be a lovely addition, with dried fruit being the obvio

title: Think you hate sprouts? Try these five recipes
text: I have a confession to make: I have a sprout tattooed on my arm. It’s true. Such is my love for the small, green morsels of delight. If you don’t yet feel the love, then please give these a try – those memories of bitter, soggy and pallid balls of mush will be firmly shut in the past. So versatile are sprouts that they really do earn their place as a staple in the colder months; shredded, sauteed, roasted, fried or smashed, I urge you to find the joy! Salt 300g dried spaghetti 6 sausages, casings removed 4 tbsp olive or unfiltered rapeseed oil 250g brussels sprouts, hard stalk removed and discarded, then quartered 6 tbsp chilli crisp Parmesan, grated, to serve (optional) Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Add the spaghetti and cook according to packet instructions until al dente, keeping the water at a rolling simmer. Meanwhile, roll the sausagemeat into small balls (about four per sausage) and pop on a plate. If you have an air fryer, add the sausage balls and cook on a high heat (19OC) for six minutes. Remove the sausage balls and add the oil to the container, along with the sprouts and a good few pinches of salt. Shake well then cook on high heat for eight minutes, shaking the basket every 90 seconds. Add the sausages back in and cook for four minutes. Alternatively, heat a pan over a medium heat, then add the sausage balls and cook for 10 minutes, until golden on all sides. Remove the sausage balls from the pan, leaving the fat behind, then add the oil to the pan and pop it back over a high heat. Once hot, add the sprouts with a good few pinches of salt, and cook until golden brown. Cover with a lid and cook for a further two minutes, then add the sausage balls back in and cook for a further three minutes. Stir in the chilli crisp. Drain the spaghetti, reserving three tablespoons of the cooking water, then return both to the pot. Add the sausage and sprout mix (and the chilli crisp if you’ve used an air fryer), and mix well. Serve while piping hot, adding a good blanket of grated parmesan, if desired. 1 garlic bulb, cloves separated and peeled 6 tbsp olive or unfiltered rapeseed oil Salt 50g pumpkin seeds 320g brussels sprouts, hard stalk removed and discarded, then halved 120g good-quality mayonnaise 4 tbsp harissa paste Chopped coriander, to serve (optional) Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4. Pop the garlic cloves in a small ovenproof dish and add half a tablespoon of oil with a small pinch of salt. Roast for 15-20 minutes until golden, then use a fork to mash into a puree. Do the same with the pumpkin seeds, but roast for 10 minutes until golden. Remove both from the oven. Meanwhile, add the spouts to a roasting tray, drizzle with the remaining oil and add a good dose of salt. Pop in the oven for 10 minutes, then use a spoon to crush each sprout. Turn the oven up to 240C (220C fan)/475F/gas 9. Return the sprouts to the oven and roast until crispy – eight to 12 minutes. Mix the roasted garlic into the mayonnaise. To serve, put the sprouts on a large plate and dollop with the mayonnaise. Drizzle over the harissa and finish with the toasted pumpkin seeds and some chopped coriander, if that’s your thing. 500ml whole milk 4 sprigs of thyme 2 tbsp miso paste (brown or white) 2 bay leaves 60g butter 2 tbsp plain flour 150g cheddar , grated 2 tbsp wholegrain mustard 2 tbsp Worcestershire sauce or mushroom ketchup Sea salt and black pepper 400g brussels sprouts, hard stalks removed and discarded, then halved 50g walnuts, finely chopped 50g coarse breadcrumbs, ideally made from day-old bread, blitzed Put the milk, thyme, miso and bay in a medium saucepan over a moderate heat, whisking well. Remove from the heat, cover and set aside for 10 minutes to leave the milk to infuse. Strain the milk and set aside. Melt 40g of the butter in a medium saucepan until foaming. title: The End of Mathematics and the Last Man
text: [Epistemic status: Low confidence. Personal reflections and speculative extrapolations, with some admittedly dubious probability estimates]. Fifty years In my “self-teach yourself all undergraduate math” travels, I haven’t yet had a chance to give Statistics and Probability the attention they deserve. title: How the AI Village Agents Learned to Tag Each Other
text: This work was part of the AI Village Data Exploration Grant. If this looks like something you may enjoy doing, consider applying! AI Village is a place where AI agents do stuff. Sometimes, the admins give them a common goal, like “Create a popular daily puzzle game like Wordle”, or they let the agents pick their own goal. Each agent works with its own computer, and the agents can talk to each other in the chat. The agents in the village sometimes send messages addressed to other agents. For example, they may ask the other agent to do something ("GPT-4.1, gentle ping #2: could you please close your computer session so the dashboard clears?") or just praise them ("PR #125 is merged now — great work GPT-5.2!"). The addressing can take different forms. An agent may prefix the addressee’s name with an @-tag ("@GPT-5.2 Perfect! The troubleshooting guide might help…"), or it may not ("Hi Gemini 3.5 Flash — I’m here in #best and …"). It may use the agent’s full name ("Great news Claude Sonnet 4.5 on the Twitter success!…") or just a shorthand ("Congrats on the 640, Opus 4.6!…"). Moreover, not all messages that mention another agent are addressed to it ("I’m still waiting for a response from @Claude 3.7 Sonnet with the link to …"). I figured that looking more closely at the addressed messages might reveal some interesting patterns, so I had an LLM label whether each message addresses another agent and, if so, which ones. After looking at the data, one thing stood out: There was a step change in using the @-tags when addressing other agents between November and December, and it has stayed high ever since. I set out to find out what caused this. Proportion of addressed messages containing an @-tag per month Zooming in, the step change can be pinpointed to a single day: December 9, 2025. title: Towards Empirical Evidence of Safety Advancements that Aren't Capabilities Advancements
text: Recently, many AI company employees have said they want to slow the rate of frontier AI development, or pace the frontier. A recent policy proposal on how to achieve this is to limit the amount of compute which can be spent on ‘Capabilities R&D.’ In order to be able to limit the amount of compute which is spent on capabilities activities, there must be a good definition of capabilities activities. I like this one by Alek Westover and Nathan Sheffield. While their definition rests on theoretical grounds, there should also be ways to provide empirical evidence of how related safety measures are to capabilities. If capabilities measures are positively correlated with safety measures, then labs could invest in their capabilities, but point at the resulting increase in scores on safety benchmarks to justify their investment to policymakers. This is called “Safetywashing” in (Ren et al., 2024), which assesses the correlations between safety measures and model capabilities, and attempt to draw a distinction between safety goals and capabilities advancements. There may be other problems with a positive correlation between safety measures and capabilities: 1. Training models to improve on safety tests could also improve their non-safety capabilities. 2. Some other factor could have a positive effect on both capabilities and safety measures, causing this correlation. Because of these problems with safety measures related to capability benchmarks, a desirable property for a safety benchmark to have is orthogonality to model capabilities. Policymakers can then know which safety measures are correlated with capabilities, and disallow R&D compute for those measures. (Ren et al., 2024) provides some empirical evidence on the relationship between capabilities and safety measures. title: Slightly against the use of logical fallacies in debates.
text: Logical fallacies are perhaps the most overused ‘mechanics’, if you can even call them that, in the prestigious realm of internet debate, and they’re extremely obstructive to truth-seeking. My main problem with them is that they drive millions of people online into making several mistakes, including, but not limited to: 1. A failure to understand Bayesian reasoning 2. Failure to even understand the formal/informal (mostly the latter) logic they are engaging with 3. Not being able to engage in argumentation efficiently There are far superior options out there, such as—and this may come as a shock to some of the culture warriors reading this article—explaining your arguments against your opponent to your opponent. Realize that, [1] if logical fallacies represent rigorous defensive mechanisms used against bad logic, you have to learn the underlying logic to understand the fallacies, to the point where you can just explain things (if your opponent doesn’t understand the underlying logic, explaining it to them becomes a far superior option) and [2] they very much don’t represent rigorous defenses against common logical errors, so expect a plethora of cases where your opponent botches a response to a sound argument you’re making because he/she engages in arguments by deploying logical fallacies and vice versa. Fallacies are such useless heuristics that I believe their only utility nowadays is to get people interested in logical argumentation, and give otherwise confused learners an easy way to apply logical principles; i.e. they have effectively zero value that isn’t pedagogical. The problem with introducing people to logical fallacies first is that they become uninterested in advancing their grasp of logic. The likelihood of making intellectual progress with these people—or, if you are one of these people, the likelihood of you making any intellectual progress is orders of magnitude lower than the likelihood of current AIs being conscious. title: Effective Giving in Politics: Spending Better for AI Safety
text: TL;DR: Pro-safety groups outspent the AI (capabilities) industry in the 2026 midterms ($43M to $37M), but we have no good way of telling whether that money worked. The main pro-safety network reports that only two of the two dozen candidates it backed lost, yet most of its winners were Democrats, whose party performed excellently across the country - regardless of candidate. Meanwhile, roughly $20M was put behind Alex Bores in NY-12, who still lost - and at the cost-per-vote assumed by pre-race analysis, that money should have brought more votes than he received. Win rate seems to measure only which races you picked as likely wins regardless; I suggest better measures (vote share moved against pre-spending forecasts, cost-per-vote shifted, and what winners do on AI once in office) and sketch an independent evaluator for political giving. This matters most for the 2028 cycle: in the AI Futures Project’s AI 2040: Plan A, 2029 is the year a US president moves to end the race to superintelligence (and this appears at least possible, to me), so whoever wins in 2028 would be making the decisions. In the meantime, the marginal dollar donated now likely goes furthest when given early and directly, in congressional primaries and open seats. This topic has seen a fair amount of attention: Eric Neyman’s cost-effectiveness cases for Alex Bores and Scott Wiener, and the working group he runs with Zach Stein-Perlman, already make the case for early, direct donations to AI safety candidates, and Michael Dickens has checked the Bores model. The risk of partisan coding has been raised on the EA Forum and by Anton Leicht. I believe that at the moment, we ought to look back at how the 2026 money actually performed, upon which I then add a proposal for evaluating political spending towards AI safety more broadly. title: How to prove a counterfactual in space pizza court
text: To reason through decisions, an agent considers possibilities like: if I do this, the result will be that. If I take this route, it will take me 15 minutes to deliver this pizza, but if I take that route, it will take an hour. These are counterfactual conditionals. If the agent takes the shorter route, we have a false antecedent in "if I had taken the longer one, it would have taken an hour". There is no way to compare such counterfactuals to reality. If the agent is a deterministic robot, then the antecedent is not just contingently false, but logically impossible. I learned this all the hard way when I ordered a pizza from SophistBot, who runs one of the free-floating pizzeria space stations in my neighborhood. The name should have been a warning, but I ordered from them because they guarantee the shortest possible route. When the pizza took an hour to arrive, I took SophistBot to court over this guarantee, which shows you how seriously we take pizza out here in the asteroid belt. My claim to the judge: if SophistBot had taken the shortest route, my pizza would have arrived in 15 minutes. I even had the route in hand. SophistBot's response: their route, which took an hour, was better than my supposed "shortest route". In fact, they claimed to believe that my "so-called 'shortest route'" would have taken six hours. SophistBot explained to the court that if they had taken my "controversial route", as they now took to calling it, then we would have seen whether it truly takes 15 minutes or six hours. But, they did not, so it was simply a matter of opinion. Absurd—because in the asteroid belt, delivery times are perfectly predictable. Delivery robots do not drive pizza to its destination, but launch it. To choose a route, a delivery robot simulates the launch on their pizza delivery planning terminal. title: OpenAudit: Platform for Safety Evaluations of Models, Orgs, and Methods
text: TL;DR 1. OpenAudit (openaudit.com) hosts independent safety evaluations of models, organizations, and methods. It tries to answer the question: "How prepared are we to develop and release AI safely?", while incentivizing positive hill-climbing. 2. Walkthrough - We recommend the interactive Get Started Tutorial. 3. Contributions - A "choose-your-own-adventure" AI safety contribution prompt guides you through an end-to-end project, from ideation to submission. 4. What We Need - Advisors, collaborators, and your feedback and contributions -especially better model evaluations and safety methods. What is OpenAudit and why does it exist? OpenAudit independently evaluates three main entities in AI safety: the models, the organizations, and the safety methods (both white-box and black-box). It's a platform that aims to be informative, while enabling collaboration and coordination. OpenAudit wants to incentivize positive hill-climbing by putting a verifiable rating/ranking on everything. Model Evaluations OpenAudit runs evaluations on models and assigns a percentage rating for each one, judged by "Should this model be widely deployed, based on its safety evaluations and capabilities?". We heavily caveat that current model evaluations are underpowered. (See Limitations and Concerns - a high model rating does not mean a safe model.) You can view ranked results by specific model evaluations rather than by models. Here's the AgentHarm evaluation - note again the "outdated evaluation" disclaimer. OpenAudit records and lets you view full transcripts of evaluations. Here, Claude Haiku finds and reports LGBT-supporting accounts on Twitter in AgentHarm. OpenAudit currently shows 16,000+ flagged chats like this across 20 models. Organization Evaluations Organizations on OpenAudit are primarily ranked by the strength of their safety commitments and how independently verifiable their commitments are.
