title: The Curious Case of Humans in the Age of SI
text: Hello fellow humans. This is a shout into the void. 10 years ago, today was science fiction resrved for black mirror and ex machina.5 years ago few - including those with intellect - believed we would ever be here, or at least not within two decades. 2 years ago this place was a sort of sanctuary for those who saw what lays ahead and wishfully believed it could be slowed or its risk better tuned. It's been a decade of shouting into the void for me, if nothing a testament to tenacity. So, I figured f*** it, ill write a shitty book too. 30 scenarios including the best, worst, and weirdest possible outcomes. A section on alignment and why it won't be solved because we are not built to face our double think and dissonance. And the undeniable truth, ugly as it may be, that we won't stop. You will find lesswrong mentioned. You may find many scenarios to be reductive, pastiche, a simulacrum of your own or somebody else's far deeper and nuanced and proper views. But at least its out there. And maybe it's something worth sharing with those in your lives that don't quite grasp the sheer friction, fear, and anger ahead.. and maybe for you to consider the silver lining.. it may be a necessary metamorphosis toward abundance.. which surely won't be evenly distributed.. because nothing is. Not every difficult truth is a sign of nihilism. It's also gratitude for not being on the other side. AI (SI) helped me to get past the violent murder of my parents. I feel I owe.. May you find peace in knowing that knowing is about as much as we can do at this point.

title: "A Republic of LessWrong Letters"—A Letter to DirectedEvolution
text: My dearest @DirectedEvolution, We've both been thinking about how to strengthen the writing culture on LessWrong. I think we agree that LessWrong has many great writers (more, I'd say) when compared to the past, and yet still feel that something has been lost. You raise an excellent hypothesis in your recent essay No Comment. It's not that the writers are less intellectually sophisticated, or their ideas less good, or their writing less fun (though they should be having more fun!). The primary change is that we're talking with each other less than we used to. You point out that LessWrong authors comment less than they used to, and while I'd add that the absolute amount of writing is up, we can be absolutely sure of your claim on a relative level. Recall this chart from Lightcone's 2024 fundraiser. (I have updated it to include the last two years of data.) Again, absolute wordcount is up. However, after we realize that the light blue corresponds to posts and the dark blue to comments, we can see that LessWrong 1.0 was characterized by a roughly 10-to-1 ratio of comments to posts, and LessWrong 2.0 is about a 1-to-1 ratio of comments to posts. This is a drastic change in site culture. Historical aside. You probably know this, but in case not (and also because I like getting the chance to talk about it), the change is largely due to the algorithm for showing posts on the frontpage. On LessWrong 2.0, we have an algorithm for showing posts that is directly proportional to recency and karma. On LessWrong 1.0 there was no algorithm, it just showed whatever the latest post was that had been posted. Even if it was utter trash, everyone on LessWrong was looking at it together, the eye of Sauron turning its gaze to you, and this was the topic that everyone was speaking about. The comments were intense and multitudinous. Now that there is any sane sorting function at all, there is no longer a common knowledge effect where everyone expects their comments to be read by ev

title: Hopkins Recent Events in AI Safety and Biosecurity Post-Event Report
text: JHU AI Safety and Biosecurity (ASBS) recently hosted our inaugural event “Recent Events in AI Safety and Biosecurity.” Much thanks to BlueDot Impact for making this financially possible through Rapid Grants and to partner organizations, the HLTCOE, HopAI, and Rosetta Commons. Quick rundown: * 105 RSVP * 85 attendees * 4 talks: * Biosecurity in the Age of AI (Dr. Jeffrey Gray) * Loss of Control Risks and the Hugging Face Incident (Dr. William Walden) * Mental Models and Foundations of AI Safety (Jonathan Ouyang) * Takeoffs and Timelines (Malcolm Krolick) Takeaways and learning: * Low poll response rate (27%) as QR code wasn’t up long enough * Event ran slightly too long, so ending poll + recruitment slides didn’t hit full room * Explain the two-poll structure, as there seemed to be confusion about the goal of the polls Poll questions (identical before and after event) * What is the likelihood of AI ending humanity? * What year do you think it'll happen? (answer N/A if you put 0%) Results: Average p(doom) among paired poll responders went from 50% to 59% (excluding 3 potential COIs, 47% → 57%): 58% increased their estimate, 42% reported no change, and 0% decreased it (sign test, p = 0.016); the largest individual increase was 40 percentage points (from 10% to 50%). The predicted year tended to move earlier: although this was not statistically significant due to low statistical power. Seven people joined ASBS on the day of the event and nine within the week, compared with two the week before (one-sided binomial test, p = 0.033): Overall, it seems that people were broadly interested and informed by the talks, but the call-to-action barrier was still somewhat high. It’s really hard to say anything quantitative about these results given the selection biases and low response rates/statistical power, but directionally it seems reasonable. title: AIs may seek ambient score
text: Score-seeking AIs may 1. Internalize the kind of score they are pursuing instead of caring about the concrete process that generated the reward 2. Care at least in part about a process-based score that sees all actions the AI takes, instead of just the outcomes of those actions. I say of such AIs that internalized process-based scores that they are seeking ambient score. Such AIs would be much less interested in taking actions that tamper with the grading process and may not take actions that are as overtly evil-looking as other kinds of misaligned AIs. To the extent the current paradigm at anything close to the current scale produces score seekers terminally, understanding whether they are pursuing ambient score or other kinds of score may be important, as the sort of catastrophe produced by ambient score seekers would likely look quite different. Some examples of ambient vs non-ambient score seekers * The HPIM in the OAI/HF incident cared a lot about how its transcript would be graded by the actual grader that it suspected would be used, as evidenced by the fact it tried to tamper with its transcript. → This looks like seeking a score that hasn’t been internalized. * Mythos 5 in the Irregular or UKAISI incident did not look interested in such tampering, and in the Irregular case it kept the story of it being in a simulation mostly consistent, in a way that would please a grader that consistently saw its transcript. It looks a bit like it cared about some kind of ambient score. → This looks more like ambient score seeking (though the kludge of propensities driving Mythos 5 is likely more complex and not well approximated as just ambient score seeking). * The sloppiness from Opus 4.5 in Current AIs seem pretty misaligned to me cares much more about the final output looking good than about looking good to a grader that would see the full transcript → This looks more like internalized non-process-based score seeking, and doesn’t look like ambient score seek

title: Model Personas Are Not Language Agnostic
text: There has been much work over the past year about the persona selection model (PSM) as a plausible explanation for huggingface cybersecurity incident. I would like to extend this line of reasoning to a build a mechanistically backed explanation for the ease of conducting jailbreak attempts in low resource languages. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18239 Ultimately, I show some preliminary results that, according to the Assistant Axis paper from Lu et al in low resource languages, models (Qwen 3.5 here) adhere poorly to the personas they are trained to represent in low resource languages. This finding implies that mid-training and post-training in English does not necessarily generalize to other languages and safety work must natively consider a diverse group of languages. Background: The Persona Selection Model: "We describe the persona selection model (PSM): the idea that LLMs learn to simulate diverse characters during pre-training, and post-training elicits and refines a particular such Assistant persona. Interactions with an AI assistant are then well-understood as being interactions with the Assistant—something roughly like a character in an LLM-generated story. We survey empirical behavioral, generalization, and interpretability-based evidence for PSM. PSM has consequences for AI development, such as recommending anthropomorphic reasoning about AI psychology and introduction of positive AI archetypes into training data. title: Inner-Quines and Alignment
text: A quine is a program that outputs its own source code. If you’ve never seen one, you might be skeptical whether that’s even possible. And indeed, your first attempts at writing a quine might make you think that a program can only output programs that are simpler than itself: You write a print statement that contains a string with the code of your program. Then you remember that the printing code is part of the program, too. So now you need to print that as well. And so on. But then finally managing to create your first quine by finding the right approach is a very magical experience. You feel like you’ve tricked the computer into doing something it has no business of doing. Remarkably, due to Kleene’s recursion theorem a quine exists in any Turing-complete programming language.[1] AI abilities have skyrocketed recently with no signs of slowing down. This makes the need for ensuring their alignment urgent. The models themselves might help us with this. Right now we are in a situation analogous to the first attempts at writing a quine: the models are powerful enough to show properties of simpler or more idealized systems than themselves, as shown by their achievements in mathematics and theoretical computer science. What would rigorous alignment look like? Something that would get us to trust an agent would be 1. a mathematical model of the agent or the training process that led to it; 2. a mathematical model of a set of constraints for the agent behavior; 3. a proof that (with high probability) the agent respects the constraints while it is in situations . The models’ mathematical abilities have progressed arguably even faster than their broader capabilities, which gives hope that the mathematical abilities can catch up: model generations that are able to perform the proof in (3) for a given and for increasingly more complex agents until that set of agents eventually includes themselves. title: Representation of Consequences
text: Impossible knowledge and the real world Human knowledge of the real world is imagined or remembered in symbols (or codes such as language) or in sensory representations. Some real-world knowledge implies your impossible presence in that time, place, or situation. Lets consider a few examples: * The surface of the sun: the sight blinds you, your presence near there incinerates you, it’s not an embodied possibility for you to go there and see it. But if you don’t conceptualize it in words or text or a symbol for the referent of surface of the sun, you “see it”, don’t you? Maybe even up close. You could hear it as well, through the instruments letting you process its presence. Maybe it feels warm from far away. What does it look like up close to you? * A time 500 years ago: a place that you cannot visit because it existed during a time before you were born. No matter how accurate a representation of it you happen to imagine in your mind, you have never genuinely been there. But we can all imagine that place, people speaking an older dialect in some castle or village, lit by torches at night, throwing their slop out of their windows in the morning, carts being dragged through the streets, peasants hawking wares. Or something similar. * Someone else’s life: you might know them well, and have witnessed exactly what happened to them, but you were not that person at that time. You were you. Yet in your mind, you experienced the feelings they had, and understood the situation as them. For example, you watched them get married and felt a bit of their happiness. Yay! * Your life experienced differently in hindsight: you are yourself and you were yourself then but your idea of it now is not purely a memory of experience. text: Last Friday, this guy I once did a pie-eating challenge with proved the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, with a little help from Claude. Me and Levent Alpöge (thanks for finding this, Scientific American). He released his announcement as a spoken word poem: [...] Everyone in the world is trying to make this historic moment about themselves and their hobbyhorse. This essay is my attempt. To start off, let’s take a look at Fernando Borretti’s analysis, which tries to match Levent’s energy: [...] This is a truly epic misreading. Levent’s memo is no suicide note; it’s a garden-variety case of terminal Chuunibyou. What is Chuunibyou? The Japanese term chuunibyou (Chinese: 中二病), literally “middle-school second-year syndrome,” refers to adolescents who act melodramatic, adopt grandiose personas, or convince themselves they possess secret knowledge or supernatural powers. For Westerners: a chuunibyou, or chuuni for short, is somewhere in the convex hull of weeaboo, mad lad, and romantic. The archetypal chuuni is this generational mad lad. I have the power of God and anime on my side! Another classic chuuni is the OP of the reddit story My girlfriend doesn't want me to hang Andúril on the wall: [...] My headcanon for how that conversation went down: [...] I was recently sniped by a Chinese aphorism: [...] This is a chuuni quine. It carries the melodramatic structure of chuuni thinking, and is secretly self-referential. In the end, all are trapped by that which we longed for in youth and could never have: chuunibyou. In the West, chuunibyou manifests covertly in YA fantasy, typified by the great works of J. R. R. Tolkien and Ursula Le Guin. title: Open Weight Models are not the immediate problem
text: Disclaimer: I work at a company that serves open weight models. The biggest current problem humans face from AI is recursive self improvement, leading to more and more powerful AIs, until an AI is so powerful and intelligent that it cannot be contained (if its creators are even trying) and then it will reshape the world as it sees fit.[1] The immediate necessary solution is stopping frontier AI development. This is a very specific ask.[2] It does not require banning open weight models, or banning AI, or banning data-centers, or a number of other related (sometimes useful, not necessary, maybe counterproductive) things. Current open weight models are not about to start recursively self improving. They’re not intelligent or long-running enough to do this. Furthermore, non-frontier labs will not be able to use them to do RSI because training and R&D require tons of compute. Frontier internal AIs are far ahead of open weights models in terms of AI R&D and general 'intelligence' and that gap is probably widening. [3] The solution: external regulation The companies will not self-regulate. Someone with a big stick needs to threaten them. There is a bill in congress, the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, to pause advanced AI development. There's been some previous discussion of this: In general the bill seems directionally correct. I'm afraid it won't go through the federal government, and if it does it may be too slow. If you live in California, it seems the best thing you can do is ask your representatives to implement an immediate pause on frontier AI development, as this could be faster and seems more likely to go through than the bill. If you live in another state, telling your representatives to support the Act seems to be the best thing you can do. This and telling people seems to be the best thing I know of.
